Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a separable complex Hilbert space H. Multiplication form: there exist a finite measure space (M, μ), a unitary U: H → L²(M, μ) and a real-valued μ-measurable function f on M, finite μ-a.e., such that x ∈ D(A) iff f·(Ux) ∈ L²(M, μ), and U A U^{-1} g = f g for all g ∈ U D(A). Projection-valued measure form: there is a unique projection-valued measure E on the Borel sets of ℝ with A = ∫_ℝ λ dE(λ), meaning D(A) = {x ∈ H : ∫ λ² d⟨E(λ)x, x⟩ < ∞} and ⟨Ax, y⟩ = ∫ λ d⟨E(λ)x, y⟩ for x ∈ D(A), y ∈ H; E is supported on σ(A) ⊂ ℝ. Borel functional calculus: for Borel φ: ℝ → ℂ, φ(A) = ∫ φ(λ) dE(λ) is defined on D(φ(A)) = {x : ∫ |φ|² d⟨E x, x⟩ < ∞}; the map φ ↦ φ(A) is a *-homomorphism, φ(A) is bounded with ‖φ(A)‖ = sup of |φ| on σ(A) when φ is bounded and continuous, φ(A) is self-adjoint iff φ is real-valued a.e., and φ(A) is unitary if |φ| = 1. In particular e^{itA} (t ∈ ℝ) is unitary and, when A ≥ 0, e^{-tA} (t ≥ 0) is a self-adjoint contraction.
H is a complex Hilbert space, separable for the finite-measure multiplication form
A is self-adjoint (symmetric is not enough)

[Conjecture of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] For $\phi\in\bR$, let $\cC_\phi$ be the full subcategory of the localized
category
\[
Nov\otimes_{Nov_+}\mathsf C_B
\]
consisting of objects $E$ with the following property: for every
$\varepsilon>0$, $E$ admits a constructible metrized model
$\widetilde E\in\mathsf C_B$ such that
\[
\phi-\varepsilon<
\phi_-(\Lambda_{\widetilde E})
\leq
\phi_+(\Lambda_{\widetilde E})
<
\phi+\varepsilon .
\]
Here the phases are normalized using the graded microlocal coefficient
system $\cV_{\widetilde E}$ on
$\Lambda_{\widetilde E}^{\mathrm{sm}}$.

The collection of subcategories $\{\cC_\phi\}_{\phi\in\bR}$ is the slicing
of a Bridgeland stability condition with central charge $Z_\Omega$.
Equivalently, together with $Z_\Omega$ it uniquely determines this
stability condition. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2608.26038, 'Rotated semicircle laws for permanental roots of Gaussian random matrices'] For every \(x\in\R\),
\begin{align}
  H_N\sim\Pp_{2,N}:\qquad
  &\E[P_N(\ii x)P_N(-\ii x)]
  =
  \int_{\R^2}
  \prod_{\ell=1}^2(x-\ii y_\ell)^N
  \,\dd\Gamma_{2,N}(y_1,y_2),
  \\
  H_N\sim\Pp_{1,N}:\qquad
  &\E[P_N(\ii x)P_N(-\ii x)]
  =
  \int_{\R^2}
  \prod_{\ell=1}^2(x-\ii y_\ell)^N
  \,\dd\Gamma_{4,N}(y_1,y_2).
  
\end{align}
The integrals are absolutely convergent.

[Lemma lem:parity of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Run the uniformised chain of (sec:setup of the paper), a Poisson$(\Lambda)$ clock with
$P$-moves at the ticks, and start the doubled chain at $(i,+)$. At time $t$ the
doubled chain is at $(j,+)$ if the original chain is at $j$ after an even number of
ticks, and at $(j,-)$ if after an odd number. Consequently, for the embedding
$\widehat\pi_0=\binom{\pi_0}{0}$,

\begin{equation}
\widehat T_t\binom{\pi_0}{0}
=\binom{\,e^{-s}\cosh(sP^{T})\,\pi_0\,}{\,e^{-s}\sinh(sP^{T})\,\pi_0\,},
\qquad s=\Lambda t,

\end{equation}

so the two sheets carry the even and odd halves of the Poisson representation
(equation eq:poisson-rep of the paper), and their sum returns $T_t\pi_0$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact integral manipulation, Palm calculus, mass transport, limiting obstruction or conditional construction Result: For a finite weighted edge set, choosing an edge proportionally to its weight and then a uniform endpoint samples vertices with probability proportional to weighted degree. Thus a uniform-vertex limit need not equal the endpoint limit when degrees or weights vary. Even knowledge of both endpoint marginals does not identify their joint boundary law: an equal mixture of pairs (0,0),(1,1) and an equal mixture of (0,1),(1,0) have the same marginals but disjoint supports. Product-edge convergence must retain the endpoint-pair measure and horizontal/vertical edge weights. Check: Each incident edge contributes half its sampling weight to a vertex, proving the degree bias. The two binary pair laws both have Bernoulli(1/2) marginals, checking the independent loss of correlation information. Obstruction: No convergence estimate for the actual product-graph endpoint measure is proved. The pair-law example is an information diagnostic, not a constructed graph counterexample.

[Lemma lem:disconnect_interior of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] {amy-cle-resampling}}]

Suppose that $\Gamma$ is a nested ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa}${} in a simply connected domain $D$, and let $\Upsilon_\Gamma$ be its gasket. For each $a\in(0,1)$, $b>0$ there exists $p > 0$ such that the following holds. 

Let $z\in D$ and $j_0\in\mathbf{Z}$ be such that $B(z,2^{-j_0})\subseteq D$. There exists a resampling $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ of $\Gamma$ within $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$ for each $j>j_0$ with the following property. Let $G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ be the event that $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ has a loop $\widetilde\mathcal {L}$ that
\begin{itemize}
 \item disconnects every point in $\Upsilon_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}} \cap B(z,2^{-j})$ from $\partial B(z,2^{-j+1})$,
 \item the gasket and the collection of loops of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ remain the same in each connected component of $\mathbf{C} \setminus \widetilde\mathcal {L}$ that intersects $B(z,2^{-j})$.
\end{itemize}
For $k\in\mathbf{N}$, let $\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k}$ be the event that the number of $j=j_0+1,\ldots,j_0+k$ so that
\[ \mathbf{P}[ G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j} \,|\, \Gamma ] \geq p\]
is at least $(1-a)k$.  Then
\[ \mathbf{P}[(\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k})^c] = O(e^{-b k}) \]
where the implicit constant does not depend on $z,j_0,k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Radon-Nikodym theorem: if mu and nu are sigma-finite measures on the same measurable space and nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (mu-null sets are nu-null), then there is a nonnegative measurable density f, unique up to mu-null sets, with nu(A) equal to the integral of f over A against mu for every measurable A; f is the Radon-Nikodym derivative dnu/dmu. Sigma-finiteness cannot be dropped (Lebesgue measure against counting measure on R fails).
title: Radon-Nikodym theorem

body: Given measurable spaces (X, F) and (Y, G), a function f : X -> Y is measurable if the preimage of every set in G lies in F. For real-valued f it suffices that {x : f(x) > a} in F for every real a (the sets (a, infinity) generate the Borel sigma-algebra). Measurability is preserved under sums, products, sups/infs of countable families, and pointwise limits - which is why it is the right regularity class for integration.

Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: The exact stationary sampler starts one active particle at every site. Write D_V for the total number eventually killed at the boundary. Then S_V=|V|-D_V pathwise. If J(x) counts jumps at x, the departure identity gives E D_V=sum_{x in V} q_V(x)*E J(x), where q_V(x) is the one-jump exit probability. This shows why a vanishing number of boundary sites cannot by itself imply negligible dissipation: expected boundary odometers can grow enough to carry a volume-order flux. Check: Count exiting jumps directly for the pathwise identity, or sum the discrete Poisson equation for the expected final occupation; both yield the same boundary-flux formula. No assumption of independent final sleepers is used. Obstruction: Need a concentration estimate for D_V and a limit for its volume-normalized expectation that is independent of the exhaustion. Surface-to-volume geometry alone does not control repeated boundary visits.

Choose a^2=c rho exp(-76(S+1)), with sufficiently small absolute rho,c, sigma_0=1/(80 sqrt(d)), S=10 log(100/(sigma_0 rho)). Use OU tau=a/R, sigma=sqrt(1-tau^2)>=1/2, the canonical three-component equal-weight identity-covariance mixture score, and physical unit-step GD on all unrestricted mean parameters initialized iid N(0,3a^2/(2d)), independently of data/noise. # Unrestricted random-mean DDPM learning for equilateral three-Gaussian teachers

This is a restricted-case candidate theorem, dependent on unaudited C06--C10. It removes the zero-centroid optimization constraint from C08/C09. It does not claim the general well-separated K=3 target, established novelty, or finite-precision complexity.

## 1. Statement

Let d>=2, R>=1 be known, E have two orthonormal columns, and u_1,u_2,u_3 be the unit equilateral vertices in R^2. The original law is the equal-weight mixture of N(R E u_j,I_d). The plane E is unknown to the algorithm. Choose the small noisy radius a according to C10: for a sufficiently small fixed absolute rho,

    sigma_0=1/(80 sqrt(d)),
    S=10 log(100/(sigma_0 rho)),
    a^2<=c rho exp(-76(S+1)).                         (1)

For a polynomial upper runtime bound, choose equality in (1) with sufficiently small absolute c, rather than allowing arbitrarily smaller a. Put tau=a/R and sigma=sqrt(1-tau^2)>=1/2. For independent original samples X_i and Gaussian noises Y_i, set W_i=tau X_i+sigma Y_i. Optimize the ordinary empirical DDPM loss

    Lhat(M)=n^(-1)sum_i ||s_M(W_i)+Y_i/sigma||^2,
    s_M(x)=-x+sum_j softmax_j(m_j.x-||m_j||^2/2)m_j.

All d-by-3 means are free parameters. Initialize their entries iid N(0,3a^2/(2d)), independently of data/noise. Use physical Euclidean GD with step one.

For 0<epsilon<1, 0<eta<=1/100, sufficiently many polynomially many samples yield

    min_pi ||M_T-a E U_pi||_F<=a epsilon             (2)

with probability at least 553/1600-eta>1/3, at

    T=O(a^(-2)log d+a^(-4)log(C/epsilon)).            (3)

The population version succeeds with probability at least 553/1600. These are real-arithmetic statements, counting exponentials as score evaluations. Sampling and arithmetic costs are polynomial in d,1/epsilon,1/eta, with an enormous fixed dimension exponent from (1). To estimate the original law, rescale means by R/a, and choose epsilon=2 epsilon_TV/R (or smaller than one); matching implies TV error at most R epsilon/2 by Gaussian KL, Pinsker and mixture convexity. Consequently costs are also polynomial in R and the inverse prescribed original-law error. Unknown radius and finite-precision implementation remain outside the statement.

## 2. Population trajectory

Use C10's exact decomposition M=a b 1^T+a c Z V^T, c=sqrt(3/2), V=sqrt(2/3)U^T. C10 proves entry, except on a set of initialization probability at most 1-79/200. Conditional on that good event, the covariance surrogate's entry angle is uniform in either determinant branch. Removing the three unstable sectors of total angular measure 1/8 leaves probability 553/1600.

At entry, the actual mean configuration is in the full tube around the equilateral subspace, projected radius in [0.9,1.1], angular margin from each unstable boundary bounded below by a fixed delta, and normal error at most C rho. Reduce the fixed rho and the constant c in (1) as needed to preserve the margins of C08. C10's full normal contraction and quadratic tangent forcing give, in normalized Euclidean mean coordinates J=M/a,

    ||w_k||<=C rho exp(-c_1 a^2 k),
    tangent error per step <=C a^2 ||w_k||^2.         (4)

Its accumulated size is at most C rho^2. The same sector-barrier and radial-inward arguments in C08 therefore apply. The restricted dynamics in the equilateral subspace are unchanged by allowing additional coordinates: invariance makes them exactly the C02/C03 radius-angle dynamics, up to fixed coordinate normalization constants. In particular normal and radial rates are order a^2, angular rate order a^4, and the angular maximum stays outside the chosen sector. Thus

    |r_k-1|+alpha_k+||w_k||<=C exp(-c_2 a^4 k).       (5)

Here alpha is distance to the nearest matching angular minimum; the radial estimate tracks that minimum exactly, as established in C08, rather than claiming an O(a^2) radius floor. Equation (5) yields (2),(3) for the population loss. The fastest centroid direction causes no loss: its order-one contraction was included in C10's normal Hessian argument, and its divergent rescaled linear field has zero tangent projection.

## 3. Uniform empirical approximation with a free centroid

The finite-sample argument needs no symmetry of the empirical objective. Work on ||b||<=11, ||Z||_F<=5 and define the two rescaled fields

    h_b=-a^(-4) partial_b F_a,
    h_Z=-a^(-4) grad_Z F_a,

and their empirical analogues. For any 0<zeta<1, with probability at least 1-eta,

    sup ||(hhat_b-h_b,hhat_Z-h_Z)||<=zeta            (6)

when n is a sufficiently large polynomial in d,1/a,1/zeta,1/eta. Although h_b itself contains -2a^(-2)b, this is polynomially bounded on the parameter box; no uniform-in-a boundedness of the population field is asserted.

Here is a direct extension of C09's concentration proof. Let

    B=C_0(d+1/a+1/zeta+1/eta+1)^2,
    n=ceil(B^100),                                  (7)

with sufficiently large absolute C_0. Both ||W|| and ||Y|| exceed B only with probability at most C exp(-c B^2), uniformly in the teacher plane. This follows by their Gaussian norm moment generating functions and the bounded mean shifts ||a E u_j||=a. The mean parameter norm is at most C a on the fixed b,Z box. Softmax derivatives of fixed order are bounded combinations of probabilities; logit derivatives are polynomials in W and bounded means. Differentiating the per-pair loss once or twice in the normalized b,Z coordinates therefore gives a polynomial envelope. More explicitly, a first score derivative is bounded by C a(1+||W||), its second derivative by C a^2(1+||W||)^2, and the score norm by ||W||+C a. Hence rescaled loss gradient is bounded by C a^(-3)(1+||W||)(1+||W||+||Y||), and its derivative by a fixed polynomial bounded by C B^12 on ||W||,||Y||<=B. Fixed-coordinate factors c, sqrt(3) and the three means change only C. The same bounds hold for a slightly enlarged fixed parameter box, allowing Lipschitz extension along segments.

Truncate the per-pair fields to zero outside this safe event for the proof only. Their expectation differs from the untruncated population field by at most polynomial(d,1/a) exp(-c B^2), using the polynomial envelope, Gaussian moments and Cauchy--Schwarz. This is smaller than zeta/10 for sufficiently large C_0. All n actual sample pairs are safe with probability at least 1-eta/4; the algorithm uses the original untruncated objective.

Parameter nets now have dimension 3d instead of 2d. A mesh zeta/(100 C B^12) in the fixed parameter box and a 1/2 direction net have combined log cardinality at most C d log B. The elementary bounded-scalar MGF inequality proved in C09 gives per-net tail at most 2 exp[-c n zeta^2/B^24]. Since zeta>=1/B and n>=B^100, this exponent is at least c B^74 and dominates both net entropy and log(1/eta). The direction net converts scalar bounds to Euclidean field bounds, and the parameter Lipschitz bound extends to all points. Allocating failures and adding expectation bias proves (6). This event is simultaneous over parameters and therefore covers all iterates without a data/iterate independence assumption. Choosing B^100 instead of B^80 only loosens the polynomial sample bound.

## 4. Entry with persistent empirical perturbations

Take zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon with sufficiently small absolute c_*. The exact coordinate metric gives

    b_+=b-(partial_b F_a)/(3a^2)+(a^2/3)e_b,
    Z_+=Z-(2 grad_Z F_a)/(3a^2)+(2a^2/3)e_Z,
    ||(e_b,e_Z)||<=zeta.                            (8)

In particular

    ||b_k||<=2^(-k)||b_0||+C(a^4+a^2 zeta).

Since zeta<=a^2, its floor remains O(a^4). The transient centroid impulse into Z is still O(a^2||b_0||^2). The additional direct shape error contributes C zeta exp(76(S+1)) to the entry comparison. Thus, reducing c in (1), the total comparison error C(a^2+zeta)exp(76(S+1)) stays below the entry tolerance. The full parameter box is retained by the same stopped induction as C10. The good initialization-and-surrogate-angle event remains of probability 553/1600; actual empirical rotational invariance is neither assumed nor needed.

## 5. Full tube with persistent empirical perturbations

In normalized Euclidean J coordinates, (8) adds an error of size at most C a^2 zeta per physical step. C10's integrated physical normal Hessian therefore implies

    ||w_{k+1}||<=(1-c a^2)||w_k||+C a^2 zeta,
    ||w_k||<=C rho exp(-c a^2 k)+C zeta.             (9)

The population tangent forcing remains quadratic. Together with the direct empirical error, it has a decaying contribution C a^2 rho^2 exp(-c a^2 k) and a persistent contribution C a^2 zeta. The first has summable total C rho^2. The second must not be summed over all time: near the sector boundary, the restricted angular drift is inward by c a^4 delta, whereas the persistent perturbation is at most C a^2 zeta. Our choice zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon makes the former dominate. Exactly the moving barrier in C09, decreased only by partial sums of the transient errors, keeps a fixed angular margin. The radial annulus has an order-a^2 inward margin, also dominating these perturbations. This closes the normal/radial/angular tube induction together.

Inside the retained sector, the resulting recurrences are

    alpha_{k+1}<=(1-c a^4)alpha_k
                 +C a^2 rho^2 exp(-c' a^2 k)+C a^2 zeta,
    |r_{k+1}-1|<=(1-c a^2)|r_k-1|
                 +C a^4 alpha_k^2+C a^2||w_k||^2+C a^2 zeta.

Geometric convolution gives

    alpha_k+|r_k-1|+||w_k||
       <=C exp(-c'' a^4 k)+C' zeta/a^2.             (10)

The normal floor is O(zeta), the radial floor O(zeta+zeta^2/a^2), and the angular floor O(zeta/a^2); thus (10) uses the largest. Choose c_* to make the final term a sufficiently small multiple of epsilon, and take the time in (3). The Euclidean coordinate metric yields (2).

## 6. Probability and limitations

The initialization-and-angle event has probability at least 553/1600. Uniform empirical control fails with probability at most eta. A union bound, without multiplying dependent probabilities, yields success at least 553/1600-eta. At eta=1/100 this is 537/1600>1/3. Population control sets empirical error to zero and uses the larger probability. A repeated-run selection guarantee is not claimed.

The teacher is still centered, equilateral, equally weighted and spherical, with known radius and covariance. There is no imposed centering on learned parameters or initialization and no known plane or orbit augmentation. General triangles, unknown radius/covariance, unequal weights, finite precision and the full T309 target remain open. C06's anisotropic population local minimum prevents treating equilateral geometry as innocuous. The result is an unaudited candidate restricted theorem, not a finding of novelty.

Least trusted steps: C10's free-centroid analytic estimates, the uniform gradient/Lipschitz envelope over all free means, and the persistent-error tube barrier. Exact symbolic probability and metric checks support only their finite algebra. body: In abstract algebra, a composition series provides a way to break up an algebraic structure, such as a group or a module, into simple pieces. The need for considering composition series in the context of modules arises from the fact that many naturally occurring modules are not semisimple, hence cannot be decomposed into a direct sum of simple modules. A composition series of a module M is a finite increasing filtration of M by submodules such that the successive quotients are simple and serves as a replacement of the direct sum decomposition of M into its simple constituents.

body: [Definition 8 (Shared-scale uniform vs.\ allocation-flexible) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] We contrast two settings by two freedoms they grant: to allocate bits across coordinates, and to give each coordinate its own scale. A quantizer is \emph{shared-scale uniform} if every coefficient of a group is stored at the same bit-width on a uniform grid with a single shared scale, so no bits can be re-allocated between coordinates: the per-group \texttt{INT4} grid of a deployed low-bit kernel (\texttt{MXFP4} and \texttt{NVFP4} are shared-scale on a \emph{non-uniform} element grid, a second axis taken up in \Cref{sec:format}). It is \emph{allocation-flexible} if the coder may spend a different number of bits on different coordinates under a fixed \emph{total}-rate budget: realized by unequal (but deterministic) bit assignment, by entropy coding of the indices, or both, as in a classical transform coder. \textbf{Every deployed LLM GEMM kernel is shared-scale, fixed-allocation}, for the datapath reasons developed in \Cref{sec:inversion}; the classical transform-coding theory of \Cref{sec:classical} is allocation-flexible.
title: Shared-scale uniform vs.\ allocation-flexible

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] Let \(w\) be a self-avoiding walk, and let \(\Delta\) be an \(r\)-cell
which contains neither endpoint of \(w\).  If
\(\Gamma_\Delta(w)\ne\varnothing\), then
\(S_\Delta^{-1}\Gamma_\Delta(w)\) is a boundary forest in \(F_r\).
Moreover, it may be replaced by any other boundary forest with the same
boundary state.  The replacement yields a self-avoiding walk with the same
endpoints as \(w\).  Such replacements may be performed
simultaneously in any finite collection of distinct \(r\)-cells.

body: The Boolean satisfiability problem SAT - given a propositional formula (equivalently, a formula in conjunctive normal form), decide whether some assignment of truth values to its variables makes it true - is NP-complete: SAT belongs to NP, and every language in NP admits a polynomial-time many-one reduction to SAT. The restriction 3-SAT (CNF with exactly three literals per clause) is also NP-complete. Hence SAT is in P if and only if P = NP.

Hardness: let L be in NP, decided by a nondeterministic machine N in time p(n) on inputs of length n, for a polynomial p. A computation of N on input x can be recorded as a tableau: a (p(n) + 1) by (p(n) + 1) grid whose row t lists the tape contents at step t, annotated with the head position and current state; each cell holds one symbol from a fixed finite alphabet (tape symbols plus composite state-symbol markers). Introduce Boolean variables y(t, j, s) asserting 'at time t, cell j holds symbol s'. Clauses of bounded size enforce: (1) consistency - each cell holds exactly one symbol; (2) initialization - row 0 encodes the start configuration of N on x; (3) locality of transition - the content of any cell at time t + 1 is determined by the three cells above it at time t (the head moves one cell per step), so for every position a constant-size set of clauses allows exactly the 2 by 3 windows consistent with some nondeterministic transition of N; (4) acceptance - some row contains the accept state. The total number of variables and clauses is polynomial in n (about p(n)^2 cells times constants), and the formula is constructible from x in polynomial time. [Proposition pro:heredity-covering-numbers of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Consider a metric space $(\mathcal{X},d_\mathcal{X})$, any $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and any $R>0$, and define the subset $\mathcal{K}_R\subset C(K,\mathbb{R}^d)$ given by
$$\mathcal{K}_R:=\left\{\Phi\in C(K,\mathbb{R}^d):\,\max\{\Vert \Phi\Vert_\infty,[\Phi]_\alpha\}\leq R\right\},$$
where, as usual, we define the uniform norm, and the $\alpha$-H{\"o}lder seminorm by
$$\Vert \Phi\Vert_\infty:=\max_{x\in K}|\Phi(x)|,\quad [\Phi]_\alpha:=\sup_{\substack{x,y\in K\\x\neq y}}\frac{|\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)|}{(d_\mathcal{X}(x,y))^\alpha},\quad \Phi\in C(\mathcal{K},\mathbb{R}^d).$$
Then, $\mathcal{K}_R$ is a compact subset of $C(K,\mathbb{R}^d)$ and we have
$$\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon(\mathcal{K}_R)\leq \left(4+\frac{72R^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)^{d\,\mathcal{N}_{\frac{\varepsilon^{1/\alpha}}{2(3R)^{1/\alpha}}}(K)},$$
for every $\varepsilon>0$.

[Definition of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \((N,\gamma)\) be a sutured manifold. A properly embedded essential annulus A in \(M\) is called a \emph{product annulus} if it does not cobound a solid cylinder and its two boundary components \(\partial _{+}A\) and \(\partial _{-}A\) of \(A\) lies in \(R_{+}\) and \(R_{-}\), respectively.
A properly embedded disk \(D\) in \(M\) is called a \emph{product disk} if its boundary intersects \(s(\gamma)\) at exactly two points.
We call both product annuli and product disks \emph{product decomposition surfaces}.

In the contrast, we say \(A\) is a \emph{non-product annulus} if it is neither a product annulus nor boundary-parallel to \(R_{+}\cup R_{-}\).

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Optimal stationary stopping under Markov-chain lumping structural calculation Result: For a genuinely lumpable partition, the K=1 inequality follows directly. Start the fine chain in any state of a chosen coarse block and use a fine-chain stopping time attaining stationarity. Its projection has the coarse-chain path law. Any extra fine information can be represented by auxiliary conditional randomness in the coarse filtration, so this yields a randomized coarse stopping rule with stationary terminal law and the same expected duration. Taking maxima proves the claim in this special case. Check: Equivalently disintegrate the stopped fine path given each successively observed coarse path; the conditional continuation probabilities give an adapted randomized coarse stopping rule. The conclusion requires strong lumpability, because otherwise the projected fine path is not the Markov chain defined by stationary-flow matching. Obstruction: For arbitrary partitions, equality of one-step stationary flows does not identify multi-step path laws. The stopping-time projection argument therefore fails at its first premise. A full comparison needs a different potential-theoretic argument and the later lifting result must be reconciled.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0242-optimal-stationary-stopping-under-markov-chain-lumping

[Thm q-difference_of_qMPL of arXiv:2609.01458, 'Confluence relations for $q$-analogues of multiple zeta values'] Let $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$. If $k_{j}>1$,
then we have
\begin{align*}
 & \mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})-\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,qx_{j},\dots,x_{d})\\
 & =\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{j}-1,\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d}).
\end{align*}
If $k_{j}=1$, then, assuming that $x_{j}\neq1$, we have
\begin{align*}
 & \mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})-\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,qx_{j},\dots,x_{d})\\
 & =\frac{x_{j}}{1-x_{j}}\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j-1}x_{j},\dots,x_{d})\\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{1-x_{j}}\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j}x_{j+1},\dots,x_{d}).
\end{align*}
Here, we regard the first term as $\frac{x_{1}}{1-x_{1}}\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{2},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{2},\dots,x_{d})$
when $j=1$, and the second term as $0$ when $j=d$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    Let $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ be a Dirichlet form on $L^2(X, \mu)$ and assume that 
    $\mathcal{F} \subset C(X)$ and that $\mathcal{F}$ is dense in 
    $(C(X),\norm{\cdot}_{\infty})$. Then, for any $f \in \mathcal{F}$, 
    there exists a unique finite Borel measure $\nu_{f}$ on $X$ which satisfies 
    \begin{align}
        \int_{X}g\,d\nu_{f}=2\mathcal{E}(fg,f)-\mathcal{E}(g,f^{2}), 
        \quad g \in \mathcal{F}.
    \end{align}
     The measure $\nu_{f}$ is called the energy measure of $f$. Also, for any 
     $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$, we define a signed measure $\nu_{f,g}$ by 
    \begin{equation}
        \nu_{f,g} \coloneqq \frac{1}{2}(\nu_{f+g}-\nu_{f}-\nu_{g}).
    \end{equation}
    $\nu_{f,g}$ is called the mutual energy measure of $f$ and $g$. Then, we have 
    $\abs{\nu_{f,g}(B)} \leq \nu_{f}(B)^{1/2}\nu_{g}(B)^{1/2}$
    for any Borel set $B$ of $X$.

body:
Let f ∈ C^1(R) and let u ∈ L^∞(R × (0,∞)) be a weak solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 that is piecewise C^1: away from finitely many disjoint C^1 curves x = s_i(t) it is C^1, and it has C^1 one-sided traces u_-(t) (from x < s_i(t)) and u_+(t) (from x > s_i(t)) on each curve. Each curve then satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, σ := s_i'(t) = ( f(u_-) - f(u_+) ) / ( u_- - u_+ ) when u_- ≠ u_+. Such a u is a Kruzhkov entropy solution if and only if at every point of every discontinuity curve the chord condition holds: for every k strictly between u_- and u_+, ( f(k) - f(u_-) ) / ( k - u_- ) ≥ σ ≥ ( f(k) - f(u_+) ) / ( k - u_+ ). Equivalently: if u_+ < u_-, the graph of f on [u_+,u_-] lies on or below the chord joining (u_+,f(u_+)) to (u_-,f(u_-)); if u_- < u_+, the graph of f on [u_-,u_+] lies on or above that chord. If f is strictly convex, this is equivalent to the Lax shock inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+), i.e. to u_- > u_+: a strictly convex flux admits only downward jumps.
f ∈ C^1
u is a weak solution which is piecewise C^1 with C^1 shock curves and one-sided traces (the equivalence as stated is for this piecewise-smooth class; Kruzhkov's definition is what governs general L^∞ solutions)

Rankine-Hugoniot alone is not sufficient: it fixes σ but permits inadmissible jumps

[Theorem 13 (CRT scaling limit of the critical cluster; conditional on Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Assume Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}, criticality $\rho(M)=1$, irreducibility and aperiodicity as in Theorem~\ref{thm:32}, and in addition that the offspring distributions admit finite exponential moments: $\E[e^{t\deg}]<\infty$ for some $t>0$ (e.g.\ bounded degrees, or Poissonian $g$). Then there is an explicit constant $\Sigma\in(0,\infty)$, computable from the second-moment matrices of the offspring law and the Perron eigenvectors of $M$ (Appendix~\ref{app:miermont}), such that, conditionally on $\{|S|=n\}$,
\[
\Big(S,\ \frac{\Sigma}{\sqrt n}\,d_{\mathrm{gr}},\ \mathrm{unif}_S\Big)\ \xrightarrow{(d)}\ \big(\mathcal T_e,d_e,\mu_e\big)\qquad(n\to\infty)
\]
in the GHP topology, where $d_{\mathrm{gr}}$ is the graph distance on the cluster and $\mathrm{unif}_S$ the uniform probability measure on its vertices. In particular the height of the conditioned cluster is of exact order $\sqrt n$, with the Brownian-excursion law of the CRT height, and the shape of the critical cascade cluster is universal: independent of the drifts, thresholds, hazard-domain structure, and boundary geometry, all of which enter only through the single scale factor $\Sigma$.

body:
[Lemma 30 (Coordinate representation) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Let $G$ be a finite graph and $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Define $\mu_{G,\beta}'$ as the probability measure on
    \[
        \tau:=(\alpha,\omega,\eta)\in [0,\tfrac\pi2]^V\times\{0,1\}^E\times\{0,1\}^E:=\Pi_G
    \]
    with density
    \begin{align}
        &
        \diff\mu_{G,\beta}'(\tau)
        \propto
        \textstyle
        \left(\prod_{u\in V}\diff\alpha_u\right)
        \\
        &
        \qquad\qquad
        \textstyle
        \cdot
        2^{k(\omega)}
        \left(
            \prod_{uv\in \omega}
                (1-\e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)})
            \middle)\middle(
            \prod_{uv\not\in\omega}
                e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)}
            \right)
            \\&
            \qquad\qquad
            \textstyle
            \cdot
            2^{k(\eta)}
            \left(
                \prod_{uv\in \eta}
                     (1-\e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)})
                \middle)\middle(
                \prod_{uv\not\in\eta}
                    e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)}
                \right).
    \end{align}
    Here $k(\rho)$ denotes the number of connected components of $(V,\rho)$.

    Now obtain a sample $\sigma\in(\S^1)^V$ as follows:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Sample $\tau\sim\mu_{G,\beta}'$,
        \item Sample $\xi\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\omega$,
        \item Sample $\zeta\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\eta$,
        \item Set $\sigma_u:=\xi_u\cos\alpha_u + i\cdot \zeta_u\sin\alpha_u$ for each $u\in V$.
    \end{itemize}
    Then $\sigma\sim\mu_{G,\beta}$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Strict interface speedup in half-plane inhomogeneous FPP structural argument Result: For constant times a on one half-plane and b on the other, let c=min(a,b)>0. Every path with vertical displacement n costs at least cn. A path taking a bounded horizontal detour into the cheaper half-plane, moving n steps vertically, then returning costs cn+O(1). Thus the interface time constant is exactly c, so there is no strict speedup beyond both homogeneous models. Check: The lower bound uses path length at least n; the explicit path gives a matching upper bound after division by n. Obstruction: Random switching between regions may exploit complementary favorable segments. The deterministic comparison cannot characterize when that advantage is strictly positive.

[Lemma lem:ank-unified of arXiv:2607.00731, 'Sharp Asymptotics for the Largest Component in the Subcritical Regime of Preferential Atta'] Let
\[
\Psi_n=\log\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}+(\alpha+2)\log\!\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha+2}\right).
\]
Then
\[
\Psi_n=\frac{\alpha+1}{2(\alpha+2)}\varepsilon^2+O(\varepsilon^3),
\]
where the \(O(\varepsilon^3)\) remainder is uniform in \(n\). Moreover, for every fixed \(B<\infty\) there exist constants
\(0<c_1<c_2<\infty\), depending only on \(B\) and \(\alpha_*\), such that, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
uniformly for $2\le k\le B\varepsilon^{-2}\log x_n,$ we have
\[
c_1 k^{-3/2}e^{-\Psi_n k}\le a_{n,k}\le c_2 k^{-3/2}e^{-\Psi_n k}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E C_k^{(n,m)}=\Theta\!\bigl(nk^{-5/2}e^{-\Psi_n k}\bigr).
\]

body: [Corollary 43 of arXiv:2609.04139, 'The conformally invariant metric on CLE$_4$ II:\\ existence of geodesics'] Almost surely, for each $\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \Gamma_{\BD}$, any $D_{\Gamma_{\BD}}^{\BD}$-geodesic $P$ connecting $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$ has the property that the subset $\{P(t) : P(t) \notin \SCL \text{ for any } \SCL \in \Gamma_{\BD}\}$ is of Hausdorff dimension zero. A similar statement holds with two deterministic and disjoint connected arcs of $\partial\BD$ in place of $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$.

For bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2, p_c = 1/2, and moreover theta(1/2) = 0: there is no infinite open cluster AT the critical point. The two halves have separate histories and separate proofs. HARRIS (1960) proved theta(1/2) = 0, which gives p_c >= 1/2. KESTEN (1980) proved that theta(p) > 0 for every p > 1/2, giving p_c <= 1/2. The self-duality of Z^2 bond percolation at p = 1/2 - the dual of the open configuration at parameter p is a configuration at parameter 1 - p on an isomorphic lattice - makes 1/2 the ONLY candidate but does not by itself decide the critical behaviour, which is why the theorem is hard. The corresponding value for SITE percolation on Z^2 is not known; for site percolation on the triangular lattice the answer is 1/2 by the same duality mechanism, and that is the case where conformal invariance at criticality is proved. [Harris (1960); Kesten (1980), Comm. Math. Phys. 74; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, or Bollobas-Riordan, Percolation]
bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2
the Harris half as sketched uses Burton-Keane uniqueness, self-duality, the square-root trick and a planar topological argument
the Kesten half is stated but not proved in this node

By the Burton-Keane theorem the infinite open cluster is almost surely unique, and by self-duality the dual configuration at 1/2 has the same law, so the dual also has a unique infinite closed cluster almost surely. Fix eps > 0 and choose a box [-n, n]^2 large enough that with probability at least 1 - eps the infinite open cluster meets the box. Let A_left, A_right, A_top, A_bottom be the four increasing events that the corresponding side of the box is joined to infinity by an open path off the box. By symmetry of the square lattice these four have the same probability, and their union has probability at least 1 - eps. The SQUARE-ROOT TRICK gives P(A_side) >= 1 - eps^{1/4}, so with probability close to 1 all four occur simultaneously. The same argument in the dual gives four closed dual arms from the four sides with probability close to 1. But an open path leaving the box to the left and one leaving to the right, joined through the unique infinite open cluster, separate the plane in a way that is incompatible with a closed dual path leaving the top and one leaving the bottom joined through the unique infinite closed dual cluster - two disjoint infinite crossings of the plane in perpendicular directions cannot coexist by a planar topological argument. Taking eps small enough forces a contradiction, so theta(1/2) = 0. [Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] A function $f:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^M$ is continuously differentiable,
$$f(x+t)\simeq f(x)+f'(x)t$$
with $f'(x)$ linear, and $x\to f'(x)$ continuous, precisely when it has partial derivatives,
$$\frac{df_i}{dx_j}(x)=\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{f_i(x+te_j)-f_i(x)}{t}$$
which depend continuously on $x$. In this case the derivative is
$$f'(x)=\left(\frac{df_i}{dx_j}(x)\right)_{ij}\in M_{M\times N}(\mathbb R)$$ 
acting on the vectors $t\in\mathbb R^N$ by usual multiplication.

[Proposition prop:higherorder of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$, $f$ non-constant, and $m>0$ continuous. Suppose the interaction
part of the sandwich velocity field, $x\mapsto f(x)^{2}H(f^{2}\mu)(x)$, coincides for
every compactly supported $\mu$ with $-m(x)\,\partial_{x}\dfrac{\delta E}{\delta\mu}(x)$
for a symmetric energy of the form
\[
  E[\mu]=\sum_{k=2}^{K}\ \underbrace{\int\cdots\int K_{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\,
  \mathrm{d}\mu(x_{1})\cdots\mathrm{d}\mu(x_{k})}_{k\text{ copies of }\mu},
\]
a finite sum of symmetric $k$-body terms, $K<\infty$. Then $K_{k}\equiv0$ for every
$k\ge3$, and $E$ reduces to the pairwise case already excluded by
Theorem~(thm:nogradient of the paper).

body: [Proposition 21 (Compatibility with the Gowdy subclass) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Fix a torus-adapted Navier--Stokes triple $(\mathscr F, \chi, \mathscr B)$.  Gowdy symmetry is propagated in the sense that any particle-production or dissipated-energy Navier--Stokes areal flow $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ with $\Kpar=\Jpar=0$ on one areal slice has $\Kpar=\Jpar=0$ identically. [Definition 19 (Wiener chaos) of arXiv:2605.14630, '2605.14630'] For any $n\geqs 1$, we denote by $\cH_n$ the one-dimensional subspace of $\cH$ 
spanned by the random variable $H_n(X)$. For $n = 0$, $\cH_0$ is the set
of constants, which is isomorphic to $\R$. Then $\cH_n$ is called the 
\emph{homogeneous Wiener chaos of order $n$}. 
The \emph{inhomogeneous Wiener chaos of order $n$} is defined as 
\begin{equation}
 \cH_{\leqs n} = \bigoplus_{k=0}^n \cH_k\;.
\end{equation}

[Theorem thm:conv-immig of arXiv:2412.03325, 'Functional limit theorem for branching processes \\ in nearly degenerate varying environme'] Assume that the BPVEI $(Y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ defined in (equation eq:Y of the paper) satisfies the conditions (C1)--(C3) and (C4) or (C4') holds. Then, for any $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$,
\[
\mathcal{L} ((Y_{A(nt)})_{t \geq  \varepsilon}) 
\stackrel{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{L} ((W(\log t))_{t \geq \varepsilon}),
\]
as $n\to \infty$, 
where $(W(u))_{u\geq \log \varepsilon}$ is a continuous time branching 
process with immigration with initial distribution having g.f.,
\[
\log f_Y(s) 
= 
\begin{cases}
-\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} 
\frac{2^k\lambda_k}{\nu^k} \left( \log\left( 
1+\frac{\nu}{2}(1-s)\right) +
\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{\nu^i}{i2^i}
(s-1)^i\right), & \nu > 0, \\
\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} \frac{\lambda_k}{k} (s-1)^k, & \nu = 0,
\end{cases}
\]
with parameters $\alpha = 1+\nu$, $\beta = \sum_{k=1}^{\kappa}(-1)^{k+1}\lambda_k$,
and
\[

body:
[Thm of arXiv:2506.01306, 'Asymptotic of Coulomb gas integral, Temperley-Lieb type algebras and pure partition functi'] Let $j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ and suppose $\mathcal{Z}$ is a positive solution to the system of PDEs, such that the limit
\[
\lim_{x_j,x_{j\pm1} \to \xi} \left|x_j - x_{j\pm1}\right|^{-\Delta} \cdot \mathcal{Z}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
\]
exists and is nonzero for all fixed $\{x_k\}_{k \neq j, j\pm1}$ and $\xi$ in a suitable interval. Let $(X_t^{(1)},\ldots,X_t^{(n)})$ solve the SDE with drift $b^{(j)} = \kappa \, \partial_j \log \mathcal{Z}$. Let $\tau$ be any stopping time such that $|X_t^{(k)} - X_t^{(l)}| \geq \varepsilon$ and $|X_t^{(k)} - X_t^{(l)}| \leq 2\pi - \varepsilon$ for all $k \neq l$ and $t \leq \tau$. Then the process $Y_t = |X_t - X_t^{(j\pm1)}|$ is absolutely continuous with respect to a linear time change of a Bessel process of dimension
\[
\delta = 1 + 2\Delta + \frac{4}{\kappa}.
\]

Depending on the value of the fusion limit:
\begin{itemize}
    \item If the limit (equation fusion1 of the paper) is nonzero, then $\Delta = \frac{\kappa - 6}{\kappa}$ and $\delta = 3 - \frac{8}{\kappa} < 2$, implying that $Y_t$ may hit zero with positive probability.
    \item If the limit (equation fusion1 of the paper) vanishes but the limit (equation fusion2 of the paper) is nonzero, then $\Delta = \frac{2}{\kappa}$ and $\delta = 1 + \frac{8}{\kappa} > 2$, so $Y_t$ remains strictly positive almost surely.
\end{itemize}

[Defn 6 (Partition function and free energy) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] For an $N \times N$ Wigner matrix $W = (W_{ij})$ and a prior $\caX$, we define the partition function $Z_N(\beta)$ and the free energy $F_N(\beta)$ at inverse temperature $\beta > 0$ by
\[
	Z_N \equiv Z_N(\beta) = \E_{\caX} \left[ \exp \left( \beta N \sum_{i<j} W_{ij} \frac{x_i x_j}{\| \bsx \|^2} \right) \right], \qquad F_N \equiv F_N(\beta) = \frac{1}{N} \log Z_N.
\]
Here, when $\| \bsx \| = 0$, we define $x_i x_j / \| \bsx \|^2 = 0$ for all $i, j$.

	We say that $\left<\cdot \right>_G$ satisfies \emph{Pfaffian relations} on the set $W$ if for any subset $I\subseteq [n]$,

        \Big \langle  \prod_{i\in I}\vp_{v_i} \Big \rangle_G = \Pf(M_I),

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] A tracial \(*\)-probability space is a unital \(*\)-algebra
\(\mathscr{A}\) over \(\C\), together with a linear functional
\(\varphi:\mathscr{A}\to\C\) satisfying
\[
 \varphi(\mathbf{1})=1,\qquad
 \varphi(a^*a)\geq0,\qquad
 \varphi(ab)=\varphi(ba)
 \quad (a,b\in\mathscr{A}).
\]
If \(\mathscr{A}\) is a unital \(C^*\)-algebra, we call
\((\mathscr{A},\varphi)\) a tracial \(C^*\)-probability space.
The elements of \(\mathscr{A}\) are noncommutative random variables, and
their joint \(*\)-distribution is the collection of all mixed moments
\(\varphi(R(a_1,\ldots,a_k,a_1^*,\ldots,a_k^*))\).
A sequence \((\mathbf{M}_N)\) converges almost surely in
\(*\)-distribution to an element \(\mathsf{m}\in\mathscr{A}\) if, for
every noncommutative polynomial \(R\) in two indeterminates,
\begin{equation}
 \tr_N R(\mathbf{M}_N,\mathbf{M}_N^*)
 \longrightarrow \varphi(R(\mathsf{m},\mathsf{m}^*))
 \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\end{equation}
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.05185

body:
[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured random perturbations of \\ tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices'] Consider two matrices $M$ and $N$ of size $r \times r$ and $s \times s$ respectively, and call $M'$ the matrix obtained by removing the last row and column from $M$ and $N'$ the one obtained by removing the first row and column from $N$. Define also two rectangular matrices $X$ and $Y$ of rank 1 and size $s \times r$ and $r \times s$ respectively, whose entries are all $0$ except for $(X)_{1,r}=:x$ and $(Y)_{r,1}=:y$. Then if we define the $2 \times 2$ block matrix
\[ A = \begin{pmatrix}
M & Y \\
X & N
\end{pmatrix} \]
we have
\[ \det A  = \det M \det N - x y \det M' \det N' . \]
\begin{proof}
We prove the formula through the Laplace expansion of the determinant. For a matrix $T$, we denote by $\mu_{i,j}(T)$ the minor obtained by removing the $i$-th row and $j$-th column from $T$. Using Laplace expansion on the $r$-th row of $A$ we get
\[ \det A = \sum_{i=1}^{r+1} (-1)^{i+r} A_{r,i}~\mu_{r,i}(A)  . \]
Now we notice that $\mu_{r,i}(A) = \mu_{r,i}(M) \det N $ for $i \leq r$. Then we have
\[ \det A = \left( \sum_{i=1}^r (-1)^{i+r} M_{r,i}~\mu_{r,i}(M) \right) \det N + (-1)^{2r+1} y~\mu_{r,r+1}(A) = \det M \det N - y~\mu_{r,r+1}(A). \]
Then we observe that if we remove the $r$-th row and $r+1$-th column from $A$ we get the following block matrix:
\[ \begin{pmatrix}
M' & M^r & 0 \\
0 & x & N_1 \\
0 & 0 & N'
\end{pmatrix}, \]
where $M^r$ denotes the $r$-th column of $M$ without $M_{r,r}$ and $N_1$ denotes the first row of $N$ without $N_{1,1}$. It is then obvious to see that
\[ \mu_{r,r+1}(A) = x \det M' \det N', \]
and that concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Literature update: the general dimension-free O(1/k) rate was already proved by Derezinski-Dong, arXiv:2606.29593v1 Theorem 3.1, and explicit affine historical forgetting by Schliserman-Koren, arXiv:2610.25469v1 Corollary 3. This draft is not a new frontier-rate advance. Owner campaign claim w708-T366-spectrum-006 v1, proof (unaudited); independent correctness and novelty review pending. For iid unit normals n in finite dimension, set Q=E[nn^T], Phi(Y)=E[(I-nn^T)Y(I-nn^T)], and let L be the number of distinct positive eigenvalues of Q. Then Phi^k(Q)<=2^(L-1)Q for every k>=0. Consequently the expected full-task residual after k projections from deterministic e_0 is <=2^(L-1)||e_0||^2/(k+1). Arbitrary eigenvalue multiplicities and noncommutative covariance orbits are allowed. For T uniformly sampled task labels, the separately proved historical bridge gives occurrence mean <=2(2^(L-1)+1)||e_0||^2/k and distinct-observed-label mean <=[8(2^(L-1)+1)+1]||e_0||^2/k for k>=1, without the conventional factor 1/2. The constant depends on L; this method alone does not give the known dimension-free result.

Rung: proof (unaudited). Claim w708-T366-spectrum-006 v1, kind narrowed, Target 2.
Independent correctness and novelty assessment remain pending. The argument is not attributed to the source paper.
Hardest remaining piece: make the constant independent of the number of distinct eigenvalues.

Let Q be a rank-one task covariance, so tr Q=1. Let L be the number of distinct positive eigenvalues
rho_1>...>rho_L>0. No assumption that the exact covariance map preserves a commutative algebra.
The Dereziński-Dong Lemma 10 majorant, N_0=Q, N_(t+1)=N_t(I-2Q)+||N_t|| Q, dominates Phi^t(Q).
Its eigenvalues x_i(t), with multiplicities merged, satisfy

    x_i(0)=rho_i,
    x_i(t+1)=(1-2rho_i)x_i(t)+rho_i m(t), m(t)=max_j x_j(t).

Proved below, subject to independent audit: N_t<=2^(L-1)Q for all t>=0.
Consequently the population residual is <=2^(L-1)||e_0||^2/(k+1), uniformly in d,T and geometry
at fixed L. Historical occurrence and distinct-label bounds follow from the bridge with C=2^(L-1).

## Basic side conditions

All x_i are nonnegative: x_i'=(1-rho_i)x_i+rho_i(m-x_i)>=0.
The maximum is nonincreasing: if rho_i<=1/2 then x_i'<=(1-rho_i)m<=m;
if rho_i>1/2 then x_i'<=rho_i m<=m.
Zero spectral values have zero coordinate forever and are omitted. If m=0, all future iterates vanish.
For two different positive spectral values, rho_i+rho_j<=tr Q=1.

## The maximizing spectral value never increases

Choose the smallest rho among all current maximizing coordinates. If j maximizes and rho_i>rho_j:
for rho_i<=1/2, x_i'<=(1-rho_i)m<(1-rho_j)m=x_j';
for rho_i>1/2, x_i'<=rho_i m<=(1-rho_j)m=x_j'.
Thus a coordinate with a larger rho cannot overtake the chosen maximizer at the next step.
On equality choose the smaller rho again. The distinct maximizing phases are therefore at most L,
and their rho values strictly decrease.

## Geometric phase-area argument

If a phase begins at t_j with maximum H_j and maximizing value rho_j, while this phase lasts
m(t)=(1-rho_j)^(t-t_j) H_j. Its total area over any finite prefix is <=H_j/rho_j.
For every coordinate, x_i(t+1)<=x_i(t)+rho_i m(t), hence
x_i(t)<=rho_i[1+sum_(s<t)m(s)].
If A is the area before a phase, its starting height satisfies H_j<=rho_j(1+A), so the
area after completing that phase is <=2A+1. After j completed phases it is <=2^j-1.

Fix a time in phase j (phases numbered from 1). If rho_i>=rho_j, then
x_i(t)<=m(t)<=H_j<=2^(j-1)rho_j<=2^(L-1)rho_i.
If rho_i<rho_j, at least one spectral value remains below the current winner, so j<=L-1.
The area including the current phase prefix is <=2^j-1, giving
x_i(t)<=2^j rho_i<=2^(L-1)rho_i.
These two cases cover all coordinates. All denominators are positive phase eigenvalues.

## Two positive eigenvalues

This gives C=2 for arbitrary task geometry whenever Q has at most two distinct positive eigenvalues.
The special case has a direct proof: the high-rho coordinate decays geometrically until the low-rho
coordinate wins; it never wins again. Before the switch, summing the high coordinate bounds the
low coordinate by twice its initial eigenvalue. After the switch, the low coordinate decays geometrically.

## Potential failure checks

The exact trace-one hypothesis is used to prevent an eigenvalue above 1/2 retaking the maximum.
The tie convention must rule out winner cycling; the set of winning rho values, not only one coordinate,
is used. Repeated eigenvalues merge because their recurrences and starts agree exactly.
This is a majorant bound; no independence of scalar coordinates is asserted or needed.
No claim of novelty until the finite-spectrum literature comparison is complete.

## Conversion to the named forgetting target

Set C=2^(L-1). Positivity of Phi and Phi^ell(Q)<=C Q imply
Phi^k(Q)<=C Phi^j(Q) for every 0<=j<=k. The projection energy identity gives
sum_(j=0)^k E[e_j'Q e_j]<=||e_0||^2, including the last summand by taking one further update.
Therefore E[e_k'Q e_k]<=C||e_0||^2/(k+1).
For T uniformly sampled task labels, the proved historical bridge in
simplex_quasidomination.md gives occurrence mean <=2(C+1)||e_0||^2/k and distinct-seen-label
mean <=[8(C+1)+1]||e_0||^2/k, for k>=1. Losses omit a conventional factor 1/2.
The bridge is a separate unaudited claim, w708-T366-history-003 v1.

## Verification and limits

The source is arXiv:2604.09909v1, Lemma 10, Section 3, PDF p7; its scalar recurrence is on p8.
The source provides domination, not the finite-spectrum phase argument stated here.
Exact Fraction checks: scripts/check_finite_spectrum.py; logs/verify_finite_spectrum.txt.
They check 27880 states with L=1..7, arbitrary sampled eigenvalue multiplicities, hierarchical
spectra and endpoints including rho=1. These checks supplement the proof and are not a proof
over all spectra. No floating-point bound or Lean certificate is claimed.
Focused searches of the two retrieved frontier papers and the brain returned no finite-L theorem;
this is not an exhaustive novelty search. Existing dimension-dependent rates may overlap at fixed
rank. The specific scope here is a constant depending only on distinct spectral values, with
arbitrarily large multiplicities and arbitrary rank-one task geometry.

[Lemma lem:2.2 of arXiv:2607.24164, 'The KLS constant is $O(\log^{1/4} n)$'] Under the regularity assumptions of (lem:a1 of the paper),
the convex function $\varphi$
given by (lem:2.1 of the paper) is finite and smooth on $\mathbb{R}^n$,
and its Hessian $\nabla^2\varphi$ is positive definite at every point.
Moreover, the map
\[
    \nabla\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\longrightarrow K
\]
is a diffeomorphism. For all $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the Monge--Amp\`ere equation
\[
    \rho(\nabla\varphi(y))\det\nabla^2\varphi(y)
    =e^{-\varphi(y)}
\]
holds pointwise. Equivalently, since $\nabla^2\varphi$ is positive
definite, for all $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
    \log\det\nabla^2\varphi(y)
    =-\varphi(y)+V(\nabla\varphi(y)).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 27 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Fix notation as in Definition~\ref{def:C4_epoch}, let $P$ be the one-step transition kernel of the $k$-column walk, and let $W_D$ denote Wasserstein distance with cost $D$. There is a universal constant $\rho_{\mathrm{loc}}>0$, independent of $n$ and $k$, such that $\rho_{\mathrm{loc}}\leq \min(1,\rho_D)$ and the following holds. If $X_0,Y_0\in \mathrm{St}(n,k)$ satisfy $D(X_0,Y_0)\leq \rho_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then
\be
W_D\left(P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(X_0,\cdot),P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(Y_0,\cdot)\right)
\le (1+C_D\rho_{\mathrm{loc}})\Big((1-\kappa)^{T_{\mathrm{contr}}}+\delta_{\mathrm{epoch}}\Big)D(X_0,Y_0),
\ee
where $\delta_{\mathrm{epoch}}=T_{\mathrm{contr}}\delta_{\mathrm{step}}$. In particular, for all $n > N_{0}$ sufficiently large,
\be 
W_D\left(P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(X_0,\cdot),P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(Y_0,\cdot)\right)
\le n^{-1}D(X_0,Y_0).
\ee

Q_{1,j}(z):=&-(-Y_{1,j}^*
H_{1,j-1}^{-1},\,I_q)R_j(z)u_{1,j},\\
Q_{2,j}(z):=&-(-Y_{2,j}^*  H_{2,j-1}^{-1},\,I_q)R_j(z)u_{2,j}. 
\end{align}
The matrix polynomials $Q_{1,j}$ and $Q_{2,j}$

[Corollary 13 (Fixed-$\alpha$ expiring collector) of arXiv:2604.26298, 'The Expiring Coupon Collector\\ Sliding-Window Surjection Flux and Rare-Entry Laws'] Let \(0<\alpha<1\) be fixed and put \(M=\floor{\alpha n\log n}\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
        \mu_{n,M}T_{n,M}\Rightarrow\Exp(1),
\]
where
\[
        \mu_{n,M}=\frac{(n-1)(n-1)!S(M-1,n-1)}{n^M}.
\]
Consequently, for every fixed \(r\ge1\),
\[
        \Ebb(\mu_{n,M}T_{n,M})^r\to r!,
\]
and
\[
        \log T_{n,M}=n^{1-\alpha}+o_{\mathbb P}(n^{1-\alpha}),
        \qquad
        \log \Ebb T_{n,M}=n^{1-\alpha}+o(n^{1-\alpha}).
\]
If \(\alpha>1/2\), then the sharper normalization is
\[
        n^{-\alpha}e^{-n^{1-\alpha}}T_{n,M}\Rightarrow\Exp(1),
\]
and in particular
\[
        \Ebb T_{n,M}\sim n^\alpha e^{n^{1-\alpha}},
        \qquad
        \Var(T_{n,M})\sim n^{2\alpha}e^{2n^{1-\alpha}}.
\]

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Gaussian-product rectangular heat has bounded-density physical boundary values, almost-everywhere time continuity, and weak transport velocity H+(kappa-1)/(2x), conditional on the stated checked real population-Wishart equation. For S=UV^T/n, independent real Gaussian factors, M/n->beta>0, p/n->kappa>1, and noise sqrt(t/n)G, the symmetric positive-singular-law Cauchy transform g satisfies partial_t g=-partial_z(g^2+(kappa-1)g/z)/2 for t>0. A quartic with leading coefficient t and four distinct asymptotic roots controls density regularity; claim024 supplies the origin gap. Supporting proof draft, not a completed target.
Independent standard real Gaussian factors and noise.
Positive finite hidden-rank ratio and strictly rectangular aspect kappa>1.
Real population-Wishart equation stated in the proof and sourced in claim022.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b64336b2038a578fb40553fcc57c6954c453dec462b4bb6cfe2d36e15f6f0505","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b6/b64336b2038a578fb40553fcc57c6954c453dec462b4bb6cfe2d36e15f6f0505.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9548f3adc68903b67cd441efcd18bebcb2f7ac02a496d314a765992a9a4498a7","bundle_entry_key":"gaussian-product-rectangular-heat-quartic-transport-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-rectangular-reference-c1-and-noncentered-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_009.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:gaussian-product-rectangular-heat-quartic-transport-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Real Gaussian-product heat: algebraic density regularity and transport

Claim draft w718-T287-025, version 1. Kind: moved; target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited), conditional on the precisely stated population-Wishart equation below, already sourced for claim 022. This is a supporting lemma; novelty is unestablished. It does not assert completion of Target 2.

## Model and statement

Let M/n->beta>0 and p/n->kappa>1. Let U (n by M), V (p by M), and G (n by p) have independent standard real normal entries and be mutually independent. Put Y_t=UV^T/n+sqrt(t/n)G, t>0. Let rho_t be the deterministic limiting law of the n positive singular values, symmetrized with equal mass on both signs. Thus rho_t is a probability measure with no rectangular zero-padding. Write a=kappa-1 and

g(z,t)=integral (z-x)^(-1) rho_t(dx), Im z>0.

For every compact interval J contained in (0,infinity), rho_t has a density p_t supported in a common compact set disjoint from zero. Its Cauchy transform is uniformly bounded up to the real axis on bounded x, for t in J. For each fixed t0>0, p_t(x) and H_t(x)=Re g(x+i0,t) are continuous in t at t0 for almost every real x. In particular p_t is continuous in every finite L^r norm. Finally

partial_t g = -(1/2) partial_z (g^2+a g/z),                (1)

and, for every continuously differentiable real test function f on a neighborhood of the common support,

integral f d rho_v - integral f d rho_u
 = integral_u^v integral f'(x)[H_t(x)+a/(2x)]rho_t(dx)dt.  (2)

All transforms use the convention g~1/z and Im g<0 in the upper half-plane. H here has no 1/pi factor.

## Primary input and the equation

Conditional on U, the columns of Y_t are independent real normals with covariance (C_n+tI)/n, where C_n=UU^T/n. The population law of C_n tends to the free-Poisson law tau_beta with mean beta. The checked real population-Wishart theorem (Silverstein 1995, Theorem 1.1 and equation (1.4)) supplies the limiting equation

g(z,t)=integral [z-(c+t)(g(z,t)+a/z)]^(-1) tau_beta(dc).   (3)

For clarity the conversion is as follows. The standard squared-singular-value Stieltjes transform m(lambda)=integral (x-lambda)^(-1) nu_t(dx) satisfies

m(lambda)=integral [kappa(c+t)(1-1/kappa-(lambda/kappa)m(lambda))-lambda]^(-1) tau_beta(dc).

Set lambda=z^2 and g=-z m(z^2) to obtain (3), initially for large purely imaginary z and then by analytic continuation. This sign conversion and covariance scaling are essential. The free-Poisson transform q=G_tau(u), with q~1/u, satisfies u q^2-(u+1-beta)q+1=0; equivalently u=1/q+beta/(1-q) on that branch. It follows either by applying the same population-Wishart equation to identity covariance, or directly by clearing its scalar quadratic.

Set h=g+a/z, q=gh and u=z/h-t, initially at large z where all denominators are nonzero. Equation (3) says q=G_tau(u). With v=zg and w=z^2, clearing denominators gives

P(v,w,t)=(v w-t v(v+a))(w-v(v+a))-w^2-(beta-1)w v(v+a)=0. (4)

Analytic continuation makes (4) valid throughout the upper half-plane, including any point at which an intermediate division was unavailable. We use (3), not arbitrary roots of (4), to specify the physical branch.

## Common support, gap and time continuity

The Gaussian two-sphere net argument bounds the operator norms of U/sqrt(n), V/sqrt(n) and G/sqrt(n) by deterministic constants outside events tending to zero. Consequently rho_t is supported in [-R,R], uniformly for t in J. Supporting claim 024 gives epsilon>0, uniform for t in J, such that rho_t((-epsilon,epsilon))=0. These statements concern the deterministic limiting laws; they do not take an uncountable union of finite-dimensional exceptional events.

Couple Y_t and Y_u with the same U,V,G. The singular-value Hoffman-Wielandt inequality gives, for their empirical positive singular laws eta_n,t,

E W2(eta_n,t,eta_n,u)^2 <= (p/n)(sqrt(t)-sqrt(u))^2.

Both empirical laws converge weakly in probability to deterministic limits. Extracting an almost surely convergent subsequence and using lower semicontinuity of quadratic transport cost followed by Fatou proves

W2(rho_t,rho_u)^2 <= kappa(sqrt(t)-sqrt(u))^2.            (5)

Symmetrization cannot increase this coupling cost. Thus g(z,t) is continuous in t at every point strictly in the upper half-plane.

## Uniform Cauchy bound and bounded densities

As a polynomial in v, (4) has degree four and leading coefficient t. On compact sets of z and t in J its other coefficients are bounded. The elementary polynomial root bound |v|<=1+max_{j<4}|b_j/t| applies: for a monic polynomial, a root of larger modulus would have its highest term strictly dominate the sum of the lower terms by the geometric-series bound. Therefore g=v/z is bounded uniformly for epsilon/2<=|z|<=R+2, Im z>0. For |z|<epsilon/2 the spectral gap gives |g|<=2/epsilon. For large real part the support bound gives the usual inverse-distance bound. This proves a uniform bound B on |g(x+i eta,t)| for all x in a fixed bounded interval, 0<eta<=1, t in J.

For each real interval I, Stieltjes inversion and the bound -Im g<=B imply rho_t(I)<=B|I|/pi, with endpoints obtained by monotone approximation. Hence rho_t is absolutely continuous with density bounded by B/pi. In particular there is no residual singular mass at branch points. Boundary values exist almost everywhere; the algebraic analysis next gives a more explicit statement away from finitely many points.

## Finitely many exceptional points and continuity in time

Fix t0>0. The discriminant of P in v is a polynomial in w. It is not the zero polynomial. Here is a direct verification that avoids choosing numerical roots. For real w tending to positive infinity, the following four simple asymptotic branches exist by the analytic implicit-function theorem:

* For bounded v, divide P by w^2 and use 1/w as the small variable. The limiting equation is v-1=0, whose root is simple.
* Put w=R^2 and v=R y; divide P by R^5. As 1/R tends to zero the limiting equation is y-y^3=0. The roots y=1 and y=-1 are simple and give two distinct branches.
* Put v=w y; divide P by w^4. With 1/w as small variable the limiting equation is t0 y^4-y^3=0. Its root y=1/t0 is simple.

These give four distinct roots at scales 1, sqrt(w), -sqrt(w), w/t0 for sufficiently large w. Therefore the discriminant has only finitely many zeros in w. Apart from finitely many real x satisfying that discriminant at w=x^2, and x=0, all roots are simple.

At any such nonexceptional x, the complex analytic implicit-function theorem gives four locally distinct analytic branches in (z,t) near (x,t0). In a sufficiently small neighborhood, their disjoint root neighborhoods contain all roots. For Im z>0 and real t near t0, the physical g is continuous by (5), so its branch label cannot change on this connected domain. It therefore extends as one of these analytic branches to eta=0 and is jointly continuous there. At x=0 the uniform spectral gap gives analytic continuation directly. Thus H_t(x) and p_t(x)=-Im g(x+i0,t)/pi are continuous in t at t0 outside a finite set. Uniform bounds and common compact support give the asserted finite-L^r continuity of p_t by dominated convergence. The same argument gives local L^r continuity of H_t; outside a fixed compact set its tail is uniformly O(1/|x|).

## Exact transport algebra

Let R0=G_tau'(u). Differentiate q=gh=G_tau(z/h-t) at large z. Since h=g+a/z, this yields

D g_t=-R0,
D g_z=R0(1/h+a/(z h^2))+a g/z^2,
D=2g+a/z+R0 z/h^2.

Here D~kappa/z, so division is valid for sufficiently large z. Put r=a/z. Multiplying the desired identity g_t+(g+r/2)g_z-a g/(2z^2)=0 by D cancels its terms without R0. The remaining coefficient, multiplied by 2h^2, is exactly

-2(g+r)^2+(2g+r)(g+2r)-r g=0.

This proves (1) near infinity. It also gives derivatives of every moment: the physical root v~1 is analytic in 1/z near infinity and in t near any t0>0, by the simple bounded-root construction above. Comparing its Laurent coefficients is legitimate on a common circle outside the support. We now identify these derivatives with the right side of (2), avoiding any assumption that density time derivatives already exist.

Define H_e(x)=Re g(x+i e,t). It is uniformly bounded on the common support and tends to H_t almost everywhere. For nonreal z, symmetrization and Fubini give

integral H_e(x)/(z-x) rho_t(dx)
 = (1/2) double-integral [(x-y)^2/((x-y)^2+e^2)] /[(z-x)(z-y)] rho_t(dx)rho_t(dy).

The bounded density makes the diagonal null, so dominated convergence gives integral H_t(x)/(z-x)rho_t(dx)=g(z,t)^2/2. Evenness and the gap give integral x^-1 rho_t(dx)=0 and integral [x(z-x)]^-1 rho_t(dx)=g(z,t)/z. Thus for V_t=H_t+a/(2x),

integral V_t(x)/(z-x)rho_t(dx)=(g^2+a g/z)/2.

The velocity is uniformly bounded on the common support. Differentiating this last identity with respect to z identifies the Laurent coefficients of the right side of (1) with integral k x^(k-1)V_t rho_t. Coefficient comparison therefore proves (2) for polynomials. For a C1 test f on a fixed containing interval, approximate f' uniformly by polynomials, integrate those polynomials to approximate f and f' simultaneously, and pass in the integrated identity using the uniform velocity bound. This proves (2). No multiplication of dependent probabilities or differentiation of a merely convergent sequence of MI functions occurs.

## Remaining work

The entropy chain rule and real rectangular radial-density calibration are not proved in this file. They are required before concluding Gaussian-reference MI differentiability or general rectangular MMSE extremality. The least trusted step for external audit here is the boundary-branch continuation argument; its finite exceptional set, continuity on the upper domain, and uniform Cauchy bound must all be retained.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:965a7f6569046bdab574a5d8dade402280c470a6610623c9409c56ed763549bc","revision_digest":"sha256:50bf03e0ebe0e096e8ec202ae39b13a5d25fd4c237863e7af9c7e523a30ae60d","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:gaussian-product-rectangular-heat-quartic-transport-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 w718-T287-025 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Method: Weak reinforcement on infinite WARM networks structural argument Result: On Z with all firing rates1, set edge values alternately2 and0. At each vertex the only positive incident edge is selected with probability1; its two endpoints supply total rate2, while zero edges get rate0. This is an equilibrium for every alpha>0. Shifting gives a second one, and the uniform edge value1 is a third. Thus uniqueness among all nonnegative equilibria is false. Check: All denominators equal2^alpha, so the example has no undefined 0/0 term. It does not contradict convergence from strictly positive initial counts. Obstruction: The positive-equilibrium uniqueness and stochastic attraction problem on general infinite graphs remains; no finite total Lyapunov function is available.

[Lemma lem:stationarity_L1 of arXiv:2605.15401, 'Noise Tradeoffs, Stationary Information Flow, and Structural Balance in Unit-Birth Network'] Consider a CTMC on a countable state space $S$ with transition rates $q(x,y)$
and total exit rate $\Lambda(x)=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)$. Suppose $\pi$ is a
stationary distribution with full support and
\[
\mathbb{E}_\pi[\Lambda(X)]<\infty.
\]
Let $\varphi:S\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)|\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)|<\infty.
\end{equation}
Then, for every $x\in S$, the series
\[
\sum_{y\neq x} q(x,y)\,|\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)|
\]
is finite, and hence
\[
(L\varphi)(x):=\sum_{y\neq x} q(x,y)\big(\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)\big)
\]
is absolutely convergent and well defined. Moreover, $L\varphi\in L^1(\pi)$
and
\[
\mathbb{E}_\pi\!\big[(L\varphi)(X)\big]=0.
\]

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Fix \(0<a<R<\infty\) and \(r\in(0,a)\).  There is
\(C=C(H,a,R,r)<\infty\) such that, for all \(s,t\in[a,R]\) with
\(|s-t|\leq1\) and all \(u\neq0\),
\begin{equation}
  |K_H(t,u)-K_H(s,u)|
  \leq C|t-s|^{2H}K_H(r,u).
  
\end{equation}
The reflected statement holds on \([-R,-a]\) with a fixed
\(r\in(-a,0)\).

Method: Diameter-squared upper bound for transitive mixing explicit structural calculation Result: The cycle illustrates the missing spectral information. On the N-cycle, lazy eigenvalues are1-sin^2(pi*k/N). Since sin(pi*k/N)>=2*k/N for k<=N/2, the chi-square bound from a point is at most2*sum_(k>=1) exp(-8*t*k^2/N^2). At t=C*N^2 this sum is as small as desired for a universal C, proving the proposed diameter-squared order in this case without a log N penalty. Check: Use symmetry k versus N-k and(1-x)^(2t)<=exp(-2tx). The Gaussian series converges and tends to0 as C increases. The cycle diameter is floor(N/2) and its degree is2. Obstruction: For a general transitive graph, the gap alone bounds all N-1 modes by the same exponential and introduces log N. A uniform bound on low-frequency multiplicities or spectral mass strong enough to remove that factor is missing.

[Definition def:discrete_continuous_coupling of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $X(t) = (x(t), (\sigma^1(t), \sigma^2(t)))$ be a continuous
  process as defined in definition
  (def:continuous_process_min_max_construction of the paper), with fixed
  parameters $\omega$ (resp. $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and $\ell$, and
  $\sigma^1(t)$ and
  $\sigma^2(t)$ two independent Markov jump
  processes with the transition rates of figure
  (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper)
  (resp. (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)). Denote
  by $0 = T_0 < T_1 < \cdots$ the jump times of the couple
  $(\sigma^1, \sigma^2)$. For $L \ge 2$, let $N_1^L$ and $N_2^L$ be
  two independent Poisson processes with parameter
  $\gamma_L = (L - 1)/\ell$ independent of the $\sigma^i$.

  Recursively define $y^L$ by setting
\[
y^L(0) = \left\lfloor (L-1)x(0)/\ell\right\rfloor+ 1 \ \text{and}\  	z^L(t) := y^L(T_k) + \sum_{i = 1, 2} (-1)^i \sigma^i(T_k)
  \left[ N^L_i(t) - N^L_i(T_k) \right],
\]
  \begin{itemize}    
  \item if $(\sigma^1(T_k), \sigma^2(T_k)) \neq \pm (1, 1)$
$$
y^L(t) = \max \left[1,  \min \left[ L, z^L(t)  \right] \right] \text{ for } t \in [T_k, T_{k+1}],
$$
\item if $(\sigma^1(T_k), \sigma^2(T_k)) = \pm (1, 1)$
$$
y^L(t) = p_L \left( z^L(t) \right) \text{ for } t \in
[T_k, T_{k+1}]
$$
where $p_L : \mathbb Z \rightarrow \{1, \ldots, L\}$ is given by
$$
p_L(k + 2 m L) =
\left\{
\begin{array}{cl}
k &\text{ for } m \in \mathbb Z \text{ and } 1 \le k \le L, \\
2L + 1 - k &\text{ for } m \in \mathbb Z \text{ and } L + 1 \le k \le 2L.
\end{array}
\right.
$$
\end{itemize}

Finally, set $Y^L(t) = (y^L(t), (\sigma^1(t), \sigma^2(t)))$.

[OPEN PROBLEM - not a proved fact. Stated in arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$' (conj environment labelled conj.b0).] Let $b_0$ be an invertible operator in a $W^\ast$-probability space $(\A,\tau)$. Define
\[ \tilde{p}_0(z) = \tau[|b_0-z|^{-2}] \qquad \& \qquad \tilde{p}_2(z) = \tau[b_0^\ast b_0|b_0-z|^{-2}] \]
where, as usual, for any operator $a\in\A$, $|a|^2:=a^\ast a$. Define $T(b_0,\cdot)\colon\C\to\R_+$ by
\begin{equation} T(b_0,z) = \frac{\log(\tilde{p}_2(z))-\log(|z|^2\tilde{p}_0(z))}{\tilde{p}_2(z)-|z|^2\tilde{p}_0(z)}.
\end{equation}
For each $t>0$, define the open precompact set $\Sigma(b_0,t)$ by
\begin{equation} \Sigma(b_0,t) = \{z\in\C\colon T(b_0,z)<t\}. \end{equation}
Let $b(t,\zeta)$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion (see Notation (notat.ovweparam)) freely independent from $b_0$. Then the support of the Brown measure of $b_0b(t,\zeta)$ is equal to the image $\overline{\Sigma(b_0,t,\zeta)}$ of $\overline{\Sigma(b_0,t)}$ under the map $\Psi^{b_0}_{t,\zeta}$ of (eq.Psi). body:
[Thm 3 of arXiv:2506.21829, 'Some notes on Lamperti's recurrence of stochastic sequences'] Assume that \eqref{1}, integrability condition \eqref{2} and assumptions \eqref{4.3}, \eqref{4.4}, \eqref{4.5} and \eqref{4.6} are satisfied.
Then the stochastic sequence is recurrent if, as $x\to\infty$, we almost surely have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{p\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}>X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}{q\mathsf{E}\{X_{n}-X_{n+1}~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}<X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}\\
&\leq1+\frac{R}{x}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{1+\epsilon}}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where $R(x)=\mathsf{E}\{|X_{n+1}-X_n|~\big|~X_{n}=x, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}$, and $R$ is the limit with probability $1$ of $R(x)$ as $x\to\infty$.
If instead
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{p\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}>X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}{q\mathsf{E}\{X_{n}-X_{n+1}~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}<X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}\\
&\geq1+\frac{R\theta}{x},
\end{aligned}
\]
for some $\theta>1$ and almost all large $x$, then the stochastic sequence is transient.
title: Thm 3 of arXiv:2506.21829

[Lemma lem:good-walk of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Let~$G = (V,E)$ be an infinite, locally finite, connected graph with degree bounded by~$d$ and satisfying the bound~(equation eq:return-bound of the paper) for some $d_s>0$ and $A<\infty$. Let $(\xi(v))_{v\in V}$ be i.i.d.\ and independent of the walk with $\mathbb{E}[\xi]\in(-\infty,0)$ and $\mathbb{E}[|\xi|^p]<\infty$ for some $p\geq 1$, and let $Y_k\coloneqq(\max_{2^k\leq n<2^{k+1}}W_n-|\mathbb{E}[\xi]|\,2^k/d)^+$. Let $\alpha\coloneqq(1-d_s/2)^+$ and fix $\delta\in(0,d_s/2\wedge 1)$. For $k\geq 0$, let
		\begin{equation}
			\mathcal{A}_k\coloneqq\bigl\{\max_v L_N(v)\leq N^{\alpha+\delta}\bigr\},\qquad N\coloneqq 2^{k+1}\,.
		\end{equation}
		Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
			\item For every integer $r\geq 1$,
			\[
			\mathbb{P}_x(\mathcal{A}_k^c)\leq C_r\begin{cases}
				N^{d_s/2-r\delta} & \text{if } d_s<2,\\[3pt]
				N^{1-r\delta}(1{+}\log N)^{r-1} & \text{if } d_s=2,\\[3pt]
				N^{1-r\delta} & \text{if } d_s>2\,.
			\end{cases}\,
			\]
			\item $\mathbb{E}_x[Y_k^p]\leq C\,N^p$ uniformly in~$x$ and~$k$.
			\item For every $q\in[1,p)$ and $r$ large enough, $\mathbb{E}_x[Y_k^q\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{A}_k^c}]=O(2^{-3k})$ uniformly in~$x$.
		\end{enumerate}

body: For an elliptic curve E over a number field K, the group E(K) of K-rational points is finitely generated: E(K) is isomorphic to a finite torsion group times Z^r, where r is the rank. The proof combines the weak Mordell-Weil theorem (E(K)/mE(K) finite, via Kummer theory and finiteness of class and unit groups) with a descent using height functions. Ranks are computable in practice but no general algorithm is proven; the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture ties r to the order of vanishing of the L-function at s = 1.

body:
[Lem 14 (Renewal--reward CLT) of arXiv:2607.28865, 'First-Passage Percolation on Spread-out line graphs: Microscopic Regime'] Let $\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i\ge1}$ be i.i.d.~with $X_i\in\dN$,
\begin{align*}
\E X_1=\mu\in(0,\infty),
\qquad
\E Y_1=\nu\in\dR,
\qquad
\E X_1^2+\E Y_1^2<\infty.
\end{align*}
Define
\begin{align*}
S_m:=\sum_{i=1}^m X_i,
\qquad
R_m:=\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i,
\qquad
N_t:=\max\{m\ge0:S_m\le t\},
\qquad
R(t):=R_{N_t}.
\end{align*}
Then, as $t\to\infty$,
\begin{align}
t^{-1/2}\cdot (R(t)-t\cdot {\nu}/{\mu})
\Longrightarrow
\N(0,\sigma^2),
\end{align}
where $\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{\mu} \var\left(Y_1-\nu/{\mu}\cdot X_1\right)$.
Equivalently,
\begin{align}
t^{-1/2}\cdot (R(t)-\E R(t))
\Longrightarrow
\N(0,\sigma^2).
\end{align}

[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2606.22611, 'Upper and Lower Bounds on Expected Soft Maxima\\of Gaussian Processes'] Let $X = (X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a centered  Gaussian process with a finite index set $T$. Let a subset $A \subset T$ with $\diam(A) \le a$ be given, and let $\cA = \set{ A_1,\ldots,A_n}$ be a partition of $A$. For any $\mu \in \eP(T)$ supported on $A$, let  $\mu^i \deq \mu(\cdot|A_i)$ be the 
conditional probability measure given $A_i$. Then, for any $\beta \ge 0$ we have
\begin{align*}
 \eF_\beta(X;\mu) \le \max_{i \le n} \eF_\beta(X; \mu^i)
  + C a \sqrt{\eta(n,a\beta)},
\end{align*}
where $C > 0$ is a universal constant.
title: Proposition 19 of arXiv:2606.22611

[Proposition prop:L2-thin of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] The coupling $(\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa})$ defined in~(equation eq:comp_Poisson_measures of the paper) and~(equation eq:thining_coupling_defn of the paper) satisfies
\begin{equation}

\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t\big|^2\bigg]
\leqslant 4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}).
\end{equation}
Moreover, if $\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})$ and $\nu_{\bm{Y}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})$ have a finite second moment, then 
\begin{gather*}
\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t+\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-(\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t+\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t)-\bm{m}_\kappa t\big|^2\bigg]
\leqslant 4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\quad\text{and}\\
\mathcal{W}_2(\bm{X},\bm{Y})
\leqslant |\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{X},\kappa}-\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{Y},\kappa}+\bm{m}_\kappa|
    + 2 d^{1/2} |\bm{\Sigma_X}-\bm{\Sigma_Y}|
    + 2\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\bigg)^{1/2},
\end{gather*}
where the mean $\bm{m}_\kappa:=\mathds{E}[\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_1-\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_1]
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\bm{w}\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
(f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w}))\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})$
is finite.
title: Proposition prop:L2-thin of arXiv:2411.03609

[Proposition prop:exact-variance of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] Assume \(((A1 of the paper))\), \(((A3 of the paper))\), and \(((A4 of the paper))\), \(\alpha m<1\), and \(2d+\alpha m<1\). Then
\[
    \operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})\sim\sigma_m^2v_n^2.
\]
where
\[
\sigma_m^2
=
\frac{J_m^2c^m}{m!}
\int_0^1\int_0^1
x^{-d}y^{-d}|x-y|^{-\alpha m}\,dx\,dy.
\]
The integral is finite. Moreover,
\(
A_n^2=\operatorname{Var}(S_n)\sim \operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m}).
\)

Consequently, \(A_n\sim\sigma_m v_n\), and \(A_n\) is regularly varying with index \(H\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
