[Lemma lem:jw-degree-law of arXiv:2607.00731, 'Sharp Asymptotics for the Largest Component in the Subcritical Regime of Preferential Atta'] Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be i.i.d.\ random variables with
\[
\mathbb P(Y_i=k)=\binom{\alpha+k-1}{k}(1-p_n)^{\alpha}p_n^k,
\]
where $$p_n=\frac{2m}{\alpha n+2m}=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\alpha+2-\varepsilon}.$$
Then
\[
d\bigl(G_{n,m}^{\alpha,\ast}\bigr)\overset{d}= (Y_1,\dots,Y_n)\,\big|\,\{Y_1+\cdots+Y_n=2m\}.
\]
In particular, if $Y^{(n)}\sim\operatorname{NBin}(\alpha,p_n)$, then for every fixed integer $k\ge 0$ and every fixed integer $r\ge 1$,
\[
\pi_k(d)=\mathbb P\bigl(Y^{(n)}=k\bigr)+O_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]
and
$$\mu_r(d)=\mathbb E\bigl[(Y^{(n)})^r\bigr]+O_p(n^{-1/2}).$$
For each fixed $r\ge 1$ one also has $\mathbb E\bigl[(Y^{(n)})^r\bigr]=O(1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 4 (\textsf{Finite-horizon KSD-SuccessiveHalving}) of arXiv:2609.02138, 'HyperMC: Multi-Fidelity Hyperparameter Tuning for Stochastic Gradient MCMC'] Suppose Assumptions~\ref{ass:envelope}--\ref{ass:ksd-concentration} hold and fix
$\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$.  Assume the terminal KSD estimate has sufficient resolution:
$$
\psi_{n,\delta}(R)<\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.
$$
Equivalently, because $\gamma(R)=0$, it is sufficient that
$$
 m_R>
 \frac{32\sigma_{\KSD}^2}{\varepsilon^2}
 \log\!\left(\frac{2nL_n}{\delta}\right).
$$
Then every $\tau_i(\varepsilon,\delta)$ is finite and belongs to $\{1,\ldots,R\}$.  If
\begin{equation}
 B_{\mathrm{eff}} \geq \eta L_n \max _{2 \leq i \leq n} i\left(1+\tau_i(\varepsilon, \delta)\right),
\end{equation}
then the output $\widehat{i}$ of KSD-SuccessiveHalving satisfies
$$
 \nu_{\widehat{i}}-\nu_1\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
$$
with probability at least $1-\delta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 1 (Coding map and coding radius) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] A measurable $\varphi:A^{\Zd}\to B^{\Zd}$ such that $\varphi\circ T^j=S^j\circ \varphi$, for all $j\in\Zd$, is called a coding map. For $x\in A^{\Zd}$ we define the (pointwise) \emph{coding radius at the origin}
\[
r\!_\varphi(x)\;:=\;\inf\Big\{r\in\N_0:\ \forall x'\in A^{\Zd},\ 
x'_{B_\infty(0,r)}=x_{B_\infty(0,r)}\ \Rightarrow\ \varphi(x')_0=\varphi(x)_0\Big\}.

\]
If the set is empty then the coding radius is infinite.
title: Coding map and coding radius

body: An n by n real matrix A = (a_{ij}) is doubly stochastic if every entry is nonnegative (a_{ij} >= 0 for all i, j), every row sums to 1 (sum_j a_{ij} = 1 for every i), and every column sums to 1 (sum_i a_{ij} = 1 for every j). The set of n by n doubly stochastic matrices is a convex set, closed under matrix multiplication. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]
title: Doubly Stochastic Matrix

Method: Exact recurrence, conditional-law calculation, or source-specific limiting obstruction Result: A compactness limit of finite-threshold processes does not automatically preserve the rule, because percolation is not a continuous local event. On Z^d, configurations with only edges inside[-n,n]^d open converge locally to the all-open configuration. Every approximating root cluster is finite, while the limiting root cluster is infinite. Thus an assertion that no finite approximation froze cannot be passed through a local limit without extra control. Check: For every fixed ball, all its edges are eventually open; this proves local convergence directly. Each finite box has finitely many vertices, so none of its open clusters is infinite. Obstruction: One must rule out discontinuous creation of infinite clusters at limiting times while enforcing the freezing equation. [Theorem Main 3 of arXiv:2609.02871, 'Estimating the number of real zeros of linear combinations of radicals of polynomials'] Let $P_k$, $k=1,\dots,n$ be real polynomials of one variable of degree at most $d$ and assume that each $P_k$ is positive on an interval $I=(a,b)$, where $a,b \in \mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}$. Let $\alpha_k$ be arbitrary real numbers. If $P_k^{\alpha_k}$ are linearly independent on $I$, $c_k$ are real and not all zero, then $$f=\sum_{k=1}^{n} c_k P_k^{\alpha_k}$$
has no more than $4n^3d+n$ distinct roots on $I$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:seed of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $d\ge1$, let $E$ carry the infection in the sense of (def:carries of the paper), and assume the
hypotheses of (thm:GS of the paper), so that a two-sided Lipschitz surface $F$ on which $E$ holds exists
almost surely. Let $D$ be the distance at which $F$ surrounds the origin, which is almost surely
finite by (thm:GSsurround of the paper), and choose $D_0$ with $\mathbb{P}[D\le D_0]\ge\tfrac34$. Put
\[
  \tau_0=D_0+1,\qquad
  \mathcal B=\big\{(i,\tau):\ 0\le\tau\le\tau_0,\ \|i\|_\infty\le2\tau_0\big\} .
\]
If $\mathbb{P}[E(i,\tau)^c]\le(4|\mathcal B|)^{-1}$ for every cell, then with probability at least
$\tfrac12$ the following holds: $E$ holds on every cell of $\mathcal B$, $F$ surrounds the origin
at distance $D_0$, and consequently, if some particle lying in the central cube $C_0$ is infected
at time $0$, then there is a cell of $F$ whose central cube contains an infected particle at the
initial time of that cell's block.

[Thm Theorem7 of arXiv:2412.05521, 'Random attractors for the stochastic Nernst-Planck-Navier-Stokes system with multiplicativ'] The random dynamical system associated with the stochastic Nernst-Planck-Navier-Stokes equations (equation b2 of the paper) has a compact random attractor in $H$.
	\begin{proof}
		It follows from Lemma (lem10 of the paper) that there exists a random closed ball in $V$, which absorbs any deterministic bounded sets in $H$. Applying the compactness of embedding $V \hookrightarrow H$, it is clear to deduce that every bounded closed sets in $V$ are asymptotically compact in $H$. Hence, one can easily obtain the existence of a compact absorbing set. With the help of Theorem (thm1 of the paper), the desired conclusion is proved. 
		\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma eq:moment-matrix of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:moment-interior}
Let
\[
 m_k=\mathbb E G^{2k}=(2k-1)!!,
 \qquad k=0,\ldots,q.
\]
There exist symmetric, compactly supported \(C^\infty\) probability densities
\(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_q\) and positive weights \(w_0,\ldots,w_q\) such that the matrix
\begin{equation}
 B_{kj}=\int x^{2k}\phi_j(x)\,\mathrm d x,
 \qquad 0\le k,j\le q,
\end{equation}
is invertible and
\begin{equation}
 m_k=\sum_{j=0}^q w_jB_{kj},
 \qquad k=0,\ldots,q.
\end{equation}
Moreover, all moment vectors sufficiently close to \((m_0,\ldots,m_q)\) in the affine hyperplane with zeroth moment equal to one admit such a representation with strictly positive weights summing to one.
title: Interior moment representation by smooth bumps

Let Assumption \ref{A2} hold and $T>0,p\geq1$ be given, then there exists constant $C(T)>0$ and $C(t,p)>0$ such that
		\begin{align}
            &
            \forall n\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{E}\sup\limits_{0\leq s\leq T}\Vert \tilde{X}^{(n)}(s)\Vert_{2\theta,\rho}^p\leq C(T,p)(1+\Vert x \Vert_{2\theta,\rho}^p),\\

[Lemma 5 (Self-selected sign and almost-sure specialization) of arXiv:2608.24007, '2608.24007'] Let $\omega^0$ have an absolutely continuous distribution on
$\mathbb S^{d-1}$, and let $(u(t),\omega(t))$ solve
\eqref{eq:self-selected-teacher-flow} with
\[
    u(0)=0,
    \qquad
    \omega(0)=\omega^0.
\]
For almost every $\omega^0$, define
\[
    \zeta
    =
    \operatorname{sign}(\Phi(\omega^0))
    \in\{\pm1\}.
\]
Then, for every $t>0$,
\[
    \zeta u(t)>0,
    \qquad
    \zeta\Phi(\omega(t))
    \geq
    |\Phi(\omega^0)|.
\]
Moreover, $\omega(t)$ is a positive time reparameterization of spherical
gradient ascent on $\Psi_\zeta=\zeta\Phi$, and, for all sufficiently large
$R$, it converges almost surely to one of the specialized maxima in
Lemma~\ref{lem:specialized-maxima}.

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Square random-profile invariant spectral calibration, proof unaudited. For biorthogonally invariant real n by n signals S_n with ||S_n||op<=C almost surely and E||S_n||_F^2/n->a, observe Y_n=sqrt(s)S_n+Z_n, with independent iid Gaussian noise variance1/n and fixed s>=0. If its empirical positive singular law converges in expected squared W2 to a deterministic compact bounded-density law eta, then I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2->Sigma(sym eta)-Sigma(semicircle_1). Input singular profiles may be random, atomic or rank deficient. The exact mixture partition function includes its input quadratic weight, so the finite MI identity is s*E||S_n||_F^2/(2n)-E Q_n(Y_n). A uniform spectral Lipschitz estimate, lemma017 quantile boxes and the signal-independent calibration019 identify every subsequential limit. No prior MI-limit assumption or unitary-to-real asymptotic-freeness extension is used. Novelty of this standard density argument is unestablished.
Real square biorthogonally invariant signal independent of Gaussian noise.
Uniform almost-sure operator-norm bound and convergent normalized mean squared Frobenius norm.
Expected squared W2 convergence of output positive singular law to a compact bounded-density law.
Fixed s>=0 and natural logarithms.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3b08fdae3bb7ff924ea3e4896262836456507449bcf8a19f7bed47185bf1cc63","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3b/3b08fdae3bb7ff924ea3e4896262836456507449bcf8a19f7bed47185bf1cc63.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f7ee46a2e3388a11ce13fc89ccd7a2a712259b34ba37615dbe0afe0e0398d634","bundle_entry_key":"random-profile-square-mi-calibration-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-near-square-c1-and-finite-variance-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:random-profile-square-mi-calibration-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Square invariant signals with random singular profiles: spectral calibration

Target 2 supporting lemma, proof draft, unaudited. Standard density
normalization argument; novelty unestablished. This removes the
deterministic-profile restriction from claim019. No generic real/complex
asymptotic freeness theorem is assumed.

Let S_n be biorthogonally invariant real n by n signals, independent of
Z_n whose entries are iid N(0,1/n). Suppose ||S_n||op<=C almost surely
for one constant C, and a_n=E||S_n||_F^2/n -> a. Fix s>=0 and put
Y_n=sqrt(s)S_n+Z_n. Assume its empirical positive singular law eta_n
satisfies E W2(eta_n,eta)^2->0 for a deterministic compact bounded-density
probability law eta on [0,infinity). Then

    I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2 -> Sigma(sym eta)-Sigma(sigma_1).    (1)

Here sigma_1 is the variance-one semicircle law and all logarithms are
natural. The input singular profiles may be random, atomic or rank
deficient. Output regularity is an explicit assumption, not a conclusion.

## Exact partition function and its Lipschitz bound

For a deterministic matrix T define

 Q_n(T)=n^-2 log E_S exp[n sqrt(s)<S,T>-n*s*||S||_F^2/2].

The expectation is with respect to a fresh sample from the signal prior.
This includes its quadratic input weight. Biorthogonal invariance makes
Q_n a function of the singular values of T. Since ||S||_F<=C sqrt(n),
uniform exponent comparison gives

 |Q_n(T)-Q_n(T')|<=C sqrt(s) ||T-T'||_F/sqrt(n).

After optimally aligning the singular frames,

 |Q_n(T)-Q_n(T')|<=C sqrt(s) W2(eta_T,eta_T').         (2)

The absolute bounds at a profile y are

 -s C^2/2-C sqrt(s*m2(eta_y)) <= Q_n(diag y)
                          <= C sqrt(s*m2(eta_y)).    (3)

These inequalities follow pointwise in the prior signal before taking
expectation and logarithm. No independence of singular values is used.

The Gaussian mixture density and the real square SVD Jacobian give the
exact ordered singular-value density

 p_n(y)=C_n exp[n^2(-m2(eta_y)/2+Q_n(diag y)+V_n(y))],               (4)
 V_n(y)=n^-2 sum_(i<j)log|y_j^2-y_i^2|.

C_n is the same signal-independent constant calibrated in claim019,
using the real Jacobian of arXiv:2203.07752 Section2.1 equation(15):

    n^-2 log C_n -> 1/2-Sigma(sigma_1).              (5)

The exact likelihood-ratio calculation now gives

    i_n(s)=s*a_n/2-E Q_n(Y_n).                       (6)

The factor1/2 differs from the fixed-profile formula for J_n in claim019,
because Q_n already contains -n*s*||S||_F^2/2. Indeed the conditional
log-density has Gaussian quadratic -n||Z||_F^2/2, while the marginal
has -n||Y||_F^2/2+n^2 Q_n(Y). Their expected difference divided by n^2
is (s/2)E||S||_F^2/n-E Q_n(Y), as asserted.

## Subsequential calibration, with all limit premises explicit

Let q_n be the midpoint-quantile profile of eta. It has bounded entries.
By (3), K_n=Q_n(diag q_n) is bounded. Along any subsequence with K_n->K,
(2), the assumed expected W2 convergence and deterministic quantile
W2 convergence imply

    E|Q_n(Y_n)-K_n|->0.                             (7)

The same expected W2 convergence implies m2(eta)=1+s*a, because
E m2(eta_n)=1+s*a_n and the square roots of second moments differ by
at most W2. This passage uses Cauchy-Schwarz to pass the squared norms;
it does not replace weak convergence by moment convergence.

For a fixed large R, P(||Y_n||op<=R)->1. This follows from
||Y||op<=sqrt(s)C+||Z||op and the Gaussian net estimate in claim019.
Thus the observed profile lies with high probability in [0,R] and in
any given small W2 neighborhood of eta. In that neighborhood, the
quadratic term and Q_n are uniformly close to their respective limits,
by bounded support and (2). The V_n uniform upper bound of claim017
then bounds the exponent in (4) above by

    c -(1+s*a)/2 +K+Sigma(sym eta)+epsilon,

where c is the limit in (5). The neighborhood volume is at most R^n.
Its probability tends to one; consequently the displayed expression
without epsilon must be nonnegative.

For the opposite direction, integrate (4) on the product boxes of radius
1/(4C_eta n^3) around q_n, where C_eta is a finite density bound of eta.
Claim017 gives their log volume o(n^2) and matching uniform energy lower
bound. Their W2 distance to q_n is O(n^-3), so (2) and the quadratic
term give the matching lower exponent. Its integral is at most one,
so that same limiting expression must be nonpositive. Therefore

    0=c -(1+s*a)/2+K+Sigma(sym eta),
    K=s*a/2+Sigma(sigma_1)-Sigma(sym eta).            (8)

Every convergent subsequence of the bounded K_n has the same limit.
Hence K_n converges, and (6)-(8) prove (1) along the full sequence.
No existence assumption for the information limit is needed.

Dependencies: proofs/quantile_vandermonde_boxes.md (claim017) and the
signal-independent Gaussian calibration and real Jacobian in
proofs/square_mi_log_energy_calibration.md (claim019). All are unaudited.

## Scope of the prospective Gaussian-product application

For the unbounded Gaussian-product prior, one still has to truncate to
a fixed operator-norm event and pay the change of MI by a small L2
coupling, then prove the expected W2 output law with a bounded density.
The exact conditional real population-Wishart representation is the
intended source route. Combining (1) with the free-heat C1 result020
also requires identifying sym eta as dilation_sqrt(s)(mu_input)
free-plus sigma_1. [Theorem thm:kpoint of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Let $z_i\in\mathbb{R}^M$ carry weights $p_i>0$, $\sum_ip_i=1$, with
$\sum_ip_iz_i=0$, and $E=\sum_ip_i\lVert z_i\rVert^2$. For every
$1\le k\le M+1$ there is a convex combination $\delta$ of at most $k$ of the
points with
\[
  \lVert \delta\rVert^2\ \le\ E\cdot\frac{M+1-k}{kM}.
\]
The constant is sharp: for the uniformly weighted regular $M$-simplex, every
convex combination supported on $k$ points has squared norm at least
$E\frac{M+1-k}{kM}$, with equality for $k$ vertices at equal weights. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $k$-point mean lemma

[Theorem 25 of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $n \geq 2$. Consider the space $\R^n$ equipped with the Lebesgue measure and the cost function $c(x,y) = -[x,y]$. Define the function $F: \R_+\to \R_+$ by $F(r) = \vol(\B)r^{\frac{n}{2}}.$
Then, $\R^n$ satisfies the cost-Santal\'o inequality associated with $\left(\frac{1}{2}, c, F \right)$ with domain $(\mathcal{B}_b(\R^n), \mathcal{B}(\R^n))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For every Borel probability measure C on [0,1]^2 whose two marginals are uniform on [0,1], let Q be the uniform product law. For squared Euclidean transport cost, W_2^2(C,Q)<=1/10. Equality holds if and only if C=Law(U,U) or C=Law(U,1-U), U uniform on [0,1]. Thus these are the only maximizers. This settles the Catalano-Lavenant conjecture recorded as open by Schrott (2026). Then $d_{\rm geo}(\widehat F)=2$ and EVERY optimal homogenized residual plane $\widehat R$ has the saturated shared-$h$ pattern: $\boxed{k_{\widehat F}(\widehat R)=r+1,\ h\notin\widehat R,\ [h]_{\widehat R}\text{ contains an old form},\ \dim S=2}$ (tag 12), with no additional merger after restriction, where $S=\operatorname{span}\{f_i-\sigma f_j:f_i-\sigma f_j\in\widehat R|_{\ker h}\}$ (tag 13). Notes: Each alternative is killed by producing an old residual of dimension $\le2$: an optimal plane leaving $\le r$ classes descends directly; if the $h$-class contains no old form, deleting $h$ removes one class; if $h\in\widehat R$, restriction loses one residual dimension and the remaining merger costs at most one; if restriction causes any extra merger; and if $\dim S<2$, adjoin one old signed difference between two remaining classes. Quantifier (S5 line 301): under old distance three EVERY optimal plane must satisfy (12), and it is enough to select ONE and apply the exclusion.

body:
[Theorem thm-12proper of arXiv:2412.03067, 'Geodesic Trees and Exceptional Directions in FPP on Hyperbolic Groups'] We fix the base-point $1$.
There exists a full measure subset $\Omega_0 \subset \Omega$ such that
for all  $\omega \in \Omega_0$, 
\begin{enumerate}
	\item $i_\omega^F: F(1,\omega) \to \Gamma$ is  proper in the sense of Lemma~(lem-proper of the paper), 
	\item $i_\omega^F: F(1,\omega) \to \Gamma$ is uniformly 2-proper in the sense of Definition~(def-2proper of the paper).
\end{enumerate}
Hence for  all  $\omega \in \Omega_0$, 
$i_\omega^F: F(1,\omega) \to \Gamma$ admits a Cannon-Thurston map. 

Further, given $\xi \in {\partial G}$, and all $\omega \in \Omega_0 \cap \Omega_{\xi}$, 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $i_\omega^T: T(\xi,\omega) \to \Gamma$ is  proper in the sense of Lemma~(lem-proper of the paper), 
\item $i_\omega^T: T(\xi,\omega) \to \Gamma$ is  2-proper in the sense of Definition~(def-2proper of the paper).
\end{enumerate}
Hence for  all $\xi \in {\partial G}$, and $\omega \in \Omega_0 \cap \Omega_{\xi}$, 
$i_\omega^T: T(\xi,\omega) \to \Gamma$ admits a Cannon-Thurston map.
Finally, (after possibly passing to a further full measure subset)
 the (boundary values of the) Cannon-Thurston maps $\partial i_\omega^F: \partial F(1,\omega) \to {\partial G}$ and $\partial i_\omega^T: \partial T(\xi,\omega) \to {\partial G}$ are surjective.

body: [Theorem 4 (Large deviations of the density of the infinite cluster [39]) of arXiv:2404.19583, 'Catalan percolation'] For any p > poc, there exist ε, c > 0 such that, for any integer n ≥1 and finite set A ⊂Z+, we have that Pp (|{a ∈A : (a, a) →L−n}| ≤ε|A|) ≤e−c|A|. Strictly speaking, [39] proves this result with {(a, a) : a ∈A} replaced by an interval of the form {(a, 0) : a ∈{1, . . . , |A|}}, but the same proof works. As noted in [39], the proof applies to oriented percolation, in addition to the contact process.

[Ppn 194 (subsequential limits) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $N\to\infty$ with parameters satisfying Assumption~\ref{a:params}. Then the measures $\Q_N$, as defined by \eqref{e:pm.on.pm.over.paths.Gamma}, are tight. Moreover, for any subsequential limit $\Q$, if $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\Gamma,\Upsilon,\mathcal{E})\sim\mu$, then $\mathcal{E}\equiv0$. The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds. 

\begin{proof}
Write $\E_N$ for expectation with respect to $\Q_N$. We use Assumption~\ref{a:params} throughout. We will argue that $\Gamma^N$ and $\Upsilon^N$ are asymptotically equivalent to
	\[
	\bar{\Gamma}^N
	\equiv \Big(
	\bar{D}^{\RomI},
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},C^{\RomIII}, Q^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,,\quad
	\bar{\Upsilon}^N
	\equiv\Big( 
	Y^{\RomII},Y^{\RomIII},Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,.
	\]
For the purposes of this proof, it is more convenient to treat $\bar{D}^{\RomI}$ separately, and group together the remaining processes as
	\[
	\bar{f}^N
	\equiv
	\Big(
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},C^{\RomIII}, Q^{\Ising},
		Y^{\RomII},Y^{\RomIII},Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)
	\,.\]
By Proposition~\ref{p:drift.kolmogorov}, for $N$ large enough we have
	\beq
	\frac{\E_N[\|
		\bar{D}^{\RomI,N}(t) -
		\bar{D}^{\RomI,N}(s)
		\|^2]}{(t-s)^2}
	\le L^{O(1)}
	\le \mathscr{C}\,.
	\eeq
Meanwhile, by Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}, together with \eqref{e:Q.naive.kolmogorov} and the definition~\eqref{e:def.r} of $C^{\RomIII}$, for $N$ large enough we also have 
	\beq
	\frac{\E_N[\|\bar{f}^N(t)-
		\bar{f}^N
		(s)\|^4]}{(t-s)^2}
	\le L^{O(1)}
	\le \mathscr{C}
	\eeq
for $N$ large enough. We next address the error terms, using Assumption~\ref{a:params}. For any function $f$ on $[0,1]$
we use $\|f\|_\infty$ to denote the supremum norm.
\begin{itemize}
\item It follows by the bound \eqref{e:Q.I.small} from Proposition~\ref{p:qv.kolmogorov}, combined with Doob's $L^2$
martingale inequality, that we have
	\[
	\E_N\bigg[ \Big( \| Z^{\RomI}\|_\infty \Big)^2\bigg]
	\le 4 \E_N[Z^{\RomI}(1)^2]
	= 4\E_N Q^{\RomI}(1)
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta
	\ll1\,,
	\]
recalling that we assumed $\delta\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
\item It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep} that
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\Big\|D^\sigma-\bar{D}^\sigma\Big\|_\infty
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\eta}{\delta}\ll1\,,
	\]
recalling that we assumed $\eta\ll\delta$.
\item It follows by the bound \eqref{e:bar.D.notI.unif} from Proposition~\ref{p:drift.kolmogorov}
that 
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\E_N \| \bar{D}^\sigma\|_\infty
	\ll 1\,,
	\]
using that $\BUCKETS \ll N\delta$.
\item It follows by the bounds \eqref{e:Q.Ising.cross.small},
\eqref{e:qv.error.unif.bound}, and \eqref{e:tildeE.III.unif}
from Proposition~\ref{p:qv.kolmogorov}
that
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
		\E_N\|\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}\|_\infty
	+\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
		\E_N\|E^{\sigma,\tau}\|_\infty
	+ \E_N\|\tilde{E}^{\RomIII}\|_\infty\ll1\,,
	\]
using that $\eta\ll \delta\ll \delta^{1/2}$ and 
$\BUCKETS \ll N\delta \ll N$.
\end{itemize}
Altogether this proves that $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges in probability to the zero path. By passing to a subsequence we can assume that $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges almost surely to the zero path.
 
Now let $J_n(H)$
be the event that $\bar{D}^{\RomI}$
fails to be $\gamma$-H\"older with constant $H$ at dyadic scale $2^{-n}$, and similarly $F_n(H)$ for the process $\bar{f}$:
	\begin{align*}
	J_n(H)
	&\equiv
	\bigg\{
	\bigg\|
	\bar{D}^{\RomI}
	\bigg(\frac{i}{2^n}\bigg)
	-\bar{D}^{\RomI}
	\bigg(\frac{i-1}{2^n}\bigg)
	\bigg\|
	> \frac{H}{(2^n)^\gamma}
	\textup{ for some }
	1\le i\le 2^n
	\bigg\}\,,\\
	F_n(H)
	&\equiv 
	\bigg\{
	\bigg\|
	\bar{f}
	\bigg(\frac{i}{2^n}\bigg)
	-\bar{f}
	\bigg(\frac{i-1}{2^n}\bigg)
	\bigg\|
	> \frac{H}{(2^n)^\gamma}
	\textup{ for some }
	1\le i\le 2^n
	\bigg\}\,.
	\end{align*}
Finally, the moment estimates above give
\[
	\E_N\big[|Y^{\Ising}(0)|^2\big]\le \mathscr{C}\,.
\]
Let $I(H):=\{|Y^{\Ising}(0)|>H\}$. Then $\P_N(I(H))\le \mathscr{C}/H^2$.

[Proposition prop:no-reappearance-old-shapes of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Suppose a shape \(\sigma\) is first added to the ground set \(\mathcal{B}(Q_i)\) at
iteration level \(i\). Then \(\sigma\) does not appear in any subsequent update:
for every \(j\ge i\),
\[
    \sigma \notin \mathcal{B}(Q_{j+1})\setminus \mathcal{B}(Q_j).
\]
Consequently, the coefficient of \(\sigma\) remains unchanged throughout all
later iterations.

body:
[Lem 6 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of $\Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ from the statement of Proposition~\ref{p:convex.body.polytope.bound.new}. 
Recall $\cD_+$ from \eqref{e:cD-plus}.
Given any $\mu$, define 
    \[
        \cD_{+,\mu}(2) \equiv \Big\{
            \YY = (\BBb,\vvv,\UUu,\www) \in \cD_+ : (\mu, \www) \le 2
        \Big\}\,,
    \]
For $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$ and $\dot{\YY}, \ddot{\YY} \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[\Big|\Surplus(\dot{\YY};\lambda,\mu) - \Surplus(\ddot{\YY};\lambda,\mu)\Big|
        \le
        \frac{4\|\Delta\YY\|_2
            +  6\|\Delta\YY\|_2^{1/2}}{\iota \min\{1,\alpha\}}\,,
    \]
where we abbreviate $\Delta\YY \equiv \dot{\YY} - \ddot{\YY}$. 
That is, $\YY \mapsto \Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ is uniformly continuous in $\cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, uniformly in $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$.

\begin{proof}
We will bound separately the differences 
	\baln
	\Delta\Cost
	& \equiv\Cost(\dot{\YY};\lambda) - \Cost(\ddot{\YY};\lambda)\,,\\
	\Delta\Budget
	& \equiv\Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu) - \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)\,.
	\ealn
Note that for any $\xxxx \in \bbR^r$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \[
        \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|
        \le \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2}
        \le \|\xxxx\|_2\,.
    \]
    Thus, abbreviating $\Delta\YY
    \equiv(\Delta\vBBb,\Delta\vvvv,\Delta\vUUu,\Delta\vwww)
    \equiv\dot{\YY}-\ddot{\YY}$, we have
    \baln
        |\Delta\Cost|
        &\le \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg\{
            |\Delta\vBBb_j|
            + |\Delta\vUUu_j|
            + \Big|
            (\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+
            \Big| 
            + 2 \Big|(\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} 
            \Big|
        \bigg\} \\
        &\le \|\Delta\vBBb\|_2
        + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        + \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        	\Big\|_2 
        + 2\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}
        \Big\|_2\,,
    \ealn
    where the operations $x\mapsto x_+$ and $x\mapsto (x_+)^{1/2}$ are applied entrywise.
    Since $x\mapsto x_+$ is a contraction,
    \[
        \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+\|_2
        \le \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu}) - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})\|_2
        \le \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2 + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2\,.
    \]
Furthermore, since $|a^{1/2}-b^{1/2}| \le |a-b|^{1/2}$ for all $a,b\ge0$, for any vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b}\in[0,\infty)^r$ we can bound
	\[
	\Big(\|\vec{a}^{1/2}-\vec{b}^{1/2}\|_2\Big)^2
	=\sum_{j=1}^r \Big((a_j)^{1/2}-(b_j)^{1/2}\Big)^2
	\le \sum_{j=1}^r |a_j-b_j| = \|\vec{a}-\vec{b}\|_1\,.
	\]
Applying this estimate gives 
    \baln
        &\bigg(\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}\Big\|_2\bigg)^2
        \le 
        \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        \Big\|_1 \\
        &\qquad \le 
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_1
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_1 
            \le r^{1/2} \Big(
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        \Big)\,.
    \ealn
    Finally, crudely upper bounding 
$\|\Delta\vBBb\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2$ by $\|\Delta\YY\|_2$,
    we obtain
    \[
        |\Delta\Cost|
        \le 4 \|\Delta\YY\|_2
        + 2
        \Big(2 r^{1/2} \|\Delta\YY\|_2 \Big)^{1/2} \,.
    \]
This gives a continuity estimate for the $\Cost$ function.

We next turn to the $\Budget$ function.
    For all $\YY  \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[
        0\le \alpha \cdot \Budget(\YY;\mu) \le (\mu,\vwww) \le 2\,,
    \]
    where the intermediate step is by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
    Therefore,
    \baln
        \alpha |\Delta\Budget| 
        &= \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2} + 
        \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}\Big| 
        \cdot 
        \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}

Consequently freely strongly unimodal real probability laws are exactly point masses. No moment assumption is required.
mu is a Borel probability measure on R
Standard unimodality permits an atom at the mode and a monotone density on either side

[Prop 12 of arXiv:2512.02538, 'On the spectral geometry of Liouville quantum gravity'] There a.s. exists a family $(\mathbf{p}_t (\cdot ,\cdot))_{t\ge 0}$ of (jointly in all three arguments) measurable functions such that for all $t \ge 0$, for all $x \in \Sigma$,
 $$\mathbf{P}_t f(x) = \int_\Sigma \mathbf{p}_t (x,y) f(y) \mu_{\ph} (\dd y).$$ This family of functions $\mathbf{p}_t (x,y)$ (a priori only defined for all $t\ge 0$, for all $x\in \Sigma$ and $\mu_\ph-$almost every $y \in \Sigma$ is called the \textbf{Liouville heat kernel} and satisfies the following properties: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Nonnegativity) For all $t \ge 0$, for all $x \in \Sigma$ and for $\mu_\ph-$almost every $y\in \Sigma$, $\mathbf{p}_t (x,y) \ge 0$. 
\item (Symmetry) For all $t \ge 0$, for all $x,  y \in \Sigma$, $\mathbf{p}_t (x,y) = \mathbf{p}_t (y,x) $.
\item (Semigroup) For all $s, t \ge 0$, for all $x \in \Sigma$ and for $\mu_\ph-$almost every $y \in \Sigma$, $\mathbf{p}_{t+s} (x, y) = \int_\Sigma \mathbf{p}_t(x,z) \mathbf{p}_t(z,y) \mu_\ph(\dd z)$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop gbf of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'] Consider a two-variable process $(G_{s,t})_{-\infty <s\le t<\infty}$ with $s,t\in \Bbb Q$, defined on some complete probability space, and satisfying 
\begin{enumerate}
        \item $G_{s_j,t_j}$ are independent if $(s_j,t_j)$ are disjoint intervals.

        \item $G_{s,t}G_{t,u}= G_{s,u}$ whenever $s<t<u$.

        \item For $n=1,2,3,4,5,6$, we have that $\Bbb E\big[ G_{s,t}^n \big] = e^{\frac{n^2}2(t-s)}.$
\end{enumerate}
These three conditions uniquely determine the finite-dimensional distributions of the process $(G_{s,t})_{s<t}$ as being the same as those of $(e^{B(t)-B(s)})_{s<t}$  for a standard Brownian motion $B$, and moreover $B$ can be defined on the same space so that the relation holds pathwise on $\Bbb Q^2$.

body: [Theorem Informal; see Theorems \ref{thm:loc_lim}, \ref{thm:extinct_1dep}, \ref{thm:giants_MCMs} and \ref{thm:dist} in the following sections of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] Consider a sequence of uniformly sampled random multipartite graphs of growing sizes, with given inter and intra partition degree sequences, and where each vertex partition has a positive proportion of vertices. Under some standard regularity assumptions on the degree sequences, the local limit of the graph sequence exists as a branching process tree. Without any assumption on the irreducibility of the local limit, there is a simple (new) criterion that checks whether the limiting tree survives, and when it does survive, is tailored to extract linear sized connected components in the pre-limit via exploration processes. Finally, in the case of survival, the typical distance is of logarithmic order in probability. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\begin{align}

body:
[Lemma delta*-gl-cc of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $\alpha\colon G\to G'$ be any homomorphism of compact Lie groups. Then the Beck--Chevalley map $\textup{BC}_!\colon\textbf{\textup{L}}\alpha_!\circ\textup{diag}\to\textup{diag}\circ\textbf{\textup{L}}\alpha_!$ is an equivalence.    
    \begin{proof}
        As a consequence of Lemma~(lemma:delta*-cc of the paper), both source and target of $\textup{BC}_!$ are cocontinuous functors ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-lvl}\to{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G'$-gl}$. In light of the presheaf description of ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-lvl}$ from Proposition~(prop:mySplev-unpar-presh of the paper), it will therefore suffice to show that the Beck--Chevalley map is an equivalence on the objects of the subcategory ${\mathfrak R\kern-.5pt\mathfrak e\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p\kern-.5pt\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_G$. It is clear that the Beck--Chevalley map is an equivalence for the zero object; every other object of ${\mathfrak R\kern-.5pt\mathfrak e\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p\kern-.5pt\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_G$ is then of the form $X\coloneqq\textbf{\textup{L}}\varphi_!\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)$ for some $\varphi\colon H\to G$ and some $H$-representation $V$. As Beck--Chevalley maps compose, we see that the map $\textup{BC}_!\colon\textbf{\textup{L}}\alpha_!\,\textup{diag}(X)\to\textup{diag}\,\textbf{\textup{L}}\alpha_!(X)$ in question is an equivalence provided that both the Beck--Chevalley maps
            $\textbf{\textup{L}}(\varphi\alpha)_!\,\textup{diag}(\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-))\to\textup{diag}\,\textbf{\textup{L}}(\varphi\alpha)_!\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)$
           and
            $\textbf{\textup{L}}\varphi_!\,\textup{diag}(\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-))\to\textup{diag}\,\textbf{\textup{L}}\varphi_!\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)$
        are so. In other words, up to replacing $\alpha$ and $G$, it suffices to treat the case where $X=\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)$ for some $G$-representation $V$.
        
        Fix a faithful $G$-representation $U$, so that the collapse map $\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,-)_+\smashp\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\to\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)$ is a cofibrant replacement of $X$. Plugging in the definitions, the Beck--Chevalley condition then amounts to saying that for some (hence any) cofibrant replacement $f\colon Y\to\textup{diag}(\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,-)_+\smashp\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-))$ in $\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ the induced map 
        \begin{equation}
            \alpha_!Y\to\alpha_!\,\textup{diag}\big(\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,-)_+\smashp\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\big)=\textup{diag}\,\alpha_!\big(\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,-)_+\smashp\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\big)
        \end{equation} 
        is a $G'$-global weak equivalence. We may choose the cofibrant replacement already in the $G$-global level model structure, and we will show that in this case $((eq:BC-unravelled of the paper))$ is even a $G'$-global \emph{level} weak equivalence, i.e.\ that for every inner product space $W$ the $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(W),G}$-weak equivalence $f(W)\colon Y(W)\to\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,W)_+\smashp\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,W)$ is sent by $\alpha_!$ to a $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(W),G'}$-weak equivalence. By Proposition~(prop:global-lvl-GSp of the paper), $Y(W)$ is $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(W),G}$-cofibrant, as is $\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,W)_+\smashp\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,W)$ by Lemma~(lemma:smash-lQ of the paper). Thus, the claim follows from Example~(ex:graph-restr-rQ of the paper).
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma delta*-gl-cc of arXiv:2608.28504

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.27569, 'Laplace and Dolbeault operators on Sasakian manifolds'] Let $(M^{2n+1},g,\xi)$ be a compact Sasakian manifold. Let $f$ be an eigenfunction of the ${\overline\partial}$-Laplacian associated with an eigenvalue $q$ of the Lie derivative, that is, $\Delta_{\overline\partial} f=\lambda f$ and  $\xi(f)=iqf$. Let $m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. 
Then there exist four linear combinations of the forms
$\alpha_m:=L^mf$, $\eta\wedge \overline\partial^*\alpha_m$, 
$\eta\wedge \partial^*\alpha_m$, and 
$\overline\partial\partial\alpha_{m-1}$ that are
eigenforms of degree $2m$ of the Hodge Laplacian corresponding 
to eigenvalues
$$\Theta_0(q,\lambda)=2\lambda-4m^2+4mn+2nq+q^2,$$
and/or 
$$\Theta_\pm(q,\lambda)=2\lambda-4m^2+4mn+4m+2nq-2n+q^2\pm 2\sqrt{2\lambda+(n+q)^2}.$$
When all of the forms $\overline\partial^*\alpha_m$, 
$\eta\wedge \partial^*\alpha_m$, and 
$\overline\partial\partial\alpha_{m-1}$ are nonzero, 
$\Theta_0(q,\lambda)$ has multiplicity two, and 
each $\Theta_\pm(q,\lambda)$ has multiplicity one. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.27569

[Proposition prop:equivariant-families of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] The set $Y_P$ is a Borel cross-section, and
\[
    (Y_P)_{[t,z]}=P_z-t,
    \qquad
    \kappa_{Y_P}([t,z])=\delta_{P_z-t}.
\]
If the family $(P_z)_{z\in Z}$ is uniformly Delone, then $Y_P$ is
a Delone cross-section and
\[
    \bigl(
        \operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}^{\mathbb R^d}(Z),
        \mu_{\Gamma,Z},
        Y_P
    \bigr)
\]
is a cross-section system.

Suppose, moreover, that there is a $\Gamma$-invariant conull
Borel set $Z_0\subset Z$ such that
\[
    P_{z'}=P_z-u
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    u\in\Gamma
    \ \text{ and }\
    z'=u.z
\]
for all $z,z'\in Z_0$ and $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Then $Y_P$ is
generating.

[Lemma 35 (Uniform local chain non-degeneracy) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Let $K_0\subset\mathsf O_0$, where $K_0$ is compact and $\mathsf O_0$ is an
open set with compact closure satisfying
$\overline{\mathsf O_0}\subset\mathsf O$, and choose the cutoff maps in
Lemma~\ref{lem:chain-compatible-cutoffs} equal to the identity near
$\overline{\mathsf O_0}$.  For $z\in K_0$, set
\[
    \widetilde A^\delta(z)=A_3^\delta(z)
    =
    \operatorname{diag}\left(
        S_r,\,
        -J_{x^1}B_2^{\delta,\mathsf O}(z)S_r,\,
        J_{x^2}B_3^{\delta,\mathsf O}(z)
        J_{x^1}B_2^{\delta,\mathsf O}(z)S_r
    \right).
\]
For a square matrix $M$, write
$s_{\min}(M):=\inf_{|v|=1}|Mv|=\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(MM^\top)}$ for its
smallest singular value.  Then
\begin{equation}
    \inf_{\substack{0\le\delta\le1\\z\in K_0}}
    s_{\min}\left(A_3^\delta(z)\right)>0,
\end{equation}
and equivalently,
\begin{equation}
    \inf_{\substack{0\le\delta\le1\\z\in K_0}}
    \lambda_{\min}\left(A_3^\delta(z)A_3^\delta(z)^\top\right)>0.
\end{equation}
That is,
\[
    \sup_{\substack{0\le\delta\le1\\z\in K_0}}
    \left(
        \left\|\widetilde A^\delta(z)\right\|
        +\left\|\left(\widetilde A^\delta(z)\right)^{-1}\right\|
    \right)<\infty .
\]
The same conclusion holds for the adjoint cutoff family.

body: Let G be a d-regular graph on n vertices with adjacency matrix eigenvalues d = lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n, and let lambda = max(|lambda_2|, |lambda_n|). For subsets S, T of the vertex set, let e(S,T) = sum_{i in S, j in T} A_{ij}, where A is the adjacency matrix. Then |e(S,T) - d|S||T|/n| <= lambda sqrt(|S||T|). [standard, e.g. Hoory, Linial and Wigderson, Expander Graphs and Their Applications]
title: Expander Mixing Lemma

body: Let X_n be an n by n random matrix whose entries are independent and identically distributed standard complex Gaussian random variables, meaning each entry has independent real and imaginary parts distributed N(0, 1/2), so that E[|X_{jk}|^2] = 1. Let M_n = X_n / sqrt(n). Then, almost surely, the empirical spectral distribution of the eigenvalues of M_n converges weakly, as n tends to infinity, to the uniform probability distribution on the unit disk {z in C : |z| <= 1}. [Ginibre (1965), Mehta; see Bai and Silverstein, Spectral Analysis of Large Dimensional Random Matrices]
title: Circular Law for the Complex Ginibre Ensemble

[Dfn 231 (row-spliced matrix) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $S\subseteq [M]$ and matrices $\bG, \hbG \in \R^{M\times N}$ with rows $(\bg^a : a\in [M])$ and $(\hat\bg^a : a\in [M])$, let $\tbG = \tbG(\bG,\hbG;S) \in \R^{M\times N}$ be the matrix with rows $(\tbg^a : a\in [M])$, where

		\tbg^a = \begin{cases}
			\bg^a & a \not\in S\,, \\
			\hat\bg^a & a\in S\,.
		\end{cases}
	\]

[Lemma 56 (No mass at chaos degree infinity) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $\mathcal U$ be a free ultrafilter and put
\[
 \cH_q=(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}.
\]
Here the factorial normalization has already been absorbed into
$x_{n,a,q}=\sqrt{q!}\,f_{n,a,q}$.
All tensor norms below are the ordinary tensor norms of these scaled coordinates.  The
product transported by the primitive--Fock unitary is the normalized product
\begin{equation}
 u\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}v
 =
 \sqrt{\frac{q!}{p!(q-p)!}}\,
 \Sym(u\otimes v),
 \qquad
 u\in H^{\odot p},\quad v\in H^{\odot(q-p)}.
 
\end{equation}
The raw contractions of Section~\ref{all:sec:infinite-feedback} are ordinary
Hilbert tensor contractions of the scaled coordinates.  The dictionary
between the two normalisations used in this paper is therefore
\[
 \underbrace{(H_n^{\odot q},q!\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}}
 _{\text{Parts II--IV, kernels }f_{n,a,q}}
 \;\xrightarrow{\ f\,\mapsto\,x=\sqrt{q!}f\ }\;
 \underbrace{(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}}
 _{\text{Parts V--VI, coordinates }x_{n,a,q}},
\]
an isometry which carries $\wtensor$ to $\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}$ and
multiplies an $s$-fold contraction of a weight-$p$ by a weight-$q$ coordinate
by $\sqrt{p!\,q!/(p+q-2s)!}$.  No statement below depends on the choice, but
all displayed constants refer to the scaled coordinates.
Under $\mathrm{QT}_2$, the represented coordinates
$x_{a,q}=[x_{n,a,q}]_{\mathcal U}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{a,q}\norm{x_{a,q}}_{\cH_q}^2
 =
 \lim_{\mathcal U}\sum_{a,q}\norm{x_{n,a,q}}^2.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently the represented packet belongs to
$\bigoplus_{q\ge1}\cH_q$ and has no additional component at an infinite chaos grade.

[Definition 13 (Boundary states) of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] A \emph{linear forest} is an acyclic graph whose vertices have degree at
most two.  A \emph{boundary forest} in \(F_m\) is a nonempty edge
subgraph \(\Gamma\subset F_m\) such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \(\Gamma\) is a linear forest;
\item every vertex of degree one belongs to \(\partial F_m\);
\item every connected component contains at least one edge.
\end{enumerate}
Thus every component is a self-avoiding path with two distinct endpoints
in \(\partial F_m\).

An \emph{abstract boundary forest} is a nonempty linear forest whose
vertex set is contained in \(V_0\) and which has no isolated vertices;
equivalently, each connected component is a path containing at least one
edge.  Let \(\cS\) be the finite set of all such abstract boundary
forests.  Thus an element \(\sigma\in\cS\) may consist of one path or of
several vertex-disjoint paths; it records only a possible finite
combination of boundary connections, not an actual walk in \(F_m\).

To pass from the actual boundary forest \(\Gamma\subset F_m\) to its
abstract boundary pattern, consider each component of \(\Gamma\) in
\(F_m\).  List the boundary vertices in the order in which the path meets
them.  Keep only these listed vertices, replace each portion
between two consecutive listed vertices by one abstract edge, and relabel the
retained vertices by \(\iota_m^{-1}\).  This compression operation is
called taking the \emph{boundary trace}.  The resulting nonempty linear
forest on \(V_0\), hence an element of \(\cS\), is the \emph{boundary
state} of \(\Gamma\), denoted by \(\operatorname{tr}_m(\Gamma)\).  It
records which boundary vertices are visited and how consecutive visits
are connected along each path; it does not record the internal vertices
or the lengths of the individual portions.

For \(\sigma\in\cS\), put
\[
  \cC_m(\sigma)
  =
  \{\Gamma\subset F_m:
    \Gamma\text{ is a boundary forest and }
    \operatorname{tr}_m(\Gamma)=\sigma\},
\]
and, for \(\beta\ge0\), define
\begin{equation}
  Z_m^\sigma(\beta)
  =
  \sum_{\Gamma\in\cC_m(\sigma)}
  e^{-\beta\#E(\Gamma)},
  \qquad
  \bZ_m(\beta)
  =
  \bigl(Z_m^\sigma(\beta)\bigr)_{\sigma\in\cS}.
  
\end{equation}
We call \(\bZ_m(\beta)\) the \emph{boundary-state partition vector}.
We adjoin the \emph{empty state} \(\varnothing\) and set
\(Z_m^\varnothing(\beta)=1\).
title: Boundary states

[Lem hypersubtreelem of arXiv:2411.00629, '\Large Transformation of Stochastic Recursions and Critical Phenomena in the Analysis of t'] Let $X_0=\delta$ and let $$M_n(t) =|\{v\in\stackrel{o}{V}(t): |v|=n\}|,$$ 
and
$$N_n(t) = |\{v\in \partial V(t): |v|\le n\}|.$$
Then, the Picard ground state iteration at generation $n$ is given by
\begin{equation}
X_n(t) = u_0^{N_n(t)}\delta^{M_n(t)}.
\end{equation}
On the event $[S<t]$ one has:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $u_0>1, \delta\in[0,1)$ implies
$X_n(t)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.
\item[(ii)] 
$u_0\in(0,1), \delta>1$ implies
$X_n(t)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
\end{enumerate}

[Definition MTP2-SMRR2 of arXiv:2507.01406, '{\Large On Iterated Lorenz Curves with Applications: The Multivariate Case }'] A strictly positive density $l:[0,1]^{d}\rightarrow
(0,\infty )$ is multivariate totally positive of order $2$ ($MTP_{2}$) if 
\begin{equation}
l(x\wedge y)\,l(x\vee y)\ \geq \ l(x)\,l(y),\qquad x,y\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d},

\end{equation}
where $\wedge ,\vee $ denote coordinatewise minimum and maximum. It is 
\textit{multivariate reverse regular of order }$2$ ($MRR_{2}$) if the
reverse inequality holds: 
\begin{equation}
l(x\wedge y)\,l(x\vee y)\ \leq \ l(x)\,l(y),\qquad x,y\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d}.

\end{equation}
We say that $l$ is strictly $MRR_{2}$ ($SMRR_{2}$) if for every compact set $
K\subset (0,1)^{d}$ there exists a set of full \textit{Lebesgue measure} in $
K\times K$ on which ((2000b of the paper)) holds with strict inequality whenever $x$
and $y$ are incomparable (i.e.\ neither $x\leq y$ nor $y\leq x$
coordinatewise). Equivalently (and more concretely), on each $K\subset
(0,1)^{d}$ on which $l$ is bounded away from $0$, ((2000b of the paper)) is strict
for all incomparable $x,y\in K$.

\]

Result: rho^D(dx) = E[Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D)] where Z^D is the (random) extremal measure; conformal covariance of Z^D gives rho^{f(D)}(f(x)) |f'(x)|^2 = E[ r_D(x)^2 |f'(x)|^{2} ... ] only for the intensity E Z^D(dx) = c r_D(x)^2 dx, not for the ratio, because the normalisation Z^D(D) is not covariant. On the unit disk, rotation invariance gives rho^D radial; a PDE characterisation would need the joint law of (Z^D(dx), Z^D(D)), which is the object Problem 16.1 asks for. Computed check: the naive guess rho^D proportional to r_D(x)^2 fails to integrate to the correct mixture (it equals E Z^D(dx)/E Z^D(D), which is a different density unless Z^D(D) is a.s. constant, which it is not). Obstruction: rho^D is a ratio expectation; without the law of the total mass Z^D(D) no closed form or PDE is available.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0004-explicit-density-of-the-position-of-the-dgff-maximum
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

body:
[Theorem thm:stab_particle of arXiv:2605.20697, 'Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for \\ Second-Order Consensus-Based Optimization'] Let \(f\) satisfy (assumption:bounded,assumption:lip of the paper). 
Let \(q>1/2\), set \(p_\ast:=\max\{8,8q\}\), and let
\(\rho_0,\tilde{\rho}_0\in\mathcal P_{p_\ast}(\mathbf R^{2d})\).
Consider two copies \((X_t^j,V_t^j)_{j=1}^J\) and
\((\tilde X_t^j,\tilde V_t^j)_{j=1}^J\) of the particle system
(equation eq: k-cbo of the paper), driven by the same Brownian motions \((W_t^j)_{j=1}^J\), with
i.i.d.\ initial data sampled respectively from \(\rho_0\) and \(\tilde\rho_0\).
Assume (assump:stab of the paper).

Then there exist constants \(C_{\mathrm{Stab},1},C_{\mathrm{Stab},2}>0\),
independent of \(J\) and \(t\), such that for all \(t\geqslant0\),
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{E}\!\left[
        \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J
        \Bigl(
            |X_t^j-\tilde X_t^j|^2
            +
            |V_t^j-\tilde V_t^j|^2
        \Bigr)
    \right]
    \leqslant
    C_{\mathrm{Stab},1}
    \mathbf{E}\!\left[
        \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J
        \Bigl(
            |X_0^j-\tilde X_0^j|^2
            +
            |V_0^j-\tilde V_0^j|^2
        \Bigr)
    \right]
    +
    \frac{C_{\mathrm{Stab},2}}{J^q}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Almost uniform-in-time stability

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2506.16259, 'Two-dimensional Rademacher walk'] Consider a simple random walk $T_n=(X_n,Y_n)$ on $\Z^2$ with steps $\pm\be_1,\pm\be_2$ and $T_0=(x_0,y_0)$. Let $\tau_0=\inf\{n:\ T_n=\mathbf{0}\}$. Then there exists a universal constant $\alpha>0$ such that
$$
\P(\tau_0\le r^3)\ge \alpha, \qquad\text{where }r=\norm{(x_0,y_0)}.
$$

body:
[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.19832, 'Sharp Convex Concentration for Symmetric Random Tensors with Subgaussian Coordinates'] Suppose that \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\) are independent and that the pairs
$(X_i,Y_i)$ are generated successively in the form
\[
 (X_i,Y_i)=F_i(Y_{<i},\xi_i),
\]
where, for every admissible value of $Y_{<i}$, the first marginal of the
resulting conditional law is $\mu_i$. Put
\[
 Z_i=\abs{X_i-Y_i},\qquad
 g_i=\E(Z_i\mid X_i,Y_{<i}),\qquad
 \widetilde g_i=\E(Z_i\mid Y_{\le i}).
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 \E(Z_i\mid X)&=\E(g_i\mid X),
 \\
 \E(Z_i\mid Y)&=\widetilde g_i.
 
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \E\big[\E(Z_i\mid X)^2\big]&\le\E g_i^2,
 \\
 \E\big[\E(Z_i\mid Y)^2\big]&=\E\widetilde g_i^2.
 
\end{align}

body:
Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 7.27 (Chapter 7, p. 259) asks whether, over arc-transitive graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau* = O(n log n), tau2 = O(n) and tau*/(2 tau0) = 1 + o(1). Our result (id P0208, 2026-09-08): all three claims are FALSE. The counterexample is the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] for odd m >= 5 - the m-cycle with every vertex split into two non-adjacent twins - which is connected, 4-regular, arc-transitive and not a cycle, on n = 2m vertices. With g(j) = j(m-j) + m the mean hitting time at cycle-distance j and 2m the twin hitting time: tau* = 2*floor(m^2/4) + 2m ~ n^2/8 (quadratic, not O(n log n)); tau2 = 1/(1 - cos(2 pi/m)) ~ n^2/(8 pi^2), because A(C_m[Kbar_2]) = A(C_m) tensor J_2 so the relaxation time is the m-cycle's own; and tau*/(2 tau0) tends to 3/2, not 1 + o(1). Verification, as the source words it: exact hitting times by linear algebra at m = 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21 (all five formulas exact at every size); arc-transitivity checked mechanically at m = 5, 7, 9 (the group generated by the rotation, one reflection and one fibre swap has order 2^m * 2m and its orbit of one arc is all 8m arcs); and a Lean file P0208.lean with nine theorems, no sorry, axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound only. Not formalised: uniqueness of the solution of (I-P)h = 1 and the tensor eigenvalue computation, both standard and checked numerically. Prior art not cleared.

[Lemma 12 (Quantile representation of \(W_1\) on the real line) of arXiv:2608.22227, '\fontsize{18pt}{20pt}\selectfont \bf Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Q'] Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb R\) with finite first
moments. Let $F_\mu(x)\coloneqq \mu((-\infty,x])$, and $F_\nu(x)\coloneqq \nu((-\infty,x])$ be their CDFs, and define their left-continuous generalized inverses by $F_\mu^{-1}(u)\coloneqq \inf\{x\in\mathbb R:F_\mu(x)\ge u\}$, $F_\nu^{-1}(u)\coloneqq \inf\{x\in\mathbb R:F_\nu(x)\ge u\}$, for all $u\in(0,1)$. Equivalently, \(F_\mu^{-1}(u)=Q_u(\mu)\) and
\(F_\nu^{-1}(u)=Q_u(\nu)\). Then $W_1(\mu,\nu)
=
\int_0^1
\left|
F_\mu^{-1}(u)-F_\nu^{-1}(u)
\right|\,du
=
\int_0^1
\left|
Q_u(\mu)-Q_u(\nu)
\right|\,du$.

body:
Let X be a compact metric space, F a closed subset of X x X, and U a closed subset with F(U) contained in the interior of U relative to X. For a set C, F(C) consists of all targets of edges whose source lies in C, and F^(-1)(C) is the image under the inverse relation. Put A=intersection over n>=0 of F^n(U) and B=intersection over n>=0 of F^(-n)(X minus interior(U)). Then every chain-recurrent point of F belongs to A union B. Here a point is chain recurrent if for every epsilon>0 a finite chain of F-edges and jumps of size less than epsilon returns it to itself. F need not be a single-valued map or invertible. A is the attractor associated to the inward set U and B its dual repeller.

closed relation F subset X x X
closed inward set U: F(U) subset int_X(U)
relation images and inverse images as explicitly defined

[Corollary 53 of arXiv:2606.15425, 'Well-posedness of stochastic parabolic equations with gradient nonlinearities and applicat'] Let $G, H$ satisfy the conditions of Proposition \ref{prop:randomcommutator}, where $G$ is $\mathcal F_t$-progressive and $H$ is $\mathcal F^\sigma_t$-progressive. Again, let $\sigma$ be a stopping time. Then the progressively measurable process 
\begin{equation} 
P(t-t \wedge \sigma)\int_0^{t \wedge \sigma}P(t\wedge \sigma-s) G_s \d {W}_s + \mathds{1}_{t \geq \sigma}\int_0^{(t-\sigma)_+} P((t-\sigma)_+ -s)H_s \d \widetilde {W}_s
\end{equation} 
is a modification of 
$$\int_0^t P(t-s)\left(\mathds1_{\{s \leq \sigma\}}G_s + \mathds1_{\{s \geq \sigma\}}H_{(s-\sigma)_+}\right) \d {W}_s.
$$ 
In particular, continuous modifications of these processes are indistinguishable.

body:
[Lemma gradient TAP of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Recall $\mathrm{TAP}$ from (equation def:TAPmu of the paper) and $k_\zeta$ from~(equation def:kqm of the paper).
		Fix $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$ and set $q=\frac{1}{N}\Vert \mathbf{m}\Vert^2$.
		Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[q,1]$. Then for every $i\in[N]$:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item (\emph{Exact gradient at the minimizer}) If $\zeta_\mathbf{m}$ is the minimizer in Definition~(def:zetam of the paper), then
			\begin{equation}
				\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})})=-\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta_\mathbf{m}}(q,m_i).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item (\emph{Exact defect formula and explicit boundary stability}) One has
			\begin{equation}
				-N\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)
				=
				k_\zeta(q,m_i)-m_i\,\xi''(q)\,\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}},
			\end{equation}
			where $\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}}$ is defined in (equation eq:def-Delta of the paper).
			Consequently, if
			\[
			\max_{j\in[N]}|m_j|\le 1-\delta
			\qquad\text{for some }\delta\in(0,1),
			\]
			and
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0,
			\]
			then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)<\infty$ such that
			\begin{equation}
				\Bigl|\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)+\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta}(q,m_i)\Bigr|
				\le \frac{C}{N\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\zeta).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:technical extended version of arXiv:2512.18435, 'Indistinguishability for recurrent clusters'] Let $\mathscr A$ be a component property and let $(G,\eta,o)$ be a random rooted network.
        Let $(v_n)$ be a stationary sequence started at $v_0=o$ on $(G,\eta,o)$, meaning that $(G,\eta,v_n)$ has the same distribution as $(G,\eta,o)$, and such that $v_n\in\mathcal P_{G,\eta}(o)$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. It can depend on $(G,\eta,o)$ and additional randomness.
    Furthermore, let $S_{G,\eta,o}$ be a $(G,\eta,o)$-measurable subset of $G$ and $\psi$ a random increasing function $\mathbb N\longrightarrow \mathbb N$ such that, almost surely:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac n{\psi(n)} >0$,
        \item $S$ is ``smallish'' for $(v_{\psi(n)})$, in the following sense, a relaxed version of being ``small'' in (lem:technical lemma for indis of the paper): for every $R\in\mathbb N$, $\limsup_{N\to\infty} \big|\big\{1\leq n\leq N : B(v_{\psi(n)},R) \cap S \not= \emptyset \big\}\big|/N = 0$.
    \end{itemize}

        Suppose there are $(G',\eta',o')$, $(v'_n)$, $S'_{G',\eta',o'}$ and $\psi':\mathbb N\longrightarrow\mathbb N$ 
         with all the same properties assumed in the previous paragraph for $(G,\eta,o)$, $(v_n)$, $S_{G,\eta,o}$ and $\psi$,
        and that they are coupled in such a way that on some event $E_{\rm co}$, for every $n\in\mathbb N$, the component $K$ of $v_{\psi(n)}$ in $G\setminus S_{G,\eta,o}$ and the component $K'$ of $v'_{\psi'(n)}$ in $G'\setminus S'_{G',\eta',o'}$ are isomorphic rooted networks with roots $v_{\psi(n)}$ and $v'_{\psi'(n)}$ and environments $\eta$ and $\eta'$.
    
    Then, conditionally on $E_{\rm co}$, up to probability zero events, $(G,\eta,o)\in\mathscr A$ if and only if $(G',\eta',o')\in\mathscr A$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $H=\sum_{j=1}^rH_j$, with
$H_j\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$, and let $H_t$ be obtained
from the thinning coupling when $\mathsf{S}=\mathsf{P}$ and from the
coordinate-refresh coupling when $\mathsf{S}=\mathsf{R}$.  Without
any lattice assumption,
\noi
\begin{align}

 =\lim_{t\downarrow0}

If $H$ satisfies the lattice condition \eqref{cond_La} with shift
$\theta>0$, then $\cJ_r(H)\geq0$.

If $F\in\cC_r^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$ and
$B=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}B_j$, with
$B_j\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$, then
\noi
\begin{align}

 \leq84\bigl(1+\norm{F}_4+\eps\bigr)^3\eps,
 
\end{align}
where
$\eps:=\sum_{1\leq j<r}\norm{B_j}_4$.

Assume that a nonnegative quantity $\rho(F)$ satisfies
\eqref{top_rho}, and put
$\mathfrak d(F):=\abs{\cD(F)}+\rho(F)$ as in
\eqref{frak_d}.  Then, without any lattice assumption,
\noi
\begin{align}

\begin{align}

\end{align}

In the Poisson setting, one has the sharper estimates
\noi
\begin{align}
 \cJ_r(F)
 &\leq4\sqrt{m_2(F)\cP(F)}+8\cP(F).
 
\end{align}

body: A sequence (x_n) in a metric space (X, d) is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is an index N such that d(x_m, x_n) < epsilon for all m, n >= N. The metric space (X, d) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, but not conversely in general: the rationals with the usual distance are not complete, while the real line R and Euclidean space R^n are complete. A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete, and a complete subspace of any metric space is closed in it.
title: Complete metric space

[Lemma of arXiv:2607.18011, 'From local giants to locality in long-range percolation'] \thlabel{lem:kernel_example}
    Let $G$ be a transitive graph of polynomial growth with $d \in \mathbf{N}$ and let $J :V \times V \to \mathbf{R}_+$ be the transitive kernel given by $J(x,y) = d_G(x,y)^{- d \alpha}$ for $\alpha > 0$.
    
    Let $(G_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ be a sequence of transitive graphs converging to $G$, let $(s_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ be a sequence converging to $d \alpha$, and let $(J_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ be the sequence of kernels $J : V_n \times V_n \to \mathbf{R}_+$ given by $J_n(x,y) = d_{G_n}(x,y)^{- s_n}$. 
    
    Then $(G_n,J_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ converges locally to $(G,J)$. Further, if $\alpha>1$, then the kernels $(J_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ are uniformly integrable.
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2607.18011, 'From local giants to locality in long-range percolation'

body: Let (mu_n) be a sequence of probability measures on R with characteristic functions phi_n(t) = integral of exp(i t x) d mu_n(x). If phi_n(t) converges pointwise, for every real t, to a limit phi(t) that is continuous at t = 0, then phi is the characteristic function of a probability measure mu, and mu_n converges weakly to mu. Conversely, if mu_n converges weakly to a probability measure mu, then phi_n converges to the characteristic function of mu, uniformly on compact sets. [Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples]
title: Levy's Continuity Theorem

multiplicity.

[Thm smasympexGOEGSE of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] There exist universal constants $C,c>0$, and a compactly supported 
distribution $\nu_k$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, such that the following 
hold. Fix any bounded $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, and define
$$
	f(\theta):= h(K\cos\theta)
	\qquad\text{with}\qquad
	K := (Cr)^{q_0}\|X_{\rm F}\|.
$$
Then for every $m, N\in \mathbb{N}$ with $m\le\frac{N}{2}$, we have
\begin{multline*}
       \left| \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}} h(X^N)]
	- \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} \frac{\nu_k(h)}{N^k} \right| 
	~\vee~
       \left| \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}} h(Y^N)]
	- \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} \frac{\nu_k(h)}{(-2N)^k} \right| 
\\
       \le
	\frac{(Cq_0)^{2m}}{m! N^m} \|f^{(2m+1)}\|_{[0, 2\pi]} 
	+
	Cre^{-cN}\big(\sobnorm{h}{0}{(-\infty,\infty)}
		+ \sobnorm{f^{(1)}}{0}{[0, 2\pi]} \big).
\end{multline*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Smooth asymptotic expansion for GOE/GSE

[Theorem thm:loclim of arXiv:2512.17747, 'On exponentially height-penalized random trees'] Let $\mu=\mu_n$ be a sequence admitting a limit $\alpha \in [0,\infty)$.
Let $\mathbf{T}_n$ be a $\mu$-height-biased tree of size $n$. If $\alpha>0$, then the random rooted tree $(\mathbf{T}_{n},\varnothing)$ converges locally to the infinite \emph{Poisson tree} of parameter $\alpha$ as defined in [abraham2020very]. Otherwise, if $\alpha=0$, equivalently $\mu=o(1)$, then the random rooted tree $(\mathbf{T}_{n},\varnothing)$ converges locally to Kesten's tree as defined in [kesten1986subdiffusive]. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 20 (Theorem~\ref{thm:micro}-(\ref{thm:sl})) of arXiv:2607.28865, 'First-Passage Percolation on Spread-out line graphs: Microscopic Regime'] Suppose Assumption~\textup{A.\ref{ass:A2}} holds and $0<\ga:=\gc\lc<2$.
Let $m_n:=\left\lfloor n/\mu_{\sfP} \right\rfloor$ and define
\begin{align}
    a_n :=\inf\left\{x>0:m_n\pr(\sfT_1>x)\le1\right\},
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    b_n :=m_n\,\E\left[\sfT_1\ind_{\{\sfT_1\le a_n\}}\right],
\end{align}
where $\sfT$ is the renewal-block passage time defined in~\eqref{eq:block-variable-notation}.
Then
\begin{align*}
    \frac1{a_n}\cdot (T_n-b_n)
    \Longrightarrow
    Z_\ga,
\end{align*}
where $Z_\ga$ is the totally right-skewed $\ga$-stable random variable characterized by
\begin{align}
    \E\left[e^{itZ_\ga}\right]
    =
    \exp\left(
        \int_0^\infty
        \left(
            e^{itx} - 1 - itx\ind_{\{x\le1\}}
        \right)
        \ga x^{-\ga-1}\,dx
    \right),
    \quad
    t\in\dR.
\end{align}
title: Theorem~\ref{thm:micro}-(\ref{thm:sl})

[Definition Doubling metric spaces of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] A metric space $(X,\rho)$ is called doubling if there exists
$\lambda_X\in\mathbb N_+$ such that every ball $B(x,r)\subseteq X$ can be covered by at most $\lambda_X$ balls of radius $r/2$.  The smallest such $\lambda_X$ is called the doubling constant of $(X,\rho)$, and the doubling dimension is
$
    \operatorname{ddim}(X,\rho)
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \log_2(\lambda_X)
$.
title: Doubling metric spaces

body:
Define the heat kernel Phi: R^n x (0,infinity) -> R by Phi(x,t) = (4 pi t)^{-n/2} exp(-|x|^2/(4t)). Then Phi is smooth and satisfies partial Phi/partial t = Delta_x Phi for all x in R^n, t>0. For every bounded uniformly continuous g: R^n -> R, u(x,t) = integral_{R^n} Phi(x-y,t) g(y) dy is smooth on R^n x (0,infinity), solves partial u/partial t = Delta u there, and u(x,t) -> g(x) uniformly on R^n as t -> 0+. Moreover Phi(.,t) is an approximate identity: integral_{R^n} Phi(x,t) dx = 1 for every t>0.
Phi is the explicit Gaussian kernel on R^n x (0,infinity) given above
g is bounded and uniformly continuous on R^n (for the convolution/initial-value statement)

body:
Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be open and F: Ω × ℝ × ℝⁿ → ℝ continuous; consider the equation F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0 in Ω. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity SUBsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every point x₀ ∈ Ω at which u − φ has a local maximum, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity SUPERsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every local minimum point x₀ of u − φ, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. (Equivalent reformulations: replace 'local' by 'strict local' or 'global' max/min, or use C^∞ test functions, or use super-/subdifferentials D⁺u(x₀) and D⁻u(x₀): the conditions read F(x₀, u, p) ≤ 0 for all p ∈ D⁺u(x₀) and ≥ 0 for all p ∈ D⁻u(x₀).) Every classical C¹ solution is a viscosity solution, and a viscosity solution that is differentiable at x₀ satisfies the equation pointwise there. For time-dependent equations u_t + H(x, Du) = 0 on Ω × (0,T) apply the same definition with the gradient variable (u_t, Du) and test functions of (x,t). SHARP EDGE — the sign of F matters: writing the same equation as −F = 0 interchanges the roles of sub- and supersolutions, so the two forms have DIFFERENT viscosity solutions. Example: on (−1,1) with boundary values u(±1) = 0, the function 1 − |x| is a viscosity solution of |u'| − 1 = 0 but NOT of 1 − |u'| = 0, while |x| − 1 is a viscosity solution of 1 − |u'| = 0 but not of |u'| − 1 = 0 (at the kink x = 0, a concave kink admits only test functions touching from above, and a convex kink only test functions touching from below). Viscosity solutions are in general only continuous, are stable under uniform limits, and for convex H coincide with Lipschitz solutions that are semiconcave; the notion is designed so that comparison/uniqueness theorems hold where classical and a.e. solutions are non-unique.
F is continuous
u is continuous on Ω
the equation is written in the form F = 0 with a fixed sign convention

body:
[Theorem result of arXiv:2607.01463, 'Two Multi--Draw Coupon Collector models with different retention rules'] Consider the  $d$ coupon collector's problem (d--CCP), where in each run we keep \textbf{all} the new observed coupons. Let $T_{N,d}$ be the number of trials until all $N$ different types of coupons, which are uniformly distributed, are collected (at least once). Then, as $N\rightarrow \infty$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb {E}\left[T_{N,d}\right]=
\frac{N}{d}\log N
+\frac{\gamma N}{d}
-\frac{d-1}{2d}\log N
+\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d-1}{2d}\gamma\right)
+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log N}{N}\right).

\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Over connected unweighted graphs on n vertices with simple random walk, max_G tau_0(G) = n^3/54 + O(n^{19/7}), settling the Kemeny half of Aldous-Fill Open Problem 6.13. The balanced barbell attains n^3/54 + 0.056 n^2 + o(n^2), so the maximum's second-order term is positive and of order n^2 and the n^{19/7} is the upper bound's looseness. Ingredients: the bridge-tree identity, a deletion comparison, the mass-capacity inequality A <= gamma (s+a_n)^2 / (2 P S^2), a distance budget, a Rayleigh test function, a stability squeeze, and the Alev-Anari-Lau-Oveis Gharan cut/resistance-diameter theorem (balance 3-a = 1+6a, a = 2/7). Exhaustively for n <= 7 every maximizer is a barbell; the optimal block fraction is 1/3 at n = 60, 120, 240.

 probability space $(\Omega,\cF,P)$
we are given random processes $\xi^{(n)}_{t}$,
$w^{(n)}_{t}$, $n=0,1,2,...$. Suppose that

 \xi^{(n)}_{t}\to \xi^{(0)}_{t},\quad w^{(n)}_{t}\to w^{(0)}_{t}
\end{equation}
in probability as $n\to\infty$
for each $t\geq0$. Finally, assume that   $w^{(n)}_{t}$ are $d_{1}$-dimensional
Wiener processes relative to some
increasing families of complete $\sigma$-fields
$\cF_{t}^{n}\subset\cF$,
$t\geq0$, $n=0,1,2,...$, the functions

$$
I^{n}_{t}:=\int_{0}^{t}\xi^{(n)}_{s}\,dw^{(n)}_{s}
$$
 are well defined for $t\geq0$, $n=0,1,2,...$ and
   $I^{n}_{t}\to I^{0}_{t}$
in probability as $n\to\infty$
for each $t\geq0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 13 of arXiv:2608.03922, 'Absolute continuity of two-dimensional polynomial random vectors'] Let $M,R>0$ and $d\in\mathbb N$. Let
$\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^\infty\mu_j$,
where $\mu_j\in\mathcal M_d(M,R)$ for every $j\in\mathbb N$.
Then, for every $f\in\mathcal P_d(\mu)$ and every sequence of cylindrical
polynomials $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of degree at most $d$ such that
$f_n\to f$ in $L^2(\mu)$, the sequence $\{\nabla f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$
converges in $L^2(\mu;\ell^2)$, and its limit does not depend on the choice
of $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$. Consequently, the gradient extends uniquely to a
bounded linear operator
$\nabla\colon\mathcal P_d(\mu)\to L^2(\mu;\ell^2)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm thm41 of arXiv:2411.13099, 'Long time behavior of killed Feynman-Kac semigroups with singular Schr{ö}dinger potentials'] ([guillinqsd]) Assume, in addition to the three previous assumptions $\mathfrak 1$, $\mathfrak 2$, and $\mathfrak 3$ above, that $Q$ has a spectral gap in $b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star} (\mathscr S)$, i.e. 
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf r_{ess}(Q|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star} (\mathscr S)})<\mathsf r_{sp}(Q|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star} (\mathscr S)}).
\end{equation}
Then, there exist  a unique couple $(\mu, \varphi) \in \mathcal P_{\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S)\times \mathcal C_{b\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S)$, where  $\varphi>0$ over $\mathscr S$ and  $\mu(\varphi)=1$, and constants $r\in ]0,1[, C\ge 1$, such that
$$
 \mu Q=\mathsf r_{sp}(Q|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star}}(\mathscr S))\mu, \ Q\varphi= \mathsf r_{sp}(Q|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star} (\mathscr S)}) \varphi
$$ 
 and
\begin{equation}
\Big \|\frac {1}{\mathsf r_{sp}(Q|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S)})^n}Q^n f - \varphi \mu(f)\Big \|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S)} \le C r^n \|f \|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star} (\mathscr S)}, \ \forall f\in b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\mu(O)>0$ for all nonempty open subset $O$ of $\mathscr S$. 
In particular, we have: 
 \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item[$\mathfrak a$.] If  $\nu\in \mathcal M_{b\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S) $  satisfies for some $\lambda \in \mathscr R$, $\nu Q= \lambda\nu$ and $\nu(\varphi)\ne0$, then $\lambda=\mathsf r_{sp}(Q|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star} (\mathscr S)})$ and $\nu=c\mu$ for some constant $c$.
 \item[$\mathfrak b$.] If $f\in b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S)$ satisfies for some  $\lambda \in \mathscr R$,  $Qf=\lambda f$  and  $\mu(f)\ne 0$, then $\lambda=\mathsf r_{sp}(Q|_{b\mathcal B_{\mathbf W_\star}(\mathscr S)})$ and $f=c\varphi$ for some constant $c$.
 \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 15 ($\mathcal{E}^f$-expectation) of arXiv:2605.04359, 'Well-posedness of reflected BSDEs with default time and irregular barrier: An application '] Let $T^{\prime} \in [0,T]$ be a deterministic time. Let $\xi \in \mathbb{L}^2_{\beta}(\mathcal{F}_{T'})$. The $\mathcal{E}^f$-expectation of $\xi$ denoted by $\left(\mathcal{E}^f_{t,T'}(\xi)\right)_{t \in [0,T']}$ is defined as the the first component of the BSDE \eqref{basic equation : classical BSDE} with default jump associated with terminal time $T'$ and data $(\xi,f)$. More generally, for each time $T'\in [0,T]$ and each terminal condition $\xi \in \mathbb{L}^2_{\beta}(\mathcal{F}_{T'})$, due to Theorem \ref{Existence and uniqueness unconstrained BSDE}, we may define an operator $\mathcal{E}^f: \left(T',\xi\right) \to \mathcal{E}^f_{\cdot,T'}(\xi)$, and we say that $\mathcal{E}^f_{\cdot,T'}(\xi)$ is the $\mathcal{E}^f$-expectation process of $\xi$.
title: $\mathcal{E}^f$-expectation

body:
[Lem 162 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $I$ be a finite, nonempty index set. Let 
  \[
    \lt(\Theta, 
    \vec{\hat{Z}}\equiv
    (\hat Z_i)_{i\in I},
    \vec{\tilde{Z}}
    \equiv(\tilde Z_i)_{i\in I}\rt)
  \]
  be a random variable where
  $(\vec{\hat{Z}},\vec{\tilde{Z}})$
  are centered, jointly gaussian, and independent of $\Theta$. 
  Assume that $\vec{\hat{Z}}$ and $\vec{\tilde{Z}}$ are equidistributed,
 and that, for distinct $i,k\in I$,
  \[
    \bbE[\hat Z_i\hat Z_k]
    =\bbE[\tilde Z_i\tilde Z_k]
    =\bbE[\hat Z_i\tilde Z_k]=0.
  \]
Let $F$ and $G$ be measurable functions
such that $F(\Theta,\hat Z)$ and 
$G(\Theta,\hat Z)$ have finite variance, and such that
	\beq
    \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big] = 0 = 
    \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]\,,
    \eeq
  $\Theta$-almost surely.
Then the covariance between $F(\Theta,\hat{Z})$ and $G(\Theta,\tilde{Z})$ is bounded by
  \beq
    \lt| \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z) G(\Theta,\tilde Z)] \rt|
    \le
    \rho_{\max} \cdot
    \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2]^{1/2}
    \bbE[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2]^{1/2}\,, 
    
  \eeq
where $\rho_i\in[-1,+1]$ denotes the correlation between $\hat{Z}_i$ and $\tilde{Z}_i$, and 
$\rho_{\max} 
   \equiv\max\{|\rho_i|: i\in i\}$.
 
\begin{proof}
Let $\sigma_i$ denote the standard deviation of $\hat{Z}_i$, and denote
  \[
    \hat W_i \equiv 
    \frac{\hat Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,, \quad
    \tilde W_i 
    \equiv \frac{\tilde Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,,
  \]
which are marginally standard gaussians. It follows from the assumptions that
$(\hat W_i,\tilde W_i)$ are independent over $i\in I$, and $\bbE[\hat W_i\tilde W_i]=\rho_i$.
Let $(h_m)_{m\geq 0}$ denote the orthonormal Hermite polynomials for the
one-dimensional standard gaussian measure. We note that if $W$ and $\tilde{W}$ are marginally standard gaussians, and $(W,\tilde{W})$ is jointly gaussian and $\rho$-correlated, then it is straightforward to verify that
	\beq
	\E[ h_n(W) h_m(\tilde{W})]
	= \ind\{n=m\} \rho^n\,.\eeq
 For a multi-index $\vec n=(n_i)_{i\in I}\in\bbZ_{\ge 0}^I$, define the multivariate Hermite polynomial
  \[
    H_{\vec n}(w)
    \equiv\prod_{i\in I}h_{n_i}(w_i).
  \]
  We expand $F,G$ in the Hermite bases of $\hat W$ and $\tilde W$ respectively, conditional on $\Theta$, to obtain Hermite coefficients $a_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ and $b_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ such that
  \begin{align*}
    F(\Theta,\hat Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}a_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\hat W)\,, \\
    G(\Theta,\tilde Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}b_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\tilde W)\,.
  \end{align*}
  The assumption \eqref{e:conditional-centering} ensures $a_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=b_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=0$, $\Theta$-almost surely.
  Consequently, expanding in the Hermite bases and applying \eqref{e:hermite.corr.ip} gives
  \begin{align*}
    &\bigg|
      \bbE\Big[
        F(\Theta,\hat Z)G(\Theta,\tilde Z) \,\Big|\, \Theta
      \Big]
    \bigg|
    \le
      \sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
         |a_{\vec n}(\Theta)b_{\vec n}(\Theta)|
         \prod_{i\in I}|\rho_i|^{n_i}\\
    &\qquad\le
      \rho_{\max}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        a_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        b_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
    =\rho_{\max}
      \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}
      \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}\,.
  \end{align*}
  Taking expectation over $\Theta$ and again applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality proves the conclusion.
\end{proof}

body:
[Theorem th:Foster-Liapunov of arXiv:2603.20078, '\bf \Large Gated Infinite Server Queues in Light Traffic'] Suppose 
	that a Markov Chain with countable state space, say $\mathbb{Z}_+$, and transition
	probability matrix $P_{ij}$ is irreducible and let $N$ be a given natural
	number. If $V:\mathbb{Z}_+\to \mathbb{R}_+$, is a non-negative and $h:\mathbb{Z}_+\to \mathbb{R}_+$ a
	strictly positive function on the state space such that
	\begin{eqnarray}
		\sum_{j\in \mathbb{Z}_+} P_{ij}V(j) &\leq  & b,\hspace{1.14in}i \leq  N,
		 \\
		\sum_{j\in \mathbb{Z}_+} P_{ij}V(j) &\leq  & V(i)-h(i) ,\hspace{0.4in} i>N,  
	\end{eqnarray}
	where $b>0$, then the Markov Chain is positive recurrent and its (unique, 
	due to its irreducibility) stationary distribution, $\pi$, satisfies $\sum_j\pi(j) h(j) <\infty$. 
	Furthermore we have 
	$\sum_{j}P_{ij}^n h(j) \rightarrow \sum_j \pi_j h(j)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Foster--Lyapunov Criterion

body:
[Proposition 30 (Scaling) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] For $\lambda>0$ define $\Phi_\lambda:\cM\to\cM$ by
$(\Phi_\lambda\mu)(A):=\lambda^{-4}\mu(\lambda A)$. Then
\[
\bN\circ\bigl(\mu\mapsto\Phi_\lambda\mu\bigr)^{-1}
\;=\;\lambda^{-2}\,\bN
\qquad\text{as measures on }\cM .
\]
In particular $\supp(\Phi_\lambda\mu)=\lambda^{-1}\Ran$, so  the family
$K\mapsto\bN(\Ran\not\subset\overline B_K)$ scales as $K^{-2}$; see
Proposition~\ref{prop:range}.

body:
[Lemma 14 (Properties of \(\psi_{s,m}\)) of arXiv:2609.01436, '2609.01436'] The function \(\psi_{s,m}\) is bounded, nonnegative, nonincreasing,
convex, and belongs to \(C_b^{1,1}([0,\infty))\), with \(\operatorname{supp}\psi_{s,m}\subset[0,L]\).  Moreover,
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
for \(0\leq x\leq s/2\), \(
 \psi_{s,m}(x)\geq(e^{-1/2}-e^{-4})^2\);
\item if \(0\leq d\leq s\) and \(0\leq x\leq L-2s\), then
\[
 \psi_{s,m}(x+d)\geq\frac{1}{(e+1)^2}\psi_{s,m}(x);
\]
\item for every finite nonnegative Borel measure \(F\) of mass \(N\),
\[
 \int_{(L-2s,\infty)}\psi_{s,m}(x)\,dF(x)
 \leq (e^2-1)^2Ne^{-2m};
\]
\item if \(L\leq\varepsilon'\), for \(x\ge 0\),
\(
 \psi_{s,m}(x)\leq\varphi_{\varepsilon'}(x).
\)

$d_{\mathrm{DS}}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{portal}})=1$ such that
\[
    R^{\mathrm{imp}}_{\mathrm{iid}}(n;\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{portal}})

    \Omega(\log n/n).
\]
For every $d\ge1$, a $d$-fold product gives a class of DS dimension $d$ with
clean risk $O(d/n)$ and adaptive risk
$\Omega(d\log(1+n/d)/n)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Let \(\boldsymbol\mu(t)\) be a solution of the nonlinear RMF equation. Then, for
all \((v,s,k)\in E\), the coordinate probabilities are absolutely continuous
in time and satisfy the following equations for almost every \(t\geq0\).

For \(v\geq1\),
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}p_i(t;v,s,k)
=
a_i(t)p_i(t;v-1,s,k)

-
\bigl[a_i(t)+\gamma+\lambda(v,s,k)\bigr]
 p_i(t;v,s,k).
\end{align}

For \(v=0\),
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}p_i(t;0,s,k)
=&
-a_i(t)p_i(t;0,s,k)

+
\gamma\sum_{u\geq1}p_i(t;u,s,k)
\\
&+
q^{+}(s-1,k-1)
\sum_{u\geq0}
\lambda(u,s-1,k-1)
 p_i(t;u,s-1,k-1)
\nonumber\\
&+
q^{-}(s+1,k-1)
\sum_{u\geq0}
\lambda(u,s+1,k-1)
 p_i(t;u,s+1,k-1).
\nonumber
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}

\beta_i(t)
=
\sum_{(v,s,k)\in E}
\lambda(v,s,k)p_i(t;v,s,k).
\end{equation}
For the hard-threshold intensity,
\begin{equation}

\beta_i(t)
=
\sum_{s,k}
\sum_{v>\alpha s^+}
p_i(t;v,s,k).
\end{equation}
