[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2607.29495, 'Fast Mixing for Low-Temperature Potts Models via Poisson Trees'] Let $\theta>1$ and $\kappa,K>0$ be arbitrary reals.  Then, for all large enough real $d$,  for  all integer $q\geq d^{\theta}$, for all real $\beta > (1+\frac{1.01}{\theta})\frac{\log q}{d}$, the following holds for all large~enough~$n$.

    
      Let $T$ be a Poisson tree with parameter $d$,  truncated at level~$h=\lfloor K\log_d n\rfloor$. Then, with probability $\geq 1 - \frac{1}{n^\kappa}$ over  $T$, 
      the mixing time for
      the Glauber dynamics for the random cluster distribution $\pi^{\pl}_{T^h;q,\beta}$ with the all-wired boundary condition
      is $\leq |E(T)|n^{o(1)}$. 
      
      In particular, both the spectral gap and log-Sobolev constants are $\geq 1/(|E(T)|n^{o(1)})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 11 of arXiv:2607.29495

body:
[Prop Vect-delta-RKE of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Evaluation at $1\in\textup{Glo}$ defines an equivalence
    \[
        {\textup{End}}_{\CMon(\Spc_\textup{Glo})}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\textup{End}}_{\CMon(\Spc)}({\mathcal{F}}_{C_2}^\amalg).
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        We factor the evaluation functor $\CMon(\Spc_\textup{Glo})\to\CMon(\Spc)$ through the $\infty$-category $\CMon(\Spc_{\textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}})$ of commutative monoids in $\hbox{$\mathcal F\kern-1.7pt\textit{in}$}$-global spaces, and we will show that each of these individual restrictions defines an equivalence on endomorphism spaces.

        For the first restriction we observe that $i\colon \textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}\hookrightarrow\textup{Glo}$ admits a left adjoint $\text{Ho}\colon\hskip 0pt minus 1pt\textup{Glo}\hskip0pt minus 1pt\to\hskip 0pt minus 1pt\textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}$ induced by the enriched functor $\mathbb B{G}\mapsto\BGcat\pi_0(G)$. As $i$ is fully faithful, $\text{Ho}$ is a (Bousfield) localization at those group homomorphisms that induce bijections of path components. It follows that $\text{Ho}^*\coloneqq{\textup{Fun}}(\text{Ho},\CMon(\Spc))$ is fully faithful with essential image those functors that invert these maps in $\textup{Glo}$. This condition is evidently satisfied for $\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta$; as $i^*$ is left inverse to $\text{Ho}^*$ this shows that it induces an equivalence
        \[
            {\textup{End}}_{\CMon(\Spc_\textup{Glo})}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\textup{End}}_{\CMon(\Spc_{\textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}})}(i^*\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta).
        \]

        To show that also restriction along $\{1\}\hookrightarrow\textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}$ induces an equivalence of endomorphism spaces, it will suffice that $i^*\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta\colon\textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}^{\textup{op}}\to\CMon(\Spc)$ is right Kan extended from $\{1\}$. As $\CMon(\Spc)\to\Spc$ is a conservative right adjoint, it suffices to show that the underlying $\hbox{$\mathcal F\kern-1.7pt\textit{in}$}$-global space $i^*\ul\textup{Rep}_\delta\colon\textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}^{\textup{op}}\to\Spc$ is right Kan extended from the point. Plugging in the definitions, this can be written as
        \[
            \textup{Glo}_{{\mathcal{F}} in}^{\textup{op}}\hookrightarrow\Cat_\infty\xrightarrow{\;{\textup{Fun}}(-,{\mathcal{F}}_{C_2})\;}\Cat_\infty,
        \]
        which is indeed right Kan extended by [swan]*{Example~2.8}.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop Vect-delta-RKE of arXiv:2608.28504

body:
[Defn Standard path of arXiv:2609.01458, 'Confluence relations for $q$-analogues of multiple zeta values'] Let 
\[
u(z)\coloneqq\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1}(z),\dots,x_{d}(z))\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
For each $z$-dependent position $i$, there is a unique integer $r$
such that
\[
x_{i}(z)=zq^{r}\qquad\text{or}\qquad x_{i}(z)=z^{-1}q^{1-r}.
\]
We call $r$ the level of position $i$. The levels are determined
by the original word $u(z)$ and remain fixed throughout the following
procedure. Starting from $u(z)$, we replace all $z$-dependent entries
one at a time, in increasing order of their levels. Entries having
the same level are replaced from right to left. At each step, the
replacement is 
\[
x_{i}(z)\quad\longmapsto\quad x_{i}(zq).
\]
The resulting finite sequence consists of formal $q$MPLs ((thm:Fn_StandardPath of the paper))
and is denoted by 
\[
\operatorname{Std}(u)=(u_{0},u_{1},\dots,u_{l}),
\]
where $u_{0}=u(z)$ and $u_{l}=u(zq)$. We call it the standard path
from $u(z)$ to $u(zq)$.
title: Standard path

body: In statistics, maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a method of estimating the parameters of an assumed probability distribution, given some observed data. This is achieved by maximizing a likelihood function so that, under the assumed statistical model, the observed data is most probable. The point in the parameter space that maximizes the likelihood function is called the maximum likelihood estimate. The logic of maximum likelihood is both intuitive and flexible, and as such the method has become a dominant means of statistical inference.

body:
[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2607.25645, 'Estimates of the total variation distance between laws of Sobolev mappings on Gaussian spa'] Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $p>4k$, and let $b>0$.
Let
\[
f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k),\quad g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k)\colon \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^k
\]
be such that
\[
f_j,g_j\in C_b(\mathbb{R}^n),
\quad
\max_{1\le j\le k}\|\nabla f_j\|_{L^p(\gamma_n)}\le b,
\quad
\max_{1\le j\le k}\|\nabla g_j\|_{L^p(\gamma_n)}\le b.
\]
Then, for every pair of functions
\[
u\in L^{\frac{p}{2k-1}}(\gamma_n)
\quad\text{and}\quad
v\in L^p(\gamma_n),
\]
one has	
\begin{align*}
&\int_{\mathbb R^n} (\Delta_g+\varepsilon)^{-1}|uv|\,d\gamma_n
\le
\|u\|_{L^{\frac{p}{2k-1}}(\gamma_n)}
\|v\|_{L^p(\gamma_n)}
\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^n} (\Delta_f+\varepsilon)^{-m_1}\,d\gamma_n\Bigr)^{1/m_1}
\\
&+
4k\varepsilon^{-1}b^{2k-1}
\|u\|_{L^{\frac{p}{2k-1}}(\gamma_n)}
\|v\|_{L^p(\gamma_n)}
\max_{1\le j\le k}\|\nabla f_j-\nabla g_j\|_{L^p(\gamma_n)}
\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^n} (\Delta_f+\varepsilon)^{-m_2}\,d\gamma_n\Bigr)^{1/m_2},
\end{align*}
where
\[
m_1:=\frac{p}{p-2k}
\quad\text{and}\quad
m_2:=\frac{p}{p-4k}.
\]

body:
Consider the variance-preserving forward diffusion dX_t=-(beta_t/2)*X_t dt+sqrt(beta_t)*dW_t with exact conditional and unconditional scores s_c and s_u. Fix guidance strength gamma and use increasing reverse-time parameter tau, with t=T-tau. The CFG-DDPM reverse drift is (beta_t/2)*x+beta_t*((1-gamma)*s_u+gamma*s_c), with diffusion sqrt(beta_t)*I. It equals a conditional DDIM/probability-flow predictor with drift (beta_t/2)*(x+s_c), followed infinitesimally by a guided Langevin corrector with drift (beta_t/2)*((1-a)*s_u+a*s_c) and diffusion sqrt(beta_t)*I, where a=2*gamma-1. Thus their time-dependent infinitesimal generators agree: Delta_CFG_DDPM(gamma)=Delta_DDIM_conditional+Delta_LD_G(2gamma-1), in the source's SDE-limit sense. With regularity ensuring well-posedness, they describe the same SDE law. This statement does not equate finite-step transition kernels or identify the terminal law with a normalized gamma-powered density.
beta_t>=0 and the exact positive conditional and unconditional densities have defined differentiable scores
All coefficients and processes are interpreted in the variance-preserving SDE limit
Equality of path laws additionally requires standard existence and uniqueness conditions for the SDE; the algebraic drift and generator identity does not prove those conditions

[Theorem thm:barbour2019longterm of arXiv:2411.18563, 'Lower tails for triangles inside the critical window'] Let $P=(Y_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a Markov chain on $\Omega$ equipped with distance $\mathrm{dist}( \cdot,\cdot)$, and let $f : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a $L$-Lipschitz function with respect to $\mathrm{dist}$. Suppose that $\Omega_{\text{typ}}\subseteq \Omega_{\text{con}} \subseteq \Omega$ are such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathrm{dist}(y,z) \leq 1$ for all $y,z\in\Omega$ such that  $P(y,z) > 0$, 
\item $\mathbb{P}(Py\neq y) \leq D$ for $y \in \Omega_{\text{typ}}$, 
\item $\Omega_{\text{typ}}^+  \subseteq \Omega_{\text{con}}$,
\item $P$ is $\rho$-contractive on $\Omega_{\text{con}}$. 
\end{enumerate}
Let $k$ be a positive integer and let
\[\mathcal{A}_k = \{Y_i \in \Omega_{\text{typ}}~\forall\,  i<k\}, \text{ and } e_k = \max_{y\in \Omega_{\text{typ}}^+}\mathbb{P}_y(Y_i\not \in \Omega_{\text{con}} \textup{ for some }i<k)\, .
\]

Then for all $y\in \Omega_{\text{typ}}$ and $m \geq 0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}_y(\{|f(Y_k) - \mathbb{E}_y[f(Y_k)]| > m\}\land \mathcal{A}_k) \leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{m^2}{4L^2(D\rho^{-1} + 12k^3e_k^2) + 4mL(1 + 6ke_k)}\right)\, .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:barbour2019longterm of arXiv:2411.18563

            + \frac{1}{2} \langle \mathfrak{P}_t,\delta C^u_t(\delta \hat{C}^u_t)^*\rangle\bigg]\Bigg],

body:
[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2607.10356, '2607.10356'] Suppose that the error $\{\CW_n: n\ge 1\}$ is a sequence of $\Bb$-valued independent random variables.
Suppose that the \emph{step size sequence} $\{\beta_n:n\ge 0\}$ and \emph{the error sequence} $\{\CW_n: n\ge 1\}$ satisfy \emph{any one} of the conditions $(J1)$--$(J3)$ given below \emph{(}in addition to \eqref{U2}, \eqref{RM}, \eqref{U5}, \eqref{U6}\emph{)}. Then 
\be  \{\CX_n:n\ge 0\} \text{ converges to }\xx^*\text{ almost surely.}\ee

\begin{itemize}
\item [$(J1)$] Suppose $\{\CW_n: n\ge 1\}$ are i.i.d. with 
\be \label {L1a}\textstyle \E(\nrm{\CW_1}^2)<\infty,\;\;\E(\CW_1)=0,\ee
\be \label {L1b}\textstyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty \beta_n^2<\infty.\ee 
\item [$(J2)$] Suppose $\{\CW_n: n\ge 1\}$ are i.i.d. and for some $\alpha\in [1,2)$ and $0<D<\infty$, we have
\be \label {L2a}\E(\nrm{\CW_1}^\alpha)<\infty,\;\; \E(\CW_1)=0,\ee
\be \label {L2b} \beta_n\le Dn^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}},\;\;\forall n\ge 1.\ee 
\item [$(J3)$] Suppose $\{\CW_n: n\ge 1\}$ is a sequence of independent random variables with mean 0 that is \emph{tight}, \emph{i.e.}, satisfies, $\forall n\ge 1$,
\begin{equation}
\E[\CW_{n}]=0,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\forall \epsilon>0,\,\exists \text{ Compact }\Kb_\epsilon\subseteq\Bb \text{ such that }\P(\CW_{n}\in \Kb_\epsilon)\ge 1-\epsilon.
\end{equation}
Suppose that for some $\alpha\in (1,2]$, we have
\be \label {L3} \sup_{n\ge 1}\E(\nrm{\CW_n}^\alpha)<\infty,\ee
\be \label {L4}\textstyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty \beta_n^\alpha<\infty.\ee 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2607.10356

body: Arrow's impossibility theorem is a key result in social choice theory, proved by American economist Kenneth Arrow. It shows that no procedure for group decision-making under ordinal utilities can satisfy the requirements of rational choice theory. Specifically, no such rule can satisfy independence of irrelevant alternatives, the principle that a choice between two alternatives A and B should not depend on the quality of some third, unrelated option, C.
title: Arrow's impossibility theorem

[Corollary cor-sup-X of arXiv:2411.13923, 'Harmonic analysis of multiplicative chaos \\ Part I: the proof of Garban-Vargas conjecture'] For any $\gamma\in(0,\sqrt{2})$, any $q>2$ and any integer $j\ge 0$, there exists a modification $\widetilde{X}_j$ of $X_j$ such that 
		\begin{align}
			\mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big( \sup_{t\ne s} \frac{|\widetilde{X}_j(t)-\widetilde{X}_j(s)|}{|t-s|^\alpha}\Big)^{q} \Big] <\infty
		\end{align}
		for any
		\[
		0\le \alpha < \frac{1}{2}- \frac{1}{q}.
		\]
		In particular, we have 
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\Big[\sup_{t\in [0,1]} \widetilde{X}_j(t)^q\Big]<\infty. 
		\]
title: Corollary cor-sup-X of arXiv:2411.13923

Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\theta \ge 0$ and variance $\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\hat\theta_n = \max(0, \bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n^* - \hat\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \sigma^2)$, the law of $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\theta = 0$) it is not: $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta) \Rightarrow \max(0, Z)$ with $Z \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n^* - \hat\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\max(0, Z + \zeta) - \max(0, \zeta)$ with $\zeta \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \to \infty$, $m/n \to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2608.06317, 'Sharp Tail Bounds Beyond Twice the Mean'] Let $(Y_i)$ be a stochastic process taking values in $[0,1]$.
Assume that its predictable mean budget is at most $a\in[0,1]$, that is,
$\sum_{i=1}^\infty\EEc{Y_i}{Y^{i-1}}\le a$. Then, for every $n\in\N$, $y>1$
\[
\PP{\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\ge y}
\le \frac{1}{y-1}\left(a-1+
\left(1-\frac{a}{n}\right)^n\right).
\]
In particular, if $u\le u_0:=\tfrac{x+1}{2}$, $w\ge 0$ and $x\ge2w-1$, $x>1$ then
\[
V_n(x,u,w)\le
\frac{x+1}{x-1}\left(\frac{2w}{x+1}-1+
\left(1-\frac{2w}{n(x+1)}\right)^n\right)
=Q_{n,w}(x).
\]

[Proposition 22 of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a non-compact connected semisimple real Lie group, $X$ be its symmetric space and ${\bf D}$ be the corona space of $X$.
    Then the sequence $\{\mu_t\}_{t\ge 1}$ is relatively compact in $\mathbf M(\mathbf D)\setminus \{0\}$.
    
    Moreover, any subsequential limit $\mu_{t_n}\overset{v}{\to}\mu\in \mathbf M({\bf D})$, $t_n\to \infty$, satisfies the following:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[{\rm(1)}] $\mu$ is $G$-invariant,
        \item[{\rm(2)}] $\mu(\{f\in {\bf D}: f(o)\le r\})<\infty$ for every $r\in \mathbb{R}$,
        \item[{\rm(3)}] $\mu(\{f\in {\bf D}: f(o)\le 0\})=1$,
        \item[{\rm(4)}] $\mu({\bf D})=\infty$,

[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2605.16733, 'Concentration Inequalities for Sample Cross-Covariances'] Let $\xi, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_N \iid \mu$ be a sequence of random variables on a probability space $(\Omega, \mu)$, and let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions on $(\Omega, \mu)$. Set
\[
\Delta(\mathcal F):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\|f\|_{\psi_2},
\qquad
\Gamma(\mathcal F):=\gamma_2(\mathcal F,\|\cdot\|_{\psi_2}).
\]
  Then, for every
\(u\ge1\), with probability at least \(1-\exp(-u)\),
\[
\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}
\left|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f^2(\xi_i)-\E f^2(\xi)
\right|
\lesssim
\frac{\Gamma(\mathcal F)\Delta(\mathcal F)}{\sqrt N}
+
\frac{\Gamma^2(\mathcal F)}{N}
+
\Delta^2(\mathcal F)
\left(\sqrt{\frac uN}+\frac uN\right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 10 of arXiv:2608.30875, 'A Decomposition Theorem for Topological Semi-small Maps'] A \textbf{perversity} 
   	$\bar{p}: \mathbb{Z}_{ \geq 2} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ is a function such that $\overline{p}(2)=0$ and
   	$\overline{p}(k+1)- \overline{p}(k) \in \{1,0\}$. The \textbf{complementary perversity} $\bar{q}$ of $\bar{p}$ 
   	is the one with $\overline{p}(k)+\overline{q}(k)=k-2$. Furthermore, the lower middle perversity is defined by $\bar{m}(k)=[\frac{k-2}{2}]$. Its complementary perversity is called the upper middle perversity and is defined by $\bar{n}(k)=[\frac{k-1}{2}]$.

body: FIRES WHEN a detection or coverage problem in a moving Boolean model has been reduced, correctly, to the volume of a union of swept regions, and you are about to call the problem solved. THE REDUCTION IS EXACT and motion-free: P(S_1 > s, S_2 > t) = exp(-lambda |A_1(s) union A_2(t)|) by the Poisson void probability, where A_i(t) is the set of grain initial conditions detecting K_i by time t. WHAT IS LEFT is the geometry, and the geometry is where the two models part. For BALLISTIC grains each A_i is a capsule with axis along -v, the axes are parallel, and the union volume is two capsule volumes minus an axial integral of the cross-sectional lens - a solid-angle computation, tractable. For BROWNIAN grains |A_1(s) union A_2(t)| is the joint volume swept by a single Brownian path around two given sets, i.e. a TWO-SET WIENER SAUSAGE volume, and that quantity has no closed form in any dimension. CONDITION OF FAILURE: Brownian, or any diffusive, grain motion. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE, and it is why this is a scar and not a complaint: it says which case to attack first, and the inertial case was settled exactly because of it.

If f is meromorphic inside and on a positively-oriented simple closed contour C, with no zeros or poles on C, then (1/(2 pi i)) times the contour integral over C of f'(z)/f(z) dz equals Z - P, the number of zeros minus the number of poles inside C, each counted with multiplicity. Equivalently it is the winding number of f(C) about the origin (the net change in arg f around C, divided by 2 pi).

\Big]
\leq
\\
C_{j,l}(1\vee\diam(D)^{j/4})

\\

body: For any ordinal \alpha, exponentiation by an ordinal \beta is defined by transfinite recursion on \beta: \alpha^0 = 1; \alpha^{\beta + 1} = (\alpha^\beta) \cdot \alpha; and for a limit ordinal \lambda, \alpha^\lambda = \bigcup_{\beta < \lambda} \alpha^\beta.
title: Ordinal Exponentiation
Thm g=1_general of arXiv:2608.25362

body: The derivative of f at c is f'(c) = lim_{h->0} (f(c+h) - f(c))/h when the limit exists; f is then differentiable at c. Differentiability implies continuity (not conversely: |x| at 0). The derivative is the slope of the tangent and the best local linear approximation f(c+h) = f(c) + f'(c) h + o(h). Standard rules (sum, product, quotient, chain) follow from the limit laws.

AUTHOR-DERIVED, UNREVIEWED finite-n identities. Let M_n=max_p sum_{v in p}g_v for n-vertex up/right paths from the origin in Z_+^2 with free endpoint and independent N(0,1) vertex weights. Define A_i as the mean of the i+1 weights on x+y=i, r_v=g_v-A_i on that layer, and H_n=sum_{j=1}^n 1/j. The layer means are Gaussian-independent of r, and M_n(g)=sum_{i=0}^{n-1}A_i+M_n(r), so Var(M_n)=H_n+Var(M_n(r)). For F_{n,beta}=log sum_p exp(beta sum_{v in p}g_v) at fixed beta>0, Var(F_{n,beta})=beta^2 H_n+Var(F_{n,beta}(r)). Under OU coupling g_t=e^(-t)g+sqrt(1-e^(-2t))g', maximizing-path overlap R_n(t) has floor sum_v P(v in P_n)^2>=H_n at every t>=0. These identities do not establish a power variance upper bound.

[Theorem thm:local-LG of arXiv:2412.01015, 'Classical beta ensembles and related eigenvalues processes at high temperature and the Mar'] Consider (standard) beta Laguerre processes $\{\lambda_i(t)\}_{i=1}^N$ in a high temperature regime where $\beta = {2c}/N$ with a positive constant $c \in (0, \infty)$. Let 
\[
	x_i(t) = \gamma_N \left(\lambda_i \left(\frac t {\tau_N}\right) - E_N\right),
\]
where $\gamma_N, \tau_N, E_N > 0$ are non-random. Let $\mu_t^{(N)}$ be the empirical measure process of $\{x_i(t)\}_{i=1}^N$ and $S_n^{(N)}(t)$ be its $n$th moment process. As $N \to \infty$ with
\[
	\epsilon_N = \frac{\gamma_N}{\tau_N} \to 0, \quad \text{and}\quad \sigma_N^2 = \frac{2\gamma_N^2E_N}{\tau_N} \to \sigma^2,
\]
for given $\sigma^2 > 0$, we get exactly the same statements as in Theorem~{\rm(thm:G-moments of the paper)} and Theorem~\rm{(thm:G-measures of the paper)}.

[Theorem thm:stopping-criterion of arXiv:2605.17082, 'Spectral Purification in Reversible Markov Chains: Hidden Parameters, Observable Equivalen'] Define the \emph{online convergence indicator}
\begin{equation}
\Gamma_k := \frac{\widehat{V}_k}{\rho_k^2} = \frac{\rho_{k+1}}{\rho_k} - 1 \;\ge\; 0.
\end{equation}
Assume that a lower bound $\tau \le 1 - (\lambda_3/\lambda_2)^2$ is known (or estimated online; see (rem:tau-estimation of the paper)). Define the critical threshold
\[
\eta(\varepsilon) := \frac{\varepsilon^4}{8} \cdot \tau^2.
\]
Then the stopping rule ``stop at the first $k$ such that $\Gamma_k \le \eta(\varepsilon)$'' guarantees
\[
\|v_k - s_2 \phi_2\|_\pi \le \varepsilon,
\]
provided that $\alpha_2(k) \ge 1/2$ at termination (which holds for all sufficiently large $k$).
title: Adaptive stopping criterion for power iteration

[Theorem 17 (Stability of the subcritical domain; conditional on Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $\mathcal M_-=\{\theta:\rho(M(\theta))<1\}$ and $\mathcal M_+=\{\theta:\rho(M(\theta))>1\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item ($\mathcal M_-$ is open.) $\rho(M(\cdot))$ is continuous (indeed real-analytic where $M$ is irreducible), so $\mathcal M_-$ is open and $\partial\mathcal M_-=\{\rho(M)=1\}$ is, where the gradient is nonzero, a smooth codimension-one submanifold (Proposition~\ref{prop:PF}(3) and the implicit function theorem).
\item (Convexity goes to $\mathcal M_+$, not $\mathcal M_-$.) In the scalar (Bethe) case $\rho=(d-1)p$, with $p$ log-concave, $\mathcal M_+=\{p>1/(d-1)\}$ is a superlevel set of a log-concave function, hence convex; $\mathcal M_-$ is its complement and is in general non-convex. Explicitly, if $p$ is jointly log-concave in $(\theta,\gamma)$ then $\mathcal M_-$ is the non-convex exterior of a convex region. Convexity of $\mathcal M_-$ cannot be deduced from log-concavity of $p$: the implication ``sublevel sets of a concave function are convex'' is false (it is superlevel sets that are convex).
\item ($\mathcal M_-$ is contractible.) $\mathcal M_-$ is star-shaped toward the zero-coupling locus $\{\gamma=0\}$: holding $(\theta,\alpha,\mu)$ fixed and sending $\gamma\downarrow0$ decreases every $p_{d,d'}$ (transmission increases in coupling), hence decreases $\rho(M)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:PF}(2)), keeping the path in $\mathcal M_-$. The straight-line homotopy $\gamma\mapsto(1-t)\gamma$ therefore retracts $\mathcal M_-$ to a point; $\mathcal M_-$ is contractible.
\item (Resolvent and gap.) On $\mathcal M_-$ the resolvent $R=(I-M)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}M^k$ converges (finite matrix, $\rho(M)<1$) to a bounded nonnegative matrix; the halting probability is $\Prob(|S|<\infty)=1$; the expected cluster size is $\E|S|=\one^\top R\,\pi$, real-analytic in $\theta$; and the spectral gap $g(\theta)=1-\rho(M(\theta))>0$ gives quantitative stability: any $\Delta\theta$ with $\|\Delta\theta\|<g(\theta)/\|\nabla_\theta\rho\|$ keeps $\theta+\Delta\theta\in\mathcal M_-$.
\end{enumerate}

Own-work draft; T419-C014 v1, proof (unaudited); elementary published-method application, no novelty claimed. Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.
Real positive definite empirical covariance; arbitrary cross matrix and finite factor initialization
Constants, sufficient step bound and excluded convergence/risk conclusions are exactly as stated

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. body:
[Theorem MainThm2 of arXiv:2608.30904, 'Entire monotone solutions of the anisotropic Allen--Cahn equation in dimension 5'] Let $F$ be the Mooney--Yang anisotropy and
\[
\Gamma
=
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2:\ |y|=\sigma(|x|)\}
\]
be its nonflat minimizing leaf.  There exists $\alpha\in(0,1)$ such that,
for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the anisotropic Allen--Cahn equation
(equation eq:main-PDE of the paper), with $H=\frac12F^2$, has a stable weak solution
\[
u_\varepsilon\in
C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^4)\cap W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^4),
\qquad
-1<u_\varepsilon<1.
\]
The solution is $O(2)\times O(2)$-invariant and is smooth on
$\{Du_\varepsilon\neq0\}$.  For every $K\Subset\Gamma$ and every
$\alpha'<\alpha$, the zero set $\{u_\varepsilon=0\}$ converges to $\Gamma$ in
$C^{2,\alpha'}(K)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$.  In particular, $u_\varepsilon$ is not
one-dimensional. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stable solution

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2609.03238, 'Representation Defects and Cassels Pairings for Congruent Number Curves'] The radical of the Cassels pairing on $\Sel_2'(E_n)$ is the image of
$\Sel_4(E_n)$.  Consequently, the pairing is nondegenerate if and only if
\[
\rk E_n(\Q)=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Sha(E_n)[2^\infty]\cong(\Z/2\Z)^{s_2(n)}.
\]
If $s_2(n)=2m$, nondegeneracy is equivalent to
$\Pf(C_{\mathcal B}(E_n))=1$ for any basis $\mathcal B$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 5 of arXiv:2609.03238

[Lemma lem:extinction of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] Let $\alpha \in (0, 2)$. Suppose $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a nonnegative continuous semimartingale
of the form $\mathrm{d} X_t=C_t\,\mathrm{d} t+\mathrm{d} M_t$, where $(C_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a predictable process with $C_t\le\kappa X_t$ for all $t\ge0$ for some
constant $\kappa>0$, and $(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a continuous local
martingale with $M_0=0$. Then, we have that for every $A>0$, $t>0$, and $D>0$,
\[ 
\mathbb{P}\left( \inf_{0\leq s\leq t} X_s >0\,, X_{0} < D, \,  \int_0^t \frac{e^{-\kappa(2-\alpha) s }}{X_s^\alpha} \, \mathrm{d}\langle M \rangle_s \geq A \  \right) \leq \frac{2D^{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}}{\sqrt{A\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)^2}}.
\]

body: [Proposition 8 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] Let $0<a\leq b<1$ and $A=[a,b]$. For any $n\geq 0$ and any real numbers $0=s_{0}<s_{1}<s_{2}<s_{n}<t=s_{n+1}$, conditionally to the event $\{e_{1}^{\varepsilon}\geq t\}$, the random vector $\begin{split}\big(N^{\varepsilon}_{(s_{i},s_{i+1}]}(A)\big)_{0\leq i\leq n}\end{split}$ converges in law, as $\varepsilon$ goes to $0$, to the random vector $\begin{split}\big({\bar{N}}_{i}\big)_{0\leq i\leq n}\end{split}$ composed of independent random variables such that for any $i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $N_{i}$ is a Poisson random variable with parameter $(s_{i+1}-s_{i})\lambda_{*}(A)$.

body:
[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] Let $f$ be a probability density on $G$ such that $\supp(f)$ is contained in some proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ with $\mu(H) > 0$ and Haar measure $\mu_H$ defined to be the Haar measure $\mu$ of $G$ restricted to $H$. 

Then if $g'$ is a symmetrizer for $\restr{f}{H}$ (the restriction of $f$ to $H$) in $H$, 
\[ g \coloneqq \begin{cases} g'(x) & x \in H \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \]
is a symmetrizer of $f$ in $G$. 

\begin{proof}
Since $g'$ is a symmetrizer for $\restr{f}{H}$, 
\begin{align*}
(g * f)(x) 
&= \int_{G} g(r)f(r^{-1}x) \,d\mu(r)\\ 
&= \int_{H} g(r)f(r^{-1}x) \,d\mu(r)
= (g' * \restr{f}{H})(x) 
= (g' * \restr{f}{H})(x^{-1}) 

= (g * f)(x^{-1}). \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. For any integer n>=64, 0<q,r<=1 and c in [-1,1], draw n independent paired standard Gaussians (Xi,Yi) of correlation c. Let F(t)=E tanh(sqrt(t)Z)^2 for standard Gaussian Z, Ui=tanh(sqrt(q)Xi)/sqrt(F(q)), Vi=tanh(sqrt(r)Yi)/sqrt(F(r)), delta=1-E(Ui Vi), A=n^-1 sum Ui^2, D=n^-1 sum Vi^2, T=n^-1 sum Ui Vi, and Dhat=1-T/sqrt(A D). Sample means are not subtracted; A and D are positive almost surely. There exists a finite universal Lambda, independent of n,q,r,c, such that E|Dhat-delta|^4<=Lambda^4 delta^4/n^2 and E|Dhat-E Dhat|^4<=16 Lambda^4 delta^4/n^2. If delta=0 then Dhat=0 almost surely. These bounds hold conditionally when q,r,c depend on a completed past and the Gaussian rows are fresh and iid conditional on that past. An explicit finite Lambda in terms of the C010 feature-curve and inverse-norm constants is given in the proof. This uses unaudited C010 v1 sections1-5; no independent audit or numerical value of Lambda is claimed. The result controls current-state sampling noise, not propagation over depth or the full Tensor Programs rate.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:48e73ff87d856f8f64113b5184222c8d995aad574fe284999fd6084843108d1a","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/48/48e73ff87d856f8f64113b5184222c8d995aad574fe284999fd6084843108d1a.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:7403637ef5b5574136264ea9884cec044a799284be3e4d5ed5596621f8cc2775","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_angular_sampling_fourth","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c015-angular-sampling-fourth","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Tensor Programs and stochastic angular-gap propagation","draft":"w712/bundle_011.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:critical-tanh-empirical-correlation-gap-conditional-fourth-moment-noise","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C015 v1: fourth moments of unequal-variance tanh angular sampling noise

Kind: moved. Target: 1, stochastic two-input Gram propagation.
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified. This supplies a conditional
fourth-moment input for a subsequent martingale argument; it does not
establish the multi-layer angular error or the full Tensor Programs rate.

## Statement

Fix 0<q,r<=1, -1<=c<=1 and integer n>=64. Draw n iid standard Gaussian
pairs (X_i,Y_i) of correlation c. Set

    F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2,
    u_q(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(F(q)),
    U_i=u_q(X_i), V_i=u_r(Y_i), h=E U_i V_i, delta=1-h,
    A=mean U_i^2, D=mean V_i^2, T=mean U_i V_i,
    Dhat=1-T/sqrt(AD).

The sample means are not subtracted. The denominators are positive almost
surely. There exists a universal finite constant Lambda, independent of
q,r,c,n, such that

    E|Dhat-delta|^4 <= Lambda^4 delta^4/n^2,          (1)
    E|Dhat-E Dhat|^4 <=16 Lambda^4 delta^4/n^2.       (2)

For delta=0 both left sides are zero. Otherwise (1) is equivalently a
uniform fourth moment of the relative sampling error, bounded by
Lambda^4/n^2. The same statements hold conditionally when q,r,c are
measurable with respect to a completed network past and the rows are
fresh iid pairs conditional on that past. Correlated coordinates within
a row, including c=+/-1, are allowed.

## 1. Exact inputs from C010, and the constants

Use T250-w712-C010 v1, sections 1-5, as an explicitly unaudited dependency.
Its hypotheses are exactly the above current-state hypotheses. Its
feature-curve lemma supplies a universal mu>0 and, for all finite p>=1,

    G_p=(E|Z|^p)^(1/p),
    B_p=(2/3)G_(3p)^3+8G_p,
    I_p=4sqrt(2)G_p+(6sqrt(2)/mu)B_p,
    ||U_i-V_i||_p<=I_p sqrt(delta),
    ||U_i^2-V_i^2||_p<=4G_(2p)I_(2p)sqrt(delta).     (3)

Here mu is the positive minimum of -R'(t) on [0,1], where

    R(t)=E[(Z^3-3Z)u_t(Z)]/[sqrt(6) E[Z u_t(Z)]],

u_0(z)=z and R is differentiated with its continuous right derivative at
zero. C010 establishes the positivity of this minimum analytically,
not numerically. We do not re-prove that feature-curve result here.

Let W_i=(U_i-V_i)^2/2 and w=mean W_i. Then E W_i=delta.
C010 equations (8)-(9), with x=A-1, y=D-1, s=A-D, give

    ||x||_8, ||y||_8 <=a/sqrt(n),
    ||w-delta||_8 <=b delta/sqrt(n),                  (4)

where

    a=max_(p in {2,4,8}) p^2(4G_(2p)^2+1),
    b=max_(p in {2,4,8}) p^2(I_(2p)^2/2+1).

Both U and V have second moment one even when q!=r. Therefore the
variables U_i^2-V_i^2 in (3) are centered. This is load-bearing in the
new order-16 estimate below.

Also C010 section 5 gives

    E A^(-20), E D^(-20) <=J,
    J=64^20 sum_(j=0)^20 binom(20,j)
                            product_(k=1)^j (64-2k)^(-1).       (5)

The empty product is 1. In particular J>=1. By monotonicity of probability
Lp norms, (5) implies, for positive t,p with tp<=20,

    ||A^(-t)||_p <=J^(t/20)<=J^t,
    ||D^(-t)||_p <=J^t.                              (6)

The deliberately loose final bounds simplify constants. C010 proves (5)
for all n>=64 by averaging size-64 row subsets and using convexity of
the inverse power. No independence of A and D is used.

Define the new finite constants

    d16=16^2 *4G_32 I_32,
    Lambda=J(b+2a)+d16^2 J^2/8.                      (7)

## 2. The only new sample-mean order

For centered iid real B_i with E|B_i|^16 finite, expansion gives

    E|mean B_i|^16 <=16^16 n^(-8) E|B_1|^16.

Indeed a term containing an index exactly once has expectation zero,
by independence and centering. All surviving index patterns partition
the 16 positions into at most 8 nonempty blocks, each of size at least 2.
There are at most 16^16 such partitions: map each position to the least
position of its block, an injective encoding into functions from a
16-element set to itself. For any partition with k<=8 blocks there are
at most n^k<=n^8 assignments of distinct row labels. Holder bounds the
absolute expectation of every term by E|B_1|^16. Divide the expanded sum
by n^16. This proves the displayed bound, also for n=1.

Taking sixteenth roots, and weakening 16 to 16^2, gives

    ||mean B_i||_16 <=16^2 ||B_1||_16/sqrt(n).

Apply this to B_i=U_i^2-V_i^2 and use (3):

    ||s||_16 <=d16 sqrt(delta/n).                    (8)

Unlike (4), this order-16 centered sample-mean estimate is new to the
normalization calculation. All row moments needed for it are already
covered by C010's all-finite-p feature-curve bound (3).

## 3. Normalization without a good-event cutoff

Put k=(AD)^(-1/2) and

    t=(sqrt(A)-sqrt(D))^2/(2sqrt(AD)).

The exact identities A+D-2T=2w and
A+D-2sqrt(AD)=(sqrt(A)-sqrt(D))^2 give

    Dhat=w k-t,
    0<=t<=s^2/(8AD).                                (9)

The inequality uses (sqrt(A)+sqrt(D))^2>=4sqrt(AD).
From (6) and Holder, without independence,

    ||k||_8 <=||A^(-1/2)||_16 ||D^(-1/2)||_16 <=J.

For g(z)=z^(-1/2), exact algebra gives
|g(z)-1|=|z-1|/[sqrt(z)(1+sqrt(z))]<=|z-1|/sqrt(z).
Therefore k-1=(g(A)-1)g(D)+(g(D)-1), and (4),(6) give

    ||k-1||_4
       <=||x||_8 ||k||_8+||y||_8 ||D^(-1/2)||_8
       <=2aJ/sqrt(n).                               (10)

For the correction t, (8),(9) and Holder give

    ||t||_4 <=(1/8)||s||_16^2 ||(AD)^(-1)||_8
             <=d16^2 J^2 delta/(8n).                (11)

In the last line ||(AD)^(-1)||_8<=||A^(-1)||_16
||D^(-1)||_16<=J^2. The largest inverse order newly needed here is 16,
and all inverse orders used in (10)-(11) are at most 20. Consequently
the width assumption n>=64 from C010 is unchanged.

Finally, rewrite the exact error as

    Dhat-delta=(w-delta)k+delta(k-1)-t.

Holder with (4),(10),(11), followed by n^(-1)<=n^(-1/2), gives

    ||Dhat-delta||_4
       <= bJ delta/sqrt(n)+2aJ delta/sqrt(n)
                            +d16^2 J^2 delta/(8n)
       <=Lambda delta/sqrt(n).

This proves (1). Since |E(Dhat-delta)|<=||Dhat-delta||_4,
the L4 triangle inequality gives
||Dhat-E Dhat||_4<=2||Dhat-delta||_4, proving (2).
When delta=0, C010 shows U_i=V_i almost surely; directly w=t=Dhat=0.
No relative division is needed in this boundary case.

## 4. Conditional form and the unpaid step

For the exact critical tanh Gram chain, define
delta_l=1-E[u_(Q_l)(X)u_(R_l)(Y)|F_l], where the fresh standard pair has
correlation c_l, and eta_(l+1)=D_(l+1)-E[D_(l+1)|F_l]. Then

    E[eta_(l+1)|F_l]=0,
    E[|eta_(l+1)|^4|F_l]<=16Lambda^4 delta_l^4/n^2.   (12)

The same Lambda is uniform in all admissible random current states;
conditioning reduces exactly to the proved deterministic-parameter
calculation. Strict positivity of the finite-depth marginal variances
holds almost surely from positive initial marginals and Gaussian rows.

Together with C010's bias bound and C014's radial mixed-source closure,
(12) supplies another required input for a martingale fourth-moment
estimate. It is not that estimate: the predictable multipliers, their
inverses, and their relation to delta_l still need a joint argument.
In particular a terminal stability product depends on future innovations
and cannot be factored out of an expectation by an independence claim.
The full normalized angular-gap propagation and readout rate remain open.

Sources: T250-w712-C010 v1 sections 1-5, specifically equations (7)-(9)
and its inverse-norm calculation; new order-16 counting and normalization
estimates are given above. C014 is contextual, not a premise of (1)-(12).

body:
[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $P_*$ and $\pi_*$ be the transition matrix and stationary distribution resp. for the RWBD chain with parameters $n,d$ and state space $\Omega_*$. Then the distance to stationary $d_*(t)$ at time $t$ is,
   \[\max_{x\in \Omega_*}\Vert P^t_*(x,\cdot) - \pi_*  \Vert_\text{TV} = \Vert P^t_*(0,\cdot) - \pi_*\Vert_\text{TV} \]
   \begin{proof}
      Fix $x\in \Omega_*$, and let $\delta_x$ be the distribution over $\Omega$ with all weight at $x$. Then,
      \begin{align*}
  \Vert P_*^t(x,\cdot) - \pi_*(\cdot) \Vert_\text{TV} &= \Vert (P^t \mu_x)(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot) \Vert_\text{TV}\tag{By Lemma \ref{d}}\\
   &= \left\Vert \sum_{x\in H_x}\frac{1}{\varphi(x)}(P^t\delta_x)(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot) \right\Vert_\text{TV}\\
   &= \left\Vert \sum_{x\in H_x}\frac{1}{\varphi(x)}\left((P^t\delta_x)(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot)\right) \right\Vert_\text{TV}\\
   &\leq \sum_{x\in H_x}\left\Vert\frac{1}{\varphi(x)} \left((P^t\delta_x)(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot)\right) \right\Vert_\text{TV}\tag{By Triangle Inequality}\\
   &= \sum_{i=1}^{\varphi(x)}\frac{1}{\varphi(x)}\left\Vert (P^t\delta_{\hat{1}})(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot) \right\Vert_\text{TV}\tag{By Transitivity}\\
   &= \left\Vert (P^t\delta_{\hat{1}})(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot) \right\Vert_\text{TV}\\
   &= \Vert P_*^t(0,\cdot) - \pi_*(\cdot) \Vert_\text{TV}
      \end{align*}
      
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 9 of arXiv:2604.07478

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.25221, 'Representing MAX functions using two-hidden-layer ReLU networks'] Fix any number $k\geq 1$. Define an {\em atom pattern of degree $k$} to be a list
\[
 P=[p_1,\ldots,p_k \mid q_1,\ldots,q_k],
\]
where $p_1, \ldots, p_k, q_1, \ldots, q_k \in \{1, \ldots, N\} \times \{1, \ldots, N\}$ be ordered pairs (with repetition allowed) of numbers in $\{1, \ldots, N\}$. 

Define the corresponding functions\[
 L_P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}m_{p_i}(x),
 \qquad
 R_P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}m_{q_i}(x),
\]
where $m_{(a,b)}(x)=\max\{x_a,x_b\}$. The {\em atom represented by $P$ is then defined as}
\[
 \A_P(x)=\max\{L_P(x),R_P(x)\}
\]
\medskip

For any permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_N$ and any ordered pair $(a,b) \in \{1, \ldots, N\} \times \{1, \ldots, N\}$, define $\sigma((a,b))= (\sigma(a), \sigma(b))$. This defines a group action of the symmetric group $\Sigma_N$ on the set of all atom patterns of degree $k$ by defining $$\sigma P = [\sigma(p_1), \ldots, \sigma(p_k)\mid \sigma(q_1), \ldots, \sigma(q_k)].$$
title: Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.25221

[Proposition 26 (Fixed-marginal target bounds) of arXiv:2608.28827, 'Quantitative Target Convergence and Uniform-in-Time\\ Propagation of Chaos for Langevin-Re'] Under Assumption~\ref{ass:core-target} and either kernel assumption, there exists a finite constant $C$ such that for fixed $k$ and $N\ge2k$, and any $t \ge 0$,
\begin{align}
    \KL(P_{N,t}^{(k)}\|\pi^{\otimes k})
    &\le Ck e^{-2\varepsilon\alpha t}+C\frac{k}{N},
      \\
    \KL(\mu_t^{\otimes k}\|\pi^{\otimes k})
    &=k\KL(\mu_t\|\pi)
    \le Ck e^{-2\varepsilon\alpha t}.
      
\end{align}

[Prop Kolmogorov equations of arXiv:2606.06187, 'How to Study Reflected Brownian Motion in a Quadrant via Kernel Functional Equations?\\ \m'] The backward equation can be written as
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\mathcal{G}_x p_t(x, y)=\partial_t p_t(x, y), \\
R_i \cdot \nabla_x p_t(x, y)=0 \text { if } x_i=0, \\
p_0(x, y)=\delta_0 (y-x) .
\end{array}\right.
$$

The forward equation (or Fokker–Planck equation) can be written as
$$ \hspace{2.1cm}
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\mathcal{G}_y^* p_t(x, y)=\partial_t p_t(x, y), \\
R_i^* \cdot \nabla_y p_t(x, y)-2 \mu_i p_t(x, y)=0 \text { if } y_i=0, \\
p_0(x, y)=\delta_0 (y-x) ,
\end{array}\right.
$$
where
$$
R^*=2 \Sigma-R=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2\rho-r_2
\\
2\rho-r_1 & 1
\end{pmatrix}

$$
and $R_j^*$ is its $j$-th column. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem t:clustering.coeff of arXiv:2601.12677, 'Stable and Fréchet limit theorem for subgraph functionals in the hyperbolic random geometr'] Let $\frac{3}{4}<\alpha<1$. As $n\to\infty$, 
$$
B_{3,\alpha} C_{3,\alpha}^{-1}n^{\frac{1}{2\alpha}} \bigg( \mathsf{CC}_n - \frac{3N_n \mathbb{E}[\mathcal C_{3,n}(X_1)]}{\sum_{i=1}^{N_n}\mathcal D_{3,n}(X_i)} \bigg) \Rightarrow \frac{3S_{2\alpha}(1)}{\widetilde S_\alpha (1)},
$$
where $B_{3,\alpha}$ and $C_{3,\alpha}$ are constants defined before Theorems (t:joint.sum.max.star of the paper) and (t:joint.sum.max.clique of the paper), and the process $(\widetilde S_\alpha(\cdot), S_{2\alpha}(\cdot))$ is a {bivariate L\'evy process with perfectly dependent stable jumps}, defined by 
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E} \big[ e^{i(v_1\widetilde S_\alpha(t) + v_2 S_{2\alpha}(t))} \big] &=  \exp\Big\{  t\int_{(0,\infty)^2} \big( e^{i (v_1 x_1 + v_2 x_2)} -1- iv_2 x_2 \big) \kappa (\dif x_1, \dif x_2) \Big\}  \\
&= \exp\Big\{  t\int_0^\infty \big( e^{i (v_1 y + v_2 y^{1/2})} -1- iv_2 y^{1/2} \big) \mathsf{m}_\alpha (\dif y) \Big\},  \ \ \ t \ge 0, \ v_i \in {\mathbb R}, \, i=1,2. \notag  
\end{align}
Here,  $\kappa$ is a L\'evy measure concentrated on the curve $\{(y,y^{1/2}):y>0\}$, and it satisfies   $\kappa\big( (y_1,\infty] \times (y_2,\infty] \big) = y_1^{-\alpha}\wedge y_2^{-2\alpha}$ for  $y_1, y_2 >0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition eq:2.18 of arXiv:2607.24164, 'The KLS constant is $O(\log^{1/4} n)$'] Let $W\sim\lambda$ be a centered random vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$. A measurable
matrix valued function $\tau_\lambda:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, understood up to
$\lambda$-almost-everywhere equality and whose entries are locally integrable
with respect to $\lambda$, is called a
\emph{Stein kernel} for $\lambda$ if, for every smooth compactly
supported function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and every $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb{E}_{W\sim\lambda}\!\left[W_i f(W)\right]
  =
  \mathbb{E}_{W\sim\lambda}\!\left[
    \sum_{j=1}^n
    \bigl(\tau_\lambda(W)\bigr)_{ij}\partial_jf(W)
  \right].
\end{equation}
If $\tau_\lambda(u)$ is symmetric for $\lambda$-almost every $u$, we call it a
symmetric Stein kernel.

[Theorem thm:finite-r-annular of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let \(0<s<1\), \(r>1\), and \(\delta>0\). Let \(U\ge0\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{E} U=1\) and
\[
2^{1-r}\mathbb{E}[U^r]\le2^{-r(s+\delta)}.
\]
Let \(\nu_\circ=f_\#\widetilde\nu\) be the circle cascade generated by \(U\).  Then there exist constants \(C<\infty\), \(c>0\), and \(\eta>0\), depending only on \(s,r,\delta\) and on the law of \(U\), such that, for every \(n\ge1\),
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\left(
\sup_{2^n\le\lvert\xi\rvert\le2^{n+1}}
\lvert\widehat{\nu_\circ}(\xi)\rvert
>
C2^{-sn/2}
\right)
\le
C\exp(-c2^{\eta n})+C2^{-cn}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
\lvert\widehat{\nu_\circ}(\xi)\rvert=O(\lvert\xi\rvert^{-s/2})
\qquad (\lvert\xi\rvert\to\infty)
\]
almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:compression-master of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$, $k\geq2$, and let
$A=(a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_{k-1})$ be an ordered real $k$-set.  If
$r=r_h(A)$, define its successive active-relation degrees by
\[
 p_i(A)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(A)\geq i\},
 \qquad 1\leq i\leq r.
\]
Put $d_A=k-1-r$.  Since $r\leq k-2$, one has $d_A\geq1$.
Then there is an integer set
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A^*&=(0=a_0^*<a_1^*<\cdots<a_{k-1}^*),\\
 a_{k-1}^*
 &\leq d_Ah^{d_A-1}\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i(A)
 \leq(k-1-r)h^{k-2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the empty product is one,
such that, simultaneously for every $1\leq j\leq h$ and every
$u,v\in\mathcal U_{j,k}$,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A^*\bigr)
 =\operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A\bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus the ordered addition tables are identical in every degree $1\leq j\leq h$;
in particular, $|jA^*|=|jA|$ for $1\leq j\leq h$.

There is a complementary intrinsic statement.  Suppose $k\geq3$ and
\[
 B=(0=b_0<b_1<\cdots<b_{k-1}=d),
 \qquad \gcd(b_1,\ldots,b_{k-1})=1.
\]
For $1\leq i\leq k-2$, define the successive relation degrees
\[
 p_i(B)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(B)\geq i\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=d\leq\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}p_i(B).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $h\geq2$,
\begin{equation}
 \max_{\substack{B\subset\mathbb Z,\ |B|=k\\r_h(B)=k-2}}
       \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=h^{k-2}.
\end{equation}

body:
[Lemma L:arc-tangent-angle of arXiv:2607.15966, 'Canonical Mandelbrot Cascades on Curves Are Rajchman'] There exists a \(C^1\) function
\(\Theta_\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
        \gamma'(t)
        =
        |\gamma'(t)|
        \bigl(\cos\Theta_\gamma(t),\sin\Theta_\gamma(t)\bigr),
        \qquad
        \Theta_\gamma'(t)
        =
        \frac{\det(\gamma'(t),\gamma''(t))}
        {|\gamma'(t)|^2}.
\]
There are constants \(0<c_\gamma\leq C_\gamma<\infty\) such that
\[
        c_\gamma\leq|\Theta_\gamma'(t)|\leq C_\gamma
        \qquad(0\leq t\leq1).
\]
Consequently, \(\Theta_\gamma\) is strictly monotone and bi-Lipschitz onto its image.

Refuted inference, not a theorem: positive free/wired marginal differences in every finite volume by themselves imply a bulk first-order transition. The length-L endpoint-wired FK path has positive differences at every L, but for each fixed 0<p<1 and q>1 those differences tend geometrically to zero; its infinite-volume law is iid Bernoulli(p/[p+q(1-p)]). A valid critical-transition bridge needs a fixed-support positive limiting witness or a different argument.
Inference is refuted in a path family; this does not refute C0048 on Z^d,d>=3
title: DRAFT refuted route: finite boundary positivity as a transition certificate

[Corollary 4 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(I=[\alpha,\beta]\subset(0,\infty)\), \(0<\alpha<\beta<\infty\), and set \(a=\beta/\alpha>1\). Then the corresponding limiting objects satisfy
\[
\Lambda_I(\theta)=\alpha^{-1}\Lambda_a(\theta),
\qquad
J_I(x)=\alpha^{-1}J_a(\alpha x),
\qquad
\mathcal{C}_I(\theta)=\mathcal{C}_a(\theta).
\]
Moreover, the variables \(N_I(L)/L\) satisfy an LDP on \([0,\infty)\) with speed \(L\) and good rate function \(J_I\), and
\[
\log\mathbb{E}\exp(\theta N_I(L))
=
L\Lambda_I(\theta)+\mathcal{C}_I(\theta)+o(1)
\]
locally uniformly for \(\theta\in S_{\pi}\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 4 of arXiv:2608.17509

[Lemma 10 (sticky resolvent kernel) of arXiv:2605.13648, 'Sticky CIR process with potential: invariant measure and exact sampling'] \label[lemma]{lem:sticky-resolvent}
The fundamental solutions of $(\alpha-\mathcal{L})f=0$ satisfying the
boundary condition~\eqref{eq:wentzell} are $f_\infty(x) = U(a,b,z_x)$
and
\begin{equation}
  f_0^{\rm sticky}(x) = M(a,b,z_x) + c_\mu\,U(a,b,z_x),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
  c_\mu = \frac{-\alpha}{\mu\,|\mathcal{W}| + \alpha U_0}.
\end{equation}
The sticky resolvent kernel is
\[
  G^{\rm sticky}_\alpha(x,y) =
  \frac{f_0^{\rm sticky}(x\wedge y)\,f_\infty(x\vee y)}{|\mathcal{W}|},
\]
with the same normalisation constant $|\mathcal{W}|$ as the reflecting
resolvent kernel.

[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Let $\hat\psi(x)=\frac12x^\top\nabla^2\psi(0_d)x$ and
\be\begin{gathered}
A = \int_De^{-\la z(u)}\dd u,\quad B =  \frac{(2\pi/\la)^{d/2}}{\la\sqrt{\det H}},\\
a(u) = e^{-\la z(u)}, \qquad b(x,t)=e^{-\la x^\top Hx/2 - \la (t-\hat\psi(x))}.
\end{gathered}\ee 
Then 
\bs
\mathrm{TV}(\pi\vert_D,\hat\pi) \leq &|1-A/B| + \frac1B\int_{D_2\cup D_3}a(u)\dd u + \frac1B\int_{\hat D\setminus D_1}b(u)\dd u \\
&+\frac1B\int_{D_1\setminus \hat D}a(u)\dd u + \frac1B\int_{D_1}|a(u)-b(u)|\dd u,
\es where $D_1,D_2,D_3$ are as in~\eqref{D123} and $\hat D = \{(x,t)\in\br^{d+1}\,:\,t\geq\hat\psi(x)\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Thm algorithmic of arXiv:2606.01627, 'The geometry of the giant component of random geometric graphs'] Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be connected compact Riemannian manifolds of dimension $d_1, d_2 \geq 2$ and volume $1$ so that $M_1$ and $M_2$ are not isometric.  Let $\Delta_c(d_j)$ denote the critical average degree for having a giant component.  There is some $K = K(M_1,M_2) < \infty$ so that there is a deterministic algorithm depending on $M_1$ and $M_2$ with run time at most $n^K$ with the following properties.  There is $\alpha = \alpha(M_1,M_2)$ so that for each $\Delta_0 > \max\{\Delta_c(d_1),\Delta_c(d_2)\}$ there is $c = c(M_1,M_2,\Delta_0)$ so for all $\Delta \in [\Delta_0, \alpha n]$, given the adjacency matrices of the random geometric graphs  $G_{M_1}(n;r_1)$ and $G_{M_2}(n;r_2)$ of expected average degree $\Delta$, the algorithm can correctly identify which came from $M_1$ and $M_2$ with probability at least $1- \exp(-c \log^2 n)\,.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm algorithmic of arXiv:2606.01627

body: A filtration on a probability space (Omega, F, P) indexed by a totally ordered set T (typically T = {0,1,2,...} or T = [0, infinity)) is a family (F_t)_{t in T} of sub-sigma-algebras of F such that F_s is a subset of F_t whenever s <= t; F_t represents the information available at time t. A stochastic process (X_t)_{t in T} is adapted to (F_t) if X_t is F_t-measurable for every t in T. The natural filtration of a process (X_t) is F_t = sigma(X_s : s <= t), the smallest filtration to which the process is adapted. [standard, e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples]
title: Filtration and Adapted Stochastic Process

[Thm 95 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $L,\alpha>0$ and let $(\cA_N)^\circ$ be a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}. Let $\cA_N$ be the perturbation of $(\cA_N)^\circ$ from Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}. By passing to a subsequence $N_j\to\infty$, we assume that $\chi_{\cA_N}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, pointwise and in $L^1$. Denote $q_0\equiv \chi(0)\in[0,1]$. The function $p\equiv\chi^{-1}$ belongs to $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ and is concave, with
\[\frac1{L^2}
\le p'(q) \le L^2\] for all $q\in [q_0,1]$. Suppose $(\mu,\mu^\Ising)$ satisfies 
	\beq
	\bbW_2\big(\mu,\mu(\cA_N)\big)
	+\bbW_2\big(\mu^\Ising,
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_N)\big)
		\le \epsilon_\textup{apx}
		\,.
	\eeq
Then there exist $C(L) > 0$ and $q_*,b,\sigma,w,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ such that the following hold. Let $B(t)$ and $W(t)$ be standard Brownian motions and
\begin{align} 
        dX(t)
        &= p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + s(t) \sigma_t\,dB(t)\,,
        \\
        dX^{\Ising}(t)
        &= w_t\,dW(t) 
        \end{align}
on the time interval $q_* \le t \le 1$, with $X(q_*)\sim\zeta$ and $X^\Ising(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$.  Then: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
$b_t=b(t,X(t))$,
$\sigma_t=\sigma(t,X(t))$,
and $w_t=w(t,Y(t))$ 
for functions $b:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[-C(L),C(L)]$ and $\sigma,w:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[0,C(L)]$, such that the functions $p'(t)^{1/2} b(t,x), s(t) \sigma(t,x), w(t,x)$, are $C(L)$-Lipschitz in $(t,x)$.
\item 
We have the diffusivity constraint
        \beq
            \max\bigg\{
            \Big|\bbE[w(t,X^\Ising(t))^2]-1
            	\Big|
	:q_* \le t\le 1
\bigg\} \leq  o(1)\,.
\eeq

\item 
    We have the approximate budget constraints
       \beq 
            \int_{q_*}^1
            \bigg\{
            \bbE\bigg[ b(t,X(t))^2+ \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}
            	(\sigma(t,X(t))-1)^2\bigg]
            -
            \frac{(\bbE w(t,X^\Ising(t)) )^2}{\alpha}
            \bigg\}_+
            \de t
            \leq o(1)\,.\eeq

 \item  The initial measures $\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ satisfy $|\bE[X(q_*)^2]|\leq o(1)$ and  $|\bE[X^\Ising(q_*)^2] - q_*|\leq o(1)$.
\item  The initial time $q_*$ lies in $[q_0,q_0+ o(1)]$ and satisfies $p(q_*) \le o(1)$. 
\end{enumerate}
Lastly, we have
\beq
\begin{aligned}
	\bbW_2(\Law(X(1)),\mu)
	&\leq 
	O(\epsilon_\textup{apx}) 
	+ o(1)\,,\\ 
	\bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(1)),\mu^{\Ising})
	&\leq  O(\epsilon_\textup{apx})
	+ o(1)\,.
\end{aligned}
\eeq
In all the above assertions, the $o(1)$ denotes an error which can tend to zero as $L^{-\Theta(1)}$. Thus, the distributions $\mu,\mu^\Ising$ are well approximated by the distributions of the endpoints of the solution to the constrained SDE described above. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 95 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Theorem Thm:Skorokhod of arXiv:2604.07497, 'The Three-Dimensional Stochastic EMHD System: Local Well-Posedness and Maximal Pathwise So'] Suppose that $H$ is a complete and separable metric space. Let $\{ \mu_n \}_{n \in {\mathbb N}}$ be a sequence of probability measure on $\mathscr{B} (H)$ converging weakly to a probability measure $\mu$. Then there exists a probability space $\left(\Omega,\mathscr{F},{\mathbb P}  \right)$, a sequence of random variables $\{X_n\}_{n \in {\mathbb N}}$ whose laws are $\{ \mu_n \}_{n \in {\mathbb N}}$ and a random variable $X$ whose law is $\mu$ such that 
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} X_n = X, \ \ \ {\mathbb P}\text{-a.s.}
\]
title: Skorokhod's representation theorem

[Definition 3 (Random clock) of arXiv:2604.11434, 'Maxima of stationary systems of randomly time-changed L\'evy particles'] Given a L\'evy process $(L_t)_{t\ge 0}$ and a bounded function $\alpha:\RR \to (0,\infty)$, we define
\begin{align*}
  A_x(t)
  \ = \
  \int_0^t
  \alpha(L_r+x)
  \,\mathrm{d}r
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  T_x(t)
  \ = \
  \inf\{s\ge 0 \mid A_x(s)> t\}
  \,,\qquad
  t\ge 0 \,, x\in\RR\,.
\end{align*}
  We call $(T_x(t))_{t\ge 0}$ the random clock, $(A_x(t))_{t\ge 0}$ the inverse random clock, and $\alpha$ the mass function.
title: Random clock

[Lemma lem:smoothcontrol of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] For any fixed $\alpha > 0$ and $\lambda_0 > 1$, there are some constants $H > 0$ and $C, c > 0$ such that
the following statement holds for all $\lambda > \lambda_0$, all $\Delta \geqslant 1$, and all large enough $T > 0$.
Let $\mathbf{X}$ denote the $\lambda$-tilted line ensemble.
Then there is a random smooth function $\Phi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}_+$ satisfying the following three properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Almost surely, we have $X^2(t) \leqslant \Phi(t)$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$. 
    \item Almost surely, we have $\Phi''(t) \leqslant \frac{1}{2}$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$. 
    \item Defining the event
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{H} \coloneqq \mleft\{ \# \mleft\{ j \in \mathbb{Z} : |j \Delta| \leqslant T \text{ and } \Phi(j\Delta) \leqslant \tfrac{H}{2} \mright\}
        \geqslant \frac{\alpha-2}{\alpha} \mleft( \frac{2T}{\Delta} - 1\mright) \mright\},
    \end{equation}
    we have $\mathbb{P} [\mathcal{H} | X^1]  \geqslant \mleft( \frac{1-\Delta/2T}{\alpha} \mright)^2$ almost surely.
    
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:smoothcontrol of arXiv:2608.05089

[Lem 15 of arXiv:2608.13976, 'Boundary Harnack principle for diffusion with jumps on metric measure spaces'] Suppose ${\bf (\wh{EP})} _{\leq , r_0, \gamma}$ holds  with  $r_0>0$ and $\gamma>0.$
  Then there is a constant $C=C(r_0, \gamma)\geq 1$ such that
  for every ball $B$ with radius $r_0$ and  $\overline B\subsetneq \sX$,
   each open $U\subset  2^{-1}B$, $\xi\in U$ and $r\in (0, r_0/4)$,
$$
\P_x \left(\wh X^B_{\wh\tau^B_{B_U (\xi, r)}} \in U \right)
=\P_x \Big(\wh \tau^B_{U}>\wh\tau^B_{B_U(\xi,r)}\Big)
\leq   C \left( \E_x \left[ \wh\tau^B_{B_U(\xi,r)} \right] / r^\gamma \right)^{1/2} \quad\hbox{ for } x\in B_U(\xi, 3r/4).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 74 of arXiv:2607.10486, 'Weak martingale solutions to stochastic Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system with transport '] Assume that  $\rU$ is a topological vector space and $\rU^\prime$ its topological dual.

A function
\[
Q: [0,\infty) \times \Omega \to \mathscr{L}^+(\rU,\rU^\prime) 
\]
is said to be  a strongly predictable process if and only if for every $f \in \rU$, the new process 
  \[
[0,\infty) \times \Omega \ni (t,\omega)  \mapsto  Q(t,\omega)[f] \in \rU^\prime 
\]  
is predictable in the sense of the previous Definition \ref{def-precictable}, i.e.  for all $f,\, g \in \rU$ the process  
    \begin{equation*}
      s \mapsto \duality{f}{Q_s g}{\rU^\prime}{\rU} \mbox{ is } \mathscr{P}(\mathbb{F})\mbox{-measurable}.
   \end{equation*}
title: Definition 74 of arXiv:2607.10486

[Lemma 15 of arXiv:2608.14802, 'Dynamical Gibbs-non-Gibbs transitions for finite-alphabet models on trees'] Let $t>0$ and $\theta>4$. Denote by $\Delta := \{ (x,y)\in (0,1)^2 : x=y \}$
the diagonal of the strictly $p_2$-dominant chamber. The map $\widetilde{g}_t^{[2]}$
satisfies $\widetilde{g}_t^{[2]}(\Delta)\subseteq \Delta$ and is componentwise
increasing on $(0,1)^2$, that is,
\begin{equation*}
    \widetilde{g}_t^{[2]}(x,y) \leq \widetilde{g}_t^{[2]}(x',y')
\end{equation*}
componentwise whenever $x,x',y,y'\in(0,1)$, $x\leq x'$, and $y\leq y'$.
Furthermore, let $d_t:(0,1)\to(0,1)$ be the map induced by $\widetilde{g}_t^{[2]}$
on the diagonal, i.e., $ \widetilde{g}_t^{[2]}(x,x) = (d_t(x),d_t(x))$.
If $d_t$ has a unique fixed point $\rho\in (0,1)$, then every discrete trajectory in
$(0,1)^2$ under $\widetilde{g}_t^{[2]}$ converges to $(\rho,\rho)$.
title: Lemma 15 of arXiv:2608.14802

body: [Lemma lem:non_trivial_convex_combination_of_double_current of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$. If $(\alpha_j)_{1\leq j\leq n}\subseteq (0,1),$ $\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j=1$  and $\mathbf{P}^{\emptyset,A} = \sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j \mathbf{P}^{\emptyset,A_j},$ then $A=A_j$ for every $1\leq j\leq n.$ In particular, there are no non-trivial convex combinations $\mathbf{P}^{\emptyset,A} = \sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j \mathbf{P}^{\emptyset,A_j}.$

[Lemma 39 (Uniform parabolic atlas from bounded geometry) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix \(n\), \(m\geq2\), \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), \(\Lambda\geq1\), and
\(L>0\).  Let \(s(t)\), \(a\leq t\leq b\), be a Ricci flow with
\(b-a\leq L\), and suppose that the inequalities in
\eqref{eq:bounded-lifted-geometry} hold with this \(\Lambda\).  Then there
are \(r_*>0\) and \(A_*<\infty\), depending only on
\(n,m,\sigma,\Lambda,L\), with the following properties.  For every
\((\widetilde x_0,t_0)\), there are harmonic
coordinates for \(\widetilde s(t_0)\) on
\(B_{\widetilde s(t_0)}(\widetilde x_0,4r_*)\).  Keeping the spatial
coordinates fixed, they remain valid on
\[
 B_{\widetilde s(t_0)}(\widetilde x_0,4r_*)
 \times\bigl([t_0-(4r_*)^2,t_0+(4r_*)^2]\cap[a,b]\bigr).
\]
Parabolic estimates may therefore be applied on backward, forward, or
endpoint-truncated subcylinders contained in this set.  In these coordinates
the coefficients of \(\widetilde s\), \(\widetilde s^{-1}\), and the
Christoffel symbols have the finite parabolic H\"older bounds through order
\(m\) needed below, all bounded by \(A_*\).  On overlaps, the transition maps
and their inverses have uniform finite-order parabolic H\"older bounds through
the same order.  Radius-\(r_*/4\) one-sided or truncated subcylinders can be
chosen to cover space-time, while the radius-\(2r_*\) cylinders have uniformly
bounded overlap and admit spatial cutoffs with uniform derivative bounds.

body: [Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.25323, 'Slow Convergence of Ising and Spin Glass Models with Well-Separated Frustrated Vertices'] Let $\Lambda$ be a square lattice region with fixed $+$ sites on the boundary of $\Lambda$ and a fixed ferromagnetic interaction $J_{ij}=1$ on each boundary edge $(i,j)$. Suppose $\Lambda$ has exactly four frustrated faces, $f_{1},\dots,f_{4}$, that are symmetric around the center of the lattice region under 90 degree rotations and are well-separated (i.e., the shortest lattice path from $f_{i}$ to $f_{i+1}$ has length $2n$, $i=1,2,3$). Then there is a universal temperature $T$ such that the Glauber dynamics ${\mathcal{M}}$ for the spin glass model on $\Lambda$ with $f_{1},...,f_{4}$ the faces with frustration has mixing time $\tau({\mathcal{M}})\geq e^{cn}$, for some constant $c>0,$ whenever $t<T$.

Author-checked lemma; a parent-agent counter-check identified the mechanism, but the full proof has no independent review. Let theta be an invertible measurable measure-preserving transformation of (E,P), with measurable inverse, and n:E->Z measurable. The law of theta^(n(Z))Z for Z~P has density g(y)=sum over k in Z of 1_{n(theta^(-k)y)=k}. Consequently g is integer-valued and finite P-almost everywhere. An arbitrary noninteger target density requires additional randomness or a projection to a marginal.
Invertible measurable P-preserving theta with measurable inverse
Measurable finite integer n(Z)

Let X_0 -> S_0 be a flat morphism of algebraic stacks and S_0 -> S a square-zero extension with ideal I. There is a canonical obstruction class ob in Ext^2(L_{X_0/S_0}, f^* I) whose vanishing is necessary and sufficient for the existence of a flat deformation X over S. When the obstruction vanishes, the set of isomorphism classes of deformations is an affine space under Ext^1(L_{X_0/S_0}, f^* I), and the automorphism group of any deformation is Ext^0(L_{X_0/S_0}, f^* I).

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables with E[X_i] = 0 and |X_i| <= M almost surely for every i, and let sigma^2 = sum_{i=1}^n Var(X_i). Then for every t > 0, P(sum_{i=1}^n X_i >= t) <= exp(- t^2 / (2 (sigma^2 + M t / 3))), and the same bound holds for the lower tail by symmetry. When sigma^2 is much smaller than n M^2, this improves on Hoeffding's inequality, which does not use the variance. [standard, e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities]
title: Bernstein's Inequality for Sums of Independent Bounded Random Variables

body:
Let lambda<=n(lambda)<=poly(lambda), and let m,N and the seed length be polynomially bounded positive integers with N>=(n+1)*m. Let F_s:{0,1}^n->{0,1} be an efficiently evaluable noisy weak-PRF family at a fixed q in[0,1/2), in the sample-oracle sense of Definitions3.1–3.2. Choose one uniform seed S, one independent uniform N-bit pad Z, and one independent uniform permutation Pi of N coordinates as the secret key. Each encoder call independently samples m uniform X_j in{0,1}^n, m independent Bernoulli(q) bits E_j, and a fresh uniform filler R of length N-(n+1)*m; it returns Pi applied to(C xor Z), where C concatenates the pairs(X_j,F_S(X_j) xor E_j) and R. For any probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher making at most Q polynomially many adaptive encoder calls, there is a polynomial-time weak-PRF sample-oracle distinguisher making at most M=Q*m calls whose advantage bounds the encoding-oracle advantage up to min(1,binom(M,2)/2^n). Here the reference encoding oracle returns a fresh independent uniform N-bit word at every call. Thus the encoder is undetectable under the noisy weak-PRF assumption. Locality of F_s and decoder robustness are not needed for this claim.
A noisy weak-PRF family with uniform random input samples; polynomial parameter lengths and n>=lambda.
One shared independent seed,pad,permutation; fresh sample inputs,noise and filler per encoding.
At most polynomially many calls,with a fixed polynomial upper bound Q.

[Definition 4 (Maximal globally hyperbolic developments) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill
		\begin{itemize} 
			\item We say that a GHD $(\mathcal{M},\vec{\Psi})$ of the initial data $\mathring{\vec{\Psi}}$ on $\Sigma$ is extendible as a GHD
		 if there is another GHD $(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\widetilde{\vec{\Psi}})$ of $\mathring{\vec{\Psi}}$
		 such that $\mathcal{M} \subsetneq \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}$
		 and such that $\widetilde{\vec{\Psi}} \restriction_{\mathcal{M}} = \vec{\Psi} $.
		\item We say that $(\mathcal{M},\vec{\Psi})$ is a \emph{maximal globally hyperbolic development} (MGHD)
			of the initial data $\mathring{\vec{\Psi}}$ on $\Sigma$ if it is not extendible.
		\end{itemize}

body: [Problem 15 of arXiv:2607.28614, 'Tampered Memory Elephant Random Walk on one-dimensional integer lattice'] Is the TMERW recurrent, that is, is $\PP \left(S_n=0 \text{ i.o. }\right)=1$? Or does it display a phase transition between recurrence and transience? If there is a phase transition, then the critical parameter should be jointly determined by $\lim_{n}\frac{|D_n|}{|D_n^c|}$ and $p$. A similar question can be asked in dimensions $d \ge 2$. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Problem 15 of arXiv:2607.28614

[Definition def:conditions of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and a send sequence~$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, and an integer $j \ge 1$. We define the following conditions. 
\begin{enumerate}[({Con}1)]
\item 
Let $d \ge 0$ be real. A tuple $\overline{m} \in (\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0})^j$ \emph{satisfies (Con(item:Con1 of the paper)) for $d$} if $\mathrm{excess}(\overline{m}, 1) \le d$.
\item A tuple $\overline{m} \in (\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0})^j$ \emph{satisfies 
(Con(item:Con2 of the paper))} if
$\mathrm{excess}(\overline{m}, \xi^{-1/3}) \le 
\lambda j/500
$. 
\item Let $\varpi,\theta,\nu \ge 0$ be real. A tuple $\overline{m} \in (\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0})^j$ \emph{satisfies
(Con(item:Con3 of the paper)) for $(\varpi,\theta,\nu)$} if,
for all $k \in [j]$ with $W_k \ge \varpi$, $p_km_k \le \nu k + (1+\theta)P_k$.

\item Let $G$ be a positive real.
A tuple $\overline{m} \in (\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0})^j$ \emph{satisfies (Con(item:Con4 of the paper)) for~$G$} if for all $k \in [j]$, $p_km_k \le G j^2$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition def:conditions of arXiv:2602.21315

[Prop 30 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] For any real numbers $R > 1$ and $\delta \in (0,1)$, the following holds w.o.p.  with respect to $\mathbb P^N_{a,b,c}$. Fix real numbers $a, b, c \in [R^{-1}, R]$; sample a uniformly random tiling on a hexagon $\mathfrak{X}_{a, b, c}$ and denote its height function by $H : \overline{\mathfrak{X}}_{a, b, c} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.

			\item  We have $\sup_{z \in \mathfrak{X}_{a, b, c}} \big| H (z) - \mathcal{H}_{a, b, c} (z) \big| \le N^{\delta-1}$.

                        \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $a,b\in(0,+\infty)$, $\eta>0$, $k,d\in\mathbb N$, and $d\ge2$. There exists
a constant $C:=C(a,b,\eta,k,d)>0$ such that, for every
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_k),Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k)\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$
satisfying
\[
a\le \operatorname{Var}(X_j)\le b,
\quad
a\le \operatorname{Var}(Y_j)\le b
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and
\[
\det \Sigma^d(X)\ge \eta,
\quad
\det \Sigma^d(Y)\ge \eta,
\]
one has
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X,Y)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X,Y)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}.
\]

In particular, if a sequence
$X_n\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$ converges in distribution to an
$\mathbb R^k$-valued random vector $X_\infty$ whose distribution is absolutely
continuous, then the convergence holds in total variation and
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X_n,X_\infty)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X_n,X_\infty)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}
\]
for some constant $C>0$ depending on the sequence and on the limiting
distribution. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.01516

[Definition QFCLT of arXiv:2411.06861, 'Quenched invariance principle for random walks in random environments admitting a cycle de'] Set $X_t^{(n)}:=\frac{1}{n}X_{n^2t}, t\geq 0$. We say the \textit{quenched functional CLT} (QFCLT) or \textit{quenched invariance principle} holds for $X$ if for $\mathbb{P}$-a.s. $\omega$ under $\Prob_0^\omega$, $X^{(n)}$ converges in law to a Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with covariance matrix $\Sigma^2=\Sigma \cdot \Sigma^T$. That is, for every $T>0$ and every bounded continuous function $F$ on the Skorohod space $D([0, T], \mathbb{R}^d)$, setting $\psi_n= \Mean_0^\omega[F(X^{(n)})]$ and $\psi_\infty= \Mean_0^{\text{BM}}[F(\Sigma \cdot W)]$ with $(W, \Prob_0^{\text{BM}})$ being a Brownian motion started at $0$, we have that $\psi_n \to \psi_\infty \mathbb{P}$-a.s.

As our main result we establish a QFCLT for $X$ under some additional moment conditions.
title: QFCLT

	\begin{enumerate}
		\item (holomorphic bisectional curvature) if

	\density(\hbc_{Z(s)}<-a_d)
]
\geq 1-  C\left(\frac{a_d+C}{d}\right)^{3r-2n+2}.$$
	\item (holomorphic sectional curvature) If $2r\geq n$,
			$$

		[

		]\geq 
		1- C\left(\frac{a_d+C}{d}\right)^{2r-n+1}.$$
		\item (Ricci curvature) $\forall d\gg1, $  $\displaystyle\mathbb E 
		[
		\density(\ricci_{Z(s)} <-a_d)
		]\geq 1-C\left(\frac{a_d+C}{d}\right)^{r(n-r)-(n-r-1)}.$
\item (Scalar curvature) 
$\displaystyle \forall d\gg1, \

[
\density(\scal_{Z(s)} <-a_d)]\geq 1-
C \left(\frac{a_d+C}{d}\right)^{\frac{1}2r(n-r)(n-r+1)}.$

[Lemma rho of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Fix $\lambda > 0$, $\alpha > 0$. Define the function
    \begin{equation}
        \rho_{\lambda, \alpha}(x) \coloneqq \left(\phi(\lambda x) - \frac{(\lambda x)^2}{2}\right) \exp\left\{- x^\alpha \right\}.
    \end{equation}
    Then for $x > 0$ it holds that
    \[
    \sgn \rho_{\lambda, \alpha}'(x) = \sgn\left(\upsilon(\lambda x) - \alpha x^\alpha\right) ,
    \]
    where
    \begin{equation}
        \upsilon(t) \coloneqq \frac{t \phi(t)}{\phi(t) - t^2 / 2} .
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma rho of arXiv:2411.07878
