[OPEN PROBLEM - not a proved fact. Stated in arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured perturbations of tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices' (conjecture environment labelled con:banded).] Consider the symbol on $[0,1] \times \T$
\[ a(x,z) = \sum_{j=-q}^p a_j(x) z^j, \]
where for all $j$ $a_j(x)$ are continuous complex-valued functions on $[0,1]$. Let $\mu_n$ be the sequence of eigenvalue-counting measures
\[ \mu_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{\lambda \in \text{sp}(R_n(a))} \delta_{\lambda}. \]

body:
Let L be an exactly quadratic loss with symmetric positive semidefinite Hessian H. At theta let G=grad L(theta) satisfy A=G^T H G>0. Let g_B be the mean of B>=1 iid finite-second-moment gradients with mean G and per-example covariance Sigma. Write C=tr(H Sigma)>=0 and B_noise=C/A. For the update theta_next=theta-eta*g_B, E[L(theta_next)]=L(theta)-eta*||G||^2+(eta^2/2)*(A+C/B), exactly. The unique real minimizing step is eta_opt(B)=||G||^2/(A+C/B)=eta_max/(1+B_noise/B), where eta_max=||G||^2/A. The optimal expected loss decrease is Delta_opt(B)=Delta_max/(1+B_noise/B), where Delta_max=||G||^4/(2*A). If B_noise>0, batch B=B_noise in the continuous interpolation achieves half Delta_max. For a general smooth loss, the source obtains these expressions from a quadratic Taylor model; without a controlled remainder they are not exact guarantees, iteration-complexity bounds, or global convergence rates.

\[

\[

\right),
& n=3,4,5.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\ee

If $u_\infty>0$ and $Y_\Omega(u)\geq r_\infty$, then
\be
\|w\|
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
O\left(\mathfrak G(u)\right)+
O\left(
\mathfrak G(u)^{\frac{(n+2)}{2(n-2)}(1+\gamma)}
\left(-\ln\mathfrak G(u)\right)^{\frac{n+2}{2n}}\right),\quad
&n\geq6,\\[5mm]
\displaystyle
O\left(\mathfrak G(u)\right), \quad
&n=3,4,5.
\end{cases}
\ee

\item[(iii)] \textbf{Estimate of the regular-part parameters.}

Suppose that $u_\infty>0$. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\bm z'|^2
={}&
o(|\bm z''|^2)+
O\left(\mathfrak G(u)^{1+\gamma}\right)+
O\left(
\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}
\lambda_k^{-\frac{n-2}{2}(1+\gamma)}
\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Under the additional assumption that
$
Y_\Omega(u)\geq r_\infty,
$
we have
\[
|\bm z'|^2
=
o(|\bm z''|^2)
+
O\left(\mathfrak G(u)^{1+\gamma}\right).
\]

\end{itemize}

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. For every finite positive integer N,P,M, let X_R=U_R V_R^T/sqrt(N) have independent Rademacher factor entries and X_G=U_G V_G^T/sqrt(N) have independent standard Gaussian factor entries. With d=NP, D=d M^2[12(N+P)+8]/N^4 and T=893026 d^5 M^10/N^5, for 0<s<=D/(322560 T), I(X_R;sqrt(s)X_R+G)-I(X_G;sqrt(s)X_G+G)>=D s^4/80 and mmse(X_R)-mmse(X_G)>=D s^3/12. Here each MMSE uses its own Gaussian observation at SNR s and Frobenius loss. The SNR interval shrinks with dimension, so this is not a counterexample to limiting Gaussian-factor extremality at fixed SNR.
N,P,M positive finite integers
All factor entries independent within each model
Independent Gaussian observation noise
Dimension-dependent SNR interval as stated

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:83f6dcaea343c2d865df41dbc0af21794cabcd9d6a0d9a3e2bf0ce3e3164b137","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/83/83f6dcaea343c2d865df41dbc0af21794cabcd9d6a0d9a3e2bf0ce3e3164b137.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:2f3275b96176775d8eb5dc40419f498be81655f87995faf6f4fc0f29ccdd72c9","bundle_entry_key":"finite-size-gaussian-factor-reversal-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-finite-moment-and-orbit-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:finite-size-gaussian-factor-reversal-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Finite-size Gaussian-factor extremality reverses at sufficiently low SNR

Target 2, finite-size special case. Proof draft, unaudited.
This does not settle extremality at a fixed SNR after the extensive-rank limit.

Let N,P,M>=1 be integers. Compare the product signals

 X_R=U_R V_R^T/sqrt(N),   X_G=U_G V_G^T/sqrt(N),

where the entries in U_R,V_R are independent uniform signs and the
entries in U_G,V_G are independent standard Gaussians; all factor
arrays are independent in their respective models. Let G be an
independent standard Gaussian observation matrix. Set d=NP, b=M/N.
Define

 D = d M^2/N^4 [12(N+P)+8] > 0,
 T = d^5 M^10/N^5 (893026),
 s_0 = D/(322560 T) > 0.

Then for 0<s<=s_0 the proposed conclusions are

 I(X_R;sqrt(s)X_R+G)-I(X_G;sqrt(s)X_G+G) >= D s^4/80,

 mmse(X_R|sqrt(s)X_R+G)-mmse(X_G|sqrt(s)X_G+G)
      >= D s^3/12.                                      (1)

Here mmse denotes E||X-E[X|Y]||_F^2, the MMSE of the scaled product.
For the unscaled product UV^T the MSE is N times larger; normalization
by NP preserves the strict comparison.

## Proof

Both vectorized products have mean zero, covariance b I_d, globally
symmetric distributions, and finite moments of every order. Their
third cumulants vanish. The fourth-cumulant formula in the expansion
proof gives

 ||K4_G||^2-||K4_R||^2
  = (M/N^2)^2 d [ (36-4)+12(P-1)+12(N-1)]
  = D.                                                   (2)

The rectangle terms cancel. The fourth moments of the factor laws are
3 and 1, respectively. In particular, the Gaussian FACTOR product has
the larger fourth-cumulant norm; it is not a Gaussian vector signal.

The tenth moments of a scalar standard Gaussian and a scalar sign
are 945 and 1. The explicit factor-moment bound (11) of
finite_moment_expansion.md gives

 E||X_G||^10+E||X_R||^10
    <= d^5 M^10/N^5 (945^2+1)=T.                         (3)

Subtracting their mutual-information expansions gives D s^4/48,
with absolute remainder at most 2688 T s^5. For s<=s_0 this is at
most D s^4/120, proving the first inequality of (1), since
1/48-1/120=1/80.

For the MMSE use equation (7) and the expansion of F from
finite_moment_expansion.md. For bounded symmetric signals,

 mmse(X|sqrt(s)X+G)
   = db-db^2 s+db^3 s^2-(db^4+||K4||^2/6)s^3+Q(s),

 |Q(s)| <= 26880 E||X||^10 s^4,                         (4)

because the fourth derivative of F is bounded by
2^4 8! E||X||^10 and the third-order Taylor remainder divides by
4!=24. This bound passes to finite tenth moments under the centered
and covariance-normalized truncation in Section C of that proof.

The needed MMSE convergence follows directly: posterior overlap is
an integral of

 ||E[X phi(y-sqrt(s)X)]||^2 / E[phi(y-sqrt(s)X)],

which converges pointwise on compact y-sets under L^2 convergence of
the signal and is bounded by E[||X||^2 phi(y-sqrt(s)X)] by conditional
Cauchy-Schwarz. Its integral outside ||y||<=L is at most
E[||X||^2 1_{||sqrt(s)X+G||>L}], which vanishes uniformly for the
truncation sequence by its uniformly bounded fourth moments and
Gaussian tails. Thus posterior overlaps and MMSE converge. The same
argument works at s=0 directly.

Subtracting (4) gives a leading difference D s^3/6 and error at most
26880 T s^4. At s<=s_0 this is at most D s^3/12, proving the second
inequality of (1).

Every denominator is positive, including N, T and 322560. The endpoint
s=0 gives equality, so strict comparison is asserted only for s>0.
The constants are deliberately conservative.

## What the statement does and does not decide

For every fixed finite triple of dimensions, Gaussian factors fail
to maximize both product MMSE and mutual information over iid
unit-variance factor priors. Rademacher factors have strictly larger
values on the displayed interval. This is compatible with the scalar
Gaussian-SIGNAL extremality theorem, which optimizes over Gaussian
input X itself rather than Gaussian U and V.

The explicit interval depends on dimension and shrinks to zero under
proportional growth. No comparison of the limiting functions at fixed
positive SNR follows. In particular this is not a disproof of the
limiting Gaussian-factor conjecture in Target 2.

Checks: N=P=M=1 gives D=32, T=893026 and leading MI difference
2s^4/3, leading MMSE difference 16s^3/3. The sign of each comparison,

body: Method (campaign status: audited-pass): Transfer from real signed projective classes to a binary quotient. Given a real residual R of dim d, replace R by R_0 = span of (every f in D_n in the zero class) and (every f - sigma*g in R, sigma in {+-1}, witnessing a class equality). R_0 is rational, contained in R, of dim d_0 <= d, and induces exactly the same classes. Put Lambda = R_0 cap Z^{n+1}; it is saturated, hence a direct summand of Z^{n+1}, so its mod-2 reduction has dimension d_0. Signs die in characteristic two, so the real signed partition (zero class included) REFINES the coset partition mod Lambda-bar. All D_n vectors have odd weight; translating by A=e_0 lands in the even-weight space E with basis u_i=e_0+e_i, sending A->0, B_i->u_i, C_i->u_i+u_{i+1}. Set W = Lambda-bar cap E, dim W <= d_0 <= d. Notes: No reduction-of-rank assumption is hidden: passing to the SATURATED lattice is precisely what stops a denominator divisible by 2 from invalidating the mod-2 argument (S10 lines 269-272, p.162). The zero class costs no lost +1 (S11 lines 104-106). Field-critical: the argument is R -> F_2 and uses sigma=+-1 |-> 1.

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. [Lem l:weakM1transf of arXiv:2605.08983, 'A functional limit theorem for self-normalized linear processes with random coefficients a'] Let $(A_{n}, B_{n})$, $n=0,1,2,\ldots$, be stochastic processes in $D^{2}$ such that, as $n \to \infty$,
\begin{equation}
(A_{n}, B_{n}) \xrightarrow{d} (A_{0}, B_{0})
\end{equation}
in $D^{2}$ with the weak $M_{1}$ topology. Suppose $x_{n}$ and $y_{n}$, $n=0,1,2,\ldots$, are elements of $D^{1}$ with $x_{0}$ and $y_{0}$ being continuous, such that, as $n \to \infty$,
$$x_{n}(t) \to x_{0}(t) \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad y_{n}(t) \to y_{0}(t) $$
uniformly in $t$. Then
$$ (A_{n} +x_{n}, B_{n} + y_{n}) \xrightarrow{d} (A_{0} + x_{0}, B_{0} + y_{0})$$
in $D^{2}$ with the weak $M_{1}$ topology. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:tropp_moment of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let independent random matrices $\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_n \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ satisfy for all $k = 1, \dots, n$, all $p = 2, 3, \dots$, with some $K > 0$ and positive-definite matrices $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k$
    \[
    \E \mathbf{X}_k = 0,
    \quad
    \E \mathbf{X}^p_k \preccurlyeq \frac{p!}{2} K^{p-2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k.
    \]
    Let $\sigma^2 \coloneqq \norm*{\sum^n_{k = 1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k}. $ Then for all $t \ge 0$
    \[
    \mathbb{P} \lr{\lambda_{\max}\left(\sum^n_{k=1} \mathbf{X}_k\right) \ge t} \le d \elr{- \frac{t^2}{2 (\sigma^2 + K t)}}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:convex-linear-bound of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N$ be i.i.d.\ mean-zero variables with finite
		variance. Let $F$ be convex in each
		coordinate and suppose that, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely, for every $1\leq i\leq N$,
		\[
			0\leq\partial_i^+F\leq b_i\, ,
		\]
		where the $b_i$ are deterministic. Then there is a universal
		$C<\infty$ such that, for every $L>0$,
		\[
			\mathbb{E}\left[\left(
			F-\mathbb{E} F-\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb{E}[\partial_i^+F]\xi_i

Let f:R^d->R be C1,P a fixed symmetric positive-definite matrix,eta>0,and beta in[0,1). Run m_(t+1)=beta*m_t+(1-beta)*grad f(x_t),x_(t+1)=x_t-eta*P^(-1)*m_(t+1),from arbitrary x_0,m_0. For ftilde(y)=f(P^(-1/2)y),unpreconditioned EMA heavy ball initialized at y_0=P^(1/2)x_0,p_0=P^(-1/2)m_0 satisfies y_t=P^(1/2)x_t,p_t=P^(-1/2)m_t for all t. For a positive-definite quadratic Hessian H,the equilibrium is linearly asymptotically stable exactly when lambda_max(P^(-1/2)H P^(-1/2))<2*(1+beta)/(eta*(1-beta)). At beta=.9 the threshold is 38/eta. Above threshold an unstable mode exists;initialization at the equilibrium still stays fixed. This is fixed-preconditioner conjugacy and its quadratic consequence,not adaptive Adam tracking. Draft,independent review pending.
Finite d>=1;C1 objective;fixed SPD P;eta>0 and0<=beta<1;arbitrary initial momentum and position.
Positive-definite quadratic H for the stability corollary;EMA normalization and no bias correction.

[Theorem 12 (The symmetric-function action) of arXiv:2609.03881, 'Eulerian insertion operators and an Eulerian form of the Pieri rule'] Let \(g\in\Lambda_m\) and \(f\in\mathrm{QSym}_N\).  Since every symmetric function is quasisymmetric, we have
$\Lambda_m\subseteq\mathrm{QSym}_m$.
Thus \(gf\in\mathrm{QSym}_{N+m}\).
Then we have
\[
 \Phi_{N+m}(gf)=\rho(g)\Phi_N(f).
\]
In particular, for every partition \(\lambda\),
$\Phi_{N+|\lambda|}(s_\lambda f)
 =\G_\lambda\Phi_N(f)$.
Moreover, for all partitions \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), we have
\[
 \G_\lambda\G_\mu
 =\sum_{\nu\vdash|\lambda|+|\mu|}
   c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}\G_\nu.
\]

body: Let D(n) be the set of |a - b| over all factorizations n = ab. For k = 2 the integers {48, 240} satisfy D(48) intersect D(240) = {8, 22} (Erdos-Rosenfeld 1997), and for k = 3 the integers {6925500, 37901500, 108448956} have the four differences {420, 3780, 14940, 76860} common to all three (Jimenez-Urroz 1999), so both cases of the problem (k positive integers whose factor-difference sets share at least k values) hold. Since d lies in D(N) exactly when d^2 + 4N is a perfect square, the integers N sharing a fixed set of differences are read off the divisors of fixed numbers; a complete enumeration of this kind shows that the only integers carrying all four differences 420, 3780, 14940 and 76860 are the three above, so no fourth integer extends this triple and a k = 4 example needs a different set of differences (Bremner 2019 gives one). The intersection is finite because every element of D(n) is at most n.

[Lemma lem:modulus of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a compact interval of length $l$ and let $\phi \colon I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and increasing.  Then there exists a continuous, strictly increasing, concave function $\omega \colon [0,l]\to[0,\infty)$ with $\omega(0)=0$ such that
\begin{equation}
    0\le \phi(b)-\phi(a)\le\omega(b-a)
    \qquad\text{whenever }a,b\in I
    \quad \text{with } a\le b.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\omega^{-1}$ is convex and strictly increasing on $[0,\omega(l)]$.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Locate the obstruction between the known polynomial regimes and a finite threshold. Result: Delocalisation is known in d = 3 for W >= N^{c} with explicit c (Yang-Yau-Yin quantum-diffusion results for W >> N^{1-eps} and later improvements), and the mean-field reduction of the source suggests W >> N^{1-eps}; a finite W_c requires an argument uniform in N at fixed W, i.e. a renormalisation-group or supersymmetric proof of diffusion for the Green function, which exists only for the density of states (Disertori-Pinson-Spencer in d = 3) and not for eigenvector delocalisation. The gap between 'W a power of N' and 'W fixed' is the same as between the T-expansion of Yang-Yau and a genuinely non-perturbative statement. A rigorous partial fact: the Thouless criterion (conductance ~ W^2 (N/W)^{2-d} ... ) predicts W_c = O(1) in d = 3 because the conductance grows with N at fixed W, and the source's heuristic is consistent; but no rigorous statement. No result. Obstruction: All rigorous delocalisation results need W to grow with N; a fixed-W argument is non-perturbative.

For a real number t write ||t|| for its distance to the nearest integer. Fix an irrational alpha and suppose alpha is DIOPHANTINE of type (C, tau): there are constants C > 0 and tau >= 1 with

  ||q alpha||  >=  C * q^{-tau}    for every integer q >= 1.

Then:

(i) (the small divisors are only polynomially small) for every nonzero integer q,
      | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 |  =  2 | sin(pi q alpha) |  >=  4 ||q alpha||  >=  4 C |q|^{-tau}.
    The upper bound | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 | <= 2 pi ||q alpha|| always holds, so the two sides are comparable to ||q alpha||.

(ii) (solving the cohomological equation) Let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle T = R/Z and let f be a C^infinity function on T with mean zero. Then the equation u(x + alpha) - u(x) = f(x) has a C^infinity solution u, unique up to an additive constant, given on Fourier coefficients by u-hat(q) = f-hat(q) / (e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1) for q nonzero. Quantitatively |u-hat(q)| <= |q|^{tau} |f-hat(q)| / (4C), so one loses tau derivatives: in Sobolev scale ||u||_{H^{s - tau}} <= (4C)^{-1} ||f||_{H^s}, and the analogous statement holds in Holder scale with an epsilon loss.

(iii) (how common the hypothesis is) For every tau > 1, Lebesgue-almost every alpha is Diophantine of type (C, tau) for some C = C(alpha) > 0; for tau = 1 the alpha satisfying the condition are exactly the badly approximable ones (bounded partial quotients), a set of Lebesgue measure zero and full Hausdorff dimension; for tau < 1 no alpha satisfies it at all, by Dirichlet's theorem.

WHERE IT FAILS. If alpha is LIOUVILLE (no such C, tau exist), the conclusion of (ii) fails badly: choose q_1 < q_2 < ... with ||q_k alpha|| < q_k^{-k} and define f by f-hat(q_k) = f-hat(-q_k)-bar = ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} and all other coefficients zero. These coefficients decay faster than any power of q_k, so f is C^infinity with mean zero, yet |u-hat(q_k)| >= ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||) = 1 / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||^{1/2}), which blows up faster than any polynomial in q_k. Hence no solution u exists in L^2, and not even a distributional solution exists. So the Diophantine condition is not a technical convenience: it is what separates solvability from non-solvability. Note also that (ii) gives no information at all about the SPEED of ergodic averages by itself, and that the estimates degrade as C -> 0, so any application that needs uniformity must track C and tau explicitly.
alpha is irrational and satisfies ||q alpha|| >= C q^{-tau} for all integers q >= 1, with C > 0 and tau >= 1
||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer
in part (ii), f is C^infinity on the circle R/Z with mean zero, and the rotation is x -> x + alpha
solutions are sought up to an additive constant; L^2 and distributional solutions are compared by Fourier coefficients
title: Small divisor estimates for a Diophantine circle rotation

coordinate shells into hyperoctahedral orbits and let $E_\lambda$ denote the
full coordinate subspace supported on the orbit $\mathcal O_\lambda$.  For

\[
 \left\lVert E_\mu A_N^jE_\lambda\right\rVert
 \leq C_JN^{a_j(\lambda,\mu)/2},
\]
with the same dimensional-edge count as in Lemma~(lem:pathbound of the paper).  The
constant is uniform over all irreducible components of the shell spaces.

body:
Theorem 6: d >= 2, E[tau_e^2] < infinity, F(0) < p_c, xhat a direction of curvature for the limit shape
Wehr-Aizenman bound chi_x >= (1 - (d-1) xi_x)/2: the hypotheses of Newman-Piza Theorem 2
Theorem 7: F(0) < p_c, E[exp(beta tau_e)] < infinity for some beta > 0, xhat a direction of curvature
chi_x >= 1/8 holds only when d = 2; xi_x <= 3/4 is stated for d >= 2
the exponents are Newman-Piza's own definitions, not Chatterjee's and not each other's

THE CURVATURE HYPOTHESIS IS NON-CONSTRUCTIVE. Directions of curvature are known to exist - at least four, by symmetry, via a non-constructive argument the survey reproduces - but no explicit direction, not even a coordinate axis, is provably one. Every consequence of Theorem 6 or Theorem 7 inherits that. The log-variance lower bound of Theorem 2 does NOT: it is direction-uniform and curvature-free.
WITHOUT curvature the best bounds on the wandering exponent are still 0 <= xi <= 1, the upper bound following directly from the shape theorem.
WHERE THE 3/4 COMES FROM: Theorem 6 combined with chi' <= 1/2, which the survey attributes to Kesten and to Alexander. The survey also gives an alternative modern route to xi_x <= 3/4 through Damron-Hanson-Sosoe's exponential concentration at chi = 1/2 + delta.
RELATION TO THE SCALING RELATION: the survey records that Theorem 6 is 'a version of the inequality chi >= 2 xi - 1', and that Newman-Piza describe their own argument as essentially a rigorous version of the Krug-Spohn heuristic for the relation.
SOURCE: Newman-Piza (1995), Ann. Probab. 23, 977-1005. Read in Auffinger-Damron-Hanson, '50 years of first passage percolation', arXiv:1511.03262v2 (AMS University Lecture Series 68, 2017), theorems 'thm:NPScaling' and 'thm:exponent_bounds' and equation 'eq:WehrAiz', tex lines 2698-2723.
VERIFICATION STATUS: survey-claim. Lane P4 did not read Newman-Piza (1995).
title: Newman-Piza (1995), Theorems 6 and 7: in d >= 2 with E[tau_e^2] < infinity and F(0) < p_c, if xhat is a DIRECTION OF CURVATURE of the limit shape then xi_x <= (1 + chi')/2; under the Theorem-2 hypotheses they also get the Wehr-Aizenman bound chi_x >= (1 - (d-1) xi_x)/2; and if in addition E[exp(beta tau_e)] < infinity for some beta > 0 then xi_x <= 3/4 and, in d = 2 only, chi_x >= 1/8. Every one of these carries the NON-CONSTRUCTIVE curvature hypothesis.

body: Let X be a Banach space, Y a normed vector space, and F a family of bounded linear operators from X to Y. Suppose F is pointwise bounded: for every fixed x in X, the set {||Tx|| : T in F} is bounded in [0, infinity). Then F is uniformly bounded in operator norm, i.e. sup over T in F of ||T|| is finite, so ||Tx|| <= C ||x|| holds for all T in F and x in X with one constant C. The proof uses the Baire category theorem, and completeness of X is essential.
title: Uniform boundedness principle (Banach-Steinhaus theorem)

[Lemma 28 of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] Let \(\mathsf a_n>0\), and suppose that
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf a_n^{1/n}=\lambda>0.

\[
  \mathcal R_n\ge b,\qquad
  \mathcal R_{n+h}-\mathcal R_n\ge-\frac{K}{n},
  \qquad n\ge n_0,
\]
then
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathcal R_n=\lambda^h.
\]

body:
[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Assume the same set-up as in Theorem \ref{thm:PoisConvAbstract} and denote by $L_{t,W}$ the length of the longest edge with midpoint in $W$, i.e., 
$$
L_{t,W} := \max\Big\{\|x-y\|:(x,y)\in\eta_{t,\neq}^2,(\eta_t-\delta_x-\delta_y)(S(x,y))=0,{x+y\over 2}\in W\Big\}. 
$$
Then, for any $t\geq 2$,
$$
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{Kol}}\big(\gamma tL_{t,W}^d-\log(t)-\log(\kappa_d/(2\gamma)),G_W\big) \leq \begin{cases}
        c\log^{-(d-2)}(t), & d \ge 3,\\
        c\log^{-1/2}(t), & d=2,
    \end{cases}
$$
where $c$ is a constant only depending on $d$, $\vol(W)$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$, and $G_W$ is a Gumbel distributed random variable with distribution function $\PP(G_W\leq s)=\exp(-\vol(W)e^{-s})$ for $s\in\RR$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 6 of arXiv:2604.09248

[Theorem 2 (Parabolic subsolution identities for Hermite energies) of arXiv:2607.07712, 'Parameter-Space Heat Flow, Gaussian Density Ratios, and Sharp Hermite Truncation Rates'] Let \(F_\tau\) solve
\[
\partial_\tau F_\tau
=
\frac12\Delta_uF_\tau
\]
in the sense above.  Then each Hermite block energy satisfies
\begin{equation}
\left(
\partial_\tau-\frac12\Delta_u
\right)
E_m(\tau,u)
=
-
\|\nabla_u\Pi_mF_\tau(u;\cdot)\|_{L^2(\gamma_d;\mathbb R^d)}^2
\le0.

\end{equation}
Similarly, each Hermite truncation-tail energy satisfies
\begin{equation}
\left(
\partial_\tau-\frac12\Delta_u
\right)
T_M(\tau,u)
=
-
\|\nabla_u(I-\Pi_{\le M})F_\tau(u;\cdot)\|_{L^2(\gamma_d;\mathbb R^d)}^2
\le0.

\end{equation}
If, in addition,
\[
F_\tau=e^{(\tau/2)\Delta_u}F_0
\]
and the heat-kernel representation is justified, then
\[
E_m(\tau,u)
\le
e^{(\tau/2)\Delta_u}E_m(0,u),
\qquad
T_M(\tau,u)
\le
e^{(\tau/2)\Delta_u}T_M(0,u).
\]

[Lemma l:decomposition-curve of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'] Let $\gamma,\tilde{\gamma}$ be two curves as in Theorem~(t:local-holonomies of the paper) such that $\gamma([0,1])=\tilde{\gamma}([0,1])$ and such that $\gamma(0)=\tilde{\gamma}(0)$. Then, one has almost surely
 $$
 \mathrm{g}_{\gamma}(1)=\mathrm{g}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(1).
 $$
 Moreover, if one decomposes $\gamma=\gamma_1\star\left(\gamma_2\star\left(\ldots\star\gamma_J\right)\right)$ into elementary pieces (including the blowup case of \S(ss:blowup-Wiener-max of the paper)), then
 $$
  \mathrm{g}_{\gamma}(1)=\mathrm{g}_{\gamma_J}(1)\ldots\mathrm{g}_{\gamma_2}(1)\mathrm{g}_{\gamma_1}(1),
 $$
 and $(\mathrm{g}_{\gamma_J}(1),\ldots,\mathrm{g}_{\gamma_2}(1),\mathrm{g}_{\gamma_1}(1))$ are independent random variables. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In computability theory, the Church–Turing thesis is a thesis about the nature of computable functions. It states that a function on the natural numbers can be calculated by an effective method if and only if it is computable by a Turing machine. The thesis is named after American mathematician Alonzo Church and the British mathematician Alan Turing. Before the precise definition of computable function, mathematicians often used the informal term effectively calculable to describe functions that are computable by paper-and-pencil methods. In the 1930s, several independent attempts were made to formalize the notion of computability:In 1933, Kurt Gödel, with Jacques Herbrand, formalized the definition of the class of general recursive functions: the smallest class of functions that is closed under composition, recursion, and minimization, and includes zero, successor, and all projections. In 1932–33, Alonzo Church created a method for defining functions called the λ-calculus. Within λ-calculus, he defined an encoding of the natural numbers called the Church numerals.
title: Church–Turing thesis

[Lemma0 of arXiv:2411.08846, 'On the Number of Crossings and Bouncings\\ of a Diffusion at a Sticky Threshold'] Let $X$ be the sticky Brownian motion of stickiness parameter $\rho>0 $, defined on the probability space $(\Omega, \bF, (\bF_t)_{t\ge 0}, \Prob_x) $ such that $X_0 = x $, $\Prob_x$-a.s..
Let $ (f_n,k_n,g_n,h_n;\,n\in\IN) $ be the functions defined for all $n \in \IN$ and $x\in \IR $ by 
$f_n(x) := \Prob_{x} \left(  X_{1/n} = 0 \right) $, 
$k_n(x) := \mathbbm{1}_{\{x\not = 0\}} f_n(x/\sqrt n) $, 
$g_n(x) := \Prob_{x} \left( x X_{1/n} < 0 \right) $, 
$h_n(x) := \sqrt n g_n(x/\sqrt n) $.
It holds that 
\begin{enumerate}
	[label={\upshape (\roman*)}]
	\item  $\lim_{n \rightarrow  \infty} f_n(0) = 1 $ and 
	$\lim_{n \rightarrow  \infty} \sqrt n (1- f_n(0)) =

body:
[Maintheorem 1 of arXiv:2609.02449, 'Finite Directional Coefficient Modules over Euler Fibers of $A$-Hypergeometric Systems'] Let $A\in\Mat_{d\times n}(\Z)$ have rank $d$, let $\bm{\beta}\in\C^{d}$, put $L=\Ker_{\Z}(A)$, and fix an $L$-generic direction $\bm{w}\in\R^{n}$.
Then the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (1)]
\item For every exponent lattice $\Lambda\in\mathfrak{L}_{\bm{\beta}}$, the classwise directed formal logarithmic solution space is represented by the finite directional coefficient module through the isomorphisms in \cref{thm:directed-coefficient-module-presentation}.
\item An exponent lattice contributes a nonzero directed formal logarithmic solution space if and only if it possesses a bounded inclusion-minimal negative-support stratum; every such stratum minimum is realized as a lowest exponent by \cref{thm:minimal-support-solutions-nonvanishing}.
\item Only finitely many exponent lattices contribute, by \cref{thm:finiteness-admissible-exponent-lattice-family}.
\item Every contributing classwise directional coefficient module and the all-lattice directional coefficient module have finite length, by \cref{thm:finite-length-classwise-all-lattice-modules}.
\item The dimension of the all-lattice directed formal logarithmic solution space is given by \eqref{eq:introduction-global-length-dimension}, and every normalized coefficient family is explicitly realized as a formal logarithmic series by \cref{thm:formal-logarithmic-realization}.
\item All realizable lowest exponents are determined by the finite criteria in \cref{thm:finite-criterion-all-classwise-realizable-exponents,thm:polynomial-colon-ideal-criterion-classwise-realizability}.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 31 (Compatible prefix time) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Fix $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm and let $W_{\C}$ be its
complexification. For every finite symmetric set
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$, define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum, the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_*\in[0,T]$ such that, for every finite symmetric
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$,
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1},
\qquad
a_\Lambda=r_{t_*}^\Lambda.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
r_{t_*}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_*}^\Lambda\bigr)
\]
for every such $\Lambda$.
title: Compatible prefix time

body: In number theory and complex analysis, a modular form is a type of function of a complex number variable that possesses a high degree of symmetry, of a certain kind. Similarly to a periodic function of a real variable, a modular form repeats or transforms in a certain way when its argument is subjected to a particular transformation. Unlike an ordinary periodic function, its symmetries include transformations such as replacing a complex number z by −1/z, and the transformation law is not an exact symmetry of the function, but more like the transformation law of a quasiperiodic function: the function picks up an additional factor, depending on the transformation. Modular forms serve as an important bridge between complex analysis, number theory, and geometry. Modular forms also appear in other areas, such as algebraic topology, sphere packing, and string theory.
title: Modular form

\]

body: [Definition 2.1 of arXiv:2605.25323, 'Slow Convergence of Ising and Spin Glass Models with Well-Separated Frustrated Vertices'] For ε > 0, the mixing time is defined as τ(ϵ) = min{t : max x∈S X y∈S ||P t′(x, y), π(y)|| ≤ϵ, for all t′ ≥t}. A Markov chain is rapidly (or polynomially) mixing if the mixing time is bounded above by a polynomial in log S, the length of a description of a state in S. A chain is slowly mixing if the mixing time is bounded below by an exponential function.

body:
[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Let  $\lambda_1(\beta)>\lambda(\beta) $ denote the next eigenvalue of
 $H_\beta $.  Then, for every compact  $K\subset\mathbb R^d $,
\begin{equation}
 Z_T(\beta,x)
 =\mathrm e^{-\lambda(\beta)T}\phi_\beta(x)\|\phi_\beta\|_1
 \left(1+O_K\!\left(\mathrm e^{-[\lambda_1(\beta)-\lambda(\beta)]T}\right)\right)
 
\end{equation}
uniformly for  $x\in K $.  In particular, the same assertion holds with
an  $O_x(\cdot) $ error for every fixed  $x $.

body:
[Lem OSSS of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] Let $f\colon\{0,1\}^N\to\{0,1\}$ be an increasing Boolean function.
  For any algorithm $\mathcal{A}$,
  \[
  \Var_p(f)\le p(1-p)\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_p(i,f;\mathcal{A})\Inf_p(i,f).
  \]
  Here,
  \[
  \Inf_p(i,f):=\mathbb{E}_p[|f-(f\circ\mathrm{Flip}_i)|]
  \]
  denotes the influence of the $i$th bit on $f$, where $\mathrm{Flip}_i\colon\{0,1\}^N\to\{0,1\}^N$ is the map that flips the $i$th value. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The OSSS inequality~\cite{OSSS2005}

body: [Theorem 2.3 (Von Neumann’s Minimax Theorem (see [Sim95]) of arXiv:2203.06168, 'Cheeger Inequalities for Vertex Expansion and Reweighted Eigenvalues'] Let X, Y be compact convex sets. If f is a real-valued continuous function on X × Y with f(x, ·) concave on Y for all x ∈X and f(·, y) convex on X for all y ∈Y , then min x∈X max y∈Y f(x, y) = max y∈Y min x∈X f(x, y). Several eigenvalue optimization problems can be formulated as semidefinite programs.

body: The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem is a fundamental result of mathematical analysis giving necessary and sufficient conditions to decide whether every sequence of a given family of real-valued continuous functions defined on a closed and bounded interval has a uniformly convergent subsequence. The main condition is the equicontinuity of the family of functions. The theorem is the basis of many proofs in mathematics, including that of the Peano existence theorem in the theory of ordinary differential equations, Montel's theorem in complex analysis, and the Peter–Weyl theorem in harmonic analysis and various results concerning compactness of integral operators.
title: Arzelà–Ascoli theorem

[Lemma 15 (Interior saturation) of arXiv:2608.30211, '2608.30211'] Given $s\in(0,1)$, there is $R=R(f,s)>0$ with the following property.  If
$D\subset\R^d$ is a domain, $u$ is a bounded positive solution of
$-\Delta u=f(u)$ in $D$ with $0<u\leq1$, and $B_R(x)\subset D$, then
\begin{equation}
 u(x)\geq s.
\end{equation}
The radius $R$ is independent of $D$ and of any boundary condition imposed on
$\partial D$.

Let~$(\tilde{p}_n)$ be a sequence in~$(0,1)$ such that~$n \tilde{p}_n\to 0$.  Then,
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}

body:
[Proposition 8 (First moment) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] For \(t<t_*\),
\begin{equation}

        m'
        =
        \frac12m^2+m-\frac12\sum_{k\geq1}q_k^2.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}

        m'\geq\frac12m(m+1),
\end{equation}
\[
        1\leq t_*\leq2\log2,
        \qquad
        \int_0^t(m(s)+1)\,ds\leq2\log m(t),\quad t<t_*,
\]
and \(m(t)\uparrow\infty\) as \(t\uparrow t_*\).

body:
For finite simple graphs G (n vertices, Laplacian L_G, eigenvalues 0 = lambda_1 <= ... <= lambda_n) and H (m vertices, L_H, 0 = mu_1 <= ... <= mu_m), the Cartesian product G box H has vertex set V(G) x V(H), with (g, h) adjacent to (g', h) when g ~ g' in G and to (g, h') when h ~ h' in H. The largest Laplacian eigenvalue of G box H is lambda_n + mu_m. If G and H are connected with at least two vertices each, the second smallest eigenvalue (algebraic connectivity) of G box H is min(lambda_2, mu_2).
G and H are finite simple graphs

body:
[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2604.24684, 'Waning Immunity Fails to Restore a Positive Epidemic Threshold on Power--Law Networks'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph with
$
\mathrm{diam}(G)\le c\log n
$, $\delta\in (0,1), \varepsilon\ge \varepsilon_1>0$,
and suppose that $G$ contains $\lceil n^{1-\delta'}\rceil$ pairwise vertex-disjoint hierarchical-stars
\[
HS(v^{(\ell)}):=\mathrm{HStar}\bigl(v^{(\ell)},\{u_i^{(\ell)}\}_{i\le \lceil n^\varepsilon\rceil },\{w_{i,j}^{(\ell)}\}_{i\le \lceil n^\varepsilon\rceil ,\ j\le  \lceil n^{\varepsilon_1}\rceil}\bigr),
\qquad
\ell=1,\dots,\lceil n^{1-\delta'}\rceil.
\]
Fix any non-empty set
$
\mathcal I\subseteq \{1,\dots,\lceil n^{1-\delta'}\rceil \}
$.
Assume that at time $0$, for every $\ell\in\mathcal I$, the center $v^{(\ell)}$ is $(\frac14 n^{\varepsilon_3},n^{\varepsilon_2})$-HS-lit with respect to $HS(v^{(\ell)})$, where
\(
\varepsilon_2=\frac{1}{200}\min\{\lambda,\rho,1\}\min\{\varepsilon,\varepsilon_1\},
\varepsilon_3=\frac14\varepsilon_2,
\varepsilon_4=\tfrac{1}{16\cdot 200}\min\{\rho, \lambda, 1\}\cdot24\varepsilon_2.
\)
Then there exists an event $A$ such that $A$ implies that, for every
$
\ell=1,\dots,\lceil n^{1-\delta'}\rceil,
$
the center $v^{(\ell)}$ is $(\frac14 n^{\varepsilon_3},n^{\varepsilon_2})$-HS-lit with respect to $HS(v^{(\ell)})$ at time $\exp(n^{\varepsilon_3/2})$, and, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
\mathbb P(A)\ge
1-\exp(-n^{\varepsilon_4/20}).
\]

body: [campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 7.27 (Chapter 7, p. 259) asks whether, over arc-transitive graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau* = O(n log n), tau2 = O(n) and tau*/(2 tau0) = 1 + o(1). Our result (id P0208, 2026-09-08): all three claims are FALSE. The counterexample is the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] for odd m >= 5 - the m-cycle with every vertex split into two non-adjacent twins - which is connected, 4-regular, arc-transitive and not a cycle, on n = 2m vertices. With g(j) = j(m-j) + m the mean hitting time at cycle-distance j and 2m the twin hitting time: tau* = 2*floor(m^2/4) + 2m ~ n^2/8 (quadratic, not O(n log n)); tau2 = 1/(1 - cos(2 pi/m)) ~ n^2/(8 pi^2), because A(C_m[Kbar_2]) = A(C_m) tensor J_2 so the relaxation time is the m-cycle's own; and tau*/(2 tau0) tends to 3/2, not 1 + o(1). Verification, as the source words it: exact hitting times by linear algebra at m = 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21 (all five formulas exact at every size); arc-transitivity checked mechanically at m = 5, 7, 9 (the group generated by the rotation, one reflection and one fibre swap has order 2^m * 2m and its orbit of one arc is all 8m arcs); and a Lean file P0208.lean with nine theorems, no sorry, axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound only. Not formalised: uniqueness of the solution of (I-P)h = 1 and the tensor eigenvalue computation, both standard and checked numerically. Prior art not cleared. odd m >= 5 simple random walk on the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] (n = 2m vertices, 4-regular, arc-transitive, not a cycle)

body:
[Thm Inverse4 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m$ odd, and let
$f_2(x)=x+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\big(c_1x+c_2x^2+x^{2q-1}\big)$ with
$c_1,c_2\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_q$
satisfying
\[
  \gamma^{3(q-1)}=1,\qquad
  1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)=\gamma^{2q-1},\qquad
  {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2\gamma^q)=0,
\]
so that $f_2$ is a permutation polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ by
Theorem~(Result2 of the paper)(3). Then
\begin{equation}
  f_2^{-1}(x)=
  \begin{cases}
    0
      & \text{if } x=0,\\[0.8em]
    x+\gamma^{q-1}\Big(h_2(x)+\dfrac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x^3)}{x^{q+1}}\Big)
      & \text{if } x\neq0,\ r=0,\\[0.8em]
    x+\gamma^{q-1}\Big(h_2(x)+\dfrac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x^3)}{x^{q+1}}
      +r^{1/3}+\dfrac{P}{r^{1/3}}\Big)
      & \text{if } x\neq0,\ r\neq0,
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
where
\[
  P=h_2(x)^2+h_2(x)\,{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\big(\gamma^{q-1}x^q\big)
    +\frac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma x)^3\,{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x)^3}{\gamma^3\,x^{2q+2}},
  \qquad
  r=P\Big(h_2(x)+\frac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x)^3}{x^{q+1}}\Big).
\]

\[
\mathbb P\bigl(G_{n,m}^{\alpha,\ast}\in \mathcal H_n \,\big|\, d(G_{n,m}^{\alpha,\ast})=d\bigr)
=
\mathbb P\bigl(\mathrm{CM}(d)\in \mathcal H_n\bigr).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition defn:fP of arXiv:2411.10829, 'Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble and its Laplace transform'] For $\vec s\in\mathscr B$, we construct another $\vec r\in\mathscr B$ without type II indices, as follows.
For each type II index $j\in J_\mathrm {II}$, and the corresponding $j'$, we let $r_j=s_j+s_{j'}$ and $r_{j'}= 0$.
For the remaining $j\in J\cup U$ we let $r_j=s_j$.
We use $\mathcal Q$ to denote the map $\vec s\mapsto \vec r$.
If $J_\mathrm {II}=\emptyset$, then $\mathcal Q(\vec r)=\vec r$.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.29536, 'Multi-hop visibility through the vacant set of Poissonian obstacles'] Let $\mathcal C$ be the occupied set of a Poisson-Boolean model in dimension $d\geq 2$, the Poisson cylinders in dimension $d\geq 3$ or the Brownian interlacements in dimension $d\geq 3$ (see Section~\ref{sec:notation+models} for the precise definitions). Let $\delta_r$ be as above and let $h_r=\sqrt{r\log r}$ for the Brownian interlacements in dimension $d=3$ and, otherwise, $h_r=\sqrt r$.
For any $N\geq 0$, there exist $c = c(d,N,\mathrm{law}(\mathcal C))$ and $C = C(d,N,\mathrm{law}(\mathcal C))$ such that 
\begin{equation}
c\,\Big(\frac{r}{\delta_r}\Big)^{d-1}\Big(\frac{h_r}{\delta_r}\Big)^{dN} f(r) 
\leq P_{\mathrm{vis}}^N(r)\leq 
C\,\Big(\frac{r}{\delta_r}\Big)^{d-1}\Big(\frac{h_r}{\delta_r}\Big)^{dN} f(r).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 1 (Conditional Tweedie identity) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Suppose that \(\E\|X_0\|^2<\infty\) and that differentiation may be
interchanged with the noising integrals in
\eqref{eq:noised-distribution} and \eqref{eq:noised-posterior-law}.  For
\(t>0\), define
\[
m_t(x)=\E[X_0\mid X_t=x],
\qquad
m_t^r(x)=\E[X_0\mid X_t=x,R=r].
\]
Then, for every \(r\) with \(0<p_R(r)<\infty\),
\begin{equation}

\nabla_x\log p_t(x\mid r)=\frac{a_tm_t^r(x)-x}{\Delta_t},
\end{equation}
and the smoothed likelihood force is
\begin{equation}

g_t(x,r):=\nabla_x\log p(r\mid X_t=x)
=
\frac{a_t}{\Delta_t}\{m_t^r(x)-m_t(x)\}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Conditional Tweedie identity

[Proposition 14 of arXiv:2605.21424, 'A dice game, a multinomial walk, and the inverted Dirichlet distribution'] Let \(\alpha>0\) and let \((G_n)_{n\in \N_{\ge 1}}\) be a sequence of random variables, where \(G_n\) has a \(\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha n,1)\) distribution, for every \(n\in\N_{\ge 1}\). Then 
\[
\lim_{n\to \infty}\P\Big(\sqrt{\alpha n}\Big(\frac{G_n}{\alpha n}-1\Big)\le b\Big)=\Phi(b),
\]
where \(\Phi(b)=\int_{-\infty}^b\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z}{2}}dz\) denotes the standard normal CDF.

[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Suppose $D$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{assume:D} and let $D_\la$ be as in~\eqref{D-Dla}. Let $R = 24 + 2(1+2N)(\log\la)/d$. Suppose $\psi\in C^{2N+2}(\us(R\e))$ and there exist constants $\CR, C_2,\dots, C_{2N+2}$ such that
\begin{align}
 \delta_\ell(R\e)\leq C_\ell d^{(\lceil\ell/2\rceil-2)_+},\quad\ell=2,\dots,2N+2,\\
d^2/\la\leq C_0, \qquad R\e \leq \min(1/3, 2/(4C_2+C_3), \rho_0),\end{align}
where $\rho_0$ is as in Assumption~\ref{assume:D} and the $\delta_\ell$ are as in \eqref{deldef}, with $H=I_d+\nabla^2\psi(0)$. Then
\bs
\mathbb P\left(\mathcal N\left(0_{d+1}, \,I_{d+1}\right)\in  D_\la\right) = \frac{e^{-\la/2}\la^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi\det H}}\left(1+\sum_{m=1}^{N-1}a_m\left(\frac{d^2}{\la}\right)^{m} + \Rem_N\right),\es where 
\bs
\max_{m=1,\dots,N-1}|a_m|&\leq C(C_2,\dots,C_{2N+2}, N),\\
|\Rem_N|&\leq C(C_0, C_2,\dots,C_{2N+2}, N)\bigg(\frac{d^2}{\la}\bigg)^{N}.\es Here, $a_m$ is as in~\eqref{amdef}, with the $\g_k$ as in~\eqref{gkdef1}, where $\g(x)\equiv1$ and $\z(x,0)=\|x\|^2/2 +(\psi(x)+1)^2/2$. In particular, 
\bs
d^2a_1 = & - 1  -\frac12\mathrm{Tr}(\nabla^2\psi_H(0_d)) +\frac{1}{12}\|\nabla^3\psi_H(0_d)\|^2_{F} + \frac18\|\langle\nabla^3\psi_H(0_d),I_d\rangle\|^2 \\
&-\frac18\langle\nabla^4\psi_H(0_d), I_d\otimes I_d\rangle-\frac18 \mathrm{Tr}^2(\nabla^2\psi_H(0_d)) -\frac14\mathrm{Tr}\left(\nabla^2\psi_H(0_d)^2\right),
\es where $\psi_H(x)=\psi(H^{-1/2}x)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn 3 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Distinguishability With Respect to Fixed Sequences] 
Fix two sequences of distributions $\mu_{n}, \nu_{n}$ that take on values in the set $\mathcal{S}_{n}$, and let $f_{n}$ be a sequence of functions from $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

We say the sequence $f_{n}$ \textit{weakly} distinguishes $\mu_{n}$ and $\nu_{n}$ if
\be 
\sqrt{\max(\Var_{\mu_{n}}(f_{n}),\Var_{\nu_{n}}(f_{n}))} = O(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |),
\ee 
and \textit{strongly} distinguishes if the LHS is 
$o(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |)$.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.17374

body: Ergodic theory is a branch of mathematics that studies statistical properties of deterministic dynamical systems; it is the study of ergodicity. In this context, "statistical properties" refers to properties which are expressed through the behavior of time averages of various functions along trajectories of dynamical systems. The notion of deterministic dynamical systems assumes that the equations determining the dynamics do not contain any random perturbations, noise, etc. Thus, the statistics with which we are concerned are properties of the dynamics.
title: Ergodic theory

body: Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. The identities above need independent coordinates. Let X_1 = X_2 = B with B uniform on {0, 1}. For f = B: H_0 = 0, H_1 = H_2 = 1/4, so the inversion formula returns W_1 = 1/2 and W_2 = -1/4; R_0 = R_1 = 0 and R_2 = 1/4, so D_2 = -1/4; and redrawing one coordinate from its correct marginal while keeping the other gives mean squared change 1/4 averaged over the two choices, while 2 R_1 = 0. For f = B - 1/2: A_0 f = 0 and A_1 f = A_2 f = f, so the formal P_1 f = 2f and P_2 f = -f, P_1 is not idempotent, and ||P_1 f||^2 + ||P_2 f||^2 = 5/4 while Var(f) = 1/4.

body:
[Corollary 17 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $P$ be the transition matrix of the RWBD chain. Then, $\Phi$ is an eigenfunction of $P$ with eigenvalue $\alpha$ if
         \[\alpha= 1 - \frac{n}{d(n-1)}\quad \text{and}\quad \Phi(x) = 1 \frac{nx}{d(n-1)}\]
         \begin{proof}
           Clearly $\alpha = \lambda_1$. Hence, consider $K_1(x)$
            \begin{align*}
            K_1(x) &= \sum_{j=0}^1 (-1)^j{x \choose j}{d-x \choose 1-j}(n-1)^{1-j}\\
            &= (-1)^0{x\choose 0}{d-x \choose 1}(n-1)^{1} + (-1)^1{x \choose 1}{d-x\choose 0}(n-1)^{0}\\
            &= (d-x)(n-1) -x\\
            &= d(n-1) -nx\\
            &\propto 1 -\frac{nx}{d(n-1)} = \Phi(x)
            \end{align*}
            Thus, $\Phi(x)$ is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\alpha$.
         \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 17 of arXiv:2604.07478

body: [Theorem 4.6 of arXiv:2110.09034, 'On the construction of cospectral nonisomorphic bipartite graphs'] Let GL and GH be bipartite graphs. Let GL be a biregular bipartite graph with distinct degrees and let GH be balanced. Then the graphs GL⊗H and GL⊗H# are nonisomorphic if and only if GH does not admit an automorphism that interchanges its partite sets.
title: Theorem 4.6 of arXiv:2110.09034: On the construction of cospectral nonisomorphic bipartite graphs

[Definition Definition_DBM of arXiv:2411.10829, 'Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble and its Laplace transform'] For a real $\beta>0$, the Dyson Brownian Motion (DBM) is the (unique,
strong) solution\footnote{For $0<\beta<1$ a special care is needed, because particles start to collide, see [cepa1997diffusing].} of the system of $N$ stochastic differential equations
\begin{equation}
 
\mathrm{d}Y_i(\tau )=\frac{\beta}{2}\,\sum_{j\neq i} \frac{1}{Y_i(\tau )-Y_j(\tau )}\,\mathrm{d}\tau +
\mathrm{d}W_i(\tau ), \quad i=1,2,\ldots,N,
\end{equation}
where $W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_N$ are independent standard Brownian motions.
title: Definition Definition_DBM of arXiv:2411.10829

body: [Corollary coro:ergodiceig of arXiv:2505.12187, 'Speeding up quantum Markov processes through lifting'] Let $\mathcal{P}_t = \exp(t \mathcal{L})$ be a QMS with an invariant state $\sigma \in \mathcal{D}_+(\mathcal{M})$. Then $\mathcal{P}_t$ is ergodic if and only if $\mathcal{L}$ has no purely imaginary eigenvalues $\lambda = i\mu$ with real $\mu \neq 0$. In this case, every eigenvalue $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ of $\mathcal{L}$ satisfies either $\lambda = 0$ or $\mathfrak{Re} \lambda < 0$. body:
[Theorem 8 (Theorem~4.1 of \cite{FK06}) of arXiv:2607.12666, 'Sample-path Large deviations for \\Scheduled Arrival Processes with Unpunctuality'] Let $\{X^{(n)}\}$ be a sequence of processes in $D([0,T])$. Suppose that
\begin{enumerate}
\item there exists a dense set $T_0\subset[0,T]$ such that, for every $t\in T_0$, the sequence $\{X^{(n)}(t)\}$ is exponentially tight in $\R$;
\item for every $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n
\log\Pbb\bigl(w'(X^{(n)},\delta,T)>\varepsilon\bigr)
=-\infty.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then $\{X^{(n)}\}$ is exponentially tight in $D([0,T])$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem~4.1 of \cite{FK06}

Let Y be finite with a distinguished always-true empty fact bot, and let p be a random probability vector with law nu. For each p put F(p)=supp(p) union {bot}, H(p)=Y\F(p). Fix O subset Y with O subset F(p) nu-almost surely, and require U=Y\O nonempty. Fix a generator g on Y and a partition Pi into nonempty cells, both fixed relative to p~nu. Define q=p^Pi by q(y)=p(B)/|B| on B in Pi and TV(q,g)=(1/2)*sum_y |q(y)-g(y)|. Then E_nu[(p(U)-TV(q,g)-g(H(p)))_+] <= max_(y in U) Pr_nu(y in F(p)) + |O|*max_(y in U) E_nu[p(y)]. In the language-model application nu is the posterior after observing training data; O, g and Pi are fixed conditional on those data. No conclusion that every uncalibrated generator hallucinates is asserted.
Finite Y, distinguished bot, F=supp(p) union {bot}, and observed O true almost surely.
Nonempty unobserved U; g and Pi fixed under the posterior draw.

body:
[Lemma lem:orbit_kernel of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Let $(m, b)$ specify a NURS orbit
\[
\mathcal{O} = (\sigma \circ \rho^i)_{i = a}^b,
\qquad a = b - 2^m + 1.
\]
Then the orbit selection kernel of NURS satisfies
\[
p_{\mathrm{orbit}}(m, b \mid \sigma, \rho)
=
\frac{1}{2^m}
\cdot
\mathbf{1}\Biggl(
\Phi(\mathcal{O})
\;\wedge\;
\bigwedge_{s = 1}^{m} \; \bigwedge_{t = 1}^{2^s}
\neg \textsc{Stop}\!\left(\mathcal{O}_{s,t}, \varepsilon, w\right)
\Biggr),
\]
where $\{\mathcal{O}_{s,t}\}$ are the dyadic sub-orbits of $\mathcal{O}$
(Definition~(def:dyadic-suborbit of the paper)), and where $\Phi(\mathcal{O})$ holds if and only if
\[
\textsc{Stop}(\mathcal{O}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
\textsc{SubStop}(\mathcal{O}_+^{\mathrm{ext}}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
\textsc{SubStop}(\mathcal{O}_-^{\mathrm{ext}}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
|\mathcal{O}| = 2^M.
\]
The forward and backward extensions are defined by
\[
\mathcal{O}_+^{\mathrm{ext}} = (\sigma \circ \rho^i)_{i = b+1}^{b+2^m},
\qquad
\mathcal{O}_-^{\mathrm{ext}} = (\sigma \circ \rho^i)_{i = a - 2^m}^{a - 1}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:orbit_kernel of arXiv:2601.07045

body:
Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a CLOSED set F contained in E with |E \ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]
f measurable and a.e. finite
|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)
the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available

REFUTED ROUTE, retained as a draft concept: matching all three pair-connectivity probabilities of a three-terminal cell was proposed to imply equality of every crossing event on a common skeleton. This implication is false: a star with three independent edges of probability 1/sqrt(2) matches each fair-site pair probability 1/2, but a connection from terminal a to the boundary set {b,c} has probability 1-1/(2sqrt(2)) rather than 1/2.
Three distinct terminals
Full cell connectivity, rather than only one fixed pair event, can enter a crossing

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:54f69bfcd0acd7996a7a998c785d6674401aa922b5a4c354b71019d63af42647","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/54/54f69bfcd0acd7996a7a998c785d6674401aa922b5a4c354b71019d63af42647.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:980764c736730308b9f646a8477bd17f79969a5ad9ec47d7cbcb728b12cbd845","bundle_entry_key":"same-second-moment-distinct-quartic-kl-gaussian-mixtures-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-quartic-lower-bound-and-second-moment-obstruction-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Extensive-rank matrix inference, Gaussian mixtures and high-noise KL expansions","draft":"w718/bundle_015.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:same-second-moment-distinct-quartic-kl-gaussian-mixtures-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Exact second-moment coefficients do not determine quartic KL

Claim w718-T287-039 v1. Target1 route-failure, proof (unaudited).
No novelty claim. This diagnoses the missing inference in the
quartic upper route. It is NOT a counterexample to T287 or a claim
that the families below are iid factor-product observations.

## Statement

There are two families of centered, covariance-I_d Gaussian mixtures
whose conditional covariance matrices differ from I_d in operator
norm by O(s), such that, after d->infinity at fixed small s,

 log(1+chi^2(P_s||Q))/d =s^4/2+O(s^8)

for BOTH families (Q=N(0,I_d)), while their normalized KL expansions
are respectively

 D(P_s||Q)/d=s^4/4+O(s^6),
 lim_(d->infinity) D(P_s||Q)/d=s^4/12+O(s^6).

Thus even the EXACT leading log-second-moment coefficient plus
centering, covariance matching, and uniformly small bounded
conditional covariance perturbations does not determine the
leading KL coefficient. Additional model-specific control is needed.

## 1. Independent balanced variance mixtures

Let q=N(0,1),
p_e=[N(0,1+e)+N(0,1-e)]/2, and P_(e,d)=p_e^tensor(d).
For |e|<1, direct Gaussian integration gives

 J(e)=integral p_e^2/q
     =[(1-e^2)^(-1/2)+(1+e^2)^(-1/2)]/2,
 log J(e)=3e^4/8+O(e^8).                             (1)

The elementary Gaussian identity used here is
integral phi_(1+a) phi_(1+b)/phi_1=(1-ab)^(-1/2),
valid whenever the variances are positive and the resulting
Gaussian precision is positive; |a|,|b|<1 suffices.

Also, as e->0,

 D(p_e||q)=3e^4/16+O(e^6).                            (2)

Here is a justification that does not assume a globally convergent
pointwise entropy series. Write L_e=p_e/q. Its expansion at zero is

 L_e(y)=1+e^2 H4(y)/8+O(e^4), H4=y^4-6y^2+3.

The Gaussian variance derivative identity is
partial_v^2 phi_v|_(v=1)=H4 phi_1/4. Normalization gives
E_q(L_e-1)=0; the coefficient of e^4 in E_q L_e log L_e is
E_q H4^2/128=24/128=3/16.

To justify differentiating the entropy integral through order6,
restrict |e|<=1/16. Derivatives through order6 of L_e are bounded
by a fixed polynomial in |y| times exp(y^2/30). Moreover the
arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives

 L_e(y)>=(1-e^2)^(-1/4)
         exp(-e^2 y^2/[2(1-e^2)])>=exp(-y^2/510).

Thus the inverse-density factors in derivatives of L_e log L_e
are bounded by exp(5y^2/510), while products of at most6 derivatives
are bounded by a polynomial times exp(6y^2/30). Their product is
integrable against q, since 6/30+5/510<1/2. The logarithm itself
is bounded in absolute value by a constant times1+y^2. These are
an explicit common integrable dominator up to a finite constant
and polynomial degree. Dominated differentiation is therefore
valid, and evenness in e gives the O(e^6) remainder in (2).

Tensorization is exact: KL(P_(e,d)||Q_d)/d=D(p_e||q),
and log(1+chi^2(P_(e,d)||Q_d))/d=log J(e). Take
e=(4/3)^(1/4)s. Equations(1)-(2) give the first family's coefficients
1/2 and1/4 as stated. Its conditional covariance is diagonal with
independent entries1+e or1-e; its average is I_d.

## 2. One shared, unbalanced variance label

Set t=s^2 and

 R_(s,d)=(1/4)N(0,(1+t)I_d)+(3/4)N(0,(1-t/3)I_d).

It is centered and covariance matched: (1/4)t+(3/4)(-t/3)=0.
For the shared binary label L, the chain rule gives

 average_label KL(N(0,(1+delta_L)I_d)||Q_d)
   =KL(R_(s,d)||Q_d)+I(L;Y),
 0<=I(L;Y)<=H(L)<=log2.

The normalized information term tends to zero, hence

 lim_d KL(R_(s,d)||Q_d)/d
 =-log(1+t)/8-3log(1-t/3)/8
 =t^2/12+O(t^3)=s^4/12+O(s^6).                       (3)

For the second moment, Gaussian integration gives a finite positive
sum over the four label pairs:

 integral R_(s,d)^2/Q_d
 =sum_(i,j) w_i w_j (1-delta_i delta_j)^(-d/2).

For sufficiently small t>0 its largest exponential base is attained
by delta_i=delta_j=t. Upper and lower bounds by this largest term
times fixed positive constants therefore give

 lim_d log integral R_(s,d)^2/Q_d /d
 =-log(1-t^2)/2=s^4/2+O(s^8).                        (4)

All measures here are finite-dimensional Gaussian probability laws
and Lebesgue measures are sigma-finite. Gaussian square integrals
are finite for the stated small parameters. Mixture expansions
have only finitely many nonnegative terms; Tonelli is applicable,
or finite linearity suffices after their explicit integrability.

## 3. Exact implication for the T287 route

[Lemma lem:johnson-spectrum of arXiv:2608.18293, 'Critical tensor covariance at the Marchenko--Pastur threshold'] Assume $1\le q<n/2$. Let $A_q$ be the adjacency matrix of the Johnson graph
$J(n,q)$: two $q$-subsets are adjacent when their symmetric difference has size
two. For a $j$-subset $T$, define
\[
  f_T(I)=\1_{\{T\subseteq I\}},
  \qquad |I|=q,
\]
and let $U_j$ be the span of the functions $f_T$ with $|T|=j$. Then
\[
  U_0\subseteq U_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_q.
\]
Set $U_{-1}=\{0\}$. If $H_j=U_j\cap U_{j-1}^{\perp}$, then $A_q$ acts on $H_j$ by the scalar
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_j=(q-j)(n-q-j)-j,
  \qquad 0\le j\le q.
  
\end{equation}
In particular, when $q<n/2$, the largest eigenvalue of $A_q$ on the orthogonal complement of the constant vector is
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_1=q(n-q)-n.
  
\end{equation}

[Lemma enormous_bound of arXiv:2606.29622, 'Affine Structure of the Brownian Signature'] Let $\bm p \in \mathcal B\,$ be of the form (equation eq:class_B_p of the paper), and define
    \begin{equation}
    
    \bm{\xi}_t := \shuexp{\bm p|_{\sigW[t,T]}} = \exp({\bracket{\bm p}{\sigW[t,T]}})\cdot \shuexp{\overline{\bm p|_{\sigW[t,T]}}}\,.
    \end{equation}
    
    Then, there exist two constants $C_{\bm p, T}, C_{\bm p, T}' > 0\,$, independent of $W$, such that for all $t\in[0, T]$ and $\sigX[] \in G$,
        \begin{align}
        \|\bm{\xi}_t\|_{\sigX[]} \leq \exp \left(\bracket{\, \mathfrak{Re}(\bm p)}{\sigW[t,T]} + M_{\bm{p}}(\sigX[])\,\zeta_{\bm p,t, T}\right) \leq \exp\left(C_{\bm p, T} \,(1 + M_{\bm p}(\sigX[]))^{\deg_{{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{1}}}}(\bm p)}\right),  
        \end{align}

body:
[Thm conformal_invariance_aut_D of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let \( \tau \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \). The drift term \( b(\boldsymbol{\theta}, u) \) is a pre-Schwarzian form, satisfying:
\[
b_i = \tau' \widetilde{b}_i \circ \tau + \frac{6 - \kappa}{2} \left(\log \tau'\right)'.
\]
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] There exists a smooth function \( F(\tau, u): \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \) such that:
    \[
    \log \psi - \log (\psi \circ \tau) + \frac{\kappa - 6}{2\kappa} \sum_i \log \tau'(\theta_i) = F(\tau, u),
    \]
    where \( F \) satisfies the functional equation:
    
    \begin{equation}
    
    F(\tau_1 \tau_2, u) = F(\tau_1, \tau_2(u)) + F(\tau_2, u).
    \end{equation}

    \item[(ii)] There exists a rotation constant \( \omega \) such that:
    \begin{equation}
    F(A_\theta, 0) = \omega \theta.
    \end{equation}

    If \( \omega = 0 \), \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \) suffices to describe conformal invariance, and \( F \) reduces to a map \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \).

    \item[(iii)] Suppose \( F_1(\tau, u) \) and \( F_2(\tau, u) \) correspond to partition functions \( \psi_1 \) and \( \psi_2 \). If their rotation constants \( \omega_1 = \omega_2 \), then there exists a function \( g(u) \) such that:
    \[
   \psi_2 = g(u) \cdot \psi_1.
    \]

    \item[(iv)] For \( \tau \in \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \), let \( \tau(u) = v \). Decompose \( \tau = T_v \circ A_\theta \circ T^{-1}_u \), where \( u, v \in \mathbb{D} \) and \( \theta \in \mathbb{R} \). Using the relations \( T_u'(u) = \frac{1}{1 - |u|^2} \) and \( T_v'(0) = 1 - |v|^2 \), define:
    \[
    \tau'(u)^{\lambda(u)} \overline{\tau'(u)}^{\overline{\lambda(u)}} := \left(\frac{1 - |v|^2}{1 - |u|^2}\right)^{2 \operatorname{Re}(\lambda(u))} e^{-2 \theta \operatorname{Im}(\lambda(u))}.
    \]
    Then:
    \[
    F(\tau, u) = \log \left(\tau'(u)^{\lambda(u)} \overline{\tau'(u)}^{\overline{\lambda(u)}}\right),
    \]
    satisfy the functional equation ((functional equation for F of the paper)), with rotation constant \( \omega = \operatorname{Im}(\lambda(u)) \).
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem6.9 of arXiv:2508.12951, '\textbf{On the central limit question for strictly stationary, reversible Markov chains}'] Suppose $y_1, y_2, y_3, \dots$ and $z_1, z_2, z_3, \dots$
are each a sequence of elements of the set $\{-1,0,1\}$.
Suppose that (i) there exists $m \in \mathbb N$ such that
$y_k = z_k = 0$ for all $k > m$, and
(ii) there exists $k \in \mathbb N$ such that $y_k \neq z_k$.

   Suppose $r_1, r_2, r_3, \dots$ is a sequence of positive numbers 
such that one of the following two conditions holds:
\hfil\break
(a) $r_{k+1}/r_k \geq 3$ for every $k \in \mathbb N$; or
\hfil\break
(b) $r_{k+1}/r_k \leq 1/3$ for every $k \in \mathbb N$.

   Then each of the sums $\sum_{k=1}^\infty r_ky_k$ and 
$\sum_{k=1}^\infty r_kz_k$ has at most finitely many non-zero summands 
(and therefore trivially converges absolutely); and they satisfy 
$\sum_{k=1}^\infty r_ky_k \neq \sum_{k=1}^\infty r_kz_k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem corrrect of arXiv:2602.22342, 'Sum of Gaussian vectors and large sets'] Let $n\geq 2$ be a positive integer. Consider probability measures $\theta_i$ on $\R$ ($i=1,...,n$), such that $\sum_{i=1}^n \theta_i = n\gamma_1$. Define $r_i\in \R$ such that $\Phi(r_i)=\frac{i}{n}$ if $i\leq \frac{n}{2}$, and $\Phi(r_i)=\frac{i-1}{n}$ if $i> \frac{n}{2}$. 
Consider independent random variables $X_i$ with respective probability distributions $\theta_i$. Then for some universal constant $C_c\geq 1$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^n \E[|X^*_i - r_i|^2]\leq C_c (\log \log n +1).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem corrrect of arXiv:2602.22342

[Proposition eq:Gaussian-divisible-slice of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:gaussian-divisible-upper-slice}
In the preceding frame-slice setting, suppose
\[
 J_{I,N}=\sqrt{1-\tau_N}\,X_{I,N}+\sqrt{\tau_N}\,G_{I,N},
 \qquad \tau_N\in[\tau_0,1],
\]
for a deterministic sequence \((\tau_N)\) and some fixed
\(\tau_0>0\), where \(X\) is an arbitrary random tensor and \(G\) is an
independent standard Gaussian tensor.  Suppose only
that the hard and smoothed slices appearing above are finite and
positive.  Gaussian convolution then supplies a global strictly
positive gradient density and a compatible conditional kernel.  For
every \(\eta>0\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak K_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)
 \ge c_{\varepsilon,\sqrt{\tau_N p}}^{\,n}\mathfrak D_{N,L}(\eta),
 \qquad
0<c_{\varepsilon,\sigma}\le1,\qquad
 \inf_{\sigma\in[\sqrt{\tau_0p},\sqrt p]}c_{\varepsilon,\sigma}
 \longrightarrow1
 \quad(\varepsilon\downarrow0).
\end{equation}
Consequently, the upper primitive defect in (equation eq:primitive-up of the paper)
vanishes, and hence so does the direct upper de-regularization defect.
The same conclusion holds for the point-incoherent slice.

[Prop 11 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $M$ be a matroid and $F, G \in \mathcal{L}(M)$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Suppose $F \subseteq G$,
        $F$ is modular in $M|_G$, and $G$ is modular in $M$. Then $F$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M|_G$.
        \item If $F, G$ are modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $(F \vee G)-G$ is modular in $M/G$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$ and $S \subseteq E(M)$ contains $F$, then $F$ is modular in $M|_S$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$ and $M$ is connected, then $M|_F$ is connected.
    \end{enumerate}

Constants in the probability bound do not depend on K; the lower restriction theta>=1/(nK) is used when converting the drift error to O_K(n^-1/2). In particular, after shrinking epsilon_0 and taking n large depending on K, theta' has E theta'<=theta throughout this range, and n E(U'-u)>=a/2. No supermartingale statement is made outside the stopped range.

## Moment bounds with n theta unbounded

For J=sum g_i^2 1{|a_i|<=2theta|g_i|}, independence of coordinates and the bounded Gaussian density give E[(g_i^2 1{|a_i|<=2theta|g_i|})^r]<=C_r theta for each positive integer r. Expanding the pth moment over distinct indices, for each fixed integer p>=2,

    E J^p <= C_p sum_{j=1}^p (n theta)^j,
    ||J||_p <= C_p[n theta+(n theta)^(1/p)].

The exponential-moment estimate E exp(lambda J)<=exp(C_lambda n theta) remains valid. Choose epsilon_0 so that C_lambda epsilon_0<lambda eta/2. This makes P(J>eta n)<=exp(-lambda eta n/2), uniformly for theta<=epsilon_0. The other Gaussian/binomial good-event failures are exponentially small as before.

The flip bounds |H|+|B|<=C theta^2 J therefore imply

    ||H/theta^2||_2+||B/theta^2||_2 <= C(n theta+sqrt(n theta)),
    E H=n(theta cos(theta)-sin(theta))/pi.

The latter identity is the exact polar integral in compact_generator.md. The chi-square estimates on central k give ||1/R-2/n||_2<=C n^-3/2 and ||C0/S||_p<=C_p n^-1/2. Products involving higher moments use the same bounds with larger p; no independence of H and R is presumed.

## Flip ratio and angular logarithm

The denominator replacement in E[H/(sin^2(theta)R);G] has error at most

    C(n theta+sqrt(n theta))*n^-3/2
    = C(theta/sqrt(n)+sqrt(theta)/n).

Deleting the small-k and other Gaussian tails contributes exponentially small terms times polynomial factors in n and theta. They are absorbed by the displayed errors uniformly for theta>=1/(nK). Projection corrections from H to Htilde are bounded by Hölder's inequality, using B=O_{L^p}(theta^2[n theta+(n theta)^(1/p)]), the inverse-S bounds, and C0/S=O_{L^p}(n^-1/2). After division by sin^2(theta)R, their first moments are bounded by C(theta^2+theta/sqrt(n)+sqrt(theta)/n). Consequently

    E[xi;G] = -2a theta
        +O(theta^2+theta/sqrt(n)+sqrt(theta)/n),
    E[|xi|^p;G] <= C_p(theta^p+theta/n^(p-1)), p=2,3.

The second bound follows directly from R>=n/8 and |Htilde|<=C theta^2 J on G. The first uses the exact mean of H, with sin^2(theta)=theta^2(1+O(theta^2)). On G, |xi|<=1/2 and Q stays in a fixed compact of (0,infinity), by the fixed J<=eta n condition. Thus Taylor remainders for log(1+xi) are controlled by fixed powers of xi.

Let z=log(theta'/theta) on G and zero otherwise. Its decomposition is

    z=z0+(1/2)log(1+xi)-log Q+E0,
    z0=(1/2)log(R/S), |E0|<=C theta^2 on G.

Define z0 to be zero off G as well. The central-k chi-square calculation gives E z0=-1/n+O(n^-2), E z0^2=2/n+O(n^-2), and E|z0|^3=O(n^-3/2), with exponentially small deletion errors. For Q=cos(theta)+sin(theta)C0/S+B/S, symmetry gives E[C0/S;central k]=0. Tail deletion is exponential, and the other terms give

    |E[log Q;G]|<=C theta^2,
    ||log Q;G||_p <= C_p(theta^2+theta/sqrt(n)), p=2,3.

For example B/S has L^p size at most C_p theta^2[theta+(n theta)^(1/p)/n], absorbed in theta^2 since theta<=epsilon_0 and n is large. The arctangent correction E0 is uniformly O(theta^2), because R/S and Q are bounded on G.

Cauchy–Schwarz controls baseline/flip covariances. It follows that, writing

    D=theta^2+theta/sqrt(n)+sqrt(theta)/n+n^-2,

one has

    Ez=-1/n-a theta+O(D),
    Ez^2=2/n+O(D),
    E|z|^3<=C(n^-3/2+theta^3+theta/n^2).

For the second line use ||log(1+xi)||_2<=C(theta+sqrt(theta/n)) and ||z0||_2=O(n^-1/2). This gives errors theta/sqrt(n)+sqrt(theta)/n+theta^2+theta/n, with theta/n absorbed into D. The third line follows by the p=3 flip bound, the baseline third absolute moment, and |E0|<=Ctheta^2. These are moments of the regularized log increment only.

## Exponentiation and the stopped supermartingale

The good-event bounds also give |z|<=C. Hence both exp(z) and exp(-z) have Taylor remainder bounded by C|z|^3. Since U'=u exp(-z),

    E(exp(-z)-1)=2/n+a theta
      +O(theta^2+theta/sqrt(n)+sqrt(theta)/n+n^-3/2),
    E(exp(z)-1)=-a theta
      +O(theta^2+theta/sqrt(n)+sqrt(theta)/n+n^-3/2).

Multiplying the first line by n u=1/theta and using theta>=1/(nK) proves the stated drift. The square-jump estimate follows from |exp(-z)-1|<=C|z| and

    Ez^2 <= C(1/n+theta^2),

where theta/sqrt(n)<=theta^2/2+1/(2n) and sqrt(theta)/n<=1/n for theta<=1. Thus u^2 Ez^2<=C(u^2/n+1/n^2).

Divide the error in the second exponential line by theta. It is bounded by C[epsilon_0+(1+sqrt(K)+K)/sqrt(n)] throughout the specified range. Take epsilon_0 small first and n large second to make it less than a/2. This proves the stopped angle supermartingale and the positive lower bound on reciprocal drift. It does not justify applying them after leaving the specified range.

Review priority: check the projection-correction bounds and exponentially small deletions uniformly in n theta; these are precisely the estimates not supplied by the original raw-moment outline. No independent review is asserted.

[Defn Monodromy of Coulomb Gas Correlation Differential of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$ be a divisor on $\mathbb{C}$ with associated Coulomb gas correlation differential
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = \prod_{j < k} (z_j - z_k)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k}.
\]
This function is multivalued due to the presence of non-integer exponents. Its multivaluedness is described by the \emph{monodromy representation} arising from analytic continuation around branch points.

To illustrate the basic mechanism, consider the case $n = 2$. Then
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = (z_1 - z_2)^{\sigma_1 \sigma_2},
\]
which is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}$. If we analytically continue this function as $z_1$ travels once counterclockwise around $z_2$, the function picks up a multiplicative factor of $e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}$. 

Thus, the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}, z_1) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_2) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}
\]
captures how the function changes under analytic continuation around the singularity at $z_2$, where $C_2$ is the loop encircling $z_2$.

In general, for $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$, the function $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}$. The fundamental group $\pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}, z_1)$ is the free group generated by loops $C_j$ encircling each $z_j$ ($j = 2, \ldots, n$), and the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}) \to \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_j) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_j}
\]
describes the multiplicative factor acquired by $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ when $z_1$ loops around $z_j$ once in the counterclockwise direction.
title: Monodromy of Coulomb Gas Correlation Differential

[Lem M1_tightness_time_changed of arXiv:2605.29073, 'Volterra clocks and their pure-jump limits: \\hitting times of curved boundaries'] We have
    \begin{equation}
        
        \mathbb E \left[X^n_t - X^n_s\right] \leq G_0^n(t) - G_0^n(s)\,, \quad s \leq t \leq T\,, \quad n \geq 0\,.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, since $G_0^n$ converges pointwise to $G_0$ which is continuous in $0$ and $T\,$,
    $$
    \sup_{n \geq 1}\, \mathbb E \left[X^n_T\right] < + \infty\,, \quad \text{and}\quad \lim_{\delta \to 0^+}\, \limsup_{n \to \infty}\, \mathbb E \left[X^n_{\delta}\right] = \lim_{\delta \to 0^+}\, \limsup_{n \to \infty}\, \mathbb E \left[X^n_{T} - X^n_{T- \delta}\right] = 0\,,
    $$
    and $\left(X^n\right)_{n \geq 1}$ is tight on $D[0\,,T]$ for the $M_1$-topology.

body:
[Theorem Geometrisation theorem of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] Suppose that $M$ is a compact, oriented, irreducible  3-manifold with $\partial M \cong \bigsqcup^k T^2$ for some $k \geq 0$.
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item  There is an $m \geq 0$ and a submanifold $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m T_i \subseteq M$ such that for every $i$, $T_i \subseteq M$ is an incompressible torus, and each component of $M$ cut along $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m T_i$ is Seifert fibred or hyperbolic.
\item  Any two minimal submanifolds with the above property are isotopic.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Ppn 208 (Kolmogorov estimates for $\vY$ and $\vY^\frozen$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] As in Definitions~\ref{d:rerand} and \ref{d:rerand.Ising}, let $\vY$ and $\vY^\frozen$ be the spatial rerandomizations of $\vX^\trunc$ and $\vX^\frozen$. We then have the quenched moment bound
    \beq
    \frac{\bE[
    (Y^{\RomI}(t)
    -Y^{\RomI}(s))^2]}{(t-s)^2}
    \le L^{O(1)} (\MAX_N)^2\,,\eeq
where $\MAX_N$ is defined by \eqref{e:MAX.N}, and satisfies
$\E[(\MAX_N)^2] \le L^{O(1)}$ as well as the bound
\eqref{e.MAX.bound}. For $N$ large enough, we also have the annealed moment bounds
    \beq
    \sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
    \frac{\E[(Y^{\sigma}(t)-Y^{\sigma}(s))^8]}{(t-s)^4}
    \le
    L^{O(1)}\,,
    \eeq
for all $q_0\le s < t\le 1$. The same bounds hold with $\vY^\frozen$ in place of $\vY$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Kolmogorov estimates for $\vY$ and $\vY^\frozen$

[Lmm lem:hom-to-inj-upper-tail of arXiv:2609.02682, 'LDP for tensor forms'] Consider $\widetilde{H}$ defined in (corH of the paper). Assume that
  $  (n\log n)^{-1/\widetilde\Delta}\ll p_n\ll 1$.
Then, for every $\rho,\varepsilon>0$, there exist constants
$c_{\varepsilon,\rho},C_{\varepsilon,\rho}>0$ such that, for all $n$,
uniformly over all $S\subseteq[n]$ satisfying $|S|\ge \rho n$, we have
\[
\mathbb P\left(
    \mathcal N_{\widetilde{H}}(S;\mathcal G_n)>
    (1+\varepsilon)p_n^{\widetilde e}(|S|)_{\widetilde v}
\right)
\le
C_{\varepsilon,\rho}\exp\left\{
    -c_{\varepsilon,\rho, \widetilde H}
    |S|^2p_n^{\widetilde\Delta}\log(1/p_n)
\right\}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Upper-tail control
