[Thm weak_convergence_hyperrough of arXiv:2605.29073, 'Volterra clocks and their pure-jump limits: \\hitting times of curved boundaries'] We consider $\lambda\,, \nu \geq 0\,$, $T > 0\,$, and $f$ satisfying Assumption (assumption:f of the paper). Let $a\,, b : \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+ \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+\,$, with $a$ non-decreasing and $b$ locally bounded and measurable, and define 
    $$
    G_0^n(t) := \int_0^t\,g_0^n(s)\,ds\,, \quad g_0^n(t) := a(t) + \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha_n)}\,\int_0^t\,(t-s)^{\alpha_n - 1}\,b(s)\,ds\,, \quad t \geq 0\,,
    $$
    for a sequence $(\alpha_n)_n \subset (0\,, 1)$ such that $\alpha_n \to 0\,$. For each $n \geq 0\,$, let $(W^n \,, X^n)$ be a weak solution to (equation eq:Volterra_clock of the paper) on $[0\,, T]$ for the input $(K^n\,, G_0^n\,, f\,, \lambda\,, \nu)\,$, where $K^n(t) := t^{\alpha_n - 1} / \Gamma(\alpha_n)\,$, which exists by Theorem (thm:weak_existence_Volterra_clock_DDS of the paper).
    Then, $(W^n\,, X^n) \Rightarrow (W^*\,, X^*)$ in $D^{\circ}[0\,,T]\,$, where $W^*$ is a standard Brownian motion, and
    $$
    X^*_t := \inf \{s \geq 0\,:\, (1 + \lambda)s - \nu W^*_{f(s)} > \bar a(t) + \bar b(t)\}\,, \quad t \leq T\,,
    $$
    with $\bar a := \int_0^{\cdot}\,a(s)\,ds$ and $\bar b := \int_0^{\cdot}\,b(s)\,ds\,$.

[Lemma lm:rho=1 of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] If $H$ has at least two cycles then $\rho(H)\geqslant 1$. Moreover, $\rho(H)=1$ if and only if 
$H$ 
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item is a cycle, or  
\item has at least two cycles and some edge $e$ for which 
each connected component of 
$H\setminus e$ has at most one cycle. 
\end{itemize}

body: [Theorem 2 of arXiv:2503.19927, 'Fully personalized PageRank and algebraic methods to distribute a random walker'] Let G = (V, E) be a directed, possibly weighted, strongly connected graph with N = |V | nodes, let c ∈RN be a positive vector. It is always possible to assign weights wij to edges (i, j) ∈E such that the eigenvector centrality of G is c.

body: [Theo Conv-Heat of arXiv:2411.19543, 'Feller property and convergence for semigroups of time-changed processes'] Assume that $\check{\bf P}_t^n$ are holomorphic for all $n\in\mathbb{N}_\infty$. Let $u_n(t), v_n$ be as before and $F_n,F$ be the respective fine supports of $\mu_n,\mu_\infty$. Assume that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|v_n - v_\infty\|_\infty =0$, $F_n,F$ are closed and that either $F_n\subset F$ for all $n$ or $\mu_n\uparrow\mu_\infty$ vaguely. Then $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|u_n(t) - u_\infty(t)\|_\infty =0$ locally uniformly in $t\in [0,\infty)$.

On the unimodular Galton-Watson tree, the default time distribution of a vertex v conditioned on the status of its parent satisfies the recursive distributional equation (RDE) tau_v = inf{ t >= 0 : x_v + Z_v(t) - c_v 1_{tau_{parent} <= t} - sum_{u in Children(v)} c_{uv} 1_{tau_u <= t} <= 0 }.
Tree structure is cycle-free
Noises Z_v are conditionally independent given degrees
title: Recursive Distributional Equation for Cascade Survival on Trees

body: [Definition of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] A \textbf{Hermitian inner product} on a $K$-vector space $V$ is a $K$-linear map $\overline{V}\otimes_K V\to K$, $(v,w)\mapsto\langle v,w\rangle$ with $\overline{\langle v,w\rangle}=\langle w,v\rangle$ and $\langle v,v\rangle> 0$ for $v\neq 0$.

[Corollary 17 of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix integers $1\le \ell\le u$, independent of $M$, and assume $t_{\ell,u}\ge0$.
Define
\[
\mathcal A_{\ell,u}
=
\{\alpha\le P:\ \ell\le L_\alpha\le u\}
\]
and
\[
\widehat\alpha_{\ell,u}(x)
=
\arg\max_{\beta\in\mathcal A_{\ell,u}}\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\beta(x).
\]
If
	\[
	\max_{\alpha\le P}\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)^c\bigr)\to0,
	\qquad
	\mathbb P(L_\alpha\notin[\ell,u])\to0,
	\]
	and
	\[
	P=o(M^{t_{\ell,u}+1}),
	\]
	then again
	\[
	\max_{\alpha\le P}
	\mathbb P\bigl(
	\widehat\alpha_{\ell,u}(x)\neq\alpha,\ 
	\alpha\in\mathcal A_{\ell,u}
	\bigr)\to 0.
	\]
title: Corollary 17 of arXiv:2604.25470

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.17562, '2608.17562'] Let $(\bm{X}_{i})_{i \ge 1}$ be a sequence of \iid random vectors with common distribution function $F$. Set 
\[
a_n \coloneq F^{\leftarrow}(1 - 1/n) \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \bm{M}_n \coloneq \max(\bm{X}_{1},\dots,\bm{X}_{n}),
\]
as well as $Z_n \coloneq a_n^{-1}M_{n}$. Let also $(V_{i,j})_{i \ge 1, j \in \lbra 1,d \rbra}$ be a sequence of \iid random variables, independent of the $\bm{X}_{i}$s and with distribution $\mathcal{U}_{[0.5, 1]}$. Then, if one sets $X_{i,j}' \coloneq X_{i,j} \oplus V_{i,j}$ and $\bm{M}_{n}' = \max(\bm{X}_{1}',\dots, \bm{X}_{n}')$, as well as $\bm{Z}_{n}' \coloneq a_n^{-1}\bm{M}_{n}'$, one gets:
\begin{align}
    \nonumber 
\mathrm{d}_{K}(\bm{Z}_{n}, \bm{Z}_{n}') \leq 2\sum_{j=1}^{d}F_{j}(1)^{n}, 
\end{align}
with $F_{j}$ the $j$-th marginal of $F$. Under the additional assumption that $\esp\big[\vert X_{1,j}\vert] < +\infty$ for every $j \in \lbra 1,d \rbra$, we have
\begin{align}
\mathrm{d}_{W}(\bm{Z}_{n}, \bm{Z}_{n}') \leq a_n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}(2 + \esp [(X_{j})_{-}])F_{j}(1)^{n-1},
\end{align}
where $x_{-} := \max(-x, 0)$.
title: Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.17562

[Proposition prop:ball-point-effective-dimensions of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] For every oracle \(A\subseteq\omega\), every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and every
\(r\in\omega\),
\[
K^A_r(x)\le K^A(x;r)+O(1)
\]
and
\[
K^A(x;r)\le K^A_{r+1}(x)+K_\omega(r)+O(1).
\]
The constants implicit in \(O(1)\) are independent of \(A\), \(x\), and \(r\).

body:
[Prop 10 of arXiv:2607.03924, 'Tree Coordinates and Range Martingales for Positive Operator-Valued Measures'] Let $E$ be a POVM on $\Omega_{m}$, and let $\left(K,P,V\right)$
be a minimal Naimark dilation of $E$. Thus $P:\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right)\to B\left(K\right)$
is a PVM, $V:H\to K$ is an isometry, 
\[
E\left(B\right)=V^{*}P\left(B\right)V,\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right),
\]
and 
\[
K=\overline{span}\left\{ P\left(B\right)Vh:B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right),\ h\in H\right\} .
\]
Then $E$ is extreme in $\mathcal{P}\left(\Omega_{m},H\right)$ if
and only if 
\[
\left\{ T\in P\left(\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right)\right)'_{\mathrm{sa}}:V^{*}TV=0\right\} =\left\{ 0\right\} .
\]

body: Finitely generated abelian group: An abelian group (G, +) is called finitely generated if there exist finitely many elements x_1, x_2, ..., x_s in G such that every x in G can be written as x = n_1 x_1 + n_2 x_2 + ... + n_s x_s for some integers n_1, n_2, ..., n_s. In this case the set {x_1, ..., x_s} is called a generating set of G, and one says that x_1, ..., x_s generate G. The cyclic groups are exactly the abelian groups having a generating set with a single element, so finitely generated abelian groups are a generalization of cyclic groups.

[Thm 23 (Stable L\'evy functional limit in the heavy-tail regime, see~{\cite[Theorem 7.4.2.) of arXiv:2607.28865, 'First-Passage Percolation on Spread-out line graphs: Microscopic Regime'] {whitt02}}]
Assume Assumption~\textnormal{A.\ref{ass:A2}} holds with $0 < \gc < 2/\lc$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:T1-tail}, $\sfT_1$ is regularly varying with tail index $\alpha := \gc\lc \in (0,2)$. Let $m_n := \lfloor n/\mu_{\sfP} \rfloor$, and choose the scaling sequence $a_n$ and the truncated centering function $b_n(t)$ as
\[
    a_n := \inf\left\{x>0 : m_n\pr(\sfT_1>x)\le 1\right\}, \qquad
    b_n(t) := \lfloor nt/\mu_{\sfP}\rfloor \E\left[\sfT_1\ind_{\{\sfT_1\le a_n\}}\right].
\]
Then, in the Skorokhod space $D([0,\infty),\dR)$ equipped with the $J_1$ topology, the passage-time skeleton process converges to a totally right-skewed $\alpha$-stable L\'evy process:
\[
    \frac1{a_n} \left(
    S_{\sfN(nt)}^{\sfT}-b_n(t)
    \right)_{t\ge 0}
    \Longrightarrow
    \left(\cL_\alpha(t)\right)_{t\ge0},
\]
where $\cL_\alpha$ corresponds to the L\'evy measure $\Pi(dx) = \alpha x^{-\alpha-1}\ind_{\{x>0\}}\,dx$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: The Ising (binary) perceptron asks for a weight vector w in {-1, +1}^n satisfying <w, x_a> >= 0 for m random patterns x_a with iid standard Gaussian (or Rademacher) entries. The storage capacity is the largest ratio alpha = m/n at which solutions exist with probability tending to one as n grows. Unlike the spherical perceptron, the solution space is discrete and dominated by isolated clusters.
title: Ising Perceptron and Storage Capacity

body:
[Question remove-delta of arXiv:2609.03856, 'Consensus time for asynchronous $\ell^p$ relaxation: graph dependence'] Fix $p\in(1,\infty]\setminus\{2\}$.  Can the factor $\Delta$ be removed from
the propagation lower bound in Theorem~(thm:propagation-lower of the paper)?  More
precisely, is there a constant $c_p>0$ such that, for every finite connected
graph, every nonconstant profile $f_0$, and every
$0<\epsilon\le\operatorname{osc}(f_0)/2$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb{E}\tau_p(\epsilon;f_0)
  \ge c_p\frac{n\operatorname{osc}(f_0)}{\lVert Sf_0-f_0\rVert_\infty}?
  
\end{equation}
The loss in the present proof occurs when all nearest-neighbor causal chains
are counted by a union bound.  A proof of
(equation eq:conjectural-degree-free-propagation of the paper) would have to average competing
influences without paying for the maximum number of possible next steps. (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Removing the maximum-degree loss

[Defi 1 of arXiv:2608.06576, 'The Resultant Distribution Method: Universality for $p$-adic Random Matrices and Polynomia'] We say that a random $p$-adic integer $\xi\in\Z_p$ is
$\epsilon$\emph{-balanced} if
$$
\mathbf{P}(\xi\equiv r\pmod p)\leq 1-\epsilon
$$
for every $r\in\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}$.

body:
Let G be a finite connected undirected graph on n>=2 vertices, with a specified symmetric support E of allowed transitions including any permitted holding loops. Among real symmetric stochastic matrices P supported on E, the second-largest eigenvalue modulus is mu(P)=max_{i>=2}|lambda_i(P)|=||P-(1/n)11^T||_2, where one stationary eigenvalue 1 is excluded and repeated stationary eigenvalues, if any, remain in the maximum. Minimizing mu(P) is the convex semidefinite program: minimize real s subject to -sI <=_PSD P-(1/n)11^T <=_PSD sI, P_ij>=0 entrywise, P1=1, P=P^T, and P_ij=0 for (i,j) outside E. The feasible matrices have uniform stationary law. This optimizes continuous transition probabilities on fixed support, not a deterministic integral matching or actual total-variation mixing time. The formulation is originally due to Boyd-Diaconis-Xiao (2004) and restated in Boyd-Diaconis-Parrilo-Xiao, arXiv:0709.0955, Section 1.1, equations (1)-(2), PDF p.2.

body:
Let M and N be NORMAL operators on a Hilbert space and let T be a bounded operator with M T = T N. Then also M* T = T N*. Taking M = N gives Fuglede's theorem: an operator commuting with a normal operator also commutes with its adjoint. A consequence used constantly: if T intertwines two normal operators then the ranges and kernels respecting one spectral projection respect the other, so T intertwines their spectral measures; in particular a normal operator commuting with T has a reducing subspace structure compatible with T.
NORMALITY of both M and N is essential;
for general operators the conclusion is false.
T need not be normal, invertible, or anything but bounded.
The boundedness of F, which Liouville needs, is exactly where normality enters through the unitarity of those exponential factors.

[Defn 13 ($\ell$-multigraph) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] We say that a multigraph $\gamma$ with nodes $1, 2, \dots, N$ is an $\ell$-multigraph if any pair of nodes can be connected by at most $\ell$ edges. The multiplicity $m^\gamma_{ij}$ between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is the number of separate edges connecting them, and we let $m^\gamma_{ij} = 0$ if the nodes $i$ and $j$ are not connected. (It is possible that $m_{kk}^{\gamma} > 0$, i.e., self-loops are allowed.) If $m^\gamma_{ij} = 1, 2, 3, 4$, we say that the edge between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is single, double, triple, quadruple, respectively.

The degree of the node $i$ is defined by
\[
	d^\gamma_i = m^\gamma_{ii} + \sum_{j=1}^N m^\gamma_{ij}.
\]
In particular, a single self-loop at the node $i$ increases the degree of the node $i$ by $2$. The size $m^\gamma$ and the length $n^\gamma$ of a multigraph $\gamma$ are defined by
\[
	m^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} m^\gamma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N d^\gamma_i, \quad n^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} > 0),
\]
respectively. The number of the single (respectively, double, triple, quadruple) edges $n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $n_2^\gamma, n_3^\gamma, n_4^\gamma$) is defined by
\[
	n_r^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} = r), \quad r=1, 2, 3, 4.
\]
Similarly, the number of the single (respectively, double) self-loops $\tilde n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $\tilde n_2^\gamma$) is defined by
\[ \tilde n_r^\gamma = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\indi(m^\gamma_{kk} = r), \quad r=1,2.\]

The set of all $\ell$-multigraphs with single and/or double self-loops is denoted by $\caG^\ell$. (The empty graph is a multigraph and included in $\caG^\ell$.)

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent real random variables with densities bounded by K, A a real symmetric n x n matrix, b in R^n, c in R, and Q = X^T A X + b^T X + c. If A has five eigenvalues of modulus at least s > 0, that is, its fifth singular value s_5(A) is at least s, Q has a density bounded by 270 K^2/s, whatever n, the other eigenvalues, the signature of A, b and c; with three such eigenvalues, sup_a E|Q - a|^{-1/2} <= 77 K/sqrt(s), and one is not enough (X_1 uniform on [0,1] and Q = X_1^2 give E X_1^{-1} = infinity). The nine-eigenvalue bound 400 K^2/s and the 17- and 33-eigenvalue versions are special cases. The proof turns 2m - 1 large eigenvalues into m large singular values of one off-diagonal block by random sign decoupling on the eigenvectors and applies a Fourier decay bound for that block. The conjecture itself, with three eigenvalues of modulus at least 1 and a universal constant, and the case of four are open; the sign-decoupling route cannot go below five.

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.23989, 'Collision Properties in Discrete and Continuous Time on Bounded-Degree Graphs'] Let~$P$ be an irreducible Markov kernel with~$n$-step transition probabilities~$p_n$, and suppose that, for some~$\alpha > 0$,
$$ \inf_{x \in \mathsf S} P^2(x,x) \ge \alpha.$$
Then, there exists~$a = a(\alpha) > 0$ such that
$$ \sum_{ \substack{\ell \ge 0: \\|\ell - m| \leq \sqrt{m}  } } \Psi(2m+\epsilon,2\ell + \epsilon) \cdot p_{2\ell + \epsilon}(x,y) \ge a \cdot p_{2m+\epsilon}(x,y) $$
for every~$x,y \in \mathsf S, m \ge 1$ and~$\epsilon \in \{0,1\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.23989

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.19549, 'The Generalized Friendship Paradox for Eigenvectors'] ({\bf Weak Convergence of the Empirical eigen-friendship bias distribution})
Consider either Model A or Model B and suppose the Assumptions A1--A3 hold. For the empirical eigen-friendship bias distribution defined in \eqref{ESDEFP} we have, as $n \to  \infty$
\[
\mu_n^E \Rightarrow \mu_{\infty} \quad \text{in probability,}
\] where $\mu_{\infty}$ is the law of 
\[
\Delta_{\infty} = \left(\frac{\rho}{K(U)}-1\right)\phi(U),
\]where $U \sim U(0,1).$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.19549

[Thm fineET of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a cooriented $C^0$-foliation on $M$ transverse to $\partial M$ with finitely many compact planar leaves. Let $L_1, \dots, L_m$ denote its unstable compact planar leaves, and let $\Lambda_1, \dots, \Lambda_k$ denote its unstable $\mathbb{T}^2$-type planar minimal sets. For each of those, choose a boundary point $p_i \in \partial L_i \subset \partial M$ and $q_j \in \partial \Lambda_j \subset \partial M$.
    
    Then $\mathcal{F}$ can be $C^0$-approximated by positive (resp.~negative) contact structures which dominate some foliation $\mathcal{G}$ on $\partial M$, obtained from $\partial \mathcal{F}$ by the following operations only:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Isotopies,
        \item Blowdowns and blowups of type $\natural/\sharp$ (resp.~$\natural/ \flat$) away from the boundaries of the aforementioned minimal sets,
        \item $\flat$ (resp.~$\sharp$) modifications near $p_1, \dots, p_m, q_1, \dots, q_k$.
    \end{itemize}
    Moreover, all of these operations can be made arbitrarily small, so that $\mathcal{G}$ is tangentially $C^0$-close to $\partial \mathcal{F}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Finest version of Eliashberg--Thurston

[Prop gl-Thom-space-la of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The global functor ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak t\kern-.5pt\mathfrak h}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}$ is a left adjoint.
    \begin{proof}
        Proposition~(prop:thom-space-marvelous of the paper) immediately implies the existence of a pointwise right adjoint. To see that these pointwise right adjoints satisfy the Beck--Chevalley condition, we may then equivalently show that ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak t\kern-.5pt\mathfrak h}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}$ satisfies the Beck--Chevalley condition with respect to the left adjoints along restriction. This follows as usual by observing that the Beck--Chevalley condition holds on the pointset level and that all functors in sight are left Quillen.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop gl-Thom-space-la of arXiv:2608.28504

[Theorem thm:U_process- of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Suppose $z=0$. For $r>0$, 
$\frac{r}{U(-r)+r}$ has distribution $\mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\delta+\widehat \delta}{2},\frac{\delta'}{2})$. 
\item The family $(Q^z,z\ge 0)$ defines a time-homogeneous Feller process. For each $z\ge 0$, the process $\left(U(-r)+r\right)_{r\ge 0}$ is a time-homogeneous $(\mathscr{W}^-_r)_{r\ge 0}$-adapted Feller process starting from $z$. 
\item Suppose $z>0$ and write $\mathrm{x}:=\inf\{r\ge 0\,:\, U(-r)>z\}$, $\mathfrak{U}:=U(-\mathrm{x})$. 
We have $\frac{z}{z+\mathrm{x}}\sim\mathcal{B}(\frac{\delta'}{2},1)$ and conditionally on  $\{{\mathrm{x}}=x\}$, $\frac{z+x}{\mathfrak{U}+x}\sim \mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\delta+\widehat{\delta}}{2},1)$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Theorem thm:U_process- of arXiv:2411.04773

[Lemma 54 of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] Let $0\le h\le h^*$, $1\le p\le q_n(h^*)$ and $1\le k\le q_n(h)$, and let $(A, \mathcal{V})$ be a $(p,h,k)$-uniform selection pair. Then for any test function $f$ defined on the value space of $\big((u^{h}_i)_{i=1,\ldots,k}, (\nu^s)_{1\le s\le h-1}\big)$, we have
\[
\mathbb{P}_n\Big[f\big(\mathcal{V}, (\nu^s)_{1\le s\le h-1}\big) \,\big|\, A\Big]
= \mathbb{P}_n\Big[f\big((u^{h}_i)_{1\le i\le k}, (\nu^s)_{1\le s\le h-1}\big)\Big].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 54 of arXiv:2511.09517

[Prop Zph2 of arXiv:2605.10617, 'Logarithmic scaling of selective sweep curves:\\ from tents to houses'] Assume that $Z_1^N$ starts in $\big\lfloor\tfrac {\log N}{\varphi_N}\big\rfloor$.
    Then for any $T$, $\delta>0$
    \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N\to\infty} \mathbb{P} \Big(  \sup_{t \leq T} \Big| \log_N^+(Z^N_{1} (t \varphi_N^{-1} \log N)) - (b+at) \Big| >\delta \Big)
        = 0,    
    \end{equation}

body: [Lemma 67 of arXiv:2608.07239, 'Unified framework for asymptotically uniform iterative construction of generalised random '] Consider integers $b\geq c\geq i\geq1$ and $a\geq0$. Let $A\subset B$ be sets of sizes $a$ and $b$ respectively. Then the probability that a uniformly random subset of $B$ of size $c$ overlaps $A$ in exactly $i$ elements is bounded from above by $$\exp\left(\tfrac12\log(2\pi c)+\tfrac{1}{12c}+\tfrac{c^2}{b-c}\right)\left(\tfrac{eca}{ib}\right)^i.$$

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2608.30875, 'A Decomposition Theorem for Topological Semi-small Maps'] Let $R$ be a closed topologically stratified space with the intrinsic stratification $R=\bigsqcup_{\alpha} S_{\alpha}$. Consider a finite decomposition $R=\bigsqcup_{\beta} T_{\beta}$ such that each $T_{\beta}$ is a topologically stratified space with a stratification $T_{\beta}=\sqcup_{\gamma} V^{\beta}_{\gamma}$. Assume the following:
    	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The inclusion $\overline{V^{\beta}_{\gamma}} \hookrightarrow R$ is locally flat, for all $\beta$ and $\gamma$.
		\item For each point $r \in R$ there is an open neighborhood that intersects finitely many connected components of finitely many $V^{\beta}_{\gamma}$. 
		\item The collection $\{ V_{\gamma}^{\beta}\}$ satisfies the frontier condition, i.e., $V^{\beta}_{\gamma} \cap \overline{V^{\beta^{\prime}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}} \neq \emptyset$ implies $V^{\beta}_{\gamma} \subseteq \overline{V^{\beta^{\prime}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}}$ for all $\gamma, \gamma^{\prime}, \beta,$ and $\beta^{\prime}$. 
	   \end{enumerate}
	   Then the decomposition $R=\bigsqcup_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma} (V_{\gamma}^{\beta} \cap S_{\alpha})$ is a topological stratification.

[Lemma 10 (Point fitting with an affine code) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $1\le S\le D$, $1\le J\le SD$, and $\eta\ge0$.  Suppose
$y_0,\ldots,y_{J-1}\in\R$ satisfy
\begin{equation*}
 \lvert y_j-y_{j-1}\rvert\le\eta,\qquad j=1,\ldots,J-1.
\end{equation*}
Write $\bmy:=(y_0,\ldots,y_{J-1})$.  There exist a one-input architecture
$\Phi^{\mathrm{fit}}\in\Arch(96,10D+24)$ and an affine map
$\calA^{\mathrm{fit}}\in\aff(3S+1,P_{\Phi^{\mathrm{fit}}})$, both depending
only on $(S,D)$, such that one can choose $\bmxi\in\R^{3S+1}$ and set
\[
 \bmtheta:=\calA^{\mathrm{fit}}(\bmxi)
\]
so that
\begin{equation}
 \left\lvert
 \Phi^{\mathrm{fit}}_{\bmtheta}(j)-y_j
 \right\rvert
 \le\eta,\qquad j=0,\ldots,J-1.
\end{equation}
Neither the architecture nor the affine map depends on the samples or on
$\eta$.

[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2609.03506, 'Divergence of decreasing rearranged Fourier series\\ on every infinite compact abelian gro'] Let \(E\subseteq\R_p^n\) and \(d\geq n\). Write
\(X=(x,z)\in\R_p^n\times\R_p^{d-n}\), and let \(Y\in\R_p^d\).
The function
\[
 F_E(X,Y)=1_E(x)\omega^{X\cdot Y}
\]
satisfies \(|F_E|=1_E(x)\) and
\begin{equation}
 \widehat F_E(a,b)=
 p^{-d}1_E(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\omega^{-a\cdot b}.
\end{equation}
In particular, \(|\widehat F_E(a,b)|\in\{0,p^{-d}\}\), also when
\(E=\varnothing\).

[Lemma lemma_adapted_homeo of arXiv:2604.04672, 'Connected components and topological ends of stationary planar forests'] Fix $\gamma\in\Gamma$ and an homeomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb{R}\to\gamma$. For each $\sigma\in\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma\}$, there exists a homeomorphism $\phi_{\sigma}$ and a non-empty bounded open interval $I_{\sigma}\coloneqq (a_\sigma,b_\sigma)\subset\mathbb{R}$ such that
        \[\text{$\Phi=\phi_\sigma$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus I_\sigma$},\quad \phi_\sigma(I_\sigma)=\sigma\setminus\gamma,\quad\text{and}\quad \Phi(I_\sigma)=\gamma\setminus\sigma.\]
    Then, one has additionally that for all distinct $\sigma,\sigma'\in\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma\}$,
        \[(\partial I_{\sigma'})\setminus\overline{I_{\sigma}}\subset \overline{I_{\sigma'|\sigma}}\quad\text{where}\quad I_{\sigma'|\sigma}\coloneqq\phi_{\sigma'}^{-1}(\sigma'\setminus\sigma).\]

[Definition def:predictable-cap-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let \(I\in\mathcal D_\ell^\circ\).  Define
\[
C_{I,n}
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
L_n\,\frac{2T_{\ell+1,n}}{M_I}, & M_I>0,\\[8pt]
+\infty, & M_I=0.
\end{cases}
\]
For a child \(J\subset I\), set \(
U_{J,n}^{\mathrm{cap}}=U_J\wedge C_{I,n}\), and define
\[
\overline U_{I,n}
=
\mathbb{E}[U_{J,n}^{\mathrm{cap}}\mid\mathcal F_\ell].
\]
This quantity is independent of the choice of the child \(J\subset I\), since the fresh child weights are independent copies of \(U\).
title: Predictable cap

body: In the mathematical field of real analysis, the monotone convergence theorem is any of a number of related theorems proving the good convergence behaviour of monotonic sequences, i.e. sequences that are non-increasing, or non-decreasing. In its simplest form, it says that a non-decreasing bounded-above sequence of real numbers converges to its smallest upper bound, its supremum. Likewise, a non-increasing bounded-below sequence converges to its largest lower bound, its infimum. In particular, infinite sums of non-negative numbers converge to the supremum of the partial sums if and only if the partial sums are bounded.
title: Monotone convergence theorem

[Lemma 3.4 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] (A step in the proof of Theorem 2.1; setting as in Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3.) Let f : Ω → R be c-Lipschitz and X be G-dependent for a Rooted and Ordered dependency tree G on [n] with parent map i ↦ p_i. Then for every i ∈ [n−1], x ∈ Ω and x'_i ∈ Ω_i, E[f(X) | X_{[i]} = x_{[i]}] − E[f(X) | X_{[i]} = x^{(i)}_{[i]}] ≤ c_i + c_{p_i}. By Lemma 3.3 the difference equals E[f(Y^{(i)}) − f(Z^{(i)})], and Y^{(i)}, Z^{(i)} differ at most in coordinates i and p_i. With McDiarmid's martingale lemma (Lemma 3.1) this gives Theorem 2.1's denominator c_n² + Σ_{i≠n} (c_i + c_{p_i})² = c_min² + Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G)} (c_i + c_j)².
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
G-dependent (Definition 1.3 of the paper): X = (X_i)_{i∈V(G)} is G-dependent when for all disjoint S, T ⊂ V(G) with no edge of G between S and T, the families (X_i)_{i∈S} and (X_j)_{j∈T} are independent; this is stronger than pairwise independence of non-adjacent coordinates.
Proof setting (Section 3 of the paper): G is a dependency tree on [n] that is Rooted (rooted at vertex n, with c_n = c_min) and Ordered (j is a descendant of i only if j < i), which a topological sort always provides; p_i is the parent of a non-root vertex i, S_i := [i+1, n] \ {p_i}, and for x ∈ Ω and x'_i ∈ Ω_i, x^{(i)} := (x_1, ..., x_{i−1}, x'_i, x_{i+1}, ..., x_n). The paper writes conditional probabilities of point events; for non-discrete Ω_i read them as conditional distributions.

body:
[Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem
with either  the  Mallows distribution
or the $P_n^{\mathcal{L}_\text{inv};\{q_n^i\}_{i=1}^n}$-type Luce distribution with  $q=q_n\in(0,\infty)-\{1\}$
in the case that the smallest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent iii.
Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac 1{1-q}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac1{1-q};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}<\frac1{1-q}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}=\frac 1{1-q}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\begin{cases}&(1-q)(1-q^{M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&1-q>\frac1e,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
$$
This limiting probability is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is
strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$.

\noindent iv. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent v.
Let $q_n=1+\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent vi. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac1{q-1}\le L<\frac q{q-1}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\frac{q-1}{q^L}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] Let $U$ and $Y$ be finite random variables, with $U$ taking values in
$\Omega$, and let $\Psi:\Delta(\Omega)\to\R$. The
{$\Psi$-information gain} from observing $Y$ is
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf I_\Psi(U;Y)
  :=\Psi(\mc{L}(U))
    -\E_Y\Psi(\mc{L}(U\mid Y)).
\end{equation}
In particular, $\mathsf I_H(U;Y)=I(U;Y)$.

DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C008 v1. For fixed integers K,q>=1 and D>=2, let X have masses proportional to exp(-t^2/2) on t=epsilon(j+b), j in Z, with b in {0,1/2}, D^-K<=epsilon<=1, and D^-K<=u<=D^K. For Y=X+uG and s=(log p_Y)', certified polynomial-time computable scalar parameters permit uniform polynomial-time construction of a constant-depth rational ReLU network f of polynomial size, coefficient magnitude and bit length with E[(f(Y)-s(Y))^2]<=D^-2q. An explicit clipping layer gives g with error <=3D^-2q and |g|<=4(q+K+10)log(D)/u. The window T=D^(2K+q+10) admits uniform error <=D^-q/4. This supplies a finite-precision implementation for the GPX phase-lattice score primitives, without an exact lattice-tie decision or circuit inversion. No novelty or independent-check claim.
K,q are fixed positive integers and D>=2
Independent standard Gaussian G
Scalar parameters admit certified rational enclosures of width 2^-l in time polynomial in D,l
The prior lattice is one-dimensional; D is the complexity parameter, not its geometric dimension
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:32fcd3043b883629d0e5c8ffd7641bd7c063ce1cbdb6f97bd153841ec34422be","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/32/32fcd3043b883629d0e5c8ffd7641bd7c063ce1cbdb6f97bd153841ec34422be.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:35db9388e6da6b094379cd3e406ed5fc45152f3b8db3d0cfaf35f16626b8e3bf","bundle_entry_key":"draft-computable-phase-lattice-gaussian-score-networks","bundle_id":"population.w740-t411-constructive-score-interface-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"diffusion priors and constructive score approximation","draft":"w740/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.sampling:draft-computable-phase-lattice-gaussian-score-networks","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Explicit phase-lattice score construction

Status: proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C008 v1, Target 2. This fills an implementation step in C007; no novelty claim about scalar Gaussian approximation is made. All complexity claims below are for fixed positive integers K and q. The calculations are analytic; numerical checks are supplementary.

## Statement and computational assumptions

Let D>=2 be an integer, K,q>=1 fixed integers, b in {0,1/2}, D^(-K)<=epsilon<=1, and D^(-K)<=u<=D^K. Let X have mass proportional to exp(-t^2/2) on t=epsilon(j+b), j in Z, and let Y=X+uG for an independent standard Gaussian G. Write s(x)=(log p_Y)'(x).

The scalar parameters are given by algorithms producing certified rational enclosures of width 2^(-l) in time polynomial in D and l. This includes rational parameters and the elementary computable parameters in the GPX source. Evaluations of x use the same convention; network construction only needs rational x. No exact comparison of arbitrary real parameters is assumed.

There is a uniform algorithm, polynomial in D for fixed K,q, which constructs a constant-depth ReLU network f with polynomially many parameters of polynomial magnitude such that

    E[(f(Y)-s(Y))^2] <= D^(-2q).

It uses only scalar exponential/arithmetic computations. A further explicit output-clipping layer gives a network g such that

    E[(g(Y)-s(Y))^2] <= 3 D^(-2q),
    |g(x)| <= 4(q+K+10) log(D)/u  for every x.

On the window |x|<=T=D^(2K+q+10), the un-clipped construction approximates s uniformly to error D^(-q)/4. The generated network has rational coefficients of polynomial bit length. The construction does not enumerate or invert a one-way function. The constants have been deliberately overestimated; the exponents are not proposed as optimal.

## 1. Conditional Gaussian lattice and its score

Completing the square in exp(-t^2/2-(x-t)^2/(2u^2)) gives a conditional lattice Gaussian with

    m=x/(1+u^2),  v^2=u^2/(1+u^2).

Let E_x denote expectation under weights proportional to exp(-(t-m)^2/(2v^2)). Differentiation of the convergent Gaussian sums gives

    s(x)=-x/(1+u^2) + E_x[t-m]/u^2,
    s'(x)=-1/u^2 + Var_x(t)/u^4.

Termwise differentiation is justified on every compact parameter/window set by Gaussian tails. These identities do not use a prior density on R.

Choose, for analysis only, an index j0 whose t0 is nearest to m. Put delta=t0-m, so |delta|<=epsilon/2, and divide every conditional weight by that of t0. Thus w0=1, and for the index offset n,

    w_n=exp(-((delta+n epsilon)^2-delta^2)/(2v^2)).

All w_n<=1. For |n|>=2,

    w_n <= exp(-epsilon^2 n^2/(4v^2)).                 (1)

Indeed the difference of squares is at least epsilon^2 |n|(|n|-1), and |n|(|n|-1)>=n^2/2. This relative normalization is essential: the unnormalized conditional mass of the nearest point can itself be exp(-poly(D)), and need not be bounded below by an inverse polynomial.

## 2. A uniform derivative bound

Because the relative partition sum is at least one, and v<=1,

    E_x[(t-m)^2]
      <=5+(9/2) epsilon^2 sum_{n>=2} n^2 exp(-epsilon^2 n^2/4)
      <=80/epsilon.                                  (2)

Here the nearest point and its two neighbors contribute at most 1/4+2(3/2)^2<5. To check the remaining constant, set alpha=epsilon/2<=1/2 and compare each summand with the integral on [n-1,n]:

    sum_{n>=1} n^2 exp(-alpha^2 n^2)
      <= integral_0^infinity (t+1)^2 exp(-alpha^2 t^2) dt
      =sqrt(pi)/(4alpha^3)+1/alpha^2+sqrt(pi)/(2alpha)
      <=2/alpha^3=16/epsilon^3.

The last inequality follows from sqrt(pi)<2 and alpha<=1/2. Substitution gives 5+72/epsilon<=80/epsilon.

The same bound applies to the conditional second moment truncated around the nearest point, since its relative partition sum remains at least one and its numerator is smaller. Therefore

    |s'(x)| <=u^(-2)+80/(epsilon u^4) <=L:=81 D^(5K)   (3)

for every real x. Also, for |x|<=T,

    |s(x)| <=T+sqrt(80/epsilon)/u^2 <=T+9D^(3K).       (4)

## 3. Certified finite evaluation of the score

Set eta=D^(-q), N=T=D^(2K+q+10), and M=2K+2q+20>=24. With the nearest-point normalization, delete the terms |n|>N. For each j=0,1,2, the deleted sum of |t-m|^j w_n is at most

    E0=1000 D^(3K) exp(-N^2/(8D^(2K)))
       <=D^(-(q+10K+20)).                            (5)

For the first inequality, use (1), epsilon<=1 and |t-m|<=|n|+1. Split exp(-n^2/(4D^(2K))) into two equal exponential factors and bound one by exp(-N^2/(8D^(2K))). The full sum of (|n|+1)^2 times the other factor is at most 1000D^(3K). This follows from the preceding integral comparison, now with alpha=1/(sqrt(8)D^K), applied to (t+2)^2; using sqrt(pi)<2 and sqrt(8)<3 gives a constant less than 200, so 1000 is sufficient.

For completeness, the elementary inequality used to absorb this exponential, and later tails, is

    D^M/32 >=(50M+100) log D  (D>=2, M>=24).         (6)

The function D^M/log D is increasing for D>=2. At D=2 it suffices that 2^M>=32(50M+100), true at M=24 and preserved by doubling. Since log 2<1, this proves (6). Also 1000<=D^10. These inequalities imply the second part of (5), because N^2/D^(2K)=D^M.

Let R and R_N be the full and truncated conditional means of t-m. The full and truncated partition sums are at least one. By (2), |R_N|<=9D^K. Equation (5) therefore gives

    |R-R_N| <=(1+9D^K)E0,
    |s-s_N| <=10D^(3K) E0 <=eta/16.                (7)

We next explain why this exact truncation can be evaluated with polynomial work, including near a lattice tie. Compute m/epsilon-b to absolute error at most 1/4 and take the floor of that rational approximation, an integer a. The exact nearest index lies within distance two of a. Use all indices in [a-N-3,a+N+3]. This set contains every term with |n|<=N, so its omitted tails satisfy (5)-(7), with the same constants. The nearest point is used in the estimates, but its exact identity is never needed by the algorithm.

Compute the energies (epsilon(j+b)-m)^2/(2v^2) on this finite set. Subtract the smallest of their rational approximations before taking negative exponentials. If each energy approximation has error at most kappa, every relative computed weight is at most exp(2kappa), and a maximum weight is at least exp(-2kappa). Thus the numerical denominator is bounded below by 1/2 once kappa is sufficiently small. There is no division by an exponentially small number. The common offset cancels from the normalized means regardless of which energy minimizes the rounded list.

Here are explicit precision budgets. Take

    kappa=eta/(2^20 D^(4K) (N+10)^3).

Obtain the individual weights and residual-weight products with absolute errors at most kappa, with a further constant-factor guard in their energy enclosures. There are at most 3(N+10) terms. For exact finite sums A,B with A>=1 in nearest-point units and |B/A|<=9D^K, errors at most 3(N+10)kappa in each sum change B/A by at most

    60 D^K (N+10) kappa.

If the implemented energy offset differs from the exact nearest energy, its common factor lies between exp(-2kappa) and exp(2kappa); allowing an additional factor four in the preceding estimate covers that normalization. After multiplication by u^(-2), this is less than eta/128 with the chosen budget. Perform the remaining scalar divisions and additions to error at most eta/128. Together with (7), the evaluation error is less than eta/8.

To see that those enclosures have polynomial cost, every index has magnitude at most O(T/epsilon+N), every residual has magnitude at most O(N), and v^(-2)<=2D^(2K). The energies, their derivatives with respect to the finitely many scalar inputs, and the reciprocal of every positive parameter denominator are bounded by fixed powers of D. Their certified evaluation to kappa accuracy needs O(poly(K,q) log D) input bits. Exponentials after the common shift have arguments bounded above by 2kappa; values below the requested precision may be replaced by a certified interval containing zero. Standard elementary-series or interval evaluation therefore has polynomial cost. There are polynomially many terms. This proves a uniform algorithm, rather than an existence assertion about network weights.

## 4. A rational ReLU network

Take n=16TL/eta, an integer under the present parameter choices, and use the n equal intervals covering [-T,T]. Their common length is Delta=eta/(8L). Compute each endpoint score to error at most eta/8 using Section 3 and retain a certified rational approximation. Interpolate the values linearly and extend constantly outside [-T,T]. Equations (3)-(4) show

    sup_{|x|<=T}|f(x)-s(x)|<=eta/4,
    |f(x)|<=H:=12 D^(3K+q+10) for every x.

Each segment slope has magnitude at most 3L, since the endpoint evaluation errors differ by at most eta/4. A continuous piecewise-linear function with knots t_i and slopes a_i, including slope zero outside the window, is represented by a constant plus sum_i (a_i-a_(i-1)) ReLU(x-t_i). Thus a two-layer network suffices, with polynomially many rational coefficients, each of polynomial magnitude and polynomial bit length. This also gives an explicit network-generation algorithm.

## 5. The tails do not hide an L2 error

The lattice normalizer is at least exp(-1/2)/epsilon: there are at least 1/epsilon lattice points in [-1,1]. For z>=2, comparing each positive lattice summand with its preceding interval of length epsilon, and doing the same on the negative side, gives

    Pr(|X|>z)<=4 exp(-z^2/8).

Indeed the two tails are at most 2 epsilon^(-1) integral_(z-epsilon)^infinity exp(-t^2/2)dt before division by the normalizer, and z-epsilon>=z/2 and >=1. Consequently

    pi_T:=Pr(|Y|>T)
      <=4 exp(-T^2/32)+2 exp(-T^2/(8u^2))
      <=6 exp(-D^M/32)
      <=D^(-(100K+100q+1000)),                       (8)

where (6) proves the last deliberately loose bound.

The Gaussian denoising identity s(Y)=-E[G|Y]/u and Jensen give E[s(Y)^4]<=3/u^4. Cauchy-Schwarz therefore bounds the error outside the window by

    E[(f(Y)-s(Y))^2 1_{|Y|>T}]
      <=2H^2 pi_T+2sqrt(3)u^(-2)sqrt(pi_T)
      <=eta^2/2.                                    (9)

For a direct check of the last inequality, its two terms are bounded by 288D^(-94K-98q-980) and 4D^(-48K-50q-500), respectively; each is at most eta^2/4 for D>=2,K,q>=1. Inside the window the squared error is at most eta^2/16. This proves the stated global L2 bound, with slack.

## 6. Bounded output and use in C007

Set B0=2(q+K+10)log(D)/u and choose a certified rational B in [B0,2B0]. Clip the network output to [-B,B], using two additional ReLU operations. Conditional Jensen applied to exp(lambda G) shows that u s(Y) is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy one. Integrating its tail gives

    E[(s(Y)-clip_B(s(Y)))^2]
      <=4u^(-2) exp(-(uB)^2/2)
      <=4D^(-2q-10).

The second inequality uses log D>=log 2>1/2 and (q+K+10)^2>2q+2K+10. Projection onto the interval is nonexpansive, so the squared error of the clipped network is at most twice the error of f plus twice this clipping error, below 3eta^2. Its magnitude is at most 2B0, as stated.

For q>K+1 this has the O(u^(-1)log(1/(u D^(-q)))) output bound used for the one-dimensional primitives in GPX Lemmas C.11/C.15. Arbitrarily fixed inverse-polynomial error budgets are obtained by increasing q, keeping polynomial complexity. Ordinary one- or two-component Gaussian primitives are even simpler finite sums and satisfy the same evaluation/interpolation argument. The source's network composition then uses these scalar primitives, its explicit decoder and forward-circuit evaluation, and switches. Composing constant-depth polynomial-size, polynomially bounded networks preserves those properties, and rounding scalar coefficients more finely by a fixed inverse-polynomial factor absorbs the polynomial sensitivity of that composition. [Corollary 17 (Unique Pinkall-modulus limit) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:anchored-profile}, orient the
profiles consistently with the reduced flow.  Let
\(\mathcal A_t\in\R/4\pi\mathbb Z\) be the oriented area class
enclosed by \(\gamma_t\), and let \(\mathcal A_T\) be the corresponding area class for
\(\gamma_T\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 
 \mathcal A_t\longrightarrow\mathcal A_T
 \qquad\text{in }\R/4\pi\mathbb Z .
\end{equation}
For \(t\) sufficiently close to \(T\), choose compatible real
representatives such that \(\mathcal A_t\to\mathcal A_T\).  Pinkall's
lattice is
\begin{equation}
 
 \Gamma_t=
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Z}
 \left\{(2\pi,0),
 \left(\frac{\mathcal A_t}{2},\frac{L(\gamma_t)}2\right)\right\},
\end{equation}
and the corresponding modulus is
\begin{equation}
 
 \tau_t=\frac{\mathcal A_t+iL(\gamma_t)}{4\pi}\in\mathbb H .
\end{equation}
It satisfies
\[
 \tau_t\longrightarrow
 \tau_T:=\frac{\mathcal A_T+iL_T}{4\pi}.
\]
Its imaginary part satisfies the quantitative bounds
\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\leq\operatorname{Im}\tau_T\leq\frac2\pi.
\end{equation}
Consequently the conformal classes
\[
 [\tau_t]\longrightarrow[\tau_T]
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal M_1=\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)
\]
have a unique finite-time limit, independent of the approaching time
sequence.  With the orientation induced by the fixed oriented profile
and the positively oriented Hopf fibres, the class \([\tau_T]\) is the
intrinsic oriented conformal class of the limiting \(C^1\) Hopf torus.
In particular, no conformal
degeneration occurs at the finite endpoint.

body: Lemma (campaign status: audited-pass): From the atom bound, as + 1 ≤ 4*4^(cs). With C* = sum_s cs and 4^beta = 16/9, a convexity calculation gives (sum_s 4^(cs))/4^(C*) ≤ m*(16/9)^(-(m-1)) ≤ 9/8, where m is the number of nonempty batches (the trivial N = 0 case is separated first). No two-shadow edge survives outside a vertex cover, hence every row support contains at most one coordinate outside C. Notes: Constant 9 explicitly not claimed sharp; the structural gain is paying dense rows their full atom loss, eliminating the old 1+ell factor. Fix a finite irreducible row-stochastic Q with stationary probability pi, p in [0,1]^d, c>0, f=cr^2 and 0<r with r+f<=1. For Z in the state space [0,1]^d, let X_i be conditionally independent Bernoulli((QZ)_i), and update Z prime=(1-r-f)Z+rX+fp. The stationary law is unique, has mean f*((r+f)I-rQ)^(-1)p, and Cov(Z) tends as r->0 to K*pbar*(1-pbar)/(2c+K) times the all-ones matrix, where pbar=pi.p and K=sum pi_i^2. For Q=(1), its exact variance is p(1-p)/(1+2c-c^2*r^2). This is a stationary moment result, not a functional diffusion convergence theorem.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:a79b386a6456c8586b0a038749eac17e42ba4fc260074089a8c88ea90bebe9d2","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/a7/a79b386a6456c8586b0a038749eac17e42ba4fc260074089a8c88ea90bebe9d2.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:cbac8f169ff863a9595053ddefd9aa680d7116085e24b8a5c3f7297ee2ff2704","bundle_entry_key":"forced-network-urn-stationary-covariance-quadratic-forcing","bundle_id":"population.w336-p0087-checked-attempt-20261010","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"w336/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.reinforcement:forced-network-urn-stationary-covariance-quadratic-forcing","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0087: stationary synchronization and covariance at f=c*r^2

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. This proves a full stationary-law limit, stationary moments and a scalar generator limit under conditional independence. It does not prove the general network's functional diffusion limit or its initial layer.

Assume a fixed finite irreducible row-stochastic Q, its stationary probability row vector pi, p in [0,1]^d, c>0, r>0, f=c*r^2 and r+f<=1. Update

    Z'=(1-r-f)Z+r X+f p,

with conditionally independent X_i given Z, and P(X_i=1|Z)=(QZ)_i. There is a unique stationary law on [0,1]^d. Its mean is z*=f*((r+f)I-rQ)^(-1)p. Write pbar=pi.p and K=sum pi_i^2. As r decreases to zero, its stationary covariance satisfies

    Cov(Z) -> [K*pbar*(1-pbar)/(2c+K)]*1*1^T.

Proof of existence/uniqueness: the transition is Feller on a compact cube. Couple two states using the same independent uniforms for their Bernoulli coordinates. Because 1-r-f>=0, the weighted L1 distance has expected next value at most (1-f) times its present value; use pi Q=pi. Thus stationary laws are unique and the transition contracts in this Wasserstein distance. Taking expectations yields the displayed mean; the matrix is invertible because its eigenvalues have positive real part.

For synchronization, let D=diag(pi), S=pi.Z, and E_Q(z)=z^T D(I-Q)z=(1/2)sum pi_i Q_ij(z_i-z_j)^2. At stationarity, with Delta=r(X-Z)+f(p-Z),

    2r E[E_Q(Z)] = 2f E[<Z,p-Z>_D] + E[||Delta||_D^2]
                   <= 2f+(r+f)^2 = O(r^2).

Irreducibility makes E_Q(z)>=gamma*||z-1*(pi.z)||_D^2 for some fixed gamma>0: the finite symmetric quadratic form has kernel precisely the constants. Hence E||Z-1*S||_D^2=O(r). Also E[S]=pbar exactly, so z*_i tends to pbar.

The martingale innovation for S has conditional variance r^2 sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i); conditional independence is used exactly here. Total variance at stationarity gives

    (2f-f^2) Var(S)=r^2 sum pi_i^2 E[(QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)].

Synchronization shows (QZ)_i-S tends to zero in L2. The variables are bounded, so for any subsequential limit V of Var(S), division by r^2 gives 2c V=K*(pbar*(1-pbar)-V). Its solution is unique. Every subsequence has that limit, and synchronization gives the full covariance limit.

For the scalar case Q=(1), stationarity gives the exact variance

    Var(Z)=r^2*p*(1-p)/(2f-f^2+r^2)
          =p*(1-p)/(1+2c-c^2*r^2).

For h in C^3([0,1]), the one-step scalar generator divided by r^2 converges uniformly to

    Lh(z)=c(p-z)h'(z)+(1/2)z(1-z)h''(z).

Indeed E[Delta]=c*r^2(p-z), E[Delta^2]=r^2*z(1-z)+c^2*r^4(p-z)^2, and |Delta|<=r+cr^2. Taylor's remainder, divided by r^2, is bounded by ||h'''||_infinity*r*(1+cr)^3/6, with the additional second-order drift term O(r^2). This identifies the candidate Wright-Fisher generator; path tightness and martingale-problem uniqueness are further steps.

Theorem (full stationary law). Under the same fixed-network assumptions and 0<pbar<1, the joint stationary law of Z converges weakly to Y*1, where

    Y ~ Beta(2c*pbar/K, 2c*(1-pbar)/K).

Proof: write S'=S+f*(pbar-S)+r*eta, where eta=pi.(X-QZ), E[eta|Z]=0, |eta|<=1 and E[eta^2|Z]=sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i). For every polynomial h, the stationary Taylor identity divided by r^2 gives

    0=c E[(pbar-S)h'(S)]
      +(1/2)E[sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)*h''(S)] + O(r).

The drift-square contribution is O(r^2), and the third-order remainder is uniformly O(r). The proved L2 synchronization implies that the sum inside the second term differs from K*S*(1-S) by a quantity tending to zero in L1. Every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence of S because [0,1] is compact. If its limiting moments are mu_k, use h(s)=s^k, k>=1, to obtain

    [2c+K*(k-1)]*mu_k = [2c*pbar+K*(k-1)]*mu_(k-1), mu_0=1.

These are exactly the moments of the displayed beta law: iterating gives the product of (2c*pbar/K+j)/(2c/K+j) for j=0,...,k-1, which also follows by integrating the beta density. A probability law on [0,1] is determined by its moments, since polynomials approximate continuous functions uniformly. Hence all subsequential limits agree and S converges weakly. Synchronization gives Z-S*1 tending to zero in probability, so the joint law converges to Y*1. If pbar=0 or 1, positivity of pi forces every p_i to be that endpoint and the unique stationary law is the corresponding point mass.

This proof uses all polynomial moments, not an inference from the first two moments. It proves convergence of stationary laws, not a limit for trajectories begun away from synchronization. Without conditional independence, the innovation variance changes. For example, Q=J_d/d, constant p, and one shared Bernoulli coin across all coordinates preserve a synchronized state and give the scalar beta parameters 2cp and 2c(1-p), rather than 2cdp and 2cd(1-p).

For reproducible finite checks, the exact covariance identity is

    V=B V B^T+r^2*diag(s*(1-s)-diag(Q V Q^T)),
    B=(1-r-f)I+rQ, s=Q z*.

Checks: the scalar exact formula; first four scalar stationary moments; exact polynomial generators; finite-network covariance systems; first four moments of the exact consensus Markov chain for Q=J_d/d at d=2,3,5; a common-coin control that changes the beta variance. The conditional-independence hypothesis is essential for K, the covariance formula and the stationary beta law.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:97f3a85196e873990e9567366e0506ef248b0ce7c5366d200c12cde129cf9cd6","revision_digest":"sha256:71f11592c93dc1af9dff028a3e3fbbd66f755b9640b9f7629f748526e31a9a8f","source_id":"owner:campaign:w336:P0087:forced-network-urn-stationary-covariance-quadratic-forcing","source_revision":"author-proof-2026-10-10; independent audit w346 pending","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
[Lemma lem:z^m of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] In the \nameref{setting} Setting, for any $m\in[d]$ and any $v\in\mathbb R^d$ there exists a vector $z^m=(z_1^m,z_2^m,\cdots,z_n^m)\in\mathbb R^n_{>0}$ such that for each $i\in[n]$ we have
\begin{align*}
    \left(\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}(z^m_j-z^m_i)\right)+(vM_i)_m&=w_i^{-1}n^{-1}(vM)_m,
\end{align*}
where $(vM_i)_m$ and $(vM)_m$ denote the $m$-th entries of the vectors $vM_i$ and $vM$, respectively.

\begin{proof}
Fix $m$. Let $\psi=(\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_n)$ denote the vector whose $i$-th entry is the $m$-th entry of the (length $d$) vector $v(n^{-1}M-w_iM_i)$; that is,
\begin{align*}
    \psi_i:=(v(n^{-1}M-w_iM_i))_m.
\end{align*}
We claim that there exists a vector $z^m$ such that
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{diag}(w)Qz^m=\psi.
\end{align}
By the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra, the image space of the matrix $\operatorname{diag}(w)Q$ is exactly the set of vectors orthogonal to the kernel of $(\operatorname{diag}(w)Q)^\intercal=Q^\intercal \operatorname{diag}(w)$. But since the Markov chain associated to $Q$ is irreducible, its stationary distribution $w$ is unique. It follows that, if $\widehat w$ is a vector with $\widehat wQ=0$, then $\widehat w$ is a scalar multiple of $w$.

But if $0=(\operatorname{diag}(w)Q)^\intercal\rho$ for some $\rho=(\rho_1,\cdots,\rho_n)^\intercal$ then
$
    0=\operatorname{diag}(w)\rho Q,
$
so in particular taking $\widehat w=\operatorname{diag}(w)\rho$ we see that $\rho$ must be a scalar multiple of the all-ones vector $\mathbf 1$. All this is to say that the kernel of $(\operatorname{diag}(w)Q)^\intercal$ is exactly the span of $\mathbf 1$, and therefore $\psi$ is in the image of $\operatorname{diag}(w)Q$ iff $\psi$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf 1$.

The scalar product between $\psi$ and $\mathbf 1$ is
\begin{align*}
    \psi\cdot\mathbf1
    &=\sum_{i=1}^n (v(n^{-1}M-w_iM_i))_m\\
    &=\left(\sum_{i=1}^nv(n^{-1}M-w_iM_i)\right)_m\\
    &=\left(v\left(\sum_{i=1}^n n^{-1}M-w_iM_i\right)\right)_m\\
    &=\left(v\left(M-M\right)\right)_m\\
    &=0.
\end{align*}
So $\psi$ is indeed orthogonal to $\mathbf 1$, and hence $\psi$ is the image of some vector $z^m$ under $\operatorname{diag}(w)Q$. Let $z^m$ be such. Notice that the $i$-th entry of $\operatorname{diag}(w)Q z^m$ is
\begin{align*}
    (\operatorname{diag}(w)Q z^m)_i
    &=\sum_{j=1}^n w_i q_{ij}z^m_j\\
    &=\left(\sum_{j\ne i} w_i q_{ij}z^m_j\right)+w_i q_{ii}z^m_i\\
    &=\left(\sum_{j\ne i} w_i q_{ij}z^m_j\right)-\sum_{j\ne i}w_i q_{ij} z^m_i\\
    &=\sum_{j\ne i} w_i q_{ij}(z^m_j-z^m_i).
\end{align*}
So equation (equation eq:diag(w)Qz=psi of the paper) tells us that for each $i$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{j\ne i} w_i q_{ij}(z^m_j-z^m_i)
    &=(v(n^{-1}M-w_iM_i))_m\\
    \sum_{j\ne i} w_i q_{ij}(z^m_j-z^m_i)+w_i(vM_i)_m&=n^{-1}(vM)_m\\
    \sum_{j\ne i}  q_{ij}(z^m_j-z^m_i)+(vM_i)_m&=w_i^{-1}n^{-1}(vM)_m.
\end{align*}
But this is exactly the equation we wanted $z^m$ to satisfy. \textit{A priori}, the vector $z^m$ need not have all positive entries. However, notice that if we add the same real number to every entry of $z^m$ then the equality above will be preserved, since the left-hand side is only a function of the differences $z^m_j-z^m_i$. Therefore, we may take every entry of $z^m$ to be positive without loss of generality.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:z^m of arXiv:2507.09421

[Theorem Fourier_laplace of arXiv:2606.29622, 'Affine Structure of the Brownian Signature'] Let $\bm{\sigma}\in T(\mathbb{C}^2)$ such that $\deg(\bm{\sigma}) = N$ for some odd $N$ such that 
    
    $\lambda := \bm{\sigma}^{{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{1}}}^{\otimes N}} \neq 0$, and let $M$ be the martingale defined by (equation eq:sig_mart of the paper). Suppose that $v = (v_1, v_2) \in \mathbb{C}^2$ is such that 
    $$
    v_1 \in \{z\in \mathbb{C} \colon \, \mathfrak{Re}(\lambda z) < 0\} \cup \{0\}, \quad  \, \mathfrak{Re}\left(\lambda^2 v_2\right) < 0,    
    $$
    and $\mathbb{E}[\exp(v_1 M_T + v_2 \langle M \rangle_T) | \mathcal{F}_t] \neq 0\,$ a.s. for all $t \in [0, T]$.
    Then,
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(v_1 M_T + v_2 \langle M\rangle_T\right)\, |\, \mathcal{F}_t\right] = \exp(\bracket{\bm{\psi}_t^{\sigW}}{{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{\varnothing}}}})\,, \quad t \in [0\,,T]\,,
    \end{equation}
    where $\bm{\psi}^{\sigW[t]}$ is a solution to the Riccati equation (equation eq:Riccati_recentered of the paper) with $\sigX[] = \sigW[t]\,$,
    
    
    
    
    
    
    and $\bm{p}$ is given by
    \begin{equation}
        \bm{p} = v_1\left(\bm{\sigma}{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{1}}} - \dfrac12\bm{\sigma}|_{{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{1}}}}{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{0}}}\right) + v_2 \bm{\sigma}^{\mathrel{\sqcup \mkern -3mu \sqcup} 2}{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{0}}}.
    \end{equation}

[Theo excha of arXiv:2507.00737, 'Dispersion models on a circle: universal properties and asymptotic results'] Consider a valid {\sf CDM}\xspace $A$, and some deterministic masses $m[k]=(m_0,\cdots,m_{k-1})$, which are either positive or zero and satisfy the total weight condition  $W(m[k])  <1$. Let $({\sf IR}_j^A,0\leq j \leq k-1)$ denote the interval relaxation processes associated with $A$. We have  
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item For a fixed $k$, the law of $\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)$ does not depend on $A$ (it is the same for all valid {\sf CDM}\xspace that are designed to treat the masses $(m_0,\cdots,m_{k-1})$.
		\item  The law of $\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)$ is invariant under the permutation of the masses:
		For any permutation $r\in {\bf S}_k$ (the symmetric group on $\{0,\cdots,k-1\}$),
		\[{\cal L}\left (\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)~|~ (m_0,\cdots,m_{k-1})\right)={\cal L}\left (\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)~|~ (m_{r(0)},\cdots,m_{r(k-1)})\right)\]
		(where we have written, as a condition, the successive masses that are used).
		\item For $k\geq 1$, the number of free CC,  ${\bf N}_k$, has (almost) a binomial distribution:
		\begin{equation}
		 {\bf N}_k \sur{=}{(d)} 1+ B(m[k]), \textrm {~~where~~} B(m[k])\sim {\sf Binomial}(k-1,R_k) 
		\end{equation}
		where $R_k=1-W(m[k])$ is the final free space available after the deposition of the first $k$ masses.
		\item Take a uniform element $\theta$ in $\{0,\cdots,b-1\}$ (independently of everything). Conditional on ${\bf N}_k=b$, 
		\begin{equation}\left(\left|\textbf{F}^{(k)}_{i+\theta {~\sf mod~} b}\right|,0\leq i \leq b-1\right)\sur{=}{(d)} R_k\, ({\bf D}_0,\cdots,{\bf D}_{b-1})\end{equation}  where $({\bf D}_0,\cdots,{\bf D}_{b-1})\sim{\sf Dirichlet}(b;1,\cdots,1)$. 
		Hence, the sequence $\left(|\textbf{F}^{(k)}_{i}|,0\leq i \leq b-1\right)$ taken according to a uniform independent rotation, is unbiased. 
		\item 
		The process $({\bf N}_k,k\geq 0)$ is a Markov chain, and its transition matrix can be computed explicitly (see (sec:qefgrethry of the paper)). 
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theo excha of arXiv:2507.00737

[Lemma lem:obstacles of arXiv:2507.09120, 'Chemical distance in graphs of polynomial growth'] Let $G = (V,E)$ be a $\Delta$-simply connected graph.
   Let $x, y \in V$, let $\beta \subset V$ be a path
   from $x$ to $y$ in $G$, and let $F \subset V$ be a finite
   set of vertices (which we think of as ``forbidden'').
   If there exists some path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$ in $G \setminus F$,
   then there exists a path $\gamma'$ from $x$ to $y$ which lies in
   $(N(F, \Delta) \cup \beta) \setminus F$.
   Here $N(F, \Delta) := \bigcup_{f \in F} B(f, \Delta)$
   is the $\Delta$-neighborhood of $F$.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The even moments of hyperspherical variables are given by
$$\int_{S^{N-1}_\mathbb R}x_i^kdx=\frac{(N-1)!!k!!}{(N+k-1)!!}$$
and the odd moments vanish. The normalized hyperspherical variables 
$$y_i=\sqrt{N}x_i$$
become standard normal, following $g_1$, and independent with $N\to\infty$.

[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2605.02093, 'An analytic approach to the finite $R$-transform'] Let $h$ be differentiable and strictly concave on $(0,\infty)$.
Then
\[
  h^*(h'(x)) = xh'(x) - h(x),
\]
and
\[
  (h^*)'(h'(x)) = x.
\]
In other words, the derivative of $h^*$ is the inverse function of $h'$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 17 (SDE for the first Malliavin derivative) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth}, and
\ref{ass:second-malliavin-uniform}(i) hold. Fix
$ 0 \le s \le u \le t $ and $ i,j \in \left\{ 1,\dots,N \right\} $. Then
$ D_s^j X_u^{i,N} $ satisfies, on $ [s,t] $,
\begin{align}

D_s^j X_u^{i,N}
&=
\sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(
\partial_x b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right) D_s^j X_r^{i,N}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right)\left( X_r^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^j X_r^{\ell,N}
\Biggr) dr
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right) D_s^j X_r^{i,N}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right)\left( X_r^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^j X_r^{\ell,N}
\Biggr) dB_r^i.
\end{align}
Equivalently, for every $ \alpha \in \left\{ 1,\dots,m \right\} $, the column
$ D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N} $ satisfies
\begin{align}

D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
&=
\sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)e_\alpha \mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(
\partial_x b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right) D_s^{j,\alpha} X_r^{i,N}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right)\left( X_r^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_r^{\ell,N}
\Biggr) dr
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right) D_s^{j,\alpha} X_r^{i,N}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right)\left( X_r^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_r^{\ell,N}
\Biggr) dB_r^i.
\end{align}

[Theorem 25 of arXiv:2505.06187, 'Preferential Attachment Trees with Vertex Death: Persistence of the Maximum Degree'] Consider the CMJ branching process $(\bp(t))_{t\geq0}$ as defined in Section~\ref{sec:embed}, where the offspring $D$ and inter-birth times $(X(i))_{i\in\N}$ satisfy Assumption~\ref{ass:appendix}.

[Theorem 3 (Uniform stability of a smooth expanding simple wave) of arXiv:2609.01589, 'Uniform stability of expanding simple waves for Euler--Poisson--Boltzmann: a singular comp'] Let Assumption~\ref{ass:pressure} hold, let $t_0\ge0$ and $T>t_0$ be fixed, and let
$(\Nr,\Vr)$ be the smooth planar simple wave constructed in
\cref{prop:smooth-simple-wave}.  For every $M\ge0$ there are
$\eps_0,\eta_0>0$ and a composite profile
$(n^a,u^a,\phi^a)$ of the form \eqref{eq:composite-intro} such that the
following holds for $0<\eps\le\eps_0$.

Suppose the initial density and velocity at $t=t_0$ satisfy the far-field
conditions, $n_0(x)\in[n_*/2,3n^*/2]$, and
\[
  \cE_{s,\eps}[r_0,v_0,\psi_0](t_0)\le\eta_0^2,
\]
where $\phi_0=\phi^a(t_0)+\psi_0$ is the unique solution of
\eqref{eq:EP-poisson}.  Then \eqref{eq:EP-mass}--\eqref{eq:EP-poisson}
has a unique classical solution on $[t_0,T]$ with
\[
  (r,v,\psi)\in C([t_0,T];H^s(\Om)),
  \qquad \eps\nabla\psi\in C([t_0,T];H^s(\Om)).
\]
Uniqueness holds among classical solutions with this regularity, positive
density in $[n_*/4,2n^*]$, the prescribed far fields, and values in the
Poisson chart \eqref{eq:poisson-map}; by continuity any classical solution
issued from the stated data lies in that class on a maximal common interval,
where \cref{lem:difference} applies.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t_0\le t\le T}\cE_{s,\eps}(t)
  \le C_{t_0,T}\bigl(\cE_{s,\eps}(t_0)+\eps^{4M+4}\bigr), 
\end{equation}
where $C_{t_0,T}$ and the smallness thresholds are independent of $\eps$.
The density stays in $[n_*/4,2n^*]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform stability of a smooth expanding simple wave

			$$
			\mathbb{P}\left[\big\{\{\mathcal{M}_i^s\}_{i=1}^k \neq \{\mathcal{M}_i^t\}_{i=1}^k \big\}\cap \mathcal{E}[W] \right] \le C (t-s)^{2/3+\delta},
			$$
			where the constant $C$ can also depend on $\theta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2607.12384, '2607.12384'] Let \(u\) be the solution to equation \eqref{eq:main equation}, and let \(G\) denote the
	corresponding heat kernel defined in \eqref{eq:G=integral}. Assume that \(d=1\).
	Fix \(T>0\), \(p\ge2\), and let \(0\le s<r\le T\), \(y,z\in\mathbb R\).
	Assume that the Malliavin derivative of \(u\) satisfies
	\begin{equation}
		\|D_{s,y}u(r,z)\|_p^2
		\le C G_{r-s}^2(z-y)
		+ C\int_s^r\int_{\mathbb R}
		G_{r-r_1}^2(z-z_1)\,
		\|D_{s,y}u(r_1,z_1)\|_p^2\,dz_1\,dr_1,
	\end{equation}
	for some constant \(C>0\) depending on \(T\) and \(p\). Then there exists a
	constant \(C_{T,p}>0\), depending on \(T\) and \(p\), such that
	\begin{equation}
		\|D_{s,y}u(r,z)\|_p^2
		\le C_{T,p}\,(r-s)^{-\frac \beta \alpha}\,G_{r-s}(z-y),
	\end{equation}
	and consequently
	\begin{equation}
		\|D_{s,y}u(r,z)\|_p
		\le C_{T,p}\,(r-s)^{-\frac{\beta}{2\alpha}}\,G_{r-s}(z-y)^{\frac 1 2}.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 10 of arXiv:2607.12384

[Corollary cor:canonical-borel-compression-traces of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every $0<a<b$, bounded real Borel function $v$, and $k\ge1$, the map
\begin{equation}
 x\longmapsto
 \Tr\!\left[(\Pi_{a,b}^x\operatorname{Mult}_v\Pi_{a,b}^x)^k\right]
 \in\mathbb R
\end{equation}
is measurable.  In particular, for rational $0<a<b$ and $v=q\in\mathcal Q_D$,
these are the power traces appearing in
(equation eq:minimal-borel-interface of the paper).

body: [Theorem 12 of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] (Asymptotic Apportionment) Let $(1,x,y(x,\tau))$ be a reduced population vector associated with a fixed $\tau$, and let $A$ be a divisor method that guarantees nonzero allocations on $M$ seats. body:
[Lem 19 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] The set $[-r,r]$ is a \emph{mobile cluster},
i.e.,
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $\eta$ such that $\eta(x)=0$ for all $x\in x_{0}+[-r,r]$. Then
there exist $\eta'\connected{}{}\eta$ such that $\eta'(x)=0$ for
all $x\in x_{0}+1+[-r,r]$.
\item Let $\eta$ such that $\eta(x)=0$ for all $x\in x_{0}+[-r,r]$. Then
there exist $\eta'\connected{}{}\eta$ such that $\eta'(x)=0$ for
all $x\in x_{0}-1+[-r,r]$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:stabilising-transient of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$.  
Let $j_0$ be a sufficiently large positive integer. Let $\tau_0$ be a  non-negative integer. Let $\Psi_0$ be the   initialising high-level state with $\tau^{\Psi_0} = \tau_0$ and $j^{\Psi_0} = j_0$. 
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be the $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule from Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-rule of the paper).  
Let $V$ be a volume process from $\Psi_0$ with transition rule $\mathrm{hls}$ send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$. 
Let $t> \tau_0$ be a positive
integer such that $\Psi(t)$ is $j$-stabilising and
$\tau^{\Psi(t)} = t$.
Then 
there is a $t'\in \{t+1,\ldots,t+j^{\phi+72}\}$ such that $\Psi(t') \neq \Psi(t)$.

[Cons 24 of arXiv:2606.08115, '2606.08115'] Let condition (C) be valid for a two-dimensional random walk $\left\{ \ov{S}_n\right\}$, the correlation coefficient of components of the random walk increments $\rho \in (0, 1)$. Then for any $\ov{x} \in \mathcal{X}_V$ and any $\alpha > 0$ the equality
$$\lim_{T \to \infty} \pr_{\bfx}^{+}\left(\exists j > T: \ov{S}_j + \ov{x} \in K \backslash K_{j, \alpha}\right) = 0$$
holds, where

body: Let Omega be a bounded domain in R^n with Lipschitz boundary, let 1 <= p < n, and let p* = np/(n-p) be the Sobolev conjugate exponent. Then the Sobolev embedding W^{1,p}(Omega) -> L^{p*}(Omega) is continuous, and the embedding W^{1,p}(Omega) -> L^q(Omega) is compact for every q with 1 <= q < p*: any sequence bounded in the W^{1,p} norm has a subsequence converging strongly in L^q(Omega). If p = n, the embedding into L^q(Omega) is compact for every finite q; if p > n, W^{1,p}(Omega) embeds compactly into C(closure of Omega). Named for Franz Rellich and Vladimir Kondrachov.
title: Rellich-Kondrachov theorem

body:
[Theorem 3 (Long-time behavior in the scalar case) of arXiv:2604.04100, '\LARGE Learning Equilibrium Fluctuation Expansions from Overdamped Langevin Dynamics'] Assume $d=1$. Let $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and let $X_\varepsilon$,  $(\bar{X}_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$,  $(a_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$ be as in Proposition \ref{thm-weak-exp-intro}. If we further assume that Assumption \ref{A2} holds, then for every $F \in C^{n+1}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying \eqref{assump-F}, the following assertions hold:\begin{enumerate}

\item[(i)] The limit
$$
b_0(F) := \lim_{t\to\infty} a_0(t,F)
$$
exists, and satisfies
\begin{equation}
b_0(F) = \mathbb{E}\Bigl[ \lim_{t\to\infty} F\bigl(\bar{X}_0(t)\bigr) \Bigr]
= F(1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0) + F(-1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0).
\end{equation}
\item[(ii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ and $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, define
$$
S_{m,i}(t) := \sum_{(j_1,\dots,j_i)\in\mathcal{D}_i^m} \prod_{k=1}^{i}\bar{X}_{j_k}(t),\quad t\ge0.
$$
We adopt the convention that a sum over the empty set is equal to $0$, and hence
$$
S_{m,i}(t):=0
\quad\text{whenever }m<0,\ i<0,\ \text{or } i>m.
$$Then the conditional limits
$$
c_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0>0],
\quad
\bar{c}_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0<0]
$$
exist and are uniquely determined by the recursion formula
\begin{equation}
    c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}c_{m-2,i-2} - \frac{3}{2}c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}c_{m,i+2}, 
    \quad 
    \bar c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}\bar c_{m-2,i-2} + \frac{3}{2}\bar c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}\bar c_{m,i+2},
\end{equation}
with $c_{1,1}=\bar c_{1,1}=0$, $c_{2,2}=\bar c_{2,2}=\frac12$ and the convention that $c_{0,0}=\bar c_{0,0}=1$, and
		$$c_{k,j}=\bar c_{k,j}=0 \quad\text{whenever } (k,j)\notin \{(0,0)\}\cup\{(k,j): k\ge1,\ 1\le j\le k\}.$$ 
The recursion \eqref{eq-c-n-intro} is understood as a nested induction: one first increases the order $m$, and for each fixed $m$, computes $c_{m,i}$ backward in $i$ from $i=m$ to $1$. The same procedure applies to $\bar c_{m,i}$.

\item[(iii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, the limit
\begin{equation}
b_m(F) := \lim_{t \to \infty} a_m(t,F)
\end{equation}
exists and is given by
\begin{equation}
    b_m(F) = \mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{c_{m,i}}{i!} F^{(i)}(1)
    + \mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{\bar{c}_{m,i}}{i!}F^{(i)}(-1).
\end{equation}
In particular, $b_m(F)=0$ for all odd $m$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Long-time behavior in the scalar case

[Theorem derivation2.414 of arXiv:2412.06246, 'The smallest singular value for rectangular random matrices with Lévy entries'] Let $N\geq n$.
    Let $T$ be an $N\times n$ matrix with decomposition $T=T_0+T_1$, where $T_0$ is deterministic, $T_1$ has independent, mean zero coordinates $(t_{ij})$ such that $\sup_{i,j}\mathbb{E}[|t_{ij}|^2]\leq \frac{M^2}{n}$ for some fixed $M>1$ and let $q>0$ be such that  $$\sup_{i,j}|t_{ij}|\leq q,\quad a.s.$$ Let $G=G_0+G_1$ be another $N\times n$ matrix where $G_0=T_0$, $G_1=(g_{ij})$ has independent mean zero Gaussian entries and share the same variance profile as $T_1$ i.e. $\mathbb{E}[g_{ij}^2]=\mathbb{E}[t_{ij}^2]$ for each $i,j$. Then on a common probability space supporting an independent copy of $G$ and $T$, we have: for any $t>0$,
     $$
\mathbb{P}(|\sigma_{min}(T)-\sigma_{min}(G)|\geq Cn^{-\frac{1}{2}}t^{\frac{1}{2}}+Cq^{\frac{1}{3}}t^{\frac{2}{3}}(\frac{N}{n})^\frac{1}{3}+Cqt)\leq 8N e^{-t},
    $$ where $C>0$ is a universal constant that only depends on $M>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition definitiontwocomponentlcds of arXiv:2504.15992, 'Repeated singular values of a random symmetric matrix and decoupled singular value estimat'] Fix some $L\geq 1$ and $\alpha_0\in(0,1)$.
Consider two vectors $X,Y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and two fixed constant $t_1,t_2>0$. We define the essential least common denominator (LCD) of the vector pair $(X,Y)$ associated with these parameters as follows:
$$
\operatorname{LCD}_{L,\alpha_0}^\mathbf{t}(X,Y):=\inf\{\|\theta\|_2:\theta\in \mathbb{R}^2,\| \theta_1X+\theta_2Y\|_\mathbb{T}\leq L\sqrt{\log_+\frac{\alpha_0\|\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^2\theta_i^2/t_i^2}}{L}}\},
$$
where $\log_+(x)=\max(\log x,0)$ and $\mathbf{t}$ denotes the tuple $(t_1,t_2)$.

[Conjecture conj:quenched full of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] For $f\in D$, let $\theta$ be the optimizer in~(equation eq:quenched conj of the paper) and $\zeta$ the minimizer
		in~(equation def:tildeLambda of the paper) for this~$\theta$.
		Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\emph{(\roman*)}]
			\item \emph{(Ultrametric structure.)} The TAP critical points at free-energy level $f$ are organized in an ultrametric tree: the overlap between any two TAP states at level $f$ taken uniformly takes values in the support of $\zeta$.
			\item \emph{(Separation of free-energy levels.)} Whenever $f\neq f_\mathrm{eq}:=\inf_\zeta \mathcal{P}\mathrm{arisi}(\zeta)$, the ancestor states in this ultrametric tree have TAP free energy $\mathcal{P}\mathrm{arisi}(\zeta)\neq f$, i.e., the ancestors live at a different free-energy level than their descendants.
			\item \emph{(Subexponential number of ancestors.)} The quenched complexity of the ancestor states is $0$: they exist, but their number grows at most subexponentially in $N$.
		\end{enumerate} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Ultrametric organization of TAP states

[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2609.04069, 'Positive and Negative Square Energies of $2$-Connected Graphs'] Let $G$ be a triangle-free $2$-connected graph of order $n$.  Then
\[
 \sneg(G)\geq n
 \quad {\it if~and~only~if}\quad
 G\ncong C_{4k+3}\quad\text{for every }k\geq1.
\]
Moreover, equality holds if and only if $G$ is an even cycle, and
every non-cycle graph satisfies $\sneg(G)>n$.

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] Let $(\Omega,B,\mathbb{P}_x)$ be the canonical Wiener space as in Section~\ref{sec:Bessel}, 
$q>1$, and $\pi=(\pi_n)_{n\geq1}$ a sequence of partitions of
$[0,T]$ such that
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|\pi_n|<\infty.
$$
Then
$$
\|\rho_{n,B}\|_{L^q([0,T])}^q
\longrightarrow
c_{q,d}T
\qquad \mathbb{P}_x\text{-almost surely},
$$
where
$$
c_{q,d}:=\mathbb{E}|Z|^{2q},
\qquad Z\sim N(0,I_d).
$$
In particular,
$$
\sup_{n\geq1}\|\rho_{n,B}\|_{L^q([0,T])}<\infty
\qquad \mathbb{P}_x\text{-almost surely}.
$$

[Defi of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] Let $V$ be a $G$–set. An \textit{abstract simplicial $G$–complex} is
a collection of finite nonempty subsets $L$ of $V$ satisfying (i) if $v\in V$, then ${v} \in L $, (ii) if $\sigma\in L$ and $\tau \subseteq \sigma$, then $\tau \in L$, (iii) if $\sigma \in L$, then $g\sigma\in L$ for all $g \in G$, and (iv) if $\sigma\in L$ and $g \in G_\sigma$, then $gv = v$ for all $v \in \sigma$. Here, the notation $G_{\sigma}$ denotes the subgroup of $G$ that preserves the subset $\sigma \subseteq V$.
title: Unnumbered defi of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'

body: In a multi-output stacking problem scored by the mean per-sample relative error $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|\hat y_i - y_i\|/\|y_i\|$, the per-output least-squares stack minimises the unweighted squared error, which is dominated by the cases with the largest $\|y_i\|$, while the score is dominated by the cases with the smallest. Interpolating the per-output weights toward one pooled simplex weight vector fitted on the relative error therefore improves the score even IN-SAMPLE on the very calibration rows on which least squares is optimal in squared error - the signature that distinguishes an objective mismatch from a generalisation (variance) effect, which can only appear out of sample. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, component Y2, 23 members, 932 calibration rows, 285 outputs): in-sample relative error 0.1105 for least squares against 0.1026 at interpolation weight 0.4 (-7.2 percent), the in-sample optimum at the same weight as the out-of-sample optimum (0.1292 to 0.1186), while the in-sample squared error is minimal at least squares (8.8e-5 against 1.2e-4); the out-of-sample gain is +15.9 percent in the smallest-norm quartile of targets and -9.6 percent in the largest, and 45 percent of the least-squares score comes from its worst decile of cases. Consequently no model of the sampling noise of the weight rows reproduces the cross-validated interpolation weight: the known-noise James-Stein amount is 0.00 and the heteroscedasticity-robust amount 0.03-0.05 where cross-validation chooses 0.10-0.40. Shrinking toward the pooled UNCONSTRAINED least-squares weights (entries up to 90 in magnitude) or toward the mean of the rows is much worse; the simplex constraint together with the relative objective carries the effect. The practical rule: when a stack is scored in a metric that weights cases differently from the fitting loss, the first question is the objective, not the estimator's variance.
