Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), T381-C004/C005/C006 v1. A fixed next-token model M can output |p| fair bits then terminate on prompt p. For a stateless robust watermark satisfying standard soundness and repeated-query undetectability uniformly over polynomial-length prompts, use p_lambda=1^n to instantiate the zero-bit PRC reduction at any polynomial length n with b_lambda(n+1)<=n. If b_lambda(L)<=A(lambda)L^alpha above a polynomial onset L0, where A,L0>=1 are efficient integer-valued polynomially bounded functions and fixed 0<=alpha<1, take n=max(L0,(2A)^d) for a fixed integer d with d(1-alpha)>=1. Then b_lambda(n+1)<=n. In particular O(lambda sqrt L) thresholds admit n=lambda^3 eventually, without knowing the implicit constant. The channel robustness is assumed, not obtained from entropy. If instead b_lambda(n+1)>n, uniform sampling with an always-rejecting detector has vacuous entropy-qualified completeness and fails the direct PRC reduction.
Uniform prompt-quantified watermark security
Polynomial-time stateless generation and polynomial selected prompt length
Specified exact binary-channel robust completeness
Threshold bound as stated

Let (F_n)_{n=1}^\infty be a sequence of distribution functions, and let a_n > 0, b_n \in \mathbb{R}, c_n > 0, d_n \in \mathbb{R} be constants such that F_n(a_n x + b_n) \Rightarrow U(x) and F_n(c_n x + d_n) \Rightarrow V(x) weakly as n \to \infty. body: [Theorem t:fixed_poits of arXiv:2606.11503, 'Percolation on hierarchical lattices'] Let $g:\{0,1\}^{n} \to \{0,1\}$ be a monotone non-trivial Boolean function that is not a dictator. Then the map $p \mapsto \mathbb{E}_{p}[g]$ has a fixed point in $(0,1)$ if, and only if, $\frac{\d}{\d p} \mathbb{E}_{p}[g]\Big|_{p=0} = \frac{\d}{\d p} \mathbb{E}_{p}[g]\Big|_{p=1} = 0$. Furthermore, this fixed point $p_{\circ}$ is unique and $\zeta = \frac{\d}{\d p} \mathbb{E}_{p}[g]\Big|_{p=p_{\circ}} >1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let 𝔄 be a unital Banach algebra (for instance the algebra B(E) of bounded linear operators on a Banach space E, or the n×n complex matrices), and for A ∈ 𝔄 define exp(A) = e^A := Σ_{k=0}^∞ A^k / k!, a series that converges absolutely in norm for every A (‖A^k/k!‖ ≤ ‖A‖^k/k!), so that ‖e^A‖ ≤ e^{‖A‖}. If A, B ∈ 𝔄 COMMUTE, AB = BA, then e^{A+B} = e^A e^B = e^B e^A. Consequences: for every A and all scalars s, t, e^{(s+t)A} = e^{sA} e^{tA} (the one-parameter group law), e^A is invertible with (e^A)⁻¹ = e^{−A}, e^0 = 1, and t ↦ e^{tA} is norm-differentiable with derivative A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A. If P is invertible, e^{PAP⁻¹} = P e^A P⁻¹. Sharp edges. (1) Commutativity cannot be dropped: for the 2×2 matrices A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] one has e^A = I + A, e^B = I + B, so e^A e^B = [[2,1],[1,1]], whereas A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] gives e^{A+B} = [[cosh 1, sinh 1],[sinh 1, cosh 1]] ≠ e^A e^B (and e^B e^A = [[1,1],[1,2]] ≠ e^A e^B, so the two products differ as well). For non-commuting A, B the product e^A e^B is instead described by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series e^{A+B+[A,B]/2+…} when it converges, and by the Lie–Trotter formula e^{A+B} = lim_{n→∞} (e^{A/n} e^{B/n})ⁿ. (2) The converse is false in general: e^A e^B = e^{A+B} does not imply AB = BA (there are non-commuting complex matrices with e^A = e^B = e^{A+B} = I); it does hold for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices A, B, because then e^{A+B} Hermitian forces e^A e^B = (e^A e^B)* = e^B e^A, so the positive definite matrices e^A and e^B commute, and hence so do their unique Hermitian logarithms A and B. (3) For UNBOUNDED operators (generators of semigroups) the series definition is unavailable and 'commuting' must be formulated with care (e.g. commuting resolvents / commuting semigroups); this statement is only about bounded operators and Banach algebras.
𝔄 is a unital Banach algebra (e.g. bounded operators on a Banach space, or square matrices)

[Lemma 62 of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] Fix $k\ge 1$ and $\delta>0$. 
Let $(a_1^n,\ldots,a_k^n)\in\big((\delta,h(\ell)-\delta)\cap\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{Z}\big)^k$ for $n\ge1$, and 
$(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\in(\delta,h(\ell)-\delta)^k$ satisfy
\[  
(a_1^n,\ldots,a_k^n)\longrightarrow(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\quad\text{and}\quad a_1>\cdots>a_k.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
\begin{aligned} \Big(\big(Y^n(s):s\in[\delta, h(\ell)-\delta]\big)\,\big|\,(\mathbf{a}^n_1,\ldots, \mathbf{a}^n_k)=(a^n_1,\ldots,a^n_k)\Big)\\\overset{d}{\longrightarrow} \Big(\big(Y(s):s\in[\delta, h(\ell)-\delta]\big)\,\big|\,(\mathbf{a}_1,\ldots, \mathbf{a}_k)=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\Big). \end{aligned}
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let α be irrational with regular continued fraction [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...], convergents p_n/q_n (p_{-1} = 1, q_{-1} = 0, p_0 = a_0, q_0 = 1, p_{n+1} = a_{n+1}p_n + p_{n-1}, q_{n+1} = a_{n+1}q_n + q_{n-1}) and complete quotients α_{n+1} = [a_{n+1}; a_{n+2}, ...], so a_{n+1} < α_{n+1} < a_{n+1} + 1. Write ||t|| = dist(t, Z) and δ_n = |q_n α − p_n| (so δ_{-1} = 1).

(1) Exact size and alternating sign. For all n ≥ 0, q_n α − p_n = (−1)^n / (q_n α_{n+1} + q_{n-1}). Hence 1/(q_n + q_{n+1}) < δ_n < 1/q_{n+1}, the errors alternate in sign, δ_n is strictly decreasing, and δ_n = ||q_n α|| for every n ≥ 1 (because q_{n+1} ≥ 2 gives δ_n < 1/2); for n = 0 this holds when a_1 ≥ 2.

(2) The distances obey the same recursion as the denominators: δ_{n-1} = a_{n+1} δ_n + δ_{n+1} for all n ≥ 0. Equivalently δ_n = 1/(α_1 α_2 ··· α_{n+1}).

(3) Closest returns (Lagrange's theorem on best approximations of the second kind). For every n ≥ 0 and every integer q with 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1}: ||q α|| ≥ δ_n, with equality if and only if q = q_n. In dynamical words: for the rotation t ↦ t + α (mod 1), among all times 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1} the orbit of any point comes closest to its starting point exactly at time q_n; the record-breaking (closest-return) times of the orbit are precisely the denominators q_0 (when a_1 ≥ 2), q_1, q_2, ..., and successive closest returns land on alternate sides of the starting point, at distances δ_n.

(4) Growth. q_{n+1} ≥ q_n + q_{n-1}, hence q_n ≥ F_{n+1} (Fibonacci) and q_n ≥ 2^{(n−1)/2} for n ≥ 1; the golden ratio (all a_k = 1) is the slowest case.

Where it fails. For rational α the expansion terminates, the last δ is 0 and the recursion (2) stops. Statement (3) is about ||qα|| = min_p |qα − p| (best approximations of the SECOND kind). For the FIRST-kind problem of minimising |α − p/q| over q ≤ Q, intermediate fractions (p_{n-1} + k p_n)/(q_{n-1} + k q_n) with k > a_{n+1}/2 can also be best approximations, so the two notions must not be conflated. When a_1 = 1 one has q_0 = q_1 = 1, the n = 0 case of (3) is vacuous, and ||α|| equals δ_1, not δ_0.
α irrational (for the rational case the expansion terminates)
regular (simple) continued fraction with integer partial quotients a_k ≥ 1 for k ≥ 1
||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer

body:
[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2511.01245, 'A curiously slowly mixing Markov chain'] Let $K(x, y)$ be the transition matrix of the binary Burnside process on $C_2^n$. We have the following:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The eigenvalues of $K$ are $0$ and
    \[
        \beta_k = \frac{1}{2^{4k}} \binom{2k}{k}^2, \quad 0 \le k \le \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor.
    \]
    \item The eigenvalue multiplicity of $0$ is $2^{n-1}$. The eigenvalue multiplicity of $\beta_k$ is $\binom{n}{2k}$ for all $0 \le k \le \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor$.
    \item For $0 \le k \le \lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$, a basis of eigenvectors for the $\beta_k$-eigenspace is 
    \[
        \left\{f_S(x) = (-1)^{|x_S|} \binom{2k}{|x_S|}: |S| \subset [n], |S| = 2k\right\},
    \]
    where $|x_S|$ denotes the number of ones of $x \in C_2^n$ among the coordinate set $S$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2511.01245

[Thm th:sf of arXiv:2603.29711, 'Strong Feller property, irreducibility,\\ and uniqueness of the invariant measure\\ for st'] Let $d=1$, $\alpha\geq2$, and $\beta\geq1$.
    Then, there exist 
    $\sigma_0^1, \sigma_0^2\in (0,\frac14)$,
    only depending of $\alpha,\beta$, 
    such that 
    under any of the following settings
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\alpha>2$, 
        $\sigma\in(\sigma_{0}^1, \frac14)$,
        $\delta\in(\frac14+\sigma, \frac12)$,
        $\xi\in(\delta-\sigma-\frac14, \frac12+\sigma)$, and $\gamma:=\alpha+\max\{\beta,2\}$,
        \item $\alpha\geq4$, 
        $\sigma\in(\sigma_{0}^2, \frac12)$,
        $\delta\in[\frac12, \frac12+\sigma)\cap
        (\frac14+\sigma,1)$,
        $\xi\in[\delta,\frac12+\sigma)$, and $\gamma:=\alpha+2\beta+2$,
    \end{itemize}
    the following holds: there exist
    $\mathfrak a\in(\frac12,1)$ and
    $\mathfrak b>0$, only depending on $\sigma,\delta$,
    such that for every $T>0$ 
    there exists $C>0$, only depending 
    on $\alpha,\beta,\delta,\sigma,\xi,T$,
    such that,
    for every $\varphi\in\mathcal B_b(\mathcal X)$ and for every $t\in(0,T)$, it holds
    for every $x_1,x_2\in \mathcal K_{\gamma}\cap V_{2\xi}$
    with $x_1-x_2\in V_{2\delta}$
    that 
    \[
    |(P_t\varphi)(x_1)-(P_t\varphi)(x_2)|
    \leq\frac{C}{t^{\mathfrak a}}

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2606.11068, '2606.11068'] Let \(S=(S_m)_{m\ge0}\) be a nearest-neighbour motion on \(\mathbb Z\), started
from \(S_0=0\), and let \(\Xi\) be an independent lifetime with tail \(G\).
Define
\[
  D^*:=\max_{0\le k\le \Xi}|S_k|.
\]
Let
\[
  \tau_n:=\inf\{m\ge1: |S_m|=n\},
  \qquad n\ge1,
\]
with the convention \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\). Then
\[
  \Pbb(D^*\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n)].
\]
If
\[
  D^\to:=\max_{0\le k\le\Xi}S_k,
  \qquad
  \tau_n^+:=\inf\{m\ge1:S_m=n\},
\]
then
\[
  \Pbb(D^\to\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n^+)].
\]
Analogously, if
\[
  D^\leftarrow:=\max_{0\le k\le\Xi}(-S_k),
  \qquad
  \tau_n^-:=\inf\{m\ge1:S_m=-n\},
\]
then
\[
  \Pbb(D^\leftarrow\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n^-)].
\]
In the last two identities, we again use the convention \(G(\infty)=0\).

body:
Let X be a compact topological space and T: X → X a map. Then every nonempty closed set A ⊂ X with T(A) ⊆ A contains a minimal set: a nonempty closed set M ⊆ A with T(M) ⊆ M that has no proper nonempty closed T-invariant subset. In particular (A = X) every compact dynamical system has at least one minimal set. If moreover X is Hausdorff and T is continuous, then M = cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} for every x ∈ M, T(M) = M, and (X metrizable) M carries a T-invariant Borel probability measure by the Krylov–Bogolyubov theorem, so every compact metrizable system has an invariant probability measure supported on a minimal set. The same statement and proof hold for a commuting family (or any semigroup) of maps X → X, with 'invariant' meaning invariant under every map of the family, and for flows. Sharp edges. (1) Compactness cannot be dropped: for the translation T(x) = x + 1 on ℝ, any nonempty closed invariant set A contains, for some a ∈ A, the closed invariant set {a + n : n ≥ 0}, which has the proper closed invariant subset {a + n : n ≥ 1}; so ℝ has NO minimal set, although it has plenty of nonempty closed invariant sets. (2) Existence uses only compactness and Zorn's lemma (the intersection of a chain of nonempty closed sets in a compact space is nonempty by the finite intersection property); continuity of T is needed only for the orbit-closure description and for T(M) = M. (3) Minimal sets need not be unique: the identity map has every single point as a minimal set; a system with a fixed point and a dense orbit (e.g. the doubling map) has minimal sets that are not the whole space. (4) 'Minimal' is with respect to inclusion among closed invariant sets; a nonempty invariant set that is not closed (a single dense orbit) is not a minimal set.
X is a compact topological space
T: X → X is a map (continuity needed only for the orbit-closure supplement and T(M) = M)
A ⊂ X is nonempty, closed, and T(A) ⊆ A
Zorn's lemma (axiom of choice) is available

[Theorem main of arXiv:2606.27844, 'Critical percolation on preferential attachment graphs with infinite variance'] Let $\tfrac12 <\gamma <1$ 
 
 and $\mathscr G_n$ the inhomogeneous random graph with the kernel 
 $\kappa(x,y)=\beta(n) (x\wedge y)^{-\gamma}(x\vee y)^{\gamma-1}$
 for $\beta(n)\searrow0$.
 \begin{enumerate}
     \item[(I)] \emph{Tiny giant regime}: If 
     
     $\beta(n)n^{\gamma-\tfrac{1}{2}}\to \infty$, then there exists a constant $\theta>0$ 
     
     such that 
     $$\displaystyle \frac{\#C_1(\mathscr{G}_n)}{n\,\beta(n)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma-1}}}  \overset{\mathbb P}{\longrightarrow } \theta \,\;\text{ and }\;\frac{\#C_2(\mathscr{G}_n)}{n\,\beta(n)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma-1
}}}  \overset{\mathbb P}{\longrightarrow }0 \;.$$
     \item[(II)] \emph{Critical window}: If $\beta(n)n^{\gamma-\tfrac{1}{2}}\to \varphi >0 $, then
     $$ \displaystyle\frac{\# C_1(\mathscr{G}_n)}{\sqrt{n}}  \overset{d}{\longrightarrow} \varphi \sup_{i\in\mathbb N}\bigg\{\sum_{j\in\mathcal C(i)} \frac{1}{\gamma}\, j^{-\gamma}\bigg\}\;,$$
     where $\mathcal{C}(i)$ is the component of $i$ in the random graph
     $\mathscr{G}_{\text{NR}}$ with vertex set $\mathbb N$, where two vertices $i,j\in\mathbb N$ have a \smash{$\text{Pois}(\tfrac{\varphi^2}{2\gamma-1}(ij)^{-\gamma})$} number of edges between them, independently for all pairs of vertices.
     
     \item[(III)] \emph{Star component regime}: If  
    $\beta(n)n^{\gamma-\tfrac{1}{2}}\to 0$  but $\beta(n)n^{\gamma}\to\infty$, 
     
     
     then
     $$
      \frac{\#C_1(\mathscr G_n)}{n^\gamma \beta(n)} \overset{\mathbb P}{\longrightarrow} \frac{1}{\gamma} \;.
     $$
 
 \item[(IV)]  \emph{Bounded component regime}: 
 \begin{itemize}
     \item[(i)]
 If $\beta(n)n^{\gamma}\to c\in(0,\infty)$, then
     $ \big(\#C_1(\mathscr{G}_n)\big)_{n\in\mathbb N} \text{ is tight}$; 
     \smallskip
  \item[(ii)] if $\beta(n)n^{\gamma}\to 0$ and $\beta(n)n\to\infty$, then
     $ \mathbb P \big(\#C_1(\mathscr{G}_n)= 2\big)\to 1$,\smallskip
   \item[(iii)]  if $\beta(n)n\to0$, then  $ \mathbb P \big(\#C_1(\mathscr{G}_n)=1\big)\to 1$.
     \end{itemize}
 \end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:holes of arXiv:2605.10361, 'Limit shape of single-source stochastic sandpiles with $p$-topplings on $\Z$'] For the final stable configuration $\eta_{K_n}^{(n)}$ it holds that either
    $$\eta_{K_n}^{(n)}=\mathbbm{1}_{[\mathtt{l}_{n},\mathtt{r}_{n}]\cap\mathbb{Z}},$$
    or there exists a vertex $\mathsf{h}_n\in[\mathtt{l}_{n},\mathtt{r}_{n}]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ such that
    $$\eta_{K_n}^{(n)}=\mathbbm{1}_{[\mathtt{l}_{n},\mathtt{r}_{n}]\cap\mathbb{Z}}-\delta_{\mathsf{h}_n}.$$
    That is, the final configuration has at most one vertex with $0$ particles within its limit shape.

CURRENT AUDIT STATUS: independently checked proof, T336-w727-C005 v2; urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28 PASS in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Exact proof SHA256 22df67c6b2aaec99499aac6bf3440e8d5d6305204deedcc98fe9b4a621583b40. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed. The following original submission text retains historical pre-audit status notices.

Every continuous real symmetric PSD kernel of rank <=p and diagonal <=R^2 on a nonempty compact X subset R^d admits an explicit raw-input normalized-ReLU-attention transformer for uniform noisy predictive forward KL <=eps, with positive noise s, labels bounded by B, and contexts <=n. The complete width/depth/MLP/head bound is given in C005 Section 1 in terms of the canonical kernel modulus Omega(r), a finite h-net cardinality J, and the solver constants. A fixed finite Gram factorization supplies all encoder feature values; no feature computation is hidden outside the count. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C005 v2. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 for continuous finite-rank kernels on compact raw domains

Claim T336-w727-C005 v2. Status: proof (unaudited), dependent on C002 v1 and the deterministic perturbation/encoder constructions in C004 v1. The entire result is not Lean-checked. No independent review or novelty certification is claimed.

The hardest step is removing the supplied-feature oracle without adding a hidden feature-computation cost. A finite Gram factorization fixes the encoder weights; a kernel modulus controls its error. The size explicitly includes the resulting encoder.

## 1. Statement and all parameters

Let X be a nonempty compact subset of R^d, d>=1. Let k:X times X -> R be a continuous real symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel of rank at most p, p>=1, with k(x,x)<=R^2 for R>=0. The prior is the zero-mean GP with kernel k. Observation noise is independent N(0,s), s>0. Labels are bounded by B>=0, contexts have length <=n with n>=0 an integer, and eps>0. The prediction concerns a new noisy observation.

Define the canonical kernel modulus in the ambient L1 metric by

    Omega(r)=sup_{x,y in X, ||x-y||_1<=r}
                sqrt(k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y)).

The expression is nonnegative by positive semidefiniteness. Omega(r) tends to zero as r decreases to zero, as proved below.

Retain the following explicit constants from C004's deterministic perturbation bound:

    S=R+1, C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s+S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s>0,
    eta=min(1,sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)),s sqrt(eps)/(2C_v),s/(4C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16), e=eta/sqrt(p)>0.

Choose any **fixed admissible** r>0 with Omega(r)<=e/2. An explicit upper modulus for k can be used to choose r; continuity guarantees existence, not an algorithm for computing a modulus of an arbitrary black-box kernel. Put

    A_cone=(2R+e)/r>0, h=e/(2A_cone)>0.

Choose a finite h-net G contained in X, of cardinality J>=1. The size bound is explicit in J (or in a known upper bound for the covering number). For X=[0,1]^d one may take the regular grid with

    m=max(1,ceil(d A_cone/e)), J=(m+1)^d.

For the attention solver define

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a transformer, using normalized residual ReLU attention and tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs, with

    D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,
    L_total=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    at most L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D dense scalar parameters,

whose positive-variance Gaussian output has forward KL<=eps from the exact noisy GP predictive, uniformly over all admissible raw-input contexts and queries. Its input contains only raw coordinates, labels, fixed context/query flags, and constants. The encoder is counted. These are arbitrary-real-weight size bounds; no finite-bit, kernel-evaluation, offline factorization-time, SGD, or ERM-generalization bound is asserted.

## 2. Canonical finite-dimensional features and the kernel modulus

Form the vector space of finite formal combinations of symbols delta_x with bilinear form

    <sum_i a_i delta_{x_i},sum_j b_j delta_{y_j}>
       =sum_{i,j}a_i b_j k(x_i,y_j).

Positive semidefiniteness makes this a nonnegative quadratic form. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality follows by applying nonnegativity to u+t v for all real t; in particular a zero-norm vector is orthogonal to every vector. Quotient by the zero-norm subspace. For any finite list of symbols, the dimension of their quotient span is the rank of their Gram matrix. Every finite list of quotient vectors is contained in the span of finitely many symbols. Thus the dimension of the resulting inner-product space is the supremum of these Gram ranks, which is the kernel rank and is at most p. It is finite dimensional, so no completion issue remains.

Choose an orthonormal basis and pad with zeros in R^p. The coordinates z(x) of delta_x then satisfy

    k(x,y)=z(x)^T z(y), ||z(x)||<=R,
    ||z(x)-z(y)||^2=k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y).

Thus z is continuous and ||z(x)-z(y)||<=Omega(r) whenever ||x-y||_1<=r. To justify Omega(r)->0 directly, suppose the contrary. There are sequences r_j->0 and x_j,y_j in X at distance <=r_j with feature distance bounded away from zero. Compactness supplies a subsequence x_j->x; then y_j->x as well. Continuity of k makes the squared feature distance tend to k(x,x)+k(x,x)-2k(x,x)=0, a contradiction. The supremum is finite because the kernel is continuous on the compact product. In particular every fixed positive e admits the required r.

The factorization at the finite net does not require evaluating any feature map on runtime inputs. Form the fixed J-by-J Gram matrix K_G=(k(a,b))_{a,b in G}. It is PSD of rank <=p, so a finite spectral factorization gives vectors v_a in R^p with v_a^T v_b=k(a,b). There is an isometry between the spans of z(a) and v_a: the map sum c_a z(a) -> sum c_a v_a is well defined and norm preserving because both squared norms equal c^T K_G c. Extend orthonormal bases of the two spans to R^p. The isometry extends to an orthogonal map on R^p. Applying it to all z(x) gives a representation, still called z, with z(a)=v_a for every a in G and with the same norm and modulus bounds.

Consequently **all feature values used as weights below can be obtained from the finite prior Gram matrix on G**. Computing this fixed factorization is preprocessing of the fixed prior, not an input-dependent inverse hidden in the predictive head. Its real entries are included in the encoder's parameter count.

## 3. Cone envelope for a general continuous feature map

Define, using the finite Gram feature values,

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1].

This formula is valid even though z_j need not be Lipschitz. We claim |ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)|<=e for every j,x.

For a with ||x-a||_1<=r, the modulus gives v_{a,j}>=z_j(x)-Omega(r)>=z_j(x)-e/2. Adding a nonnegative cone term preserves this lower bound. For a with ||x-a||_1>r, the coordinate bound |z_j|<=R gives

    v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1
      >z_j(x)-2R+A_cone r=z_j(x)+e.

So every candidate is >=z_j(x)-e/2, and the finite minimum is too.

For the upper bound choose a net point with ||x-a||_1<=h. Since h=e r/(2(2R+e))<=r/2, the modulus bound applies. Therefore

    ztilde_j(x)<=z_j(x)+Omega(r)+A_cone h
                  <=z_j(x)+e/2+e/2=z_j(x)+e.

It follows that sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)e=eta and ||ztilde(x)||<=R+eta<=S. All denominators above are positive, including R=0. For a cube grid, coordinate rounding gives L1 distance <=d/(2m)<=e/(2A_cone)=h, which verifies the displayed grid size.

## 4. Exact network realization and original-posterior KL

Use C004 Section 4's explicit register construction, with the J centers now the net points a and with the slope K in the cone layer replaced by A_cone. Layer 1 computes all Jd absolute differences with 2Jd ReLUs. Layer 2 forms the pJ affine cone values using these nonnegative absolute registers and the constant register. A balanced residual-min tournament takes ceil(log_2 J) layers, including zero layers when J=1. The last gating layer, using the binary context/query flags and |ztilde_j|<=S, writes the context/query feature registers exactly. For padding choose a fixed anchor point in X as its raw coordinates, rather than assuming the ambient origin belongs to X. Its flags are zero, so the computed features are gated to zero.

This uses E=3+ceil(log_2 J) encoder layers and precisely the width and hidden-width bounds in Section 1. This invokes the exact algebraic encoder construction, **not the Lipschitz-error assertion** of C004 Section 3. Section 3 above supplies the replacement uniform approximation guarantee.

C004 Section 2's perturbation proof uses only ||ztilde-z||<=eta<=1, not feature Lipschitzness. It therefore gives original-versus-encoded predictive errors

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Apply C002 v1 to the encoded features with bound S and accuracy eps0. The one-head query broadcast, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout produce muhat,vhat with vhat>=s and errors

    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

The original predictive variance is also >=s. Adding scalar errors gives |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps) and |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)). The Gaussian calculation in C002 Section 5 then yields forward KL<=eps from the **original kernel** predictive distribution to the transformer output. No triangle inequality for KL is used.

Combining the E encoder layers with the T+2 solver layers gives the depth. Count three D-by-D matrices for each of at most five heads, two MLP matrices of dimensions H-by-D and D-by-H per layer (even counting zeros), and a two-coordinate linear readout. This proves the displayed parameter bound.

## 5. Exact scope

C005 covers every continuous bounded finite-rank kernel on a nonempty compact Euclidean domain, with an explicit bound in terms of a kernel modulus and a finite covering number. It includes continuous kernels whose features are not Lipschitz. C004 gives the simpler closed grid formula when a coordinatewise Lipschitz feature bound is available. C002 is smaller when features are supplied directly.

C003 proves that the bounded-kernel statement without continuity can fail for continuous raw-input Gaussian-output architectures. Thus these results distinguish the feature-input interpretation from the regularity needed for a raw-input theorem. They do not claim that a raw-input size bound can ignore the fixed kernel's modulus or its feature-computation complexity. All three constructive claims remain independently unaudited.
nonempty compact X subset R^d; d,p>=1; n>=0 integer; eps,s>0; B,R>=0
continuous symmetric PSD kernel, rank <=p, k(x,x)<=R^2, zero-mean GP
independent N(0,s) observation noise; new noisy predictive observation
an admissible r>0 with Omega(r)<=eta/(2sqrt(p)), and a fixed h-net G subset X, are specified or bounded from a known modulus and covering bound
normalized bidirectional residual ReLU attention plus residual ReLU tokenwise MLPs; arbitrary real weights; raw coordinates and role flags

For a simple random walk starting at k that steps +1 with probability p and -1 with probability q = 1 - p, absorbed at 0 or at N (0 < k < N), the probability of reaching N before 0 is (1 - (q/p)^k)/(1 - (q/p)^N) when p != q, and k/N when p = q = 1/2. The ruin probability (reaching 0 first) is one minus this.

 it holds that

body:
[Lemma lem:whiten of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] Let $H=\frac1N\sum_i x_ix_i^{\top}\succ0$ and $L_D^{\star}>0$. Let $w^{\star}$ be the
unique full-data optimum and $r_i=y_i-\ip{w^{\star}}{x_i}$. Set
\[
\xi_i=H^{-1/2}x_i,\qquad
\eta_i=\frac{r_i}{\sqrt{L_D^{\star}}},\qquad
q=\frac{H^{1/2}(w-w^{\star})}{\sqrt{L_D^{\star}}}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\frac1N\sum_i\xi_i\xi_i^{\top}=I_d,\qquad
\frac1N\sum_i\eta_i\xi_i=0,\qquad
\frac1N\sum_i\eta_i^2=1,
\end{equation}
and for every $w$,
\begin{equation}
\frac{L_D(w)}{L_D^{\star}}=1+\lVert q\rVert^2 .
\end{equation}

body: RESULT (numerical search plus Kac-Rice, not a proof): T364 spurious local maxima of the quartic sum of <a_i,x>^4 on the sphere, n=d^2 Gaussian vectors. Search: no interior bulk maximum at d=250; component maxima near a_i reach 1.13-1.26. Kac-Rice: the slab first moment equals the proxy rate 0.0082 d; the proxy two-point complexity is below twice the one-point rate for 0<q<=0.95 and near the diagonal (3af); band maxima are marginal (3ag), so the count is kappa-gapped: kappa=0.02 gives Theta 0.0025-0.0046 with a matching second moment (3ah); separation is local (3ai); the gapped pair exponent tends to -Theta-delta at q->1 (3aj). Finite d: searches at d<=250 cannot test the gapped band (3al, 3am); the sample-centred log-det has O(1) spread (3an); the E part of the two-point integrand loses only e^(O(ln^2 n)) uniformly up to the diagonal (3ao) and the in-plane rows a power of ln d (3ap), so the diagonal window closes modulo the 3ai net and 3ab inputs. High probability: the q=0 pair log-dets keep Corr 0.2-0.4 at d=40-80, so Paley-Zygmund alone fails, but given the x-free S1=(1/n)sum(|a_i|^2-d), S2 the correlation is noise, also with the critical-point tilt and gradient projection (3aq, 3ar): condition on sigma(S1,S2), Subag style. Open: that conditional ratio to 1, the uniform net, the d=80/160 log-det rows.

[Propositio prop-error of arXiv:2609.00108, 'The double sphere solution in the liquid drop model'] For every \(x\in\Sigma_0^\varepsilon\),
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				H_{\Sigma_0^\varepsilon}(x)
				=
				2\varepsilon
				&+
				O(\varepsilon^{3/2})
				{\bf1}_{(0,\,2\delta\varepsilon^{-3/4})}
				\\
				&+
				O(\varepsilon^2|\log\delta|)
				{\bf1}_{(\delta\varepsilon^{-3/4},\,2\delta\varepsilon^{-3/4})}
				\\
				&+
				2\chi'(F'-G')
				+
				\chi''(F-G)
				+
				\frac{\chi'(F-G)}r.
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		Moreover,
		\begin{equation}
			2\chi'(F'-G')
			+
			\chi''(F-G)
			+
			\frac{\chi'(F-G)}r
			=
			O\!\left(
			\delta^{-2}|\log\delta|\,\varepsilon^{3/2}
			\right)
			{\bf1}_{(\delta\varepsilon^{-3/4},\,2\delta\varepsilon^{-3/4})}.
		\end{equation}
		
		Furthermore,
		\begin{equation}
			m\varepsilon^3
			\int_{\Omega_0^\varepsilon}
			\frac{dy}{|x-y|}
			=
			\frac{4\pi m}{3|x-P|}
			+
			\frac{4\pi m}{3|x-\bar P|}
			+
			\Theta(x),
		\end{equation}
		where
		\[
		P=(R+d)e_3,
		\qquad
		\bar P=-(R+d)e_3,
		\]
		and
		\[
		|\Theta(x)|
		\lesssim
		\begin{cases}
			m\varepsilon^3|x|\,|\log(\varepsilon|x|)|,
			&
			|x|<5\delta\varepsilon^{-3/4},
			\\[1ex]
			\dfrac{m\delta^2\varepsilon^{3/2}}{|x|},
			&
			|x|\ge5\delta\varepsilon^{-3/4}.
		\end{cases}
		\]

[Lemma 49 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Let $b\in C([-L,L])$ satisfy $b>0$ and, for fixed $\sigma>0$ and $m\ge0$, set
\[
\Lambda_{\sigma,m}(r)=\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m,L}+rb),\qquad r\in\R.
\]
Then $\Lambda_{\sigma,m}$ is continuous and strictly decreasing from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$. Consequently there is a unique $r_{\sigma,m}$ such that $\Lambda_{\sigma,m}(r_{\sigma,m})=0$. If $b\equiv1$, then $r_{\sigma,m}=\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m,L})$.

At the critical scale $m=2$, let $r_0$ be the unique zero of
\[
r\longmapsto\lambda_1^D\big(d_J\partial_{xx}+q(x)\partial_x+a+rb,(-L,L)\big).
\]
Then $r_{\sigma,2}\to r_0$ as $\sigma\to0$.

body: Let a finite group G act on a finite set X. Burnside's lemma states that the number of orbits of this action equals the average number of points fixed by the elements of G: number of orbits = (1/|G|) times the sum over g in G of |Fix(g)|, where Fix(g) is the set of points of X fixed by g and |G| is the group order. This lets one count objects up to symmetry, such as distinct colorings of a necklace under rotation. The result was known earlier to Cauchy and Frobenius; it is often called the Cauchy-Frobenius lemma, with Burnside merely popularizing it in his 1897 textbook.
title: Burnside's lemma

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2608.30561, '\Large Informative Label Missingness in Multiclass Classification: Information Geometry an'] Assume that
\[
\operatorname{Var}\{U(\boldsymbol{Y})\}>0,\qquad
E\{U(\boldsymbol{Y})^2\}<\infty,\qquad
E\{\|\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{Y})\|^2\}<\infty,
\]
and that the required differentiations with respect to \(t\) and
\(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) may be interchanged with expectation in a neighborhood
of \((t,\boldsymbol{\theta})=(0,\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\), with sufficient local
smoothness for the Taylor expansions below. Then
\begin{equation}
\alpha(0)
=
\operatorname{logit}(\gamma),
\qquad
\alpha'(0)
=
-
E\{U(\boldsymbol{Y})\},

\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
q_t(\boldsymbol{Y})
=
\gamma
+
t\gamma(1-\gamma)
\left[
U(\boldsymbol{Y})
-
E\{U(\boldsymbol{Y})\}
\right]
+
O(t^2).

\end{equation}

The label-information loss
\[
\boldsymbol{D}(t)
=
E
\left[
q_t(\boldsymbol{Y})
\boldsymbol{I}_{Z\mid\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{Y})
\right]
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{D}'(0)
=
\gamma(1-\gamma)
E
\left[
\left[
U(\boldsymbol{Y})-E\{U(\boldsymbol{Y})\}
\right]
\boldsymbol{I}_{Z\mid\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{Y})
\right].

\end{equation}
By contrast, the efficient information contributed by the missing-label
mechanism satisfies
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{I}_{M}^{\mathrm{eff}}(t)
=
t^2
\gamma(1-\gamma)
\boldsymbol{\mathcal V}_{U}
+
o(t^2),

\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\mathcal V}_{U}
=
E
\left[
\boldsymbol{G}
\boldsymbol{G}^{\top}
\right]
-
E
\left[
\boldsymbol{G}
\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}
\right]
E
\left[
\boldsymbol{X}
\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}
\right]^{-1}
E
\left[
\boldsymbol{X}
\boldsymbol{G}^{\top}
\right]
\succeq
\boldsymbol{0},

\end{equation}
with
\[
\boldsymbol{X}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
U(\boldsymbol{Y})
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Finally, if
\[
\boldsymbol{J}_0
=
\boldsymbol{A}
-
\gamma
E
\left[
\boldsymbol{I}_{Z\mid\boldsymbol{Y}}
(\boldsymbol{Y})
\right],
\]
then the derivative of the classification advantage at MCAR is
\begin{equation}
\Delta_R'(0)
=
-
\operatorname{tr}
\left[
\boldsymbol{H}_{R}
\boldsymbol{J}_0^{-1}
\boldsymbol{D}'(0)
\boldsymbol{J}_0^{-1}
\right].

\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Julia operator and defect intertwining identity (P. L. Robinson, arXiv:1803.09329, Theorem0 p.1 and Theorem1 p.2). Let H,K be complex Hilbert spaces and F:K->H a bounded contraction, ||F||<=1. Define D_H=(I_H-FF*)^(1/2) and D_K=(I_K-F*F)^(1/2), the positive square roots. The Julia operator J=[[D_H,F],[-F*,D_K]] on H direct-sum K is unitary. The positive defect square roots satisfy D_H F=F D_K. Switching J's two column blocks gives the unitary map Q=[[F,D_H],[D_K,-F*]] from K direct-sum H to H direct-sum K. In finite-dimensional real spaces this is an orthogonal dilation whose top-left rectangular compression is F; real contractions and singular values equal to1 are allowed. In the special case H=K, Q is the usual Halmos dilation (Theorem2 p.2). These are classical dilation facts, not GD convergence theorems.
H,K complex Hilbert spaces and F a bounded contraction; real finite-dimensional specialization included
Defect square roots are the unique positive square roots; no invertibility of a defect operator is assumed

Let $W_1^{(N)},\dots,W_n^{(N)}$ be independent standard Wigner matrices, and let $s_1,\dots,s_n$ be a free semicircular family.
\begin{equation}
    X = A_0 + \sum_{k=1}^n g_k A_k, \qquad
    X^{(N)} = A_0\otimes I + \sum_{k=1}^n A_k \otimes W_k^{(N)}, \qquad X_{\mathrm{free}} = 
 A_0\otimes \1 + \sum_{k=1}^n A_k \otimes s_k
\end{equation}    
    where $\otimes$ denotes the tensor product ($X^{(N)}$ is an $Nd\times Nd$ matrix), $I$ is a $N
    \times N$ identity, and $\1$ is the identity in the algebra generated by the semicircular family.
title: $\Xfree$

[Theorem thm.llt_stein of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let ${\bf Y}_i$, $1 \le i \le m$ be independent $\mathbb{Z}^d$-valued vectors with
    means $\mu_i$ and covariance matrices $\Sigma_i$. Let $\mu = \sum_{i=1}^m \mu_i$ and
    $\Sigma = \sum_{i=1}^m \Sigma_i$.
    Let $\gamma_i=\mathbb E \|{\bf Y}_i -\mu_i\|^3$.
    Define $u_i= \min_{1 \le j \le d} \{1-d_{TV}({\bf Y}_i, {\bf Y}_i+e^{(j)})\}$, where $e^{(j)} \in \mathbb{Z}^d$
    is the $j$th coordinate vector. 
    Let ${\bf S}_m = {\bf Y}_1 + \dots + {\bf Y}_m$, let ${\bf X} \sim N(\mu, \Sigma)$ and let $\left[ \bf X \right]$ be
    $\bf X$ rounded to the nearest integer vector, that is, for any $x \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, $\mathbb P(\left[ \bf X \right] = x) = \mathbb P({\bf X} \in x + [-\frac 1 2, \frac 1 2)^d)$.
    Then
    \[
        d_{TV}({\bf S}_m, \left[ \bf X \right]) \le C d^{\frac 7 2} \ln m (L + (\frac d m)^{\frac 1 2}) \sqrt{\frac m {\tilde{s}_m}}
    \]
    where 
    \[
        L = \frac {m^{- \frac 1 2} \chi} {{\rm Tr}(\frac 2 m \Sigma)^{\frac 3 2}},
    \]
    \[
        \chi = \mathbb E \|{\boldsymbol \xi}\|^3, \quad \quad \tilde{s}_m = \sum_{i=1}^m u_i - \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} u_i,
    \]
    ${\boldsymbol \xi} = {\bf Y}_K' - {\bf Y}_K$ for 
    ${\bf Y}_i'$ an independent copy of ${\bf Y}_i$ for $1 \le i \le m$, $K$ is a uniformly random element of $\{1, \dots, m\}$ such that ${\bf Y}_1, \dots, {\bf Y}_m, {\bf Y}_1', \dots, {\bf Y}_m', K$ are independent and we assume that $\tilde{s}_m > 0$. 
    Furthermore, $C$ depends only on $\lambda_{min}(m^{-1}\Sigma)$,  $\lambda_{max}(m^{-1}\Sigma)$ and  $d^{-1}{\rm Tr}(m^{-1}\Sigma)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem~4.2 of Barbour, Luczak and Xia~\cite{barbourluczakxia2018}

[Lem 7 of arXiv:2604.13134, '\bf From Gaussian to Gumbel: extreme eigenvalues of complex Ginibre products with exact ra'] Let $(S_{j, 1})_{1\le j\le n}$ be defined as above. The following assertions hold:
\begin{enumerate}	
	\item[\textup{(a)}.]  For the moments and moment generating function, we have:
	\begin{align*}
		\mu:=\mathbb{E}[\log S_{j, 1}] = \psi(j)&, \quad\quad
		\sigma^{2}:={\rm Var}[\log S_{j,1}] = \psi'(j); \\
		\mathbb{E}[S_{j, 1} \log S_{j, 1}] = j \psi(j+1)&, \quad\quad
		\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda \log S_{j,1}}] = \frac{\Gamma(j+\lambda)}{\Gamma(j)}.
	\end{align*}
	
\item[\textup{(b)}.] For sufficiently large $j$, the skewness and kurtosis correction terms for $\log S_{j,1}$ are given by:
$$\gamma_{1}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}(\log S_{j,1}-\mu)^{3}}{6\sigma^{3}}=-\frac{1}{6\sqrt{j}}(1+O(j^{-1}))\quad \textup{(skewness correction)};$$
$$\gamma_{2}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\log S_{j,1}-\mu)^4] - 3\sigma^4}{24\sigma^4} =\frac{1}{12j}(1+O(j^{-1}))\quad \textup{(kurtosis correction)}.$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 2 (A unified sufficient condition) of arXiv:2608.24294, 'Existence of densities and atoms for the running maximum of time-inhomogeneous jump diffus'] Fix $p>1$ and let $\Theta=(h,v)\in \Hb_{\infty-}\times \Vb_{\infty-}$.
Assume that for every $t\in[0,T]$ we have $X_t\in W^{1,p}_\Theta$, that $\Xstar_T\in L^p(\Omega)$, that $D_\Theta X$ admits a right-continuous version with
\[
\E\Big[\sup_{0\le t\le T}|D_\Theta X_t|^p\Big]<\infty,
\]
and that
\[
\Pbb\big(D_\Theta X_t>0,\ \forall t\in(0,T]\big)=1.
\]
Then $\law(\Xstar_T)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\R$.

Consider a fixed constant $D> \left\{\frac{2m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}, \frac{2m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right\}$ entering only in the case of a second order reaction $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $S_i + S_k \rightarrow S_j + S_r$. \begin{align*}

[Definition def:double-in-banach of arXiv:2506.17168, '{\bf Scaling limits for sample autocovariance operators of Hilbert space-valued linear pro'] Let $(\mathbb Y,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space, and let $\{W^{(r)}\}_{r \in \mathbb Y}$ be a family of Gaussian random measures on $(\mathbb R, \lambda)$ with covariances (equation eq:covWW of the paper). Consider a kernel $f: \mathbb Y^2 \times \mathbb R^2 \to \mathbb R$. We say that there exists an $L^2(\mathbb Y^2)$-valued double Wiener-It\^o integral of the kernel $f$, denoted $\mathcal{I}_2(f)$, if there exists a sequence $\{f_{(n)}: n \geq 1\}$ of $L^2(\mathbb Y^2)$-valued special kernels, defined on $\mathbb Y^2 \times \mathbb R^2$, such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $\lim_{n \to \infty} \|f^{(r,s)} - f_{(n)}^{(r,s)}\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)} = 0$ $\mu^{\otimes 2}$-a.s.,
    
    \item the sequence $\{\mathcal{I}_2(f_{(n)}): n \geq 1\}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^1(\Omega:L^2(\mathbb Y^{2}))$.
    
\end{enumerate}
In that case, we define the double Wiener-It\^o integral by 
\[
\mathcal{I}_2(f) \doteq \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathcal{I}_2(f_{(n)}),
\]
where the limit is again understood in $L^1(\Omega:L^2(\mathbb Y^{2}))$. For an $\mathbb R^d-$valued kernel $f = (f_1,\dots,f_d)$ such that $\mathcal{I}_2(f_i)$ exists for all $i = 1,\dots,d$, we fix the notation $\mathcal{I}_2(f) \doteq (\mathcal{I}_2(f_1),\dots,\mathcal{I}_2(f_d))$.
title: Definition def:double-in-banach of arXiv:2506.17168

[Dfn 207 (coarsened buckets) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Definition~\ref{d:buckets}
the progressive partition
$\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$. 
For each time $q_d$, and for each of the spatial blocks $J_{\vl}$ defined by \eqref{e:J.blocks}, we now define a single bucket
	\beq
	B^{\frozen,\coarse}
	\equiv B^{\frozen,\coarse}(q_d,J_{\vl})
	\equiv \bigg\{
	a\in [M^+]
	: \vX^\frozen(q_d,a) \in J_{\vl}
	\bigg\}\,.\eeq
Each such $B^{\frozen,\coarse}$ is a union of buckets $B^\frozen\in\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$.
For any $B^\frozen\in\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$ not covered by one of the above (i.e., singleton buckets corresponding to particles that have left $[-\trK,\trK)^3$), we define simply
$B^{\frozen,\coarse} = B^\frozen$.
We define $\mathcal{C}^\frozen(q_d)$
to be the coarsening of $\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$ given by all these buckets $B^{\frozen,\coarse}$. We analogously define
the coarsening $\mathcal{C}^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_d)$ of $\mathcal{B}^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_d)$.
title: coarsened buckets

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Second-order expansion of E[|level set|] by the local CLT for the DGFF at a point, then a variance computation from the two-point Gaussian density. Result: The first-order correction to the mean is computable: with h_x ~ N(0, g log N + O(1)) the mean of the level-set size is N^{2(1-lambda^2)} times (c + O((log N)^{-1/2})) where the (log N)^{-1/2} term comes from the Gaussian tail with the boundary correction G_N(x,x) - g log N. The variance is dominated by pairs at distance N^{1-lambda^2 t} for t in (0,1) and its exponent is 2(1-lambda^2) + something strictly positive, so the normalised fluctuation is not of CLT type but is driven by the field at mesoscopic scales; the natural conjecture is that the fluctuation is Z^D_lambda-mixed Gaussian with variance proportional to the integral of e^{2 alpha lambda h} over a scale window, but I could not close the identification of the mixing measure. Obstruction: No local limit theorem for pairs at every mesoscopic distance uniformly; the fluctuation law is a functional of the whole scale ladder, not of one scale.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0002-fluctuations-and-large-deviations-of-intermediate-level-sets-of-the-2d

[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $G,H$ be compact Lie groups, and let $X$ be a $G$-free and Hausdorff $(G\times H)$-space. Then the quotient map $\eta\colon X\to X/G$ (i.e.\ the unit of the adjunction $(-)/G\dashv{\textup{triv}}_G$) is a $\mathcal G_{H,G}$-equivariant fibration.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $K\subset H$ be any closed subgroup and let $\varphi\colon K\to G$ be any continuous group homomorphism. Using the homeomorphism $((eq:splitting-of-fp of the paper))$, we may identify $\eta^\varphi$ with the quotient map $X^\varphi\to X^\varphi/C(\im\varphi)$ followed by the inclusion of a disjoint summand. The latter is clearly a Serre fibration, while the former is so by Lemma~(lemma:quotient-map-is-fib of the paper).
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'

[Lemma lem:hypoqms of arXiv:2505.12187, 'Speeding up quantum Markov processes through lifting'] Let QMS $\mathcal{P}_t = \exp(t \mathcal{L})$ be ergodic with an invariant state $\sigma \in \mathcal{D}_+(\mathcal{M})$, and let $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{L})$ be the fixed-point algebra defined in (equation def:fixedpointspace of the paper). 
Then we have $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{L}) \subset \ker(\mathcal{L} + \mathcal{L}^\star)$, and 
$\mathcal{P}_t$ is hypocoercive, i.e., $C > 1$ in (equation ex:expdecay of the paper), if and only if 
\begin{align*}
    \dim \ker(\mathcal{L} + \mathcal{L}^\star) > \dim \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{L})\,,
\end{align*}
that is, $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{L})$ is a strict subspace of $\ker(\mathcal{L} + \mathcal{L}^\star)$.

body:
For a doubly indexed family (a_{ij}) of NONNEGATIVE reals, sum_i sum_j a_{ij} = sum_j sum_i a_{ij} = sup over finite rectangles of the partial sums, all three being equal in [0, infinity] with no further hypothesis; this is Tonelli's theorem for two copies of counting measure, which is sigma-finite. For SIGNED a_{ij} the interchange is valid as soon as sum_i sum_j |a_{ij}| < infinity (absolute summability), and can fail otherwise even when both iterated sums exist and are finite. Concrete failure: index i, j >= 1 and set a_{ii} = 1, a_{i,i+1} = -1, and a_{ij} = 0 otherwise. Every row sums to 1 - 1 = 0, so sum_i sum_j a_{ij} = 0. The column j = 1 has only the entry a_{11} = 1 and sums to 1, while every column j >= 2 has entries a_{jj} = 1 and a_{j-1,j} = -1 and sums to 0; hence sum_j sum_i a_{ij} = 1. Both iterated sums exist, both are finite, and they differ. [standard; the counterexample is classical]
for the unconditional statement: a_{ij} >= 0
for the signed statement: sum_{i,j} |a_{ij}| < infinity

Then $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n:n\geqslant 2\right\}$ converges in probability in the extended fringe sense (Def.~(def:local-weak of the paper)~(equation it:fringe-b of the paper)) to the unique infinite {\tt sin}-tree with fringe distribution $\boldsymbol{\varpi}_{{\sf Poisson} , 1}$.      \[
\frac{N_k(n)}{n} \stackrel{P}{\longrightarrow} \frac{e^{-1}}{(k-1)!} \text{ as } n\to\infty,
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] A \emph{sutured manifold} \((N,R_{+},R_{-},\gamma)\) is a compact oriented 3-manifold \(N\) with boundary together with a set \(\gamma\subset \partial N\) satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\gamma\) consists of pairwise disjoint annuli \(A(\gamma)\) and tori \(T(\gamma)\). A component of \(A(\gamma)\) is called a \emph{sutured annulus} and a component of \(T(\gamma)\) is called a \emph{sutured torus}.
\item Each sutured annulus contains a homologically nontrivial oriented simple closed curve, called a \emph{suture}.
\item \(R_{+}\cup R_{-}= \partial N\setminus \operatorname{int}(\gamma)\) is oriented such that the orientation of \(R_{\pm}\) is coherent with the orientation of sutures in \(\partial R_{\pm}\) by boundary orientation principle.
Denote by \(R_{+}(\gamma)\) (resp. \(R_{-}(\gamma)\)) the components of \(\partial N\setminus \operatorname{int}(\gamma)\) whose normal vectors point out of (resp. into) \(N\).
\end{enumerate}
In practice, we usually abbreviate the notation to \((N,\gamma)\), or more simply to \(N\), when there is no ambiguity.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'

body: In mathematics, low-rank approximation refers to the process of approximating a given matrix by a matrix of lower rank. More precisely, it is a minimization problem, in which the cost function measures the fit between a given matrix and an approximating matrix, subject to a constraint that the approximating matrix has reduced rank. The problem is used for mathematical modeling and data compression. The rank constraint is related to a constraint on the complexity of a model that fits the data. In applications, often there are other constraints on the approximating matrix apart from the rank constraint, e.g., non-negativity and Hankel structure.
title: Low-rank approximation

[Lemma 3 (Galligo--Najnudel--Vu) of arXiv:2607.16954, 'Repeated differentiation of deterministic polynomials with asymptotically radial root dist'] Suppose $k$ is a non-negative integer and $m$ is a positive integer and suppose $P$ is a polynomial of the form
\[
P(z)=z^k p(z^m),
\]
where $p$ is a nonconstant polynomial with real, positive roots. Then $P'(z)$ has the form
\[
P'(z)=mz^{m-1}p'(z^m),\quad (k=0)
\]
and
\[
z^{k-1}\tilde p(z^m),\quad (k>0),
\]
where $\deg(\tilde p)=\deg(p)$ and where $\tilde p$ has all real, positive roots. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm 4 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] Let $d$ be fixed, and let $\mathbf X = (X_1,\dotsc,X_n)$ be the exchangeable unconditional base vector. If 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\E X_1^2 \to 1$, 
        \item  $\E(X_1^2X_2^2) - \E(X_1^2)\E(X_2^2) \to 0$, and
        \item  there exists some $\epsilon > 0$ such that $\sup_n \E(\abs{X_1}^{4d + \epsilon}) < \infty$,
    \end{enumerate} then the three conditions in \cref{thm:main} are satisfied, and we have with probability $1$ that \[\ESD(K_{\PrincipalT}) \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$
  G_{k,n}(y)

  \EE[G_n(X_{0,k}+y)]

  \int_{\mathbb{R}} G_n(x) f_k(x-y)\mathrm{d}x
  \,.
$
  Then the following statements hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item
    $\EE|G_n(X_{0,k}+y)|^r<\infty$ for all $k\in \NN \cup \{\infty\}$,  $n\in\NN$, $y\in\RR$, and for all $r\in (0,\alpha)$.

With the notation of Lemma~\ref{lem:f},
    for all $k>k_0$ or $k=\infty$, it holds that the function $G_{k,n}$ is continuously differentiable with
  \begin{align*}
    G_{k,n}'(y)
    \ := \
     \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}
     G_{k,n}(y)
     \ = \
    -
    \int_{\RR}
    G_n(x)
    f'_{k}
    (x-y)
    \,\mathrm{d}x
    \ < \ \infty
    \qquad\text{for all}\ y\in\RR\,.
  \end{align*}
  \end{enumerate}

body:
[Lemma lmm:m1m2 of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] With the above notations, we have
    \[
    m_2 = \frac{d-1}{d}am_1
    \]
and $1 \le a \le ( 2 \log (1/p))^{1/2}$.
Furthermore, assuming $a\le \sqrt d/2$, we have
\[ \zeta^2 \asymp pa^{2} \lesssim h(p)\,,
\]
where we recall that $\zeta$ is defined by ~((eq:zeta-def of the paper)).

\begin{proof}
In this proof, we fix $d$ and suppress it from the notation.  We abbreviate $\mathbb{P}=\nu$, and write $\mathbb{E}$ for expectation with respect to $\nu$.  We also abbreviate $c\equiv c_{d,1}$ and $f(t)\equiv f_d(t)$. Define
    \[ g(t)
    = c \bigg(1-\frac{t^2}{d}\bigg)^{(d-1)/2}\,,
    \]
and note that
    \begin{align*}
    \frac{d}{dt} g(t) &= -\frac{d-1}{d}  t f(t)\,,\\
    \frac{d}{dt} [tg(t)]
        &= -(t^2-1) f(t)\,.
    \end{align*}
It follows that
    \begin{align*}
    &m_1
    = \mathbb{E}[T;T\ge a]
    = \int_a^{d^{1/2} } t f(t)\,dt
    = \frac{d}{d-1} g(a)
    = \frac{cd}{d-1} \bigg(1-\frac{a^2}{d}
        \bigg)^{(d-1)/2}\,,\\
    &\mathbb E[T^2; T \ge a]-p
    =\int_a^{d^{1/2}} (t^2-1) f(t)\,dt
    =ag(a)
    = \frac{d-1}{d}am_1\,.
    \end{align*}
Rearranging the last expression gives
    \[
    m_2
    = \mathbb E[T^2 K(T)]
    = \mathbb E[T^2;T\ge a]-p
    = \frac{d-1}{d}am_1\,,
    \]
which proves the first claim. Next, recalling that $p=\mathbb{P}(T\ge a)$, to bound $a\ge1$ it suffices to prove that $\mathbb{P}(T\ge 1)> p$. In fact it is easy to argue that $\mathbb{P}(T\ge 1)$ is lower bounded by an absolute constant: $T$ is equidistributed as
    \[
    \frac{d^{1/2} Z}{(Z^2 + S)^{1/2}}
    \]
where $Z$ is a standard gaussian random variable, and $S$ is a chi-square random variable with $d-1$ degrees of freedom, independent of $Z$. If $Z \ge 2^{1/2}$ and $S \le 2(d-1)$ then the above ratio is $\ge1$, so we conclude
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(T\ge1)
    \ge \mathbb{P}(Z \ge 2^{1/2}) \mathbb{P}(S \le 2(d-1))
    \ge \frac{\mathbb{P}(Z \ge 2^{1/2})}{2}
    \ge 0.03\,.
    \]
This proves $a\ge1$, as claimed. On the other hand the upper bound on $a$ is equivalent to the bound 
\[p = \mathbb{P}(T\ge a) \le \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(-\frac{a^2}{2}\bigg)\,,\] which follows from the fact that $T$ is $1$-subgaussian (Lemma~(lem:beta.mgf of the paper)). Next, recalling the definition ~((eq:zeta-def of the paper)) of $\zeta$, it is clear that $\zeta\gtrsim p^{1/2}a$. For the upper bound, we recall that the integration by parts above gives
    \[m_1 = \frac{d}{d-1} f_d(a) 
    \bigg(1-\frac{a^2}{d}\bigg)
    \leq 2 f_d(a)\,.
    \]
It is shown later in 
Lemma~(l:cap-tail-moment of the paper)
that under the assumption $1\le a\le \sqrt d/2$ we have
$p\geq c f_d(a)/a$ for some numerical constant $c$ (see display ~((eq:p-lb of the paper))). It  follows that
\[\zeta^2 = \frac{m_1^2}{p(1-p)}
\lesssim \frac{(ap)^2}{p} = pa^2
\lesssim h(p)\,,
\] as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lmm:m1m2 of arXiv:2607.02013

[Proposition 9 (Bernoulli relative anticoncentration) of arXiv:2606.25204, 'Exponential Rank Bounds for Random Matrices'] For every \(0<\rho\leq 1/2\) there are constants
\(\alpha_{3.1}=\alpha_{3.1}(\rho)>0\),
\(\gamma_{3.1}=\gamma_{3.1}(\rho)<1\), and
\(k_{3.1}=k_{3.1}(\rho)\) such that the following holds.  Let
\(B=(B_1,\ldots,B_n)\) have independent coordinates with
\[
   B_j\sim {\rm Bernoulli}(q_j),
   \qquad
   q_j\in[\rho,1-\rho]
   \quad (1\leq j\leq n),
\]
and let \(Z\) be defined by \eqref{eq:lazy-def-noniid} with
\(\alpha=\alpha_{3.1}\).  If \(V\subseteq\R^n\) is a linear subspace of
codimension \(k\ge k_{3.1}\), then
\begin{equation}
   \sup_{a\in\R^n}\PP\{B\in a+V\}
   \leq
   \gamma_{3.1}^k \PP\{Z\in V\}.
\end{equation}

DRAFT proof-method concept; this special-case argument was independently checked by w355 and assigned referee w356. No novelty or full KLS claim. Let d>=2, K=(d+1)(d+2), X be uniform on Delta_d={x_i>=0,sum_i x_i<=1}, m=(1,...,1)/(d+1), Sigma=(I-J/(d+1))/K with J the all-ones matrix, A=Sigma^(-1/2), Y=A(X-m), a=sqrt(2K), and v=Ae_1/a. Put Z=Proj_(v-perp)Y, T=<v,Y> and S=sum_(j=2)^d X_j. Given 0<epsilon<1, choose a nonzero smooth eta supported in (epsilon/4,epsilon/2) and put f(Y)=eta(S) sin(pi T/(a(1-S))). Each such f has finite full energy, E[f|Z]=0, E Var(f|Z)=E eta(S)^2/2 and E|partial_v f|^2=(pi^2/(2a^2)) E[eta(S)^2/(1-S)^2]. Its directional quotient is at least (2K/pi^2)(1-epsilon)^2, and the support has positive probability. Letting epsilon go to zero proves that the optimal directional conditional coefficient is 2K/pi^2. This card records the localized admissible witness method, rather than duplicating the common simplex-constants card. It does not bound the full-gradient KLS constant.
Integer d>=2
eta is nonzero smooth with the indicated support
Each fixed-epsilon full gradient energy is finite
Independent KEEP receipts are in w354 REFEREE_VERDICTS.json and w355 W354_AUDIT.md
title: Isotropic simplex: localized admissible Neumann modes attain the sharp directional bound

[Definition d:EnergyMeas of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let $(X,d,\mu,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ be an MMD space.
		The \emph{energy measure} $\Gamma(f,f)$ of $f\in\mathcal{F}$
		associated with $(X,d,\mu,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ is defined,
		first for $f\in\mathcal{F}\cap L^{\infty}(X,\mu)$ as the unique ($[0,\infty]$-valued)
		Borel measure on $X$ such that
		\begin{equation}
			\int_{X} g \, d\Gamma(f,f)= \mathcal{E}(f,fg)-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}(f^{2},g) \qquad \textrm{for all $g \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_{\mathrm{c}}(X)$,}
		\end{equation}
		and then by
		$\Gamma(f,f)(A):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Gamma\bigl((-n)\vee(f\wedge n),(-n)\vee(f\wedge n)\bigr)(A)$
		for each Borel subset $A$ of $X$ for general $f\in\mathcal{F}$. The signed measure $\Gamma(f,g)$ for $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$ is defined by polarization.
title: Definition d:EnergyMeas of arXiv:2510.13659

[Proposition prop:cond-band-noncrit of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Fix $q\in[0,1)$ and a finite-step order parameter
		$\eta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$. For each \(N\), let
		\(\mathbf{a}_N\in(-1,1)^N\) satisfy
		\[
		q_{\mathbf{a}_N}=q,
		\qquad
		F_{\mathrm{TAP}}(\mathbf{a}_N)=F_{\mathrm{TAP},\eta}(\mathbf{a}_N).
		\]
		Let \(f_N\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(g_N\in\mathbf{a}_N^\perp\). When \(q=0\), take
		\(\mathbf{a}_N=0\), \(f_N=P_\eta\), and \(g_N=0\). Condition on
		\[
		F_{\mathrm{TAP},\eta}(\mathbf{a}_N)=Nf_N,
		\qquad
		P_{\mathbf{a}_N^\perp}\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\eta}(\mathbf{a}_N)=g_N.
		\]
		Then
		\[
		\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
		\limsup_{N\to\infty}
		\left[
		\frac1N
		\mathbb{E}\left[
		\sup_{\mathbf{m}\in\mathrm{Band}_{\le1-\varepsilon}(\mathbf{a}_N)}
		\bigl(
		F_{\mathrm{TAP}}(\mathbf{m})-F_{\mathrm{TAP}}(\mathbf{a}_N)
		\bigr)
		\,\middle|\,
		\mathcal J_{\mathbf{a}_N}(f_N,g_N)
		\right]
		-
		\mathscr D_\eta(\mathbf{a}_N,g_N)
		\right]
		\le0.
		\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    \[
      \mathbb{P} \left( 
      \frac{r d^\lambda_r(\mathring{p},\mathring{q})}{\mu(\lambda) d_M(p,q)} \in 
      [e^{-\varepsilon},e^\varepsilon]
      \right)
      \geq 1 - \exp(-c \log^2 n)

    for all $n \geq n_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own work draft; proof (unaudited), no novelty established. For a centered equilateral equal-weight three-Gaussian teacher with covariance I_d, exact population DDPM GD on centered mean parameters, physical step 1 and centered Gaussian factor initialization, converges to the teacher up to permutation with probability at least 7/20. At the inverse-polynomial noisy radius chosen in C07, normalized mean accuracy epsilon costs O(a^(-2) log d+a^(-4) log(C/epsilon)) iterations, hence polynomial d and 1/epsilon. Here M=a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T, V=sqrt(2/3)U^T for unit equilateral vertices U, and Z_0 has iid N(0,1/d) entries. Mean error is ||M-M_teacher,permuted||_F<=a epsilon. This enforces zero centroid, known weights, covariance and radius; no empirical or arbitrary-triangle theorem is claimed.

centered equilateral teacher and equal weights 1/3
known identity component covariance
known teacher radius for choosing smoothing time
centered-parameter exact population GD with physical step 1
Gaussian factor initialization at noisy scale, independent entries N(0,1/d)
a and fixed small rho chosen as in C07, with a^2 proportional to rho*(rho/(8000 sqrt(d)))^760
real arithmetic only

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:f0c6d14fab384b7fe8c06fe1bd69fb68554b30c51ff83b3861f618460b245efa","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/f0/f0c6d14fab384b7fe8c06fe1bd69fb68554b30c51ff83b3861f618460b245efa.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f7692cf4f4e3cbbd58ca3826a6a28ccd46d9a1f069ecd58c0fd5466a710fd2f4","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c08","bundle_id":"population.t309-centered-equilateral-random-init-population-learning-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:gaussian-mixture-ddpm-equilateral-centered-random-initialization-convergence","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Own work draft; proof (unaudited), T309-w721-C08 v2, Target 2.

# Population DDPM learning from centered Gaussian initialization: equilateral teacher

This is a restricted population result toward the named K=3 target. It combines the random-entry bridge C07 with C03 and C05. These dependencies are themselves unaudited drafts; this file does not confer independent verification. No novelty claim is made. The result does not treat arbitrary triangles, an unconstrained centroid, or finite samples.

## 1. Statement

Use the teacher, factor coordinates, population loss and physical unit GD step of C07: equal weights, identity component covariance, centered equilateral teacher of noisy radius a, M=a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T, and iid N(0,1/d) entries in Z_0. There is an absolute rho_*>0 such that choosing rho=rho_* in C07, and choosing a^2 equal to a sufficiently small constant times

    rho*(rho/(8000 sqrt(d)))^760,

gives the following. With probability at least 7/20, for every 0<epsilon<1 there is a permutation pi such that after

    O(a^(-2) log d + a^(-4) log(C/epsilon))             (1)

iterations, ||M-M_*pi||_F<=a epsilon. The same good-initialization event works for all accuracies; the trajectory converges to a permuted teacher. All constants and polynomial exponents are independent of d and epsilon. As in C07, this is a real-arithmetic, exact population-gradient result. No sample or bit-complexity theorem is asserted.

For original equilateral means of radius R, choose OU time exp(-t)=a/R and rescale the fitted means by R/a. The resulting mean error is at most R epsilon; if a distributional TV error is desired, choose epsilon proportional to that error divided by R. This follows by matching components and applying Pinsker to each pair of identity-covariance Gaussians. A known radius and imposed zero centroid remain assumptions.

## 2. Uniform angular anti-concentration at entry

Let G be precisely the good Gaussian event in C07 Section 3. It has probability at least 2/5. It is invariant under every rotation of the teacher plane, acting on the initialization as Z_0 -> T Z_0 where T is a plane rotation and the identity on its perpendicular complement. The conditions defining G are Frobenius norms, the first planar column norm, and the absolute perpendicular component of the second planar column. Each is unchanged by these rotations.

The covariance-factor flow f(Z)=(P-ZZ^T)Z is equivariant under that rotation group. At the deterministic entry time s_N=N*(2a^2/3), E^T Z(s_N) is invertible on G: its covariance is (I+K)^(-1), positive definite, by C07. Its unique orthogonal polar factor O_s is therefore rotation-equivariant. Conditional on G and on either determinant branch of O_s with positive probability, its angle is uniform modulo 2pi. This follows because its conditional law is invariant under every circle rotation; the only invariant probability measure on the circle is normalized arc length. One can see the uniqueness directly by equal probabilities for equal-length arcs, first at rational partitions and then by continuity. Independence between angle and a noninvariant event is not being assumed.

Take delta=pi/24. In either determinant branch there are three unstable equilateral angles, spaced 2pi/3 apart. Their open delta-neighborhoods occupy fraction 3delta/pi=1/8 of the circle. Reflection of the unit equilateral triangle is a label transposition, so the same description applies to the determinant-minus branch. Consequently

    P(G and flow entry angle at least delta from all maxima)
       >=(2/5)*(7/8)=7/20.                            (2)

This statement concerns the surrogate flow, whose continuous rotational symmetry is exact. The exact DDPM objective has only the discrete teacher symmetries; its entry angle is transferred by C07 rather than assumed uniform.

At this time the flow is within rho/4 of EO_s and the exact DDPM iterate within rho/4 of the flow. Thus the exact factor is within rho/2 of EO_s. Its projection onto the corresponding conformal equilateral subspace has radius r=1+O(rho) and angle within 4rho of the flow angle, for rho sufficiently small. Here is an elementary way to bound this last assertion. In the determinant-plus branch, the angle of a planar matrix A close to R_theta is the argument of (A_11+A_22)+i(A_21-A_12), whose value at R_theta is 2exp(i theta). Its change has modulus at most sqrt(2)||A-R_theta||_F. The argument is Lipschitz on the disk of radius 1 about 2exp(i theta). For the other branch first multiply by a fixed reflection, an isometry. The same formula also identifies the angle of orthogonal projection onto the conformal subspace. The constant 4 is more than sufficient for ||A-R_theta||<=rho/2.

Choose rho so 4rho<=delta/4 and so the entry radius and normal error lie strictly inside the tube considered next. On the event in (2), the exact entry angle is at least 3delta/4 from all unstable angles.

## 3. Off-family tangent forcing is quadratic

Work in centered factor coordinates, after a fixed label permutation selecting the proper determinant branch. Let L={r E R_theta:r>=0,theta in R}, a two-dimensional linear subspace when expressed using the two conformal basis matrices. Write Z=v+w with v=Pi_L Z and w perpendicular to L, and ||v||_F=sqrt(2)r. The exact population vector field in rescaled time is f_a=-a^(-4)grad_Z F_a; the GD update is Z'=Z+gamma f_a(Z), gamma=2a^2/3.

C02 supplies exact invariance f_a(L) subset L. Its proof uses the fixed space of simultaneous cyclic label permutation and spatial rotation, plus perpendicular reflection. Since f_a is a gradient field, Df_a(v) is self-adjoint. Differentiating invariance along L shows Df_a(v)L subset L, hence

    Pi_L Df_a(v) w=0      for w perpendicular to L.

Uniform third-derivative bounds for F_a/a^4 on a fixed bounded factor ball therefore give

    ||Pi_L f_a(v+w)-f_a(v)||_F<=C||w||_F^2.           (3)

These derivative bounds follow by the same finite-span softmax domination used for (3) in C07, now with three rather than two parameter derivatives; the span remains bounded independently of d. The leading covariance loss is quartic and has bounded derivatives on this ball; the higher-order remainder has the same property. Thus (3) does not conceal a factor a^(-2) or a dimension-dependent norm.

C05's normal contraction, after the fixed coordinate rescaling, gives in a sufficiently small tube, for absolute c_0,C>0,

    ||w_{n+1}||_F^2<=(1-c_0 gamma)||w_n||_F^2.        (4)

The exact constants may change under the fixed scaling sqrt(3/2); their positivity and dimension independence do not. C05 initially makes (4) conditional on the radial annulus. We preserve that annulus below.

## 4. Radial confinement and angular barrier

Use r in [0.9,1.1] and a normal tube ||w||<=eta_0 for a sufficiently small absolute eta_0. The exact restricted angular derivative from C03 is

    partial_theta F_a=a^6(3r^3/4+O(a^2)) sin(3theta),

uniformly on the annulus, with its usual smooth extension at zeros of sin(3theta). This extension and positivity follow from the reflection and cyclic symmetries and the C^2 angular expansion. The exact restricted discrete step thus has angular map

    T_r(theta)=theta-gamma a^2 k(r,theta) sin(3theta),

where k is uniformly bounded above and below by positive constants. The harmless step dependence is included in k: the exact angle is an atan2 of radial and angular components, with positive radial denominator. Since gamma a^2 is small, T_r is increasing, fixes every minimum and maximum, and moves an interior angle toward its nearest minimum without crossing it.

On L the normalized radial update is

    r'=r+gamma[(1-r^2)r+O(a^2)]+O(gamma^2 a^4).

The leading radial field is strictly positive at 0.9 and strictly negative at 1.1. By (3) the projected update off L differs by at most Cgamma||w||^2. Choose a and eta_0 small. This preserves the annulus: in fixed narrow boundary layers the radial increment points inward, while elsewhere its bounded size cannot jump a boundary when gamma is small. Equivalently its restricted radial map has positive r derivative 1+gamma(1-3r^2)+O(gamma a^2), maps the two endpoints inward, and the off-family error is smaller than the inward boundary margin. Polar coordinate derivatives are bounded throughout this annulus. This argument and (4) close simultaneously by induction. Entry at r=1+O(rho), ||w||=O(rho), is strictly inside for small rho.

The true projected angular recurrence differs from T_r by an error e_n satisfying

    |e_n|<=C gamma ||w_n||^2,
    sum_{n>=0}|e_n|<=C'||w_0||^2<=C''rho^2.          (5)

No independence or martingale claim enters this sum; (4) is a pointwise deterministic geometric bound. Shrink the fixed rho further so C''rho^2<=delta/4. Because T_r moves away from the unstable angles within each sector, the distance to the nearest sector boundary decreases by at most |e_n| in one step. Starting at margin 3delta/4, summing (5) keeps that distance at least delta/2 forever. The trajectory cannot cross into a neighboring sector.

## 5. Convergence and rate

Let alpha_n be angular distance to the sector's minimum. Throughout the preserved sector, alpha<=pi/3-delta/2. On this compact interval sin(3alpha)>=c_delta alpha for an absolute positive c_delta. The exact restricted map and (5) imply

    alpha_{n+1}<=(1-c_1 gamma a^2)alpha_n
                                      +C gamma ||w_n||^2.  (6)

Take a small enough that c_1 a^2<c_0/2. Summing (6) with (4) gives

    alpha_n<=C exp(-c_2 gamma a^2 n).                  (7)

The constants do not contain inverse powers of a. In discrete form the convolution is gamma times the difference of the slow and fast geometric powers divided by their ratio difference, whose magnitude is at least c gamma. The faster normal forcing therefore has bounded total effect even as a decreases.

To control the final radius, write b_n=r_n-1. The leading radial field has negative derivative uniformly on the annulus. At r=1, the exact restricted radial field is O(a^2 alpha^2): it vanishes at the realizable teacher angle, is even in alpha, and its covariance leading term vanishes at r=1, leaving order a^2 after dividing F by a^4. Its r derivative changes the leading contraction only by O(a^2). The length correction from the angular component of the discrete step is O(gamma^2 a^4 alpha^2), which is absorbed below. Together with (3) this yields

    |b_{n+1}|<=(1-c_3 gamma)|b_n|
                        +C gamma a^2 alpha_n^2
                        +C gamma ||w_n||^2.            (8)

Equations (4),(7),(8), or their geometric-series sums, show

    |b_n|+alpha_n+||w_n||<=C exp(-c_4 gamma a^2 n).    (9)

For (8), choose c_4 smaller than each fast contraction constant and smaller than half the angular constant; convolution with the faster radial kernel is then bounded uniformly. In particular repeated equal fast rates can be bounded by a slightly slower exponential. These estimates establish convergence to r=1, w=0, and the fixed sector's minimum, hence to a permuted teacher, rather than just convergence to an O(a^2) radial neighborhood.

Since gamma=2a^2/3, (9) costs O(a^(-4)log(C/epsilon)) physical iterations after entry. Adding C07's O(a^(-2)log d) entry cost gives (1), and the mean-factor isometry gives the claimed mean error after adjusting an absolute constant inside the logarithm. The probability is exactly the good-entry-and-angle event bounded in (2), with no multiplication of unverified conditional probabilities.

## Remaining target gaps and review priorities

This removes the unknown-plane and generic-centered-shape entry assumptions for the equilateral population case. It leaves free-centroid initialization, unaugmented empirical optimization, bit complexity, unknown radius, unequal weights and arbitrary well-separated triangles open. In particular it does not overcome the anisotropic high-noise trap C06. A general K=3 Target 2 proof is not supplied.

Review should focus on the quadratic tangent-forcing claim (3), radial annulus closure, the exact angular factorization, and the conditional rotation argument. The proof depends on the exact versions C03 v2, C05 v1, C07 v2. principal-pivot presentations $P_C,P_H,P_G$ listed explicitly in
(lem:pn1 of the paper) below, and by exchange and reversal
of the two carrier rails.  A \emph{circuit state} $\tau$ records, before
evaluation,
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item every original $p\vee r$ circuit, its ordered oriented interval
fragments, and one base fragment on that circuit;
\item the ten named physical gaps, every component, defect, and retained
root port, with their source and target tensor words; and
\item either one ordered pair of root fronts or one existing opaque
two-front token.
\end{enumerate}
The finite root states $\Pi_{\rm root}$ record the twenty ordered choices
of distinct core occurrences together with this data.

For later use we make the signed transport in this definition explicit.
Identify the five core vertices with $\mathbb F_5$ by
\[
 \kappa_5(0)=0,\qquad \kappa_5(1)=1,\qquad \kappa_5(2)=4,
 \qquad \kappa_5(3)=2,\qquad \kappa_5(4)=3.
\tag{2.2.6a}
\]
In these coordinates the oriented left and right rails are respectively
$x\mapsto x+1$ and $x\mapsto x+2$.  The transport group is
\[
 \mathscr O_{20}=\{g_{\alpha,\beta}:x\mapsto\alpha x+\beta:
       \alpha\in\mathbb F_5^\times,\ \beta\in\mathbb F_5\}.
\tag{2.2.6b}
\]
It acts on vertices through $\kappa_5^{-1}g_{\alpha,\beta}\kappa_5$.
Multiplication by $\alpha=1,4,2,3$ sends the ordered pair of oriented
rails $(L,R)$ to
\[
 (L^+,R^+),\qquad (L^-,R^-),\qquad
 (R^+,L^-),\qquad (R^-,L^+),
\tag{2.2.6c}
\]
respectively.  If $x_v^s$ is the gap leaving $v$ on the oriented rail
$s$ and $g$ sends $s$ to $t$ with orientation $\epsilon$, then
\[
 g(x_v^s)=
 \begin{cases}
 x_{g(v)}^t,&\epsilon=+1,\\
 (x_{\operatorname{pred}_t(g(v))}^t)^*,&\epsilon=-1.
 \end{cases}
\tag{2.2.6d}
\]
At a curvature gate the induced dart permutation carries the two physical
wedge pairs to the two physical wedge pairs.  Reversal within a wedge pair
contributes its skew sign, whereas exchange of the two wedge pairs is
signless.  Thus the product of the five local curvature signs is
\[
 \chi(g_{\alpha,\beta})=
 \begin{cases}+1,&\alpha\in\{1,4\},\\-1,&\alpha\in\{2,3\}.
 \end{cases}
\tag{2.2.6e}
\]
\Crefrange{eq:2.2.6a}{eq:2.2.6e}, including the formal adjoints in (eq:2.2.6d of the paper),
are part of every transported circuit state.

For an ordered pair $r\ne s$, put
\[
 R=\{r,s\},\qquad S=V(K_5)\setminus R.
\]
Excise the five selected coefficient gates and cut each of the ten rail
segments at its two incidences with the core.  The resulting typed
boundary word $\mathscr U_{rs}$ has two half-darts on the edge internal to $R$, six on
the three edges internal to $S$, and twelve on the six $R$--$S$ edges.
For any typed boundary word $\mathscr U$, let
$\mathscr H(\mathscr U)$ be the ordered tensor product of its indicated
$H$, $\Lambda^2H$, and dual factors.  Fixing the complete complement also
fixes an output boundary word $\mathscr O_{rs}$.
A \emph{joint attachment}
\[
 \mathcal A_{rs}[\Xi]:\mathscr H(\mathscr U_{rs})
       \longrightarrow\mathscr H(\mathscr O_{rs})
\tag{2.2.7}
\]
is the contraction made from the complete complement of those five
gates, the original circuit wiring, all ten simultaneous gap contexts,
signed boundary maps, and ancillary identities.  In pass mode its total
token degree is one and its unique opaque token is denoted $\Xi$; here
\emph{token degree} means the number of occurrences of this distinguished
formal token generator in the raw complement.  In root
mode the attachment has token degree zero.  No selected core gate belongs
to the attachment, and the complement supplies every named gap context
exactly once.  The token may lie in one gap context or may couple several
gap slots.  Only the finite boundary type of $\mathcal A_{rs}$ belongs to
the port-state set; its contents remain opaque.

[Corollary 8 of arXiv:2608.27143, 'An approximate zero bias transformation for random sums: Applications to sampling with out'] Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. mean zero random variables with finite variance. Let $W=\sum_{i=1}^N X_i$, where $N$ is  a binomial random variable  with parameters $n$ and $p$, independent of $\{X_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$.
	Define $\sigma^2 := \Var(W) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty Var(X_i) P(N\ge i)$. Let $I$ be as in \eqref{Idef}. Then
			$$d_1\left(\mathcal{L}(W/{\sigma}), \mathcal{L}(Z) \right)= \frac{1}{\sigma^3}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\E|X_1|^3 + 2\E X_1^2 \E|X_1|\right) P^2(N \ge i)  +{2\sqrt{2} \over \sqrt{\pi}}\cdot\displaystyle{\left(1-{1\over np}\sum_{i=1}^nP^2(N\ge i)\right)},$$ where $Z$ is a standard normal random variable.

[Lemma 29 of arXiv:2511.06414, 'Non-uniform Edgeworth expansions for weakly dependent random variables and their applicati'] Suppose that $\sig>0$.
For $\bbP$-a.a. $\om$ there exists an increasing sequence $(B_n(\om))_{n=1}^\infty$ so that 
$$
\sig_{\om,n}^2=\|S_n^\om-\mu_\om(S_n^\om)\|_{L^2(\mu_\om)}^2=B_n(\om)+O(1).
$$
As a consequence, the couplings with the properties described in Corollary \ref{ASIP} always exist (for all $m$) for  $S_n=S_n^\om-\mu_\om(S_n^\om)$.

[Theorem 16 (Warren's strict-sign theorem) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $r,n,d_{\mathrm{pol}}\in\N^+$ with $n\ge r$, and let
$q_1,\ldots,q_n$ be $n$ distinct nonzero real polynomials in $r$ variables,
each of total degree at most $d_{\mathrm{pol}}$.  A vector
$\bmsigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n)\in\{-1,1\}^n$ is a consistent nonzero
sign assignment if there exists $\bmmu\in\R^r$ such that
$\sigma_j q_j(\bmmu)>0$ for every $j$.  The number of such assignments
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \Bigl\lvert
 \bigl\{
  \bmsigma\in\{-1,1\}^n:
  \text{there exists }\bmmu\in\R^r
  \text{ such that }\sigma_j q_j(\bmmu)>0
  \text{ for every }j
 \bigr\}
 \Bigr\rvert
 \le
 \left(\frac{4ed_{\mathrm{pol}}n}{r}\right)^r.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Warren's strict-sign theorem

[Lemma lem:stochastic-order-distribution of arXiv:2411.01364, 'Global Dynamics of Granular Media Equations via Stochastic Order'] Let $\mu_1,\mu_2\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R)$ be two probability measures on $\mathbb R$, and let $F_1,F_2:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ be their cumulative distribution functions.
Then $\mu_1\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\mu_2$ if and only if $F_1(x)\geq F_2(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.

[Lem 18 of arXiv:2609.00739, '2609.00739'] Let $\Gamma\subset\partial\Omega$ be a $C^2$ arc and let
\[
 T_j=\upnu_j I_2-(\upmu_{j,ab})_{a,b=1}^2
 \stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}T
\]
be the Allen--Cahn stress measures in original coordinates.  If $\tau$
and $n$ are the unit tangent and inward unit normal along $\Gamma$, then,
as Radon measures on $\Gamma$,
\begin{equation}
 T_{nn}\llcorner\Gamma=0,
 \quad T_{\tau n}\llcorner\Gamma=0,
 \quad T\llcorner\Gamma
 =2(\tau\otimes\tau)(\zetastar\llcorner\Gamma).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\zetastar\llcorner\Gamma$ has no atoms.
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \upmu_{\star,n\tau}\llcorner\Gamma&=0,\\
  (\upmu_{\star,nn}-\upmu_{\star,\tau\tau})\llcorner\Gamma
  &=2\zetastar\llcorner\Gamma,\\
  \nustar\llcorner\Gamma&=\upmu_{\star,nn}\llcorner\Gamma.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Combine the known factorial-type lower bound heuristics with Graham's Borel-type bounds. Result: The source cites Graham's Borel-type bounds on the remainder; if the coefficients a_i satisfy |a_i| >= c K^i i! for infinitely many i then the radius is zero, and the computed a_i (Clisby-Liang-Slade) grow consistently with factorial growth. A rigorous proof of divergence would follow from a lower bound on the number of lace diagrams contributing with the same sign at order i, i.e. a non-cancellation statement; the lace expansion for SAW has alternating-sign contributions (pi^{(N)} with sign (-1)^N) so cancellation cannot be excluded without an explicit asymptotic analysis of the diagram sums. A standard trick for proving zero radius is to exhibit a singularity of the generating function at every point of a circle, which is unavailable here since the 'function' is only asymptotic. I tested the computed coefficients' ratio a_{i+1}/a_i (from the source's cited values, not recomputed here): the ratios increase roughly linearly in i, consistent with factorial growth, but 11 terms cannot certify it. No proof; the conjecture is recorded with the concrete criterion (non-cancellation of leading lace diagrams) that would prove it. Obstruction: Alternating-sign lace contributions may cancel; no asymptotic diagram count with sign control.

piecewise linear path $\gamma\colon [-1,1] \to \R^{d\times n}$ consisting of at

times $t_1 < \dots < t_L$ only, and for every $\ell \in \{1,\dots,L\}$ and
every $B \in \mathcal B$ the point $\gamma(t_\ell)$ lies on at most one wall
$D_{B,I}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
