[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2608.07239, 'Unified framework for asymptotically uniform iterative construction of generalised random '] Consider the IMFIS process on $(G,F,R,\b)$ with $G=(V,E)$ $2$-uniform. Assume $\ell$ is fixed, and let $\alpha\to\infty$. Then
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item $\begin{aligned}[t]
				|V|=n_{\alpha}=(1+O(\alpha^{-1}))\tfrac{\ell}{2}\alpha^2,
			\end{aligned}$
			\item $\begin{aligned}[t]
				|F|\leq\alpha F_{\max}\leq\alpha M,
			\end{aligned}$
			\item $\begin{aligned}[t]
				|R^*(U)|\leq|U|R_{\max}^{(a)}\leq|U|M,\ \forall U\subset V.
			\end{aligned}$
		\end{enumerate}

body: In mathematics, especially group theory, two elements $a$ and $b$ of a group are conjugate if there is an element $g$ in the group such that $b=gag^{-1}.$ This is an equivalence relation whose equivalence classes are called conjugacy classes. In other words, each conjugacy class is closed under the maps $a\mapsto gag^{-1},$ with $g$ an element of the group.

[Proposition Separating_Surface_Prop of arXiv:2603.28520, 'The Supercritical Loop O(1) and Random Current Models: Uniqueness and Mixing'] Let $q\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2},$ $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and let $E_1,E_3\subseteq E$ be disjoint. Denote $E_2:=E\setminus (E_1\cup E_3).$ Suppose that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $E_1$ and $E_2$ are finite.
    \item The induced graph $G(E_2)$ is connected.
    \item Any path $(\gamma_j)_{1\leq j\leq n}$ in $G$ with $\gamma_1\in G(E_1)$ and $\gamma_n\in G(E_3)$ must have a $1<j<n$ with $\gamma_j\in G(E_2).$
\end{enumerate}
Then, $\pi_{G(E_1)}(\ker(\partial^G))=\pi_{G(E_1)}(\ker(\partial^{G(E_1\cup E_2)})).$ In particular, for any $A\in (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{V(G(E_3))}$ with $\sum_v A_v=0$,
$$\operatorname{UD}^A_G[\eta|_{\mathcal{O}(E_1)} \in \cdot\;]=\operatorname{UD}_{G}[\eta|_{\mathcal{O}(E_1)} \in \cdot\;]=\operatorname{UD}_{G(E_1\cup E_2)}[\eta|_{\mathcal{O}(E_1)}\in\cdot\;].$$ Furthermore, for $\eta\sim \operatorname{UD}^A_G,$ the random variables $\eta|_{\mathcal{O}(E_1)}$ and $\eta|_{\mathcal{O}(E_3)}$ are independent.
title: Proposition Separating_Surface_Prop of arXiv:2603.28520

[Dfn 101 (coordinate sum) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any measure $\rho$ on $[0,1]\times\R^d$, let $\bar{\rho}$ be the measure on $[0,1]\times\R$ that satisfies
	\[
	\int_{t,y} f\bigg(t, \sum_{i=1}^d y^i\bigg)
	\,\rho(dt\,dy)
	= \int_{t,x} f(t,x)
	\,\bar{\rho}(dt\,dx)\,,
	\]
where $t\in[0,1]$, $y\in\R^d$, and $x\in\R$.
As above, let $\vY$ be an $\R^d$-valued semimartingale with drift $\vD$ and covariation $\vQ$. We now consider the one-dimensional projections
	\[
	Y = \sum_{i=1}^d Y^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i=1}^d D^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d Q^{ij}\,.
	\]
Then $Y$ is a (one-dimensional) semimartingale with drift $D$ and covariation $Q$. We hereafter abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation measure of $\vY$ defined in Definition~\ref{d:intro.cts.occ}.
Then the occupation measure of $Y$ is $\bar{\rho}$. The occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $Y$ are
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{D^i}\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{Q^{ij}}\,.	
	\]
Let $\hvY$ be as defined by Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr},
and let $\iY$ be the one-dimensional projection, so $\iY(t)=Y(t-\sss)+\mathfrak{x}$ where $(\sss,\mathfrak{x})\sim\bar{\varphi}$ (the density $\varphi$ integrated over $x^1 + \ldots + x^d=\mathfrak{x}$). It follows that $\iY$ has occupation measure $\overline{\rho*\varphi}=\bar{\rho}*\bar{\varphi}$. Similarly, the occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $\iY$ have densities
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}
	\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}
		*\varphi}\,.	
	\]
Then, analogously to \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv}, we define (with $x$ now a scalar)
	\begin{align}
	
	B(t,x) 
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
		{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,,\\
	A(t,x)
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i,j=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
	{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Let $\iX$ be the solution to the (one-dimensional) SDE
	\[
	d\iX(t)
	= B(t,\iX)\,dt
	+A(t,\iX)^{1/2}\,dW(t)\,,
	\]
where $W$ is a one-dimensional standard Brownian motion.
title: coordinate sum

       F \left(\sqrt{\mu_\mathbb{D} \big(\tfrac{a}{\sqrt{\pi}}\big)} \right) \delta_\Omega( \delta_\Omega+2) +  G \left(\sqrt{\mu_\mathbb{D} \big(\tfrac{a}{\sqrt{\pi}}\big)} \right) \delta_\Omega,
    \end{equation}
    where $F$ and $G$ are as in (equation Eq:def_FG of the paper). In particular,
    \begin{equation} 
        |\Omega| \, \mu_\Omega \bigg(\frac{a}{\sqrt{|\Omega|}}  \bigg)
        - \pi \, \mu_\mathbb{D} \bigg(\frac{a}{\sqrt{\pi}}  \bigg) 
        \leqslant C_{\mathrm{PW}} \delta_\Omega( \delta_\Omega+2) + \pi j_{0,1} \delta_\Omega
    \end{equation}
    and the equality holds if and only if $\Omega$ is a disk. Here, $C_{\mathrm{PW}}>0$ is the constant in (equation Eq:PW_Dirichlet of the paper).

[Lemma lem:truncation-coupling of arXiv:2608.26745, 'Moderate Deviations for the Largest Eigenvalue of a Randomly Deformed Gaussian Unitary Ens'] There are constants $c,C>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P(\widehat\lambda_N\ne\lambda_N)
 \le CN e^{-c\tau_N}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for
\[
 \upsilon_N\in
 \left\{a_N^{3/2},\,a_N^3,\,\alpha_N^2a_N^2\right\},
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1{\upsilon_N}
 \log\mathbb P(\widehat\lambda_N\ne\lambda_N)=-\infty.
\end{equation}
In particular, at each of these speeds, the scaled variables
$\sqrt N(\widehat\lambda_N-R_N)/\alpha_N$ and $Z_N$ are exponentially
equivalent.

[Theorem 40 (The one-dimensional Stokes tree) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(F\) be a tame Morse polynomial of degree \(m\) in one variable and
fix an admissible direction.  Denote by
\[
 E_0,\ldots,E_{m-1}
\]
the \(m\) decay sectors at infinity.  There is a canonical boundary
isomorphism
\begin{equation}
 \partial:
 H_1^{\mathrm{rd}}(F;\mathbb Z)
 \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
 \widetilde H_0(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{m-1}\};\mathbb Z).
 
\end{equation}
If \(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_{m-1}\) is a distinguished integral thimble
basis, join two vertices whenever the corresponding thimble has its two
ends in those sectors.  The resulting oriented graph \(T\) is a spanning
tree.

Let \(\gamma\) be an admissible contour directed from \(E_p\) to \(E_q\).
Then
\begin{equation}
 [\gamma]
 =
 \sum_{e\in[p,q]_T}
 \epsilon_e(p,q)[\Gamma_e],
 \qquad
 \epsilon_e(p,q)\in\{-1,1\},
 
\end{equation}
where \([p,q]_T\) is the unique path from \(p\) to \(q\), and the sign is
positive precisely when the orientation of \(e\) agrees with that path.
Thus the physical Betti row is obtained by a finite path search and all
of its entries belong to \(\{0,\pm1\}\).  If the contour lies on a Stokes
direction, the two lateral trees give the two lateral rows, related by
\eqref{eq:Betti-wall-crossing}.

[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2608.31145, 'Gauge-compatible tensors on statistical manifolds: splitting and submanifold geometry'] Let $(M,g,\nabla,\nabla^{*},\Theta)$ be a $\Theta$-statistical manifold. Then
\[
R^{\nabla}(X,Y)\Theta Z
=
\Theta\,R^{\nabla^{*}}(X,Y)Z,
\]
for all $X,Y,Z\in\Gamma(TM)$.

If $\Theta$ is invertible, then
\[
R^{\nabla}(X,Y)
=
\Theta\circ R^{\nabla^{*}}(X,Y)\circ\Theta^{-1}.
\]

Moreover, for every piecewise smooth loop $\gamma$ based at $p$,
\[
\mathcal{P}^{\nabla}_{\gamma}\circ\Theta_p
=
\Theta_p\circ\mathcal{P}^{\nabla^{*}}_{\gamma}.
\]
Hence, if $\Theta_p$ is invertible,
\[
\operatorname{Hol}_{p}(\nabla)
=
\Theta_p\circ
\operatorname{Hol}_{p}(\nabla^{*})
\circ\Theta_p^{-1}.
\]

[Proposition 169 (Fundamental spacetime energy--null-flux identities) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill
	
	\noindent \underline{\textbf{Wave equation spacetime energy--null-flux identity}}.
	Suppose that on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubar)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,u]}$, the scalar function $f$ is the solution to the inhomogeneous covariant wave equation $\upmu \Box_{\gfour} f = \mathfrak{G}$. Then the following identity holds for $q \in [0,\infty)$:
	\begin{align}
		\begin{split} 
			& \ingoingfluxwave{q}[f](\ubar,u) + \outgoingfluxwave{q}[f](\ubar,u) + \frac{1}{2} \spacetimecoercive{q}[ \angrmD f](\ubar,u)   			+ \frac{q}{2} \newspacetimecoercive{q-1}\left[ \sqrt{\upmu + 2\ReciprocaluLunitAppliedtoTimeFunction \upmu} \, \nullangrmD f\right](\ubar,u) + 2 q \newspacetimecoercive{q-1}\left[ \newuL f\right](\ubar,u)  \\
			& = \ingoingfluxwave{q}[f](\leftubar,u) + \outgoingfluxwave{q}[f](\ubar,\moreinterestingu_1) - \int_{\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubar)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,u]}} \left\{ \Lunit f + 2 \upmu \Transport f \right\} \mathfrak{G} \, \weight^{q} \ReciprocalLunitAppliedtoTimeFunction \voldiamond  \\
			& \ \
			+ \int_{\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubar)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,u]}}  
			{^{(\multipliervectorfield)}\mathfrak{B}}[f]\, \weight^{q} \ReciprocalLunitAppliedtoTimeFunction \voldiamond  + 2q \int_{\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubar)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,u]}}  \MagnitueofinnerproductofnewLandnewuL  (\ToriTangentVectorfieldAssociatedToDoubleNullFolliations f )(\newuL f) (\newL \weight) \, \weight^{q-1} \voldiamond
		\end{split}
	\end{align}
	The error term ${^{(\multipliervectorfield)}\mathfrak{B}}[f]$ appearing 
	in the last integral on RHS\,\eqref{E:ENERGYNULLFLUXINTEGRALIDENTITIESWAVE}
	can be decomposed as follows: 
	\begin{align}  
		{^{(\multipliervectorfield)}\mathfrak{B}}[f] 
		& \eqdef \frac{1}{2} \left| \angrmD f\right|^2_{\gtorus} \mathbf{1}_{\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubar)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,u]} \setminus \smallneighborhoodofcreasearg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot]}}  +
		\sum_{i=1}^6 {^{(\multipliervectorfield)}\mathfrak{B}_{(i)}[f]},
	\end{align}
	where:
	\begin{subequations}
		\begin{align}
			{^{(\multipliervectorfield)}\mathfrak{B}_{(1)}[f]} 
			&

[Proposition mainestimate of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] Consider a family of probability measures $(\mu_t)_{t>0}$ verifying  $M_\beta$ for some $\beta>0$. Let moreover $\varepsilon>0$. 
    \par There exists a constant $C_\beta$ such that for integers $n < m$ and $l$, and independent random variables $(X^j_u)_{\substack{1\leqslant j\leqslant l \\ 1\leqslant u \leqslant n  }}$ and $(Y^j_v)_{{\substack{1\leqslant j\leqslant l \\ 1\leqslant v \leqslant m-n  }}}$ such that 
\[\mathbb{P}(X^j_u\in \mathrm{d} g)= \mu_{s^j_u}(\mathrm{d} g) \text{ and } \mathbb{P}(Y^j_v\in \mathrm{d} g)= \mu_{t^j_v}(\mathrm{d} g), \]
 where 
 \[\max\Bigg (\max_{\substack{1\leqslant j\leqslant l \\ 1\leqslant u \leqslant n  }} s^j_u, \max_{{\substack{1\leqslant j\leqslant l \\ 1\leqslant v \leqslant m-n  }}} t^j_u\Bigg )\leqslant \varepsilon,\]
we have 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\left[\left\vert \sum_{j=1}^l \log(X^j_1\cdots X^j_n Y^j_1\cdots Y^j_{m-n})-\log(X^j_1\cdots X^j_n)  \right\vert^{2\beta}\right] \leqslant C_\beta l^{\beta} \left( (m-n)^\beta \varepsilon^\beta +n^{2\beta-}\varepsilon^{2\beta}\right).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a sequence of finite, possibly random, rooted graphs G_n, local weak (Benjamini-Schramm) convergence means that for every finite radius r, the distribution of the isomorphism class of the r-ball around the (uniformly, or otherwise canonically) chosen root converges weakly to that of a limiting, typically infinite, random rooted graph (G*, o). The objective method, due to Aldous and Steele, is the broader program of analyzing this limiting infinite object directly, such as a Poisson weighted infinite tree or a unimodular Galton-Watson tree, to compute limiting constants for combinatorial optimization functionals on the finite graphs, such as the minimum spanning tree constant or the limiting value in the random assignment problem, by solving a recursive distributional (fixed-point) equation on the infinite limit rather than working with finite-n computations directly. It does not by itself establish that a given sequence converges locally weakly, which typically must be separately verified via a subsequential compactness argument together with uniqueness of subsequential limits, and it does not directly give convergence of global, extensive functionals without an additional concentration or summation argument beyond the purely local statement. Typical failure: Assuming that local weak convergence of the underlying random graph automatically implies convergence of a global extensive functional, such as the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, at the same per-vertex limiting rate; local convergence controls only typical local neighborhoods, and passing to a global average requires an additional uniform-integrability or concentration argument, often the genuinely hard part of an objective-method proof, which is easy to overlook once the local limit has been identified. Canonical reference: Benjamini and Schramm, 2001, Electronic Journal of Probability; Aldous and Steele, 2004, in Probability on Discrete Structures, Springer; Aldous and Lyons, 2007, Electronic Journal of Probability.
a sequence of (random) rooted graphs with controlled local neighborhoods, such as bounded degree, sufficient for tightness
existence of a limiting infinite, typically unimodular, random rooted graph as the local weak limit
the functional of interest is expressible as, or well approximated by, a sum or average of local, root-based quantities
for extensive functionals: an additional argument, such as subadditivity or concentration, to pass from the local limit to a law of large numbers for the global sum

A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). [Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Fix a compact interval $\mathcal I\subset \R$.
For any $f\in \mathbf{M}$ satisfying \eqref{eq:TwistCondition}, there exists a coupling between the $\alpha_p$ and an iid sequence $Z_p \sim \cN^{\C}(0,1)$  
such that
the error function 
\[
  E_{N,0}(x) \coloneqq S_{N,0}(x) - G_{N,0}(x)  = \sum_{p\leq N} \frac{f(p)}{\sqrt{p}} (\alpha_p-Z_p) p^{-ix}
\]
converges almost surely in $L^{\infty}(\mathcal{I})$ to a random continuous function $E(x)$. Moreover, for each $\lambda\geq 0$, we have the exponential moment bound
\begin{align}
  \E\big[\exp\big(\lambda \sup_{N\geq 0} \|E_{N,0}\|_{L^\infty(\cI)}\big) \big]<\infty\,,
\end{align}
which in particular implies 
\begin{align}
  \E \big[\exp(\lambda\|E\|_{L^\infty(\cI)})\big] < \infty \,.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.13687

[Theorem 131 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider a discrete ensemble satisfying Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}, \ref{Assumptions_basic}, \ref{Assumptions_offcrit}, \ref{Assumptions_analyticity} and the additional Assumption~\ref{Assumptions_extra}. For $h,h_1,h_2 \in [H]$, we set
\begin{equation}

\begin{split}
W_{2;h_1,h_2}^{[0]}(z_1,z_2) & = \mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2), \\
W_{1; h}^{[1]}(z) & = \Op_{h}\Bigg[\bigg(\frac{q^{+,[1]}_{g}}{s_g^{\circ}}\bigg)_{g = 1}^H\,;\,\boldsymbol{0}\Bigg](z_1), \\
W_{1;h}^{[2]}(z) & = \Op_{h}\Bigg[\bigg(\frac{1}{s_g^{\circ}}\Big\{q^{+,[2]}_{g} + q_g^{-,[1]} \big\langle\bth_g \cdot \boldsymbol{W}_{1}^{[1]}\big\rangle + \frac{q_g^+}{2}\big\langle\bth_g\cdot \boldsymbol{W}_{1}^{[1]}\big\rangle^{2} \\
& \qquad\qquad + \frac{q_g^+}{2} \big\langle \bth_g(\bth_g - 1)\cdot \partial \boldsymbol{W}_{1}^{[1]}\big\rangle
+ \frac{q_g^+}{2} \big\langle \bth_g^{\otimes 2}\cdot \boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}}_{\bullet,\bullet}(*,*) \big\rangle \Big\}\bigg)_{g =
1}^H;\, \boldsymbol{0}\Bigg](z).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where $z \in \amsmathbb{M}_{h}$ and $z_i \in \amsmathbb{M}_{h_i}$ for $i \in \{1,2\}$.

Then, for any $\eps >0$ and compact sets $\amsmathbb{K}_h \subset \amsmathbb C\setminus [\hat a^{\mathfrak m}_h,\hat b^{\mathfrak m}_h]$ indexed by $h \in [H]$, there exist a sequence of positive constants $(C_n)_{n \geq 1}$ depending only $\eps$, the compacts, and the constants in the assumptions, such that for any $n \in \amsmathbb{Z}_{> 0}$, $h_1,\ldots,h_n \in [H]$ and $z_i \in \amsmathbb{K}_{h_i}$ for $i \in [n]$, we have
\begin{align}
 \big|W_{1;h}(z) - W_{1;h}^{[1]}(z) - \N^{-1}W_{1;h}^{[2]}(z) \big| & \leq C_1\,\N^{-\frac{3}{2} + \varepsilon}, \\
 \max_{ l = 1,2} \big|W_{1;h}^{[l]}(z)\big| & \leq C_1, \\
 \big|W_{2;h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2) - W_{2;h_1,h_2}^{[0]}(z_1,z_2)\big| & \leq
C_2\,\N^{-\frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon}, \\
 \big|W_{2;h_1,h_2}^{[0]}(z_1,z_2)\big| & \leq C_2
\end{align}
and for $n \geq 3$
\begin{equation}
 \big|W_{n;h_1,\ldots,h_n}(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\big| \leq C_n\,\N^{-\frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 131 of arXiv:2601.16377

$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be positive measures on M. One says that mu and nu are MUTUALLY SINGULAR, written mu perp nu, if there exists a set E in M with mu(E) = 0 and nu(X minus E) = 0; equivalently, X splits into two measurable pieces, one carrying all of nu and mu-null, the other carrying all of mu and nu-null. The relation is symmetric. For signed or complex measures the definition is applied to the total variations: mu perp nu means |mu| perp |nu|. Basic consequences: mu perp mu holds if and only if mu = 0; if nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu << mu) and nu perp mu, then nu = 0; if nu_1 perp mu and nu_2 perp mu then (nu_1 + nu_2) perp mu. CAUTIONS. (1) Mutual singularity is much stronger than 'nu is not absolutely continuous with respect to mu': a measure can fail to be absolutely continuous without being singular, and in general a measure splits into an absolutely continuous and a singular part (Lebesgue decomposition). (2) Singularity is a measure-theoretic, not a topological, smallness statement: the measure sum over n of 2^(-n) times the Dirac mass at the n-th rational is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure on R yet has full support, and the Cantor-Lebesgue measure is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure while being atomless. (3) The witness set E must be measurable; without that requirement the notion is vacuous or ill-posed. (4) Mutual singularity is not preserved by arbitrary uncountable sums of measures.
(X, M) is a measurable space
mu and nu are positive measures on M (for signed or complex measures the definition is applied to their total variations)
the separating set E is required to belong to M
title: Mutually singular measures

Let X,Y solve the synchronous Skorokhod equations in {|x|>=R}, R>0, with the same continuous driving path and inward-to-domain normal X/R or Y/R on the boundary. Write r=|X-Y| and let L_X,L_Y be their boundary regulators. Before r reaches zero, d log r = (1/(2R))(1-(|Y|^2-R^2)/r^2) dL_X + (1/(2R))(1-(|X|^2-R^2)/r^2) dL_Y. For reflected Brownian motions the same identity holds pathwise because the common Brownian increments cancel in X-Y. Thus coalescence at infinity is equivalent to this signed occupation functional tending to minus infinity. No sign or long-time behavior of that functional is proved here.

boundary regulators supported on |X|=R or |Y|=R

body: [Proposition prop:pilot of arXiv:2608.23638, 'Replicable Conformal Prediction'] Split a public pilot of $n_p=2m$ scores (disjoint from all calibration data): $\hat q_p$ is the conformal quantile of the first half, $N_W$ counts second-half scores in $W=[\hat q_p-h,\hat q_p+h]$ with $h\le\Delta/2$, and $\hat f_{\mathrm L}:=\max\{N_W,1\}/\big((1+c)\,2hm\big)$ for an accuracy $c\in(0,1)$. If $e_m(\delta_p/3)\le f_{\min}\Delta/2$ and $m\ge3\log(3/\delta_p)/(2c^{2}hf_{\min})$, then on a pilot event $\mathcal{G}_p$ of probability $\ge1-\delta_p$: $W\subseteq I$ and $\tfrac{1-c}{1+c}f_{\min}\le\hat f_{\mathrm L}\le f_{\max}$. Set $\beta:=2\hat\kappa B_n/(\hat f_{\mathrm L}\rho)$, $B_n$ as in Theorem~(thm:upper of the paper), with shared offset $u=\beta V$, $V\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1)$. For every pilot realization in $\mathcal{G}_p$, under Appendix~(app:upper of the paper)'s explicit side conditions ($\overline\beta_n\le\Delta/2$, tail $\le\rho/2$), two analysts satisfy $\mathbb{P}[\tau\ne\tau'\mid\mathcal{D}_p]\le\rho$; unconditionally $\mathbb{P}[\tau\ne\tau']\le\rho+\delta_p$, made exactly $\rho_\star$ by running the construction at $\rho_0=(\rho_\star-\delta_p)/(1-\delta_p)$ (for $0<\delta_p<\rho_\star$). Marginal coverage $\ge1-\alpha$ holds for \emph{every} pilot and offset realization, and the conditional band holds with rounding excess at most $\tfrac{2(1+c)}{1-c}\hat\kappa\kappa B_n/\rho$. A valid $\hat\kappa\ge\kappa$ remains the one input that cannot be certified from data, and $\hat\kappa=1.5$ was consistent with the target in every configuration of the safety study (Section~(sec:exp of the paper)). (Full statement and proof: Appendix~(app:upper of the paper).) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The free cumulants $\kappa_1,\kappa_2,\kappa_3,\ldots$ appear as a modification of the moments $M_1,M_2,M_3,\ldots\,$, and uniquely determine $\mu$. We have
$$\kappa_1=M_1$$
$$\kappa_2=-M_1^2+M_2$$
$$\kappa_3=2M_1^3-3M_1M_2+M_3$$
$$\kappa_4=-5M_1^4+10M_1^2M_2-2M_2^2-4M_1M_3+M_4$$
$$\vdots$$
in one sense, and in the other sense we have
$$M_1=\kappa_1$$
$$M_2=\kappa_1^2+\kappa_2$$
$$M_3=\kappa_1^3+3\kappa_1\kappa_2+\kappa_3$$
$$M_4=\kappa_1^4+6\kappa_1^2\kappa_2+2\kappa_2^2+4\kappa_1\kappa_3+\kappa_4$$
$$\vdots$$
with in both cases the correspondence being polynomial, with integer coefficients.

[Proposition 21 (The neutral face lies in the separatrix) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Let $(\Delta_{m-1},C)$ be a spectral duality structure and let
$\pi$ be supported on neutral sites, $\sigma(z)=z$ for every
$z\in\operatorname{supp}\pi$. Then
\[
C(\pi,\gamma)=C^\ast\qquad\text{for all }\gamma\in(0,1).
\]
In particular $C(e_{z_0},\cdot)\equiv C^\ast$ at every neutral
site $z_0$: the entire neutral face of the simplex is contained
in~$\Sigma$.

[Lemma 23 (Matrix exponential bounds) of arXiv:2605.24445, 'Matrix concentration inequalities for time-inhomogeneous Markov chains'] \label[lemma]{lem:exp_bounds}
For any \(H\in\mathbb{C}^{m \times m}\), \(\|e^H\|_{\op} \le e^{\|H\|_{\op}}\).
For any \(A,B\in\mathbb{C}^{m \times m}\),
\[
\|e^{A}-e^{B}\|_{\op}\le e^{\max\{\|A\|_{\op},\|B\|_{\op}\}}\ \|A-B\|_{\op}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\|e^{A}-e^{B}\|_{\mathrm F}\le e^{\max\{\|A\|_{\op},\|B\|_{\op}\}}\ \|A-B\|_{\mathrm F}.
\]

[Theorem backgeodlargedev of arXiv:2601.05361, 'Noise sensitivity in last-passage percolation'] For every $\delta \in (0, \frac{1}{2})$, there exist constants $c, C, r_0 >0$ such that for all $\lambda \in (\delta, 1-\delta)$, $r \geq r_0$ and all $s \in [0, r^{1/3}]$
\[
{\mathbb{P}} \Big(\pi(\lambda; -\infty, 0)\cap H_{- \lfloor r \mathbf{u}_{\lambda} \rfloor}   \subseteq \big[ - \lfloor r \mathbf{u}_{\lambda} \rfloor - s r^{2/3} \mathbf{e}_1 , - \lfloor r \mathbf{u}_{\lambda} \rfloor + s r^{2/3} \mathbf{e}_1 \big]  \Big)
\geq 1 - C \exp(-c s^3).
\]

PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. Exact critical tanh two-input Gram chain: given current Gram [[q,c sqrt(qr)],[c sqrt(qr),r]], draw n iid centered Gaussian pairs (Ai,Bi) with that Gram and set Qnew=mean tanh(Ai)^2, Rnew=mean tanh(Bi)^2, Cnew=mean tanh(Ai)tanh(Bi). Write D=1-C/sqrt(QR), S=Q+R, V=Q^2+R^2, F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2, and delta=1-E[tanh(Ai)tanh(Bi)]/sqrt(F(q)F(r)). Probability norms and expectations are over the exact chain.  Initialize Q0=R0=s in (0,1], c0 in [-1,1], D0=1-c0; H_L=sum_(j=1)^L 1/j. Let K,Lambda be the finite uniform C010/C015 raw angular moment constants: conditional absolute bias <=K delta/n, raw squared error <=K delta^2/n, raw fourth error <=Lambda^4 delta^4/n^2. Put M=12K+3Lambda^4 and B_T=8650752 s exp(210+(639/2)T). For integer n>=27648 and L<=Tn, ||D_L exp(96 S_L)||_2 <=exp(192+MT/4) D0[1+61 B_T L H_L/n]. In particular for fixed 0<eps<1 and L<=n^(1-eps), this is at most C_eps D0, where Bstar=8650752 exp(1059/2) and C_eps=exp(192+M/4)[1+61 Bstar(1+1/(e eps))]. This is an amplitude estimate, not an angular approximation-error or complete Tensor Programs rate.
Fresh iid Gaussian rows and layers; zero bias, variance1/n, exactly tanh; deterministic equal initial variances s<=1. Uses C010,C011,C014,C015 v1 unaudited, plus audited C002 v2 and C004 v1. Universal K,Lambda are the current-state bias/MSE/fourth-noise constants.
Only C002 v2 and C004 v1 among these inputs have reviewer PASS; new dependencies remain unaudited.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:6d4f3b75a6d73553539e29d35baef5f7f3c0d532bb6839c6530919e0fcb82e19","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/6d/6d4f3b75a6d73553539e29d35baef5f7f3c0d532bb6839c6530919e0fcb82e19.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:42bd0e2f7a01df611b6326a10dbc750466d99342d5d46b7c00409a28757f9ee0","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_unstopped_angular_amplitude","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c017-c018-unstopped-angular-energy","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Tensor Programs and stochastic Gram propagation","draft":"w712/bundle_013.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:critical-tanh-unstopped-angular-amplitude","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C017 v1: unstopped angular-gap amplitude by exponential variance weighting

Kind: moved. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified.
This controls the angular gap itself without stopping. It does not yet
estimate its error relative to the deterministic GP gap, remove C016's
particular stopping indicator, or prove the full readout rate.

## Statement and inputs

Use the exact zero-bias critical tanh two-input Gram chain. Its deterministic
initial state is Q_0=R_0=s in (0,1], C_0=s c_0 with -1<=c_0<=1.
Conditional on the completed past F_l, draw n iid centered Gaussian pairs
(A_i,B_i) with covariance [[Q_l,C_l],[C_l,R_l]], and update the Gram
by averaging tanh(A_i)^2, tanh(B_i)^2 and tanh(A_i)tanh(B_i).
Let c_l=C_l/sqrt(Q_l R_l), D_l=1-c_l, e_l=Q_l-R_l,
S_l=Q_l+R_l, V_l=Q_l^2+R_l^2, and H_l=sum_(j=1)^l 1/j, H_0=0.
Marginal variances are positive almost surely at finite depth and at most 1.

Use the universal constants K,Lambda of C010 v1 and C015 v1. At each
current state, if delta_l is the population postactivation angular gap,
these give

    |E[D_(l+1)|F_l]-delta_l|<=K delta_l/n,
    E[(D_(l+1)-delta_l)^2|F_l]<=K delta_l^2/n,
    E[(D_(l+1)-delta_l)^4|F_l]<=Lambda^4 delta_l^4/n^2. (1)

Define M=12K+3Lambda^4 and, for T>0,

    B_T=8650752 s exp[210+(639/2)T].

This B_T is exactly the constant in C014 v1's radial bound

    (E e_l^4)^(1/2)<=B_T D_0 H_l/n, 0<=l<=Tn.       (2)

Claims C010, C011, C014 and C015 are explicitly unaudited dependencies;
the scalar contraction and angular derivative estimates from C002/C004
have exact-version reviewer PASS. We use these claims as inputs, not as
newly re-proved results.

For every integer n>=27648 and 0<=L<=Tn,

    ||D_L exp(96 S_L)||_2
       <=exp(192+MT/4) D_0 [1+61 B_T L H_L/n].       (3)

In particular ||D_L||_2 is bounded by the same right side, with no
stopping event. For every 0<eps<1, uniformly over integers
1<=L<=n^(1-eps), this is at most C_eps D_0, where one explicit choice is

    B*=8650752 exp(1059/2),
    C_eps=exp(192+M/4)[1+61 B* (1+1/(exp(1)eps))].   (4)

The constants are finite and deliberately conservative; no numerical
evaluation or claimed sharpness is involved. D_0=0 is the exactly
coincident-input case and all gaps are then zero.

## 1. A raw conditional fourth moment close to its population value

Fix the completed past and write delta=delta_l, epsilon=D_(l+1)-delta.
Conditional Cauchy-Schwarz and (1) give
|E epsilon^3|<=sqrt(K)Lambda^2 delta^3/n^(3/2).
Expand (delta+epsilon)^4 about delta, retaining the possibly nonzero
first moment of epsilon. Since delta>=0,

    E[D_(l+1)^4|F_l]
      <=delta^4[1+10K/n+4sqrt(K)Lambda^2/n^(3/2)+Lambda^4/n^2]
      <=delta^4(1+M/n).                              (5)

For the second inequality use n>=1 and
4sqrt(K)Lambda^2<=2K+2Lambda^4. The case delta=0 follows directly
from (1), without dividing by delta.

## 2. Conditional exponential drift of the sum of marginal variances

Fix current values q,r and let V=q^2+r^2, S=q+r. A row contributes
Y=tanh(A)^2+tanh(B)^2 to S_(l+1). It lies in [0,2]. Its centered
version X lies in [-2,2], and

    Var(Y)<=2Var(tanh(A)^2)+2Var(tanh(B)^2)<=6V.

The last inequality uses tanh(t)^2<=t^2 and Gaussian fourth moments.
It does not assume A and B independent. For |z|<=1, the exponential
series gives exp(z)<=1+z+z^2. Therefore, if 4a/n<=1,

    E exp[(2a/n)X] <= exp[(2a/n)^2 Var(Y)].

Only now use independence of the n fresh rows to multiply their mgfs:

    E[exp(2a S_(l+1))|F_l]
      <=exp[2a(F(q)+F(r))+24a^2 V/n],

where F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2. Audited C002 gives
F(q)+F(r)<=S-V/6. Taking the square root of the preceding expectation
and imposing n>=144a gives

    (E[exp(2a S_(l+1))|F_l])^(1/2)
       <=exp[a S-(a/6-12a^2/n)V]
       <=exp[a S-aV/12].                            (6)

This width assumption also implies 4a/n<=1. The conditional moment
calculation allows arbitrary within-row correlation and arbitrary
dependence between the two marginal chains.

## 3. Population angular amplification and radial immigration

Let H(q,r,c) be the population correlation of the normalized tanh
features, so delta=1-H(q,r,c). The angular derivative bound of C004 is
0<=partial_c H(q,r,c)<=1+8(q^2+r^2). At c=1, C011 v1's comparison
with the equal-variance state (s=q there) gives

    0<=1-H(q,r,1)<=(121/2)(q-r)^2<=61(q-r)^2.

Integrate the angular derivative from c to 1 to obtain

    delta_l<=(1+8V_l)D_l+61e_l^2.                   (7)

This uses the comparison at c=1: its term proportional to 1-c is zero.
An absolute parameter bound at general c would introduce an unnecessary
linear-in-|q-r| angular amplification and is not used.

## 4. The exponential weight absorbs amplification

Set a=192 and rho=(1+M/n)^(1/4). Conditional Cauchy-Schwarz, (5), and
(6) give

    E[D_(l+1)^2 exp(a S_(l+1))|F_l]
      <=rho^2 delta_l^2 exp[a S_l-aV_l/12].           (8)

No factorization between D_(l+1) and S_(l+1) is made. Write
u_l=||D_l exp(a S_l/2)||_2. Take expectations in (8), then take square
roots and apply the L2 triangle inequality to (7):

    u_(l+1)
      <=rho ||exp(aS_l/2-aV_l/24)(1+8V_l)D_l||_2
           +61rho ||exp(aS_l/2-aV_l/24)e_l^2||_2
      <=rho u_l+61rho exp(192)(E e_l^4)^(1/2).       (9)

Indeed a/24=8, exp(-8V)(1+8V)<=1 for V>=0, and S_l<=2.
Thus the weight absorbs the random angular multiplier before any
unconditional expectation is estimated. In particular, this argument
does not raise the radial input from a fourth to an eighth moment.

Initially u_0=D_0 exp(192s)<=exp(192)D_0. Iterating (9), with rho>=1,

    u_L<=rho^L exp(192)[D_0+61sum_(l<L)(E e_l^4)^(1/2)]
       <=exp(192+MT/4)D_0[1+(61 B_T/n)sum_(l<L)H_l],

because rho^L<=exp(ML/(4n))<=exp(MT/4). Finally
sum_(l<L)H_l<=L H_L. This proves (3), including L=0.

## 5. Mesoscopic uniformity and scope

For L>=1, H_L<=1+log L. If L<=n^(1-eps),

    L H_L/n <=n^(-eps)(1+log n)<=1+1/(exp(1)eps).

For the last step set x=log n>=0 and use
x exp(-eps x)<=1/(exp(1)eps). Take T=1 in (3) and use
B_1<=B* (since s<=1). This proves (4).

The estimate is about the absolute angular-gap amplitude relative to
its initial value, not the error D_L-Dbar_L. It does not give an exit
probability for C016's inverse-product normalization. The next route is
to apply the same exponential drift to the squared angular error while
retaining conditional centering of the sampling innovation under the
weight. Bias and deterministic-GP radial forcing must also be included.
Neither that centered-error argument nor a full GP readout coupling is
claimed here.

dependence handling, not independent review. No Lean certificate is
claimed. Sources: C002 v2 scalar contraction; C004 v1 angular derivative;
C010 v1 equation(1); C011 v1 population radial comparison at c=1;
C014 v1 equations(1)-(4); C015 v1 equation(1).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:dbd8a6c5a827add2c3289bada6bf9e734985d00fd855f40cd24f9a9e38084111","revision_digest":"sha256:796afde54fb639cf03081399b72baf7b625b84ebf4285be1c4549f212b07c690","source_id":"own-work:T250-w712-C017-v1","source_revision":"T250-w712-C017-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

CURRENT AUDIT STATUS: independently checked proof, T336-w727-C003 v1; urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28 PASS in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Exact proof SHA256 871d621cbc24aaa88e57770194527ceb78d17debf276473333b5cce6d7414821. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed. The following original submission text retains historical pre-audit status notices.

A rank-one bounded PSD kernel on [-1,1], k(x,xprime)=1{x>=0}1{xprime>=0}, with observation noise variance 1, prevents every continuous raw-input Gaussian predictor from achieving uniform forward KL below log(9/8)/4 > 1/36. An empty context, or one observation (-1,0), yields predictive variances 1 left of zero and 2 at zero. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C003 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Raw-input obstruction for Target 1

Claim T336-w727-C003 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a scope obstruction to the literal bounded-kernel raw-input statement; it does not contradict C002's supplied-feature theorem. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed.

## Statement

There is a rank-one bounded positive-semidefinite kernel on the compact raw-input domain [-1,1], observation-noise variance s=1, and bounded context labels, such that every predictor with continuous Gaussian output parameters (mu(x),v(x)), v(x)>0, has worst-case noisy predictive forward KL at least

    c0=(1/4) log(9/8)>1/36.

The conclusion applies in particular to every finite transformer whose raw-input encoding and subsequent operations are continuous and whose output is a Gaussian with positive continuous variance. It applies to normalized ReLU attention and softmax attention under these conditions. Therefore boundedness, compactness, finite rank, and positive observation noise alone cannot imply the raw-input version of Target 1 for arbitrarily small eps.

## Kernel and posterior

Define phi(x)=0 for x<0 and phi(x)=1 for x>=0. Set k(x,x')=phi(x)phi(x'). For any finite coefficients a_i,

    sum_{i,j} a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)=(sum_i a_i phi(x_i))^2>=0.

Thus k is positive semidefinite, bounded by 1, and of rank exactly one (because k(0,0)=1). The GP can be represented as f(x)=Z phi(x), with Z~N(0,1). Observations add independent N(0,1) noise.

Use the empty context if allowed. Alternatively, for any n>=1 use one observation at x=-1 with label y=0, which satisfies every B>=0. This observation is pure noise independent of Z, so the posterior law of Z remains N(0,1). For either context, the new noisy predictive distribution is

    P_x=N(0,1) for x<0; P_x=N(0,2) for x>=0.

Hence the example does not rely on whether a context of length zero is included.

## Continuity forces two incompatible approximation requirements

Fix this context and any continuous output mu(x),v(x)>0. Let E=sup_x KL(P_x || N(mu(x),v(x))). If E is infinite the bound is immediate. Otherwise put mu0=mu(0),v0=v(0)>0. At x=0,

    D_2:=KL(N(0,2)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

Take x_j=-1/j tending to zero from below. Since mu,v are continuous and v0>0, the explicit Gaussian KL formula is continuous along this sequence; all denominators remain positive near the limit. Therefore

    D_1:=KL(N(0,1)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

No dominated convergence, probabilistic conditioning argument, or exchange of a supremum with a limit is used: every term in this deterministic convergent sequence is <=E.

For a>0 define

    D_a=(1/2)(log(v0/a)+(a+mu0^2)/v0-1).

Writing w=3/(2v0)>0 and combining logarithms gives the exact identity

    (D_1+D_2)/2
      = (1/4)log(9/8)+(1/2)(w-1-log w)+mu0^2/(2v0).

The inequality log w<=w-1 follows by integrating 1/t from 1 to w, separately for w>=1 and 0<w<=1, or by differentiating w-1-log w. Both additional terms are nonnegative. Consequently

    E >= (D_1+D_2)/2 >= (1/4)log(9/8).

Finally log(9/8)=integral_1^{9/8} dt/t > (1/8)(8/9)=1/9, since 1/t>8/9 except at the right endpoint. Thus c0>1/36. Every denominator and logarithm argument above is strictly positive.

## Interpretation for the dossier

C002 supplies phi as an input, so its input encoding itself is discontinuous as a function of raw x in this example; the continuity hypothesis here then fails. There is no contradiction. To close Target 1, the architecture must explicitly permit the fixed feature map in the input representation, or the theorem must add assumptions that make raw-input feature computation possible and account for its cost. Merely calling the kernel finite rank does not settle this issue.

The example is an obstruction to a named target interpretation, not a claimed solution of the entire T336 problem. The remaining feature-input theorem C002 and this obstruction both await independent review.
Raw-input mean and positive variance are continuous
Kernel continuity is not assumed in the literal target
A new noisy observation is predicted

(a) If $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ and $\hat f(n)=0$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$, then $f=0$ almost everywhere. (b) If $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ and $\hat f(\xi)=0$ for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$, then $f=0$ almost everywhere. (c) If $\mu$ is a finite complex Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$ (or on $\mathbb T$) whose Fourier-Stieltjes transform $\hat\mu(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}d\mu(x)$ vanishes identically (on $\mathbb Z$ for $\mathbb T$), then $\mu=0$; in particular a probability measure is determined by its characteristic function. Equivalently, two $L^1$ functions with the same transform agree a.e. Consequence: if $f\in L^1$ and $\hat f\in L^1$, then $f$ agrees a.e. with the continuous function $\int\hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}d\xi$.

(b): f integrable on R^d
(c): mu a finite complex Borel measure

[Theo eq:limTh-intro-height of arXiv:2607.01877, 'Coupling some conditioned L\'evy trees with the Kesten tree'] We assume the infinite variation setting and the Grey condition. 
The (sub-)critical Lévy tree ${\mathcal T}$ conditioned under the excursion measure to have height $h$, say ${\mathcal T}^{\mathbf{\mathrm{height}}}_h$, with its only vertex $X_h$ at distance $h$ from the root ${\varrho}$, is distributed as $({\mathcal K}^{\mathbf{\mathrm{height}}}_h,h)$:
\[
({\mathcal T}^{\mathbf{\mathrm{height}}}_h, X_h)
   \, \overset{\text{(d)}}{=} \,
   ({\mathcal K}^{\mathbf{\mathrm{height}}}_h,h).
\]
Furthermore 
 the ``increasing'' sequence $({\mathcal K}^{\mathbf{\mathrm{height}}}_h)_{h\ge 0}$  converges  to the Kesten tree ${\mathcal K}$ in $({\mathbb T}, {d_\mathrm {LGH}})$. In particular, we have the following  local   convergence in distribution:
 \begin{equation}
   
      {\mathcal T}^{\mathbf{\mathrm{height}}}_h  \xrightarrow[h\rightarrow
   +\infty]{\text{(d)}}
      {\mathcal K}
     \quad\text{in}\quad

That is, p ∩Nκ(γ 1 3 [a,b], c) ̸= ∅.
title: Definition 1.2 of arXiv:2603.24423: First passage percolation preserves sublinearly Morse boundaries

	\[
	\mathbf{u}_j=e^{\varphi_j}(u_j^\sharp+u_j^\flat),
	\]
	
	with 
	
	\[
	\varphi_j(t,x)=i|\nu|^2t+\nu_j\cdot x,
	\] 
	
	\[
u_j^\sharp(t,x)=[e^{it\Delta'}\check {f_j}](Q_je_1\cdot x,\ldots, Q_je_{n-1}\cdot x),
        \]
        
and $u_j^\flat$ as constructed in subsection (sect: CGO of the paper). Here $Q_j\in O(n)$ is a rotation such that $Q_je_n=\nu_j/|\nu_j|$.

\begin{equation}
\left|\int_{\Sigma} (V_1-V_2)u^\sharp_1\overline{u^\sharp_2}\right| \leq C \left(\mathrm{dist}_{\delta,\varepsilon}(\mathcal{U}_T^1, \mathcal{U}_T^2)e^{2\varepsilon s^{(1+\varepsilon)/\varepsilon}}+s^{-1/2}\right)\|f_1\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})} \|f_2\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})}.
\end{equation}

[Corollary cor:parking_constant of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] For the parking constant $\xi(a,b)= \lambda(a,b)(a+b)/2$, it follows that
\begin{equation}
    \xi(a,b)
    =
    \frac{1+\frac{b}{a}}{4} \int_0^\infty \bigg(2+e^{-t\cdot \frac{b}{a}}-e^{-t}\bigg)\exp \bigg( \int_0^t \mleft(-2+e^{-s(1+\frac{b}{a})/2}+e^{-s}\mright) \frac{\,\mathrm{d} s}{s}\bigg) \,\mathrm{d} t
    =
    \xi\big(1,\tfrac{b}{a}\big).
\end{equation} Thus, we may without loss of generality assume that $a=1$ and $b \in [0,1]$ when working with $\xi(a,b)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 17 (Inversion of the surrogate objectives) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Regard both distortions as functionals of the transformed energy vector $v$ at
fixed $E=\sum_k v_k$, the shared-scale one on a \emph{uniform} grid.
\begin{itemize}
\item The \textbf{allocation-flexible} coding surrogate (\Cref{sec:classical})
$D_{\mathrm{vr}}(v)\propto(\prod_k v_k)^{1/d}$ is the geometric mean, the form the
variable-rate distortion takes while every coordinate draws positive rate
(\Cref{prop:schur}(i); once the water level of \Cref{prop:waterfill} rises above a
coordinate's energy the true distortion is floored by the un-coded coordinates' energy,
so the vanishing limit below is an idealization of the surrogate). It is strictly
Schur-\emph{concave} wherever all coordinates are positive and identically zero elsewhere; it decreases under majorization, so it is driven down by
\emph{concentration}, the direction in which the KLT moves the profile, reaching the
majorization-maximal \emph{reachable} one, the spectrum (\Cref{thm:klt}).
\item The \textbf{shared-scale AbsMax} surrogate (\Cref{sec:inv-flatness})
$D_{\mathrm{fr}}(v)=\sum_g\max_{k\in g}v_k$ obeys the max-vs-mean bound of
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii), so among all $v$ of fixed sum it is minimized at the
\emph{flat} $v$, the direction in which incoherence processing and the Hadamard move the
profile (\Cref{prop:rht}), and maximized under within-group concentration.
\end{itemize}
Over all $v$ of fixed total energy, then, the two surrogates are driven apart. The
geometric mean is strictly Schur-concave on the positive orthant, so every majorization
step toward concentration strictly lowers $D_{\mathrm{vr}}$ while every coordinate remains
positive, and it is maximized at the flat $v$;
while $E/G\le D_{\mathrm{fr}}\le E$, the lower bound attained exactly when every group
is internally uniform and the upper bound when each group's mass sits on a single
coordinate. Concentrating energy \emph{within} a group therefore strictly lowers the first whenever every coordinate remains positive, and never lowers the second, strictly raising it as soon as the group maximum rises; flattening within groups does the reverse. Along no \emph{within-group} step of the order do the two objectives move the same way.

[Theorem 57 ({\cite[Theorem 4) of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] {gotze_bounds_2008}}]

    Let $n,d \in \N$ and $p > 2$. Let $(D_j)_{1 \leq j \leq n}$ be independent $\R^d$ valued random variables. We suppose that there exists $\lambda,\Lambda >0$ such that the following holds for all $1 \leq j \leq n$:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\E D_j =0$.
        \item For all $v \in \R^d$, $\E (v \cdot D_j)^2 \geq \lambda |v|^2$.
        \item $\E |D_j|^p \leq \Lambda^{p/2}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then there exists $C(p,d, \Lambda/\lambda)>0$ and (on perhaps a larger probability space) mutually independent $\R^d$-valued Gaussian random variables $(Z_j)_{1 \leq j \leq n}$ (though \textit{not independent of the $D_j$}) so that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\E Z_j =0$,
        \item $\E Z_j \otimes Z_j = \E D_j \otimes D_j$,
    \end{enumerate}
    and we have the approximation bound
    \[\E\bigg[\sup_{1\leq k\leq n} \Big|\sum_{j=1}^k (D_j-Z_j)\Big|^p\bigg]^{1/p}\leq C \Lambda^{1/2} n^{1/p}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] Suppose $X\in \mathcal{H}$.
\begin{description}
  \item[\rm (i)]
 For any $\delta>0$,
$$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \V\big(|X|\ge \delta \sqrt{n\log\log n} \big)<\infty \;\; \Longleftrightarrow C_{\V}\left[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\right]<\infty.
$$
 \item[\rm (ii)]
   If $C_{\V}\left[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\right]<\infty$, then for any $\delta>0$ and $p>2$,
$$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\mbE\big[\big(|X|\wedge (\delta \sqrt{n\log\log n})\big)^p\big]}{(n\log\log n)^{p/2}}<\infty. $$
 \item[\rm (iii)] $C_{\V}\left[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\right]<\infty$, then for any $\delta>0$,
 $$ \mbE[X^2\wedge (2\delta n\log\log n)]=o(\log \log n) $$
 and $$ \breve{\mathbb E}[(|X|-\delta \sqrt{2  n\log\log n})^+]=o(\sqrt{\log\log n/n}).\;\;  $$
\end{description} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let N>=1 and d_0,...,d_N be positive integers, with d_j>=min(d_0,d_N) for 1<=j<N. Let Phi be a real d_N-by-d_0 matrix of full rank min(d_0,d_N). For real matrices W_j of size d_j-by-d_{j-1}, write P=W_N...W_1 and L(W_1,...,W_N)=||P-Phi||_F^2/2. All layers are updated simultaneously by W_j(t+1)=W_j(t)-eta grad_{W_j} L(W_1(t),...,W_N(t)). Assume c>0 and ||P(0)-Phi||_F<=sigma_min(Phi)-c, where sigma_min denotes the min(d_0,d_N)-th singular value. Put delta=c^2/(256 N^3 ||Phi||_F^{2(N-1)/N}). Assume ||W_{j+1}(0)^T W_{j+1}(0)-W_j(0) W_j(0)^T||_F<=delta for all 1<=j<N. Choose 0<eta<=c^{(4N-2)/N}/(6144 N^3 ||Phi||_F^{(6N-4)/N}). For every integer t>=0, ell(t)<=ell(0) exp(-eta c^{2(N-1)/N} t). Consequently, if ell(0)>0 and epsilon>0, any integer T>=max(0,ceil(log(ell(0)/epsilon)/(eta c^{2(N-1)/N}))) satisfies ell(T)<=epsilon. If ell(0)=0 the loss remains zero. This is a conditional deterministic convergence theorem: it does not assert that independently Gaussian-initialized layers satisfy both initialization conditions with high probability.
positive integer depth and layer dimensions; no hidden bottleneck
real full-rank target Phi
loss is one half squared Frobenius error of the end-to-end product (equivalently the whitened-data objective after dropping its constant)
positive deficiency margin c at initialization
adjacent-layer Gram imbalance at most delta=c^2/(256 N^3 ||Phi||_F^{2(N-1)/N})

body: [Lem hpcabc of arXiv:2412.09535, 'Local limit theorem for joint subgraph counts'] A necessary condition for $n$ to be $(p, \pm)$-HPC is that $\frac{1}{b}(h_\pm+a\binom{n}{2})$ is an integer and $b^8 \mid 2h_\pm(n-2)$. A sufficient condition for $n$ to be $(p, \pm)$-HPC is that $\frac{1}{b}(h_\pm+a\binom{n}{2})$ is an integer and $b^{12} \mid n-2$.
title: Lem hpcabc of arXiv:2412.09535

body:
Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); D0010-C003 v1; audits w668:PASS. For n>=3 and 0<=lambda<=1, the density f(x)=lambda*(n-1)*(1-x)^(n-2)+(1-lambda)*(2n-1)*(2n-2)*x*(1-x)^(2n-3) on [0,1] is unimodal, has mean 1/n, and is n-CM. It is the common-center mixture of Beta(1,n-1) and Beta(2,2n-2) simplex marginals. Its mode lies inside (0,1) when lambda<C/[C+(n-1)(n-2)], C=(2n-1)(2n-2); otherwise the density is nonincreasing. This is a special sufficient family; novelty is not asserted.
n integer >=3
lambda in [0,1]

Status: proof (unaudited). Known Dirichlet/Beta construction plus an elementary mixture calculation; novelty not asserted.

For n>=3 and 0<=lambda<=1, the density on [0,1]

 f_lambda(x)=lambda*(n-1)*(1-x)^(n-2)
       +(1-lambda)*(2n-1)*(2n-2)*x*(1-x)^(2n-3)

is continuous, unimodal, has mean 1/n, and is n-CM. When

 lambda < (2n-1)*(2n-2) / [(2n-1)*(2n-2)+(n-1)*(n-2)],

its mode is strictly inside (0,1), so it is not monotone (the mode is 1/(2n-2) when lambda=0). Otherwise it is nonincreasing. Thus it gives concrete extra sufficient structure in the D0010 boundary regime, without invoking the density-floor theorem.

1. Gamma/Dirichlet construction. For alpha>0 draw n independent positive variables G_i with density g^(alpha-1) exp(-g)/Gamma(alpha). Put T=sum G_i and Z_i=G_i/T. By changing coordinates from the G_i to (T,Z_1,...,Z_{n-1}), with Z_n=1-sum_{i<n}Z_i, the Jacobian is T^(n-1). The joint density becomes

 T^(n alpha-1) exp(-T) product_i Z_i^(alpha-1) / Gamma(alpha)^n.

Integration over T gives density Gamma(n alpha)/Gamma(alpha)^n times the product on the simplex. In particular the vector is invariant under coordinate permutations and sums to one, so the common marginal is n-CM with mean 1/n.

2. Marginal formula. Fix Z_1=x. On the remaining (n-2)-dimensional simplex write Z_i=(1-x)V_i for i>=2. The resulting power of (1-x) is (n-1)(alpha-1)+(n-2)=(n-1)alpha-1. Applying the normalization formula from Step 1 for n-1 coordinates gives marginal

 Gamma(n alpha)/[Gamma(alpha)Gamma((n-1)alpha)]
          * x^(alpha-1)*(1-x)^((n-1)alpha-1).

For alpha=1 this is (n-1)(1-x)^(n-2). For alpha=2 it is (2n-1)(2n-2)x(1-x)^(2n-3). Each is n-CM, has total mass one and mean 1/n, since its coupling sums to one and has identical marginals.

3. Choose an independent Bernoulli label, selecting the alpha=1 vector with probability lambda and the alpha=2 vector otherwise. Every outcome still has sum one, and each marginal has f_lambda. Thus f_lambda is n-CM and has boundary mean 1/n.

4. Unimodality. For x in (0,1), divide the derivative by the positive factor (1-x)^(n-3), and put C=(2n-1)(2n-2). Its sign is the sign of

 D(x)= -lambda*(n-1)*(n-2)
       +(1-lambda)*C*(1-x)^(n-1)*(1-(2n-2)x).

On [0,1/(2n-2)] the second factor R(x) is strictly decreasing, because

 R'(x)=(n-1)*(1-x)^(n-2)*(-3+2n*x)<0

there for n>=3. Beyond that interval R(x) is nonpositive, so D(x)<=0. For lambda below the threshold, D(0)>0 and D(1/(2n-2))<=0, with a unique crossing in the open interval (including lambda=0, where the crossing is at the endpoint 1/(2n-2), see correction immediately below). For lambda at or above the threshold, D(0)<=0 and the density is nonincreasing.

Endpoint clarification: for lambda=0 the mode is exactly 1/(2n-2). Accordingly the precise interior-mode statement is: when 0<lambda<threshold the mode is in (0,1/(2n-2)); when lambda=0 the mode is at 1/(2n-2). All below-threshold cases have a mode strictly inside (0,1).

The construction is sufficient for this explicit family, not a necessary condition for general unimodal laws. [Prop 11 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] Given two
floors $H_-,H'_-:D\mapsto \mathbb R$ with $ H_-\le H'_-$, two ceilings $H_+,H'_+:D\mapsto \mathbb R$ with $H_+\le H'_+$ and two
initial conditions $\eta_0,\eta'_0\in\Omega_D$ satisfying $ \eta_0\le \eta'_0$, ${\eta_0}\in\Omega_{H_\pm}, {\eta'_0}\in\Omega_{H'_\pm}$, the Glauber  dynamic $\eta_t$ in $D$ constrained between $H_\pm$ and the dynamic $\eta'_t$ constrained between $H'_\pm$
can be coupled in such a way that $\eta_t\le \eta_t'$ for all times $t$, with probability $1$.
{In particular, it holds that $\pi_{H_\pm}\preceq \pi_{H'_\pm}$}.

[Theorem te:protection of arXiv:2606.15339, 'Uniform integrability of the distance to the nearest leaf in random trees'] Let $v_n$ be a uniformly chosen vertex of $\mathcal{T}_n$. As $n\to\infty$ along those $n$
for which $\mathcal{T}_n$ is defined,
\[
\partial_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathcal{T}_n,v_n) \xrightarrow{d} \partial(\mathcal{T}),
\qquad
\mathbf{E}\bigl[\partial_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathcal{T}_n,v_n)^p\bigr] \to \mathbf{E}\bigl[\partial(\mathcal{T})^p\bigr]
\quad(p\ge 1),
\]
where $\mathcal{T}$ is a Bienaym\'e--Galton--Watson tree with a specific offspring distribution $\xi$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Protection number of a random vertex

body:
[Proposition Prop:finite-horizon-lower-bound of arXiv:2608.19643, 'Time-Uniform Self-Normalized Concentration for Discounted Least Squares: Limits and Correc'] Consider the same scalar Gaussian process as in (Eq:counterexample-recursion of the paper). Fix \(T\geq1\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\). Let \(C_T(\delta)\) be any deterministic boundary satisfying
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\max_{1\leq t\leq T}
\frac{\lvert S_t^\gamma\rvert}{\sqrt{\widetilde V_t^\gamma}}
\leq C_T(\delta)
\right)\geq1-\delta .
\]
Then
\[
C_T(\delta)
\geq
\frac{R}{(1+\gamma)\sqrt{\lambda+(1-\gamma^2)^{-1}}}
\,
\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{1+(1-\delta)^{1/T}}{2}\right),
\]
where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. In particular, for fixed \(\gamma\) and \(\lambda\), there are positive constants \(c_{\gamma,\lambda}\) and \(x_0\) such that, for \(\delta\in(0,1/2]\) and \(T/\delta\geq x_0\),
\[
C_T(\delta)\geq c_{\gamma,\lambda}R\sqrt{\log\frac{T}{\delta}}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Finite-horizon lower bound

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03924, 'Beyond normal fluctuations in local laws for Wigner matrices'] We identify non-Gaussian corrections to the central limit theorem for the global and local laws, i.e. for Stieltjes transform of the empirical eigenvalue distribution of a large real symmetric or complex Hermitian Wigner matrix. We find that in the real case the rate of convergence in this CLT is substantially slower than in the complex case. For the proofs, we develop new static and dynamic hierarchies of extended cumulants up to any order that can be analysed by a refinement of the zigzag strategy.

body: A non-degenerate distribution function G is called max-stable (or an extreme value distribution) if for every integer n \ge 2, there exist constants a_n > 0 and b_n \in \mathbb{R} such that G(x)^n = G(a_n x + b_n) for all x \in \mathbb{R}. That is, the maximum of n i.i.d. random variables with distribution G has the same distribution as G up to an affine rescaling.
title: Extreme Value (Max-Stable) Distribution

body: Ergodic theory is a branch of mathematics that studies statistical properties of deterministic dynamical systems; it is the study of ergodicity. In this context, "statistical properties" refers to properties which are expressed through the behavior of time averages of various functions along trajectories of dynamical systems. The notion of deterministic dynamical systems assumes that the equations determining the dynamics do not contain any random perturbations, noise, etc. Thus, the statistics with which we are concerned are properties of the dynamics.
title: Ergodic theory

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2606.09121, 'Truncated Signature Information for Mixed Fractional Brownian Paths'] Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K$ be distinct real numbers and let $a_r,b_r\in\mathbb R$.  If
\[
    f(x)=\sum_{r=1}^K(a_r+b_rx)e^{\alpha_rx}
\]
is not identically zero, then $f$ has at most $2K-1$ real zeros counted with multiplicity.

[Thm 7 ($L^1$-stability and uniqueness) of arXiv:2607.28238, 'Well-posedness and large deviations for the obstacle problem of first-order stochastic con'] Let \textbf{Hypotheses (H1) and (H2)$'$} hold.
Let $(u_1,\nu_1)$ and $(u_2,\nu_2)$ be two kinetic solutions of the lower obstacle problem for \eqref{eq:intro-reflected-model} in the sense of Definition \ref{def:dfn-1},
with corresponding initial values satisfying
\[
u^0_{1},u^0_{2}\in L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^N),
\qquad
u^0_{i}\geq \psi(\cdot,0)\quad\text{a.e. on }\mathbb{T}^N.
\]
Then, for almost every $t\in[0,T]$,
\begin{equation}
\E\Vert u_1(t)-u_2(t)\Vert _{L^1(\mathbb{T}^N)}
\leq
\Vert u^0_{1}-u^0_{2}\Vert _{L^1(\mathbb{T}^N)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $u^0_{1}=u^0_{2}$ a.e. on $\mathbb{T}^N$, then
\[
u_1=u_2
\quad\text{in }L^1(\Omega\times\mathbb{T}^N\times[0,T]),
\]
and the reflection measures coincide:
\[
\nu_1=\nu_2
\quad\text{as Radon measures on }\mathbb{T}^N\times[0,T),
\quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Thus, the kinetic solution pair $(u,\nu)$ is unique.

$x \in [1, \infty)$ is convex.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked_criterion_controlled_against_the_papers_own_deterministic_benchmark] This is the broader partial answer reported for both cases of the open question in Remark 5.3(ii) of arXiv:2607.07410. Let V be a two-sided (r_0,alpha)-semi-selfsimilar Levy process with alpha in (0,2), whose value at time one has positive probability of each sign, and let nu be its Levy measure. For delta > 0 consider the two diffusion forms with reference densities exp(-|x|^delta - V(x)) and exp(|x|^delta - V(x)), each with energy (1/2) integral |f'|^2 times the corresponding density. The record claims noncompactness, with essential-spectrum bottom zero, for every delta, when nu has negative jumps in the first case or positive jumps in the second. The written quiet-window proof covers delta > 1; the paper's Proposition 5.2 covers 0 < delta <= 1/alpha. Together these give all delta when alpha <= 1, which includes alpha < 1, where nu must charge both half-lines. For alpha in (1,2) and 1/alpha < delta <= 1 the claim is not established by the written argument. For alpha > 1, delta > 1 and no negative jumps, the record also sketches compactness at the +infinity end of the first diffusion via the bound B_l(x) <= C^2 x^(2-2delta). Here B_l is the integral of the reciprocal density from a fixed positive x_0 to x times the integral of the density from x to infinity, and C is a finite path-dependent constant. The record explicitly leaves the uniform near-field estimate unwritten, so this converse is a sketch. Compactness at one end does not by itself establish compactness of the full two-sided operator. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The converse is explicitly a sketch, with a missing uniform estimate.

body: Cantor's diagonal argument is a mathematical proof that there are infinite sets which cannot be put into one-to-one correspondence with the infinite set of natural numbers – informally, that there are sets which in some sense contain more elements than there are positive integers. Such sets are now called uncountable sets, and the size of infinite sets is treated by the theory of cardinal numbers, which Cantor began.
title: Cantor's diagonal argument

[Corollary 13 (Bridge to the Gaussian-base factor of Dytso et al.) of arXiv:2606.18458, 'Stable size-biasing and the positive scale-mixture order of generalized Gaussian laws'] Let $0<r\le2$, and let $V_{G,r}$ denote the Gaussian-base factor of \citet{Dytso2018}, defined by
\[
X_r\stackrel{d}{=}V_{G,r}X_2,
\qquad
V_{G,r}>0,\qquad V_{G,r}\perp X_2 .
\]
Then
\[
V_{G,r}\stackrel{d}{=}V_{r,2},
\]
and
\[
V_{G,r}\ \text{is Stieltjes moment-determinate}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
r\ge \frac25 .
\]
Equivalently,
\[
V_{G,r}\ \text{is Stieltjes moment-indeterminate}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0<r<\frac25 .
\]
Thus \citet[Proposition~8]{Dytso2018} is recovered and sharpened: their sufficient condition $r\ge2/5$ is the exact Gaussian-base threshold.

body:
Let X be a compact metric space and T : X -> X a continuous surjection. T is TOPOLOGICALLY EXACT, also called locally eventually onto, if for every nonempty open set U there is an integer n >= 1 with T^n(U) = X. Two consequences are what proofs actually use. (a) UNIFORMITY IN n: if T^n(U) = X then T^m(U) = X for every m >= n, because T is onto; hence for each nonempty open U there is N with T^n(U) = X for ALL n >= N. (b) DENSE BACKWARD ORBITS WITH ALL LARGE PERIODS: for every x in X and every nonempty open U there is N with U intersect T^{-n}(x) nonempty for every n >= N; in particular the full backward orbit of any point is dense. Property (b) is a genuine aperiodicity statement that topological transitivity does not give and that even topological mixing of an invertible system cannot give. Relations: topological exactness implies topological mixing, which implies topological transitivity; the converses are false. An invertible map is never topologically exact unless X is a single point, since T^n(U) = X forces U = X for a homeomorphism, so exactness is a hypothesis reserved for genuinely non-invertible maps: expanding maps of the circle or of a compact manifold, one-sided mixing subshifts of finite type, and Chebyshev-like interval maps are the standard examples.
X is a compact metric space
T : X -> X is continuous and surjective
the definition quantifies over all nonempty OPEN subsets U
title: Topological exactness (locally eventually onto)

body:
[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Let $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}\in \R^d$ be i.i.d. random vectors such that $x_1=(x_{1j})_{1\leq j\leq d}$ has indpenedent coordinates satisfying
	\begin{equation}
		\E[x_{1j}]=0,\qquad \E \left[x_{1j}^2\right]=1,\qquad
		\E \left[x_{1j}^4\right]=\kappa,\qquad \sup_{j\le d}\|x_{1j}\|_{\psitwo}\le K_x,
	\end{equation}
    where $\kappa>1$ and $K_x>0$ do not depend on $n,d$. Let
	$n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d^2\to\alpha\in(0,\infty)$.  There is an explicit
	threshold $\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:alpha-star-def},
	which depends only on $\kappa$, such that the following holds.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
		\item If $\alpha<\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one, there exists an ellipsoid fitting all $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$:
		\[
		\exists R\succ 0,\quad\textnormal{such that}\quad x_i^{\top}R x_i=1\quad \textnormal{for all}\quad 1\leq i\leq n.
		\]
		Moreover, such $R\in \R^{d\times d}$ can be chosen to be well-conditioned: $\lambda_{\max}(R)/\lambda_{\min}(R)=O(1)$. 
		\item If $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one
		there is no $R\succeq0$ such that $x_i^\top R x_i=1$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$. Moreover, the optimal squared fitting error converges in probability:
		\begin{equation}
			\Gamma_X:=\inf_{R\succeq0, \operatorname{Tr}R=d}\,\inf_{r\geq 0}\,
			\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x_i^\top Rx_i}{\sqrt{d}}-r\right)^2
			\pto e_\star(\alpha,\kappa),
		\end{equation}
        where $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)$ is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:optimal-fitting-error-main}. For $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)>0$ holds, thus an approximate ellipsoid fitting is not possible with any $R\succeq 0$ with $\Tr R=d$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27372

[Lem measure_2arm of arXiv:2604.14122, 'The scaling limit of random walk and\\ the intrinsic metric on planar critical percolation'] Fix an annulus $A$ and $r>0$. For each $\delta > 0$, let $X_\delta$ be the set of points $x \in A^{\inn}$ such that there are two disjoint (open or closed) arms crossing $B(x,r)\setminus B(x,\delta)$. Then
    \[
    \lim_{\delta\searrow 0} \mathbf{E}[\mu^A(X_\delta)] = 0 .
    \]
    In particular, the set of points with two disjoint arms to distance $r$ has measure $0$ almost surely.
title: Lem measure_2arm of arXiv:2604.14122

Let K ⊂ ℝⁿ be nonempty and closed and let d(x) := dist(x, K) = min_{y ∈ K} |x − y| (the minimum is attained because K is closed). Then: (a) d is 1-Lipschitz, d ≥ 0, and d(x) = 0 exactly when x ∈ K. (b) [minimal-time / control representation] d(x) = inf { T ≥ 0 : there is an absolutely continuous ξ: [0,T] → ℝⁿ with |ξ'(s)| ≤ 1 for a.e. s, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K } = inf { ∫_0^T |ξ'(s)| ds : ξ absolutely continuous, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K, T ≥ 0 } — the distance is the value function of the minimal-time problem for the control system ξ' = α, |α| ≤ 1, with target K, and the straight segment from x to a nearest point of K is an optimal trajectory. (c) [variational characterization] d is the largest 1-Lipschitz function that is ≤ 0 on K: if u: ℝⁿ → ℝ is 1-Lipschitz and u ≤ 0 on K then u ≤ d everywhere, and d itself is admissible; equivalently d(x) = max { u(x) : u 1-Lipschitz, u ≤ 0 on K }. (d) [eikonal equation] d is a viscosity solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in the open set ℝⁿ \ K, and a viscosity subsolution of |Du| − 1 ≤ 0 on all of ℝⁿ. Sharp edges. (1) The sign convention matters: d solves |Du| − 1 = 0 but is in general NOT a viscosity solution of 1 − |Du| = 0 (for K = {−1, 1} ⊂ ℝ, d = 1 − |x| on (−1,1) has a concave kink at 0 which is admissible for the first form only). (2) Uniqueness of viscosity solutions of |Du| = 1 in ℝⁿ \ K vanishing on K FAILS without a sign or growth restriction: for K = {0}, the function u(x) = −|x| is a classical (hence viscosity) solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in ℝⁿ \ {0} with u(0) = 0, different from d(x) = |x|. The distance is singled out among solutions by (c), or by nonnegativity/boundedness-below conditions that this lemma does not assert. (3) For K not closed the minimum in the definition of d must be replaced by an infimum and d vanishes on the closure of K, not only on K.
K ⊂ ℝⁿ is nonempty and closed
the Euclidean norm is used (for the eikonal equation |Du| = 1 the ball of the same norm is the unit speed set)
the eikonal equation is taken in the form |Du| − 1 = 0

[Lem Steinhaus of arXiv:2602.22342, 'Sum of Gaussian vectors and large sets'] There is a $\delta>0$
such that for any dimension $n\geq 1$, for any closed set $A$ in $\R^n$ with $\gamma_n(A)\geq \frac{2}{3}$,   
$$B(0,\delta)\subset A+A$$
where $B(0,\delta)$ is the closed Euclidean ball of radius $\delta$ centered at $0$. In particular, given any $D>0$, there is an integer $p=O(D)$ such that
$$B(0,D)\subset A_{(p)}.$$

[Definition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] For a Banach couple $(E_0, E_1)$, denote by $\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)$ the class 
    of functions $F: \Bar{S} \to E_0 + E_1$ satisfying
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $F$ is continuous on $\Bar{S}$ and analytic on $S$
        \item $F(it) \in E_0$ and $F(1+it) \in E_1$ for all $t \in \mathds{R}$
        \item $\|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)} \coloneqq 
        \max \Big\{ \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(it)\|_{E_0}, \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(1+it)\|_{E_1}           \Big\} < \infty$ 
    \end{itemize}
    Then, for $0 \leq \theta \leq 1 $, the \textbf{complex interpolation space} $[E_0, E_1]_\theta$ is the 
    Banach space defined by
    \[
        [E_0, E_1]_\theta \coloneqq \{h \in E_0 + E_1: h = F(\theta) \ \ \text{for some} \ F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)\}
    \]
    equipped with the norm
    \[
        \|h\|_{[E_0, E_1]_\theta} \coloneqq \inf_{\substack{F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1) \\
        F(\theta) = h}} \|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)}
    \]
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'

[Defn defi_kin_sol of arXiv:2608.30548, 'Finite speed of propagation and waiting time phenomena for stochastic porous media equatio'] Let $u_0\in L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)$ be non-negative and assume  (equation equation_n_m_together of the paper)  and (equation Eq_ass_B1 of the paper)--(equation Eq_ass_B3 of the paper). Then, a kinetic solution to (equation Eq_SPME_intro of the paper) is a non-negative, continuous, $\mathscr{F}$-adapted, $L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)$-valued process $u\in L^1(\Omega \times [0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^d)$, such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
	\item mass is conserved, i.e., $\mathbb{P}$-a.s, we have  $\|u(t)\|_{L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)} = \|u_0\|_{L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)}$ for all $t\in [0,T]$,
	\item it holds $\sigma(u) \in L^2(\Omega \times [0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^d)$,
	\item  we have $((K\wedge u )\vee 1/K) \in  L^2(\Omega \times [0,T]; H^1(\mathbb{T}^d))$ for all $K\in \mathbb{N}$,
	\end{enumerate}  
and there exists  a kinetic measure $q$ with 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
	\setcounter{enumi}{3}
	\item $\mathbb{P}$-a.s, $m\delta(v - u)v^{m-1} |\nabla u|^2 \le q $ in the sense of measures on $\mathbb{T}^d \times (0,\infty) \times [0,T]$,
	\item  $q$ vanishes at infinity in the sense that $\lim_{M\to\infty} \mathbb{E} [ q(\mathbb{T}^d \times [M,M+1] \times [0,T])] = 0$,
	\item and for every $\psi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d\times (0,\infty ))$, it holds $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.\ 
	\begin{align}\begin{split}&\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}
		\mathbf{1}_{\{0<v <u(t,x)\}} \psi(x,v)
		\,\mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} v \,=\, \int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}
		\mathbf{1}_{\{0<v <u_0(x)\}} \psi(x,v)
		\,\mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} v\\&\qquad -\,m\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^d}
		u^{m-1}\nabla u \cdot (\nabla \psi )(x, u)
		\,
		\mathrm{d} x
		\mathrm{d} s\,-\, \frac{1}{2}\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\bigl[\Psi_1 (\sigma'(u))^2 \nabla u \,+\, \sigma'(u) \sigma(u)\Psi_2 \bigr] \cdot (\nabla \psi )(x, u) \,\mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} s
		\\&\qquad -\,\int_0^t  \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \partial_v \psi (x,v) \,\mathrm{d} q\,+\,\frac{1}{2}\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \bigl(
		\sigma(u)\sigma'(u)\nabla u \cdot \Psi_2 \,+\, \Psi_3 \sigma^2(u)\bigr) (\partial_v\psi)(x,u) 
		\,\mathrm{d} x
		\mathrm{d} s
		\\&\qquad - \sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^\infty \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \psi(x, u) \partial_i ( \psi_k \sigma (u)) \,\mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} \beta_k^{(i)}(s)		
		,
		\end{split}
	\end{align}
	for all $t\in [0,T]$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Kinetic solution to \eqref{Eq_SPME_intro}

[Lemma 67 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] For each $p \in (0,1)$ there exist $N \in \N$ and $\epsilon > 0$ such that the following is true. Let $D$ be a simply connected domain and $\varphi\colon \h \to D$ a conformal transformation. Let $j,k \in \N$ be such that $\abs{\varphi'(i)} \ge 2^{-j}$, and suppose that
 \[ \abs{\shortcutscales \cap \{j,\ldots,j+k\}} \ge N . \]
 Let $(\eta'_1,\eta'_2)$ be a bichordal \slekp{} in $(D,\varphi(0),\varphi(\infty))$, and given $(\eta'_1,\eta'_2)$, sample a \clekp{} and the internal metrics in the region between $\eta'_1,\eta'_2$. Let $G_{D,\varphi}$ be the event that there are $x,y \in \eta'_1 \cap \eta'_2$ with
 \[ 
 \frac{\rmet{x}{y}{\Gamma}}{\rmett{x}{y}{\Gamma}} \le \sqrt{c_1 c_2} 
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \rmet{x}{y}{\Gamma} \ge \epsilon\,\median[2^{-j-k}]{} .
 \]
 Then
 \[ \p[ G_{D,\varphi} ] \ge p . \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 67 of arXiv:2512.04807

Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p <= infinity. Then L^p(mu) is complete: every Cauchy sequence in the L^p norm converges in that norm to an element of L^p(mu), and a subsequence converges almost everywhere. In the Hilbert-space form: if (e_n) is an orthonormal sequence in L^2(mu) and (c_n) is a sequence of scalars, the series sum c_n e_n converges in L^2 if and only if sum |c_n|^2 < infinity, and when (e_n) is an orthonormal basis the map f |-> (<f, e_n>)_n is an isometric isomorphism of L^2(mu) onto l^2. For Fourier series on the circle this says that every square-summable coefficient sequence is the coefficient sequence of exactly one L^2 function.
(Omega, F, mu) any measure space (no sigma-finiteness needed)
1 <= p <= infinity
the Hilbert-space form: (e_n) orthonormal in L^2(mu), an orthonormal BASIS for the isomorphism statement

[Theorem 41 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Suppose $\g\in C^{2}(\us(R\e)), \z \in C^{4}(\us(R\e))$, $R\geq1$, and
\be
\left(R^2c_3(R)\frac{d}{\sqrt\la}\right)^2 + c_4(R)\frac{d^2}{\la}\leq \Clap.
\ee Then
$$
\frac{1}{\mathcal Z}\int_{\us(R\e)}\g(x)e^{-\la \z (x)}\dd x = \g(0_d)+ \Rem_1,
$$ where
\bs
|\Rem_1| \les_{\Clap} &\bigg\{c_{0,\g}(R)(c_3(0)^2+c_4(R))+d^{-1}c_{2,\g}(R) + d^{-1}c_{1,\g}(R)\big(c_3(0)+\frac{d}{\sqrt\la}c_4(R)\big)\bigg\}\frac{d^2}{\la} \\
&+ \left(|\g(0_d)|+ \frac{d}{\sqrt\la}c_{1,\g}(0)\right)e^{-(R-1)^2d/4}.
\es

UNREVIEWED DRAFT, not a solution of C0056. Real symmetric finite matrices with all eigenvector squared components and IPR equal to 1/N can have local measures converging to singular-continuous Cantor measure. With N=2^k and eta=N^-1/2, the diagonal smoothing contribution is 1/(2pi sqrt(N))->0, while the full second moment is at least N^((1-log(2)/log(3))/2)/(5pi)->infinity. The abstract counterexample refutes an IPR-only inference, not the Anderson conjecture.

[Definition 11 (Signature of tfBm) of arXiv:2512.04646, '\textbf{Canonical Rough Path over Tempered Fractional Brownian Motion: Existence, Construc'] The \emph{signature} of $\mathbf{B}_{H,\lambda}$ over $[s,t]$ is
the formal power series
\[
S(\mathbf{B}_{H,\lambda})_{s,t}
= \Bigl(1,\;B_{H,\lambda}(s,t),\;
  \mathbb{B}_{H,\lambda}(s,t),\;
  \mathbb{B}^{(3)}_{H,\lambda}(s,t),\ldots\Bigr)
\in T((\mathbb{R}^d)),
\]
where $T((\mathbb{R}^d))=\prod_{k=0}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)^{\otimes k}$
is the completed tensor algebra and $\mathbb{B}^{(k)}_{H,\lambda}$
denotes the $k$-th iterated integral, defined recursively by
Chen's relation.
title: Signature of tfBm

Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent identically distributed random variables with E X_1 = 0, E X_1^2 = sigma^2 > 0 and rho = E |X_1|^3 < infinity. Let F_n be the distribution function of (X_1 + ... + X_n) / (sigma sqrt(n)) and Phi the standard normal distribution function. Then sup_x |F_n(x) - Phi(x)| <= C rho / (sigma^3 sqrt(n)) for an absolute constant C. The constant satisfies 0.4097 < C <= 0.4748 (the upper bound from Shevtsova, 2011). A version for independent but non-identically distributed summands holds with the third-moment ratio sum E|X_i|^3 / (sum sigma_i^2)^{3/2} and a slightly larger constant.

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.30138, 'High-frequency wave propagation for the viscoelastic wave equation with singular memory'] For $k=0,1,\dots$, let $F\in C([0,T];H^k(\Omega))$, and
assume that \eqref{m-int-k} holds with $k+1$ in place of $k$. 
Then the Volterra equation 
\begin{equation}   
\Delta_{\sigma_\eps} u (t) -  \eps\nabla \cdot \int_0^t \mathfrak{m}(s,\cdot) \nabla u(t-s)\,\d s=F(t)
\end{equation}
has a unique solution $u\in C([0,T]; \, H^{k+2}(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega))$. Moreover, the norm of the solution operator $F\mapsto u$ is uniformly bounded in $\eps\in [0,\eps_0]$, for $\eps_0\ll1$ possibly depending on $m$.

body: [Definition of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] We say a point $m = (m_1, m_2)$ is a cut-point of $\Gamma$ if $m \in \Gamma$ and the intersection of $\Gamma$ and the vertical line $x = m_1$ is the point $m$. That is, $\gamma$ only crosses the line once, and so in particular no components of $\underline{{\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}}$ or finite regions $D_i$ cross the line.

[Proposition prop:q-refining-homeomorphism of arXiv:2604.05941, 'Banach spaces of continuous paths with finite $p$-th variation'] Let $q\ge2$ and let $\mathbb P=(\mathbb P^n)_{n\ge0}$ be a dense $q$-refining partition sequence. Then there exists a unique increasing homeomorphism $\phi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ such that
    \[
        \phi(t_i^n)=\frac{i}{q^n},\qquad i=0,\dots,q^n,\ \ n\ge0.
    \]
    Equivalently, $\mathbb P^n=\phi^{-1}(\mathbb{T}_q^n)$, for $n\ge0$.

body:
[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] For every \(n\in [1:\kappa+\zeta]\), let \(\ell=\lceil n/2\rceil\). Then the homogeneous components of the Schwinger--Dyson kernel satisfy
\begin{equation}
K_0(s,t)=1 +  \int_s^t  K_{1}(s,u) d\mathbf{X}_u du,
\qquad
K_n(s,t)
=
-\int_s^t \sigma_n\bigl(K_{\ell-1}(s, \cdot),K_{n-\ell}(\cdot, t)\bigr)_u\,d\mathbf X_u .
\end{equation}
Here, for every word \(I=i_1\cdots i_n\) over the alphabet \(\{1,\dots,d\}\), we set
\(
\tilde I:=i_1\cdots i_{\ell-1},\,
\hat I:=i_{\ell+1}\cdots i_n,
\)
and,given a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) of \(V\), define
\begin{align*}
&\sigma_n:
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(\ell-1)},\mathbb R\bigr)\boxtimes
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(n-\ell)},\mathbb R\bigr)
\to
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V,\mathrm{Hom}(V^{\otimes n},\mathbb R)\bigr),\\
&\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_I)
=
\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_{\tilde I}\otimes e_{i_\ell}\otimes e_{\hat I})
=
\eta(e_{\tilde I})\,\delta_{i_\ell j}\,\xi(e_{\hat I}),
\end{align*}
for every word \(I\) of length \(n\), and extend linearly on \(V^{\otimes n}\).

[Definition 10 of arXiv:2609.01020, '2609.01020'] Let $F$ be a sheaf of $\CC_X$-modules on $X$. 
Then we say that $F$ is (complex) constructible if there exists a (complex 
analytic) stratification 
$X=\bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A}X_\alpha$ of $X$ such that for any $\alpha \in A$ 
we have an isomprphism $F|_{X_\alpha}\simeq\CC_{X_\alpha}^{\oplus r_\alpha}$ 
locally on $X_\alpha$ for some $r_\alpha \geq 0$.

[Theorem thm:GP:restriction of arXiv:2605.28106, 'Gaussian Processes with Sample Paths in Reproducing Kernel Banach Spaces'] Let \( \xi : T \times \Omega \to \mathbb{R} \) be a centered Gaussian process, and suppose that there exists \( \Omega_0 \in \mathcal{A} \) with \( \mu(\Omega_0) = 1 \) such that \( \xi(\cdot,\omega) \in X \) for all \( \omega \in \Omega_0 \).
    Then the random element \( \eta : \Omega \to X \) defined by \( \xi \) is a centered Gaussian random element.

For arbitrary L/R words w in {L, R}^m and marked columns, the joint expectations of the height observables E[prod_{j=1}^k H(x_j, y_j)] under the doubly free-boundary Macdonald process are given by k-fold nested contour integrals of the form (1 / (2*pi*i)^k) * oint ... oint det[1 / (z_a - z_b)] * prod_{a=1}^k F_w(z_a; x_a, y_a) * prod_{a < b} S(z_a, z_b) dz_1 ... dz_k, where F_w contains the spectral rail-yard data and S(z_a, z_b) is the universal reflection kernel.
Contours enclose specified poles of F_w while excluding reflection poles

body:
[Lemma lem:vertical-concatenation of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Given a backbone-dangling shape $\tau$, its deviation vector $\eta_\tau = L(\tau) \in \mathbb{R}^m $, and $w_\tau = M^{-1} \eta_\tau$, write \[ 
\mathsf{correct}(\tau) \coloneqq \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \left( \mathcal{L}^*(w_\tau ) - \gamma \cdot \mathsf{M} _\tau  \right)=   \mathsf{Proper}(\eta_\tau) + \mathsf{Error}(\eta_\tau)\,,
 \]
 where $\mathsf{Proper}(\eta_\tau)$ is a weighted linear combination of proper backbone-dangling shapes,	
 and $\mathsf{Error}$ are the remaining terms. We have
 \[ 
 \mathrm{Var}( \mathsf{Proper}(\eta_\tau))  = \frac{1}{1-\gamma}\cdot \mathrm{Var}(\eta_\eta)+o_d(1)=  \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\cdot \mathrm{Var}(\tau) + o_d(1) 
 \]
 and
  \[
 \|\mathsf{ErrorShapes}\|_{sp} = o_d(1)\,.
  \]
We remind the reader that for a matrix $X$, we define its variance as $\mathrm{Var}(X)\coloneqq \frac{1}{\dim(X)} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\Tr(XX^\top)] $ and analogously for a vector. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Linearizing Deviation Attachment into Proper Shapes

body:
[Lemma 22 (Basic Properties of Wishart Matrices) of arXiv:2609.02790, 'Full-Model Optimality for Tunable Linear Generative Priors in Compressed Sensing'] If $W\sim \mathcal W_p(\Sigma,n)$, then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $W$ is almost surely symmetric positive semidefinite.
    \item $\mathbb{E}[W]=n\Sigma$.
    \item If $n\ge p$, then $W$ is almost surely invertible.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Basic Properties of Wishart Matrices
