[Proposition expvar of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let  $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$  be a {\em stationary} marked point process  
   on $\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{K}$ with non-null, finite intensity
     $\rho$.  Let $\xi : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \hat\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a translation invariant marking function.
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item  
Let $\xi$ be fast \textnormal{BL}-localizing on all finite windows of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ as in 
(equation Lp-stab of the paper) for $p = 1$ and 
assume $\xi$
also
satisfies  a $(1 + \varepsilon)$-moment condition on {\em finite windows} 
as at~(equation e:xinpmomcopied of the paper) for {\em some} $\varepsilon > 0$. Then for almost all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ as $n\to\infty$ the Palm distributional limit of $\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)$, 
given by  $\Upsilon_{\0}$
in (equation e.xil-0 of the paper), exists and for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}

\Big| n^{-1} \mathbb{E}  \mu_n^\xi(f) -  \rho \mathbb{E} [\Upsilon_{\0}]\int_{W_1}f(x)\,\mathrm{d} x\Big| = O(n^{-1/d}).
\end{equation}
If $\xi$ satisfies (equation Lp-stab of the paper)  for $p=1$ with
$\varphi_{1}$ only decreasing to zero, then the right-hand side of (equation expasy of the paper) is $o(1)$.

 
\item   
Assume $\xi$ is fast  \textnormal{BL}-localizing on finite windows of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$  as in (equation Lp-stab of the paper) for $p \in \{1,2\}$  and assume 
$\xi$ satisfies a $(2 + \varepsilon)$-moment condition on finite windows as at~(equation e:xinpmomcopied of the paper) for some $\varepsilon > 0$. 
Then for \(\rho^{(2)}\)-almost all \(x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}^d\) as $n\to\infty$ the Palm distributional limit of $(\xi(\tilde{x}_1,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n),\xi(\tilde{x}_2,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n))$
given by $\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}=(\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}[1],\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}[2])$, $z=x_2-x_1$,
in (equation e.xil-xy of the paper) exists.

Further, if $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ has  summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations as in Definition~(def.A2 of the paper) then for all $f \in  \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}

\lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-1} {\rm Var} \,\mu_n^{\xi}(f) =  \sigma^2(\Upsilon) \int_{W_1} f(x)^2 \,\mathrm{d} x \in [0,\infty),
\end{equation}
whereas for all $f, g \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}

\lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-1}  {\rm{Cov}} ( \mu_n^{\xi}(f) , \mu_n^{\xi}(g) )  =  \sigma^2(\Upsilon) \int_{W_1} f(x) g(x) \,\mathrm{d} x,
\end{equation}

where 

\begin{align}  
\sigma^2(\Upsilon) =
\rho\mathbb {E} [\Upsilon_{\0}^2]  \ + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left( \mathbb {E} \Bigl[\Upsilon_{
(\0,z)}[1]\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}[2]\Bigr] \rho^{(2)}(\0,z) - \rho^2\mathbb {E} [\Upsilon_{\0}]^2 \right) \mathrm{d} z \in [0, \infty).
\end{align}

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:674197501cd9286c5f75463ef8485319e2234a6184e83f7a667fe9e194f803cc","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/67/674197501cd9286c5f75463ef8485319e2234a6184e83f7a667fe9e194f803cc.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:62b37a0e5b3f43f2b597c9eb36466623aae3077347358d7d6bad31f4eae5889b","bundle_entry_key":"balanced-orientation-global-endpoint","bundle_id":"population.t232-square-two-gaussian-second-step-chain-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"deep linear networks; asymmetric factorization; saddle-to-saddle dynamics","draft":"w704/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.deep_linear_networks:balanced-orientation-global-endpoint","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T232 Target 1: balanced orientation excludes every nonglobal terminal rank

Status: proof draft (unaudited). No novelty or priority claim. This theorem concerns a selected balanced width-two orbit; it does not establish a general-data canonical escape limit.

## Theorem
Let M be invertible and Sigma symmetric positive definite, both 2x2. Let B,A be SQUARE 2x2 factors solving gradient flow for C(BA)=tr((BA-M)Sigma(BA-M)^T)/2. Suppose initially
  B^T B=AA^T,
  B and A are invertible,
  sign det(BA)=sign det M,
  C(BA)<C(0).
Then the factors converge to finite limits B*,A* with B*A*=M. No isotropy or commutation assumption is imposed, and no assumption of an initially best-rank-one saddle is made.

## 1. Global boundedness, analytic convergence, and finite-time full rank
The balance K=B^T B-AA^T is conserved, hence remains zero. Loss decreases and Sigma positive definite bounds P=BA. The exact invariant identity
  ||B^T B||F^2+||AA^T||F^2=2||BA||F^2+||K||F^2
bounds both factors when w=2; their trace norms are bounded by the corresponding Frobenius norms times sqrt(2). Thus the forward polynomial ODE is global and bounded.

The bounded analytic gradient trajectory has a finite-length tail and converges to a stationary factor pair, by the elementary local Lojasiewicz argument given in C002: at a cluster point choose a local analytic gradient inequality, integrate the square-root energy dissipation to bound remaining length, and trap the late trajectory inside that neighborhood. This is the analytic convergence ingredient, not an inference that boundedness alone implies a point limit.

Put W=A^T and U=(B;W). The stacked flow is U'=-H(P-M)U, with H(D)=[[0,D Sigma],[Sigma D^T,0]]. On every finite time interval the linear fundamental matrix of this prescribed continuous coefficient is invertible, so U keeps column rank two. If Wc=0, balance gives ||Bc||^2=c^T B^T Bc=c^T W^T Wc=0, hence Uc=0 and c=0. Thus W and B stay invertible at every finite time. Define O=B W^(-1). Balance gives O^T O=I, and its constant determinant is
  delta=sign det O=sign det(BA)=sign det M.
This equality of signs does not assert det(BA) is constant in magnitude.

## 2. Classify possible limiting ranks
Balance passes to the limit, so B*,W* have the same Gram matrix and the same rank. If that rank is zero then both vanish, contradicting C(P*)<=C(P(0))<C(0). If their common rank is two, stationarity and invertibility give G*=(B*W*^T-M)Sigma=0, hence B*W*^T=M.

It remains to rule out common rank one. Their equal rank-one Gram matrices imply
  B*=b h^T, W*=a h^T,
where ||h||=1 and ||a||=||b||=rho>0. Then P*=ba^T, and stationarity gives G*a=0 and G*^T b=0. Since M has rank two, G* cannot be zero; it has rank exactly one.

## 3. A rank-one limit forces increasing determinant, a contradiction
Choose oriented orthonormal frames L=[b/rho,J2 b/rho], R=[a/rho,J2 a/rho], J2=[[0,-1],[1,0]]. In these frames G*=L diag(0,gamma)R^T, with gamma!=0. Let Hinv=R^T Sigma^(-1)R. From M=P*-G*Sigma^(-1), direct determinant expansion yields
  det M=-rho^2 gamma (Hinv)22.
Since (Hinv)22>0, delta=sign det M=-sign gamma.

Although B*,W* are singular, O(t) still converges: choose any index j with h_j!=0. For all late times the nonzero jth columns w_j(t),b_j(t) converge to nonzero multiples of a,b. An orthogonal 2x2 map of fixed determinant delta is uniquely determined by its action on one nonzero vector. Explicitly
  O(t)=L_j(t)diag(1,delta)R_j(t)^T,
using the oriented normalized column frames. Hence O(t)->O*=L diag(1,delta)R^T. If h_j<0, both oriented frames change sign together and the same formula results.

The exact input-factor equation is W'=-G^T O W. Since W is invertible at every finite time, Jacobi's formula gives
  d/dt log|det W|=-tr(G^T O).
At the alleged rank-one endpoint this coefficient tends to
  -tr(G*^T O*)=-delta gamma=|gamma|>0.
Therefore for all sufficiently late times |det W| grows at least exponentially with positive rate |gamma|/2. This contradicts the previously established boundedness of W (and also its rank-one limit). Thus common rank one is impossible. Only common rank two remains, and its stationary product equals M. QED, subject to independent analytic audit.

## Why the energy hypothesis cannot be omitted
In dimension two the same graph determinant component contains the negative map as well as the positive one. Let M=diag(3,1), Sigma=I, choose W(0)=c I with c>0 and B(0)=-W(0). Then O=-I has determinant +1=sign det M and balance is exact, but P=-WW^T. The coordinate-diagonal invariant flow has positive diagonal w_i satisfying w_i'=-(m_i+w_i^2)w_i, so W and B tend to zero. Its initial loss is greater than C(0), outside the theorem. Thus determinant orientation alone is insufficient and cannot be used to drop the strict energy hypothesis.

## Canonical escape connection and remaining obligation
At any nonzero balanced rank-one critical factor zstar and its positive residual vector v, the two columns zstar,sqrt(eta)v form a balanced J-null rank-two plane. Their graph determinant is sign det M by the same endpoint determinant identity. For eta sufficiently small their loss is below C(0), because the critical rank-one product has strictly lower loss than zero and the perturbation is small. The finite-eta balanced outgoing factor flows therefore meet this theorem.

For a limiting canonical escape orbit, one must ALSO ensure it remains a nonconstant rank-two factor realization in this component, with loss below C(0) at a finite time. These are expected from its nonzero normal mode, but are not supplied merely by taking limits of rank-two finite-eta orbits: rank can drop in a limit. The pending dominant Gram escape proof must verify the canonical normal-mode expansion, balanced realization and nonzero normal coefficient before invoking this endpoint theorem. Do not interchange the eta limit and t->infinity based on finite-eta convergence alone.

For the final connection paragraph, the strict critical energy inequality is exact: C(P)-C(0)=-tr(P Sigma P^T)/2+<G,P>. At any rank-one stationary product <G,P>=b^T G a=0; nonzero P and positive-definite Sigma make C(P)<C(0). This does not assume that P is best rank one.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:34bc22cb3481f5c38302f01d1fa56a8cf139f838fb0e985f87f9681f103548ce","revision_digest":"sha256:7f7355b46f9a74f292fdcd8da948418090dd4840d067411c51d863dcc85295b8","source_id":"own-work:w704:T232-w704-C010:v2","source_revision":"v2-as-read-2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Def Def_Exch of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $(\xi_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of random variables.
Given $n\in \mathbb{N}$, the random variables $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n$ are called {\sl exchangeable} if for any permutation $\sigma$ of $(1,2,\ldots,n)$,
 the law of $(\xi_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,\xi_{\sigma(n)})$ coincides with that of $(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)$.
The sequence $(\xi_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb{N}}$ is called exchangeable if, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$,
 the random variables $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n$ are exchangeable.
title: Def Def_Exch of arXiv:2606.22183

body: A group is cyclic if it is generated by a single element g (every element is a power g^k). Up to isomorphism the cyclic groups are the integers Z (infinite order) and Z/nZ (order n). Every subgroup and every quotient of a cyclic group is cyclic; a finite cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing n. A finite group is cyclic iff it has an element whose order equals the group's order.
title: Cyclic Group

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The number of possibilities of choosing $k$ objects among $n$ objects is
$$\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$$
called binomial number, where $n!=1\cdot2\cdot3\ldots(n-2)(n-1)n$, called ``factorial $n$''.

body:
In binary uplift modeling, the subpopulation of never-takers consists of units for which the outcome does not occur regardless of treatment: $\{i \mid Y_i(1) = 0 \text{ and } Y_i(0) = 0\}$. For never-takers, the individual treatment effect is zero: $\tau_i = 0 - 0 = 0$.
Potential outcomes are binary Y \in {0, 1}

[Corollary coro of arXiv:2412.02486, 'On the curvatures of \\ random complex submanifolds'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~(theorem1 of the paper),
	for any $\epsilon \in (0,1]$,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item (holomorphic bisectional curvature) if 
		$3r\geq 2n-1$ and  $0<\eta < \epsilon (3r-2n+2),$
			there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$
			\density(\hbc_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}.$$
		\item (holomorphic sectional curvature) If $2r\geq n$ and $0<\eta < \epsilon(2r-n+1)$,
			there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$
		\density(\hc_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}.$$
		\item (Ricci curvature) If  $0<\eta < \epsilon(r(n-r)-(n-r-1))$, 	there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$		
		\density(\ricci_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}
		.$$
		\item (Scalar curvature) 
		If  $0<\eta < \epsilon(\frac{1}2r(n-r)(n-r+1))$, 	there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$	
		\density(\scal_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}
		.$$
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:root-fused-allocation of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For every fixed $L$ there are $A_L<\infty$ and a numerical $B$ with the
following property.  Put $N=\binom n2$ and $r\le L\log n$.  Fix one
reflected residual word with its $r$ labelled nonconstant occurrences;
one fully declared, once-normalized circuit-anchored spatial atom
$\Gamma$ with positive terminal projective majorant
$\mathfrak a_\Gamma$; all status,
incidence, reversal, Jacobi, finite-Green, and nonroot chronological data;
a selected root set $R=R_{\rm ord}\sqcup R_{\rm sp}
=\{\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_q\}$ with
$|R_{\rm ord}|\le r$, $|R_{\rm sp}|\le B_0$, and hence
$q\le r+B_0$; and the set $F$ of
exactly those still-unrecorded port-open singleton occurrences whose
weak-order node is one of the selected root supernodes.
Here $B_0$ is numerical.  The special set consists only of complete
paired-marked blocks and complete aggregate-Ricci blocks with a
distinguished literal-$W$ coupon.  At an aggregate-Ricci block, a
same-color full-centered occurrence is classified only after the complete
coefficient pairing has been fixed: an immediately adjacent string stays
inside the root and is covered by
(lem:aligned-ricci-string of the paper); an external one-box $q$-packet
vanishes; and an external multibox $q$-packet is the closed plane-blind
scalar of (lem:plane-blind-ricci-packet of the paper).
(cor:zero-gap-special-environment of the paper) is used only for its constant-zero
and exposed-seed bookkeeping, not to bound an aligned $\mathsf V$ block
before the root cancellation.  Every other selected root is ordinary and
contains a labelled nonconstant occurrence, giving the displayed bound
on $|R_{\rm ord}|$.
If the special set contains an aggregate-Ricci root $R$, the assertion of
this theorem is restricted to the packet-attached subfiber
$\mathcal P_R(\phi)\ne\varnothing$; the packetless subfiber is outside
its scope.  If there is no aggregate-Ricci root, no such restriction is
imposed.

For each ordinary root, designate its one endpoint resource
$\mathfrak e_\rho$.  If this is a packet token, let
$\mathcal E_{\rm ord}$ be the set of packets supplying those tokens;
their carrier factors are left bare in $\mathfrak a_\Gamma$, while the
disjoint normalized $N^{-1}$ tokens occur only in
$\mathfrak e_\rho$.  These endpoint packets contain their selected hard
root supernode, whereas a mobile packet consists only of occurrences in
$F$ whose root has not yet been selected.  Hence
$\mathcal M\cap\mathcal E_{\rm ord}=\varnothing$.  A linear Jacobi endpoint is treated in the same
way, without adding a packet to $\mathcal E_{\rm ord}$.  When the
special set contains the unique coupled pure-Weyl marked root, its
nonmobile marked packet $P_\star$
instead keeps its normalized correlated-front weight
\[
 w_{P_\star}

Let phi : G -> H be a group homomorphism. Then the kernel K = ker(phi) is a normal subgroup of G, the image phi(G) is a subgroup of H, and the map G/K -> phi(G), g K |-> phi(g), is a well-defined group isomorphism. Consequently every homomorphic image of G is isomorphic to a quotient of G by a normal subgroup, and |G| = |K| . |phi(G)| when G is finite. The same statement holds word for word for rings (kernel an ideal, image a subring) and for modules over a ring (kernel and image submodules); the second and third isomorphism theorems, H N / N congruent to H / (H cap N) for H a subgroup and N normal, and (G/N) / (M/N) congruent to G/M for normal subgroups N and M of G with N contained in M, are its corollaries.

[Theorem 33 (Crossing probability) of arXiv:2607.27786, 'Gaussian free field in annulus: \\BPZ equations and crossing probabilities for level lines'] Fix $r>0$ and an even number $n=2N$. 
For $\bs{\alpha}, \bs{\beta}\in\LX_n$, we write $\bs{x}=\ee^{\ii\bs{\alpha}}$ and $\bs{y}=\ee^{\ii\bs{\beta}-r}$. 
Let $\varphiann{n}$ be the bounded harmonic function in annulus $\A_r$ with alternating boundary data~\eqref{eqn::boundarydata}.
Suppose $\Gamma$ is Dirichlet GFF in annulus $\A_r$. 
Let $\gamma^j$ be the level line of $\Gamma+\varphiann{n}$ starting from $x_{j}$ for $1\le j\le n$ and denote $\bs{\gamma}=(\gamma^1, \ldots, \gamma^n)$.
We define $\cross(\bs{\gamma})$ and $\wind(\bs{\gamma})$ as in~\eqref{eqn::crossingevent_def} and~\eqref{eqn::windingevent_def}. 
We have 
\begin{align}
&\PP[\cross(\bs{\gamma}), \wind(\bs{\gamma})=(m;\ell)]=\frac{\LZcro{n}^{(\ell)}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \beta_{2m+1}, \ldots, \beta_{2m+n})}{\LZann{n}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \bs{\beta})}, \quad \text{for $m\in\{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\ell\in\Z$};\\
&\PP[\cross(\bs{\gamma})]=\sum_{m=1}^N\frac{\LZcro{n}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \beta_{2m+1}, \ldots, \beta_{2m+n})}{\LZann{n}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \bs{\beta})}.
\end{align}
where $\LZann{n}, \LZcro{n}^{(\ell)}, \LZcro{n}$ are partition functions defined in~\eqref{eqn::LZann_def}-\eqref{eqn::LZcro_def}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Crossing probability

[Corollary coro:Wegner_orbital of arXiv:2604.20215, '\bf Edge Universality for Inhomogeneous Random Matrices II: Markov Chain Comparison and Cr'] \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] \textbf{Frozen regime:} Given   any  fixed integer $D\geq 2$,  if
         \(M^{\frac13}\lambda \ll 1\), then for any fixed integer  $k\geq 1$ with $s_N=M^{-2/3}$,
       $ (T_{s_N})_*  R_{N,\lambda}\bigl(dx_1,\dots,dx_k\bigr)$
        converges vaguely to the corresponding limits  of $D$ independent GUE/GOE matrices.

    \item[(ii)] \textbf{Skellam regime:} Given   any  fixed integer $D\geq 2$,  if
         \(M^{\frac13}\lambda \to \mu \in (0,\infty)\) with $s_N=M^{-2/3}$, then
       $ (T_{s_N})_*  R_{N,\lambda}\bigl(dx_1,\dots,dx_k\bigr)$converges vaguely to a new point process \(R^{\mathrm{(Skellam)}}_{\mu;k}(dy_1,\ldots,dy_k)\) defined by definition (def:skellam_process of the paper) that interpolates between Airy and Poisson  statistics.

    \item[(iii)] \textbf{Diffusive regime:}  If $d=1$, \(M^{\frac13}\lambda \gg 1\),
       then  the $k$-point correlation measure  converges
       to those of the corresponding $1d$ 2-stable random band matrix with effective bandwidth $W=\sqrt{\lambda}M$ and $N=DM$.
\end{enumerate}

[Definition def:halfcross of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $B=Q\times[s,s+h]$ with $Q=y+[-w,w]^d$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $T(B)$ is the event that there is an open path contained in $B$ whose trace has duration
  at least $h/2$.
\item For $1\le i\le d$, $S^+_i(B)$ is the event that there is an open path contained in $B^+$
  whose trace starts at a point with $x_i\le y_i+\vartheta w$ and later reaches a point with
  $x_i\ge y_i+w$; and $S^-_i(B)$ is its mirror image, obtained by replacing $x_i-y_i$ by
  $y_i-x_i$.
\end{itemize}
The \emph{half-crossing event} of $B$ is
$H(B)=T(B)\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^d\big(S^+_i(B)\cup S^-_i(B)\big)$.
title: Half-crossings

body: Let X and Y be Banach spaces and let T : X -> Y be a linear map. If the graph of T, consisting of all pairs (x, Tx) for x in X, is a closed subset of the product space X times Y (with the product topology), then T is automatically continuous (bounded). Equivalently, if x_n -> x in X and Tx_n -> y in Y together force y = Tx for every such sequence, then T is bounded. The theorem follows from the open mapping theorem and can fail if either X or Y is not complete.
title: Closed graph theorem

body: In probability theory, concentration inequalities provide mathematical bounds on the probability of a random variable deviating from some value. The deviation or other function of the random variable can be thought of as a secondary random variable. The simplest example of the concentration of such a secondary random variable is the CDF of the first random variable which concentrates the probability to unity. If an analytic form of the CDF is available this provides a concentration equality that provides the exact probability of concentration. It is precisely when the CDF is difficult to calculate or even the exact form of the first random variable is unknown that the applicable concentration inequalities provide useful insight.
title: Concentration inequality

PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. Exact critical tanh two-input Gram chain: given current Gram [[q,c sqrt(qr)],[c sqrt(qr),r]], draw n iid centered Gaussian pairs (Ai,Bi) with that Gram and set Qnew=mean tanh(Ai)^2, Rnew=mean tanh(Bi)^2, Cnew=mean tanh(Ai)tanh(Bi). Write D=1-C/sqrt(QR), S=Q+R, V=Q^2+R^2, F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2, and delta=1-E[tanh(Ai)tanh(Bi)]/sqrt(F(q)F(r)). Probability norms and expectations are over the exact chain.  At any admissible current state q,r in (0,1], c in [-1,1], let eta=Dnew-E[Dnew|past], with E[eta^2|past]<=K delta^2/n and E[eta^4|past]<=16Lambda^4 delta^4/n^2. Set a=192. For integer n>=48 a^2(1+K), any finite past-measurable real x and alpha with |alpha|<=1+8V satisfy E[exp(a Snew)(alpha x+eta)^2|past] <=exp(aS)[x^2+(1+4Lambda^2)delta^2/n]. K,Lambda are finite nonnegative uniform constants supplied by C010/C015. The innovation and weight use the same fresh rows; no independence or stopping is assumed. This is a one-step estimate; multilayer forcing and readout coupling remain open.
Current q,r in (0,1], valid Gaussian Gram; fresh iid Gaussian rows and tanh; n integer >=1769472(1+K), finite K,Lambda>=0. Uses C017 joint-norm mgf, C002 scalar drift, C010 conditional variance and C015 centered fourth moment (the latter components unaudited).
Only C002 v2 and C004 v1 among these inputs have reviewer PASS; new dependencies remain unaudited.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e88f710dcfdf9884299c5d3c01716e24b4280ae1782dc83c823ada304b1b7716","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e8/e88f710dcfdf9884299c5d3c01716e24b4280ae1782dc83c823ada304b1b7716.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:42bd0e2f7a01df611b6326a10dbc750466d99342d5d46b7c00409a28757f9ee0","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_weighted_centered_error_energy","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c017-c018-unstopped-angular-energy","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Tensor Programs and stochastic Gram propagation","draft":"w712/bundle_013.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:critical-tanh-weighted-centered-error-energy","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C018 v1: exponential weighting preserves centered angular-noise energy

Kind: moved. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified.
This is a one-step conditional error-energy estimate, without stopping.
Its iteration with deterministic-GP radial and bias forcing is not claimed
as completed here.

## Statement

Fix a completed network past F. Current variances q,r are in (0,1] and
the current Gram is positive semidefinite. Draw n fresh iid centered
Gaussian pairs of that covariance, and let Qnew,Rnew be the empirical
tanh-square marginal variances. Put S=q+r, V=q^2+r^2,
Snew=Qnew+Rnew. Let eta be the centered empirical angular-gap innovation
from these same rows, and delta its F-measurable population gap.
Assume the C010/C015 bounds

    E[eta|F]=0,
    E[eta^2|F]<=K delta^2/n,
    E[eta^4|F]<=16Lambda^4 delta^4/n^2.              (1)

These are unaudited dependencies, with finite universal K,Lambda>=0.
Take a=192 and integer n>=48a^2(1+K)=1769472(1+K).
For every finite F-measurable real x and every F-measurable alpha with
|alpha|<=1+8V,

    E[exp(a Snew)(alpha x+eta)^2|F]
       <=exp(aS)[x^2+(1+4Lambda^2)delta^2/n].         (2)

The innovation and Snew may be arbitrarily dependent subject to the
stated model and (1). In particular they come from the same fresh rows;
no independence between the exponential weight and eta is assumed.

## 1. Exponential moments and a covariance estimate

Set mu=E[Snew|F]=F(q)+F(r), where
F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2, and set Z0=Snew-mu.
The joint marginal-norm mgf calculation in C017 section 2, before using
the scalar drift, gives

    E[exp(t Z0)|F]<=exp(6t^2 V/n), t=a,2a.          (3)

Indeed the centered contribution of one row has range [-2,2] and
variance at most 6V. The series estimate used there requires 2t/n<=1;
our width assumption implies this. Audited C002 also gives
mu<=S-V/6. These are the only distributional properties of Snew used.

Let z=24a^2 V/n. Since V<=2 and n>=48a^2, 0<=z<=1.
Jensen gives E[exp(a Z0)|F]>=1. Consequently

    E[(exp(a Z0)-1)^2|F]
       <=exp(z)-1<=2z=48a^2 V/n.                   (4)

The inequality exp(z)-1<=2z on [0,1] follows from convexity and
exp(1)<3. Conditional centering in (1), followed by Cauchy-Schwarz,
now yields, with C_a=a sqrt(48K),

    |E[eta exp(a Snew)|F]|
       =exp(a mu)|E[eta(exp(a Z0)-1)|F]|
       <=exp(a mu) C_a delta sqrt(V)/n.             (5)

This is order n^-1, rather than the order n^-1/2 obtained by discarding
the centering. Equality in (5)'s first line uses E[eta|F]=0 exactly.

For the squared-noise term, Cauchy-Schwarz with the fourth moment in
(1) and (3) gives

    E[eta^2 exp(a Snew)|F]
       <=4Lambda^2 delta^2/n *exp(a mu+12a^2 V/n).  (6)

## 2. Drift absorbs the remaining cross term

Our width bound implies n>=144a. Combining (3) with mu<=S-V/6 gives

    E[exp(a Snew)|F]<=exp(aS-aV/8),
    exp(a mu+12a^2V/n)<=exp(aS-aV/12).              (7)

For the first inequality, 6a^2/n<=a/24; for the second,
12a^2/n<=a/12. Also |alpha|<=1+8V<=exp(8V).
Expand the square in (2), using (5)-(7). Since a=192, this yields

    E[exp(a Snew)(alpha x+eta)^2|F]/exp(aS)
       <=exp(-8V)x^2
          +exp(-24V) 2C_a |x|delta sqrt(V)/n
          +4Lambda^2 delta^2/n.                    (8)

The first exponent is -a/8+16=-8; the cross-term exponent is
-a/6+8=-24. No conditional expectations have been multiplied here.
For the cross term use exp(-24V)<=exp(-8V) and 2uv<=u^2+v^2:

    exp(-24V) 2C_a |x|delta sqrt(V)/n
       <=exp(-8V)[(C_a^2/n)V x^2+delta^2/n].        (9)

Finally C_a^2/n=48K a^2/n<=K/(1+K)<=1, and
exp(-8V)(1+V)<=1. Inserting (9) into (8) proves (2).
If V=0 the algebra remains valid, though the actual normalized angular
model assumes positive marginal variances. If delta=0, (1) forces eta=0
conditionally and all noise terms vanish. The proof never divides by
V, delta, or an angular stability product.

## 3. What this does and does not settle

For the GP angular-error recursion, x is its current error, alpha the
positive population angular secant, and the remaining predictable
forcing consists of the finite-width bias and the radial comparison
with the deterministic GP state. Inequality (2) handles its homogeneous
error and centered innovation jointly, without C016's stopping event.

Those forcing terms are not zero. Their iteration, using C017's
unstopped amplitude and C014's radial fourth moment, still needs to be
written and checked before claiming an angular error rate. A final
Gaussian covariance coupling is another separate step toward Target 1.

drift; C010 v1 conditional variance; C015 v1 conditional centered fourth
moment. [Theorem 2.1 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let f : Ω → R be c-Lipschitz and let the Ω-valued random vector X be G-dependent. If G is a tree, then for every t > 0, P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t² / (c_min² + Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G)} (c_i + c_j)²)), where c_min is the minimum entry of c.
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
G-dependent (Definition 1.3 of the paper): X = (X_i)_{i∈V(G)} is G-dependent when for all disjoint S, T ⊂ V(G) with no edge of G between S and T, the families (X_i)_{i∈S} and (X_j)_{j∈T} are independent; this is stronger than pairwise independence of non-adjacent coordinates.

[Lemma lem:single-step of arXiv:2607.05693, 'Free multiplicative convolution and Erlang moments in monitored quantum transport'] Let $S\in U(N)$, and let $P$ be an orthogonal projection of rank $(1-c)N$.
Then the eigenvalues of
\[
  (PS)^\dagger(PS)=S^\dagger P S
\]
are exactly $1$ with multiplicity $(1-c)N$ and $0$ with multiplicity $cN$.
Hence
\[
  \ESD\bigl((PS)^\dagger(PS)\bigr)
  =
  \nu_c=(1-c)\delta_1+c\delta_0
\]
for every $S\in U(N)$.

[Lemma lem:finite-rank-chaos-upper of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] Let \(E\subset D_{\mathbb R}\) be finite-dimensional, and let
\(
    Q_t\in E^{\odot m},
    \qquad
    0\le t\le T,
\)
be continuous in \(t\). Then, almost surely, the sequence
\[
    \left\{
        t\mapsto
        \frac{I_m(Q_t;W_n)}{(2\log\log n)^{m/2}}:
        n\ge3
    \right\}
\]
is relatively compact in \(C[0,T]\), and every cluster point belongs to
\(
    \left\{
        t\mapsto
        \langle Q_t,\xi^{\otimes m}\rangle:
        \|\xi\|_{\mathfrak H_{\mathbb R}}\le1
    \right\}.
\)

[Definition of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] For  $s\in (0,1)$ and $\alpha \in [0,1]$, we define the  weighted tensorized H\"older space $T^{s, \alpha}C(\mathbb{R}^2)$ as the space of functions $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ of $L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ such that there is $c>0$ with
    \begin{align*}
&|f(x_1+h_1,x_2+h_2)- f(x_1, x_2+h_2) - f(x_1+h_1,x_2)+ f(x_1,x_2)| \\
& \hspace{6cm} \leq c \, \min\{|h_1|,|h_2| \}^{(1+\alpha)s} \max\{|h_1|,|h_2| \}^{(1-\alpha)s},
    \end{align*}
    and 
$$|f(x_1+h_1,x_2)- f(x_1,x_2)| \leq c \, |h_1|^{(1+\alpha)s} \quad \text{and} \quad |f(x_1,x_2+h_2)-  f(x_1,x_2)| \leq c \,  |h_2|^{(1+\alpha)s}$$
for all $x_1,x_2,h_1,h_2 \in \mathbb{R}$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields'

body: In the classical Wasserstein topology on process laws, essential stochastic operations such as the Doob decomposition, optimal stopping, and conditional expectations are discontinuous because the classical topology ignores the temporal structure of filtrations. The adapted Wasserstein distance $\mathcal{AW}_p$ constrains couplings to be bicausal (non-anticipative), making the Doob decomposition continuous and providing the appropriate geometry for dynamic stochastic analysis.
title: Discontinuity of Doob Decomposition in Classical Wasserstein Topology

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, A proof of Atanassov's conjecture and other generalizations of Sperner's lemma (arXiv:1708.07175, version 3) gives a simple proof of Atanassov's conjecture, a generalization of Sperner's lemma, based on the Brouwer degree of maps. The conjecture had been proved before (J. A. De Loera, E. Peterson and F. E. Su, A polytopal generalization of Sperner's lemma, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 100, 2002); the abstract describes the new proof as much simpler than the original proofs, so this is a new proof of a known theorem, not its first solution. The paper also presents a generalization of the conjecture and proves a new theorem similar to Sperner's lemma.

body:
[Theorem 39 (Quota Violation Probability) of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] Let $M$ be the total number of seats, and let $A$ be the Modified Jefferson, Modified Webster, Dean, or Huntington-Hill method with divisor function $\delta$. Let $(1,x,y)$ be a reduced population vector with $1 < x < y$, drawn from a probability distribution with joint density $f(x,y)$.

For each $\tau \in \left(-\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3}\right)$, the $\tau$-line parametrization in $x$ is 
$$
x = x(y,\tau) := \frac{1}{2}y - \frac{3}{2}\tau y + \frac{1}{2},
$$
Let the set of ultimately violatory $\tau$ values be
$$
V = \bigcup_{k= \lfloor M/2 \rfloor + 1}^{M-1} 
\left( 1 - \frac{2M}{3k}, \, 1 - \frac{2M}{3\bigl(k + D(k)\bigr)} \right),
$$
where
$$
D(k) =\frac{(M-k)\delta(k-1)-k\,\delta(M-k-1)}{\delta(k-1)+\delta(M-k-1)}.
$$

For each $\tau$, let $y^F_\tau$ denote the floor-stabilization threshold and $y_\tau$ the agreement with asymptotic apportionment threshold defined in Lemma \ref{y_tau.def}. Define
$$
y_\tau^{\max} :=
\begin{cases}
\infty & \text{if } \tau \in V,\\
y_\tau & \text{if } \tau \notin V.
\end{cases}
$$

Then the probability of a quota violation caused by a guaranteed seat is
$$
\Pr(\text{quota violation})
=
\int_{-1/3}^{1/3}
\int_{y_\tau^F}^{y_\tau^{\max}}
f\bigl(x(y,\tau),\,y\bigr)\,
\frac{3}{2}y
\, dy \, d\tau.
$$

Along each such line, Lemmas~\ref{y_tau.def} and \ref{y_tau.def2} define the guaranteed-seat threshold $y_\tau^F$ and the agreement with asymptotic apportionment threshold $y_\tau$. 

By the preceding lemmas, a quota violation caused by the guaranteed seat of state 1 occurs precisely when $y > y_\tau^F$ and $y \le y_\tau^\mathrm{max}$, where
$$
y_\tau^\mathrm{max} =

\infty, & \tau \in V \text{ (ultimately violatory)},\\

body:
PROOF (UNAUDITED). For every 0<q,r<=1, -1<=c<=1 and n>=64, let n independent standard Gaussian pairs have correlation c. Apply tanh(sqrt(q)*X) and tanh(sqrt(r)*Y), and let Dhat be one minus their uncentered empirical Gram correlation. If delta=1-E[tanh(sqrt(q)*X)tanh(sqrt(r)*Y)]/sqrt(F(q)*F(r)), there is a finite universal K independent of q,r,c,n such that |E Dhat-delta|<=K*delta/n, E(Dhat/delta-1)^2<=K/n and Var Dhat<=K*delta^2/n whenever delta>0. Delta=0 exactly at q=r,c=1 and then Dhat=0 almost surely. The conditional estimates therefore hold at arbitrary unequal-current-variance fresh-weight tanh states. The proof constructs K from the positive minimum of minus the derivative of the third-to-first Gaussian coefficient ratio of the normalized tanh feature curve. No numerical value of that minimum is certified. No contraction against the deterministic multi-layer GP gap is asserted.
n>=64; q,r in (0,1]; independent fresh paired Gaussian rows; uncentered empirical correlation.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:172bbda704bebde4058b12f6c2d33d457888d36337ba799cca551cfb4517f483","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/17/172bbda704bebde4058b12f6c2d33d457888d36337ba799cca551cfb4517f483.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:06128067af9ef3d1e0e86630d68fdbd5ceb9a15228fc0e995db98ca2000ea141","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_unequal_relative_gap","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c010-unequal-relative-gap-noise","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Gaussian-process limits and empirical Gram matrices","draft":"w712/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:unequal-variance-tanh-gram-gap-relative-conditional-noise","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C010 v1: unequal-current-variance relative noise for the tanh Gram gap

Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: moved. Target: T250(a), conditional-noise component of the reviewer's two-input gap rung. Novelty unverified. Full multi-layer relative-gap propagation remains open.

## Statement

Fix 0<q,r<=1, -1<=c<=1, and n>=64. Let (X_i,Y_i), i=1,...,n, be independent standard Gaussian pairs of correlation c. Define

    F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2,
    u_q(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(F(q)),
    U_i=u_q(X_i), V_i=u_r(Y_i), h=E U_i V_i, delta=1-h,
    A=mean U_i^2, D=mean V_i^2, T=mean U_i V_i,
    Dhat=1-T/sqrt(AD).

Sample means are NOT subtracted. This is the normalized empirical Gram correlation. The sample denominators are positive almost surely. There is a finite universal constant K, independent of q,r,c,n, such that, whenever delta>0,

    |E Dhat-delta|<=K delta/n,
    E(Dhat/delta-1)^2<=K/n,
    Var(Dhat)<=K delta^2/n.                              (1)

Delta=0 exactly when q=r and c=1; then Dhat=0 almost surely. Unlike C009, this statement does not require equal current variances and so applies conditionally at EVERY finite-depth state of the two-input fresh-weight tanh chain with nonzero initial marginal variances at most one. Its population delta is computed at the current random state, not at the deterministic GP state.

The proof gives a formula for K using a strictly positive universal feature-curve constant mu. No numerical lower bound on mu, numerical value of K, independent audit, or literature novelty is claimed.

## 1. A uniformly regular normalized feature curve

Set h_q(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(q) for q>0, and h_0(z)=z. The scalar inequalities in audited C002 v2 give

    1/2<=||h_q||_2<=1, |h_q(z)|<=|z|,
    u_q=h_q/||h_q||_2, u_0(z)=z,
    |u_q(z)|<=2|z|, Lip_z(u_q)<=2.                     (2)

For t>=0,

    tanh(t)-t sech(t)^2=integral_0^t 2s sech(s)^2 tanh(s) ds
                         <=2t^3/3.

Differentiating h_q therefore yields |partial_q h_q(z)|<=|z|^3/3. The limit at zero is -z^3/3, obtained from the third-order Taylor expansion of tanh at zero. The displayed bound dominates this limit in every finite Gaussian Lp space. Thus q -> h_q and q -> u_q are continuously right-differentiable at zero and continuously differentiable elsewhere in every such Lp space. Since

    |partial_q ||h_q||_2|<=||partial_q h_q||_2<=sqrt(15)/3<2,

we obtain, for p>=1,

    ||partial_q u_q||_p <= B_p:=(2/3)G_(3p)^3+8G_p,      (3)

where G_p=(E|Z|^p)^(1/p). All bounds hold uniformly on q in [0,1]. The weaker bound 8|z| in the normalization derivative uses ||h_q||_2^(-2)<=4.

## 2. An inverse-Lipschitz estimate from two Gaussian coefficients

Let

    a_1(q)=E[Z u_q(Z)],
    a_3(q)=E[(Z^3-3Z)u_q(Z)]/sqrt(6),
    R(q)=a_3(q)/a_1(q).

The two test polynomials have Gaussian L2 norm one; no full Hermite expansion is used. Weighted Jensen with density Z^2 dgamma and tanh(x)^2>=x^2/(1+x^2) gives

    1>=a_1(q)>=E[Z^2/sqrt(1+qZ^2)]>=1/sqrt(1+3q)>=1/2.

Also |a_3(q)|<=1. For q>0, normalization cancels in the ratio:

    R(q)=(m(q)-3)/sqrt(6),
    m(q)=E[Z^3 tanh(sqrt(q)Z)]/E[Z tanh(sqrt(q)Z)].

Let nu_q be the probability measure with density z tanh(sqrt(q)z)/E[Z tanh(sqrt(q)Z)] relative to Gaussian measure. Its density is nonnegative, positive except at zero, and m(q)=E_(nu_q) Z^2. Differentiation under the Gaussian integral, for each fixed q>0, gives

    m'(q)=Cov_(nu_q)(Z^2, s_q(Z)),
    s_q(z)=z/[sqrt(q) sinh(2sqrt(q)z)],
    s_q(0)=1/(2q).

The score s_q is bounded and strictly decreasing as a function of |z|>0. Indeed t/sinh(2t) is strictly decreasing, since sinh(2t)-2t cosh(2t)<0, equivalent to tanh(2t)<2t. The covariance is strictly negative: for independent Z,Z' under nu_q, twice the covariance equals

    E[(Z^2-Z'^2)(s_q(Z)-s_q(Z'))]<0.

The product is negative whenever |Z|!=|Z'|, an event of probability one. All integrals are finite. Hence R'(q)<0 for q>0.

The endpoint q=0 must be checked separately. Divide numerator and denominator of m by sqrt(q), and use h_0(z)=z, partial_q h_0(z)=-z^3/3. Gaussian moments give

    B(0):=E[Z h_0]=1, B'(0)=-1,
    N(0):=E[Z^3 h_0]=3, N'(0)=-5,
    m'(0)=(-5)*1-3*(-1)=-2.

The derivative envelope in section 1 justifies these limits and continuity of R' on [0,1]; the divided denominator B(q)=E[Zh_q(Z)]=a_1(q)||h_q||_2 is at least 1/4 throughout the interval. Therefore

    mu:=min_{q in [0,1]}[-R'(q)]>0.                    (4)

This is an analytic compactness conclusion: a continuous, everywhere strictly positive function on a compact interval has positive minimum. It is not inferred from sampled numerical values.

By the mean value theorem and Cauchy-Schwarz for the two unit test polynomials,

    mu|q-r|<=|R(q)-R(r)|
       <=2|a_3(q)-a_3(r)|+4|a_1(q)-a_1(r)|
       <=6||u_q-u_r||_2.                               (5)

Thus the feature curve has a uniform inverse-Lipschitz constant. The first coefficient alone would not suffice: its derivative vanishes at zero, whereas the ratio above has R'(0)=-2/sqrt(6).

## 3. The population gap controls BOTH angle and variance mismatch

For standard Gaussians X,Y of correlation c, Price's identity gives

    partial_c E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)]=E[u_q'(X)u_r'(Y)]>=0,

on (-1,1), and the inequality extends to the endpoints by continuity. The functions are increasing and smooth with polynomially bounded derivatives; the hypotheses of Voigtlaender, arXiv:1710.03576, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2, apply. At q=0 the limiting function is linear, and the same identity holds directly. Hence

    delta>=1-E[u_q(Z)u_r(Z)]=||u_q-u_r||_2^2/2.

Combining with (5) gives |q-r|<=6sqrt(2delta)/mu. Separately write u_q(z)=a_1(q)z+v_q(z), with E[Zv_q(Z)]=0. Gaussian conditioning annihilates the linear-residual cross terms even when q!=r. Consequently

    2delta=(a_1(q)-a_1(r))^2+2a_1(q)a_1(r)(1-c)
                 +E[v_q(X)-v_r(Y)]^2 >=(1-c)/2.

Therefore

    1-c<=4delta, |q-r|<=6sqrt(2delta)/mu.               (6)

These inequalities also prove the stated characterization of delta=0, since (5) makes the feature curve injective. No assumption that empirical variances stay equal has entered.

## 4. Increment moments at arbitrary current variances

The triangle inequality, (2),(3),(6), and Gaussian X-Y give

    ||u_q(X)-u_r(Y)||_p <= I_p sqrt(delta),
    I_p:=4sqrt(2)G_p+(6sqrt(2)/mu)B_p.                  (7)

Indeed split the difference into u_q(X)-u_q(Y) and u_q(Y)-u_r(Y). The first uses the input Lipschitz bound and 1-c<=4delta; the second integrates (3) along the parameter interval between q and r.

Let W_i=(U_i-V_i)^2/2, so E W_i=delta. From (7) and ||U+V||_p<=4G_p,

    ||W_i-delta||_p <=(I_(2p)^2/2+1)delta,
    ||U_i^2-1||_p,||V_i^2-1||_p <=4G_(2p)^2+1,
    ||U_i^2-V_i^2||_p <=4G_(2p)I_(2p)sqrt(delta).       (8)

The LAST variable is centered for UNEQUAL q,r as well, because each normalized marginal has second moment one. This supplies exactly the moment input that equal current variances supplied in C009.

Define positive finite constants

    a=max_{p=2,4,8} p^2(4G_(2p)^2+1),
    b=max_{p=2,4,8} p^2(I_(2p)^2/2+1),
    d=max_{p=2,4,8} p^2*4G_(2p)I_(2p).

For a centered iid sample mean, expansion of its even p-th power shows

    ||mean B_i||_p<=p^2||B_1||_p/sqrt(n), p=2,4,8.

Only index tuples in which every index occurs at least twice survive; their number is at most p^(p+1)n^(p/2), and Holder bounds each expectation by E|B_1|^p. This proves the assertion for every n, not just sampled n.

With x=A-1, y=D-1, w=mean W_i, s=A-D, (8) thus gives

    ||x||_p,||y||_p<=a/sqrt(n),
    ||w-delta||_p<=b delta/sqrt(n), ||w||_p<=(1+b)delta,
    ||s||_p<=d sqrt(delta/n), p=2,4,8.                 (9)

## 5. Inverse empirical norms and the normalization calculation

For EVERY q in (0,1], u_q(z)^2>=z^2/(1+z^2). For a size-64 subset of rows, its sample norm A_I is at least S/[64(1+S)], where S is chi-square with 64 degrees of freedom. Direct integration gives E S^(-j)=product_{k=1}^j(64-2k)^(-1) for j<=20<32. Hence, with

    J=64^20 sum_{j=0}^{20} binom(20,j)product_{k=1}^j(64-2k)^(-1),

we have E A_I^(-20)<=J. Averaging over all size-64 subsets gives the full A exactly; Jensen for z^(-20) then proves E A^(-20)<=J for every n>=64. The same proof works for D with parameter r. Thus ||A^(-t)||_p,||D^(-t)||_p<=J^t when tp<=20. No independence between A and D is asserted or used.

Put k=(AD)^(-1/2) and t=(sqrt(A)-sqrt(D))^2/(2sqrt(AD)). Algebra gives

    Dhat=w k-t, 0<=t<=(A-D)^2/(8AD).

Holder with (9) and the inverse-norm bounds gives

    ||t||_2<=d^2J^2 delta/n,
    ||k-1||_4<=2aJ/sqrt(n).                            (10)

For g(z)=z^(-1/2), Taylor's remainder satisfies

    g(A)=1-x/2+r_A, |r_A|<=(3/8)x^2(1+A^(-5/2)).

Define R=k-1+(x+y)/2. Then R=r_A g(D)+r_D-(x/2)(g(D)-1). Applying Holder first with L4 factors and then L8 factors yields

    ||R||_2<=(a^2/n)[(3/8)(1+J^(5/2))(1+sqrt(J))+sqrt(J)/2]
             <=2a^2J^4/n.                             (11)

The largest inverse moment used is 20, from ||A^(-5/2)||_8; it is within the range proved above. These are the same algebraic estimates as C009 sections 3-4, now with moment inputs (9) established for arbitrary q,r.

Since E x=E y=0 and E w=delta,

    E[w(k-1)]=-(1/2)E[(w-delta)(x+y)]+E[wR].

Equations (9)-(11) prove

    |E Dhat-delta|<=[ba+2(1+b)a^2J^4+d^2J^2]delta/n,
    ||Dhat-delta||_2<=[b+2(1+b)aJ+d^2J^2]delta/sqrt(n).

Let H=1+a+b+d+J>=2 and K=H^12. The first bracket is at most 4H^7<=K; the square of the second is at most 16H^8<=K. This proves (1), including the variance inequality, since variance is no larger than the squared deviation from a fixed number.

## 6. Conditional use and exact remaining gap

All constants are independent of the current parameters. Conditioning on the full past of a fresh-weight tanh chain therefore yields, at each state, delta_l=1-H(Q_l,R_l,c_l) and

    |E[D_(l+1)|past]-delta_l|<=K delta_l/n,
    Var(D_(l+1)|past)<=K delta_l^2/n.

If delta_l=0 the update is exactly zero. This removes C009's equal-current-variance restriction and closes that specific applicability obstruction.

It does not establish contraction of delta_l divided by the deterministic GP gap. The still-unpaid step is a multiplicative comparison between 1-H(Q_l,R_l,c_l) and 1-H(s_l,s_l,bar c_l) that includes the radial contrast Q_l-R_l. The old absolute parameter Lipschitz estimate loses the small gap factor. A coupled radial-contrast recurrence or a sharper parameter estimate is needed before the C003-style multi-layer relative argument can be claimed. Targets involving transposes and non-Lipschitz activations remain open.

Sources: audited C002 v2 scalar inequalities; Voigtlaender arXiv:1710.03576 Theorem 1 and Corollary 2 for Price's identity; C009 v1 for the preceding equal-variance normalization calculation, reproduced here with the new moment inputs. \begin{align*}
F&=E[F]+\int_{0}^{T}\varphi^{X}(t)\,\mathrm{d}B^{X}_t+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}}\psi^{X}(t,x)\widetilde{N}^{X}(\mathrm{d}t,\mathrm{d}x)\notag\\
&=E[F]+\int_{0}^{T}\varphi^{X}(t)\,\mathrm{d}B^{X}_t+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\psi^{X}(t,x)\widetilde{N}(\mathrm{d}t,\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}y).

body:
Let N=N(n) with N/n->c in (0,infinity). For all n,i,j let X_ij^(n) be real independent identically distributed random variables with mean zero, variance one, and E|X_ij^(n)|^(4+epsilon)<infinity for some epsilon>0. Let sigma_ij(n) be deterministic real numbers uniformly bounded in absolute value. Let A_n be deterministic real N-by-n matrices whose row Euclidean norms and column Euclidean norms are uniformly bounded over all n and all rows and columns. Put (Y_n)_ij=sigma_ij(n) X_ij^(n)/sqrt(n) and Sigma_n=Y_n+A_n. For the relevant N,n, write A=A_n and sigma_ij=sigma_ij(n), D_j=diag(sigma_1j^2,...,sigma_Nj^2), and Dtilde_i=diag(sigma_i1^2,...,sigma_in^2). Let S_plus consist of the functions z->integral_[0,infinity) (lambda-z)^(-1) nu(dlambda) for probability measures nu on [0,infinity), analytically continued to C minus [0,infinity). Define the unique S_plus-valued solution psi_i,psitilde_j by psi_i(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(Dtilde_i Ttilde(z))/n)] and psitilde_j(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(D_j T(z))/n)], where Psi=diag(psi_i), Psitilde=diag(psitilde_j), T(z)=[Psi(z)^(-1)-z A Psitilde(z) A^T]^(-1), and Ttilde(z)=[Psitilde(z)^(-1)-z A^T Psi(z) A]^(-1). Both trace terms in these canonical equations use division by n. Let P_n be the empirical eigenvalue probability measure of Sigma_n Sigma_n^T, and let pi_n be the deterministic probability measure with Stieltjes transform tr(T_n(z))/N. For every bounded continuous f:[0,infinity)->R, integral f dP_n-integral f dpi_n->0 almost surely. The analogous conclusion holds for Sigma_n^T Sigma_n and the deterministic measure with transform tr(Ttilde_n(z))/n. This compares two sequences of measures and does not require either sequence to have a single limiting probability law. The test function in this corollary is bounded.

[Definition of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] A \emph{labelled} rooted tree $\underline{\tau} = (N,E,r)$ is a \textit{connected acyclic graph} with finite node set $N \subset \N$, edge set $E \subset N^{(2)}$, and a distinguished root node $r \in N$. 
 We often write $N(\underline{\tau}) = N$, $E(\underline{\tau}) = E$ and $r(\underline{\tau}) = r$. 

We write $\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$ for the set of all labelled rooted trees, and often just call elements of $\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$ labelled trees. 
We also write, for any $r\in\N$, $\circ_r$ for the labeled tree with a single node $N(\circ_{r}) = \{r\}$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'

body:
Let G be a finite undirected graph with k>=3 distinct terminals and mutually independent Bernoulli edges with probabilities in [0,1]. If the all-separated and all-connected terminal partitions both have positive probability, some strictly intermediate terminal partition has positive probability. Thus no such graph realizes a terminal law supported only on the two extreme partitions with both masses positive. If G has m optional edges whose probabilities lie in [epsilon,1-epsilon], 0<epsilon<=1/2, its partition law has total variation distance at least min(q,1-q,epsilon^m) from the selector assigning probability q to all-connected and 1-q to all-separated, for 0<q<1.
Finite undirected graph; k>=3 distinct labeled terminal vertices.
All Bernoulli edges are mutually independent.
The quantitative conclusion requires m optional edges and 0<epsilon<=1/2 bounding their probabilities away from zero and one.

[Lemma 12 (Local-to-global Wasserstein contraction) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $(E,D)$ be a compact geodesic metric space and let $K$ be a Markov kernel on $E$. Let $W_D$ denote Wasserstein distance with cost $D$. Suppose that, for some $\rho>0$ and $\lambda\in[0,1)$,
\be
W_D(K(x,\cdot),K(y,\cdot))\leq \lambda D(x,y)
\qquad \text{whenever }D(x,y)\leq \rho.
\ee
Then, for all $x,y\in E$,
\be
W_D(K(x,\cdot),K(y,\cdot))\leq \lambda D(x,y).
\ee
Consequently, for all probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $E$,
\be
W_D(\mu K,\nu K)\leq \lambda W_D(\mu,\nu).
\ee (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Local-to-global Wasserstein contraction

[Lem 6 of arXiv:2604.25964, 'Strong convergence rate of Euler-Maruyama approximations in temporal-spatial H\"older-norm'] For $\delta \in \widetilde{\mathbb{S}},$ $s, \widetilde{s} \in [0,T],$ $t\in [s, T],$  $x \in\mathbb{R}$, let $(X^{\delta,x}_{s,t})_{t\in[s,T]}:[s,T]  \times\Omega\to\mathbb{R} $ 
be an $(\mf_t)_{t\in[s,T]}$-adapted stochastic process with c\`adl\`ag  sample paths satisfying equation \eqref{y01}. Then, for all $\mathbb{X}=(\mathbb{X}_r)_{r\in [s, t]}, \mathbb{Y}=(\mathbb{Y}_r)_{r\in [s, t]} \in \{ (x)_{r\in [s, t]}, (X_{\widetilde{s},\max\{\widetilde{s},\delta(r)\}}^{\delta,x})_{r\in [s, t]}, (X_{\widetilde{s},\max\{\widetilde{s},\delta (r) \}}^{\iota,x})_{r\in [s, t]}  \}$ and $p\ge 2,$ there exists a positive constant $C_p=C_p(T,m_2,m_p)$ such that
\begin{align*}
&\left[\mathbb{E} \left[\left| \int_s^t (\mu(\mathbb{X}_r)-\mu(\mathbb{Y}_r)) dr \right|^p \right]\right]^{1/p} + \left[\mathbb{E} \left[\left| \int_s^t (\sigma(\mathbb{X}_r)-\sigma(\mathbb{Y}_r)) dW_r \right|^p \right]\right]^{1/p} \notag \\ 
& \quad + \left[\mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \int_s^t \int_{\bR_0} (\gamma(\mathbb{X}_{r-})-\gamma(\mathbb{Y}_{r-})) z \widetilde{N}(dr, dz) \right|^p \right]\right]^{1/p} \notag \\
 & \leq c  C_p  |t-s|^{1/p} \sup_{r\in [s, t]} \left[ \mathbb{E} \left[\left| \mathbb{X}_r-\mathbb{Y}_r \right|^p \right]\right]^{1/p},
\end{align*}
where the constant $c$ is given in {\bf A1}.

body: [Defi defn:MRSC of arXiv:2605.03151, 'Giants through Higher-Order paths in Random Simplicial Complexes'] The $d$-dimensional multi-parameter random simplicial complex model with vertex set $[n]$ and probability parameters $\bm{p} = (p_1, \dots, p_d) \in [0,1]^d$ is constructed recursively as follows. The set $[n]$ is the $0$-dimensional skeleton and each pair of vertices is connected by an edge with probability $p_1$, independent of all the other pairs. In general, for each $k$, let $S_{k}'$ denote the set of all potential $k$-dimensional simplices upon the constructed $(k-1)$-dimensional skeleton. Each $k$-dimensional simplex in $S_{k}^{'}$ is included with probability $p_{k}$. This goes on until $k = d$ or $S_{k}' = \emptyset$ for some $k \leq d$. This model is denoted by $\MRSC_d(n; \bm{p})$. Throughout, the abbreviation MRSC is used to refer to the multi-parameter random simplicial complex.
title: Multi-parameter random simplicial complex (MRSC)
Thm box-crossing of arXiv:2605.14910

body: FIRES WHEN a source, or your own reading of one, states a stochastic dominance between two random variables that you can check have equal means. MINIMAL COUNTEREXAMPLE, or rather the minimal IMPOSSIBILITY: if X >= Y in the usual stochastic order and E X = E Y < infinity, then E(X - Y) = integral (P(X > t) - P(Y > t)) dt = 0 with a nonnegative integrand, so the survival functions agree everywhere and X and Y are equal in law. There is no example to find; the hypothesis is already the conclusion. CONDITION UNDER WHICH THE ROUTE FAILS: equal means. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD: the intended relation is the CONVEX or dilation order, under which the variance inequality c^2 >= 1 is immediate. In the E0078 case this is a reading issue in the source's own statement, not a mathematical obstacle - and reading it as the usual stochastic order would have made Conjecture 4.2 imply Conjecture 4.1 for a trivial and wrong reason. The lesson generalises past this problem: when a claimed ordering would be vacuous under a moment identity the problem also asserts, the ordering has been mis-transcribed.

Suppose $g:[1, \infty) \to [1, \infty)$ is a function such that
$\lim_{x \to \infty} g(x) = \infty$. 
  
   Then there exists a (real) strictly stationary, countable-state,
irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain 
$X := (X_k, k \in \mathbb Z)$ which is reversible, such that
$E[X_0^2]< \infty$ and $E[X_0] = 0$ and 
\begin{align}
   
    &\int_0^{(1/x)^p} Q_{|X(0)|}^2(u)\, du\ <<\ 
(1/x) \cdot g(x)\ \ {\rm as}\ x \to \infty, 
\quad  {\rm and}\\
   
    &\alpha_X(n)\ \leq\ \beta_X(n)\ 
    \leq\ (1/n)^p\ \
    {\rm for\ all}\ n \in \mathbb N,  
\end{align}
and conclusions (iii) and (iv) in Theorem (thm3.4 of the paper) hold,
and conclusion (iv) in Theorem (thm4.4 of the paper) holds as well [with $g_n = g(n)$]. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary cor:lipschitz-drift of arXiv:2608.01279, 'Stochastic heat equation with nondegenerate Hölder diffusion coefficient: uniqueness below'] Let $b:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be a measurable function. Let $G$ satisfy the assumption in Theorem~(thm:vector-valued of the paper). Assume that $b$ is globally Lipschitz continuous:
\[
    |b(z)-b(z')|
       \leq L_b|z-z'|,
    \qquad\forall z,z'\in\mathbb{R}^d.
\] Then the following SHE with drift
\begin{equation}\partial_tU
      =\Delta U+b(U)+G(U)\dot W,\quad U(0)=u_0\in L^2(\mathbb{T},\mathbb{R}^d)
\end{equation}
has a unique weak mild solution.
In particular, \(b\) is allowed to have linear growth. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Thrampoulidis-Oymak-Hassibi convex Gaussian min-max optimizer-norm transfer. For each n>=1 let m=m(n)>=1, let S_x,n subset R^n and S_y,n subset R^m be deterministic nonempty compact convex sets, and let psi_n:S_x,n times S_y,n to R be deterministic, continuous, convex in x and concave in y. Let G_n, g_n and h_n have mutually independent standard Gaussian entries, with dimensions m-by-n, m and n. Define Phi_n=min_{x in S_x,n} max_{y in S_y,n} [y^T G_n x+psi_n(x,y)], v_n(x)=max_{y in S_y,n}[||x||_2 g_n^T y+||y||_2 h_n^T x+psi_n(x,y)], and phi_n=min_{x in S_x,n} v_n(x). Choose measurable global minimizers x_P,n of Phi_n and x_A,n of phi_n. Let ||.||_n be a deterministic norm on R^n, possibly different from the Euclidean norms inside the auxiliary optimization. Suppose there are constants d_star in R, alpha_star>=0 and tau>0 independent of n such that phi_n converges in probability to d_star, ||x_A,n||_n converges in probability to alpha_star, and P(v_n(x)>=phi_n+tau*(||x||_n-||x_A,n||_n)^2 for every x in S_x,n) tends to one. Then ||x_P,n||_n converges in probability to alpha_star. The optimizer conclusion requires a uniform auxiliary quadratic-growth gap; value convergence alone is insufficient. The result concerns compact problems; applying it to unbounded feasible sets requires a separate valid compactification argument. This is TheoremII.1(iii), not a new result or a proof of the data-pruning max-margin limit.
Deterministic nonempty compact convex index sets and deterministic continuous convex-concave offsets at every n.
Independent standard Gaussian primary matrix and auxiliary vectors of the displayed dimensions.
Measurable global minimizers; arbitrary deterministic comparison norm.
Auxiliary value convergence, auxiliary norm convergence, and one fixed positive uniform quadratic-growth constant with probability tending to one.

[Theorem thm-CLT-det of arXiv:2411.14876, 'Limit theorems for stochastic exponentials of matrix-valued L\'evy processes \\'] Let $L=(L_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a Lévy process in $\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ fulfilling (equation eq-nonsingular of the paper) and let $D=(D_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be the determinant process of its stochastic exponential defined in (equation eq-detprocess of the paper). 
	Set
	$$T_1(x):= \nu_L\big(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}: |\det(\Id+x)|\in (0,e^{-x})\cup (e^x,\infty)\}\big),$$
	and 
	$$T_2(x):=\nu_L\big(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}: |\det(\Id+x)|\in  (e^x,\infty)\}\big) - \nu_L\big(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}: |\det(\Id+x)|\in (0,e^{-x})\}\big). $$
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Assume $T_1(x)=0$ for some $x>0$. If $\sigma_{\check{D}}= \sum_{m,n=1}^d \sigma_{(m,m),(n,n)}>0$, then 
		$$\frac{\log |D_t| - t \big(\gamma_{\check{D}} + T_2(1)+\int_{(1,\infty)} T_2(y) dy\big)}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\check{D}} \cdot t}} \overset{d}\longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad t\to \infty.$$
		\item Assume $T_1(x)>0$ for all $x>0$. If
		$$\frac{\sigma_{\check{D}}+\int_{[-x,x]} z^2 \nu_{\check{D}}(dz)}{x^2 T_1(x)} \to \infty, \quad x\to \infty,$$
		then there exist measurable functions $a(t), b(t)>0$ such that
		$$\frac{\log|D_t| - a(t)}{b(t)}  \overset{d}\longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad t\to \infty.$$
	\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 2604171624 of arXiv:2609.02626, 'Comparison principles and symmetry for subquadratic fractional $p$-Laplacian equations'] Let $N\ge 1$, $s\in (0, 1)$ and $p>1$. Assume that $\mathcal{U}$ is an open set such that $\overline{\mathcal{U}} \Subset \mathbb{R}^N_+$, and $K\Subset \mathbb{R}_+^N\backslash \overline{\mathcal{U}}$. Then
\[
\int_{K}\frac{1}{|x-y|^{N+sp}} {\rm d}y\le {\rm dist}(\mathcal{U}, K)^{-N-sp}|K|\quad \mbox{for all }x\in \mathcal{U},
\]
and 
\[
\underset{x\in \mathcal{U}, y\in K}{\sup}\frac{|x-y|}{|x-y^*|}<1,
\]
where ${\rm dist}(\mathcal{U}, K)=\inf{\{|x-y|: x\in \mathcal{U}, y\in K\}}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let M be real m-by-2 of rank two with m>=2 finite, Sigma be symmetric positive definite, and F(b,a)=(-G a,-G^T b), G=(b a^T-M)Sigma. T232-w704-C015 v1. Kind: moved; Target 1, local-arrival spectral component only. Status: proof (unaudited). No complete second-step or novelty claim.

## Statement
Let M be real m-by-2 of rank two, m>=2 finite, and Sigma be 2-by-2 symmetric positive definite. Consider the rank-one factor field
 F(b,a)=(-G a,-G^T b),  G=(b a^T-M)Sigma.
Let (b,a) be stationary with NONZERO PRODUCT b a^T, equivalently F=0 and both a,b nonzero. Let Q be an orthonormal basis of col(M), and N an orthonormal basis of its orthogonal complement. Then a,b are both nonzero, b lies in col(M), G has rank one, and its columns lie in col(M).

Put kappa=a^T Sigma a>0, Gtilde=Q^T G, and s=||G||op>0. In the orthogonal coordinates delta_b=Q x+N y, delta_a=h, the frozen dormant matrix L=[[0,-G],[-G^T,0]] splits as Lred on (x,h) and zero on y. Its eigenvalues are s,-s and zero of multiplicity m. The active derivative J=DF(b,a) splits exactly as
 J = Jred direct-sum (-kappa I_(m-2)),
where Jred is the derivative for the square reduced target Q^T M at (Q^T b,a). In particular its largest eigenvalue r equals that of Jred and satisfies 0<=r<s. For m=2 the transverse block is absent.

## 1. Stationarity confines the endpoint
If a=0, then G=-M Sigma and G^T b=0, so b could be nonzero in ker(M^T). Thus a weaker nonzero-factor assumption alone would NOT imply both factors are nonzero in a rectangular problem.

The theorem therefore explicitly requires nonzero product, equivalently a!=0 and b!=0. Stationary zero-product factors outside col(M) are excluded. This distinction is necessary when applying a square endpoint argument in a rectangular space.

Under this corrected assumption, G a=0 gives
 b (a^T Sigma a)=M Sigma a,
so b belongs to col(M). Thus both terms of G have their columns in col(M). Since a is a nonzero vector in R^2 and G a=0, rank(G)<=1. If G=0, invertibility of Sigma would give M=b a^T, contradicting rank(M)=2. Therefore rank(G)=1. Projection by Q is isometric on G, so its sole singular value s is also that of Gtilde.

## 2. Exact active and dormant blocks
For an increment xi=(d,h), set T xi=d a^T+b h^T and S(P)=P Sigma. Direct differentiation gives
 J xi=L xi-T^* S T xi,
where T^* P=(P a,P^T b). S is self-adjoint positive definite for the Frobenius inner product, and hence J is symmetric.

If d=N y and h=0, then G^T N=0 and N^T b=0. Consequently
 L(Ny,0)=0,
 T^* S T(Ny,0)=(Ny (a^T Sigma a),0),
so J(Ny,0)=-kappa(Ny,0). On the orthogonal subspace d=Qx the formula remains inside that subspace and equals exactly the reduced square formula with Mtilde=Q^T M. Orthogonality of Q,N proves the displayed direct sum without omitted coupling terms. The dormant direct sum follows immediately from G^T N=0. The reduced 4-by-4 dormant block has eigenvalues s,-s,0,0; adding m-2 transverse zeros gives total zero multiplicity m, and total dimension m+2 as required.

## 3. Strict active/dormant gap
The factor-scaling curve (exp(t)b,exp(-t)a) consists of stationary factors, since its product is constant and Ga=G^T b=0. Its nonzero tangent (b,-a) belongs to ker J. Thus r>=0. Since -kappa<0, the transverse block cannot change the largest active eigenvalue, so r=rred.

As J=L-T^*ST and T^*ST is positive semidefinite, r<=s. Suppose equality held, and take a maximizing unit eigenvector x of J. Equality in
 <x,Jx>=<x,Lx>-<Tx,S Tx><=s
forces x into the simple top eigenspace of L and Tx=0. Write its unit top vector as v=(p,q)/sqrt(2), with ||p||=||q||=1 and -Gq=s p, -G^T p=s q. From G^T b=0 and Ga=0 one gets p perpendicular to b and q perpendicular to a. Hence
 ||Tv||_F^2=||p a^T+b q^T||_F^2/2
            =(||a||^2+||b||^2)/2>0.
This contradicts Tv=0 and positive definiteness of S. Therefore r<s. Also v is perpendicular to (b,a). The dormant orthogonal complement of v has only nonpositive eigenvalues, as required by the cone argument; the added transverse modes have eigenvalue zero, not a new positive rate.

## 4. Scope and the first detected rectangular pitfall
A nonzero FACTOR is not necessarily a nonzero PRODUCT when m>2. For example take M with columns e1,e2, Sigma=I, a=0 and b=e3. Then G=-M, Ga=0 and G^T b=0: it is stationary, but b is outside col(M). This counterexample refutes the weaker hypothesis discussed in Section 1, not the corrected nonzero-product theorem proved here.

A canonical first path with strictly lower loss than the zero product cannot end at a zero product. C012's analytic endpoint argument is still unaudited; this note does not silently certify it. The reduction theorem here requires nonzero product explicitly. C014 does not by itself prove every later local-arrival and escape hypothesis.

The scalar gap is pointwise for fixed data. No uniform lower bound for (s-r)/s is asserted. This note verifies the rectangular spectral component only; the full local-arrival continuation and complete rectangular second-step composition remain to be recorded and independently checked.

[Lemma lem:Bochner++ of arXiv:2609.01464, 'Removability of non-isolated singularities for Einstein metrics and RCD spaces'] Let $n\geqslant 2$ be an integer and $K\in\mathbb R$. Let $U$ be an open set of a smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $(M^n,g)$. Let us assume $\mathrm{Ric}\geqslant K$ on $U$. Let $f\in C^{\infty}(U)$ be a bounded function on $U$ such that $\Delta f=-\lambda f$ on $U$ for some $\lambda\geqslant 0$.

    \[
    u:=(1+|\nabla f|^2)^{\beta},
    \]
    we have

    \Delta u \geqslant -cu, \qquad \text{on $U$}.
    \end{equation}

[Proposition 37 (Near-flat entry into a uniform stability neighborhood) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix \(\rho\in(0,1)\).  There exist an integer
\(m_{\mathrm{flat}}\geq2\), a number
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{flat}}>0\), a fixed model torus
\(\TT^3_*\), a compact set \(\mathcal F\) of flat metrics on
\(\TT^3_*\), and a uniform \(h^{2+\rho}\)-stability neighborhood
\(\mathcal U_{\mathcal F}\) of \(\mathcal F\), as in
Proposition~\ref{input:flat-stability}, with the following property.

Let \(q\) be a smooth metric on \(\TT^3\), put
\(D=\diam(\TT^3,q)>0\), and suppose that
\begin{equation}
 D^{j+2}\sup_{\TT^3}|\nabla^j\Rm_q|_q
 <\varepsilon_{\mathrm{flat}},
 \qquad 0\leq j\leq m_{\mathrm{flat}}.
\end{equation}
Then there is a connected finite covering map
\[
        p_{\mathrm{st}}:\TT^3_*\longrightarrow\TT^3
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
        p_{\mathrm{st}}^*(D^{-2}q)\in\mathcal U_{\mathcal F}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the Ricci flow starting from the metric in
\eqref{eq:near-flat-entry-conclusion} converges exponentially in fixed
coordinates to a flat metric.

[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2606.03661, '2606.03661'] Let $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ be such that
$$
a=\lambda_1+\lambda_2,
\qquad 
b=\lambda_1\lambda_2 ,
$$
and consider the differential equation \eqref{2nd.order.eq}. 
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textrm{(i)}] If $\lambda_1\neq \lambda_2$, the general solution of eq.\eqref{2nd.order.eq} is
\begin{equation}

f(t)=c_1\Psi_\alpha^\nu(-\lambda_1 t)
+c_2\Psi_\alpha^\nu(-\lambda_2 t).
\end{equation}
where $\Psi_\alpha^\nu$ is defined in eq.\eqref{eq.solution.final} 
and the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ are chosen so that $f(t)$ is real-valued
whenever $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are complex conjugates. 
\item[\textrm{(ii)}] If $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$, the general solution of eq.\eqref{2nd.order.eq} is
\begin{equation}

f(t)=c_1^\prime \Psi_\alpha^\nu(-\lambda_1 t)
+c_2^\prime \Psi_\alpha^{\nu+1}(-\lambda_1 t) ,
\end{equation}
where $c_1^\prime$ and $c_2^\prime$ are real constants. 
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 48 of arXiv:2607.08536, 'Soft edge limit of the Laguerre beta-ensemble at the lower edge'] For $1\le k\le n_0$, we have 
    \begin{align*}
        \ev[Z_{1,k}] &= \frac{k}{n}+O(n^{-1}),\qquad  \Var[Z_{1,k}]=O(n^{-1}),\\
       \ev[Z_{2,k}]&= \frac{k}{n}+O(n^{-1}),\qquad \Var[Z_{2,k}]=\frac{4}{\beta n}+O(kn^{-2}),\\
         \Cov[Z_{1,k},Z_{2,k}]&=O(n^{-1}),\qquad \ev[Z_{1,k}^4]=O(n^{-2}), \qquad \ev[Z_{2,k}^4]=O(n^{-2}). 
    \end{align*}
    For $n_0\le k\le n_1:=\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ we have   \begin{align*}
        \ev[Z_{1,k}] &= \frac{2k}{\sqrt{n-k}(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{n-k})}+O(n^{-1}), \qquad \Var[Z_{1,k}]=O\Big(\frac{1}{n-k}\Big),\\
        
        \quad \ev[Z_{2,k}] &= \frac{2k}{\sqrt{n-k}(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{n-k})}+O(n^{-1}),
        \qquad \Var[Z_{2,k}]=\frac{4}{\beta(n-k)}+O\Big(\frac{k^2}{n^2}\Big).
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 54 of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] The element $q$ is a unit in $\Hab$, the natural map
$\Z[q^{\pm1}]\to\Hab$ is injective, and every root of unity $\zeta$
defines a ring homomorphism
\[
 \operatorname{ev}_\zeta:\Hab\longrightarrow\Z[\zeta].
\]
If $a_k\in(q;q)_k\Z[q^{\pm1}]$, then $\sum_{k\ge0}a_k$ converges in
$\Hab$ and, when $\zeta$ has order $L$,
\[
 \operatorname{ev}_\zeta\!\left(\sum_{k\ge0}a_k\right)
 =\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}a_k(\zeta).
\]

[Definition def:generalized-mass-conservation of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Let $T>0$ and let $u \colon [0,T]\times X\to[0,\infty)$ be a pointwise solution of the (eq:GPME of the paper) with initial datum $u_0$.
We say that $u$ satisfies the \emph{generalized mass balance} on $[0,T]$ if
\begin{equation}\tag{MB}
     \sum_{x\in X}u(t,x)\mu(x)
    +\int_0^t\sum_{x\in X}\kappa(x)\,\phi(u(s,x))\,\mathrm d s
    =\sum_{x\in X}u_0(x)\mu(x)
    \qquad \text{for all } 0\le t\le T.
\end{equation}
title: Generalized mass balance

body: Hilbert's problems are 23 problems in mathematics published by German mathematician David Hilbert in 1900. He intended to rival the master of French mathematics, Henri Poincaré, and to prove that he was cut from the same cloth. They were all unsolved at the time, and several proved to be very influential for 20th-century mathematics. Hilbert presented ten of the problems at the Paris conference of the International Congress of Mathematicians, speaking on August 8 at the Sorbonne. The complete list of 23 problems was published later, and translated into English in 1902 by Mary Frances Winston Newson in the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society. Earlier publications appeared in Archiv der Mathematik und Physik.
title: Hilbert's problems

body: There is a Hermitian matrix with a repeated eigenvalue whose individual eigenvectors are unstable under arbitrarily small perturbations while the cluster is stable: for A = diag(0, 0, 3) and E = eta (e_1 e_2^T + e_2 e_1^T) with eta > 0, A + E has eigenvalues -eta, eta, 3 (each moved by at most ||E|| = eta), its invariant subspace for the cluster is still span(e_1, e_2), and its eigenvectors there are (e_1 +- e_2)/sqrt(2), at 45 degrees to e_1 and e_2, however small eta is.

body:
[Cor inv of arXiv:2606.21049, '\textsc{Locality of rough path lifts}'] Let $H \in (1/4,1/2]$, $\eta\in (0,H)$ as in (thm:localfbm of the paper), and $\boldsymbol{X}$ be a local, square-integrable $\eta$-RPL of $X$. Let $\varphi = (0, \varphi^{(2)}, \varphi^{(3)})$ be as in (thm:localfbm of the paper). In the following, statements regarding third levels should be omitted if $H > \frac 13$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item  $\boldsymbol{X}$ is stationary jointly with the underlying noise in the sense that $\boldsymbol{X}_{s,t} \sim \boldsymbol{X}_{0,t-s}$ if and only if $\varphi_{s,t}^{(n)} = (t-s)A^{(n)}$ with $A \in \mathcal G^{\lfloor 1/H \rfloor}(\mathbb R^d)$ for $n = 2,3$.

\item  $\boldsymbol{X}$ is scale-invariant in the sense that $\boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}_{s,t} \sim (t-s)^{nH} \boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}_{0,1}$ for $n = 2,3$ if and only if it is stationary as above and either $H = \frac 12$, $H = \frac 13$ with $A^{(2)} = 0$, or $A = 0$.

\item  $\boldsymbol{X}$ is coordinate permutation-invariant in the sense that $\sigma_*\boldsymbol{X} \sim \boldsymbol{X}$ for $\sigma \in \mathfrak S_d$ if and only if $\varphi^{\alpha\beta} = 0$ and
\begin{align}
\varphi^{\alpha\beta\gamma} = (\delta^{\alpha\beta} - 2 \delta^{\alpha\gamma} + \delta^{\beta\gamma})\phi
\end{align}
for some $3\eta$-H\"older function $\phi\colon [0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, all three conditions can only hold if either $\varphi = 0$ or for $H = \frac 13$, and in the latter case there is a one-dimensional continuum of such rough paths, namely for $\varphi^{\alpha\beta} = 0$ and $\varphi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}$ as in (equation eq:phiequi of the paper) with $\phi(t) = \lambda t$, $\lambda \in \mathbb R$.

[Prop equiv-sp-pw-univ-property of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $f\colon T\to\textup{Glo}$ be any functor, and let ${\mathcal{C}}^\otimes$ be a fiberwise presentably symmetric monoidal $T$-$\infty$-category. Then the map
    \[
        {\textup{Hom}}_{{\textup{Fun}}(T^{\textup{op}},\CAlg(\textup{Pr}^{\textup{L}}))}(f^*{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}^\otimes,{\mathcal{C}}^\otimes)\to
        {\textup{Hom}}_{{\textup{Fun}}(T^{\textup{op}},\CAlg(\textup{Pr}^{\textup{L}}))}(f^*\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_*^\otimes,{\mathcal{C}}^\otimes) 
    \]
    induced by $\textbf{\textup{L}}\Sigma^\infty$ is an inclusion of path-components, and its image consists precisely of those functors that send representation spheres to invertible objects.
    \begin{proof}
        For any compact Lie group $G$, [gepnermeier2020equivTMF]*{Proposition C.9} shows that $\textbf{\textup{L}}\Sigma^\infty\colon{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{G,*}^\otimes\to{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_G^\otimes$ is the initial example of a map in $\CAlg(\textup{Pr}^{\textup{L}})$ inverting representation spheres, i.e.~it exhibits $\smash{{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_G^\otimes}$ as a left adjoint object with respect to the functor $i\colon\textup{Pr}^{\textup{L}}\to\Ar(\CAlg(\textup{Pr}^{\textup{L}}))$ sending a symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category to the inclusion of the full subcategory of tensor invertible objects. [Thm reac-diff-domain-thm of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Let $\lambda$ be the largest eigenvalue of the problem 
    $$
    d\Delta\Big(\frac{u}{K(x)}\Big) + (r(x)-E(x))u = \lambda u
    \qquad \textrm{on } D
    $$ 
    with the same (Neumann) boundary conditions imposed on (equation reac-diff-domain of the paper). If $\lambda > 0$, then there is some $\overline \epsilon > 0$ such that for all $\epsilon < \overline \epsilon$, (equation reac-diff-domain of the paper) is stochastically persistent in the sense that: 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For every $\delta > 0$ there are $0 < b < B < \infty$ such that for any nonnegative initial condition $u_0 \neq 0$, $$
        \liminf_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T}m\Big(\Big\{t \leq T \mid b \leq \int_D u_t \leq B\Big\}\Big) \geq 1 - \delta
        $$ 
        almost surely, where $m$ is the Lebesgue measure.
        \item There is an invariant measure $\mu_+$ for (equation reac-diff-domain of the paper) with $\mu_+(\{0\}) = 0$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm reac-diff-domain-thm of arXiv:2601.19145

body: Given functors F, G from C to D, a natural transformation eta : F => G assigns to each object A of C a morphism eta_A : F(A) -> G(A) such that for every morphism f : A -> B the naturality square commutes: G(f) o eta_A = eta_B o F(f). If every eta_A is an isomorphism, eta is a natural isomorphism.
title: Natural Transformation

body:
[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.23401, 'Limit Theorems for the Pitman-Yor Frequency Spectrum'] Assume \eqref{N1}. We have for  $\nu\in\R$, 
$\bfu_n\in\R^n$ and $k\in \N_n$, 
  \bea
  &&
\EE\Big(
\exp\Big(\nu\bfu_n^T\Big(\frac{\bfM_n}{K_n}-\bfq_n\Big)\Big); K_n=k\Big)
\cr
&&  \hskip1cm 
=
\EE\Big(\exp\Big(
  \frac{ \nu }{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k}
   \big(V_{in}^{(\bfu_n)}- \EE(V_{in}^{(\bfu_n)})\big)\Big)\Big)\times
\frac{\PP\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{k} \wh X_{in}^{(\nu\bfu_n)}
=n\Big)}
{ \PP\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{k} \wh X_{in}^{(0)}=n\Big)}
 \times \PP(K_n=k).
 \eea
 The 
 $\big(\wh X_{in}^{(\nu{\bfu_n}  )}\big)_{1\le i\le k}$ are i.i.d. with the distribution 
\be
\PP\big(\wh X_{1n}^{(\nu{\bfu_n}  )}=j\big) 
=
\frac{q_{j}e^{ \nu u_{jn}/k} }
{\sum_{\ell=1}^n q_{\ell } e^{ \nu u_{\ell n}/k}}, \ 1\le j\le n,
\ee
the  $\big(\wh X_{in}^{(0 )}\big)_{1\le i\le k}$ are i.i.d. with
\be
\PP\big(\wh X_{1n}^{(0 )}=j\big) 
= q_{jn} 
:= \frac{q_j}{q_{+n}}
=
\frac{q_{j} }
{\sum_{\ell=1}^n q_{\ell } },\ 1\le j\le n,
\ee
and the  $(V_{in}^{(\bfu_n)})_{1\le i\le k}$  are i.i.d. with 
 \be
 P(V_{1n}^{(\bfu_n)}= u_{jn})= q_{jn},\ 1\le j\le n.
 \ee
     The $V_{in}^{(\bfu_n)}$ have 
     \be
      \EE(V_{1n}^{(\bfu_n)})= \bfu_n^T\bfq_n
      \quad {\rm  and}\quad
       {\rm Var}(V_{1n}^{(\bfu_n)})= \bfu_n^T\bfQ_n\bfu_n,
       \ee
 where the matrix $\bfQ_n$ is  the $n\times n$ matrix  with 
diagonal elements $q_{jn}(1-q_{jn})$ and 
off-diagonal elements $-q_{jn} q_{\ell n}$, $1\le j\ne \ell \le n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.23401

[Proposition 30 (Standard neck continuation and selection) of arXiv:2608.25971, 'Positive \texorpdfstring{$\tau$}{tau}-bi-Ricci curvature and Mean curvature flow with surg'] For the parameters fixed above, the neck-continuation and neck-selection
construction of \cite{HS09}*{Lemmas~7.4, 7.10, and~7.12,
Theorem~8.2, and the proof of Theorem~1.1 on pp.~216--218} applies to the
surgically modified flow.  Whenever $H_{\max}$ first reaches $H_3$, it produces
finitely many pairwise disjoint normal necks of radius $r_*$.  Standard
replacement on these necks, followed by discarding the recognized
high-curvature components, gives
\begin{equation}
  H_{\max}(t+)\leq H_2.
\end{equation}
All constants are uniform over the surgery times.

body:
[Lem Re1 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m>1$, let $c_1,c_2,c_3\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$ and let
$\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_q$. Put
\[
  A:={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\!\bigl(c_3\gamma^3+\gamma^{q+2}\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
  f_1(x)=x+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\!\bigl(c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+x^{q+2}\bigr)
\]
is a permutation polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ if and only if $m$ is odd,
\[
  A\neq 0,\qquad
  {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma^2)+(c_3\gamma+\gamma^{q})^{q+1}=0,\quad
  \mbox{~and~} \quad A\bigl(1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)\bigr)+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2^2\gamma^4)=0 .
\]
title: Lem Re1 of arXiv:2609.01350

[Theorem 22 of arXiv:2603.26936, 'Sharp Riemannian heat kernel estimates on the cut locus and the Parabolic Anderson model'] Let $f_1,f_2\in C(M)$, and denote by $u_i$ the solutions to equation \eqref{eq: SHE} starting from initial conditions $f_i(x)m(dx)$ for $i=1,2$. 

\begin{enumerate}
    \item[\textup{(i)}] If $f_1(x)\leq f_2(x)$ for all $x\in M$, then we have
    $$\mathbb{P}\left[u_1(t,x)\leq u_2(t,x)\ \mathrm{for\ all}\ t\geq0, x\in M\right]=1.$$
