[Definition 13 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] A densely defined form $\mathfrak a$ is sectorial with vertex
$\omega\in\mathbb R$ and semi-angle $\alpha<\pi/2$ if
\[
  \mathfrak a[f]-\omega\|f\|^2\in\overline{\Sigma_\alpha},
  \qquad f\in\mathcal D(\mathfrak a).
\]
Equivalently, after a real shift, its imaginary part is controlled by its real
part: there is $C<\infty$ such that
\[
  |\Im \mathfrak a[f]|
  \leq C\bigl(\Re\mathfrak a[f]-\omega\|f\|^2\bigr),
  \qquad f\in\mathcal D(\mathfrak a).
\]
If $\omega=0$ and $\Re \mathfrak a[f]\geq0$, the form is called
accretive.

body: Let X be a Banach space and A a subset of X. Then A is relatively weakly compact (its weak closure is weakly compact) if and only if A is relatively weakly sequentially compact, meaning every sequence in A has a subsequence that converges weakly to some point of X. In particular, on a Banach space, weak compactness and weak sequential compactness of a subset coincide, even though the weak topology need not be metrizable. [Prop 7 (Pro\"inov Theorem (1984)) of arXiv:2605.03528, '\bf Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance and discrepancies {\em versus} Wasserstein distances'] Let $d$, $n \!\in \N$ and let   $\big([0,1]^d\big)^n$-valued $n$-tuple $(\xi_k)_{k=1,\ldots,n}$. Then there exists a real constant $C_d\!\in [1,4]$ such that 
\[
{{\cal W}_1^{\ell^{\infty}}\Big( \frac 1n \sum_{k=1}^n \delta_{\xi_k}, {\cal U}([0,1]^d) \Big)\le C_d D^{\star, {\cal U}([0,1]^d)}\big((\xi_k)_{k=1,\ldots,n}\big)^{\frac 1d},}
\]
where ${\cal W}_1^{\ell^{\infty}}$ denotes the  Wasserstein distance w.r.t. the $\ell^\infty$-norm on $[0,1]^d$. Moreover when $d=1$, then $C_1=1$ and both error moduli attain their minimum, $n$ being fixed, at $\Big(\frac{2k-1}{2n}\Big)_{k=1,\ldots,n}$ with a common resulting value $\frac{1}{2n}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Pro\"inov Theorem (1984)

body:
Let X be a metric space, x_0 a limit point of X, and f_n : X \ {x_0} -> R (or into any complete metric space). Suppose (i) f_n -> f uniformly on X \ {x_0}, and (ii) for each n the limit A_n = lim_{x -> x_0} f_n(x) exists. Then (A_n) converges, lim_{x -> x_0} f(x) exists, and the two iterated limits agree: lim_n lim_{x -> x_0} f_n(x) = lim_{x -> x_0} lim_n f_n(x). Uniformity in (i) is not removable: with f_n(x) = x^n on (0,1) one gets lim_n lim_{x->1} f_n = 1 and lim_{x->1} lim_n f_n = 0. Uniform convergence may be replaced by uniform convergence of the OTHER family (in n, uniformly in x) - only one of the two limits needs to be uniform. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.11]
f_n -> f uniformly on a punctured neighbourhood of x_0 (or the analogous uniformity in the other variable)
each f_n has a limit at x_0
the target space is complete

body:
[Prop 4 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] Let $(u,\nu)$ be a stochastic kinetic solution of the obstacle problem for \eqref{eq:main} under Definition \ref{def:def of stochastic kinetic solution}, and $\chi$ be a kinetic function of $u$.
Then, $\chi$ admits almost surely left and right limits at all points $t\in[0,T]$, which means that for all $t\in[0,T]$ there exist some kinetic functions $\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{\pm}$ on $\Omega\times\mathbb{T}^d\times\mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.
\[
\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\chi(x,\xi,t\pm\epsilon)\phi(x,\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}x\to \int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{\pm}(x,\xi)\phi(x,\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}x,\quad \text{as }\epsilon\to 0,
\]
for all $\phi\in C_c^{1}(\mathbb{T}^d\times(0,\infty))$ and almost surely
\begin{align}
&\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big[\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{+}(x,\xi)-\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{-}(x,\xi)\big]\phi(x,\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}x\\
&=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi)\mathbf{1}_{\{t\}}(s)\mathrm{d}q(x,\xi,s)
-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,\psi(x,s))\mathbf{1}_{\{t\}}(s)\mathrm{d}\nu(x,s)\nonumber.

\end{align}
In particular, almost surely, the set of $t\in[0,T]$ such that $\tilde{\chi}_{t}^{-}\neq\tilde{\chi}_{t}^+$ is countable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 4 of arXiv:2605.15501

Fong-Yang Theorem 3.4 proves: if W_t>=2+delta eventually for some delta>0, then sum_t ||x_t||^2<infinity and w_i,t tends to w_i,max. Thus every trajectory with limsup_t ||x_t||>0 has liminf_t W_t<=2. Also limsup_t W_t>=W_diag(beta1,beta2), where the explicit cutoff satisfies W_diag(0.9,0.999)>=1.9. These are distinct subsequential bounds; they do not assert convergence W_t->2 or shrinking-band confinement. The theorem is for uncorrected Adam, not the empirically studied bias-corrected variant.

[Theorem thm:controlling of arXiv:2510.13733, 'Internal Diffusion Limited Aggregation \\ with Critical Branching Random Walks'] Let $d \geq 3$.   There  exists $\alpha_0>0$, $c >0$ and $N_0 < \infty$ such that 
 the following holds. 
 For any  $\alpha > \alpha_0$, $N> N_0$, 
  $
  R \leq \frac{1}{\alpha}  \sqrt{  \frac{\log N} {N} },
   $
  any particle configuration $\eta$ with support 
   $\partial B_{ R }$  and number of particles $N$, we have 
   $$
   \mathbb{P}  \Big ( \mathscr{S}(\eta) \not\subset B_{  R +  c \,    \alpha^2 \,  {N }^{\frac{1}{d}} {\log (N)}^\rho }  \Big ) \leq 
    \frac{1}{ N^{\alpha}},
  $$
  where $\rho=\frac{7}{2}$ if $d=3$ and $\rho=1$ if $d>3$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem T:dd main of arXiv:2507.01236, 'Disintegration theorem for multifunctions, \\ with applications to empirical Wasserstein d'] Let $\mathfrak{X} = [0, 1]^D$ be the unit cube in dimension~$D$, endowed with the $\ell^{\infty}$ metric $d$ and its Borel $\sigma$-field,
and let~$\mu$ be an absolutely continuous probability measure on~$\mathfrak{X}$ with density $f$ satisfying
\[
c\leq f(x)\leq C\mbox{\rm \ for every $x \in \mathfrak{X}$},
\]
where $0<c\leq C<\infty$. Given $\alpha \in (0, \infty)$, let
\begin{equation}

  r(n)\equiv r(n,D,c,\alpha) := c^{-1/D}(4 \cdot 3^{D - 1})^{1/D} (2 + \alpha)^{1/(2D)} \left( \frac{\ln n}{n} \right)^{1/(2 D)}.
\end{equation}
Then there exists $n_0\equiv n_0(D,c,C,\alpha)$ such that for every $n\geq n_0$, the space $(\mathfrak{X},d,\mu)$ is $(n^{-\alpha},r(n))$-disintegrable.
title: Theorem T:dd main of arXiv:2507.01236

 \]

body:
[Conjecture eq:sparse-lower of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[conjecture]{conj:sparse-lower}
For smooth centered unit-variance entry laws satisfying the preceding large-deviation hypothesis and stability of the conditional critical-point exponent under an \(o(1)\) perturbation of the exposed block,
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 \ge\sup_{r\ge0}\sup_{\substack{A\in\mathbb R^{[r]^p}:\\ \mathcal J_\mu(A)<\infty}}
 \left\{\underline\Phi_{p,\mathrm{sf}}^{J,A}(V)-\mathcal J_\mu(A)\right\}.
\end{equation}
Under the additional hypothesis (equation eq:deformed-background-univ of the paper),
the right-hand side could be written with the Gaussian spike-free
pressure, but the preceding bounded example shows that this hypothesis
is not available under finite moment matching and entrywise cutoff.
The \(r=0\) term is merely the cutoff residual branch: for bounded
disorder it equals the full non-Gaussian pressure and already contains
the mesoscopic obstruction.  Thus the conjecture is informative only
when that residual branch has been controlled separately.  The
one-entry instance proved in (thm:one-spike of the paper) is a coarse form of
the bound; general \(A\) allows localized clusters and mixed
spike--bulk critical points. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Finite-spike lower bound

Then:

$(\mathcal Q, \mathcal E)$ has a unique minimal class (i.e. $|\mathcal M|=1$) if and only if $(\mathfrak V,\mathfrak E)$ admits a rooted arborescence.

Let $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, identified with $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure, and $f\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$. The Fourier coefficients are $\hat f(n)=\int_0^1 f(x)e^{-2\pi i n x}\,dx$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, with $|\hat f(n)|\le\|f\|_1$; the Fourier series is $\sum_n\hat f(n)e^{2\pi i n x}$. Convolution on $\mathbb T$ is $(f*g)(x)=\int_0^1 f(x-y)g(y)\,dy$ and $\widehat{f*g}(n)=\hat f(n)\hat g(n)$. The symmetric partial sums are $S_Nf(x)=\sum_{|n|\le N}\hat f(n)e^{2\pi i n x}=(f*D_N)(x)$ with the Dirichlet kernel $D_N(x)=\sum_{|n|\le N}e^{2\pi i n x}=\sin((2N+1)\pi x)/\sin(\pi x)$; $D_N$ is even, $\int_0^1 D_N=1$, but it changes sign and its Lebesgue constants $\|D_N\|_{L^1(\mathbb T)}=\frac{4}{\pi^2}\log N+O(1)$ tend to infinity. The Fejer (Cesaro) means are $\sigma_Nf=\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_{k=0}^N S_kf=f*F_N$ with the Fejer kernel $F_N(x)=\frac{1}{N+1}\left(\frac{\sin((N+1)\pi x)}{\sin(\pi x)}\right)^2=\sum_{|n|\le N}\left(1-\frac{|n|}{N+1}\right)e^{2\pi i n x}$; $F_N\ge0$, $\int_0^1F_N=1$, and $F_N(x)\le\min\{N+1,\;1/((N+1)\sin^2(\pi x))\}$. Periods other than 1 are handled by rescaling (for period $2\pi$: $\hat f(n)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(t)e^{-int}dt$).
f is 1-periodic and Lebesgue integrable over one period

[Theorem discreteIPS of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let the input process for the discrete-time interacting particle system be 
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}} = \left\{(x, M(x),\mathbf{L}_x)\in\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M}  \times \mathbb{L}^J\right\}$,
where $J \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbf{L}_x$ are vectors of i.i.d.
elements of $\mathbb{L}$, independent of $\sum_x \delta_{(x,M(x))}$. Put
\begin{equation}

\mu_n^{\xi} := \sum_{x \in \mathcal{P} \cap W_n} \xi (\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)  \delta_{n^{-1/d}x}.
\end{equation}
If 
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ and $\xi$ respectively satisfy assumptions~(i.thmIPS of the paper) and~(iii.thmIPS of the paper) in Theorem ~(thmIPS of the paper), 
$\Phi_j$ are update rules as at ~(equation e:updaterulef-discrete of the paper) with respect to a stabilizing interaction graph $\Psi$ on finite windows with respect to $\mathcal{P}$ as in (equation e:ddecay of the paper), then
 the random measures $(\mu_n^{\xi})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfy the central limit theorem. That is, for every test function $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ such that
$
{\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)] = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$,
we have
$$
({\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)])^{-1/2} \big(\mu_n^{\xi}(f) - \mathbb {E} [\mu_n^{\xi}(f)]\big)  \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,$$
where $Z$ is a standard Gaussian random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2604.25336, 'Central limit theorem for slow-fast system under mixed fractional Brownian motion'] Under assumptions \textbf{A1}-\textbf{A3} and \(\bar g (x)= \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} g(x,y)\mu(dy)=0\). Define that 
\begin{equation}
\Psi(x,y) =\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{P}_t g(x, Y_t) \dd t.
\end{equation} 
The \(\Psi(x,y)\) is the solution to the Poisson equation \eqref{Poisson_eq} where \(h\) is replaced by \(g\).
Moreover, \(\Psi(x,y)\in C^2\). For all \((x,y)\in \mathbb{R}^n\times \mathbb{R}^m\), \(D_x\Psi(x,y)\) and \(D^2_{xx}\Psi(x,y)\) is linear growth. \(D_y\Psi(x,y), D^2_{xy}\Psi(x,y), D^2_{yy}\Psi(x,y)\) is globally bounded. 
Furthermore, since \(Y\) is independent of \(x\), \(\Psi\in C^2\) is Lipshitz continuous with respect to \(y\) uniformly over all \(x\) . (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma orth-spc-ev-lrQ of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] For any $V\in\textbf{\textup{L}}$, the functor $\ev_V\colon\cat{$\bm G$-\textbf{\textup{L}}-Top}\to\cat{$\bm{({\textup{O}}(V)\times G)}$-Top}$ is both left and right Quillen for the level model structure on the source and the $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(V),G}$-model structure on the target.
    \begin{proof}
        The functor $\ev_V$ has both adjoints (given by enriched Kan extension), and it is clear from the definitions that it preserves weak equivalences and fibrations. It only remains to show that it also preserves cofibrations, for which it again suffices to show that $\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,V)\times_\varphi G=\varphi_!(\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,V))$ is a cofibrant in the $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(V),G}$-model structure for every homomorphism $\varphi\colon H\to G$ and any finite faithful $H$-representation $U$. 
        
        By Example~(ex:graph-restr-rQ of the paper), it will suffice to treat the case $\varphi=\textup{id}$. If $\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,V)=\emptyset$, there is nothing to prove, otherwise we may identify $U$ with a subspace of $V$. Then the homeomorphism ${\textup{O}}(V)/{\textup{O}}(V-U)\to\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,V)$ from Remark~(rk:L-top-explicit of the paper) is just the restriction map, which is easily seen to be $(H\times G)$-equivariant with respect to the action on the source via pre- and postcomposition. By Illman's theorem, ${\textup{O}}(V)$ admits the structure of an $({\textup{O}}(V-U)\times {\textup{O}}(V)\times H)$-CW-complex; moreover, the isotropy of any cell of this decomposition has to be contained in $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(V-U)\times {\textup{O}}(V),H}$ as $H$ acts freely on ${\textup{O}}(V)$ by faithfulness of $U\subset V$. Thus, ${\textup{O}}(V)$ is $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(V-U)\times {\textup{O}}(V),H}$-cofibrant, and hence $\textbf{\textup{L}}(U,V)\cong{\textup{O}}(V)/{\textup{O}}(V-U)$ is $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(V),H}$-cofibrant by another application of Example~(ex:graph-restr-rQ of the paper)
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2608.30859, 'Conservation Laws with Discontinuous Flux:\\ A First Application to Traffic Flow'] Given a constant $a>0$, let $v:[0,\tau]\times\R \rightarrow \R$ be a function with properties:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] The function $x\rightarrow v(t,x)$ increases at all times.
    \item[(ii)] For every Lipschitz curve $t\rightarrow\gamma(t)$ with derivative $\dot\gamma(t)\ge a - \varepsilon$, the composite function $t\rightarrow v(t,\gamma(t))$ is decreasing. 
\end{itemize}
Consider any couple of Lipschitz functions $y,z:[0,\tau]\rightarrow \R$ such that 
\[
y(0)=z(0)=0, \quad \dot y(t) \ge a,  \ \dot z(t)\ge a \quad \mbox{for a.e. } t\in[0,\tau],
\]
and define 
\[
v_{max}=\sup_{t,x} v(t,x), \quad v_{min}=\inf_{t,x} v(t,x), \quad \delta(t) = \sup_{0<s<t}|y(s)-z(s)|.
\]
Then, for every $t\in[0,\tau]$ one has
\begin{equation}
    \int_0^t |v(s,y(s))-v(s,z(s)))| ds \leq 2 \delta(t)\,\frac{v_{max}-v_{min}}{\epsilon}.
\end{equation}

[Prop 15 of arXiv:2607.03924, 'Tree Coordinates and Range Martingales for Positive Operator-Valued Measures'] Let $\left(K,P,V\right)$ be a minimal Naimark dilation
of $E$, and let $c>0$. If $F\in\mathcal{M}_{+}\left(\Omega_{m},H\right)$
satisfies $F\leq cE$, then there is a unique positive operator $T\in B\left(K\right)$
such that 
\[
0\leq T\leq cI_{K},
\]
\[
TP\left(B\right)=P\left(B\right)T,\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right),
\]
and 
\[
F\left(B\right)=V^{*}P\left(B\right)TV,\qquad B\in\mathcal{B}\left(\Omega_{m}\right).
\]
Conversely, every such operator $T$ defines an element $F\in\mathcal{M}_{+}\left(\Omega_{m},H\right)$
satisfying $F\leq cE$ by this formula. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary cor:Stein.Wishart.generator.step.1 of arXiv:2606.04859, 'Stein's method for the Wishart distribution'] Let $\alpha\in (d-1,\infty)$ and $\Sigma\in \mathcal{S}_{++}^d$ be given. Then
\[
\mathfrak{W}\sim \mathcal{W}_d(\alpha, \Sigma) \qquad \Leftrightarrow \qquad \mathsf{E}\big[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{W}} f(\mathfrak{W})\big] = 0 ~~\forall f\in C_{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{W}}}^2(\mathcal{S}_{++}^d),
\]
where, for $\mathfrak{W}_{\infty}\sim \mathcal{W}_d(\alpha, \Sigma)$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
C_{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{W}}}^2(\mathcal{S}_{++}^d)
&\vcentcolon= \Big\{f\in C^2(\mathcal{S}_{++}^d) :
\mathsf{E}[|\mathrm{tr}\{\Sigma \nabla f(\mathfrak{W}_{\infty})\}|] < \infty, ~\mathsf{E}[|\mathrm{tr}\{\mathfrak{W}_{\infty} \nabla f(\mathfrak{W}_{\infty})\}|] < \infty, \Big. \\[-2mm]
&\hspace{43.7mm} \Big. \mathsf{E}[|\mathrm{tr}\{\mathfrak{W}_{\infty} \nabla \Sigma \nabla f(\mathfrak{W}_{\infty})\}|] < \infty, ~\mathsf{E}[|f(\mathfrak{W}_{\infty})|] < \infty, \Big. \\[-2mm]
&\hspace{68.4mm} \Big.\text{and } \mathsf{E}\big[\|\mathfrak{W}_{\infty}^{1/2}\nabla f(\mathfrak{W}_{\infty})\Sigma^{1/2}\|_F^2\big] < \infty~\Big\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Status: proof draft (unaudited). This lemma replaces an unproved extension of the published local-minimum Gram theorem; it does not assume that extension.

## General local ODE lemma
Let F be C^2 near zero in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, F(0)=0, and J=DF(0) symmetric. Let lambda>0 be its largest eigenvalue, E its full eigenspace, and P the orthogonal projection onto E. The multiplicity of lambda is arbitrary. Fix a unit u in E. Let initial data d_epsilon satisfy
  P d_epsilon=p_epsilon u, p_epsilon>0, p_epsilon->0,
  ||d_epsilon||<=C p_epsilon.
Then the solutions shifted by tau_epsilon=log(1/p_epsilon)/lambda converge uniformly on every compact interval where the canonical solution exists to a unique path h solving
  h'=F(h),
  h(t)=exp(lambda t)u+integral_-infinity^t exp(J(t-v))N(h(v))dv,
  N(x)=F(x)-Jx.
In particular h(t)=exp(lambda t)u+O(exp(2lambda t)) backwards. The canonical path is defined on a negative half-line and extended by its ODE. Forward compact convergence is asserted only up to its maximal forward lifetime unless an independent global-existence argument is available.

## Proof
On a small ball, ||N(x)||<=K||x||^2 and ||N(x)-N(y)||<=K(||x||+||y||)||x-y||. In shifted time the initial time is -tau. The free evolution obeys
  ||exp(J(t+tau))d||<=C exp(lambda t), t>=-tau,
since J is symmetric and every eigenvalue is <=lambda. In a weighted supremum ||x(t)||exp(-lambda t), Duhamel bounds the quadratic term by
  (K/ lambda) A^2 exp(lambda T)
on [-tau,T] whenever the weighted norm is <=A. Choose a fixed negative T so a continuity bootstrap from C to 2C cannot cross 2C, and so the resulting ball stays in the local domain of F. Thus ||x_epsilon(t)||<=2C exp(lambda t) there, uniformly in epsilon.

The top part of the free evolution is exactly exp(lambda t)u. For an eigenspace with eigenvalue nu<lambda its free part has norm bounded by
  C p_epsilon^(1-nu/lambda) exp(nu t),
which tends to zero uniformly on each fixed shifted compact interval. No convergence of the bounded normalized lower initial components is needed. On each such interval, the solutions and their derivatives are uniformly bounded. Diagonal Arzela-Ascoli therefore yields a locally uniform subsequential limit on (-infinity,T].

The nonlinear integrand is bounded uniformly by
  exp(lambda(t-v)) K(2C)^2 exp(2lambda v)
    =K(2C)^2 exp(lambda t)exp(lambda v),
which is integrable at minus infinity. A fixed-tail split passes Duhamel to the displayed Volterra equation. Its operator is a contraction in the exp(lambda t) weighted ball on a sufficiently negative half-line: its Lipschitz constant is bounded by a fixed multiple of exp(lambda T)/lambda. Thus its solution is unique in the class O(exp(lambda t)); for two possible bounds choose a common larger bound and a more negative T. Existence follows from the subsequential limit. Uniqueness identifies every subsequential limit, proving whole-family convergence. Integrating the same quadratic bound gives the O(exp(2lambda t)) backward remainder. Finite-interval continuous dependence extends convergence along every compact part of the canonical solution. QED, subject to independent review.

## The two essential restrictions
The normalized FULL top projection must be fixed (or converge to u with an explicit equivalent argument). A rotating top vector need not converge when the top eigenspace has dimension above one. Also ||d||=O(p) cannot be omitted: for J=diag(2,1), initial data (p,sqrt(p)) have top projection p e1 but at the shift log(1/p)/2 their lower coordinate stays of order one and changes the limit. This is an exact linear boundary, not numerical evidence.

## Application to the actual rank-one saddle
Use the full parameter space of B,A and its Euclidean factor metric, centered at theta1=[zstar,0,...,0], where zstar is a nonzero balanced rank-one critical factor. The factor flow is negative gradient of the scalar loss, so its Jacobian is symmetric. Direct differentiation at zero dormant columns makes it block diagonal:
  Jfull=diag(Jact,Lstar,...,Lstar).
C009 proves largest eigenvalue(Jact)=r<s. Each frozen dormant block has eigenvalues s,0,0,-s. Thus the full largest eigenvalue is s, with multiplicity w-1, and its full eigenspace consists of v times arbitrary dormant hidden rows. A nonminimal active saddle does not change this strict spectral separation.

At the aligned arrival supplied by C009, the active endpoint error is O(p^2), the dormant norm is O(p), and the row v^T X has norm p. Make a hidden orthogonal rotation of the DORMANT columns only, fixed for the subsequent flow, taking that row to (p,0,...,0). This leaves theta1 unchanged. The full top parameter projection is now EXACTLY p times the fixed vector u having v in the first dormant column and zero elsewhere; total parameter error is O(p). The general lemma applies with lambda=s even though its top eigenvalue is multiple. This is a parameter theorem; it does not smuggle a simple-top assumption into a multiple-top Hessian.

## The canonical path has a nonzero width-two realization
The subspace with only the active and first dormant columns nonzero is invariant under the factor ODE. It is also preserved by J and the Volterra map because every zero factor column has identically zero derivative. Uniqueness therefore makes the canonical path have exactly this width-two realization. The backward expansion gives
  z(t)=zstar+O(exp(2st)),
  x(t)=exp(st)v+O(exp(2st)).
The input part of v is a nonzero residual singular vector perpendicular to astar, and its output part is perpendicular to bstar. The input and output square factors consequently have determinants with nonzero leading terms of order exp(st); both are invertible for all sufficiently negative finite t. This proves a nonzero rank-two canonical mode; rank is not inferred from limits of finite-rank matrices alone.

The factor balance matrix is conserved and tends to its value at theta1, which is zero, so the canonical width-two factors are exactly balanced. In the oriented endpoint frames, v=(delta lperp;rperp)/sqrt(2) up to simultaneous sign, with delta=sign det M by C003's determinant identity. The graph determinant of the canonical two-column plane is therefore delta at sufficiently negative times and remains so. Its loss is strictly below the first critical loss because the path is nonconstant gradient flow, and that critical loss is strictly below C(0) by the stationary energy identity in C010. C010 therefore gives global forward existence, factor convergence and endpoint product M for this canonical path.

## Clocks and original factor rotations
The parameter shift in this lemma is log(1/p)/s. At the actual C009 arrival, z-zstar=O(p^2) and v perpendicular to zstar, so
  a=v^T Z v=p^2+(v^T z)^2=p^2+O(p^4).

[Proposition prop:HI-before-HS of arXiv:2606.27573, 'Conditional Path Decomposition at the Infimum and Maximum Drawdowns for Spectrally Negativ'] Under $\mathbb{P}_{a,b}^{<}$, the pre-$H_I$ process, the intermediate process
$$
\{X_{H_I+u}:0\le u\le H_S-H_I\},
$$
and the post-$H_S$ process are independent.  Their laws are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The pre-infimum process is the Doob transform of the process killed on leaving $(a,b)$ through the lower boundary, with
\begin{equation}\hspace{-1,4cm}
h_1(x)=
\frac{W^{(\gamma)\prime}(x-a)W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)-W^{(\gamma)\prime}(b-a)W^{(\gamma)}(x-a)}
     {\big(W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)\big)^2},
\qquad a<x<b.
\end{equation}

\item The intermediate process has the law of $a+\Gamma$, where $\Gamma$ is the Doob transform of a spectrally negative L\'{e}vy process killed at $\tau_{b-a}^+\wedge\tau_0^-$, with
\begin{equation}
h_2(z)=e^{-\Phi(\gamma)(b-a-z)}\frac{W^{(\gamma)}(z)}{W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)},
\qquad 0<z<b-a.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, in the original coordinate $x=a+z$,
\[
h_2^a(x)=e^{-\Phi(\gamma)(b-x)}\frac{W^{(\gamma)}(x-a)}{W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)}.
\]

\item The post-$H_S$ process is the Doob transform of the process killed on leaving $(a,b)$ before $T$, with
\begin{equation}
h_3(x)=1-Z^{(\gamma)}(x-a)+\big(Z^{(\gamma)}(b-a)-1\big)\frac{W^{(\gamma)}(x-a)}{W^{(\gamma)}(b-a)},
\qquad a<x<b.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Decomposition under $H_I<H_S$

Let d>=2, p=d-1, S a nondegenerate centered p-simplex, A invertible, c(y)=c_0+y*c_1, and r(y)=alpha+(beta-alpha)y with alpha,beta>=0 and alpha+beta>0. [Lemma lem:chirurgieloc of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Fix a rooted graph in $\Omega^{\mathrm{very\, good}}$ then fix a family of weights $w(e)_{e \in E(G_n)}$ and pick $e_1 \in B_H(G_n,o_n)$.
         Assume that $i(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1})+i(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1})=1$.
         Then there exists $e_2 \sim e_1$ such that $i(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2})+i(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2})=1$ and:
         \begin{itemize}
             \item If $e_1\in M_{\mathrm{opt}}$ then there exists $a>0$ such that setting $w'(e_2)=a$ and $w'=w$ elsewhere gives $\max(Z_-(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2}),Z_+(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2}))+\max(Z_-(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2}),Z_+(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2}))<w'(e_2)=a.$
             \item If $e_1 \notin M_{\mathrm{opt}}$, then there exists $b>0$ such that setting $w'(e_1)=b$ and $w'=w$ elsewhere gives $\max(Z_-(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1}),Z_+(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1}))+\max(Z_-(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1}),Z_+(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1}))<w'(e_1)=b$.
         \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 38 (Uniform moments for the \texorpdfstring{\eqref{eq:kTULA}}{kTULA} scheme) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Let Assumptions~\hyperref[ass:PJG]{(A1)}--\hyperref[ass:D]{(A4)} hold.
There exists $\lambda_{\max}>0$ such that for all $0<\lambda\le\lambda_{\max}$ the following holds.
Let $(\widehat X_n)_{n\ge0}$ denote the kTULA iterates and let $\widehat X_t$ be any continuous
interpolation on $[n\lambda,(n+1)\lambda]$ satisfying $\widehat X_{n\lambda}=\widehat X_n$.
Then for every $p\ge2$ there exists a constant $c_p<\infty$ such that for all $t\in[n\lambda,(n+1)\lambda]$,
\[
  \E\|\widehat X_t\|^{2p}
  \;\le\;
  (1-a(t-n\lambda))(1-a\lambda)^n\,\E\|\widehat X_0\|^{2p}
  + c_p\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{a}\Bigr).
\]
In particular,
\[
  \sup_{t\ge0}\E\|\widehat X_t\|^{2p}
  \;\le\;
  \E\|\widehat X_0\|^{2p} + c_p\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{a}\Bigr)
  <\infty.
\]

A Borel subtree class as specified

Let $n$ be a large positive integer and $p\in (0, 1)$ a probability satisfying $1/3\geq p\geq n^{-1/5}(\log n)^A$, where $A$ is a large absolute constant. For every $d\geq C_\varepsilon n^3p^3 (\log p^{-1})^3$, we have
\[\TV(G(n, p), G(n, d, p))\leq \varepsilon.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (M,g) be a connected Riemannian manifold with induced distance function d. The following are equivalent: (1) (M,d) is a complete metric space; (2) M is geodesically complete, i.e. for every p in M the exponential map exp_p is defined on all of T_pM; (3) M is geodesically complete at some single point p, i.e. exp_p is defined on all of T_pM for at least one p; (4) every closed and bounded subset of M is compact. If any of these hold, then any two points of M can be joined by a minimizing geodesic, a geodesic segment whose length equals the distance between its endpoints.
M is a connected smooth Riemannian manifold

[Proposition p:mppmix_double of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Fix $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r \in (0, \infty)$. Assume that $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ satisfies condition~(ii:mppmix_double of the paper)  of Lemma~(p:mppmixcl_double of the paper). Let $\xi: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{K}'$ be a marking function such that $\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) =  \xi^{(r)}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) =\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}\cap B_r(x))$ for all $(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}}$. Consider the marked point process $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}=\sum_{x \in \mathcal{P}} \delta_{(x,V(x))}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d\times \mathbb{K}'$ where $V(x) := \xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})$.  

Then, for  all $f \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^p),$   $g \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^q)$, for almost all $\bk x1{p+q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d(p+q)}$ such that $s:=d(\bk x1p,\bk x{p+1}{p+q}) >4r$, and with ${w}_0= 4(p+q)\theta_d r^d$
we have
\begin{align} \nonumber
& \Big| \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{p+q}}[f(\bk V1{p})g(\bk V{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(p+q)}(\bk x1{p+q}) -
\mathbb {E} _{\bk x1p}[f(\bk V1p)] \rho^{(p)}(\bk x1{p}) \; \mathbb {E} _{\bk x{p+1}{p+q}}[g(\bk V{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(q)}(\bk
x{p+1}{p+q}) \Big|
\\
&\le 
\phi( \frac{s}{2})\sum_{l=1}^\infty \frac{w_0^l}{l!}  C_{l+p+q}
=:\phi( \frac{s}{2})\hat{C}_{p+q}<\infty.
\end{align}

Thus the marked point process
 $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the inequality~(equation e.Bmppmixing of the paper)  in Definition~(B-omega-mixing of the paper)(Bmixing of the paper) 
for $s>4r$, with  $\omega_{p+q}(s):=\hat C_{p+q}\phi(s/2)$ where  $p,q,\phi$ are as above.

[Proposition prop:2.8 of arXiv:2607.24164, 'The KLS constant is $O(\log^{1/4} n)$'] Let $W\sim\lambda$ be log-concave, and let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be locally
Lipschitz. Suppose that $f,\partial_i f\in L^2(\lambda)$ and
\[
  \mathbb{E}_{W\sim\lambda}\partial_i f(W)=0,
  \qquad 1\leqslant i\leqslant n.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  \Var_{W\sim\lambda}\bigl(f(W)\bigr)
  \leqslant
  \sum_{i=1}^n
  \norm{\partial_i f}_{H^{-1}(\lambda)}^2.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma zygmund-marcinkiewicz of arXiv:2411.07737, 'On Asymptotic Behavior of Extinction Moment of Critical Bisexual Branching Process in Rand'] Let $\{ \xi_n \}_{n = 1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. r.v. with $\ER \abs*{\xi_n}^{\alpha} < \infty$, where $1 \leq \alpha \leq 2$, and $\ER \xi_n = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
    Then, there is a constant $c_{\alpha} > 0$ such that
    \[
        \left( \ER \abs*{ \sum_{i = 1}^n \xi_i } \right)^{\alpha}
        \leq \ER \abs*{ \sum_{i = 1}^n \xi_i }^{\alpha}
        \leq c_{\alpha} \sum_{i = 1}^n \ER \abs*{\xi_i}^{\alpha}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequality,~\cite{Marcinkiewicz1938}

body:
[Prop P:two-point-bd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $n \in \mathbb{N}$, parameter $\alpha \ge 1/2 - n^{-1/6}$, and $x, y, z_0 \in \llbracket0, n/100 \rrbracket$, $a > 0$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
	
C_0 \max \left(\frac{z_0^2}{n}, \frac{z_0 |y-x|}{n}, z_0(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0 \right) < a < C_* z_0,
\end{equation}
where $C_0>0$ is a universal constant, and $C_*>0$ is any large enough number.
Then for a constant $c>0$ depending only on $C_*$, we have
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{z \in\llbracket0,z_0 \rrbracket} \left|\bar X[x, 1; y + z, n]_\textsf{L} - \bar X[x, 1; y, n]_\textsf{L} \right| \ge a \right) \le 2\exp(- c a^2/z_0) + 2 \exp(-c \sqrt{n}).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop P:two-point-bd of arXiv:2604.10020

[Cor 15 of arXiv:2604.25725, 'What is The Probability That A Random Graph With A Given Degree Sequence is Connected?'] Fix $0<\eps<10^{-6}$ and let $\cD$ be such that $m$ is large enough and $n_1,n_2 \le 10^{-6} m$.
    Let $v\in[n]$ be fixed. Then the probability that there exists an $i$  with  $1\leq i \leq m$  such that  $2|E(H_{i-1})|+|X_{i-1}| \leq \eps m$, and such that neither
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item $X_i \ge 0.9\sum_{j=1}^i d_j(v_j)-\frac{m}{\log m}$, nor
    \item  $D^*\ge \epsilon m$ and 
    $H_i$ contains a vertex of degree at least $\sqrt{m}(\log m)^{-2}$
\end{enumerate}
holds, is at most $e^{-m^{1/11}}$.
title: Cor 15 of arXiv:2604.25725

u_h(B_{\xi\wedge\eta})^{- eta}$ for some $ eta>0$ determined by the transmission/Martin exponents, where $\xi\wedge\eta$ is the confluence depth. Then
 egin{align*}
\|K_\infty\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2&=\iint_{\partial T	imes\partial T}|k_\infty(\xi,\eta)|^2\,d
u_h(\xi)\,d
u_h(\eta)\
&\asymp\sum_{n\ge0} r(T)^{2n eta}\cdot
u_h\otimes
u_h ig(\{|\xi\wedge\eta|=n\} ig)\asymp\sum_{n\ge0} r(T)^{n(2 eta-1)}
\end{align*}
whenever $2 eta\ge1$ and $g$ is supercritical ($ r(T)>1$). For the Martin-kernel construction one has $ eta\ge1$, since $K(x,\cdot)\asymp
u_h(B_{|x|})^{-1}$ on the cylinder of $x$ (the Martin kernel is the harmonic-measure density $d
u_h^x/d
u_h$). Hence $K_\infty$ is not Hilbert--Schmidt, and the Krein--Rutman route through Hilbert--Schmidt compactness is unavailable.

[Theorem 61 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] Let $\Sigma = \Sigma_{g,p}$ be a punctured surface with $g\geqslant 2,p\geqslant 1$. Let $s\in\{\pm 1\}^p$ and $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
    \item $p_+(s)=1$ and $n=\chi(\Sigma)+1$, or
    \item $p_-(s)=1$ and $n=-\chi(\Sigma)-1$
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathcal{NH}^s_n$ has measure zero.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03634, 'Joint Laws of Maximum Drawdown and Maximum Drawup for Spectrally Negative L\'{e}vy...'] Let $X$ be a spectrally negative L\'{e}vy process observed up to an independent exponential time $T$ with parameter $\gamma>0$. We study the joint law of the maximum drawdown and the maximum drawup of $X$ on $[0,T]$. The path is decomposed according to the two possible orderings of its infimum and supremum. Conditional on the values of these extrema and on their ordering, the resulting pre-, intermediate, and post- components are independent. We identify their laws as Doob $h$-transforms of killed spectrally negative L\'{e}vy processes and express the corresponding distribution functions explicitly in terms of the $\gamma$-scale functions $W^{(\gamma)}$ and $Z^{(\gamma)}$ and their derivatives. Combining the conditional laws with the joint densities of the extrema yields integral representations of the joint distribution and moments.

body:
[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.

		c_1 t^\beta \leq \mathbb{P}(W \leq t) \leq c_2 t^\beta

		\[
		f(x)\sim C\,x^{-1/d_F}
		\qquad\text{as } x\to\infty,
		\]
		for some constant $C>0$.
		Moreover $f(x) \xrightarrow[x \to 0]{} L$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A standard Brownian motion, or Wiener process, is a real-valued stochastic process (W_t)_{t >= 0} on a probability space such that (i) W_0 = 0 almost surely; (ii) for 0 <= s < t the increment W_t - W_s is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance t - s; (iii) increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; (iv) almost every sample path t |-> W_t is continuous. Existence is Wiener's theorem (constructed for instance by the Levy-Ciesielski series or as the Kolmogorov-extension limit with continuity from Kolmogorov's criterion, since E|W_t - W_s|^4 = 3 (t - s)^2). Consequences packaged with the definition: the covariance is E[W_s W_t] = min(s, t); paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable and have unbounded variation on every interval, with quadratic variation t; Brownian scaling c^{-1/2} W_{c t}, time inversion t W_{1/t}, and reflection are again Brownian motions; W is a continuous martingale and a Markov process with transition density the Gaussian kernel. Conditions (i)-(iii) characterise the finite-dimensional laws; (iv) selects the continuous version, which is the object meant in every theorem about paths.

[Corollary c:classical-observables of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'] Let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2:[0,1]\rightarrow\Sigma$ be two $\mathcal{C}^1$ curves such that $\gamma_1(0),\gamma_1(1)$ belong to $W^u(a_1)$ and $\gamma_2([0,1])\subset W^u(a_1)$. Then, the maps
$$
A\in\Omega^1(\Sigma,\mathfrak{g})\mapsto \lim_{T\rightarrow +\infty}\operatorname{Hol}_{\gamma_1}(A_{T}) \in G,
$$
and
$$
A\in\Omega^1(\Sigma,\mathfrak{g})\mapsto\int_{\gamma_2} A_\infty\in\mathfrak{g}
$$
induce maps from the moduli space $\Omega^1(\Sigma,\mathrm{g})/\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\Sigma,G)$ to $G/\mathbf{Ad}$ and $\mathfrak{g}/\operatorname{Ad}$ respectively, where $A_1\sim A_2\in \Omega^1(\Sigma,\mathfrak{g})$ means that $A_2=\mathrm{g}^{-1}d\mathrm{g}+\mathrm{g}^{-1}A_1\mathrm{g}$ for some $\mathrm{g}\in C^\infty(\Sigma,G).$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Classical admissible observables

Under this limit, Macdonald polynomials P_lambda(x; q, t) degenerate to Jack symmetric functions P_lambda^(1/alpha)(x).

body:
In population dynamics, environmental stochasticity is modeled via multiplicative noise sigma_ext(N) = sigma * N dB_t, representing climate or exogenous fluctuations affecting all individuals identically; its diffusion variance is quadratic in population size and creates strong boundary absorption at zero. By contrast, internal demographic noise arises from independent individual events with variance sigma_int^2(N) ~ O(N), which becomes negligibly small relative to drift near the origin, preserving the invariance of the positive state space.
Comparison between linear diffusion sigma*N and sublinear diffusion sqrt(N)
title: Comparison of Internal and Environmental Stochasticity

of $\nu$.

Now write $s=\sech^2 y$ with $y\ge 0$.  Then \eqref{e:r-def} becomes
\[
r(s(y))=
\frac{2}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\sech^2 y\,e^{-\frac{y^2+h^2}{2\sigma^2}}\cosh\left(\frac{hy}{\sigma^2}\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{d}{dy}\log r\big(s(y)\big)
=-2\tanh y-\frac{y}{\sigma^2}+\frac{h}{\sigma^2}\tanh\left(\frac{hy}{\sigma^2}\right).
\]
Set $c=h/\sigma^2\le 1$.  Then for $y\ge 0$,
\[
c\tanh(cy)\le c\tanh y\le \tanh y,
\]
so
\[

		\[

body:
[Lemm l:mesh-geo-deloc of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] For $u=(0,z;\delta^{3/2},w)$ with $z,w\in J^\delta$, 
    let $\Gamma_u$ be the mesh geodesic (see (def:discrete-LPP of the paper)).
    For $k\in\llbracket1,n-1\rrbracket$, we define the event
    \begin{align*}
        \mathsf{MeshGeoDeloc}^k_u \coloneqq  
        \left\{
            (\bm{\mathcal{L}}^{\mathrm{near}}, \bm{\mathcal{L}}^{\mathrm{far}}, \bm{\mathcal{L}}^{\mathrm{bdry}}) : 
            \left|
                \Gamma_u(t_k)
            \right|
            \wedge
            \left|
                \Gamma_u(t_{k+1})
            \right|
        > \varepsilon\log^4(1/\varepsilon)
        \right\},
    \end{align*}
    where $t_k,t_{k+1}$ were defined in (equation e:eps-mesh-times of the paper).
    Note that the above event depends on $\varepsilon$.

    There exists $C>0$ such that for all small $\delta>0$ and $\varepsilon\leqslant \delta^{100/\gamma}$,
    \begin{align*}
        \sup_u
        \max_{k\in\llbracket 1,n-1\rrbracket}
        \mathbb{P}\left(\neg \mathsf{MeshGeoDeloc}^k_u\right) \leqslant  C \varepsilon^{1-3\gamma},
    \end{align*}
    where the supremum is over all $u=(0,z;\delta^{3/2},w)$ with $z,w\in J^\delta$.
title: Mesh geodesic delocalization

 \[

 \]

 \[

 \hat A+\hat B+\hat C-\hat{\mathfrak{t}}&& \textnormal{if}\,\,\max(\hat B,\hat C)\leq \hat{\mathfrak{t}}<\hat B+\hat C, \end{array} \right.
\]
 and the equilibrium measure of the discrete ensemble \eqref{eq_Hahn_hole_ensemble} has a band in each of the segments $[\hat a'_1+\eps,\hat b'_1-\eps]$ and $[\hat a'_2+\eps,\hat b'_2-\eps]$.

Fix a finite class set Y, positive weights w_i summing to1, means mu_i in R^d, and a shared positive-definite covariance Sigma. Under the forward Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model dU_s=-U_s ds+sqrt(2)dW_s, put Sigma_s=exp(-2s)*Sigma+(1-exp(-2s))*I and p_s(x,i)=w_i*N(x;exp(-s)*mu_i,Sigma_s). Let p_s(x)=sum_i p_s(x,i) and q_s(i|x)=p_s(x,i)/p_s(x). Fix a class y, finite horizon T>0 and a constant guidance increment eta>=0. In increasing sampling time t, s=T-t, define guided DDIM by dX_t/dt=b_eta(X_t,t), b_eta(x,t)=x+grad_x log p_s(x,y)+eta*grad_x log q_s(y|x). Unguided DDIM is dZ_t/dt=b_0(Z_t,t). Let Phi_t be the guided flow and J_t(a)=D_a Phi_t(a), with J_0=I. Let M_t solve M_dot=(I-Sigma_(T-t)^(-1))*M, M_0=I; the unguided flow is affine Z_t=M_t Z_0+xi_t. For all a in R^d and 0<=t<=T, 0<det J_t(a)<=det M_t. For the fixed model and finite horizon, det J_t(a) is bounded above and bounded away from zero uniformly in a and t. This is the determinant comparison used in the paper's entropy proof; its constants are not dimension-free or uniform over eta.
Finite Gaussian mixture with strictly positive class probabilities and shared positive-definite covariance; arbitrary component means.
Exact conditional and marginal scores of the stated OU model; deterministic continuous-time DDIM.

body: Brouwer's fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem in topology, named after L. E. J. (Bertus) Brouwer. It states that for any continuous function f mapping a nonempty compact convex set to itself, there is a point x_0 such that f(x_0) = x_0. The simplest forms of Brouwer's theorem are for continuous functions f from a closed interval I in the real numbers to itself or from a closed disk D to itself. A more general form than the latter is for continuous functions from a nonempty convex compact subset K of Euclidean space to itself.

body: [Theorem thm:h00 of arXiv:2608.26564, 'Real ideal points, Conway spheres, and left-orderable Dehn fillings'] Let $B$ be a real half-branch as in Proposition (prop:branchmodel of the paper), with associated representations $\rho_u$ and meridian-normalized lifts $\widetilde\rho_u$. Suppose the homological longitude admits a four-longitude decomposition $\lambda=\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3\ell_4$ in positive parabolic normal form along $B$. Then for $u$ sufficiently small, the expanding eigenline $v_u\in\mathbb RP^1$ of $\rho_u(\mu)$ is well-defined and depends continuously on $u$. The pairs $(\widetilde\rho_u,v_u)$ form a continuous family of augmented peripherally hyperbolic representations, and $\operatorname{EV}(\widetilde\rho_u,v_u) = \bigl(x(u),y(u);0,h_1+h_2+h_3+h_4\bigr)$, where $x(u)=\log|a_\mu(u)|$ and $y(u)=\log|a_\lambda(u)|$, and $a_\mu(u),a_\lambda(u)$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho_u(\mu),\rho_u(\lambda)$ on $v_u$. Consequently, the image of this family is an augmented holonomy arc contained in $H_{0,h_1+h_2+h_3+h_4}(M)$.

    balanced standard extremal sequences of random variables
    for strongly balanced sequences
    $(\alpha_i, i \in\{1,\dots,m\})$ and $(\alpha_i', i \in \{1,\dots, m\})$ 
    respectively.
    
    
    
    
    Assume furthermore, that for each $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ there are integers $t_i$ such that
    \[
        
        \frac 1 K \le \alpha_i' \le  \alpha_i   = \frac {t_i} {K^2}  \le 1 - \frac 1 K, \quad  \alpha_i' \in \left[\frac {t_i-1} {K^2}, \frac {t_i} {K^2}\right].
    \]

    Let $Y$ be a symmetric log-concave integer random variable, independent of both the sequences. 
    

    Then 
    \[
        \mathbb P(X_1' + \dots + X_m' + Y = 0) \ge \mathbb P(X_1 + \dots + X_m + Y=0)(1-  39  K^{-\frac 1 6}) 
    \]

\[
 G_{n,d}(u)=d\sqrt u+
 \sqrt{du\log(e+n/u)},\qquad u>0.
\]
There are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that, for $0<s\le c\sqrt n$,
\begin{equation}
 c\mathcal I_{n,d}(s)

\end{equation}
The supremum of the empty set is understood as zero.

[Theorem thm:cc of arXiv:2605.26048, 'Classification of the eternal solutions and multiple coalescing shocks in the KPZ fixed po'] For almost-every $\omega$, the following hold. 
    \begin{enumerate} [label=(\roman*), font=\normalfont]
        \item For every $b \in \mathcal{B}_\omega$, the set $\pmb{\xi}^b$ is at most countable. 
        \item For every $\varphi \in \Phi_\omega$, $\pmb{\xi}^{W \star \varphi} = \operatorname{Dom}(\varphi)$, and this set is dense in $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$. 
        \item  For every $\varphi \in \Phi_\omega$, $\xi \in \pmb{\xi}^{W\star \varphi}$, and $(x,t) \in \mathfrak{C}^{W\star \varphi}(\xi)$,
        \[
        (W\star \varphi)(x,t) = \varphi(\xi) + W^\xi(0,0;x,t). 
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Defn localization of measure of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] Let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ be a simply connected domain, and let $u$ be a marked boundary point. Let $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n$ be distinct prime ends of $\partial \Omega$, and let $U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n$ be disjoint closed neighborhoods of $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n$ in $\Omega$ such that $u \notin U_j$ for all $j$ and $U_i \cap U_j = \emptyset$ for $1 \leq i < j \leq n$. 

We consider probability measures
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}
\]
on $n$-tuples of unparametrized continuous curves, where each curve starts at $z_j$, is contained in $U_j$, and exits $U_j$ almost surely. 

A family of such measures, indexed by different choices of neighborhoods $\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)$, is called \emph{compatible} if for all $U_j \subset U_j'$, the measure $\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}$ is obtained from 
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1', U_2', \ldots, U_n'\right)}
\]
by restricting each curve to the portion before it first exits the smaller domain $U_j$.
title: Localization of measures

[Cor cor_upper_boundary_examples of arXiv:2606.23648, '\textsc{Optimal Stopping for a Diffusion with Unobserved Bernoulli Drift}'] Assume that the hypotheses of Proposition
    (prop_upper_boundary_asymptotics of the paper) hold.

    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
        \item For power costs
        \(
            k(s)=\alpha s^\beta+\gamma,
            \, \alpha>0, \beta>1,
        \)
        one has
        \(
            b(x)\to+\infty,
        \)
        and more precisely
        \begin{equation}
            b(x)
            =
            y_0+\frac12\log\frac{2x}{\beta}+o(1), \qquad x \to \infty.
        \end{equation}

        \item For exponential costs
        \(
            k(s)=\alpha(e^{\lambda s}-\gamma),
            \, \alpha>0, 0<\lambda<2,
        \)
        one has
        \begin{equation}
            b(x)\to
            y_0+\frac12\log\frac{2-\lambda}{\lambda}.
        \end{equation}

[Prop eq:q(t|s) of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] The SMC jump chain $(X_{n})$ defined by ((eq:Xn+1 of the paper)) has
transition density
\begin{equation}
q_{\mathrm{SMC}}(t\mid s)=\frac{e^{-t}\left(e^{s\wedge t}-1\right)}{s},\quad s>0, t>0.
\end{equation}
It is irreducible and reversible with respect to 
\[
\mu(dt)=te^{-t} dt,
\]
and $\mu$ is the unique invariant probability measure.

The SMC' jump chain $(X'_{n})$ has transition density
$q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(t\mid s)$ given above. 
It is irreducible and reversible with respect to 
\[
\mu'(dt)=\frac{3}{8} \bigl(2t+1-e^{-2t}\bigr)e^{-t} dt.
\]
and $\mu'$ is the unique invariant probability measure. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop eq:q(t|s) of arXiv:2604.20629

[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2608.30549, '\vspace{-1cm}Maximally Spread Out Measures and Implications\\{} for Phase Transitions in A'] Let $\nu \geq 1$ and fix $0 < \varrho_0 \leq \frac{1}{4} < \frac{1}{2} \leq \varrho_1 < 1$.
  Then, the set
  \[
    \SC
    := \bigl\{ \indicator_{S} \,\,:\,\, S \in \mathrm{STAR}^2 (\nu; \varrho_0, \varrho_1) \bigr\}
    ,
  \]
  considered as a subset of $\XX = L^2 (\R^2)$, satisfies $\md(\SC) = 1$ and
  there exists a Borel probability measure on $\XX$ that is critical for $\SC$.

  Moreover, there exist a suitable \emph{cone-adapted shearlet system}
  (see \cite[Definition~5.6]{VoigtlaenderPeinAnalysisVSSynthesisSparsityAlphaShearlets}),
  a suitable enumeration $\CalG = (g_n)_{n \in \N}$ of this system,
  and a polynomial $P$ such that the family
  $(\CalA_n)_{n \in \N} = \bigl(\Sigma_n (\CalG, P)\bigr)_{n \in \N}$
  defined in \Cref{prop:PolynomiallyBoundedNTermApproximationControlledComplexity}
  is optimal for $\SC$ in the class of families of controlled complexity in $L^2(\RR^2)$.
  In particular, a phase transition as in
  \Cref{thm:PhaseTransitionForFamiliesWithControlledComplexity} occurs. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 12 (Harmonic dimension and directional energy) of arXiv:2608.24007, '2608.24007'] The dimension of $\mathcal V_{r,K}$ is
\[
    H_{r,K}
    =\binom{K+r-1}{r}-\binom{K+r-3}{r-2}.
\]
Let $P_{r,K}$ be orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal V_{r,K}$.  For every
unit vector $q\in\mathbb R^K$,
\[
    \left\|P_{r,K}h_r(q^\top z)\right\|_{L^2}^2
    =\alpha_{r,K},
\]
where, writing $r=2m$ or $r=2m+1$,
\[
    \alpha_{2m,K}
    =\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}
      \frac{K+2j-1}{K+2m+2j-2},
\]
and
\[
    \alpha_{2m+1,K}
    =\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}
      \frac{K+2j-1}{K+2m+2j}.
\]
For every fixed $r$, $H_{r,K}=\Theta_r(K^r)$ and
$\alpha_{r,K}\to1$ as $K\to\infty$.

body:
[Theorem thm:honest-region of arXiv:2608.20295, 'Physical-Support Confidence Sets for Highly Coherent Dictionaries'] Under Assumption~(ass:frozen-shell of the paper) and the calibration coverage condition
in Equation~(equation eq:training-rectangle of the paper), the totalized correspondence
$\widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}$ is measurable, nonempty, and
compact-valued. Uniformly over $\mathfrak P^p_{q,r}(s)$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb P_{p_\star,\nu_\star,D_\star}^N
\left[
\mathbb P_{\mu_\star,\sigma_\star}^T
\left\{
    \vartheta_\star
    \in
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
    \mid Y_{1:N}
\right\}
\ge1-\alpha_T
\right]
\ge1-\alpha_D.

\end{equation}
Consequently, by independence of the calibration and deployment experiments,
with
\[
    \alpha
    =
    1-(1-\alpha_D)(1-\alpha_T),
\]
\begin{equation}
\inf_{\xi\in\mathfrak P^p_{q,r}(s)}
\mathbb P_\xi^{N,T}
\left\{
    \vartheta(\xi)
    \in
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
\right\}
\ge1-\alpha.

\end{equation}

For $N$ above the fixed block threshold of the robust calibration-moment
construction, define
\begin{equation}
\rho_N(s)
=
C\left[
    (s\wedge\epsilon_N)
    +
    \left(s\wedge\frac{\epsilon_N}{s}\right)
    +
    \left(s\wedge\frac{\epsilon_N}{s^2}\right)
\right].

\end{equation}
Any two dictionaries retained by the same nonempty calibration region have
quotient-dictionary distance at most $\rho_N(s)$.  If
$\epsilon_N\le CN^{-1/2}$, then
\begin{equation}
    \rho_N(s)
    \le
    C\left(
        s\wedge\frac{1}{\sqrt N\,s^2}
    \right).
    
\end{equation}
Below the block threshold, retaining the full compact shell yields the same
order after adjustment of fixed constants.

For every realization,
\begin{align}
\operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{pr}}
\left(
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
\right)
\le{}&
C\rho_N(s)
\notag\\
&+
Cs\,
\mathbf 1
\left\{
    2\tau_{T,q}\ge m_S(\rho_N(s))
\right\}
\notag\\
&+
C\,
\mathbf 1
\left\{
    2\tau_{T,q}\ge m_G(\rho_N(s))
\right\}.

\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Coverage and resolution of the cross-dictionary correspondence

Let P_X be an input probability law and P_F a law on measurable functions F:X->{-1,1}, with measurable evaluation. Draw F and F_prime independently from P_F. Draw X_1,...,X_m iid from P_X, independently of both functions, where m>=1 is an integer; each sampled function is held fixed throughout the batch. Define CP_infinity = E_{F,F_prime}[(E_X F(X)*F_prime(X))^2]. Define CP_m=E[((1/m) sum_{i=1}^m F(X_i)*F_prime(X_i))^2]. Then CP_m=1/m+(1-1/m)*CP_infinity. Equivalently, for K(x,x_prime)=E_F[F(x)*F(x_prime)], CP_infinity=E_{X,X_prime}[K(X,X_prime)^2], with X,X_prime independent under P_X. Thus0<=CP_infinity<=1, CP_m>=1/m and CP_1=1. No balanced-label assumption is needed for these identities.
Binary-valued functions; measurable evaluation and the stated probability laws.
The input batch is iid and independent of two iid function draws.
The same function pair is reused throughout the batch; it is not redrawn per input.

[Satz thm:HigherOrderIndep of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Let $X$ be a random vector with independent components, $f: \mathcal{X} \to {\mathbb R}$ a measurable function satisfying $f = f(X) \in L^\infty(\IP)$, ${\mathbb E} f(X) = 0$ and $d \in {\mathbb N}$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Assuming that $\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(j)} f}_{\mathrm{op},1} \le 1$ for all $j=1,\ldots,d-1$ and $\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(d)} f}_{\mathrm{op},\infty} \le 1$, it holds that
        \[
        {\mathbb E} \exp\Big\{c |f(X)|^{2/d} \Big\} \le 2,
        \]
        where a possible choice of the constant $c$ is given by
        \[
        c = \frac{(\sqrt{2}-1)^2}{64 \kappa e}.
        \]
        \item For any $t\ge 0$, it holds that
        \[
        {\mathbb P}(|f(X)| \ge t)\le
        2 \exp\Big\{- \frac{C}{d^2} \min\Big(\min_{j=1, \ldots,d-1} \Big(\frac{t}{\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(j)} f}_{\mathrm{op},1}}\Big)^{2/j}, \Big(\frac{t}{\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(d)} f}_{\mathrm{op},\infty}}\Big)^{2/d}\Big)\Big\},
        \]
    where a possible choice of the constant $C$ is given by
    \[
    C = \frac{\log(2)}{16 \kappa e^2} > \frac{1}{217}.
    \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Coro 16 of arXiv:2605.23292, 'Second-order Poincaré inequalities and localization on the Poisson space'] (normal approximation for the sum of power weighted edge lengths of the $k$-nearest neighbor graph in $d$-dimensional hyperbolic space)
We work in the setup of Theorem~\ref{thm:hyperbolic}. Let $X_\la=W_\la=B(p,\la) \subset \hyp$ by a ball of radius $\la\geq2$ and $p\in\hyp$ a fixed point. Let $\mathcal{P}_\la$ be a Poisson measure of intensity $\nu$ on $W_\la$ and let $k\text{NN}(\P_\la)$ be the  undirected $k$-nearest neighbor graph on 
$\P_\la$. For $\alpha \sg 0$ we consider the sum of power weighted edge lengths
\[
H_\la^\alpha := \sum_{\text{edges } e \in k\text{NN}(\P_\la)} \text{length}(e)^\alpha.
\]
Then the functional $H_\la^\alpha$ satisfies \eqref{dKhyp} and \eqref{dWhyp} with $\nu(W_\la) \leq \Gamma_d e^{(d-1)\la}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 40 (Merge operation, see Figure \ref{fig:merge}) of arXiv:2605.09459, 'Multipoint connectivity in the branching interlacement process'] Let $T$ be a tree with an internal node $\partial$ only attached to an external vertex $x$ and another node $z$. Denote by $T'$ the copy of $T$ without the vertex $\partial$ and where the edges $\{x,\partial\}$ and $\{z,\partial\}$ have been merged into a single edge $\{x,z\}$. Let $\alpha_{T'}$ be a weight function for $T'$, which coincides with $\alpha_T$ except that
  \[
    \alpha_{T'}(x,z) = \alpha_T(x,\partial) + \alpha_T(z,\partial) - d.
  \]
  Suppose that $\alpha_T(x,\partial)$ and $\alpha_T(\partial,z) < d$ and $\alpha_T(x,\partial) + \alpha_T(z,\partial) > d$. Then for any function $\varphi : V(T)\backslash\{\partial\} \to \mathbb{Z}^d$,
  \[
    \sum_{y\in\mathbb{Z}^d} p_{\varphi_y}(T) \lesssim p_\varphi(T').
  \]

[Lemma 11 (Endpoint reduction and contact identities) of arXiv:2608.06523, 'On the Gardner Transition in the Ising Pure $p$-Spin Glass II'] For the measure in \eqref{eq:mu},
\begin{equation}
 \partial_x\Phi_\mu(x,q)=\tanh x,\qquad
 \partial_{xx}\Phi_\mu(x,q)=\cosh^{-2}x.
 
\end{equation}
For every smooth test function $\varphi$ such that
$\varphi,\varphi',\varphi''$ have at most exponential growth and which
does not depend on $m$ or $\xi'(q)$,
\begin{equation}
 \E[\varphi(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]
 =\frac{\E\!\left[
 \varphi(\sqrt{\xi'(q)}z)\cosh^m(\sqrt{\xi'(q)}z)\right]}
 {\E[\cosh^m(\sqrt{\xi'(q)}z)]},
 \qquad \E e^{W_\mu(q)}=1.
 
\end{equation}
At a stationary marginal point,
\begin{align}
 \Gamma_\mu(q)
 &=\E[\tanh^2(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]=q,
 \\
 q&=(p-1)\xi'(q)
 \E[\cosh^{-4}(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}],
 \\
 \E[\cosh^{-2}(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]&=1-q,
 \\
 \E[\cosh^{-4}(M(q))e^{W_\mu(q)}]
 &=\frac{q}{(p-1)\xi'(q)}.
 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:vary of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\mathcal W$ be a white noise with respect to some filtration $\mathcal F$. Let $\overline{\delta}$ be a drift function with respect to $\mathcal F$. We call a collection of continuous processes $\mathcal S=(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)_{r\in {\mathbb R},a\ge 0}$ a ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta})$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$ if 
   
    (1) The restriction of $\mathcal S$ to each $A_i$ is a ${\rm BESQ}^{\delta_i}$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$.

    (2) The regularity conditions of Definition (def:BESQflow of the paper) hold.
 

If $E$ is a (possibly random) Borel set, we call $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow killed on $E$ the flow obtained from the $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow by absorbing the flow line $\mathcal S_{r,\cdot}(a)$ at $0$ at time $\inf\{x \in E\cap (r,\infty) \,:\, \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)=0\}$.

 If $E={\mathbb R}$, we will simply say that $\mathcal S$ is a killed  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow. We call general  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow a $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow or a  killed $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow.
title: Definition def:vary of arXiv:2411.04773

body:
[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $V$ be a $k[H]$-module. Let $R$ be such that it contains $R_s$. Let $t\in\mathbb Z\setminus p\mathbb Z$. Let $o$ be the order of $[t]_{p^s}\in (\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^{\times}$. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (1.a)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.b)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.c)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is strongly indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.d)} We have $\imath_V\in\{0,1\}$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.e)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.f)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic and strongly indecomposable.

\medskip
{\bf (2)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal H$ to $R$ which is an end-hull of $V$ and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules. Moreover, if $\jmath_V=0$, then we can also assume that $r_{\mathcal H}=0$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} Suppose that $V$ is cyclic. Let $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ be two lifts of $V$. Then the $R[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ are isomorphic if and only if the $B[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1\otimes_R B$ and $\mathcal V_2\otimes_R B$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} The $k[H]$-modules $V$ and $V^{(t)}$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (5)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (5.a)} There exists a lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules (resp.\ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules with $r_{\mathcal V^H}=0$).

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (5.b)} For each $b\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket\setminus o\llbracket1,\lfloor\frac{p^s}{t}\rfloor\rrbracket$ such that $\mu_V(b)\neq 0$, $\mu_V(b)$ is a sum of cardinals of orbits of the action of $[t]_{p^s}$ on $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$), equivalently of subsets $\Phi$ of $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$) with $[t]_{p^s}\cdot\Phi=\Phi$.

\medskip
{\bf (6)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$ (equivalently, $o=2$) and $\dim_k(V)$ is even. Then $V$ has a lift to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant.

\medskip
{\bf (7)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$, $\mu_V(d)$ is even for each odd $d\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$, and $\jmath_V=0$. Then $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant with $r_{\mathcal V}=0$.

[Lemma 18 (Ricci quadratic estimate; cf.\ Lemma A.1 of \cite{Brendle2019}, Lemma 4.7 of \cite{Chen2024}) of arXiv:2608.26598, 'Pinching cones for positive isotropic curvature in dimensions seven and eight'] Let $0\le\zeta\le1$ and $0<\varrho\le1$, and let $H$ be a symmetric two-tensor whose largest
    eigenvalue is at most $\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,H$ and whose two smallest eigenvalues have sum at
    least $\frac{2(1-\zeta)}{n}\mathrm{tr}\,H$. Then, with
    $H^0=H-\frac1n\mathrm{tr}(H)\,\mathrm{id}$, every orthonormal pair $\{e_1,e_2\}$ satisfies
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{n-2}{n}\,\mathrm{tr}(H)\,\bigl(H_{11}+H_{22}\bigr)
        -\varrho\bigl((H^0)^2_{11}+(H^0)^2_{22}\bigr)
        \ge\frac{2}{n^2}\left((n-2)(1-\zeta)-2\zeta^2\varrho\,
        \frac{n^2-2n+2}{(n-2)^2}\right)\mathrm{tr}(H)^2.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition lem:EOTPotentialBounds of arXiv:2609.03094, 'Discrete Gromov--Wasserstein Duality: Algorithms and Isomorphism Testing'] Fix $(\mu_0,\mu_1)\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X_{0})\times \mathcal P(\mathcal X_1)$ and $c:\mathcal X_0\times \mathcal X_1\to\mathbb R$. Then,  there exist EOT potentials $(\varphi_0,\varphi_1)$ for (equation eq:EOTDual of the paper) defined on $\mathcal X_0$ and $\mathcal X_1$  which satisfy  (equation eq:SchrodingerSystem of the paper) on $\mathcal X_0\times \mathcal X_1$ and for which $\max\left\{\| \varphi_0\|_{\infty,\mathcal X_0},\| \varphi_1\|_{\infty,\mathcal X_1}\right\}\leq \frac 32 \|c\|_{\infty,\mathcal X_0\times \mathcal X_1}$. As such, the EOT plan $\pi^{\star}$ satisfies
           $
                \frac{d\pi^{\star}}{d\mu_0\otimes \mu_1}(x,y)\geq e^{\frac{-4\|c\|_{\infty,\mathcal X_0\times \mathcal X_1}}{\varepsilon}}>0\text{  for each $(x,y)\in\supp(\mu_0)\times \supp(\mu_1)$.}           $ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:Unique_loop_qversion of arXiv:2603.28520, 'The Supercritical Loop O(1) and Random Current Models: Uniqueness and Mixing'] Let $q\in \mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}$, $d\geq 2$ and $x>x_{slab}$. For any Gibbs measure $\ell^q_{\mathbb{Z}^d,x}$ of the $q$-flow model, there exists a weak limit $\phi_{\mathbb{Z}^d,p,q}$ of finite-volume random-cluster measures such that 
$$
\ell^q_{\mathbb{Z}^d,x}[\;\cdot\;]=\phi_{\mathbb{Z}^d,p,q}[\operatorname{UD}_{\omega}[\;\cdot\;]].
$$
In particular, whenever $x>x_{slab},$ there is a unique Gibbs measure for the $q$-flow model if and only if $\phi^1_{\mathbb{Z}^d,p,q}=\phi^0_{\mathbb{Z}^d,p,q}$.

Fix a globally Lipschitz activation rho with E rho(G)=0 and v=E rho(G)^2>0 for G~N(0,1). Define W_jk=f_j^T f_k/d and C_jk=E_g rho(f_j^T g/sqrt(d))rho(f_k^T g/sqrt(d)). With b=(E G rho(G))^2 and tau=v-b, C=tau I+bW+E where E_jj=0, |E_jk|<=tau|W_jk|^2 and E||E||_F^2<=3 tau^2 p(p-1)/[d(d+2)]. The Schur product contraction gives ||C||<=v||W||. Hence C has limiting empirical law law(tau+b MP_psi), since its resolvent trace differs from that of tau I+bW by at most ||E||_F/(sqrt(p) s^2) at every s>0. Operator-norm equivalence is not asserted. For variance-one centered ReLU rho(t)=sqrt(2 pi/(pi-1))[max(t,0)-1/sqrt(2 pi)], b=pi/[2(pi-1)], tau=(pi-2)/[2(pi-1)]. Its second Hermite coefficient square is 1/[2(pi-1)]. body: The nerve of a finite collection A of nonempty sets is the simplicial complex N(A) := {sigma : nonempty sigma subset of A with intersection over B in sigma of B nonempty}. If the sets are convex subsets of R^d (in the paper, the grains x + K of the union Z_W), the union is homotopy equivalent to the nerve (a variant of the Nerve Theorem, Edelsbrunner-Harer p. 76). For general sets contractibility of the intersections is not enough; the usual hypotheses are open sets, or closed convex sets.

The planar set C={(x,y): x>0 and |y-x^2|<1} is open, connected and unbounded, but contains no straight ray with nonzero direction. A ray with negative x direction exits x>0, a vertical ray exits the bounded vertical strip at its fixed x, and a ray with positive x direction has y-x^2 tending to minus infinity quadratically. This is a geometric counterexample to an unbounded-component implies straight-visibility inference; no permitted mirror configuration or reflected-ray trapping is asserted.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Status: proofs written; w346 KEEP pending. Neither result constructs an all-ray trapping mirror configuration.

Lemma 1. Every unbounded open convex set C in R^d contains an unbounded straight ray starting at each x in C. Therefore, if a mirror-complement component is unbounded, open and convex, an origin in it has an unobstructed escaping launch direction and cannot have every reflected ray bounded.

Proof: choose r>0 with B(x,r) contained in C and y_k in C with |y_k-x| tending to infinity. A subsequence of d_k=(y_k-x)/|y_k-x| tends to a unit direction d. For fixed t>=0 and sufficiently large k, convexity gives a ball centered at x+t*d_k with radius (1-t/|y_k-x|)*r contained in C. Eventually this radius exceeds 3r/4 and the center is within r/4 of x+t*d, so B(x+t*d,r/2) is in C. This holds for every fixed t with the same subsequential direction d, proving the entire ray stays inside C. No collision occurs along it.

Lemma 2. C={(x,y): x>0 and |y-x^2|<1} is open, connected and unbounded but contains no unbounded straight ray.

Proof: (x,u)->(x,x^2+u) is a homeomorphism from (0,infinity) times (-1,1), proving the first three properties. For a ray (a+bt,c+dt), t>=0, with nonzero direction: b<0 eventually violates x>0; b=0 and d!=0 eventually violates the strip condition; b>0 makes y-x^2 a quadratic with leading coefficient -b^2, whose magnitude diverges. Thus all possible directions leave C in finite time.

This gives an explicit algebraic version of the previous spiral-corridor obstruction: unbounded connected vacancy alone does not supply a straight ray. The corridor is not represented as a permitted mirror arrangement, and absence of straight rays does not establish trapping of reflected rays. Convexity is a sufficient special-case condition, not a necessary one.

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The orthogonal polynomials with respect to $\mu$ are given by
$$P_k=c_k\begin{vmatrix}
M_0&M_1&\ldots&M_k\\
M_1&M_2&\ldots&M_{k+1}\\
\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\
M_{k-1}&M_k&\ldots&M_{2k-1}\\
1&x&\ldots&x^k
\end{vmatrix}$$
where $M_k=\int_\mathbb Rx^kd\mu(x)$ are the moments of $\mu$, and $c_k\in\mathbb R^*$ can be any numbers.

[Prop lamclass of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Suppose $\Lambda$ is a minimal lamination on $M$ transverse to $\partial M$. Then at least one of the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\Lambda$ has a leaf $\lambda$ such that $\pi_1(\lambda)$ is not normally generated by boundary parallel curves.
        \item $\Lambda$ is a compact planar surface.
        \item $\Lambda$ has a leaf with a noncompact boundary component inside a Reeb, $\sharp$, or $\flat$ annulus on $\partial M$.
        \item $\Lambda$ is a $\mathbb{T}^3$-type planar lamination.
        \item $\Lambda$ is a $\mathbb{T}^2$-type planar lamination.
    \end{enumerate}

Define the elementary factors E_0(w) = 1 - w and, for p ≥ 1, E_p(w) = (1 - w) exp(w + w^2/2 + ... + w^p/p). Let m ≥ 0 be an integer and let (a_n) be a finite or infinite sequence of nonzero complex numbers, repetitions allowed, with |a_n| → ∞ if the sequence is infinite. Choose nonnegative integers p_n such that the series Σ_n (r/|a_n|)^{p_n + 1} converges for every r > 0 (the choice p_n = n - 1 always works). Then the product P(z) = z^m Π_n E_{p_n}(z/a_n) converges absolutely and uniformly on compact subsets of C and defines an entire function whose zero set is exactly {0} (with multiplicity m, omitted if m = 0) together with the points a_n, each with multiplicity equal to the number of times it is listed. Conversely, every entire function f whose zeros are exactly these (with these multiplicities) has the form f(z) = exp(g(z)) P(z) for some entire function g. Consequently every entire function admits such a factorization, and every meromorphic function on C is a quotient of two entire functions.
the prescribed zeros form a sequence with no finite accumulation point (|a_n| → ∞ if infinite)
the integers p_n satisfy Σ_n (r/|a_n|)^{p_n+1} < ∞ for every r > 0
multiplicities are encoded by repetition in the list

Let H be a complex Hilbert space. (a) If A is self-adjoint on H, then U(t) = e^{itA} (Borel functional calculus) defines a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, U(t)* = U(−t), and t ↦ U(t)x is continuous on ℝ for each x. Moreover D(A) = {x ∈ H : lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/t exists} and for x ∈ D(A) that limit equals iAx; D(A) is invariant under each U(t). (b) Conversely, let (U(t))_{t ∈ ℝ} be a family of unitary operators with U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, and t ↦ U(t)x continuous for each x ∈ H. Then there is a unique self-adjoint operator A with U(t) = e^{itA} for all t, namely Ax = lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/(it) on the set where the limit exists. (c) Weak continuity suffices in (b): if t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ is continuous for all x, y, the group is strongly continuous, since ‖U(t)x − x‖² = 2‖x‖² − 2Re⟨U(t)x, x⟩. If H is separable, weak measurability of t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ already implies strong continuity (von Neumann). (d) A subspace D ⊂ D(A) that is dense in H and invariant under every U(t) is a core for A (Nelson's criterion via invariant domains).
H is a complex Hilbert space
in (a): A is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric
in (b): U(t) unitary for every real t, group law on all of ℝ, and strong (or weak) continuity

[Lemma bound_on_4th_moment of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Fix $\alpha > 0$. 
    Let a random matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ be such that $u \coloneqq \norm[\big]{\norm{\mathbf{X}}}_{\psi_{\alpha}} < \infty$ and $\sigma^2 \coloneqq \lambda_{\max}(\E \mathbf{X}^2)$. 
    Then for any $z > 0$ such that $\alpha z^\alpha \ge 4$
    \[
    \E \mathbf{X}^4 \preccurlyeq z^2 u^2 \lr{\E \mathbf{X}^2 + 2 z^2 u^2 e^{-z^\alpha} \mathbf{I}}.
    \]
    In particular, for $z = z(u, \sigma; \alpha)$ defined by~(equation eq:def_z of the paper),
    \[
    \lambda_{\max}(\E \mathbf{X}^4) \le \frac{5}{3} (\sigma u z)^2.
    \]
title: Lemma bound_on_4th_moment of arXiv:2411.07878

[Corollary 6 (Finite-family covariance domination) of arXiv:2608.27657, '\bfseries Stein Kernels and Normal Approximation\\ for Log-Concave Bilinear Forms'] Assume the estimates in \cref{thm:letwin}.  Let
\(A_1,\ldots,A_k\in\mathsf S_n\), and define
\[
  K_{ij}
  =
  \Cov\!\left(\Tr(A_iH),\Tr(A_jH)\right),
  \qquad
  G_{ij}
  =
  \Tr(A_iA_j).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  0\preceq K\preceq4G.
  \tag{3.19}
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) are Hilbert--Schmidt orthonormal,
then \(K\preceq4I_k\).  For two arbitrary directions this also gives
\[
  \left|
  \Cov\!\left(\Tr(AH),\Tr(BH)\right)
  \right|
  \leq
  4\sqrt{\Tr(A^2)\Tr(B^2)}.
\]

[Lem ulX_ut of arXiv:2411.01849, 'A tamed-adaptive Milstein scheme for stochastic differential equations with low regularity'] For any $p \in (0, p_0]$, and $T>0$, there exists a finite positive constant $K$ such that, 
$$\sup_{t\geq 0} \mathbb{E}[ |X_{\underline{t}}|^p] \leq K.$$
Moreover, when $\gamma<0$, constant $K$ does not depend on $T$.

    \frac{r}{2}$, where $r$ is defined in (equation eq:cU of the paper). Let $p_t:=\pi_\mathcal{M}(x_t), n_t:=x_t-p_t$. If $\eta \le \min\{\frac{1}{50L},\frac{r}{4G}\}, \epsilon \le \min\{\frac{1}{512\eta(G\kappa+L)},\frac{r}{4E_t}\}$, then we have that $\mathrm{dist}(x_{t-1},\mathcal{M})
    \le
    \frac{r}{2}$, and with
\begin{align*}
    \textstyle V(x):=f(\pi_\mathcal{M}(x))+\frac{1}{160\eta}\|x-\pi_\mathcal{M}(x)\|^2,
\end{align*}
we have
\vspace{-15pt}
\begin{align*}
   \textstyle V(x_{t-1})
    \le
    V(x_t)
    -
    \frac{\epsilon\eta}{480}\|\mathrm{grad}_\mathcal{M} f(p_t)\|^2
    -
    \frac{\epsilon}{2000\eta}\|n_t\|^2
    +
    \frac{6\epsilon}{\eta}E_t^2.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lyapunov descent with inexact projection

[Definition 5 (Conical complex) of arXiv:2609.00183, '2609.00183'] Let $(X,d)$ be an NPC space and let $O_X \in X$. For $\mu \in [0,1],$ define the mapping
\[
R_{O_X,\mu}:X \to X
\]
by letting $R_{O_X,\mu}(P)$ be the point lying a fraction $\mu$ of the way from $O_X$ to $P \in X$ along the unique geodesic joining them. We say that $X$ is {\bf conical with respect to $O_X$} if 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item for any $P,Q \in X$ and $\mu \in [0,1]$
            \[
                d\bigl(R_{O_X,\mu}(P), R_{O_X,\mu}(Q)\bigr) = \mu d(P,Q).
            \]
    \item $R_{O_X,\mu}$ is surjective for any $\mu \in (0,1].$ 
\end{enumerate}
The point $O_X$ is called the {\bf cone point} of $X.$
title: Conical complex

$(v_j)_{j=n}^{n+m-1}$ with $a:=\max\|v_j\|_{j,\omega}\leq \del_0$

Set $\cA_{j}(g)=\cL_j(e^{iv_j}g)$ and 
$

Then

[Proposition prop:KW of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $\Lambda$ be a finite cubical subcomplex of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $\mathbb{G}$ a finite abelian group, $1\leq k\leq d$, $(J_{\mathbf{c}})_{\mathbf{c}\in \Lambda^{*,k}}$ be positive coupling constants and $h:\mathbb{G}\to \mathbb{R}$ be even. Let $\Omega:=\mathrm{Im}(\partial_{d-k+1})$  and $\Sigma:=C^{k-1}$. Define $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ by $f(\eta) = \{\sigma \in \Sigma \mid d^k(\sigma) = \eta^* \} = (*\circ d^k)^{-1}(\eta)$ and
     $$
     \rho[\eta]\propto \prod_{\mathbf{c}\in {\Lambda_{d-k}}}\exp(J_{\mathbf{c}} h(\eta_{\mathfrak{c}})), \;\forall \eta\in \Omega, \qquad \gamma[\sigma]\propto 1,\;\forall\sigma\in\Sigma.
     $$
     Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is the spin model $\mu^{*}_{\Lambda^{k-1}}$. 
        For each $\eta \in\Omega$,  the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta]$ is the uniform measure on $f(\eta)$, that is the uniform assignment of a spin configuration consistent with the domain walls $\eta$.
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is the domain wall measure $\mu_{\Lambda_{d-k}}$.  For each $\sigma \in\Sigma$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \sigma] = \delta_{(d^k(\sigma))^*}$, the Dirac measure on the dual of the co-boundary of $\sigma$ corresponding to taking the domain walls of the spin configuration. 
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Spin Models and Domain Walls

[Conjecture of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] For each $d \ge 2$ and each $1 \le k \le d - 1$, there exists $0 < \lambda_{c,k}<\infty$
    such that the following holds.
    For $\lambda \in (0,\infty)$,
    let $X^n$ be a Poisson point process with intensity measure $ndM = (\lambda/r^d) dM$
    on a Riemannian manifold of $M$ of dimension $d$ and volume 1,
    and let $
    \mathcal{C} = VC_r(X^n)$
    be the associated Vietoris-Rips complex
    with radius $r$.
    Then, if $ \lambda > \lambda_{c,k}$, then
    \[
        \mathbb{P}(\mbox{the natural map }
        H_k(\mathcal{C}) \to H_k(M)
        \mbox{ is surjective})
        \to 1
    \]
    as $r \to 0$. Moreover, there exists
    some function $s_\lambda:[0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$
    with $s_\lambda(r) = o_{r \to 0}(1), s_\lambda(r) = \omega(r)$
    such that
    \[
        \mathbb{P}(\mbox{the natural map }
        Z_k(\mathcal{C})/
        Z_k^{s_{\lambda}(r)}(\mathcal{C})
        \to H_k(M)
        \mbox{ is an isomorphism})
        \to 1
    \]
    as $r \to 0$,
    where $Z_k^{s_\lambda(r)}(\mathcal{C})$
    is the submodule
    of $Z_k(\mathcal{C})$
    generated by $k$-cycles of diameter
    at most $s_\lambda(r)$.
    \\
    On the other hand,
    if $\lambda < \lambda_{c,k}$, then
        \[
        \mathbb{P}(\mbox{the natural map }
        H_k(\mathcal{C})
        \to H_k(M)
        \mbox{ is the zero map})
        \to 1
    \]
    as $r \to 0$. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
