{"artifact_digest":"sha256:61540c5a30665f23d715dfa877ed36851d4f5e6b8bcc57c61ae9d265cd7eb3e0","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/61/61540c5a30665f23d715dfa877ed36851d4f5e6b8bcc57c61ae9d265cd7eb3e0.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:7c673ab1f544f0e3955fcd92879e554a7907834c68728a34330c1cedd7cbda10","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-tangent-shared-quadratic-form","bundle_id":"population.t244-tanh-tangent-shared-wishart-noise-017","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_017.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-tangent-shared-quadratic-form","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Critical tanh: exact tangent kernel and its shared Wishart noise

20 October 2026. C050/C051; Target 3. Proof drafts, unaudited.
These are infinitesimal-angle one-step results, not a two-input tanh
diffusion theorem or an all-order cumulant expansion. No novelty asserted.

## C050: exact positive-variance kernel

Fix n>=2 and q>0. Let g,h be independent N(0,I_n) vectors. For two inputs
with equal preactivation variance q and angle theta, the next activated
vectors are exactly distributed as

    x = tanh(sqrt(q) g),
    y(theta) = tanh(sqrt(q)(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h)).

The independent Gaussian weight rows give these conditional marginals
given the present Gram matrix. The tanh critical weight variance is 1/n;
thus the next diagonal variance is K'=||x||^2/n and the radial multiplier
is M_q=||x||^2/(nq). There is no width-dependent shaping normalizer.

Set D=diag(sech^2(sqrt(q)g_i)), P_x=I-xx^T/||x||^2. Then the right-hand
derivative H_q of the angle between x and y(theta) at theta=0 is

    H_q^2 = q h^T D P_x D h / ||x||^2.

Proof: y(0)=x and y'(0)=sqrt(q)Dh. The derivative of y/||y|| is
sqrt(q)P_x Dh/||x||, whose norm is the nonnegative angular speed.
Almost surely x is nonzero and this speed is positive for n>=2.

Conditionally on g, Q_q=h^T D P_x D h is a sum of n-1 independent
chi-square_1 variables with positive weights equal to the nonzero
eigenvalues lambda_j of D P_x D. These satisfy

    d_min^2 <= lambda_j <= 1,
    d_min = min_i sech^2(sqrt(q)g_i).

Indeed these nonzero eigenvalues equal those of P_x D^2 P_x restricted
to x-perp, whose Rayleigh quotients lie in that interval. Both M_q and
the conditional weights depend on the same g. In particular the exact
positive-q model must retain this conditioning; replacing Q_q by an
independent chi-square is a different kernel. Even the radial sum
||x||^2/q is bounded above by n/q, unlike a chi-square variable.

For fixed n, q decreases to zero gives jointly, almost surely under the
original (g,h) coupling,

    M_q -> S/n,      H_q -> sqrt(R/S),
    S=||g||^2 ~ chi-square_n,
    R=h^T P_g h ~ chi-square_(n-1),  R independent of g and hence of S.

The independence follows because the conditional law of R given g is
the same chi-square_(n-1) law for every nonzero g. The SAME S appears in
the radial multiplier and angular denominator. For n=1 the tangent
speed is zero, so logarithmic angular statements below exclude n=1.

## C051: uniform leading noise at the critical variance scale

For every fixed C<infinity, uniformly over 0<q<=C/n, define

    A_q=log M_q,       B_q=log H_q.

As n increases,

    n Cov((A_q,B_q)) -> [[2,-1],[-1,1]].

Here Cov is centered covariance. Equivalently, replacing B_q by the
logarithmic reciprocal-angle multiplier -B_q changes both off-diagonal
entries to +1. This only identifies one-step noise, not a drift limit.

### Coupling and quantitative error

Draw g and, independently, eta_1,...,eta_(n-1) iid standard normals.
Use a measurable ordering of the eigenvalues above and put

    Q_q^* = sum_j lambda_j(g) eta_j^2,
    R^* = sum_j eta_j^2,       S=||g||^2.

The pair (M_q, sqrt(q Q_q^*/||x||^2)) has EXACTLY the required joint
law (M_q,H_q), by the conditional quadratic-form law. Also S and R^*
are independent chi-squares with the stated degrees of freedom.
Thus this construction verifies both coupled marginals. No pointwise
comparison with the original h projection is being asserted.

For z>=0, sech^2(z) <= tanh(z)/z <= 1, with the continuous value at zero.
Consequently, with Z=max_i |g_i|,

    d_min^2 <= ||x||^2/(qS) <= 1,
    d_min^2 <= Q_q^*/R^* <= 1.

Since log(cosh z)<=z^2/2, this yields the deterministic coupling bounds

    |A_q-log(S/n)| <= 2q Z^2,
    |B_q-(1/2)log(R^*/S)| <= q Z^2.

A Gaussian union bound P(Z^2>r)<=min(1,2n exp(-r/2)), integrated as
E Z^4=integral_0^infinity 2r P(Z^2>r)dr, gives
||Z^2||_2 <= C_0 log(2n). Hence each logarithmic error has L2 norm at
most C_1 q log(2n), without deleting any event or inverse tail.

### Covariance calculation

Let A_0=log(S/n), B_0=(log R^*-log S)/2. Gamma integration gives

    Var A_0 = psi_1(n/2),
    Cov(A_0,B_0) = -(1/2)psi_1(n/2),
    Var B_0 = (psi_1((n-1)/2)+psi_1(n/2))/4.

The trigamma series psi_1(z)=sum_(k>=0)(z+k)^(-2) and integral comparison
give psi_1(z)=1/z+O(z^-2). These identities can alternatively be obtained
by differentiating E S^t=2^t Gamma(n/2+t)/Gamma(n/2) at t=0.
The displayed baseline covariance therefore has the claimed limit
after multiplying by n, and its centered L2 norms are O(n^-1/2).

For centered random variables, covariance perturbation by L2 errors e
has size at most C(n^-1/2 ||e||_2 + ||e||_2^2); centering an error costs
no more than its L2 norm. After multiplying by n, our bound is

    O(sqrt(n) q log(2n) + n q^2 log(2n)^2)
       = O_C(log(2n)/sqrt(n) + log(2n)^2/n),

uniformly over 0<q<=C/n. This tends to zero and proves C051.

## Scope left open

The limits are: first the angle derivative at zero for fixed n,q,
then n -> infinity with q<=C/n. C051 does not justify exchanging the
infinitesimal-angle limit with a finite-angle network evolution, does
not give the order-1/n drift, and does not establish that actual tanh
input correlations approach one. The scalar critical-tanh diffusion
and cumulant-rate work remain separate claims C026-C027 and C044-C047.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:22c6d532d863fd81ef53240a00570657817f6c17e8e5fb0515c76a33cfbda523","revision_digest":"sha256:85f5ca6e4c11faf59b3859d20fd8b9c840a142c102084630954bf5c6cc79c24a","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C050:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T13:53:12.705197","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: Let X be a Banach space and (x_n) a sequence in X converging weakly to x. Then there exists a sequence (y_k) of finite convex combinations of the x_n, that is, each y_k = sum_i lambda_i^{(k)} x_i for finitely many indices i with lambda_i^{(k)} >= 0 and sum_i lambda_i^{(k)} = 1, such that y_k converges to x in norm. Equivalently, the norm-closed convex hull of {x_n : n >= 1} contains x and equals its weak closure. [standard, e.g. Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and PDEs]
title: Mazur's Theorem (Convex Combinations of a Weakly Convergent Sequence)

Method: Source-specific calculation, conditional implication or exact obstruction Result: A naive Mermin-Wagner deformation estimate based on absolute Hessians is divergent. For V(r)=r^-s, the Hessian has size of order r^-s-2. Multiplication by a displacement difference bounded crudely by a constant times r gives the second-order energy integral of order integral r^(d-1)*r^2*r^-s-2 dr = integral r^(d-s-1)dr. Check: The tail integral diverges whenever s<=d, covering the long-range regimes. For the logarithmic case the corresponding Hessian r^-2 gives the same limiting power at s=0. Obstruction: One needs a deformation adapted to neutrality or screening, with cancellation of long-range contributions and control of rare configurations. Absolute Hessian integrability cannot establish the stated symmetry theorem. Existing periodic-limit uniqueness is not automatically a theorem for every Gibbs state.

[Lemma of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $P(r_{j\wedge\tau}<r_{(j+1)\wedge\tau}\,|\,\tau>j)=1$ and, therefore, $K_{j\wedge\tau}$ is almost surely in descending order.
    \begin{proof}
        The first descent in the permutation of cards that appear is uniquely seen after card $n$ is shown. Prior to card $n$ being shown, the cards are in ascending order. After card $n$ is shown, the cards are in descending order. This is because card $n$ is the first card placed into the pile. Cards must be placed, from the bottom of the deck, on top or on the bottom of the pile. This preserves the relative order if placed on the top and reverses the relative order if placed on the bottom.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear (H(p)/|p| → ∞), let L = H* be its Legendre transform, and let g: R^n → R be Lipschitz. Define u(x,t) := min_{y ∈ R^n} ( t L((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) for t > 0, u(x,0) := g(x). Then: (i) the minimum is attained, u(·,t) is Lipschitz with constant at most Lip(g) for every t > 0, and |u(x,t) - g(x)| ≤ C t with C = max( |L(0)| , max_{|p| ≤ Lip(g)} |H(p)| ); hence u is Lipschitz on R^n × [0,∞) and attains the initial data continuously. (ii) u is differentiable almost everywhere in R^n × (0,∞), and at every point of differentiability u_t(x,t) + H(Du(x,t)) = 0. (iii) u is a viscosity solution of u_t + H(Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,∞) with u(·,0) = g. (iv) If in addition g is bounded, then for every T > 0, u is the unique viscosity solution of this Cauchy problem in the class of bounded Lipschitz functions on R^n × [0,T].
H: R^n → R finite, convex, superlinear (continuity is automatic from finiteness and convexity)
L = H* so that L is finite, convex and superlinear and L* = H
g: R^n → R Lipschitz continuous
for (iv): g in addition bounded, and uniqueness asserted only among bounded Lipschitz viscosity solutions
(ii) asserts the equation only at points of differentiability; a.e. solutions are not unique, so (ii) alone does not characterize u

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For f: {-1,1}^n -> R with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_S hat{f}(S) chi_S and the noise operator T_rho, which independently resamples each coordinate to a fresh uniform sign with probability 1-rho (equivalently, flips each coordinate with probability (1-rho)/2, so that each coordinate keeps correlation rho with the input), the Bonami-Beckner inequality states ||T_rho f||_q <= ||f||_p whenever 1 <= p <= q and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.
uniform (or explicitly known-bias) product measure on {-1,1}^n or {0,1}^n
f in the relevant L^p space, typically boolean or bounded
the noise parameter rho within the sharp Bonami-Beckner range 0<=rho<=sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))
a well-defined Fourier-Walsh expansion, i.e. finite n or a suitable limiting argument

[Theorem 15 (Matched-spectrum orientation dependence) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Let $X_0\sim\calN(0,\Sigma)$ with eigenvalues
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d>0$, let $1\le d_y\le d$, let
$A\in\R^{d_y\times d}$, and let $R_A=AX_0+\varepsilon$ with
$\varepsilon\sim\calN(0,\sigma_y^2\Id_{d_y})$.  Assume
$AA^\top=\Id_{d_y}$.  Thus every admissible $A$ has the same nonzero singular
values; isotropic measurement noise leaves orientation relative to \(\Sigma\)
as the only design variable.  Define
\[
C_\gamma=(\Sigma^{-1}+\gamma\Id_d)^{-1},
\qquad
\Sigma_A^{\rm post}
=
(\Sigma^{-1}+\sigma_y^{-2}A^\top A)^{-1},
\qquad
\psi_\gamma(\lambda)
=
\frac12\log
\frac{\sigma_y^2+\lambda}
{\sigma_y^2+\lambda/(1+\gamma\lambda)}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}

\mathcal M_\gamma(A)=\MI(R_A;Y_\gamma)
=
\frac12\log
\frac{\det(\sigma_y^2\Id_{d_y}+A\Sigma A^\top)}
{\det(\sigma_y^2\Id_{d_y}+AC_\gamma A^\top)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, among all row-orthonormal rank-$d_y$ measurements,
\begin{align}

\frac12\sum_{i=d-d_y+1}^{d}
\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lambda_i}{\sigma_y^2}\right)
&\le \MI(X_0;R_A)
\le
\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d_y}
\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lambda_i}{\sigma_y^2}\right),\\

2\MI(X_0;R_A)
&=
\log\frac{\det\Sigma}{\det\Sigma_A^{\rm post}},\\

\sum_{i=d-d_y+1}^{d}\psi_\gamma(\lambda_i)
&\le \mathcal M_\gamma(A)
\le
\sum_{i=1}^{d_y}\psi_\gamma(\lambda_i).
\end{align}
For every $\gamma>0$, $\psi_\gamma$ is strictly increasing.  Equality in the
upper (respectively, lower) bounds is attained by choosing the row space of
$A$ to be the span of the largest (respectively, smallest) $d_y$ prior
eigenvectors.  If the boundary eigenvalue is repeated, the extremizing row
space need not be unique: the required dimensions may be chosen arbitrarily
within that eigenspace.  Hence equal operator
singular values do not determine clean
measurement information, posterior covariance-volume contraction, or
reverse-path assimilation once the prior is anisotropic. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Matched-spectrum orientation dependence

The characteristic exponent \alpha \in (0, 2] of a stable distribution determines the decay rate of its tails. When \alpha = 2, the distribution is normal (Gaussian), all moments exist, and the tails decay exponentially. When 0 < \alpha < 2, the distribution has heavy tails: \mathbb{P}(|X| > x) \sim c x^{-\alpha} as x \to \infty, so \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] < \infty for all 0 < p < \alpha, but \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] = \infty for all p \ge \alpha.
\alpha \in (0, 2]

body: Concept (campaign status: open, evidence strong): CONJECTURE - for every linear NAE triangle system, SOME choice of one pair per triangle yields a pair-sum span that is an admissible residual space (valid_R). Since c = k*beta - ell is intrinsic, every choice-graph shares one Z, so the choice is free on the Ising side, and the lemma would give d_cb <= |V| - b and hence Conjecture RC for ALL linear systems via cut-inflation. Evidence: on the single system where the fixed shared-pair rule failed, 725 of 729 pair-choices are admissible (min dim 5); a 60-system chosen-pair sweep found zero systems with no admissible choice, tight on trees (slack exactly 0). Structure of the obstruction: a signed extra like e_0 - e_1 + e_2 is covered exactly when the choice-graph places its two same-signed coordinates in one component on the same bipartition side (their difference then dies in R) or in a non-bipartite component (whose generator vanishes) - so the general lemma is a simultaneous matching problem over the 3^k choices.

\[
D^{\infty}(\mu,\nu) \ge  \sup_{x,\, y\in [0,1]^d} \big| \mu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big) -  \nu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big)\big|.
\]
$(b)$ If furthermore, $\mu\big((0,1]^d\big)= \nu\big((0,1]^d\big) =1$, then 
\[
D^{\infty}(\mu,\nu) = \sup_{x,\, y\in [0,1]^d} \big| \mu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big) -  \nu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big)\big|.
\]
$(c)$ Without the additional assumption of $(b)$, we have:
\[
D^{\infty}(\mu,\nu) = \sup_{x,\, y\in [0,1]^d, x\preceq y} \big| \mu\big(]\![x,y]\!]\big) -  \nu\big(]\![x,y]\!]\big)\big|,
\]
where $]\![x,y]\!]$ is defined by 
$$]\![x,y]\!]=\begin{cases}
]\!]x,y]\!]\textnormal{ if $x^i>0,\,\forall \, i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$}\\
 \left\{u\in[0,1]^d, x^i<u^i\le y^i \textnormal{ if  $x^i>0$}, 0\le u^i\le  y^i \textnormal{ if  $x^i=0$}\right\}\textnormal{ otherwise.}
 \end{cases}
 $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.31300, 'Cone-Additive Functions for Random Walks on Free Products of Graphs'] Consider a function 
$$
f: \Pi\to\mathbb{R}, \pi \mapsto f(\pi).
$$
Then $f$ is called  \textit{cone-additive} w.r.t. $P$ if the following two properties hold:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item 
Additivity property: for all $n\in\N$,
$$
f\bigl([X_0,\ldots,X_n]\bigr)= \sum_{j=1}^{\mathbf{k}(n)} f(\pi_j) + f(\pi^\ast_{n}) \quad \textrm{ almost surely.}
$$
\item Shift invariance: for all $j\in\N$, 
\begin{equation}
f(\pi_j)=f\bigl(X_{\e_{j-1}}^{-1}\pi_j\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.31300

body:
Let p and q be probability mass functions on a nonempty finite set and p x q their independent coupling, whose disagreement probability is 1 - sum_x p(x) q(x). The following are equivalent: (i) p x q has the least disagreement d_TV(p, q) among couplings; (ii) it has the greatest, 1 - max_x (p(x) + q(x) - 1)_+; (iii) all couplings of p and q have the same disagreement probability; (iv) p and q have disjoint supports, or p or q is a point mass. Otherwise the independent coupling's disagreement lies strictly between the least and the greatest.

Let V be an affine algebraic set containing the origin 0. For any non-zero polynomial f, let f^{in} denote its initial form (the non-zero homogeneous component of lowest degree). The tangent cone of V at 0, denoted C_0(V), is the algebraic set defined by the initial ideal in(I(V)) = (f^{in} : f in I(V)). For an arbitrary point p, C_p(V) is defined by translation of p to the origin.

[Prop P:weighted-quadrangle of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Consider a weighted directed acyclic graph $G = (V, E, M)$, and let $H = (V, E, M')$ be another one with the same vertices and edges, but different weights satisfying $M' \le M$, with equality on a set $W \subset V$. Consider vertices $x_1 \prec y_1$ and $x_2 \prec y_2$ and suppose that we have the following {\bf path-crossing} property:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Let $\tau$ be any path from $x_1$ to $y_1$ and $\pi = (\pi_0, \dots, \pi_k)$ be any path from $x_2$ to $y_2$. Then if $\pi_i \notin W$ for some $i \in \llbracket1, k-1 \rrbracket$, there are indices $i^- < i < i^+$ such that the vertices $\pi(i^-), \pi(i^+)$ are on the path $\tau$.
\end{itemize}
Then
$$
H(x_1; y_1) + G(x_2 ; y_2)  \le G(x_1; y_1) + H(x_2 ; y_2).
$$

body: In spectral graph theory, the Alon–Boppana bound provides a lower bound on the second-largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix of a -regular graph, meaning a graph in which every vertex has degree . The reason for the interest in the second-largest eigenvalue is that the largest eigenvalue is guaranteed to be due to -regularity, with the all-ones vector being the associated eigenvector. The graphs that come close to meeting this bound are Ramanujan graphs, which are examples of the best possible expander graphs.

body:
[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $m,n\in\Nsf$, $[S,T]\subseteq\Rsf$ be an interval, $p\in[1,3)$, and $\omega$ a control function on interval $[S,T]$. Let $X=(X^\tau)$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $M$ be an $m$-dimensional manifold and let $f: M\to R_n^2M$ be a rough velocity field. Let $Y:[S,T]\to M$ be a continuous function such that for every $r\in [S,T]$ there exists
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\itemsep0em
    \item an interval $[u,v] \subset [S,T]$ that contains $r$ in its relative interior and such that we either have $v = T$ or $\omega(r,v) > 0$,
    \item a chart $(U, x)$ whose domain contains the image of $[u,v]$ under $Y$, and
    \item a constant $C\in (0,\infty)$
\end{enumerate}
such that inequality~\eqref{eq:integral-curve}, where $(Y^i)$ is the representation of $Y$ in the chart $(U,x)$ and $(f^i_\tau)$ is the representation of $f$ in the induced chart $(\overline{U},\overline{x})$, holds for every $i\in \llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta [u,v]$. Then $Y$ is an integral curve of the rough velocity field $f$ driven by the rough path $X$.

Let X be a real N-by-n design of rank q>=1 with q<n, Y an N-by-m response matrix, and hidden width h>=min(m,n). Consider continuous Euclidean gradient flow on L(U,V)=||Y-X U V^T||F^2/2, U n-by-h, V m-by-h. Choose an orthonormal basis Phi1 of the data row space, set U1=Phi1^T U, and let a=lambda_q(X^T X)>0 be the smallest positive design-covariance eigenvalue. The latent imbalance D=U1^T U1-V^T V is constant along the flow. Using decreasing eigenvalues with lambda_i=0 when i exceeds the matrix dimension, define delta_eff=max(lambda_q(D),0)+max(lambda_m(-D),0). If delta_eff>0 at initialization, the excess over the unrestricted linear-regression optimum obeys L(t)-L_star<=exp(-2a delta_eff t)(L(0)-L_star) for every t>=0. This is the sufficient-imbalance specialization of Min, Tarmoun, Vidal and Mallada, Convergence and Implicit Bias of Gradient Flow on Overparametrized Linear Networks, arXiv:2105.06351, Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 (printed pp.9-10), with the zero-padding convention on p.4 and delta_eff in equation (20), p.8. Positive definiteness of the h-by-h D alone is insufficient when q>h: its q-th eigenvalue is zero by convention, while all eigenvalues of -D are negative (or zero-padded). This is a continuous-time sufficient condition, not a discrete-GD or proper-bottleneck initialization theorem.
Real finite data with 1<=rank(X)=q<n; hidden width h>=min(m,n)
Euclidean continuous gradient flow; unrestricted linear-regression comparator
Effective imbalance delta_eff>0, with the precise zero-padded eigenvalue indices

[Prop Sigma-oo-lev-ff of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let ${\mathcal{C}}$ be any pointed globally cocomplete global $\infty$-category. Then
    $\ev_{\mathbb S}\colon{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{L}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl},{\mathcal{C}})\to{\mathcal{C}}(1)$ admits a both a fully faithful left adjoint $\mathbb S_!$ and a fully faithful right adjoint $\mathbb S_*$.
    \begin{proof}
        By the previous lemma and 2-functoriality of ${\textup{Fun}}^\text{L}(-,{\mathcal{C}})$, the restriction functor $-\circ\textbf{\textup{L}}\Sigma^\infty\colon{\textup{Fun}}^\text{L}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl},{\mathcal{C}})\to{\textup{Fun}}^\text{L}(\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl},*},{\mathcal{C}})$ has a fully faithful left adjoint given by ${-}\circ\Omega^\infty$ (here we are using that $\Omega^\infty$ is also a \emph{left} adjoint). Combining this with the universal property of $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl},*}$ from Corollary~(cor:gl-pointed of the paper), we conclude that $\ev_{\mathbb S}$ has a fully faithful left adjoint, and it only remains to show that it also admits a right adjoint, which will then automatically be fully faithful as before.

        For this we observe that ${\textup{Fun}}^\text{L}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl},{\mathcal{C}})\hookrightarrow{\textup{Fun}}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl},{\mathcal{C}})$ preserves colimits by [martiniwolf2022presentable]*{Lemma 2.6.1.3}, so that $\ev_{\mathbb S}\colon{\textup{Fun}}^\text{L}({\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl},{\mathcal{C}})\to{\mathcal{C}}(1)$ is cocontinuous. As the source is presentable (Proposition~(prop:FunL-presentable of the paper)), the existence of a right adjoint then follows from the (non-parametrized) Adjoint Functor Theorem.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop Sigma-oo-lev-ff of arXiv:2608.28504

More precisely, if is a compact set of points in -dimensional Euclidean space whose Hausdorff dimension is strictly greater than , then the conjecture states that the set of distances between pairs of points in must have nonzero Lebesgue measure.

 -\frac1{m_i^S(z)}=z+\sum_jS_{ij}m_j^S(z),
 \qquad
 \overline m^S(z):=\frac1N\sum_i m_i^S(z),
\end{equation}
and let \(m(z)=m_{\rm sc}(z)\).  On every fixed analytic LSS contour
\(\Gamma\) at positive distance from \([-2,2]\), with the standard spectral
confinement cutoff,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{z\in\Gamma}\E\left|
 \left[\Tr(H-zI)^{-1}-N\overline m^S(z)\right]
 -\left[\Tr(\widetilde H-zI)^{-1}-Nm(z)\right]
 \right|^2=o(1).
\end{equation}
Consequently, uniformly for \(z,w\in\Gamma\),
\begin{align}
 &\left[\E\Tr(H-zI)^{-1}-N\overline m^S(z)\right]
 -\left[\E\Tr(\widetilde H-zI)^{-1}-Nm(z)\right]=o(1),
 \\
 &\Cov\!\left(\Tr(H-zI)^{-1},\Tr(H-wI)^{-1}\right)
 \nonumber\\
 &\qquad-
 \Cov\!\left(\Tr(\widetilde H-zI)^{-1},
              \Tr(\widetilde H-wI)^{-1}\right)=o(1).
 
\end{align}
The same comparison holds for joint characteristic functions of finitely many
analytic LSS after subtracting the exact Dyson centering
\(-N(2\pi\ii)^{-1}\oint\varphi\overline m^S\) at the \(H\) endpoint and the
scalar semicircle centering at the \(\widetilde H\) endpoint.

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a population of size $N\in\mathbb N$, with $m\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$ of these objects having a certain feature, the probability of having $s$ successes, when performing draws without replacement, and stopping after $r\in\{0,\ldots,N-m\}$ failures, is
$$P(s)=\frac{\binom{s+r-1}{s}\binom{N-r-s}{m-s}}{\binom{N}{m}}$$
with this being called negative hypergeometric law of parameters $(N,m,r)$. When doing this with replacement, we obtain a negative binomial law of parameter $m/N$.

[Lemma 12 (Separation of boundary hits and fixed-time atomlessness) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] For the limiting and regularized forward and adjoint processes, simultaneous
first hits of distinct boundary components among $\partial A$, $\partial B$,
and $\partial\calD$ have probability zero.  Moreover, for every fixed $t>0$,
\[
    \Pbb_z\left(Z_t\in\partial A\cup\partial B\cup\partial\calD\right)=0,
\]
and
\[
    \Pbb_z^\delta\left(
        Z_t^\delta\in\partial A\cup\partial B\cup\partial\calD
    \right)=0.
\]
Consequently, the hitting times of these boundary components and their minima
are atomless at every deterministic time.  The same statements hold for the
adjoint processes.

[Lemma corollary3.6chap9 of arXiv:2504.15992, 'Repeated singular values of a random symmetric matrix and decoupled singular value estimat'] Let $B>0$, $\zeta\in\Gamma_B$ and $A_n\in\operatorname{Sym}_n(\zeta)$. Fix any $\kappa>0$. Fix two locations $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\in[-(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n},(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n}]$ and any $\sigma\in(0,1)$. Then for any $c_0>0$ we can find constants $C_1,C_2,C_3>0$ depending only on $B$, $\kappa$ (they do not depend on $c_0$) such that

\mathbb{P}\left(  \frac{C_1\sqrt{n}}{k}  \leq \mu_{k}(\lambda_i)\leq  \frac{C_2\sqrt{n}}{k}\text{ for both $i\in\{1,2\}$ and all } c_0n^\sigma\leq k\leq C_3n\right)\geq 1-e^{-\Omega(n^\sigma/2)},
\end{equation} where the constant in the error term $\exp(-\Omega(n^\frac{\sigma}{2}))$ depends also on $c_0>0$. 

In particular, we can find $C_4>1$ depending only on $\kappa$ and $B$ so that for any $c_0>0$,
$$
\left(\mu_{\frac{k}{C_4}}(\lambda_i)\geq {10}\mu_k(\lambda_j) \text{ for all } c_0n^\sigma\leq k\leq C_3n\text{ and  }\text{ for all } i,j\in\{1,2\}\right)\geq 1-e^{-\Omega(n^{\sigma/2})}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm-ig1 of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\kappa>0$, a vector $\underline{\rho}$ of weights and a vector $\underline{x}$ of force points. Let $(K_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be the hull at time $t$ of the SLE$_\kappa(\underline{\rho})$ process $\eta$ described by the Loewner flow (equation eqn-def-sle of the paper) with $(W_t, V_t^{i,q})$ solving (equation eqn-def-sle-rho of the paper). Let $\mathfrak{h}_t^0$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb{H}$ with boundary values 
	 	$$
	 	-\lambda(1+\sum_{i=0}^j \rho^{i,L})\ \ \text{on} \ [V_t^{j+1, L}-W_t, V_t^{j,L}-W_t)\ \  \text{and}\ \ \lambda(1+\sum_{i=0}^j \rho^{i,R})\ \text{on}\ \ [V_t^{j, R}-W_t, V_t^{j+1,R}-W_t)
	 	$$
	 	where $\rho^{0,R} = \rho^{0,L}=0$, $x^{0,L} = 0^-, x^{0,R} = 0^+, x^{k+1, L} = -\infty, x^{\ell+1, R} = +\infty$, $V_t^{0,L} = g_t(0^-)$ and $V_t^{0,R} = g_t(0^+)$. Set $\mathfrak{h}_t(z) = \mathfrak{h}_t^0(g_t(z))-\chi\arg g_t'(z)$. Let $\mathcal{F}_t$ be the filtration generated by $(W, V^{i,q})$. Then there exists a coupling $(K,h)$ where $h = \tilde{h}+ \mathfrak{h}_0$ with $\tilde{h}$ being a zero boundary GFF on $\mathbb{H}$ such that the following is true. For any $\mathcal{F}_t$-stopping time $\tau$ before the continuation threshold, $K_\tau$ is a local set for $h$ and the conditional law of $h|_{\mathbb{H}\backslash K_\tau}$ given $\mathcal{F}_\tau$ is the same as the law of $\mathfrak{h}_\tau+\tilde{h}\circ g_\tau$. Moreover, the curve $\eta$ is measurable with respect to $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm-ig1 of arXiv:2411.19810

Fixing $\kappa>0$, then we can find positive constants $C_{(corollary8.5 of the paper)}$ and $c$ depending only on $\kappa$ such that, for all $s\geq C_{(corollary8.5 of the paper)}$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$ that satisfy $sk\leq n$, uniformly for all $\lambda_i\in[-(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n},(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n}]$,
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\mu_k(\lambda_i)\cdot k}\geq s\right)\lesssim\exp(-c(sk)^\frac{1}{2}).
$$
We also have, uniformly for all $\lambda_i\in[-(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n},(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n}]$, for all $k\in\mathbb{N},$
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\mu_k(\lambda_i)\geq \frac{\sqrt{n}}{C_{(corollary8.5 of the paper)}k}\right)\lesssim \exp(-ck^\frac{1}{2}).
$$

body: [Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.21255, 'Laws of the iterated logarithm for random Dirichlet series with general weights'] Let $N$ be a positive nonincreasing integer-valued function satisfying $\lim_{s\to 0+}N(s)=\infty$ and $\lim_{s\to 0+}s\log N(s)=0$. Let $\rho=\rho(\gamma)$ and $(s_n)_{n\geq 1}$ be as in Lemma \ref{4} with the only difference that $\gamma\in (0,1/2)$. Then $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{s\in [s_{n+1}, s_n]}\, g(s)\Big|\sum_{k>N(s)}\frac{a_k}{k^{1/2+s}}\tilde \eta_{k,\,\rho}(s)-\sum_{k>N(s_{n+1})} \frac{a_k}{k^{1/2+s_{n+1}}}\tilde \eta_{k,\,\rho}(s_{n+1})\Big|=0\quad\text{{\rm a.s.}}$$

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Same structural obstruction as C0064, with the oriented triangle diagram. Result: For oriented percolation the lace expansion converges when the oriented triangle (bubble) diagram is small, controlled by the random-walk return probabilities of the d-dimensional walk, of order 1/d; the nearest-neighbour model in d = 5, 6, 7 has no small parameter, exactly as for unoriented percolation below d = 11. The NoBLE-type numerical bootstrap has not been carried out for oriented percolation in the source's account; the threshold would need to be beaten at d = 5, where the bubble diagram is of order 1. A rigorous partial fact: the bubble condition (finiteness) holds for all d > 4 by the Gaussian bound of the infrared type only after the infrared bound is proved, so there is no unconditional finiteness statement below the lace-expansion regime; the differential inequalities of Barsky-Aizenman give the mean-field exponents from the bubble condition, so the entire problem is the bubble condition for d in {5, 6, ...} below the numerical threshold. No new input. Obstruction: No small parameter for nearest-neighbour oriented percolation in d = 5, 6, 7.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0078-mean-field-behaviour-of-nearest-neighbour-oriented-percolation-for-all

[Lemma PSn012Rn0 of arXiv:2604.07227, 'Transition probabilities of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $S$ be a usual SRRW on $(\mathbb{Z}_L,+)$ with parameter $\alpha\in [0,1)$ and step distribution $\mu$, and let $(R_n(x))_{n\geq 1}$ be elephant polynomials with the same parameter $\alpha$. \\
(i). If $L=2$ and $\mu(0)=\mu(1)=1/2$, then for $n\geq 1$, 
$$\mathbb{E} \chi_1^{(2)}(S_n)=2\mathbb{P}(S_n=0)-1=\mathrm{i}^n R_n(0).$$ 
(ii). If $L\geq 3$ and $\mu(-1)=\mu(1)=1/2$, then for any $j\in [L-1]$ and $n\geq 1$, $\mathbb{E} \chi_k^{(L)}(S_n)=R_n(\cos (2 k\pi/L) )$.

body: [Proposition prop:15 of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\gamma\in (0,2)$ and consider a whole plane GFF $h$ and the associated LQG metric $D_h$. Then, almost surely, simultaneously for all $D_h$-geodesics $P: [0,T] \to \mathbb{C}$ and $0<s<t<T$, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that for every point $u\in \mathcal{B}_\delta(P(s)), v\in \mathcal{B}_\delta(P(t))$, and every geodesic $\Gamma_{u,v}$, we have $P\lvert_{[s+\varepsilon,t-\varepsilon]}\subseteq \Gamma_{u,v}$ and $\Gamma_{u,v}\lvert_{[\varepsilon, D_h(u,v)-\varepsilon]}\subseteq P$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 7 (Generalized It\^o class) of arXiv:2606.17517, 'Killed resolvents and measure-valued stopping gains for reflected optimal stopping with ma'] A continuous function $u:\R^2_+\to\R$ is said to belong to the generalized
It\^o class for $X$ if the following holds. Whenever the distribution
$(\mathcal L-r)u-c$ is represented in the interior by a signed Radon measure
$\mu_u$, there is a corresponding signed continuous additive functional
$A^{\mu_u}$ such that, after localization,
\[
   e^{-rt}u(X_t)
   =
   u(x)
   +\int_0^t e^{-rs}c(X_s)\,ds
   +\int_0^t e^{-rs}\,dA_s^{\mu_u}
   +M_t
   +\text{reflection boundary terms},
\]
where $M$ is a local martingale. If $u$ satisfies the reflected Neumann
condition in the trace sense, the reflection boundary terms vanish.
title: Generalized It\^o class

[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked, no independent read.] This is an exactly solved adjacent case of Open Problem 14.12 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). For n>=3 let C_n be the simple cycle on n vertices. Start a particle at every vertex. Each particle independently jumps at rate one to a uniformly chosen neighbor, and particles merge on meeting. Let T_coal be the first time only one particle remains. Then E[T_coal]=(n^2-1)/6. If P is the cycle's discrete-time simple-walk matrix, define its mean spectral hitting-time quantity K=sum_{j=2}^n 1/(1-lambda_j(P)); then K=(n^2-1)/6 also. Thus E[T_coal]=K exactly. Its relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-cos(2pi/n)) satisfies tau_2/K -> 3/pi^2, so this family has the equality conclusion even though the small-relaxation-time hypothesis in the source problem fails. In the extracted optional-stopping proof, EC in a stopping-time subscript denotes the random coalescence time; the final displayed EC denotes its expectation. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Continuous-time rate-one simple walks; one initial particle per vertex.
n>=3 and coalescence occurs on occupying the same vertex.

			\wtilde{\E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\big(\|u(t)\|_{H_0^1(\bO)}^2+ \|u(t)\|_{L^p(\bO)}^p\big)\bigg]+	\wtilde{\E}\bigg[\int_0^T\big(\|\Delta u(t)\|_{L^2(\bO)}^2+ \|u(t)\|_{L^{2p-2}(\bO)}^{2p-2}\big)dt\bigg]<\infty.

[Proposition 21 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] The comparison and rigidity arguments used below are collected in the following proposition.

\textup{(i)} Assume that for some compact interval $K$, $\delta>0$ and $W\ge1$,
\[
W(x)\to+\infty,\; (\cA_\R+\lambda)W\le-\delta W\;\hbox{in }\R\setminus K.
\]
Let $U$ be one of the two components of $\R\setminus K$. If $u\in C^1(U)$ extends continuously to the interaction collar of $U$, satisfies $u^+=o(W)$ at the infinite end, $(\cA_\R+\lambda)u\ge0$ in $U$, and $u\le0$ on the finite interaction collar of width $R_J$, then $u\le0$ in $U$.

\textup{(ii)} Let $\lambda_p=\Lp(\R)$. Assume that there exist a compact interval $K$, $\delta>0$ and $W\in C^1(\R)$ such that $W\ge1$, $W(x)\to+\infty$, and
\[
(\cA_\R+\lambda_p)W\le-\delta W\;\hbox{in }\R\setminus K.
\]
Suppose that every positive eigenfunction associated with $\lambda_p$ is $o(W)$. Then every such eigenfunction has $W$-minimal growth, and $\lambda_p$ is simple in the positive cone: any two positive eigenfunctions associated with $\lambda_p$ are proportional.

\textup{(iii)} Assume the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:simplicitycore}. Let $u>0$ satisfy $u=o(W)$ and $(\cA_\R+\lambda_p)u\le0$ in $\R$, where $\lambda_p=\Lp(\R)$. Then $u$ is a positive multiple of the principal eigenfunction. In particular the inequality is necessarily an equality.

\textup{(iv)} Under the same hypotheses, let $f\in C_c(\R)$ satisfy $f\ge0$ and $f\not\equiv0$. There is no positive $u\in C^1(\R)$ with $u=o(W)$ satisfying $(\cA_\R+\lambda_p)u=-f$ in $\R$.

\textup{(v)} Assume the Lyapunov hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:simplicitycore}. Let $u,v>0$, $u=o(W)$, $v=o(W)$, satisfy
\[
(\cA_\R+\lambda_p)u\ge0,\qquad (\cA_\R+\lambda_p)v\le0.
\]
If $u\le Cv$ on one compact interaction collar containing the Lyapunov core, then $u\le Cv$ on $\R$. If equality of the optimal constant is attained at one point and both differential inequalities are equalities, then $u$ and $v$ are proportional.

[Theorem 10 (Simple bounded-degree configuration model: pointwise version) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\), that is, the pairing model conditioned on simplicity. Assume that
\[
1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
\qquad\text{for all }i,n,
\]
and
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho.
\]
Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\). If
\[
\rho>2c_{\theta,u}
=
2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr),
\]
then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
\[
t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\rho)+\delta,
\]
one has
\[
\Pbb\!\left(
\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Simple bounded-degree configuration model: pointwise version

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); no independent PASS or established priority. Use C014's setting: finite m>=2,w>=2, real rank-two m-by-2 M, SPD 2-by-2 Sigma, distinct positive singular values s1>s2 of M Sigma. Write D=[[0,M Sigma],[Sigma M^T,0]], H(P)=[[0,P Sigma],[Sigma P^T,0]], and let v1,v2 be its positive unit eigenvectors. Fix one finite seed U0=(B0;A0^T) and one hidden orthogonal rotation R with v1^T U0 R=(c1,0,...,0), c1>0. Write U0 R=[z0,X0] and assume c2=v2^T X0 is nonzero. Start the factor flow at alpha U0 R. Put tau=log(1/alpha)/s1 and epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), and write shifted U_alpha(t)=[z_alpha(t),X_alpha(t)] for physical time tau+t.

For the exact c1 canonical path zbar of C014, on every FIXED shifted compact I,
 sup_I ||z_alpha-zbar||<=C_I epsilon.
The constant depends on I, seed and data. This is an entire active-vector bound, including the extra output directions, not a substitution of frozen dormant transport for active variation.

Moreover C014, this estimate, the reduced square transport C003 and C016 imply the following proposed Gaussian-arrival conclusion. For almost every ONE fixed iid standard Gaussian seed, subsequently scaled by alpha, there are physical arrival times T_alpha and p_alpha>0 tending to zero with
 ||z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar||=O(p_alpha^2),
 ||X_alpha(T_alpha)||_F=O(p_alpha),
 ||vstar^T X_alpha(T_alpha)||_F=p_alpha,
 ||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar zstar^T||_F<=K p_alpha^2,
 vstar^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)vstar>=p_alpha^2.
Here zstar is the nonzero-product critical endpoint of the canonical first path, Z_alpha=U_alpha U_alpha^T, and vstar is the unit top frozen residual vector. In these arrival formulas z_alpha and X_alpha are evaluated in physical time, with the first fixed hidden rotation R. K is fixed for the chosen seed and data. Thus arrival is strongly relatively aligned without an initial alignment hypothesis. This statement alone does not construct the subsequent canonical escape or its forward endpoint.

Fix one finite seed U0=(B0;A0^T) and one hidden orthogonal rotation R with v1^T U0 R=(c1,0,...,0), c1>0. Write U0 R=[z0,X0] and assume c2=v2^T X0 is nonzero. Start the factor flow at alpha U0 R. Put tau=log(1/alpha)/s1 and epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), and write shifted U_alpha(t)=[z_alpha(t),X_alpha(t)] for physical time tau+t.

For the exact c1 canonical path zbar of C014, on every FIXED shifted compact I,
 sup_I ||z_alpha-zbar||<=C_I epsilon.
The constant depends on I, seed and data. This is an entire active-vector bound, including the extra output directions, not a substitution of frozen dormant transport for active variation.

Moreover C014, this estimate, the reduced square transport C003 and C016 imply the following proposed Gaussian-arrival conclusion. For almost every ONE fixed iid standard Gaussian seed, subsequently scaled by alpha, there are physical arrival times T_alpha and p_alpha>0 tending to zero with
 ||z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar||=O(p_alpha^2),
 ||X_alpha(T_alpha)||_F=O(p_alpha),
 ||vstar^T X_alpha(T_alpha)||_F=p_alpha,
 ||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar zstar^T||_F<=K p_alpha^2,
 vstar^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)vstar>=p_alpha^2.
Here zstar is the nonzero-product critical endpoint of the canonical first path, Z_alpha=U_alpha U_alpha^T, and vstar is the unit top frozen residual vector. In these arrival formulas z_alpha and X_alpha are evaluated in physical time, with the first fixed hidden rotation R. K is fixed for the chosen seed and data. Thus arrival is strongly relatively aligned without an initial alignment hypothesis. This statement alone does not construct the subsequent canonical escape or its forward endpoint.

## 1. Negative-half-line comparison
C014's proof gives, on [-tau,T] for a sufficiently negative FIXED T,
 ||U_alpha(t)||,||zbar(t)||<=C exp(s1 t),
 ||X_alpha(t)||_F<=C epsilon exp(s2 t),
 zbar(-tau)=alpha c1 v1+O(alpha^3).
These follow from the full operator bounds and weighted bootstrap, including all zero modes.

Let e=z_alpha-zbar. At -tau,
 e(-tau)=alpha(z0-c1 v1)+O(alpha^3).
The displayed first vector has zero v1 component EXACTLY. The spectrum of D outside v1 is bounded above by s2: it consists of s2, -s1, -s2, and m-2 zeros. Hence for t>=-tau its first free term is bounded by
 C alpha exp(s2(t+tau))=C epsilon exp(s2 t).
The O(alpha^3) remainder propagates to at most C alpha^2 exp(s1 t). After division by epsilon exp(s2 t), its size is at most
 C alpha^(1+s2/s1) exp((s1-s2)T).
This is bounded and tends to zero. In particular there is no uncontrolled O(alpha) remainder in the fastest free direction. The transverse zero-mode free terms, though larger than negative-mode terms in normalized dormant matching, are smaller than the positive s2 bound used here.

Put N1(z)=H(b a^T)z. On the segment between actual and reference active vectors, its cubic derivative is bounded by C exp(2s1 t). With X=(V;W), the exact equation is
 e'=De-[N1(z_alpha)-N1(zbar)]-H(VW^T)z_alpha.
The last term is bounded by C epsilon^2 exp((s1+2s2)t). No frozen-transport equation is used for e.

Using ||exp(D(t-u))||<=exp(s1(t-u)), define the finite weighted supremum A_t=sup_{-tau<=u<=t} ||e(u)||/(epsilon exp(s2 u)). The Lipschitz integral, after division by this weight, is at most
 [C exp(2s1 T)/(s1+s2)] A_t.
Indeed its remaining integral is exp((s1-s2)t) integral_{-tau}^t exp((s1+s2)u)du. The dormant-feedback integral is at most
 C epsilon exp((s1+s2)T)/(2s2),
since its remaining integral is integral_{-tau}^t exp(2s2 u)du. Both denominators are positive. Thus
 A_t<=C_free+[C exp(2s1 T)/(s1+s2)]A_t+C epsilon exp((s1+s2)T)/(2s2).
Shrink T until the bracket is below 1/2, and absorb it. For alpha small with -tau<=T and alpha<=1, the rightmost term is bounded uniformly. This proves a uniform bound on A_t through T. All constants are independent of alpha for the fixed data and seed.

## 2. Extension to fixed compacts only
C014 gives uniform bounded factors and X_alpha=O(epsilon) on each fixed interval [T,T1]. The active vector field is Lipschitz on the relevant fixed bounded set, and dormant feedback is O(epsilon^2). Finite-interval Gronwall propagates e(T)=O(epsilon) to e=O_I(epsilon). No interval with T1 depending on alpha is covered. This proves the quantitative active assertion.

## 3. The first endpoint and ideal transport reduce exactly to square dimension two
Let Q span col(M) orthonormally. C014 places both bbar and chi_b inside col(M), and the reduced equations are exactly those for the invertible square Mtilde=Q^T M and the same Sigma. Their positive origin singular values remain s1,s2. The first canonical path is balanced and nonconstant, bounded by its energy sublevel and balance identity. The analytic-gradient convergence argument in C012 Section 2 gives a stationary limit. A fixed finite-time loss is strictly below C(0), hence the limiting loss is also strictly below C(0). It cannot have zero product. In the reduced square representation, zero outer product forces one factor zero and balance forces the other zero. Thus zstar has NONZERO PRODUCT, the premise needed by C015 and C016. This transfers back isometrically to the rectangular output space.

The reduced canonical pair has the two positive origin boundary modes and their canonical Volterra prescriptions. Thus it is exactly the square pair of C006, with its J-null graph orientation. C003 applies to the nonzero first endpoint and implies chi/||chi|| tends, up to sign, to its positive frozen residual vector. This statement does not require exponential endpoint convergence. The full rectangular residual has columns in col(M), by C015, and rank one. Its unique positive vector vstar is the isometric lift of the reduced vector; all added output directions are dormant zero eigenvectors. Therefore the same normalized transport alignment holds in the full rectangular space. The nonzero solution chi of a continuous linear ODE never vanishes at a finite time; c2 is fixed and nonzero.

## 4. One fixed cone entrance, followed by the separate local argument
Choose a single sufficiently late shifted first-path time T0 so the reference remains inside C016's endpoint neighborhood and chi(T0)c2 lies strictly inside its prescribed cone. Such T0 exists by the transport limit just proved. It is chosen before alpha tends to zero. By C014,
 X_alpha(T0)/epsilon -> chi(T0)c2.
Consequently there are fixed positive c0,c1 and a fixed small-alpha cutoff such that the actual projected dormant row has norm between c0 epsilon and c1 epsilon and the actual block is inside the cone. The strict cone margin absorbs any eventually-small normalized error; no false O(epsilon) bound on that normalized error is imposed.

Sections 1-2 give ||z_alpha(T0)-zbar(T0)||<=C0 epsilon at the SAME fixed T0. These are all of C016's entrance hypotheses, with uniform constants for the fixed seed and data. Apply C016 with epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), a monotone parametrization tending to zero. Its own local comparison inequalities and all-smaller-epsilon diagonal cutoffs give the physical arrival times and O(p_alpha^2) active endpoint error stated above. This uses C016 to control the growing local interval; it does not extrapolate Section 2 Gronwall beyond a fixed compact.

## 5. Gaussian event, status and remaining piece
For iid Gaussian U0 the two orthonormal eigenrows v1^T U0 and v2^T U0 are independent standard Gaussian rows in R^w. Almost surely c1>0 and the projection of the second onto the (w-1)-dimensional complement of the first is nonzero. This is an initialization statement, not later-flow independence. The seed is fixed while alpha varies.

C014-C017 are unaudited rectangular drafts. C003/C006/C008/C009/C010/C011/C012 have PASS only at their recorded square or general-ODE scopes; no PASS is inherited merely by analogy. The strongest remaining obligation for the full rectangular second-step theorem is the canonical escape and forward-endpoint composition: verify its full parameter Jacobian, fixed full-top projection, invariant output/hidden subspaces at the negative-infinite boundary, and apply C010 only after reducing the canonical path to square width two. That composition is not asserted here. Literature priority remains unresolved.

[Corollary No finite-moment determination of annealed complexity of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:no-finite-moment}
For every fixed integer \(r\ge2\) and every \(p\ge3\), there exist two
symmetric, centered, unit-variance sub-Gaussian laws \(\mu_1,\mu_2\), both
with strictly positive \(C^\infty\) densities and with identical moments
through order \(r\), and a compact interval \(B\subset(0,\infty)\), such
that
\[
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_{\mu_1}\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 >
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_{\mu_2}\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B).
\]
Thus no prescribed finite collection of moments forces the Gaussian
energy-window rate for the spatially unrestricted, unregularized annealed
count: the non-Gaussian liminf may be strictly larger.  The statement
does not assert existence of the non-Gaussian limit. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 55 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let $X$ be a smooth proper $k$-scheme of dimension $d$.
We assume $\omega_X \simeq \cO_X$.
Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X$ is HT-split.
\item The homomorphism
\[
H^d(X,\cO_X) \xrightarrow{F^{\dR}_X} H^d(X,F_*\Omega_X^{\bullet})
\]
is injective.
\item The Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence is $E_1$-degenerate.
\end{enumerate}

    eta = min(p_c/2, (delta_star-delta)/(2M)) > 0.

Own-work draft: C024 v2, proof (unaudited); independent audit and literature novelty assessment pending. Finite-accuracy bound only, not arbitrary accuracy for a fixed nonzero tail. Let d>=2, X standard Gaussian, u a unit teacher, fixed +1 outer weights, sphere directions, student f_rho(X)=E_rho sigma(w.X), and risk E[(f_rho(X)-sigma(u.X))^2] without 1/2. Let sigma be smooth with Gaussian-L2 expansion sum c_k He_k/sqrt(k!), c1=0, a_k=c_k^2, sum_{k>=2}a_k=1, A=a2>0 and sum k^4 a_k finite. The arbitrary constant coefficient cancels. Put tau=sum_{k>=3}k a_k; odd degrees are allowed. For 0<eps<=1 define delta=sqrt(eps)/8, S=log(32d/delta^3), T=S/(8A delta), H=min(delta^2/16,1/(256A^2T^2)), K=8(1+16AdT)^6 and lambda0=H/(8dTK). If tau<=eps/32 and tau^2<=H/(64KT^2), population sphere MFLD from the uniform law with lambda(t)=lambda0/(1+t/T) has R(rho_T)<=43eps/384<eps/4. Time and inverse positive temperature have explicit polynomial bounds in d,1/eps,1/A. The allowed tail threshold also has a polynomial reciprocal bound. The altered-kernel coupling uses h prime<=16A r_nu h+16A h^(3/2)+8tau sqrt(h)+2d lambda; only the quadratic reference residual enters the integrated clock. It bypasses mixing by tracking that noiseless reference, and supplies no finite-particle guarantee. An explicit entire activation is sqrt(A)He2/sqrt(2)+eta[exp(z-1/2)-1-z-He2/2], with A=1-eta^2(exp(1)-5/2). Every a_k=eta^2/k! for k>=3 is nonzero. Choose Tbar=S/(4delta), Hbar=min(delta^2/16,1/(256Tbar^2)), Kbar=8(1+16dTbar)^6, eta^2=(1/2)min(1/2,eps/32,sqrt(Hbar)/(8Tbar sqrt(Kbar))). Then A>7/8, tau=eta^2(exp(1)-2)<eta^2, and the hypotheses hold. This activation depends on d and eps. For a fixed tail tau>0, the condition tau<=eps/32 fails for sufficiently small eps; no fixed-tail sign-selection or mixing theorem is asserted.

On $\Omega_0$, exchanges inside $B_0$ force $b=\beta\mathbf1_{12}$ and comparison of the three minority states forces $c=\gamma\mathbf1_3$, so the old part of the lower row lies in the span of the two upper rows. On $\Omega_1$, with $R_\xi=(0,\mathbf1_3)$, $R_{\eta,p}=(\mathbf1_{12},p)$ and slice sums $s_j=q-p\cdot\xi^{(j)}\in\{0,0,2\}$, slice exchanges give $b=\beta\mathbf1_{12}$ and a linear form constant on the three minority states has three equal coefficients, so $(b,c)=\beta R_{\eta,p}+\lambda R_\xi$. Subtracting cancels all fifteen upper coordinates, leaving a nonzero row supported on at most two old coordinates -- contradicting projective simplicity. [Lemma number hitting points of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] Let $\xi \in \partial \mathbb{H}^d$, and $\beta \in [0,\pi]$. Let $B\subset \partial \mathbb{H}^d$ be the set of all $\zeta$ such that $\angle([0,\xi),[0,\zeta))<\beta$ and set
\[A:= \bigcup_{\zeta \in B}\big\{x \in [0,\zeta)\big\}.\]
Further, let $\alpha \in (\beta,\pi]$ and $H=H(\alpha)$ be a barrier as defined in (equation barriers of the paper), i.e.
\[ H(\alpha) = \bigcup_{\eta} \bigg\{x \in G: d_{{\mathcal G}}(x,o)\geq n \text{ and } d_{\mathbb{H}}(\psi(x),[0,\eta))<C_0\bigg\}.\]
Let $\lambda>0$ be the multiplicative constant for the rough similarity of the Bonk-Schramm embedding (equation rough similarity of the paper).
Then there exist $C_1,C_2>0$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $n(m):= \abs{\{g\in H : \lfloor d_{{\mathcal G}}(g,o)\rfloor =m\}} \leq C_1$.
\item$N(m):= \abs{\{g\in G : \lfloor d_{{\mathcal G}}(g,o)\rfloor =m, \psi(g)\in A\}}\geq C_2 {\rm e} ^{m}$, as long as $\psi^{-1}(B)\ne \emptyset$. The constant $C_2$ might depend on $\alpha.$
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition proposition4.7 of arXiv:2504.15992, 'Repeated singular values of a random symmetric matrix and decoupled singular value estimat'] [[WOS:000542157900013], Lemma 6.1]
    Let $B>0$, and $\zeta\in\Gamma_B$ be a random variable having a finite, $n$-independent log-Sobolev constant. Consider $A_n\sim\operatorname{Sym}_n(\zeta)$, and denote by $\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_n$ the eigenvalues of $A_n$. Define the empirical measure $\rho_{A_n}^n$ via 
$$\rho_{A_n}^n:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{\frac{\sigma_i}{\sqrt{n}}},$$ 
where $\delta_\cdot$ is the delta measure. Then there exists $\kappa_{(proposition4.7 of the paper)}\in(0,\frac{1}{10})$ such that 
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\ln\mathbb{P}[d(\rho_{A_n}^n,\rho_{sc})>n^{-\kappa_{(proposition4.7 of the paper)}}]=-\infty,
\end{equation}
    where $\rho_{sc}$ is the semicircle law (equation semicircle of the paper) and the distance $d$ is the Dudley (i.e., bounded Lipschitz) distance defined as follows: for two probability measures $\mu$ and $\nu$,
    $$
d(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\|f\|_L\leq 1}\left|\int f(x)d\mu(x)-\int f(x)d\nu(x)\right|,
    $$
    where $\|f\|_L:=\sup_{x\neq y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|}+\sup_x |f(x)|$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn def:size-biased-tree of arXiv:2601.00119, 'The largest common subtree of two random trees'] Let $\tau_\infty$ be a random infinite plane tree and $U_\infty=(J_i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a sequence of random positive integers. Set $U_0=\varnothing$ and $U_n=(J_1,\ldots,J_n)$ for all $n\geq 1$. We say that $(\tau_\infty,U_\infty)$ is a \emph{size-biased Bienaymé tree with offspring distribution $\mu$} if it satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] For all $n\geq 0$, $U_n$ is almost surely an element of $\tau_\infty$.
    
    \item[(b)] The random pairs $(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty),J_{n+1})$ for $n\geq 0$ are i.i.d.~and distributed as follows:
    \[\forall k,j\in\mathbb{N}^*,\quad \mathbf{P}(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty)=k\, ;\, J_{n+1}=j)={\mathbf 1}_{\left\{j\leq k\right\}}\mu(k)/m_\mu.\]
    
    \item[(c)] Conditionally given $(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty),J_{n+1})_{n\geq 0}$, the random plane trees $\theta_{U_n*(j)}\tau_\infty$ for $n\geq 0$ and $j\in \{1,\ldots,\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty)\}\setminus\{J_{n+1}\}$ are independent Bienaymé trees with offspring distribution $\mu$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Defn def:size-biased-tree of arXiv:2601.00119

[Lemma lem:Bernoulli_calYr_representation of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] For every $r \in [0,1]$, the set $\{\hat{f}_k^r \mid k \in I^r \}$ is a basis for ${\rm aff}(\Sym^r)$.

That is, for all $r \in [0,1]$ and $f \in \Sym^r$, there exist constants $\alpha_k^r = \alpha_k^r[f]$ such that 
\[ f = \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r. \]
where $\alpha_0^1[f] = \frac{pf(-1)-qf(1)}{p-q}$ and
$ \alpha_k^r[f] = \frac{2(pf(-2k-r) - qf(2k+r))}{p-q}$
for all other $k,r$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:Bernoulli_calYr_representation of arXiv:2607.29020

[Theorem thm:observable-distance-eb of arXiv:2608.25551, 'Beyond Optimal Rates in Stochastic Optimization: Trajectory-Adaptive Stopping Rules'] Suppose Assumptions~(assump:strong-convexity of the paper)--(assump:stepsize-bound of the paper) and~(assump:bounded-stochastic-gradients of the paper) hold, and suppose~(equation eq:eb-integrability-condition of the paper) is satisfied. Let $R_0$ be an $\mathcal{F}_{t_0 - 1}$-measurable quantity satisfying $R_0 \ge Z_{t_0}$ almost surely. Then, for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, the recursively defined process $\{\widehat U_{t+1}^{\mathrm{dist,EB}}(\alpha)\}_{t \ge t_0}$ is well defined and fully observable from $R_0$ and the SGD trajectory. Moreover,
\[
    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \forall t \ge t_0:\
        Z_{t+1}
        \le
        \widehat U_{t+1}^{\mathrm{dist,EB}}(\alpha)
    \right)
    \ge
    1 - \alpha.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In statistics and control theory, Kalman filtering is an algorithm that uses a series of measurements observed over time, including statistical noise and other inaccuracies, to produce estimates of unknown variables that tend to be more accurate than those based on a single measurement, by estimating a joint probability distribution over the variables for each time-step. The filter is constructed as a mean squared error minimiser, but an alternative derivation of the filter is also provided showing how the filter relates to maximum likelihood statistics. The filter is named after Rudolf E. Kálmán.
title: Kalman filter

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2608.27166, 'Well-posedness and regularity of stochastic heat equations on moving domains'] Let $D\subset\R^n$ be bounded and $C^{1,1}$, and let $p>n+2$. Let $v$ solve

\begin{equation*}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&dv
=
\Delta_D v\,dt+h_i\,dw_t^i,
&& (t,x)\in(S,2T_0]\times D,
\\
&v
=0,
&& (t,x)\in(S,2T_0]\times\partial D,
\\
&v(S)
=0,
&& x\in D.
\end{aligned}
\right.
\end{equation*}
If $h$ is predictable and
$$
h\in L^p\bigl(\Omega\times(S,2T_0]\times D;\ell^2\bigr),
$$
then there are $\alpha_1\in(0,1)$ and $C>0$, depending only on $n,p,T_0,D$, such that
\begin{align*}
\E\|v\|_{C^{\alpha_1/2,\alpha_1}([T_0,2T_0]\times\overline D)}^p
+
\E\|\nabla v\|_{L^p((T_0,2T_0]\times D)}^p
&\leq
C\E\|h\|_{L^p((S,2T_0]\times D;\ell^2)}^p .
\end{align*}
Moreover,
\begin{align*}
\E\|D^2v\|_{L^p((T_0,2T_0];W^{-1,p}(D))}^p
&\leq
C\E\|h\|_{L^p((S,2T_0]\times D;\ell^2)}^p .
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 11 of arXiv:2608.27166

[Defn def:weak_sewing of arXiv:2606.21049, '\textsc{Locality of rough path lifts}'] Recall the set $B\supset \mathcal{C}_2$ from (equation eq:B_def of the paper).
A \emph{weak $\gamma$-sewing map} is a map $\Lambda \colon \delta_2(\mathcal{C}_2) \cap \mathcal{C}_3^\gamma \to B$ such that $\delta_2 \Lambda = \mathbbm 1$.
We say that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item
$\Lambda$ is \emph{local} if for all $(s,t) \in \triangle$ and $\Xi, \Xi' \in \delta_2(\mathcal{C}_2) \cap \mathcal{C}_3^\gamma$ such that $\Xi|_{\triangle^3[s,t]} = \Xi'|_{\triangle^3[s,t]}$, it follows that $\Lambda \Xi|_{\triangle[s,t]} = \Lambda \Xi'|_{\triangle[s,t]}$,

\item
$\Lambda$ \emph{vanishes locally at zero}
if for all $\Xi \in \delta_2(\mathcal{C}_2) \cap \mathcal{C}_3^\gamma$ and $(s,t)\in\triangle$ such that $\Xi|_{\triangle^3[s,t]} = 0$,
one has $\Lambda \Xi|_{\triangle[s,t]} = 0$,

\item $\Lambda$ is \emph{time translation--invariant} if for all $(s,t) \in \triangle$ and $\tau >0$ such that $t+\tau\leq 1$ and $\Xi \in \delta_2(\mathcal{C}_2) \cap \mathcal{C}_3^\gamma$
such that $\Xi_{a,b,c} = \Xi_{a+\tau,b+\tau,c+\tau}$ for all $(a,b,c)\in\triangle^3[s,t]$,
one has $(\Lambda \Xi)_{s,t} = (\Lambda \Xi)_{s+\tau,t+\tau}$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Defn def:weak_sewing of arXiv:2606.21049

[Lemma 10 (\cite{MMO26}) of arXiv:2609.03558, 'Local well-posedness of the higher-order nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation on the half-li'] Suppose $0 \le s < \frac12$, $2 \le \lambda \le \frac{7-2s}{1-2s}$, and
$$
(\mu,r)=\left(\frac{6\lambda}{(1-2s)(\lambda-1)},\frac{2\lambda}{1+2(\lambda-1)s}\right).
$$
Then,
$$
\bigl\||\varphi|^{\lambda-1}\varphi\bigr\|_{L_t^1((0,T);H_x^s(\mathbb{R}))}
\le c(s,\lambda)T^{\frac{\mu-\lambda}{\mu}}
\|\varphi\|_{L_t^\mu((0,T);H_x^{s,r}(\mathbb{R}))}^{\lambda},
$$
and
$$
\bigl\||\varphi|^{\lambda-1}\varphi-|\psi|^{\lambda-1}\psi\bigr\|_{L_t^1((0,T);H_x^s(\mathbb{R}))}
\le c(s,\lambda)T^{\frac{\mu-\lambda}{\mu}}
\left(
\|\varphi\|_{L_t^\mu((0,T);H_x^{s,r}(\mathbb{R}))}^{\lambda-1}
+
\|\psi\|_{L_t^\mu((0,T);H_x^{s,r}(\mathbb{R}))}^{\lambda-1}
\right)
\|\varphi-\psi\|_{L_t^\mu((0,T);H_x^{s,r}(\mathbb{R}))}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For compact full-dimensional convex C in R^d, d>=1, with centroid mu, every linear functional with range [a,b] on C has mean m satisfying a+(b-a)/(d+1)<=m<=b-(b-a)/(d+1). Brunn-Minkowski makes section density to the power 1/(d-1) concave; comparison to a cone density and a monotone-likelihood-ratio covariance identity give the bounds (d=1 is the interval midpoint). Consequently -(C-mu)/d is contained in C-mu, and n*mu-C is contained in (n-1)C for every n>=d+1. This necessary pointwise balancing condition always passes for uniform convex bodies and does not enforce all uniform marginals.

body:
Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and f a square-integrable function of them, Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n). Let X_1', ..., X_n' be an independent copy of the X_i and Z_i' = f(X_1, ..., X_i', ..., X_n) the value with the i-th coordinate resampled. Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - Z_i')^2] = sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - E_i Z)^2], where E_i denotes expectation over X_i alone (Efron and Stein 1981; Steele 1986 for the constant 1/2). Equivalently Var(Z) <= sum_i E[Var_i(Z)]. The inequality is tight for linear f. It needs independence of the coordinates (it is the sum over coordinates of one-coordinate variances, a tensorization statement) but no boundedness; the bounded-differences (McDiarmid) inequality is the exponential-tail counterpart under the extra assumption that changing one coordinate changes f by at most c_i, in which case Var(Z) <= (1/4) sum c_i^2.
X_1, ..., X_n independent (not necessarily identically distributed)
f(X) square-integrable
no boundedness or Lipschitz assumption; those are needed only for the exponential tail (McDiarmid), not for the variance bound
title: Efron-Stein inequality (variance of a function of independent variables)

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The circular measure has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\varepsilon$ has equal density at $q,q^{-1},-q,-q^{-1}$.

\item The odd moments of $\varepsilon$ are $0$.

\item The even moments of $\varepsilon$ are half-integers.

\item When $X$ has norm $\leq 2$, $\varepsilon$ is supported by the unit circle.

\item When $X$ is finite, $\varepsilon$ is discrete.

\item If $K$ is a solution of $d=K+K^{-1}$, then $\varepsilon=law(K)$. 
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma eq:dpi_InfEps of arXiv:2512.20338, 'Up-down chains and scaling limits: \\ application to permuton- and graphon-valued diffusio'] For any permuton $\mu$, pattern $\pi$ of size $k \ge 1$, and $ \varepsilon $ in $[0,1]$, we have
  \begin{multline}
  \mathbb E\Big[ d _\pi^o \big( \textrm{Inf}^{\,  \varepsilon }(\mu) \big) \Big]
  = (1- \varepsilon )^{k}  d _\pi^o(\mu)

  + (1-p) \sum_{m \ge 1} \binom{k}{m} \frac{(1- \varepsilon )^{k-m}  \varepsilon ^m}{k-m+1} \left( \sum_{(\tau,i) \in {\mathcal D}_m(\pi)}  d _\tau^o(\mu)  \right).
\end{multline}

[Lemma lem:MittagLeffler_diff of arXiv:2604.10602, 'Fractional Navier-Stokes Equations with Caputo Derivative Driven by Hermite Noise'] For $0<t_1<t_2\le T$ and $0\le\nu<2$, there exists $C>0$ such that
\[
\|(E_\alpha(t_2)-E_\alpha(t_1))\chi\|_\nu \le C (t_2-t_1)^{\frac{\alpha\nu}{2}} \|\chi\|.
\]
For $t_1=0$, the same estimate holds provided $\chi\in\dot{H}^\nu$ (not merely $\dot{H}^0$). The same estimate holds for $E_{\alpha,\alpha}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma conjugating piecewise linear lip maps of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(0 \leq a_1 < b_1 \leq 1\) and \(0 \leq a_2 < b_2 \leq 1\). Let 
    \[f_i(t) = 
    \begin{cases}
        2t-a_i, \quad &t \in [a_i,a_i + \frac{b_i-a_i}{3}] \\
        \frac{1}{2}t+\frac{1}{2}b_i, \quad &t \in [a_i + \frac{b_i-a_i}{3},b_i].        
    \end{cases}\]
    Then there is a homeomorphism \(\varphi: [a_1,b_1] \to [a_2,b_2]\) such that \(\Lip(\varphi) = \frac{b_2-a_2}{b_1-a_1}\), \(\Lip(\varphi^{-1}) = \frac{b_1-a_1}{b_2-a_2}\) and \(\varphi \circ f_1 = f_2 \circ \varphi.\)

(equation eq:pole-coefficient-class of the paper) and (equation eq:pole-weight-threshold of the paper), with
$0\leq\alpha<1/2$.  Fix an integer $N_{\mathrm H}\geq1$,
$0<\theta<1$, $K\geq K_\theta^\star(a)$, $0<r\leq T$, and
$0<\varepsilon<1$.  Let
$\varphi=\Pi_{\mathrm{hi}}\varphi$ belong to
\begin{equation*}
 W^{1,2}\bigl([\varepsilon,1];L^2(\gamma_d)\bigr)
 \cap L^2\bigl([\varepsilon,1];\mathscr D_\gamma\bigr),
\end{equation*}
with $\varphi=0$ on a strip immediately below $s=1$.  Suppose that, for some
$C_{\mathrm{hi}}>0$, for almost every $s\in(\varepsilon,1)$ and every
$\vartheta\in\mathscr D_\gamma$ satisfying
$\vartheta=\Pi_{\mathrm{hi}}\vartheta$, the fixed-time estimate
\begin{equation}
 \norm{\nabla^{\mathsf A_r^{-1}}\vartheta}_{L^2(\gamma_d)}^2
 \leq\frac{C_{\mathrm{hi}}}{N_{\mathrm H}}
       \norm{\mathsf A_r^{1/2}\operatorname{Hess}_{\mathsf A_r^{-1}}\vartheta
                     \,\mathsf A_r^{1/2}}_{L^2(\gamma_d)}^2
 
\end{equation}
holds, and put
$\Theta_{\mathrm{hi}}
:=\theta+(1-2\alpha)C_{\mathrm{hi}}/N_{\mathrm H}$.  Then
\begin{equation*}
 (1-\Theta_{\mathrm{hi}})
 \left\lVert \mathcal J_r\varphi\right\rVert_{\mathscr Y_{\alpha,K,r};(\varepsilon,1)}^2
 \leq4\left\lVert \mathcal P_r\varphi\right\rVert_{\mathscr X_{\alpha,K,r};(\varepsilon,1)}^2.
\end{equation*}
The estimate is uniform in $\varepsilon$.

Every regular Dirichlet form (E, F) on L^2(E; m) admits a unique Beurling-Deny representation: for any u, v in F cap C_0(E), E(u,v) = E^{(c)}(u,v) + iint_{E x E \ diag} (u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y)) J(dx, dy) + int_E u(x) v(x) k(dx), where E^{(c)} has the strong local property, J is a symmetric Radon jumping measure off the diagonal, and k is a Radon killing measure.
(E, F) is regular Dirichlet form on L^2(E; m)
title: Beurling-Deny Decomposition of a Regular Dirichlet Form

[Lemma lm:tensor-bil of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $S\subset T$ be a cleft and let ${\mathcal{C}}^\otimes$ be an $S$-cocomplete symmetric monoidal $T$-$\infty$-category such that the tensor product is $S$-bilinear. Then also $\smash{{\mathcal{C}}_{/X}^\otimes}$ is $S$-cocomplete, and the tensor product is $S$-bilinear.
    \begin{proof}
        By [martiniwolf2022presentable]*{Corollary~A.1.4}, the underlying $T$-$\infty$-category of $\smash{{\mathcal{C}}_{/X}^\otimes}$ is $S$-cocomplete, and the forgetful functor is $S$-cocontinuous. Using that the latter is also conservative and symmetric monoidal, we immediately see that the tensor product on $\smash{{\mathcal{C}}_{/X}^\otimes}$ preserves $S$-colimits in each variable as this holds in ${\mathcal{C}}^\otimes$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lm:tensor-bil of arXiv:2608.28504

body:
[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2607.19873, 'Local limit theorem for the operator norm of products of random matrices'] Let $M$ be a metrizable compact group acting continuously on the right on the compact metrizable space $\wt B$. 
Then, the following statements hold. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For each $x \in \wh M$, 
the operator $\pi_x$ is a continuous projection of $C^0(\wt B)$ whose range is the closed subspace $\bigcap_{\substack{x' \in \wh M \\ x' \neq x}} \ker \pi_{x'}$.

\item
The linear subspace $\bigoplus_{x \in \wh M} \pi_x (C^0(\wt B))$ is dense in $C^0(\wt B)$. 

\item
The linear map $f \otimes \psi \mapsto \langle f, \psi \rangle: V_x^* \otimes W_x^0 \to C^0(\wt B)$ is a continuous surjection onto $\pi_x (C^0(\wt B))$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 16 of arXiv:2607.19873

[Lemma 57 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(d\ge3\), \(1\le k<d\), \(r_b>0\), and \(\Lambda\ge1\).  There
exist constants
\[
 a_0=a_0(d,k,r_b,\Lambda)>0,
 \qquad
 R_0=R_0(d,k,r_b,\Lambda)<\infty
\]
with the following property.  Let \((M^d,h)\) be a Riemannian manifold
and \(p\in M\).  Suppose that \(\exp_p\) is a diffeomorphism from
\(B_{T_pM}(0,2r_b)\) onto its image and that, in these exponential
coordinates,
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda^{-1}g_{\rm E}
 \le \exp_p^*h\le\Lambda g_{\rm E},
 \qquad
 \|\exp_p^*h\|_{C^2(B(0,2r_b))}\le\Lambda.
\end{equation}
Let
\[
 H:\exp_p\bigl(B_{T_pM}(0,2r_b)\bigr)\longrightarrow\R^k
\]
be smooth, with \(H(p)=0\), and suppose that
\begin{equation}
 |dH|_h+|\nabla dH|_h\le\Lambda
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda^{-1}|a|^2
 \le
 \left|\sum_{\alpha=1}^k a_\alpha dH^\alpha\right|_h^2
 \le\Lambda |a|^2
 \qquad(a\in\R^k).
\end{equation}
Then the component of \(H^{-1}(0)\) through \(p\) contains an embedded
closed \((d-k)\)-disk \(\mathcal D_p\) such that
\begin{align}
 \mathcal D_p
 &\subset
 B_{H^{-1}(0),\,h|_{H^{-1}(0)}}(p,R_0),
 \\
 \Vol_{h|_{H^{-1}(0)}}(\mathcal D_p)
 &\ge a_0.
 
\end{align}
The ball in \eqref{ti:eq:level-disk-intrinsic-ball} is intrinsic to the
regular level.

\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in V} H(Dv(x),x).

Let K=[0,1]^2, c1=(0,0), c2=(1,0), c3=(0,1), phi_i(x)=max(0,1/2-||x-c_i||_1), and f(x)=sum_i phi_i(x)v_i, where the planar v_i are unit vectors at pairwise angle 120 degrees. Put Y=f(K), with ambient Euclidean metrics on both K and Y. The map f has no continuous right inverse Y -> K. If alpha:K -> R^m is continuous and constant on every f-fibre, it factors continuously as alpha=psi composed with f. If also D composed with alpha=f, then psi embeds Y; for finite PL alpha its three initial positive tangent rays are distinct and span dimension at least two. Such fibre constancy is not automatic for hidden features of an exact biased ReLU network. For any Lipschitz s:Y -> K with approximation error e=sup_y ||f(s(y))-y|| satisfying 0<e<1/2, e Lip(s)>=1/sqrt(6). For every 0<e<=1/4 an explicit finite PL s attains equality. Therefore uniformly Lipschitz approximate source sections cannot replace a source section as the error tends to zero. These facts do not imply a bound on network parameter cost: a link between source lifts and hidden features is still missing, and full T276 remains open.

Write K=[0,1]^2, c1=(0,0), c2=(1,0), c3=(0,1),
phi_i(x)=max(0,1/2-||x-c_i||_1), and f=sum_i phi_i v_i, with unit
120-degree leg vectors v_i. Put Y=f(K), and let T_i={||x-c_i||_1<=1/2}.
The positive support interiors are disjoint. Consequently if f(x)=t v_i
for t>0 then x lies in T_i (indeed in its relative positive interior).

There is no continuous right inverse s:Y -> K of f. If one existed,
s(t v_i) would lie in T_i for every 0<t<=1/2. Continuity at the common
vertex 0 and closedness of T_i would imply s(0) belongs to every T_i.

than the sum 1 of their radii. This is a contradiction.

endpoint cannot exist. The branch vertex is a whole collapsed fibre,
not a source point at which all three positive legs meet. Translating
hidden features by one chosen source feature does not fix this issue.

Here is the exact additional hypothesis under which a hidden branch
center does exist. Suppose alpha:K -> R^m is continuous and constant
on each fibre of f. Then there is a unique continuous psi:Y -> R^m
with alpha=psi composed with f. Indeed, define psi(f(x))=alpha(x).
This is well-defined by fibre constancy. The continuous surjection f
from compact K to Hausdorff Y is a closed quotient map, so psi is
continuous. If also a suffix D satisfies D composed with alpha=f,
then D composed with psi=id_Y. Thus psi is injective, and compactness
makes it a homeomorphism from Y onto its image.

If alpha is finite PL, psi is finite PL on each of the three legs.
For example set u=(1/2-t)/2 for 0<=t<=1/2 and use the affine lifts
x_1(t)=(u,u), x_2(t)=(1-u,u), x_3(t)=(u,1-u).

which is harmless because fibre constancy identifies their alpha values.
Thus psi(t v_i)=alpha(x_i(t)) is PL. Close enough to t=0 it equals
psi(0)+t u_i for a fixed nonzero vector u_i. Injectivity implies that
no two u_i are positive multiples, since otherwise the two small image
segments overlap. Three distinct positive rays cannot all lie in one
linear line. Their joint linear span therefore has dimension at least 2.

Fibre constancy is not automatic for exact representations. The valid
hidden encoder alpha(x)=x+(1,1) has nonnegative outputs on K and is
implemented by a ReLU layer with W=I,b=(1,1). The suffix z -> f(z-(1,1))

p=(1/2,1/2) and q=(3/4,3/4), both in f^{-1}(0).

enforce fibre constancy. This construction does not have cost below 2
per layer and gives no counterexample to Jacot's conjecture.

features, but an arbitrary exact network need not have such features.

# Approximate sections cannot have uniformly bounded Lipschitz constants

Let f:K=[0,1]^2 -> Y be the dossier map with corners c1=(0,0),
c2=(1,0), c3=(0,1), phi_i=max(0,1/2-||x-c_i||_1), and unit leg
directions v_i at pairwise angle 120 degrees. Give K and Y their ambient
Euclidean distances. Let E(s)=sup_{y in Y} ||f(s(y))-y||.

For any Lipschitz s:Y -> K with 0<E(s)<1/2,

                   E(s) Lip(s) >= 1/sqrt(6).                 (1)

If E(s)=0, no continuous s exists, as established in the preceding
no-section artifact. Thus a sequence of approximate sections whose
errors tend to zero cannot have uniformly bounded Lipschitz constants.

Proof of (1). Put e=E(s). For e<t<=1/2, the image f(s(t v_i))
must lie on the positive i-th leg: every other leg, including the
vertex, is at distance at least t from t v_i, since their angles
are obtuse. Thus s(t v_2) lies in T_2={||x-c2||_1<=1/2}, and
s(t v_3) lies in T_3={||x-c3||_1<=1/2}.
On T_2 we have x-y>=1/2, while on T_3 we have x-y<=-1/2.
Cauchy-Schwarz therefore gives distance(T_2,T_3)>=1/sqrt(2).
Equality is attained at (3/4,1/4) and (1/4,3/4).
Since ||t v_2-t v_3||=sqrt(3)t, we obtain
Lip(s)>=1/(sqrt(6)t). Let t decrease to e to obtain (1).

For clarity the divergence is unavoidable geometry, not an artifact
of a poor approximate lift. For each 0<e<=1/4 there is a finite PL s
with E(s)=e and Lip(s)=1/(sqrt(6)e), as follows.
Set delta=e/(1-2e), so 0<delta<=1/2, p=(1/2,1/2), and
u(t)=(1/2-t)/2. The exact affine lifts along the separate legs are

 x1(t)=(u(t),u(t)), x2(t)=(1-u(t),u(t)), x3(t)=(u(t),1-u(t)).

Define s(0)=p and, on the i-th leg, define

 s(t v_i)=p+(t/delta)(x_i(delta)-p),   0<=t<=delta,
 s(t v_i)=x_i(t),                    delta<=t<=1/2.

The two definitions agree at delta and the three branches agree at 0.
The images stay in the convex square. On the inner part no other
positive support is encountered and direct substitution gives

 f(s(t v_i))=max(0,-1/2+(1/2+delta)t/delta) v_i.

The coefficient is between 0 and t. The error increases up to
t0=delta/(1+2delta)=e and then decreases to zero at delta.
The outer part is exact, so E(s)=e.

The Euclidean slope along each inner leg is
M=(1+2delta)/(2 sqrt(2) delta)=1/(2 sqrt(2)e).
The outer slope is 1/sqrt(2), which is at most M for e<=1/4.
For points on different legs with parameters t,q>=0, their distance

=1/(sqrt(6)e). The universal lower bound (1) proves equality.

body:
Compact operators are completely continuous: they send weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent ones. The converse needs the domain to be reflexive, because the proof runs 'bounded sequence -> weakly convergent subsequence -> norm convergent image', and the first arrow is exactly reflexivity (with the Eberlein-Smulian theorem). The counterexample is the identity of l^1: by Schur's property, every weakly convergent sequence in l^1 converges in norm, so the identity is completely continuous, yet it is not compact because l^1 is infinite-dimensional. A related trap in the other direction is the use of weak sequential compactness of the unit ball: in a nonreflexive space such as c_0 or L^1([0,1]) a bounded sequence need not have any weakly convergent subsequence, so arguments of the form 'the sequence is bounded, so pass to a weakly convergent subsequence, and then apply compactness of T' are invalid there. Also note that the older literature uses 'completely continuous' as a synonym for 'compact'; when reading a classical source, check which meaning is in force before transporting a statement.
the domain is reflexive for the converse direction
compactness always implies complete continuity, with no reflexivity needed
terminology must be checked in older sources, where 'completely continuous' can mean 'compact'
title: Pitfall: 'Maps Weakly Convergent to Norm Convergent' Implies Compact Only for Reflexive Domains

body: In mathematics, subadditivity is a property of a function that states, roughly, that evaluating the function for the sum of two elements of the domain always returns something less than or equal to the sum of the function's values at each element. There are numerous examples of subadditive functions in various areas of mathematics, particularly norms and square roots. Additive maps are special cases of subadditive functions.
