[Proposition prop:averaging of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] A proof cannot either rely on selections that keep the original weights on a
subset. With $w_e=p_ip_jd_{ij}$, $y_e=w_eB_{ij}$,
$U=\sum_ew_e^2$, $Q=\sum_e\lVert y_e\rVert^2$, $R=4\sum_ip_i^2$,
$V=2\sum_ip_i^2|z_i|^2$, the exact averages over all $k$-subsets $S$ (with
$D_S=\sum_{e\subset S}w_e$, $G_S=\sum_{e\subset S}y_e$, and binomials
$A=\binom{N-2}{k-2}$, $B=\binom{N-3}{k-3}$, $H=\binom{N-4}{k-4}$) are
\[
  \sum_{|S|=k}\lVert G_S\rVert^2=(A-2B+H)Q+(B-H)V,\qquad
  \sum_{|S|=k}D_S^2=H+(A-2B+H)U+(B-H)R .
\]
For the fifth-roots system $t_j=\zeta_5^j$, $z_j=t_j^2$, $p_j=\frac15$ one
gets $U=\frac3{25},R=\frac45,Q=\frac15,V=\frac25$, so the best
original-weight three-point ratio guaranteed by these averages is
$\frac{Q+V}{U+R}=\frac{15}{23}>\frac58$: reweighting inside the selected
triangle (the freedom quantified by Lemma~(lem:closure of the paper)) is essential.

+

\[
\boxed{
l_{xx}
+
\frac1{2t}
+
\frac1{x^2}
\geq0 ,
}

where

\[
l=\log w .
\]

Hamilton.

body: In combinatorial mathematics and extremal set theory, the Sauer–Shelah lemma states that every family of sets with small VC dimension consists of a small number of sets. Here, the VC dimension is the largest size of a set with the property that all of its subsets can be formed by intersecting it with a member of the family. If the family has elements in its union, then the Sauer–Shelah lemma states that its number of sets is at most proportional to .

[Theorem Restatement of \cref{gaussian recursion} of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] Let ${\bf x} \sim \gauss{0}{\mathbb{I}_n}$ and $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in [n]^d}$ be a sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a degree-$d$ homogeneous Gaussian polynomial random matrix as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in [n]^d} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b \in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{2t}^{2t} ~\leq~ (2^d \sqrt{2}t)^{2t} \left( \sum_{1 \leq a+b
    \leq d}\norm{{\mathbb E} {\bf F}_{a,b}}_{2t}^{2t} \right).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 15 of arXiv:2609.02808, 'Minimizers of Laplace eigenvalues under a lower curvature bound'] Let $(X_n)\subset\overline\Cc$ satisfy $\mathcal H^2(X_n)\to0$ and
$\diam(X_n)\to D>0$, and equip each with its normalized measure
$\mathfrak m_n=\mathcal H^2\llcorner X_n/\mathcal H^2(X_n)$. Then, after passing to a
subsequence, $(X_n,d_n,\mathfrak m_n)$ converges in the mGH
topology to
\[
X=\bigl([0,D],\,|\cdot|,\,c\,\varphi\,ds\bigr),
\]
where $c>0$ normalizes the mass and $\varphi$ is continuous on $[0,D]$, positive on
$(0,D)$, and satisfies $\varphi''+\varphi\le0$ distributionally, that is
\eqref{eq:intro-density}.

[Theorem 1 (Classification of entire logarithmic signatures) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be continuous and of bounded variation, and put
\[
\overline\gamma_t=\gamma_t-\gamma_0,
\qquad
 g=S(\gamma),\qquad l=\log g,\qquad v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0.
\]
Assume $R(l)=\infty$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $v=0$, then $g=1$; equivalently, $\gamma$ is tree-like.
\item If $v\neq0$, there is $t_*\in[0,T]$ such that, with
\[
\alpha=\overline\gamma|_{[0,t_*]},
\qquad a=S(\alpha),
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
S(\gamma)=a\e^v a^{-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Conversely, if $a$ is a bounded-variation signature, then $a\e^v a^{-1}$ has an entire logarithmic signature for every $v\in V$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Classification of entire logarithmic signatures

[Definition def:box-counting-dimensions of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] {Falconer2014}}]

For a nonempty bounded set \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\delta>0\), let
\(N_\delta(F)\) be the least number of closed balls of radius \(\delta\)
needed to cover \(F\).  The upper box-counting dimension of \(F\) is
\[
\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}(F)
=
\limsup_{\delta\to0}
\frac{\log N_\delta(F)}{-\log\delta}.
\]
The base of the logarithm is immaterial in this ratio.

The upper modified box-counting dimension of a set
\(E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is defined by
\[
\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm{MB}}(\emptyset)=0,
\]
and, for \(E\ne\emptyset\), by
\[
\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm{MB}}(E)
=
\inf
\left\{
\sup_j \overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}(E_j):
\begin{array}{l}
E\subseteq\bigcup_{j\in\omega} E_j,\\
E_j\ne\emptyset\text{ and }E_j\text{ is bounded for every }j
\end{array}
\right\}.
\]

body: [Proposition prop-cone-unif-embed of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $W>0$ and $\alpha = Q - \frac W{2\gamma}$. Sample $(\mathcal{V}, T, \theta)$ from $\mathcal{M}^\mathrm{cone}(W) \times dT \times \mathds{1}_{\theta \in [0,2\pi)}\frac1{2\pi} d\theta$ and let $(\mathbb{C}, \psi_0, 0, \infty)$ be an embedding of $\mathcal{V}$ chosen in a way not depending on $(T, \theta)$. Let $f_{T, \theta}(z) = e^{T+i\theta}z$. Then the law of $\psi = f_T \bullet_\gamma \psi_0$ is $(Q -\alpha)^{-1} \mathrm{LF}_{\mathbb{C}}^{(\alpha, 0), (2Q-\alpha, \infty)}$.

[Definition def-srr2 of arXiv:2507.01406, '{\Large On Iterated Lorenz Curves with Applications: The Multivariate Case }'] A density $h(u,v)$ on $[0,1]^{2}$ is \textit{strictly
reverse regular of order 2} ($SRR_{2}$) if 
\begin{equation}
h(u_{1},v_{1})\,h(u_{2},v_{2})\;<\;h(u_{1},v_{2})\,h(u_{2},v_{1})

\end{equation}
for all $0\leq u_{1}<u_{2}\leq 1$ and $0\leq v_{1}<v_{2}\leq 1$ such that
all four points lie in a region where $h>0$.

Equivalently (under standard regularity so that conditional expectation and
density exist), for $H$ a bivariate distribution with density $h$, the
conditional mean $x\mapsto m_{2|1}^{H}(x)=E[\,X_{2}^{H}\mid X_{1}^{H}=x\,]$
is strictly decreasing on every compact subinterval of $(0,1)$.
title: Definition def-srr2 of arXiv:2507.01406

body: [Lemma lem:excursion of arXiv:2609.04138, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ I:\\ subsequential limits of the non-simple C'] Suppose that we have the same setup as in~(lem:markovian_cpi_exploration of the paper). Recall that the set of outermost true loops of all the $\cwBCLE_{\kappa^\prime}(0)$'s has the law of a non-nested $\CLE_{\kappa^\prime}$. Let $\SCI$ be a connected arc of some loop of this non-nested $\CLE_{\kappa^\prime}$. Suppose that $\SCI$ is contained in $D_{\tau}$ (hence it does not intersect $\eta_z([0,\tau])$). Then $\SCI$ is contained in some loop of the non-nested $\CLE_{\kappa^\prime}$ associated with the iterated $\cwBCLE_{\kappa^\prime}(0)$/$\ccwBCLE_\kappa(-\kappa/2)$ construction in $D_{\tau}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma mgf_X_bound of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ be a random matrix such that
    \[
    \E \mathbf{X} \preccurlyeq 0, \quad
    \E \mathbf{X}^2 = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \quad 
    \norm*{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{X})_+}_{\psi_{\alpha}} = U < + \infty,
    \]
    for some $\alpha > 0$.
    
    Fix $\lambda > 0$. Let $y > 0$ satisfy 
    \begin{equation}
        \upsilon(\lambda y) \le \alpha \left(\frac{y}{U}\right)^\alpha.
    \end{equation}
    If $\alpha < 1$, let $\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{X}) \le \tau ~~\text{a.s.}$ for some $\tau > 0$ satisfying~(equation eq:condition_lambda of the paper), i.e. $\upsilon(\lambda \tau) \le \alpha \left(\frac{\tau}{U}\right)^\alpha.$
    Then
    \[
    \E \exp\left\{\lambda \mathbf{X} \right\} \preccurlyeq \mathbf{I} + \frac{\phi(\lambda y)}{y^2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} + 2 \left(\phi(\lambda y) - \frac{\lambda^2 y^2}{2}\right) \elr{- \left(\frac{y}{U}\right)^\alpha} \mathbf{I}.
    \]
title: Lemma mgf_X_bound of arXiv:2411.07878

body: [Lem 24 of arXiv:2608.26698, 'Mapping class groups of simply connected closed spin 5-manifolds with no 2- and 3-torsion '] Let $f : V_g \rightarrow V_g$ be a cellular map acting trivially on homology. Suppose \[f_*([j_k]) = \sum_{1 \leq l \leq g} d_{k,l}[i_l \circ \eta] + \sum_{1 \leq l < h \leq g} d_{k,l,h}[i_l, i_h] + [j_k] \in \pi_3(V_g)\] for each $k$. Then the cup products of elements of $H^2({(V_g)}_f)$ are given by \[\overline{x}_k^2 = \sum_{1 \leq t \leq g} d_{t,k}\overline{y}_t, \quad \overline{x}_k\overline{x}_l = \sum_{1 \leq t \leq g} d_{t,k,l}\overline{y}_t.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma lem: individ1 of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] There exist absolute constants $C_1, C_2, C_3, c_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}>0$ such that the following holds. Let $C_3 \log n \le d\le n/2$, and let $\varepsilon\in [\varepsilon_0, 0.01]$. Set $m_0=\max\{1, \lfloor  \varepsilon n/2d\rfloor\}$, and let $m_1, m_2$ be such that
    \[
    1\le m_1\le m_2\le n-m_1.
    \]
    Assume that $x\in \mathbb{C}^n$ satisfies
    \[
    \forall i>m_2:\, \, \,      x_{m_1}^*>2/3+x_i^*.\]
     Let $y\in \mbox{span}\{\1\}$ and $z\in \mathbb{C}$. Let $m=\min\{m_0, m_1\}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{(lem: rowsum of the paper)}=\mathcal{E}_{(lem: rowsum of the paper)}(\varepsilon)$. Consider the event
     \[\mathcal{E}_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}'(x,y,A,k)=
     \lr{\mathcal{E}_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}(x,y,M)\cap \Omega_{2k,\varepsilon} \cap \mathcal{E}_{(lem: rowsum of the paper)}} \cup \lr{\mathcal{E}_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}(x,y,M^T)\cap \Omega_{2k,\varepsilon} \cap \mathcal{E}_{(lem: rowsum of the paper)}},
     \]
     where $k=m_0$ or $k=m_1$ and for $A=M$ or $A=M^T$,
    \[
     \mathcal{E}_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}(x,y,A):=\set{M\in \mathcal{M}_{n, d}:\, \|(A-z\mathbf{I}_n)(x+y)\|_2\le \sqrt{c_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}md}}.
    \]
       Then
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item in the case $m_1\le m_0$, one has $\quad \mathbb{P}\lr{\mathcal{E}_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}'(x,y,A, m_1)}\leq (5/6)^{m_1d/2};$
     
     
     
        \item in the case $m_1>C_1 m_0$ and $\varepsilon=0.01$, one has 
        $\quad \mathbb{P}\lr{ \mathcal{E}_{(lem: individ1 of the paper)}'(x,y,A, m_0)}\leq  \lr{\frac{C_2 n}{m_1d}}^{m_0d/4}$.
     
     
     
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem: individ1 of arXiv:2604.10446

body:
[Lem 7 of arXiv:2607.24170, '\large\bf ON NON-MONOTONICITY OF LOGARITHMIC ENERGY\\ FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Let $f$ be a bounded probability density supported on $[-L,L]$, and
let $\mathbf{M}_n$ be real symmetric with independent upper-triangular
entries, all with density $f$.  Then
\[
 \rho_n\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
 \E[\mu_{\mathbf{M}_n/\sqrt n}]
\]
has a density bounded by
\begin{equation}
 C_{n,f,L}\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
 \sqrt n\,\|f\|_\infty^n(4L)^{n-1},
\end{equation}
and is supported on $[-L\sqrt n,L\sqrt n]$.  Consequently,
$\cE(\rho_n)\in\R$.

[Lem ito of arXiv:2411.11759, 'Milstein-type schemes for McKean--Vlasov SDEs driven by Brownian motion and Poisson random'] For any real-valued $F\in \mathcal C^2(\mathbb R^d\times\mathscr{P}_2(\mathbb R^d))$
\begin{align*} 
	F(&x_t^{i,N},\,\mu_t^{x,N})=F(x_0^{i,N},\mu_0^{x,N})+\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak{D}_x^bF(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})ds
	-\int_{0}^{t}\int_Z \mathfrak D_{x}^{\gamma(z)} F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N}) \nu(dz)ds	\notag
	\\
	&
	+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak{D}_\mu^b F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})ds
	-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\int_{0}^{t}\int_Z
	\mathfrak D_{\mu}^{\gamma(z)} F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})\nu(dz)ds
	\\
	&+\sum_{\ell=1}^m\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak D_x^{\sigma^\ell}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})dw_s^{i\ell} \notag
	+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\ell=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak D_\mu^{\sigma^\ell}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})dw_s^{k\ell} \notag
	\\
	&+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{xx}^{\sigma}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})ds 
	+\frac{1}{N}\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{x\mu}^{\sigma} F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})ds   \notag
	\\
	&+\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{y\mu}^{\sigma}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})ds
	+\frac{1}{2N^2}\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{\mu\mu}^{\sigma}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})ds \notag
	\\
	&+ \sum_{k=1}^{N}\int_{0}^{t}\int_Z\Big\{F\big(x_{s-}^{i,N}+1_{\{k=i\}}\gamma(x_s^{k,N},\mu_{s}^{x,N},z),\mu_{s-}^{x+\gamma(k,z),N}\big)
	-F(x_{s-}^{i,N},\mu_{s-}^{x,N})
	\Big\}n_p^k(ds,dz) 
\end{align*}
almost surely for  $t \in [0,T]$ and $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ where $\mu_{s-}^{x+\gamma(k,z),N}=\displaystyle \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\delta_{x_{s-}^{j,N}+1_{\{j=k\}}\gamma(x_s^{j,N}, \,\mu_{s}^{x,N}, \,z)}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:variance of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] For any $P$ with stationary distribution $\pi$,
\[
  \mathrm{Var}_\pi(r)
  :=
  \sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\bigl(r(x)-\bar r_\pi\bigr)^2
  \;\le\;
  \bar r_\pi\,M\,(1-L(P)).
\]
This bound is sharp: equality holds for any chain in which $r(x)\in\{0,M\}$
for $\pi$-a.e.\ $x$.

body:
[Ppn 26 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $F^{\riv}$ from \eqref{e:F.iv}, and
$F^{\rv}$ from \eqref{e:F.rv}. 
    For sufficiently large $N$, we have for all $t\in \R$
    \[
    \P(F^{\riv} \ge t)
    \le \P\bigg(
    F^{\rv}+ \frac{\epsilon'}{5}
    \ge t
    \bigg) + e^{-cN} \,.
    \]
That is, $F^{\rv}$
approximately stochastically dominates
$F^{\riv}$.

\begin{proof}
For each $j\in[r]$, let
    \[\bv_1(B_j)\equiv
    \frac{\bz(B_j)}{\|\bz(B_j)\|}\,,\]
and complete this to a (Haar random)
orthonormal basis
$(\bv_a(B_j) : 1\le a \le |B_j|)$
of $\R^{|B_j|}$. Let $\tau_j \equiv \|\bz^{B_j}\|^2 / |B_j|$. Then we can rewrite \eqref{e:F.v} and \eqref{e:bar.F.U} as
    \begin{align*}
    F_v(\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a=1}^{|B_j|}
        (
         \bv_a(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2
         \,,\\
    \bar{F}_U(\bG,\bz,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
        ( \bv_1(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
If we split off the $a=1$ term of $F_v$ and combine it with $\bar{F}_U$, then we see that $F_v+\bar{F}_U$ is the same as the sum of the two terms
    \begin{align*}
    F_{v\setminus1}(\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a=2}^{|B_j|}
        (
         \bv_a(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2
         \,,\\
    \bar{F}_{U+}(\bG,\bz,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j+
            \tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
        ( \bv_1(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Fix arbitrary representatives $a_j \in B_j$, and denote
    \begin{align*}
    \acute{F}_{v\setminus}
    (\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a\in B_j\setminus a_j}
        (\bg^a,\by)^2
    \le F_v(\bG,\by)\,, \\
    \acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j+
            \tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
    (\tbmeta^{r+j},\by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Recalling $F_w$ from \eqref{e:F.w} and
$\bar{F}_B$ from \eqref{e:bar.F.B}, define
    \begin{align*}
    \acute{F}_-(\bG,\tbmeta,\by)
    &\equiv F_w(\by)
    +\acute{F}_{v\setminus}
        (\bG,\by)
    +\bar{F}_B(\tbmeta,\by)
    +\acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    \\
    &\le F_w(\by)
    +\acute{F}_v(\bG,\by)
        +\bar{F}_B(\tbmeta,\by)
        +\acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    \equiv\ddot{F}(\bG,\tbmeta,\by)
    \end{align*}
By gaussian rotational invariance,
$\bar{F}$ has the same distribution (as processes indexed by $\by$) as $\acute{F}_-$, which in term is dominated by $\ddot{F}$. Finally, the difference between $\ddot{F}$ and $\acute{F}$
is bounded, for all $\|\by\|^2=N$, by
\[
        \bigg|\sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{(\tau_j-1) \hU_j}{MN}
        (\tbmeta^{r+j}, \by)^2\bigg|
        \le \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{|\tau_j-1| |\hU_j|}{M}
        \|\tbmeta^{r+j}\|^2\,.
    \]
It holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ that
    \[|\tau_j-1| \le \frac{\alpha \iota \epsilon'}{20r},\quad
    \max_{j\in[r]}
    \frac{\|\tbmeta^{r+j}\|}{N^{1/2}}
     \le 2\,.
    \]
On this event, the above quantity is bounded by 
    \[
        r \cdot \frac{\alpha \iota \epsilon'}{20} \cdot \frac{\|\hU\|_\infty}{M} \cdot 4N 
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:fp-normalization-bd}}{\le} \frac{\epsilon'}{5}\,,
    \]
which concludes the proof.\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let (Omega, F, mu) be a finite measure space and (f_n) a sequence in L^1(mu) converging in measure to a measurable function f. If the family {f_n} is uniformly integrable, that is, sup_n integral over {|f_n| > K} of |f_n| d mu tends to 0 as K tends to infinity, then f is in L^1(mu), f_n converges to f in L^1(mu), and integral of f_n d mu converges to integral of f d mu. This generalizes the dominated convergence theorem, which is the special case where |f_n| <= g for a fixed integrable g. [standard, e.g. Folland, Real Analysis]
title: Vitali Convergence Theorem

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let mu_1, mu_2 be strictly positive probability measures on a common finite distributive lattice (e.g. {0,1}^E ordered coordinatewise). If the Holley condition holds, mu_1(x v y) mu_2(x ^ y) >= mu_1(x) mu_2(y) for all configurations x, y, then mu_1 stochastically dominates mu_2, meaning mu_1(A) >= mu_2(A) for every increasing (monotone) event A. This is a purely combinatorial, pointwise sufficient condition for stochastic domination between two measures that need not be product measures, and it strictly generalizes the FKG inequality, which is recovered as the special case mu_1 = mu_2. It is the standard tool for comparing Gibbs measures with different boundary conditions or parameters in the Ising model, the random-cluster model, and other lattice systems, and for monotone-coupling arguments more generally. The theorem does not establish the Holley condition itself, which can be as hard to verify as the comparison one is trying to prove; it gives only qualitative stochastic domination, with no quantitative bound on the total-variation distance between mu_1 and mu_2; and it requires strict positivity of both measures on the entire lattice. Typical failure: Assuming the Holley condition holds because mu_1 looks larger than mu_2 in some averaged or marginal sense; the condition is a pointwise, multiplicative statement that must hold for every pair of configurations including their join and meet, and it can fail even when mu_1 does stochastically dominate mu_2 for unrelated reasons, or when only checked on a generating set of configurations rather than genuinely all pairs. Canonical reference: Holley, 1974, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Georgii, Haggstrom and Maes, 2001, in Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena, vol. 18, Academic Press.
mu_1 and mu_2 strictly positive on a common finite distributive lattice closed under meet and join
the pointwise Holley ratio condition mu_1(x v y) mu_2(x ^ y) >= mu_1(x) mu_2(y) holding for all pairs x, y
events being compared are increasing with respect to the same partial order used to define the lattice

[Proposition 13 (The inverse chain map is the Wick forest) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] For a monomial
\[
 x_{\boldsymbol i}=x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n}
\]
and a partial matching \(M\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), put
\[
 \Contr_{C,M}(x_{\boldsymbol i})
 =
 \left(\prod_{\{a,b\}\in M}C_{i_ai_b}\right)
 \prod_{a\notin |M|}x_{i_a}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \exp\!\left(\pm\frac12\Delta_C\right)x_{\boldsymbol i}
 =
 \sum_M(\pm1)^{|M|}
 \Contr_{C,M}(x_{\boldsymbol i}).

\end{equation}
Thus \(\Theta_B\) is the signed aggregation of all partial matching
forests, while \(\Theta_B^{-1}\) is their positive Wick aggregation.

[Definition 32 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] (\textbf{Snake-pseudometrics}) Let $\zeta \ino (0, \infty)$ and let $(h,w)\ino \fSigma ([0, \zeta])$. Recall from (\ref{djhczkk}) the definition of $m_h (\cdot, \cdot)$ and recall  that $\widehat{w}_s\eqo w_s( h(s))$, $s\ino \bbR_+$. 
For all $s_1, s_2\ino [0, \zeta]$, we set
\begin{eqnarray}

M_{h,w} (s_1, s_2) \!\! \! \! \!& =&\!\!  \! \!\!  \min \! \Big( \!  \min \! \big\{  w_{s_1} (r) ; r\geqo m_h (s_1, s_2) \big\}  ,  \min \! \big\{ w_{s_2} (r) ; r\geqo m_h (s_1, s_2)\big\} \! \Big)  \nonumber \\
 &   &\!\!\!\! \!\!\!\! \!\!\!\! \!\!\!\!  \textrm{and} \quad d_{h,w} (s_1, s_2)\! = \! \widehat{w}_{s_1}+  \widehat{w}_{s_2} -2M_{h,w} (s_1, s_2) \; .
\end{eqnarray}

We call $d_{h,w}$ the \textit{snake-pseudometric associated with $(h,w)$} (see Lemma~\ref{Hermagor_fix} below). \cq

[Lemma lem:rep-h of arXiv:2601.10568, 'Hydrodynamic Limit with a Weierstrass-type result'] Fixed $M\in\mathbb{N}_+$, for each $0\leq m\leq M$ and $u,v\in[0,1]$ let

\begin{align}

\mathfrak{V}_{m,M}(\inner{\tau^x\eta_{N^2 s}}_{\ell_N},\inner{\tau^x\eta_{N^2 s}}_{L})

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.13107, 'Discrepancy and Fisher information'] Let $K \subset \R^d$ be a convex, centrally symmetric set with nonempty interior. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n \in \R^d$ be fixed vectors, and let $\e_1,\ldots, \e_n$ be independent Rademacher random variables. Let $\pi(\cdot)$ be a probability density supported in the interior of $K$. Then there exists an online algorithm that discards some steps $\e_j v_j$ such that, for each $k$,
	$$
	\sum_{j \le k \text{ accepted}} \e_j v_j \in 2K
	\quad \text{deterministically},
	$$
	and
	\begin{equation}	
		\E \#\{\text{discarded}\}
		\le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{v_j^\tran \I_\pi v_j}, 
	\end{equation}
	where $\I_\pi$ denotes the Fisher information matrix defined in \eqref{eq: Ipi}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.13107

  for all non-negative Borel measurable functions $f$ and $g$ on $M$, 
  $\int_M E^i_x[f(X^i_t)] g(x)\, \mu(dx) = \int_M f(x) E^i_x[g(X^i_t)]\, \mu(dx)$
  for all $t \geq 0$,
  where $E^i_x$ denotes the expectation with respect to $P^i_x$.
  Then Assumption~(assum:smooth of the paper) is satisfied, 
  and thus the collision local time $(C_t)_{t \geq 0}$ is well defined.

[Theorem 23 of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] [The geometric wave-transport-divergence-curl formulation of the compressible Euler equations]
	
	Let $\overline{\varrho} > 0$ be any constant background density,\footnote{Recall
	that $\LogDensity$ depends on $\overline{\varrho}$; see Def.~\ref{D:LOGDENS}.}
	and assume that $(\LogDensity,v^1,v^2,v^3,\Ent)$ is
	a solution
	to the compressible Euler equations 
	\eqref{E:BVIEVOLUTION}--\eqref{E:BENTROPYEVOLUTION}
	in three spatial dimensions under an arbitrary equation of state $p = p(\varrho,\Ent)$ with positive sound speed 
	$\Speed$ (see \eqref{E:SOUNDSPEED}).
	Let $\Transport$ be the material derivative vectorfield defined in \eqref{E:MATERIALDERIVATIVEVECOTRFIELD},
	let $\gfour$ be the acoustical metric from Def.~\ref{D:ACOUSTICALMETRICDEF},
	let $\square_{\gfour}$ be the corresponding covariant wave operator from Def.~\ref{D:COVWAVEOP},
	let $\almostRiemannfunction  = \almostRiemannfunction(\LogDensity,\Ent)$ be the function from
	Def.~\ref{D:ALMOSTRIEMANNINVARIANTS},
	and let 
	$\vortrenormalized$,
	$\GradEnt$,
	$\VortVort$,
	and
	$\DivGradEnt$
	be the higher order variables from Def.~\ref{D:HIGHERORDERFLUIDVARIABLES}.
	Then the scalar-valued functions
	$\LogDensity$,
	$v^i$, 
	$\almostRiemann_{(\pm)}$, 
	$\Ent$,
$\vortrenormalized^i$,
$\GradEnt^i$,
$\Flatdiv \vortrenormalized$,
$\VortVort^i$,
$\DivGradEnt$,
and
$(\Flatcurl \GradEnt)^i$,
	($i=1,2,3$),
	also solve the following equations,
	where $\upepsilon_{ijk}$ is the fully antisymmetric symbol normalized by $\upepsilon_{123}=1$, 
	and \textbf{the Cartesian component functions $v^i$ are 
	treated as scalar-valued functions
	under covariant differentiation on LHS~\eqref{E:VELOCITYWAVEEQUATION}}:

\medskip

\noindent \underline{\textbf{\upshape Covariant wave equations}}.
	\begin{subequations} 
	\begin{align}
		\square_{\gfour(\wavearray)} v^i
		& = 
			- 
			\Speed^2 \exp(2 \LogDensity) \VortVort^i
			+ 
			\nullform_{(v)}^i
			+ 
			\mathfrak{L}_{(v)}^i,
				\\

	\square_{\gfour(\wavearray)} \LogDensity
	& = 
		-
		\exp(\LogDensity) \frac{p_{;\Ent}}{\overline{\varrho}} \DivGradEnt
		+
		\nullform_{(\LogDensity)}
		+
		\mathfrak{L}_{(\LogDensity)},
			 
				\\
	\square_{\gfour(\wavearray)} \Ent
	& = 
		\Speed^2 \exp(2 \LogDensity)  \DivGradEnt
		+
		\mathfrak{L}_{(\Ent)}.
	
\end{align}
\end{subequations}\medskip

\noindent \underline{\textbf{\upshape Transport equations}}.
\begin{subequations}
\begin{align}	\Transport \vortrenormalized^i
	& = \mathfrak{L}_{(\vortrenormalized)}^i,
		
		\\
	\Transport \Ent
	& = 0,	
		
			\\
	\Transport \GradEnt^i
	& = \mathfrak{L}_{(\GradEnt)}^i.
		
\end{align}
\end{subequations}\medskip	
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{\upshape Transport-divergence-curl system for the specific vorticity}}.
\begin{subequations}
\begin{align} 
	\Flatdiv \vortrenormalized
	& = 
		\mathfrak{L}_{(\Flatdiv \vortrenormalized)},
		\\
\Transport \VortVort^i
& = 
	\mainnullform_{(\VortVort)}^i 
	+ 
	\nullform_{(\VortVort)}^i
	+	
	\mathfrak{L}_{(\VortVort)}^i. 
	 
\end{align}	
\end{subequations}\medskip

\noindent \underline{\textbf{\upshape Transport-divergence-curl system for the entropy gradient}}.
\begin{subequations}
\begin{align} 	
\Transport \DivGradEnt
	& =  \mainnullform_{(\DivGradEnt)} +
			\nullform_{(\DivGradEnt)},
 
			\\
	(\Flatcurl \GradEnt)^i & = 0.
	
\end{align}
\end{subequations}
	Above, the main terms $\mainnullform_{(\VortVort)}^i$ and $\mainnullform_{(\DivGradEnt)}$ 
	in the transport equations for the modified fluid variables are 
	the \textbf{null forms relative to} $\gfour$ (see Def.~\ref{D:STANDARDNULLFORMS})
	defined by:\footnote{Actually, the last the last term on
 RHS\,\eqref{E:TRANSPORTDIVGRADENTMAINTERMS} is not a null form, but rather 
	a simpler harmless error term.}
	\begin{subequations}
	\begin{align}
	\begin{split} 
		\mainnullform_{(\VortVort)}^i & \eqdef 
		- 
		2 \updelta_{jk} \upepsilon_{iab} \exp(-\LogDensity) (\partial_a v^j) \partial_b \vortrenormalized^k
		+
		\upepsilon_{ajk}
		\exp(-\LogDensity)
		(\partial_a v^i)

[Theorem 25 (Sharp careless stationary high-tail constant) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] For fixed $p\in(0,1)$ and $q=1-p$,
\[
        \nu_n(n)\sim \frac1{(q;q)_\infty}\frac{n!}{n^n}q^{n(n+1)/2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
        \mu_n=\nu_n(n)(1-q^n)
        \sim \frac1{(q;q)_\infty}\frac{n!}{n^n}q^{n(n+1)/2}.
\]

[Definition $\varepsilon$-nets, covering numbers, and packing numbers of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space and let $\varepsilon>0$.  A set
$\mathcal X_\varepsilon\subseteq X$ is called an $\varepsilon$-net of $X$ if
$
    X
    \subseteq
    \bigcup_{x\in\mathcal X_\varepsilon}
        B(x,\varepsilon).
$
The $\varepsilon$-covering number of $X$ is
\[
    \mathcal N(X,\rho,\varepsilon)
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \inf
    \left\{
        |\mathcal X_\varepsilon|
        :
        \mathcal X_\varepsilon\subseteq X
        \text{ is an } \varepsilon\text{-net of }X
    \right\}.
\]
title: $\varepsilon$-nets, covering numbers, and packing numbers

body:
[Theorem th:GFF of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Fix $y_0 \in (0, \infty)$. Let $\phi = \phi_N : V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ be a test function of the form
	\[ \phi (x,y) = \sum_{k=2}^K \alpha_k(y) f_k^N(x) \]
for some finite integer $K \geq 2$ independent of $N$, where each coefficient $\alpha_k$ does not depend on $N$ and is differentiable on a neighbourhood of $y_0$ with bounded derivative there.
Let $\varphi = \varphi_N : V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ be the extension
	\[ \varphi (x,y) \coloneqq \phi \Big( x , \frac{y}{a_N} \Big)\,, \qquad (x,y) \in V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} \,, \]
with $a_N$ as in~(equation eq:aN of the paper). Assume that Assumption~(a:spectral of the paper) holds for each $2 \leq k \leq K$, and that
	\[ a_N \gg \log N + \log_+ a_N \qquad \text{as } N \to \infty\,. \]
Let
	\[ \sigma^2(\phi) \coloneqq \sum_{k=2}^K \alpha_k(y_0)^2 \, \frac{1 - e^{-2\g_k y_0}}{2\g_k} \,\geq\, 0\,. \]
Then, with $T = N \lfloor y_0 a_N \rfloor$,
	\begin{equation}
	 \frac{1}{\sqrt{Na_N}} \langle \! \langle D_T , \varphi \rangle \! \rangle \Rightarrow
	\mathcal{N} \big( 0\,,\, \sigma^2(\phi) \big)
	\end{equation}
as $N\to\infty$. 

Here $\Rightarrow$ denotes convergence in distribution, and $\mathcal{N} (0, \sigma^2)$ denotes a normal distribution with $0$ mean and variance $\sigma^2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 17 of arXiv:2512.05687, '$L^p$-Boltzmann-Gibbs principle \\ via Littlewood-Paley-Stein inequality'] (cf.\ Lemma 5.7 of \cite{BFS}) 
Let $p\ge 4$ and let $f$ be a local $L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})$ function on
$\mathcal{X}_N$ for some $p'>p$ depending only on $\eta_{\La_{\ell_0}}$  
such that $\tilde f(u_0)=0$ and $\tilde f'(u_0)=0$.  Then, there exists a constant 
$C = C(u_0,\ell_0)$ such that, for $\ell \geq  \ell_0$, and a function
$h$ on $[0,T]\times \T_N$, we have
\begin{align}   
&E_{\mu_{u_0}}\Big[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Big|\int_0^t\sum_{x\in{\T_N}}h(s,x)\\
& \hskip 10mm \times
\Big\{E_{\mu_{u_0}}\big[f(\tau_x\eta_s^N)|\eta_s^{N,(\ell)}(x)\big] 
-\frac{1}{2} \tilde f''(u_0) \Big((\eta_s^{N,(\ell)}(x) - u_0)^2- \tfrac{{\rm var}(u_0) }{2\ell +1}\Big)\Big\} ds \Big|^p\Big] 
\notag \\
& \hskip 5mm\leq \ CT^{p-1} N^p \ell^{-3p/2} \|f\|^p_{L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})}
\int_0^T \frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in \T_N}|h(t,x)|^p dt.
\notag
\end{align}
On the other hand, when only $\tilde f(u_0)=0$ is known, we have
\begin{align}  
&E_{\mu_{u_0}}\Big[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Big|\int_0^t\sum_{x\in{\T_N}} h(s,x) \\
& \hskip 20mm \times\Big\{E_{\mu_{u_0}}[f(\tau_x\eta_s^N)|\eta_s^{N,(\ell)}(x)] 
-\tilde f'(u_0)
\big(\eta_s^{N,(\ell)}(x)-u_0\big) \Big\} ds\Big|^p\Big] 
\notag  \\
& \hskip 10mm
 \leq \ CT^{p-1} N^p \ell^{-p} \|f\|^{p}_{L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})} \int_0^T \frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in \T_N}|h(t,x)|^p dt.  \notag
\end{align}

body:
Let Omega in R^n be open, k >= 0 an integer and 0 < alpha <= 1. For a function v on a set S, [v]_{alpha;S} = sup over x, y in S with x != y of |v(x) - v(y)| / |x - y|^alpha. For bounded Omega, C^{k,alpha}(closure of Omega) is the space of u in C^k(Omega) such that every derivative D^beta u with |beta| <= k extends continuously to the closure and ||u||_{C^{k,alpha}} = sum_{|beta| <= k} sup_Omega |D^beta u| + sum_{|beta| = k} [D^beta u]_{alpha;Omega} is finite; it is a Banach space. The local space C^{k,alpha}(Omega) consists of u in C^k(Omega) with u in C^{k,alpha}(closure of U) for every open U with compact closure in Omega. C^{0,1} is the Lipschitz class; C^{1,1} (bounded second difference quotients, equivalently W^{2,infinity} locally) is strictly larger than C^2. A bounded open set Omega is a C^{k,alpha} domain if every boundary point has a neighborhood U such that, in suitable rotated coordinates, Omega intersected with U = {x in U : x_n > g(x_1, ..., x_{n-1})} for some g of class C^{k,alpha}. Schauder theory uses 0 < alpha < 1 strictly; it fails for alpha = 0 (mere continuity) and alpha = 1 (Lipschitz).
Omega open in R^n (bounded for the global space)
k >= 0 integer
0 < alpha <= 1
title: Hoelder Spaces C^{k,alpha} and C^{k,alpha} Domains

body:
Let X, B, Y be Banach spaces with X embedded COMPACTLY in B and B embedded continuously in Y. Let 1 <= p < infinity and 1 <= q <= infinity, and set W = { u in L^p(0,T; X) : the distributional time derivative u' lies in L^q(0,T; Y) }. Then W is embedded COMPACTLY in L^p(0,T; B) (and, when p = infinity and q > 1, compactly in C([0,T]; B)). The typical PDE use is X = H_0^1, B = L^2, Y = H^{-1}: a sequence bounded in L^2(0,T;H_0^1) whose time derivatives are bounded in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}) has a subsequence converging strongly in L^2(0,T;L^2), which is what lets one pass to the limit in a nonlinear term.
COMPACTNESS of the embedding X into B is essential - continuity is not enough.
The time derivative must be controlled in the WEAKER space Y;
controlling it in B would be a much stronger and usually unavailable hypothesis.

Let d>=1, L>=m>0 and R>0. Let U:R^d->R be C1, have an everywhere-existing Hessian and globally L-Lipschitz gradient, with grad U(0)=0. Put Omega=R^d minus B(0,R). Assume V(x)=U(x)-(m/2)||x||_2^2 is convex on Omega in this precise sense: V(sum_j a_j x_j)<=sum_j a_j V(x_j) whenever a_j>=0, sum_j a_j=1, all x_j belong to Omega and their barycenter also belongs to Omega. Let mu have density proportional to exp(-U), and define rho_U by Ent_mu(g^2)<= (2/rho_U) integral ||grad g||_2^2 dmu for smooth compactly supported g, where Ent_mu(h)=integral h log(h/integral h dmu) dmu. Then rho_U >= (m/2) exp(-16 L R^2). In particular the deterioration is governed by L R^2; polynomial-dimensional consequences require that this quantity and the other algorithmic parameters be controlled.
d>=1; L>=m>0; R>0
U is C1 with globally L-Lipschitz gradient and Hessian existing everywhere
grad U(0)=0, as in Appendix A
Writing V(x)=U(x)-(m/2)||x||^2 and Omega=R^d minus B(0,R), V is convex on Omega in the authors' nonconvex-domain sense: V(sum_j a_j x_j)<=sum_j a_j V(x_j) for nonnegative coefficients summing to one whenever every x_j and their barycenter belong to Omega

[Theorem thm:locFriendClust of arXiv:2603.16824, 'Age-dependent random connection models with arc reciprocity: clustering and connectivity'] For all \(\beta>0,\gamma\in(0,1),\delta>1,\) and \(\Gamma\geq 0\), we have, in probability as \(t\to\infty\),
    \[
    	c^\textup{fc}_\textup{av}(\mathscr{D}_t) \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_o c^\textup{fc}(\0,\mathscr{D}_o),
    \]
    where
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{aligned}
            \mathbb{E}_o c^\textup{fc}(\0, \mathscr{D}_o) & = 
            \int_0^1 \mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(u)}\leftrightarrow\boldsymbol{X}^{(u)}) \mu^f_2(\,\mathrm{d} u),
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation*}
    
    and \(\boldsymbol{X}^{(u)}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(u)}\) are two independent random variables distributed according to the normalised measure \(\lambda_u^f/\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))\) with
        \[
       \lambda_{u}^\textup{f}(\,\mathrm{d}(x,s)) =  \Big((\tfrac{s}{u})^\Gamma\rho\big(\beta^{-1} s^{\gamma}u^{1-\gamma}|x|^d\big)\1_{\{s<u\}}+(\tfrac{u}{s})^\Gamma\rho\big(\beta^{-1}s^{1-\gamma}u^\gamma |x|^d\big)\1_{\{s\geq u\}}\Big) \,\mathrm{d} s \, \,\mathrm{d} x,
    \]
    and \(\mu^f_2\) is the distribution on \((0,1)\) with density proportional to 
    \[
        1-e^{-\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))}-\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))e^{-\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $M$ be a complex manifold with a contact structure $ D \subset TM$. 
Denote by $\fc \subset H^0(M, TM)$ the Lie algebra of contactomorphic vector fields on $M$, namely, holomorphic vector fields on $M$ whose local flows preserve $D \subset TM$. Let $L := TM/D$ be the line bundle with the quotient map $TM \to L$. Then the induced homomorphism $H^0(M, TM) \to H^0(M, L)$ sends $\fc$ isomorphically to $H^0(M, L)$. [Theorem thm:deywu23_SK of arXiv:2510.26960, 'Free energy fluctuations in SK and related spin glass models: \\ A literature survey'] {DeyWu23}}] 
Consider the SK model with Gaussian disorder. Assume that the external field is scaled as $h = \rho N^{-\alpha}$ for some positive constants $\rho$ and $\alpha$. Let
 \begin{equation} 
v_1^2 := -\frac12\log(1-\beta^2) - \frac{\beta^2}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad v_2^2 := \frac{\beta^2}{2(1-\beta^2)}.
 \end{equation} 
We then have the following statements of convergence in distribution. 
\begin{enumerate}
     \item (Sub-critical) For $\alpha>1/4$ and $\beta<1$,
        \[
        N \left(F_N - \left(\log(2\cosh h)+\frac{N-1}{4N}\beta^2\right)\right) \to \mathcal{N}(-\frac12 v_1^2, v_1^2).
        \]
        \item (Critical) For $\alpha=1/4$ and $\beta<1$,
        \[
        N \left(F_N - \left(\log(2\cosh h)+\frac{N-1}{4N}\beta^2\right)\right) \to \mathcal{N}(-\frac12 \left(v_1^2 + \rho^4 v_2^2 \right), v_1^2+\rho^4 v_2^2).
        \]
        \item (Super-critical) There exists $\beta_0\leq 1$ such that, for $\alpha<1/4$ and $\beta<\beta_0$,
        \[
        \frac{\sqrt{N}}{h^2}\left(F_N - \left(\mathbb{E} \log(2\cosh(\beta\sqrt{q}\eta+h))+\frac14\beta^2(1-q)^2\right)\right) \to \mathcal{N}(0,v_2^2),
        \]
        where $\eta$ is a standard Gaussian random variable and $q\in [0,1]$ is the solution to 
        \[
        q = \mathbb{E} \tanh^2(\beta \sqrt{q}\eta +h).
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Every wake-chain state has the same total k. On a cycle, the complement-of-one-site window therefore has variance rho_N*(1-rho_N)<=1/4 under the unique stationary law, where rho_N=k/N; the whole torus has variance zero. More generally, translation invariance forces sum_y Cov(I_x,I_y)=Cov(I_x,k)=0, but this finite-volume cancellation does not imply mesoscopic hyperuniformity. For comparison, uniform k-subsets have Var(S_B)=|B|*rho_N*(1-rho_N)*(N-|B|)/(N-1), which is volume order for |B|=o(N). Check: Under the uniform k-subset comparison law, E I_x=k/N and E I_x I_y=k*(k-1)/(N*(N-1)); substitution yields the displayed variance. This comparison law is not asserted to be the ARW stationary distribution. Obstruction: The literal all-window lower bound is false; the meaningful small-window transition is unresolved. Exact global covariance cancellation alone cannot prove a subvolume variance bound.

[Theorem 11 (Extremizers for all smoothing times) of arXiv:2605.11451, '2605.11451'] Let $1\le p<2$, $n\ge2$, and $t\ge0$. Then for every $\theta\in\sphere$,
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\diag)
 \le
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\theta)
 \le
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(e_1).
\end{equation}
The right equality occurs exactly for coordinate directions $\{\pm e_i\}$, and the left equality occurs exactly for diagonal directions
\[
 \left\{\frac1{\sqrt n}(\pm1,\ldots,\pm1)\right\}.
\]
The same statement holds for the unstandardized profile $A_{p,n,t}$.

[Prp 14 of arXiv:2608.13976, 'Boundary Harnack principle for diffusion with jumps on metric measure spaces'] Suppose assumption (A1) holds. Let $B$ be a ball in $\sX$
so that $\overline{B}\subsetneq \sX$,
and  $D$ be an open subset of  $\sX$.  Let  $U$ and $V$ be relatively compact  open sets in $B$ with $\overline V  \subseteq U$ and $D\cap V\neq \varnothing.$
  Suppose $h$ is a nonnegative  regular   harmonic function with respect to $X^B$in $D\cap U$ and
    vanishes on $(D^c)^r\cap U$.
 Then
 there exist a sequence of Radon measures $\{\mu_n; n\geq 1\}$ on $(D\cap U)\setminus V$
  so that     $G^B_{D\cap U}\mu_n(x):= \int_{(D\cap U)\setminus V} G^B_{D\cap U}(x, y) \mu_n (dy)$   is uniformly bounded on $D\cap V$ and increasing   in $n\geq 1$,  and for $x\in   D\cap V,$
  \begin{eqnarray}
h(x)& = &  \lim_{n\to \infty} \int_{(D\cap U)\setminus  V} G^B_{D\cap U}(x, y)\mu_n(dy) \nonumber\\
&&  + \int_{D\cap U} G^B_{D\cap U}(x,y)\int_{B\setminus U}h(z) J(y, dz)\,m_B(dy).
\end{eqnarray} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let A be a real m x n matrix, the payoff matrix of a two-player zero-sum game in which the row player chooses a mixed strategy x in the simplex Delta_m = {x in R^m : x >= 0, sum_i x_i = 1}, the column player chooses y in Delta_n, and the row player's expected payoff is x^T A y (the column player's payoff being its negative). Then max_{x in Delta_m} min_{y in Delta_n} x^T A y = min_{y in Delta_n} max_{x in Delta_m} x^T A y. This common value v is called the value of the game, and any x*, y* attaining the respective maximum and minimum together form an optimal pair of strategies (a Nash equilibrium) for the game.
A is a real m x n matrix defining a finite two-player zero-sum game
x and y range over the mixed-strategy simplices Delta_m and Delta_n respectively

A relative local limit is a sufficient fixed-length transfer premise. Let Gamma_delta be curves in a common metric space and let L_delta be an integer length. Suppose Q is a probability law, h_delta>0 tends to zero and rho>0. For every bounded continuous f, assume E[f(Gamma_delta) 1_{L_delta=n_delta}]=h_delta rho Q(f)+o(h_delta), and P(L_delta=n_delta)=h_delta rho+o(h_delta). The conditional laws given L_delta=n_delta then converge weakly to Q, by dividing these asymptotics. This criterion is conditional draft material; its SAW hypotheses are not proved here and independent review is pending.

Independent review pending. Let T be the rooted tree in which each vertex at level n-1 has 8 children if n is a power of two and 2 children otherwise, for n>=1. T is infinite, connected, simple and locally finite, with maximum degree 9. For iid Bernoulli bond percolation, p_c(T)=1/2 and the root survives at criticality with probability at least 4/5. At p=1/2 the open generation mean is M_n=4^(1+floor(log_2 n)), and its normalized second moment is 1+(1/2)sum_{j<=n}1/M_j<=5/4. Two independent uniform-child rays on the host have E[2^K]=5/4, where K counts their common undirected edges. Below 1/2, M_n<=4n^2(2p)^n tends to zero. The degree-8 root is unique, so every automorphism fixes it and T has infinitely many vertex orbits. This example excludes replacing quasi-transitivity by bounded degree; it does not refute critical extinction on quasi-transitive graphs.

Independent Bernoulli bond percolation

[Theorem 16 (Randomly initialized neurons specialize) of arXiv:2608.24007, '2608.24007'] Under \cref{data:neuron-specialization}, \cref{train:neuron-specialization} and \cref{init:neuron-specialization}
there are universal constants $R_0,C<\infty$ such that the following holds
for every $R\geq R_0$. For almost every draw of
$\omega_1^0,\ldots,\omega_m^0$, there are cluster labels
$J_1,\ldots,J_m\in[K]$ and orientations
$\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_m\in\{\pm1\}$ such that, for every $\delta>0$, there
exist a finite time $T_\delta$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$ for which
\[
    0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \left\|
        \frac{w_j(T_\delta)}{\|w_j(T_\delta)\|_2}
        -\tau_j v_{J_j}
    \right\|_2
    \leq
    \delta+\frac{C}{R}
    \qquad\text{for every }j\in[m].
\]
Thus every neuron specializes, up to orientation and a vanishing
$O(R^{-1})$ routing component, to the predictive direction of one cluster.

The selected labels $J_1,\ldots,J_m$ are independent and uniformly
distributed on $[K]$. Consequently,
\[
    \mathbb P\left(
        \text{every cluster is covered by a specialized neuron}
    \right)
    \geq
    1-Ke^{-m/K}.
\]
In particular, if
\[
    m\geq K\log\left(\frac{K}{\eta}\right),
\]
then all $K$ clusters are covered with probability at least $1-\eta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Randomly initialized neurons specialize

[Corollary c:CSAgen of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Consider the CSA model with input  point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ given in~(equation e:IPS-input of the paper), with state space $\mathbb {M} =\{0,1\}$ and clocks having uniformly distributed marks in $\mathbb{L}=[0,1]$. As in Theorem~(thmIPS of the paper),we assume $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ has {\em summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations},  and  Palm moment bounds~(equation e:bd_palmcorr of the paper) for all $p, m \in \mathbb{N}$. We assume  Markovian update rules~ (equation e:updaterulem of the paper) with (equation e.CSA2 of the paper) on a stabilizing interaction graph $\Psi$ on finite windows with respect to $\mathcal{P}$ as in~(equation e:ddecay of the paper).
Put $\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) = M_n(x,t_0)$  for
$t_0 \in (0, \infty)$.
Then the measures $(\mu_n^{\xi})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ at (equation IPS of the paper) satisfy the conclusions of Theorem~(thmIPS of the paper).
When $f \equiv 1$ this yields the asymptotic normality for the total number of accepted particles in $W_n$ up to time~$t_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title:
Limit theory for the number of accepted particles
 in CSA

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured random perturbations of \\ tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices'] Define
\[ \gamma(z) = \lim_n \frac{1}{n} \log \vert \det(T_n - zI) \vert. \]
If
\[
\varepsilon_n=\max_{1\le j\le n}\Bigl( |d_j^{(n)}-d_0|+|b_j^{(n)}-b_0|+|c_j^{(n)}-c_0| \Bigr) \longrightarrow 0
\]
in probability, then for every $\epsilon>0$ we have
\begin{equation}

\prob \left(
\bigl| \log |\det(P_n-zI)| - n\gamma(z) \bigr| \ge n\epsilon
\right) \longrightarrow 0
\qquad\text{as } n\to\infty.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2604.20617

body:
[Theorem 15 of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] For any $k\in\mathbb{N}_+$, the tree $\mathcal{T}^{\ell,\sigma}_k$ admits the following construction:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Sample $k$ heights independently with density \(\frac{\ell(x)}{I(\ell)}\,\mathrm{d}x\), and reorder them so that \(x_1 > \cdots > x_k\).
\item Sample a piecewise Kingman coalescent 
\(Z^{(k)}=\big(Z^{(k)}_s(x_1,\ldots,x_k): s>0\big)\) in which each pair of lineages coalesces at rate $\frac{4}{\ell^\sigma(s)}$.
\item Conditionally on \(Z^{(k)}\), sample uniformly from the set of rooted ordered real trees whose lineage counts at each height agree with \(Z^{(k)}\).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 15 of arXiv:2511.09517

body:
[Corollary 21 (No transfer) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] A transform proven optimal for one regime carries no optimality guarantee for the other. In particular, for a generic spectrum the KLT (\Cref{thm:klt}), optimal for allocation-flexible
coding, leaves the energy profile bounded away from the within-group flatness that the
AbsMax step-size surrogate rewards (\Cref{thm:inversion},
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii)). Because that surrogate is not a functional of the global order at
all, the change relative to an arbitrary starting basis is not even signed: what fails to
transfer is the guarantee, the signed opposition of \Cref{thm:inversion} being a within-group
statement rather than a global one. The one exception is degenerate: if the spectrum is constant on every scale group in the eigenvalue-sorted order (plateaus of multiplicity $G$ aligned with the group boundaries, \Cref{rem:inv-scope}), the sorted KLT sits on the fixed-rate floor $E/G$ and both surrogates are minimized at once.

[Prop trans-large-and-small of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] There exists a choice of $\varepsilon$ and $\beta$ such that every state is evanescent for the model in Example (ex:trans-large-and-small of the paper) for both $\kappa$ sufficiently large and $\kappa$ sufficiently small, but such that there nevertheless exist intermediate values of $\kappa$ for which the model is exponentially ergodic.
\begin{proof}
Notice that this model consists of two two-species submodels which do not interact. By Proposition (prop:switching ergodic monomolecular of the paper), for any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ the first submodel (the one with species $S_1,S_2$) is evanescent when $\kappa$ is small enough and exponentially ergodic when $\kappa$ is large enough. Let $\kappa_{\min}$ be large enough (implicitly depending on $\varepsilon$) that the first submodel is exponentially ergodic whenever $\kappa>\kappa_{\min}$.

Similarly, the second submodel (the one with species $S_3,S_4$) is a version of the model from Example (ex:basic switching transient of the paper), but with the speeds scaled up ($\beta>1$) or down ($\beta<1$) by a factor of $\beta$. Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ going forward to be small enough that the model from Example (ex:basic switching transient of the paper) is exponentially ergodic for small $\kappa$, and let $\kappa_{\max}$ be small enough that said model is exponentially ergodic whenever $\kappa<\kappa_{\max}$. It follows that the second submodel here is exponentially ergodic whenever $\kappa\beta^{-1}<\kappa_{\max}$ but is transient whenever $\kappa\beta^{-1}$ is sufficiently large (see Figure (fig:rescaling of the paper) for more explanation).

[Lem e:Phi of arXiv:2504.07255, 'A Tail-Respecting Splitting Numerical Scheme\\ for L\'evy-Driven SDEs With Superlinear Dri'] Let assumption $\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{Lip}_+}_A$ hold.
Then the ODE (equation e:ODE of the paper)
has a unique global solution that satisfies the following estimates for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $t\in[0,\infty)$:
\begin{align}

&\|\Phi(t,x)\|\leq  \|x\| \mathrm{e}^{Lt} + \|A(0)\|\frac{\mathrm{e}^{Lt}-1}{L},\\

&\|\Phi(t,x)-x\|\leq \|A(x)\|\frac{\mathrm{e}^{Lt}-1}{L}.
\end{align}

[Lemma 13 (Codimension-one filling) of arXiv:2609.03916, 'Halfspace Theorems for Anisotropic Minimal Surfaces and Perimeter Minimizers'] Let $S$ be a compactly supported integral $n$-cycle in $\R^{n+1}$.  Then
there exists $g\in BV(\R^{n+1};\mathbb Z)$ with compact essential support
such that
\begin{equation}
 S=\partial\llbracketset{g},
 \qquad
 \supp g\subset\operatorname{conv}(\supp S).
\end{equation}
Here $\supp g$ denotes the essential support of $g$.
The normalization that $g=0$ on the unbounded component of
$\R^{n+1}\setminus\supp S$ determines $g$ uniquely.

A real-valued stochastic process Z satisfies the downward crossing property if for any almost surely finite stopping time tau, P(forall h > 0, inf_{s in [0, h]} (Z(tau + s) - Z(tau)) < 0) = 1. This property ensures that upon hitting any boundary, the process immediately enters the lower half-plane with probability 1.
Z is a real-valued stochastic process
title: Downward Crossing Property of Driving Processes

[Defn Standard module of arXiv:2506.01306, 'Asymptotic of Coulomb gas integral, Temperley-Lieb type algebras and pure partition functi'] The standard module $V_{n,p}$ is defined as the graded piece
\[
V_{n,p} := M_{n,p} / M_{n,p+1},
\]
which is a representation of $\mathrm{TL}_n(\beta)$ via diagram concatenation. Its dimension is given by:
\[
\dim V_{n,p} = d_{n,p} = \binom{n}{p} - \binom{n}{p-1},
\]
the $(n,p)$-entry of the Catalan triangle.

body:
[Proposition 11 (Poissonized ratio Tauberian theorem) of arXiv:2608.24616, '2608.24616'] Retain the standing assumption $\Pp\{Y>0\}>0$, and fix $p>1$.  The following
statements are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is a constant $c>0$ such that
\[
 m_t(p)\longrightarrow c \qquad (t\to\infty).
\]
\item For some $\beta\in[0,1)$,
\[
 \overline G(x)=\Pp\{Y>x\}\in\RV_\infty(-\beta).
\]
\end{enumerate}
When these statements hold, $\beta$ is unique and
\begin{equation}
 c=\frac{\Gamma(p-\beta)}{\Gamma(p)\Gamma(1-\beta)}.
 
\end{equation}
The result remains valid when $\mu_Y$ has an atom at zero and when its
restriction to $(0,\infty)$ is atomic or has lacunary support.
title: Poissonized ratio Tauberian theorem

body:
[Corollary cor:constant-overshoot-families of arXiv:2607.04620, 'The Exact Ville Identity\\ \large From the Absorbing Case to the General Law\\ with an App'] Consider the first passage of an additive mean-zero walk above an integer level.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \emph{Bounded integer up-steps (C1).} If the increments take integer values with maximal up-step $+1$, the walk lands exactly one unit above the level, so $\omega=1$. (For any such $X$, $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>0]=1$.)
\item \emph{Geometric positive increments (C(2,$\cdot$)).} If the positive increment has the geometric law on $\{1,2,\ldots\}$ with success probability $q\in(0,1)$, namely $\mathbb{P}(X=k)=q(1-q)^{k-1}$, then by the memorylessness of the geometric the conditional overshoot is again geometric with the same law, and $\omega=1/q$. (Equivalently, the companion's parametrization gives $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>k]=k+p/(1-p)$ in the decay-ratio convention; see (rem:geometric-param of the paper).)
\item \emph{Exponential right tail (C(3,$a$)).} If the positive increment has an exponential right tail, $\mathbb{P}(X>y)=c e^{-ay}$, then by the memorylessness of the exponential the overshoot is exponential with mean $\omega=1/a$, and $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>y]=y+1/a$ (the constant $c$ is irrelevant).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Constant-overshoot families

body: In probability theory, the central limit theorem states that, under certain circumstances, the probability distribution of the scaled mean of a random sample converges to a normal distribution as the sample size increases to infinity. Under stronger assumptions, the Berry–Esseen theorem, or Berry–Esseen inequality, gives a more quantitative result, because it also specifies the rate at which this convergence takes place by giving a bound on the maximal error of approximation between the normal distribution and the true distribution of the scaled sample mean. The approximation is measured by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance. In the case of independent samples, the convergence rate is n−1/2, where n is the sample size, and the constant is estimated in terms of the third absolute normalized moment. It is also possible to give non-uniform bounds which become more strict for more extreme events.
title: Berry–Esseen theorem

[Definition Local and global appearances of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Consider a fixed block-walk. An appearance of a labeled vertex within a given block is called a \emph{local appearance}, whereas an appearance of that vertex anywhere in the full block-walk is called a \emph{global appearance}.

    A labeled vertex or edge makes its \emph{global first} or \emph{global last appearance} if the corresponding occurrence is its first or last appearance in the entire walk. Similarly, it makes its \emph{local first} or \emph{local last appearance} if the corresponding occurrence is its first or last appearance within the current block.
title: Local and global appearances

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2607.17087, 'Transportation-cost inequalities for invariant measures of stochastic reaction-diffusion e'] Let $p>2$, let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $(e_k)_{k\geq 1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H$. Let $W$ be an $H$-cylindrical Wiener process.
Let
\[
\Phi: [0,T]\times\Omega \longrightarrow \mathcal{L}\big(H,L^p([0,1])\big)
\]
be an operator-valued progressively measurable process. Assume that
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\int_0^T \Vert G(t)\Vert_{L^p([0,1])}^2\,dt <\infty,
\end{equation}
where
\[
G(t,x):= \bigg( \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \big|\big(\Phi(t) e_k \big)(x) \big|^2 \bigg)^{1/2}, \qquad x\in[0,1] .
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E} \left\Vert \int_0^T\Phi (t)\,dW(t) \right\Vert_{L^p([0,1])}^2
\leq (p-1) \mathbb{E}\int_0^T \Vert G(t)\Vert_{L^p([0,1])}^2\,dt.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 7 of arXiv:2607.17087

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). After the optimism reading was refuted (P20), the gain was located row by row: the per-evaluation-row relative-score gain of the long-only stack over least squares against the bootstrap variance of the least-squares stack at that row. P22 (a) REFUTED at the pre-registered 0.2: the within-cell median Spearman between a row's gain and the least-squares variance load at that row is 0.13 over the 40 EMIT cells (positive in 36 of 40; 0.37 on Y2, 0.01 on Y1); (b) HELD on Y2, REFUTED as an every-group claim: the top-decile-load rows carry 47 pct of Y2's gain (a uniform spread gives 10) but only 11 pct on Y1 (20 on Y3, 32 on Y4); (c) HELD: across the 40 EMIT cells the gain rank-correlates 0.54 with the variance-load share of least squares' error, and 0.65 with the share the constraint removes (least squares minus nn1) - the between-cell statistic that optimism (P20) failed to be; (d) REFUTED as written: the OCO-2 top-decile share reaches 0.40 on sco2, but as the share of a gain of -0.55 pct it is the ratio of two near-zero numbers and does not test the clause; falsifier (within-cell correlation at or below zero) not triggered. Reading: where the gain is large (Y2, +18) it sits where least squares is uncertain - row-level rank correlation 0.37, 47 pct of the gain on the tenth of rows with the largest variance; where it is modest (+5 to +6) it is spread over the rows; between cells the variance-load share of least squares' error predicts the gain (0.54) and the variance the constraint removes predicts it better (0.65). The calibration and evaluation rows share the same target-norm distribution, so this is not a split shift; the gain leans toward the small-norm evaluation rows the reported metric weights most. Cell level: the variance the constraint removes (least squares' bootstrap variance share minus the long-only stack's) predicts the gain within every output group (Spearman 0.79, 0.87, 0.54, 0.43 on Y1-Y4; 0.69 across 40 cells with the group effect removed), while the L1 norm of the least-squares weights does not survive the group adjustment (0.02): the constraint pays what it saves in estimation variance at the rows it is scored on. Fresh-split replication (split C, SPLIT_SEED 11): P23 (a) REFUTED at the per-group 0.5, HELD in the aggregate: on split C the within-group Spearman between the gain and the variance removed is +0.59, +0.49, +0.64, +0.22 on Y1..Y4 and +0.74 across the 40 cells with the group effect removed (split B: +0.69); (b) REFUTED: the split-B variance-removed share predicts the split-C gain only on Y1 and Y2 (+0.72, +0.47; Y3 +0.09, Y4 -0.24; demeaned +0.17), and the split-B gain itself predicts the split-C gain only weakly (Y1 +0.82, Y4 +0.47, Y2 +0.15, Y3 -0.14); (c) HELD: the long-only stack beats least squares on 35 of 40 split-C cells (mean +9.59 against +8.83 on split B); falsifier (any group at or below 0.2, or the demeaned correlation at or below 0.3) not triggered. Fresh-split check of the calibration-side correlates (P32, the P20 driver on split C): P32 (a) HELD: on split C the between-cell Spearman of the gain with the least-squares L1 is +0.55 and with n_eff -0.44; (b) REFUTED: group-demeaned, L1 +0.29 and members kept +0.21; (c) HELD: the nn0 RMSE gain with the smallest relative eigenvalue +0.29 and with the condition number -0.31; falsifier (L1 above +0.3 after the group adjustment) not triggered. The gain off the tail (P36, the top tenth of evaluation rows by |gain| removed): P36 (a) HELD for the sign, REFUTED for the size: the trimmed gain is positive on 36 and 36 of 40 EMIT cells (splits B, C) but reads +7.67 and +8.30 against untrimmed +8.83 and +9.59 - the body keeps 87 pct of the gain, not less than half; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the trimmed gain is +0.25 against -0.18 untrimmed; (c) REFUTED: the smallest trimmed gain is on Y4, not Y1; falsifier (negative trimmed gain on EMIT) not triggered. Removing the two-sided tail leaves 87 pct of the EMIT gain: the constraint pays broadly across the rows, and the non-transfer between splits comes from the tails' noise, not from where the gain sits.

[Lemma 1 (Criteria for PRM convergence) of arXiv:2506.12632, 'Point process convergence of extremes in $K$-symmetric exclusion'] Let $\{\theta_t : t \ge 0\}$ be a sequence of point processes on $\R$ and $\mu$ a locally finite measure on $\R$. 
 The following are equivalent: 

	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]

	\item $\displaystyle \theta_t \underset{t\to\infty}{\Longrightarrow} \text{PRM}\,(\mu)$. 
	
	\item $\displaystyle \theta_t(B) \underset{t\to\infty}{\Longrightarrow} \text{Poisson}\,(\mu(B))$ for any $B \in \sU$. 
	
	\item $\displaystyle \theta_t(A_1) + \theta_t(A_2) + \cdots + \theta_t(A_m) \underset{t\to\infty}{\Longrightarrow} \text{Poisson}\,(\mu(A_1) + \mu(A_2) + \cdots + \mu(A_m))$ for any finite collection of disjoint, finite intervals $A_k = (a_k, b_k]$, $1 \le k \le m$. 	
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); T232-w704-C016 v1. No independent PASS or established novelty/priority. Let finite m>=2,w>=2, rank-two M in R^(m-by-2), and SPD 2-by-2 Sigma define the asymmetric factor gradient flow. Suppose a balanced rank-one reference zbar(t) converges to a stationary endpoint zstar=(bstar;astar) with NONZERO PRODUCT bstar astar^T. Put Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma and let v be the unit top eigenvector of Lstar=[[0,-Gstar],[-Gstar^T,0]]. At one sufficiently late FIXED entrance time, write actual flows U_epsilon=[z_epsilon,X_epsilon]. Assume uniformly for all small positive epsilon that ||z_epsilon(0)-zbar(0)||<=C0 epsilon, c0 epsilon<=||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F<=c1 epsilon with fixed 0<c0<=c1, and ||(I-vv^T)X_epsilon(0)||_F<=h||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F for a sufficiently narrow fixed cone aperture h. The reference future tail must be inside the chosen fixed local endpoint neighborhood. Then convergence alone permits thresholds delta_epsilon tending to zero and first-hit times t_epsilon tending to infinity with p(t_epsilon)=||v^T X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F=delta_epsilon, ||z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-zstar||<=D delta_epsilon^2, and ||X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F<=sqrt(1+h^2)delta_epsilon, for fixed D. For Z_epsilon=U_epsilon U_epsilon^T and Z1=zstar zstar^T, a fixed K>0 gives ||Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-Z1||_F<=K delta_epsilon^2 and v^T Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)v>=delta_epsilon^2, hence strong relative Gram alignment at least 1/K. C015 supplies the strict active/dormant gap and the nonpositive dormant complement. No exponential reference rate or actual-family balance is needed. This does not prove the Gaussian active O(epsilon) entrance premise: C014's qualitative convergence alone is insufficient. It does not prove the complete rectangular second-step composition.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4a054a169c86083274f88d6e8fb68681913e099c83326d578db28eb6369c9656","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4a/4a054a169c86083274f88d6e8fb68681913e099c83326d578db28eb6369c9656.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9450ac9294b900eb84b74e677731622c7384c7a2f2eb38a2ba5a8657212dc693","bundle_entry_key":"rectangular-strong-gram-arrival","bundle_id":"population.t232-rectangular-origin-spectrum-arrival-20261021","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"deep linear networks; asymmetric factorization; saddle-to-saddle dynamics","draft":"w704/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.deep_linear_networks:rectangular-strong-gram-arrival","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Rectangular local arrival: strong Gram alignment from a fixed cone entrance

T232-w704-C016 v1. Kind: moved; Target 1, conditional local arrival on the whole m-by-2 range. Status: proof (unaudited). This is not a complete Gaussian second-step theorem. Dependencies C015 v1 and the proof below require independent audit; the square C009 PASS does not certify this extended statement.

## Theorem and load-bearing entrance hypotheses
Let m>=2 and w>=2 be finite, M in R^(m-by-2) have rank two, and Sigma be 2-by-2 symmetric positive definite. Let a balanced rank-one reference zbar(t)=(bbar;abar) solve the factor gradient flow and converge to a critical endpoint zstar=(bstar;astar) with NONZERO PRODUCT bstar astar^T. Set Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma, Lstar=[[0,-Gstar],[-Gstar^T,0]], s=||Gstar||op, and let v be its unit top eigenvector.

Choose a sufficiently late reference time as the fixed local time zero. Consider any actual width-w flow family U_epsilon=[z_epsilon,X_epsilon], with positive epsilon tending to zero, satisfying at this ONE fixed entrance time, with constants independent of epsilon,
 ||z_epsilon(0)-zbar(0)||<=C0 epsilon,
 c0 epsilon<=||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F<=c1 epsilon,  0<c0<=c1,
 ||(I-vv^T)X_epsilon(0)||_F<=h||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F.
Here h>0 is a sufficiently narrow fixed aperture, and all entrance conditions hold for every sufficiently small epsilon. No independence of evolving factors, exponential reference convergence, or balance of the actual family is assumed.

Then there are first-threshold times t_epsilon tending to infinity and positive thresholds delta_epsilon tending to zero such that
 p(t_epsilon)=||v^T X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F=delta_epsilon,
 ||z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-zstar||<=D delta_epsilon^2,
 ||X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F<=sqrt(1+h^2)delta_epsilon.
With Z_epsilon=U_epsilon U_epsilon^T and Z1=zstar zstar^T, a fixed K>0 satisfies
 ||Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-Z1||_F<=K delta_epsilon^2,
 v^T Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)v>=delta_epsilon^2.
Hence the liminf of their relative alignment ratio is at least 1/K>0. Constants may depend on fixed data, endpoint, reference and entrance constants; there is no uniform quantitative lower bound across data.

## 1. Rectangular spectral premises
C015 proves, under exactly the nonzero-product endpoint premise, rank(Gstar)=1, s>0, simple top s of Lstar, nonpositive complementary spectrum (one -s and m zeros), and v perpendicular to zstar. The full active derivative Jact=DF(zstar) is symmetric with top rate r satisfying 0<=r<s. Its added m-2 transverse active directions have eigenvalue -astar^T Sigma astar<0. Thus neither the dormant zero modes nor the additional active directions introduce a competing positive top rate.

Choose rplus in (r,s). Continuity makes the largest eigenvalue of DF at most rplus on a small convex active ball of radius R about zstar. Choose h>0 and then eta>0 small enough that
 eta(1+h)^2<h s,
 a=s-eta(1+h)>rplus,  b=s+eta(1+h).
These choices are possible since rplus<s. Fix active and dormant balls, of radii R and R_X, so the exact dormant generator differs from Lstar by at most eta throughout them. The generator difference is -H(P-Pstar), where P=z_b z_a^T+VW^T for X=(V;W). It is continuous and vanishes at (zstar,0). Shift the reference sufficiently late that its entire future tail lies in the active ball of radius R/4. The theorem assumes the uniform entrance hypotheses at that chosen time.

## 2. Dimension-independent cone and active comparison
Write Y=v^T X, Q_X=(I-vv^T)X, p=||Y||_F, q=||Q_X||_F. Up to first exit from the local balls, the exact equation X'=(Lstar+R(t))X has ||R(t)||op<=eta. For p>0,
 sp-eta(p+q)<=p'<=sp+eta(p+q).
The symmetric nonpositive complementary spectrum gives D^+q<=eta(p+q), including q=0 by the norm triangle inequality. At q=hp,
 D^+(q-hp)<=[eta(1+h)^2-hs]p<0.
Thus the cone q<=hp is invariant before exit. The initial p is positive, and p'>=ap preserves positivity. Inside the cone,
 ap<=p'<=bp,  ||X||_F^2<= (1+h^2)p^2.
This calculation uses only a nonpositive complement, not its dimension or absence of zeros.

The exact active equation is z'=F(z)-H(VW^T)z. On a fixed bounded active ball, ||H(VW^T)z||<=C||X||_F^2, for a fixed C. With E=||z-zbar||, symmetry of DF and integration along the segment between z,zbar give
 D^+E<=rplus E+C(1+h^2)p^2.
For u<=t, lower cone growth gives p(u)<=p(t)exp(-a(t-u)). Integration therefore yields
 E(t)<=C0 epsilon exp(rplus t)+C1 p(t)^2,
 C1=C(1+h^2)/(2a-rplus).
The denominator is strictly positive because a>rplus>=0. This uses the full active derivative; frozen dormant transport is not substituted for it.

## 3. A uniform cutoff for each fixed threshold
Set k=rplus/a<1 and C_H=max(1,C0 c0^(-k)). Choose delta0 in (0,1) so
 (1+C1)delta0^2<R/4,  sqrt(1+h^2)delta0<R_X/2.
For any fixed delta in (0,delta0], reference convergence supplies a finite t_delta>=0 such that ||zbar(t)-zstar||<=delta^2 for every t>=t_delta. Impose
 epsilon<=epsilon_ent,
 epsilon<=delta/(2c1),
 epsilon<=[delta^(2-k)/(2C_H)]^(1/(1-k)),
 epsilon<=delta exp(-b t_delta)/(2c1).
Here epsilon_ent is the fixed entrance cutoff. All four bounds are positive at fixed delta and hold for every smaller epsilon as well.

Before the first threshold p=delta or the first exit, lower growth gives the elapsed-time upper bound T_upper=log(delta/(c0 epsilon))/a: an interval without either event cannot extend past this value. Therefore its homogeneous active error is at most
 C0 epsilon exp(rplus T_upper)<=C_H delta^k epsilon^(1-k)<=delta^2/2.
Consequently E<=(C1+1/2)delta^2<R/4 and z remains within R/2 of zstar, while ||X||<R_X/2. There is a strict margin to both exit boundaries. Smooth local continuation in these bounded balls excludes exit first and, by the lower growth bound, ensures that the threshold is attained by T_upper.

Upper growth gives the stopping-time lower bound
 t_stop>=log(delta/(c1 epsilon))/b>=t_delta+log(2)/b.
Thus the reference endpoint error is at most delta^2 at this stop. Combining it with E yields
 ||z-zstar||<=D delta^2,  D=C1+3/2.
The Gram expansion gives
 ||zz^T+XX^T-zstar zstar^T||_F<=K delta^2,
 K=2||zstar||D+D^2 delta0^2+1+h^2.
Indeed the active difference is bounded by 2||zstar||||z-zstar||+||z-zstar||^2, and ||XX^T||_F<=||X||_F^2. Positivity gives v^T Z v=(v^T z)^2+||v^T X||^2>=delta^2. In particular K is fixed independently of delta and epsilon.

## 4. One diagonal selection; all smaller epsilon, not a subsequence only
Let delta_n=delta0 2^(-n), n>=1. Choose epsilon_n strictly below half of epsilon_(n-1) for n>1, delta_n^n/2, epsilon_ent/2, and half of each of the other three cutoffs in Section 3 evaluated at delta_n. Every epsilon_n is positive, epsilon_n strictly decreases to zero, and the delta_n stop is valid for EVERY epsilon<=epsilon_n.

For epsilon<=epsilon_1 set n(epsilon)=max{n>=1:epsilon<=epsilon_n}. This set is nonempty and finite because epsilon_n tends to zero. Its maximum tends to infinity as epsilon tends to zero. Choose the actual first delta_n(epsilon) stop and put delta_epsilon=delta_n(epsilon). All estimates above apply uniformly there, so delta_epsilon tends to zero and the claimed alignment follows. Moreover epsilon<delta_n^n implies
 t_stop>=[(n-1)log(1/delta_n)-log c1]/b,
which tends to infinity. This checks the index direction and the number n-1 explicitly.

The reference convergence modulus t_delta may be arbitrarily slow. It only shrinks positive epsilon cutoffs; no rate or interchange of growing-time limits is used. QED, subject to independent review.

## Remaining frontier obligations
This establishes conditional local arrival over the whole m-by-2 range if its proof and C015 are correct. It does NOT establish the entrance hypotheses for Gaussian initialization, a complete rectangular canonical escape or its forward endpoint. C014 supplies fixed-compact origin matching and ideal output confinement, not a growing-time comparison or an active O(epsilon) error estimate by itself. In particular normalized dormant convergence cannot be substituted for the active O(epsilon) entrance premise without a separate argument. That Gaussian handoff remains the hardest open link of the rectangular extension.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Use the Apollonian structure of the limit to predict the local statistics in each patch. Result: The Pegden-Smart limit is a piecewise-quadratic function whose Hessian takes values in the set Gamma of integer superharmonic matrices; inside a patch where the Hessian is a fixed matrix A in Gamma, the sandpile is (Levine-Pegden-Smart) a periodic pattern determined by A, so the height-j fraction in a patch converges to the frequency of height j in that periodic pattern, which is a computable rational number. Hence the refinement holds in the interior of every patch; the question reduces to the boundary set between patches (the Apollonian gasket of patch boundaries), which has Lebesgue measure zero in the limit but whose discrete neighbourhood might carry a positive fraction of sites at scale n if the boundary layers have width of order n^{alpha}, alpha > 0... the patches are of all sizes (Apollonian), and the total area of patches of diameter < eps tends to zero as eps -> 0 (the gasket has Hausdorff dimension < 2), so for any delta the fraction of sites within the small patches is < delta for eps small, and within large patches the convergence holds; therefore the height-j fraction converges PROVIDED the discrete configuration inside a large patch is exactly the periodic pattern except in a boundary layer of o(n) width, which is the content of the Levine-Pegden-Smart 'Apollonian structure in the abelian sandpile' theorem (they prove the patterns appear; the width of the transition layers is what I could not confirm from memory). Conditional resolution recorded: the height-fraction convergence follows from the patch-pattern theorem plus an o(n) transition-layer bound plus the measure-zero gasket; the identity-element scaling limit remains open beyond the Caracciolo-Paoletti-Sportiello special case. Key identity: Inside a patch with Hessian A the height-j frequency is the frequency of j in the A-pattern; the gasket of boundaries has area zero, so convergence reduces to o(n) transition layers. Obstruction: Transition-layer width between patches not confirmed; identity element limit open.

Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and T: X -> X continuous. For n >= 1 define the Bowen metric d_n(x,y) = max_{0 <= i <= n-1} d(T^i x, T^i y). A set E contained in X is (n, eps)-SEPARATED if d_n(x,y) > eps for all distinct x, y in E; let s_n(eps) be the largest cardinality of an (n, eps)-separated set. A set F is (n, eps)-SPANNING if for every x in X there is y in F with d_n(x,y) <= eps; let r_n(eps) be the smallest cardinality of an (n, eps)-spanning set. Both are finite by compactness. THEOREM (Bowen, Dinaburg): h_top(T) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log s_n(eps) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log r_n(eps), and this common value coincides with the Adler-Konheim-McAndrew topological entropy defined through open covers. The limits in eps exist in [0, +infinity] because s_n(eps) and r_n(eps) are nonincreasing in eps, so the inner quantities are nonincreasing in eps. The two counts are comparable at shifted scales: r_n(eps) <= s_n(eps) <= r_n(eps/2). SHARP EDGES. (a) The order of the limits is not negotiable: for a FIXED eps the quantity limsup_n (1/n) log s_n(eps) is in general strictly smaller than h_top(T) (it is the 'entropy at scale eps'), and it is only after eps -> 0 that one gets the entropy. The single exception worth remembering is an expansive homeomorphism, where any eps below the expansive constant already gives the answer. (b) Compactness is used to make the counts finite and to make the value a topological invariant. Bowen's extension to a uniformly continuous map of a possibly non-compact metric space, taking the supremum of the above over compact subsets, defines a quantity h_d(T) that depends on the METRIC and not only on the topology: uniformly equivalent metrics give the same value, but merely topologically equivalent ones need not, so on non-compact spaces 'the topological entropy' is not well defined without naming the metric. (c) Separated and spanning counts measure ORBIT distinguishability over a finite time window; they say nothing by themselves about invariant measures. The link to measures is the variational principle, h_top(T) = sup over T-invariant Borel probabilities mu of h_mu(T), which is a separate theorem and is not proved by the counting argument below. (d) The definition uses only forward iterates 0, ..., n-1, and for a homeomorphism this already gives the entropy of T; the two-sided window max over |i| <= n gives the same number, not twice it.
(X,d) is a compact metric space
T: X -> X is continuous
for the non-compact extension, T is uniformly continuous and the entropy is taken as a supremum over compact subsets, and then depends on the uniform equivalence class of d

If A is an element of U v T^{-1}U v ... v T^{-(n-1)}U then A has d_n-diameter at most eps, so A contains at most one point of any (n,eps)-separated set. Hence s_n(eps) <= N(U v ... v T^{-(n-1)}U), which gives limsup_n (1/n) log s_n(eps) <= h_top(T,U) <= h_top(T). Letting eps -> 0 gives the '<=' half. LOWER BOUND. Let U be any finite open cover and let delta > 0 be a Lebesgue number for it. Take eps < delta/2 and let F be an (n,eps)-spanning set of minimal size r_n(eps). For each x in F and each 0 <= i <= n-1 the ball B(T^i x, eps) has diameter below delta, so it lies in some element U_i of U; therefore the d_n-ball of radius eps around x is contained in the element U_0 ∩ T^{-1}U_1 ∩ ... ∩ T^{-(n-1)}U_{n-1} of the refinement. Since these d_n-balls cover X, we get N(U v ... v T^{-(n-1)}U) <= r_n(eps) <= s_n(eps), whence h_top(T,U) <= liminf_{eps->0} limsup_n (1/n) log s_n(eps). Taking the supremum over U gives the '>=' half. The inequalities r_n(eps) <= s_n(eps) <= r_n(eps/2) come from: a maximal (n,eps)-separated set is (n,eps)-spanning (maximality), and distinct points of an (n,eps)-separated set cannot share the same centre of an (n,eps/2)-spanning set by the triangle inequality in d_n.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:b37e769019af9c3c806bc40c8bcd035f4ed3ab30f89685ef51d9f4cfa8dc0756","revision_digest":"sha256:885e1c5ce5a142a5b0817a051568e1c6290d72f8e2a8225eed7dad76bf607388","source_id":"wikipedia:Topological_entropy","source_revision":"as-read-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}
